en: Preface to the Commentary on the Extensive Version of the Vimalakīrti Sūtra:
The *Vimalakīrti Sūtra-vyākhyāna* in twenty-eight fascicles was previously requested by the assembly at Hiei-zan, including Huisun and others, who desired to have it carved for publication.
They entreated me to provide the words; however, as I have been afflicted by chronic illness in recent years, I consented but failed to carry it through. Alas!
The Great Being Vimalakīrti used his illness as an occasion to give instruction, whereas I have become ill and lost my resolve; how great is this disparity!
Thus, filled with shame and self-reproach, I prostrated three times and took up my brush, saying:

"Consider that when the Great Master Zhìzhě propagated the Dharma for thirty years, his eloquent and unrestrained expositions relied entirely upon his disciples to compile them so that they might be transmitted to future generations. Alone...
This work was personally annotated by Prince Jin himself; its exposition of the four teachings is profound, penetrating, and lucid, leaving no further obscurities.

No later person’s veneration and faith have surpassed it. However, it is regrettable that after the deletions and revisions made at Piling, the original text became sparse, existing as if barely present or having vanished altogether.
When the Tiantai teachings were included in the canon during the Song dynasty, this work unfortunately was omitted, and thus it has rarely been transmitted among the people until now.
The Hu-Yuan (Mongol Yuan) dynasty has ultimately perished, and Master Xu of Lingfeng has once again spread [the teachings] like a pillar in the center. His letter states:

"The commentary on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* has long been suppressed in the lands east of the sea; if we rely on your great power to illuminate it here once more, it would be a marvelous event for all eternity. Day and night I pray for this. Alas!
Given the literary heritage of the Central Kingdom (*Zhōnghuá*), that it should have been lost and not transmitted, sought for but not found—how could this be anything other than the Great Dharma?

That it has spread eastward from there while here it is parched and overflowing—is this not a matter of principle that can do nothing about? Yet, it would be better to rejoice that a single copy remains in an ancient repository;
for if it were not carved into woodblocks and widely disseminated, even though it exists, it would be the same as being lost.

Moreover, in those lands of literary excellence, seekers have employed every means to find the works of our masters, yet the pearl was never recovered. That it should now survive here among us is truly remarkable.
To have previously stored this away in a chest and obscured its light—how could one say that such a person understood me? Now, Hui-shun and others are courageous in practicing righteousness;
how can their resolve not be praised? Although I am unworthy, my efforts lie in upholding the school; I shall likewise plant the roots of virtue and perform acts of benefit.
Once this book is issued, people will increasingly honor and trust it; if they cultivate themselves according to the teachings, we may hope to approach the state of non-duality.
The gates were opened wide, and the illnesses of sentient beings were healed; thus, he inscribed this and gave it to them.
Composed respectfully by Prince Jun, a First-Rank Duke of the Three Palaces, in the first month of the year of Xin-si, the eleventh year of the Huanghe Baoli era.
Preface to the Newly Carved Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra:
It is heard that the teaching of purifying the Buddha-lands is the great thoroughfare of the Mahāyāna and the essential ford for those who study the Buddha-way.

Yet, as its profound traces are deep and recondite, one must look up to the guidance of the Four Reliances; and as the ocean of Dharma is vast and expansive, it depends upon [the assembly] to realize its depths.

The bridge for those crossing to the next life was constructed by Maitreya across the heavens when he composed his treatises during the Jin dynasty; Jingying [Daoshi] expounded its chapters during the Sui era.

Although these works are rich in expression and vast in meaning, one has never heard of a comprehensive exposition that unifies the four types of pure lands and encompasses the five categories of causes and conditions.
Thus, our High Ancestor, the Holy Master, while at Mount Taiqiao, once lectured on the Great Canon of Vimalakīrti, moving the azure... [text truncated].
The auspicious sign of the Eye descending upon the hall seats was personally composed by the Prince of Jin as a family commentary;

the omen of the seven jewels pouring into the pavilions and galleries resulted in the "Hanging Discourse" which elucidates the three meanings, where both teaching and contemplation are fully harmonized.

The two commentaries on the *Mysterious Text* (*Xuanyiwen*) provide a complete explanation of the sutra’s intent—what had never been revealed before is now all brought to light, and whatever was obstructed is now opened up by me. Thus it is put into practice.
That when a person places their foot upon the ground, it does not miss the earth—this is what is meant by the Pure Land Dharma-gate reaching its ultimate consummation at Tiantai without remainder;
this is indeed a statement that cannot be refuted. Beginning with Emperor Sui Wen, he was first commanded to lecture in the Eastern Capital (Luoyang).

His compilation was included in the *Xuanyilu* (Records of Manifestation), which is praised as a model of elegant and orthodox scholarship. Jingxi Zhiyi subsequently composed commentaries and exegeses, and further produced an abridged version that became widely circulated.

During the Five Dynasties period, the various lineages within the realm gradually declined and perished; by the time Ciyun’s [Zhiyuan] version was included in the canon, the two meanings of *Guanshi* had already been lost, and furthermore, the extensive version had been omitted from the separate circulation outside the canon.
Down to the Yuan and Ming dynasties, even the brief commentaries were submerged, with only a single copy of the *Sijiao yi* (Meaning of the Four Teachings) remaining.
Alas! Is it not a pity that such true treasures so easily sink while the traces of the teachings are so difficult to transmit? How fortunate!

Ah! In our own country, the propagation [of these teachings] has been as continuous as a succession of chariots, and the transmission of the Dharma has not ceased. Thus, the complete canon of the Ānanda Garden remains flourishing and worthy of admiration.
Yet, it is a regret that one volume of the *Wenshu* (Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra) has been lost at the original mountain;
of the few scrolls that remain, they consist only of fragmentary slips insufficient for study. In years past, Jìtóu Cíyuàn recovered the ancient collection from Nínglè, including that of Jīngxī.

The records of the rare and secret texts brought from afar were subsequently examined by Jue, Chang, Hui, Shun, and others; they praised them and eventually granted permission for their widespread dissemination.

Consequently, we were able to follow the imperial decree of the Great King Dongrei to include them within the *Dingxin zang* (Treasury of the Concentrated Mind). Shortly thereafter, we planned to have them carved into printing blocks and commissioned me to proofread them.
Some remarked: "Since the *Lüeshu* (Abridged Commentary) has already been circulated throughout the world, what further use is there for this vast and elaborate work?"
I, Yu, maintain that this is not the case. When the First Patriarch compiled the *Xuánwén*, he produced thirty-four fascicles;

the *Xuánsū* consists of six fascicles. Since these have circulated for a long time, it is appropriate to supplement them with the twenty-eight fascicles of the *Wénsū*, so that the complete works may circulate together in the world.

Jingxi’s purpose in pruning the redundancies was to ensure that both the extensive and the concise versions could coexist. This point is explained in the writings of the Hanlin Scholar of the Liang dynasty.
The preface exclusively values the abbreviated version, which was not the intention of the Venerable Master;

the three-fascicle record explains its extensive commentary, which has recently been published in woodblock form, yet people remain ignorant of its origins. Furthermore, this text originated at Zhaoti Monastery and was frequently cited by the masters of the Shanjia school.
For these reasons, how could one discourage its carving and printing? As for those who weary of its lengthy chapters, they may simply prefer it.

That this work should be extensively transcribed is not something I dare to insist upon. In the Gengchen year of the Baoli era, certain śramaṇas, including [Name], courageously sacrificed their resources and were thus able to obtain the original woodblock.
We are fortunate that Your Majesty has granted a preface, which shall serve to stabilize and preserve these scrolls.

For when the Great Dharma is about to spread, it depends upon the wise and enlightened to bring forth reverence and protection for the true teachings, so that these surviving texts and ancient chapters may endure.
Though many ages have passed, it remains ever new; could there indeed be anyone who surpasses those entrusted with the task of its restoration and flourishing?
Therefore, I have briefly recorded the origins of this matter to serve as a preface to the volume.
Written in the eighth month of autumn, the year of Xinsi (761), during the Baoli era, by the former abbot of Ryūju-ji on the northern valley of Mount Hiei, the śramaṇa Honjun.
I have carefully observed and recorded these general principles:
for the first twenty-five fascicles, the commentary on the sutra’s meaning follows the format established in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. I look toward this as my model.

In this final age, those who have mastered the commentaries on the sutras are sufficiently qualified to serve as models; however, when the sutra and its commentary are written continuously, beginners are easily confused.
Therefore, I have now standardized the characters—both high and low—to facilitate the reader's study.
The final three fascicles were subsequently supplemented by Zhāng'ān; they do not accord with the original text of the scripture.

I have now followed the format of the preceding fascicles and combined them with the Song edition of the scripture, which is why their structure differs from that of the previously existing "Accordant Edition" (Huìběn).
In each fascicle, there are discrepancies, omissions, and additions; furthermore, no complete version exists for thorough collation.
For the most part, one should consult various editions and briefly annotate them to follow the correct readings.

Commentary on the Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra, Volume One:
Explanation of the "Buddhakṣetra" Chapter, Part One.
First, clarifying the entry into this sūtra’s text is primarily divided into five points. The first clarifies that the sūtra’s translation is not exhaustive; the second...
Section Three: A Brief Analysis of the Text; Section Four: Discerning the Meaning of the Buddha-land; Section Five: Explaining the Chapter. Part One: Entering the Main Text of the Sūtra.

First, regarding the clarification that the sūtra’s translation is not exhaustive: although these five sections differ between the earlier and later translations, both the ancient and modern versions consist of exactly three fascicles each.
Having personally investigated the intent behind the arrival of this sūtra, it is evident that its full meaning has not yet been realized.

The literary meanings in the Western lands are vast and numerous. How is this known? For example, when [the Buddha] commanded ten disciples to inquire after his illness, each had a response and discourse that was so extensive it could not be recorded in the sūtra;
it would have amounted to nearly ten sheets of paper. Likewise, he commanded five hundred śrāvakas, but they also declined, saying they were unable to do so.
These expressions of inability were all beyond measure. Next, he commanded the four great bodhisattvas...

Śāriputra likewise repeatedly and firmly declined, recounting past instances of being rebuked in several scrolls; subsequently, he was commanded to address the various great bodhisattvas, yet he again declined, stating his inability.
These words of inability were all recorded as not having come to save [others]. Inferring from this, the number of such scriptural volumes is not small.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī entered the chamber to inquire after the illness, transmitting the Tathāgata’s intent with immeasurable earnestness, including the account of the eight thousand [bodhisattvas].
Each of the Bodhisattvas expounded the Dharma-gate of Non-duality; these various discourses would surely occupy more than half a scroll.

Furthermore, when [the Buddha] emerged from his chamber and proceeded to the Āmra Garden to proclaim the teachings before the Tathāgata and debate the meaning of the Buddha-lands, the subsequent expositions and dialogues—how could they have been contained in merely a few sheets of scripture?
My intention is that the spiritual faculties of the people of China [are such that they require this].
Being of narrow capacity, I am unable to fully read, recite, and uphold it;
however, that wealthy man [the Master] has extracted its essential framework and transmitted it to this land, preserving its meaning in brief. Question:

This sutra exists in the Western Regions with such vast and extensive wording—is it not the very *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* which clarifies that the Buddha spoke an inconceivable sutra consisting of one hundred thousand verses?
Answer: Some masters explain that this is what is meant by "the present," but this is not so.
The *Acintya-sūtra* elucidated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* is merely another name for the *Avataṃsaka*. Thus, the Śāstra states: "There are two kinds of Prajñāpāramitā:

one taught in common with the Two Vehicles, and one not taught in common with the Two Vehicles. That which is not taught in common with the Two Vehicles is, for example, the 'Inconceivable' (*acintya*)."
Accordingly, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "This sūtra does not fall into the hands of those of the two vehicles;
those who preach it together with those of the two vehicles are [preaching] the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, the various *Vaipulya* sūtras, and this very sūtra. Question:
Is the name *Avataṃsaka* not itself inconceivable? Furthermore, since this sūtra has the single name "Inconceivable Liberation," why is it translated as being "not so"?
Answer: This sutra has two direct titles: first, it is called *The Teaching of Vimalakīrti*, and second, it is called *The Dharma-Door of Inconceivable Liberation*.
How could it be that only the *Avataṃsaka* lacks alternative names?

Yet, if one carefully examines the various citations from the *Acintya-sūtra* found throughout the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, they are all passages from the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, such as the passage concerning Oṣadhīśvara.

The account of Bhadrapāla explaining the number of sentient beings to be delivered to the Bodhisattva Sudhana refers to the events heard by Sudhana as he entered the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) as described in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.

If one were to cite this scripture, it would be called the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* rather than the *Acintya-sūtra*. As for the textual passage of the second division, it contains two distinct meanings.
First, it clarifies how various Dharma masters of past and present have differed in their expositions of the sutra; second, it clarifies the interpretation of our own school.
Regarding the first point, concerning the differences among the various Dharma masters: this sutra consists of fourteen chapters.

Master Kumārajīva, Master Daosheng, and other ancient masters did not divide the text into formal sections, but instead provided a direct commentary on the prose. However, Master Sengzhao stated: [text continues]
It begins with the Pure Land and concludes with the Dharma-offering; although what is elucidated between these points differs, they are all equally inconceivable and one.
Thus, the section prior to Ratnakūṭa’s inquiry serves as the introduction, while the "Entrustment" chapter serves as the dissemination;
everything in between constitutes the main teaching. Next, Master Lingwei judged that this title of the sutra...

Since it is stated that all from the "Expedient Means" chapter (*Upāya-paṭala*) onward are the "Correct Teaching" (*samyag-deśanā*) as expounded by Vimalakīrti, Master Kaishan divided the text of this sutra into four sections:
first, the "Introductory Section," ending with the "Bodhisattva" chapter; second, the "Correct Teaching," consisting of the six chapters within the house;
third, the "Section on Verification," consisting of the two chapters on the Bodhisattva Practice and the Buddha Akṣobhya; and fourth, the "Propagation Section."
Regarding the two chapters on the "Dharma-offering" (*dharmapūjā*) and the "Entrustment" (*parindanā*):

if one follows the interpretations of Zhuangyan and Guangzhai, the first four chapters constitute the introductory exposition (*nidāna*), the next six chapters constitute the main exposition (*samyag-deśanā*), and the final four chapters constitute the dissemination (*pravartana*).

The late masters of the Sanlun school also provide this same interpretation. However, the Northern Dilun masters take the single chapter "The Buddha-land" (*buddhakṣetra*) as the introductory exposition.

The first eleven chapters, ending with the "Chapter on the Manifestation of Akṣobhya Buddha," constitute the primary exposition (*dharmadeśanā*); the final two chapters constitute the dissemination (*parīndanā*).
However, as interpretations differ between ancient and modern traditions, those who have inherited and practiced these teachings each maintain their own school.

Consequently, many Chan masters, encountering these discrepancies, have frequently engaged in protracted disputes; thus, in interpreting the text of this sutra, they do not employ formal structural divisions.
This merely clarifies the intent of entering the Way through the gate of contemplation. Second, regarding the present school’s critical interpretation:
if one does not establish topical divisions (*kōdan*), one will fail to discern the beginning and end of the sūtra text;

if the Buddhist teachings are not thus traced, disputes will proliferate and the dharma of liberation will be needlessly burdened with entanglements. Now, I shall specifically describe this school’s method of investigating the sūtras.

The underlying intent follows the ancillary scriptures to open up the topical divisions rather than adhering rigidly to them. Although the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma arises from diverse sources, it is invariably excellent in its beginning, middle, and end; the textual structure is necessarily complete. Now, based on these three excellences, we shall employ them to correspond with the Introduction, the Main Body, and the Dissemination, thereby establishing three points of interpretation: first, the formal opening of this sutra; second, the application to the contemplation of the mind; and third, the differentiation from other schools. Regarding the formal division of this sutra into sections, whether the sutra be large or small, there are generally three parts: first, the introduction; second, the main exposition;

and third, the dissemination. As for the introduction: when a Great Sage is about to preach the Dharma, he invariably manifests auspicious omens to signal its commencement and serve as a basis for it.
For example, when he wished to preach the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, he emitted light of various colors from his limbs and joints to signify his intent to preach the *Prajñā*.
If he emits light from the white tuft between his eyebrows to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, it signifies the teaching of the Middle Way and the true reality (*tathatā*);
now, this sutra joins the canopy and manifests the land to signify the desire to preach on the Buddha-land.

Since these manifested signs differ according to their causes and conditions, they represent the diversity of the teaching gates that respond to the capacities of sentient beings, stirring their sentiments so that all may believe and aspire.

I have composed this preface because Guizong has a purpose for it. Second, regarding the "Correct Exposition" (Zhengshuo): when the fourfold assembly beheld the auspicious signs, they all looked up with joy and were capable of hearing the Sage’s intent.
The Great Sage, knowing the time and responding to their capacities, preached the teaching; the assembly heard the sutra and all partook of its Dharma benefit.
Therefore, it is called the "Correct Exposition. Third, regarding the "Circulation" (Liutong): "Flowing" is likened to water pouring downward, and "penetration" means...
Without stagnation or obstruction, the Tathāgata’s great compassion preaches the Dharma with impartiality;

it is not merely for the sake of those in the present, but is intended to reach far back through the periods of the True, Semblance, and Final Dharma, so that all who have the karmic affinity may be moistened by the Dharma.
Thus, the flow of the Dharma-water shall provide moisture without end, and future disciples alike shall partake of this benefit; therefore, it is called "circulation. Now, I open this sutra.
The text is divided into three parts: first, from "Thus have I heard" up to the seven-character verses spoken by Ratnakūṭa;
this constitutes both the general and specific prefaces, and because it provides the necessary basis for the formal exposition, it is termed the Introductory Section (*nidāna*).
Second, from Ratnakūṭa’s inquiry regarding the causes and conditions of the Buddha-land onwards, up to the end of the *Aksobhyatathāgatasyavyūha-parivarta*.
The eleven chapters and a half of the sutra text all clarify the inconceivable liberation and the causes and conditions of the Buddha-land;
these are all teachings adapted to the capacities of sentient beings, and their present benefits constitute the primary exposition.

From the "Dharma Offering" chapter through the "Entrusting" chapter, it clarifies how the Heavenly Emperor Śakra vows to propagate the sutra, the Tathāgata’s seal of approval, his exhortation, and his entrustment for its proclamation.
To ensure that it reaches the future and its transmission remains unceasing—all of these pertain to the category of "circulation" (liutong).
Question: The title of this sutra is called *The Teachings of Vimalakīrti*; why then is the "Chapter on the Buddha-land" taken as the primary designation for the teaching? Answer:

Vimalakīrti received the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha to assist the land in propagating the transformation [of beings]. Because he was instrumental in guiding and transforming others, the sutra is named after him.

For example, it is like a king who commands his ministers to administer the government; when they perform meritorious service, the ministers receive the reward, yet the authority of the administrative edict resides with the king.

While the ministers take credit for the achievement, it cannot be said that the ministers alone provide the correct teaching while the king’s bestowal of governance is merely a peripheral discourse. Thus, Vimalakīrti has received the seal of certification from the Buddha.

Only then is it established as the "Correct" [teaching], and thus it is named the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*. Second, regarding the analysis of the Prologue, the Main Body, and the Circulation by way of contemplating the mind:

this refers to the three divisions [of the sūtra]. The first two contemplations serve as the "expedient means," which corresponds to the meaning of the Prologue; attaining entry into the Middle Way constitutes the "Main Body";
and the simultaneous illumination of the Two Truths, wherein every thought-moment is quiescent and naturally flows [into the ultimate], constitutes the "Circulation."
The "ocean of sarvajñā" (all-knowledge) refers to the meaning of circulation and dissemination. Third, regarding the distinction from other schools: Question:

Why do you not follow Master Kumārajīva and the various Chan masters in not dividing the text into sections? Answer: If one were to discuss the practice of the Way and contemplative cultivation, there would indeed be no need for such elaborate divisions.
However, I now wish to enable students to understand the beginning and end of the scriptural text, so that they may recognize how the Sages respond to conditions.

Skillful words do not arise in isolation; they must necessarily be followed by subsequent ones. If there is no obstruction regarding the phrasing and sentences, and one provides a close commentary, then the contemplative practice will become increasingly clear.
Question: Why did you not employ the entirety of Master Zhaoshan’s commentary? Answer: The "Dharma-offering" belongs to the section on the correct exposition (*samyag-vāk*);
it would not be appropriate [to apply it here]. Question: For what reason did you not rely on the *Lingwei* commentary? Answer: Because it employs the Buddha’s [teachings].

Regarding the introductory explanation of the "Buddha-land" (*buddhakṣetra*), the meaning should not be understood in that way. Why is this so? The Buddha is the King of Dharma and the sovereign of the three thousandfold world-system;

whatever he proclaims must surely be correct. However, as for the request made by Ratnakūṭa and the Buddha’s response thereto, these were delivered in accordance with the specific capacities and conditions of the occasion.
When the assembly heard the sutra and realized the Way, they attained the fruits of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. How could this be otherwise?
It may be divided to serve as a preface; furthermore, since Vimalakīrti assists the Buddha in expounding the Dharma, he is truly one who promotes and completes the Buddhist teachings.
How could it be that what a disciple assists in explaining is treated as the primary teaching, while what the Great Master himself has spoken is instead relegated to a preface?

Question: Why is this not the same as the Kai-shan school’s division of the text into four sections? Answer: Whether a sutra is Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna, there are generally three intended meanings [in its composition]. Why?

Regarding the fourth point, that this sutra alone opens [the section on] the "Four": Question: What is the intention behind this being different from the *Zhuāngyán* (Zhuangyan), the *Guāngzhái* (Guangzhai), and the masters of the Three Treatises (*Sānlùn*)?
Answer: The *Fóguó* (Foguo) takes [the "Introductory Chapter"] as its preface; the objections are the same as before.

Furthermore, they take the "Bodhisattvacaryā-prakaraṇa" and the "Akṣobhyavyūha-parivarta" as belonging to the "Circulation" (Prakīrṇaka) section. I fear this is not so. Why? Because in the "Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa," the palm [of Vimalakīrti] upholds the great... [text fragment].
Only when the assembly of Āmra addressed the Buddha and confirmed what was spoken within the inner chamber could it truly become a sūtra.

Furthermore, when the Buddha again addressed Vimalakīrti to distinguish the causes and effects of the Buddha-lands, he summarized the beginning and end of the scripture so that its central tenets became clear; the great assembly thereby received benefits exceeding those of the inner chamber.
This constitutes the definitive teaching (*nītārtha*); how can it be called merely a provisional transmission (*neyārtha*)? Why not rely on the Great [Commentary] of the Northern Region?
The Master Chengshi replies that using the "Buddha-land" (*buddhakṣetra*) as the introduction serves as a refutation for our own school; the meaning is the same as before.
Regarding the third chapter, the "Chapter on the Buddha-land": this chapter clarifies the inquiry into the Buddha-land made by the Elder’s son Ratnākara.

Regarding the "Chapter on the Buddha-land": When the World-Honored One answered concerning the causes and effects of the Buddha-land, and Śāriputra gave rise to doubt, the Buddha used his supernatural powers to manifest the appearance of a pure land.
At that time, the great assembly attained the benefits of the Mahāyāna. When he returned to the defiled land, those seeking the vehicle of the śrāvakas attained the path of the Hīnayāna.
It is based on this that the title is established; thus it is called the "Buddha-land Chapter. Since this sutra takes the Buddha-land as its theme...
To establish our thesis, one must understand the meaning of the Buddha-land; I shall now briefly explain it in eight sections: first, a general clarification of the Buddha-land;
second, a specific clarification of the Buddha-land; third, clarifying the cultivation of the causes for the Buddha-land; fourth, clarifying the differences in perceiving the Buddha-land;
fifth, clarifying rebirth there; sixth, clarifying the preaching of the teachings; seventh, [clarifying] by way of contemplating the mind; eighth, [the conclusion].
Using the meaning of "Buddha-land" to provide a comprehensive explanation of this sutra, first, the general clarification of the Buddha-land:

Previously, the Great Sage extensively elucidated the *Samantabhadra-parivarta* (The Universal Assembly Sutra) and other texts in various directions, primarily clarifying the Dharma-body as the primary retribution (*pratyaya-vipāka*).

Now, because Ratnakūṭa offered a parasol and the Tathāgata joined the parasols to manifest a land, this immediately signifies the intention to explain the environmental retribution (*adhiṣṭhāna-vipāka*). Why is this so? Because of the primary retribution...

Since this has already been indicated, it must now be explained in detail regarding the *niśraya-vipāka* (the environment or external retribution). For example, if one speaks of a king, his ministers, and his subjects, one must necessarily know the territory, its administration, and its affairs.
What is called a "Buddha-land" (*buddhakṣetra*) refers to the domain in which he dwells; therefore, it is named a "Buddha-land.
For instance, although a royal kingdom is inhabited by the king, his ministers, and his subjects together, the kingdom is designated by the name of the king, such as "the kingdom of King So-and-so."

Now, although the Buddha dwells together with sentient beings who have a karmic affinity with him, it is from the Buddha that they receive the name "the land of such-and-such a Buddha," which is also called the "Buddha-field" (*buddhakṣetra*).
It is called the "Buddha-field" because it is the place upon which the Buddha-body relies. It is also called the "Buddha-world" (*buddhaloka*).

It is called a "Buddha-land" (*buddhakṣetra*) because it is the demarcated boundary of the place where the Buddha resides. Within this dwelling place of the Buddha, the myriad phenomena of all objects appear.

Because they are identical, they are called "lands" (*kṣetra*). There is both the phenomenal aspect and the noumenal aspect of a Buddha-land. The phenomenal aspect refers to the domain where the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) resides.
The noumenal aspect, however, pertains to the realm illuminated by ultimate wisdom; therein, the ultimate truth is void and quiescent, fundamentally lacking any distinction between object and wisdom.

How, then, could there be any differentiation regarding the boundary domains where one might reside? It is merely for the sake of responding to the capacities of sentient beings and transforming them that the True and the Responsive are spoken of.

Because there are two bodies, it is clear that there are two lands of principle and phenomena; yet, since there are no traces without a fundamental source, there are manifested forms and manifested lands.
Since there are no traces without which the fundamental cannot be revealed, these lead sentient beings to return together to the true land of the Dharma-body.
Therefore, this sutra says: "Although one contemplates the lands of all Buddhas as eternally quiescent like space, they manifest in various ways."
If one were to purify a Buddha-land, it would follow that there should be common boundaries between ordinary beings and sages;

yet the fruits and retributions of ordinary beings and sages appear with distinct differences in status, and the manifestation of purity and impurity would likewise be untenable. Therefore, the *Yingluo jing* states:
"It corresponds to all sentient beings and corresponds to all lands. Some commentators explain that "corresponds" (*ying*) means that the lands are the collective karma of sentient beings.
Because it is what is experienced, this sutra states: "The categories of sentient beings are the pure land of the Bodhisattva; it is through the power of the sages' compassion that these appear.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "He enters the decayed and dilapidated fire-houses of the three realms in order to deliver sentient beings from birth, old age, sickness, and death.
Some commentators have explained that the Dharma-body of all Buddhas is like a bright mirror.
All forms and images appear within it; thus, all lands emerge from the fundamental land of the Dharmakāya.
Because they arise from the Buddha, they are called "Buddha-lands. Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "Now these three realms are all mine;
the sentient beings therein are all my children. Now, if we carefully examine these words:
If one says that the land arises from the Dharma-body, it is self-arising; if one says it arises from the karma of sentient beings, it is other-arising;
if one says it exists because sentient beings encounter the Dharma-body, it is co-arising;
if one says there is a land that exists apart from both karma and the Dharma-body, it is arising without causes and conditions. All of these fall [into error].

The meaning of the four types of nature (*gotra*) must be refuted; this can be understood by analogy with what preceded. One should know that whether a land is pure or defiled, it cannot be said to exist [inherently];

however, because there are causes and conditions, it may be spoken of according to the *siddhānta* and the capacities of sentient beings, such that all four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) may be asserted.
Second, to specifically clarify the Buddha-lands: these are the distinct characteristics through which the Buddhas benefit sentient beings in accordance with conditions.
The immeasurable and boundless [realms] are now briefly categorized into four types: first, the defiled and pure lands, where ordinary beings and sages dwell together;
second, the lands with remainder, where those practicing through skillful means reside;
third, the lands of retributive fruition, inhabited solely by great bodhisattvas of the dharma-body, which are the unobstructed lands like Indra’s net; and fourth, the lands of ultimate fulfillment.
Fourth is the Land of Constant Quiescent Light, which is the dwelling place of ultimate wondrous enlightenment.

Regarding these four lands, the first two are both the lands where the Responsive Buddhas (*nirmāṇa-buddha*) and the Responsive-Response Buddhas (*nirmāṇa-nirmāṇa-buddha*) reside. The third land is the dwelling place of both the Responsive and the Retribution Buddhas (*vipāka-buddha*).
The final land is solely true purity; it is neither responsive nor retributive, but belongs to the Dharma-body Buddha (*dharmakāya-buddha*).
That which is their dwelling place is what is called a "defiled or pure land. This refers to the fact that sentient beings of the nine realms dwell together in mutual intermingling.
Why is this so? Because the six destinies all possess the vulgar and defiled dharmas of both *dṛṣṭi* (views) and *kleśa* (afflictions), they are termed "defiled.

Because the three vehicles equally perceive the True Truth (*satyadharma*), sever the fetters of the three realms, and are free from the defilements of views and afflictions, they are termed "pure. Thus, the six [realms]...
Because the three vehicles dwell together therein, it is called the Land of Defilement and Purity, also known as the Land of Common Dwelling for Ordinary Beings and Sages.
Regarding this Land of Defilement and Purity, there are two types: first, the defiled; second, the pure. As for the defiled, there are ordinary beings who abide in both good and evil;
these ordinary dwellings are of two kinds, and the dwellings of the sages are likewise of two kinds. Regarding the two kinds of ordinary dwellings, the first is that of the evil multitude.
The first is the dwelling place of those born in the four evil destinies (*catur-apāya*). The second is the dwelling place of virtuous sentient beings, namely humans and devas.

Regarding the two types of the "Dwelling Place of Shared Residence with Sages" (*ārya-sāṃvāsika*), the first is the residence of actual sages (*bhūta-ārya*) and the second is the residence of provisional sages (*upāya-ārya*).

Actual sages include those who have attained the three fruits of the *śrāvaka* path, Arhats in their final body, Pratyekabuddhas, those of the Shared Teaching up to the sixth stage, those of the Distinct Teaching up to the ten stages of abiding (*daśa-vihāra*), and those of the Perfect Teaching from after the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) onward.
Although the afflictions within the mental realm have been severed, the retribution body still remains within the three realms.
Those who dwell together with the two provisional sages in the Land of Expedient Means—the Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas—receive the partial, true Dharma-nature body.

For the sake of benefiting sentient beings with whom they share a karmic affinity, they vow to manifest and respond by being born in the Land of Common Residence, the Land of Real Reward Without Obstruction, and the Land of Eternal Quiescent Light.

The Bodhisattvas of the Perfectly True Dharma-Nature Body and the Buddhas of Sublime Enlightenment manifest their appearance and take birth in the Land of Common Residence for the benefit of sentient beings with whom they have a karmic affinity;
these are all provisional dwellings. Because such holy ones reside together with ordinary beings, it is called the "Impure Land of the Co-residence of Ordinary Beings and Sages.
As for what is termed "impure," it means defiled and evil, because this land...
First, it is called a "defiled land" because the beings of the four evil destinies dwell together therein. Second, regarding the Pure Land where ordinary beings and sages dwell together:

although the Western Land of Immeasurable Life possesses a karmic reward far superior to this world—such that it is difficult to find an analogy for—it is nevertheless a land where defiled and pure ordinary beings and sages dwell together. Why is this so? Because, although that land lacks the four evil destinies...
Regarding the two paths of humans and devas toward which [beings] proceed, how is this known? It is because those born in that land are not necessarily all people who have attained the Way.

Thus, the Sūtra says: "Even those who have committed grave offenses, if at the moment of death they repent and practice the visualization of Buddha-remembrance (*buddhānusmṛti*), their karma will immediately be transformed and they shall attain rebirth there.
If only those who have attained the Way were born in that land, then ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) would be unable to perform such practices.
How can humans aspire to be born in that Buddha-land? Thus we know that even those possessed of afflictions and defilements may dwell in that land.
One may infer from this that the births of the sages have both provisional and ultimate aspects; this is called the "Pure Land where the defiled and the pure, the ordinary and the sage, cohabit.
It is called "pure" simply because it lacks the four evil realms of existence; by citing this case, one may analogously understand other similar instances.

The superiority or inferiority of the lands where they dwell is not uniform; although there are many varieties of defilement and purity, as explained in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* regarding the predictions granted to the various disciples concerning the lands in which they shall dwell, these are all collectively categorized as belonging to the "Land of Common Abode for Ordinary Beings and Sages.

Question: From which sutra do the names of these defiled and pure lands originate? Answer: They are explained in the *Candraprabha-kumārabhūta-paripṛcchā-śāstra* (the *Si-yi lun*) as being derived from the light of the sun and moon.
The Buddha commanded Brahmā to come to this land, saying: "You should travel through that world by means of ten dharmas. The *Śāstra* states:
"The Sahā world-realm is called a world of defilement and purity; 'defilement' refers to ordinary beings, while 'purity' refers to those who are correct. [An objection is raised:

"It may be granted that the ten unwholesome paths produce the four realms of rebirth and that both the primary and secondary retributions in these impure lands are indeed defiled; however, as for the fruit of the ten wholesome paths..."

Question: Since the causes for the Pure Land cultivated by the Sages are the same [as those in the defiled land], why is it that the two types of retribution—the primary and the secondary—are so suddenly and vastly different? Answer:
Although the names of the wholesome causes cultivated in both places are the same, the cultivation of goodness in the Pure Land is more subtle and superior.

Consequently, the two types of retribution—the primary and the secondary—attained by ordinary beings and sages there are exquisitely distinct and unlike those in the defiled land. Second, to clarify the Land of Residual Phenomena (sāvaśeṣa-bhūmi), there are two parts.
This is the dwelling place of Bodhisattvas who have mounted the threefold path of skillful means for realization.

Why is this so? If one cultivates the two contemplations and, through skillful means, exhausts all pervasive delusions within the realms and severs the remaining distinct ignorance—vast as the sands of the Ganges—such that the afflictions of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) are not yet severed, one abandons the body of分段 (segmentary birth) and is born outside the realms, receiving a Dharma-nature body (*dharmatā-kāya*), which is subject to transformation and change (*pariṇāmika*).
The realm where one dwells while receiving retribution for birth and death is called the Land of Remainder (*śeṣabhūmi*).
The *Lotus Sūtra* states: "I shall become a Buddha in another land"; based on this, the name "Land of Remainder" is established.

It is also known as the dwelling place of those who practice through skillful means (*upāya*). Thus, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* explains that there are seven kinds of birth and death; this [land] is the first among them.
The four skillful means are the dwelling lands of *saṃsāra*. Question: From which sutras or treatises does the existence of other lands originate?

Answer: The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "After my parinirvāṇa, there may be disciples who have not heard this sutra and, regarding the merits they have attained, conceive the notion that they have reached parinirvāṇa.
I shall become a Buddha in another land under a different name, and these people [will encounter me there]."
Although they conceive the thought that [the Buddha] has entered parinirvāṇa, they seek the Buddha’s wisdom in that land and hear this sutra, attaining parinirvāṇa solely through the Buddha-vehicle.

Furthermore, it says that they see the Buddha constantly on Vulture Peak, surrounded by a great assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas as he preaches the Dharma; this also clarifies that there is still something remaining.
Regarding the culture of the land, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that although Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas enter nirvana and are not reborn within the three realms,
there exists a pure land outside the realms where they receive the Dharma-nature body (*dharmatā-kāya*).

This "land of the fruit-retribution of the three knowledges" (*trividyā-vipāka-deśa*) is precisely the Indra’s Net Lotus Treasury World (*indrajāla-padmagarbha-lokadhātu*), which consists entirely of Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-body.

It is the dwelling place [of the Dharmatā-nirmāṇakāya]. Because one contemplates the single ultimate truth (ekasatyam), one is able to shatter ignorance and manifest the Dharma-nature, thereby attaining the fruit of reality;

yet, as ignorance is not yet exhausted, it remains moistened by ignorance, and through uncontaminated karma (anāsrava-karma), one receives the retribution body of the Dharma-nature (dharmatā-nirmāṇakāya).

The pure realm that serves as the supporting environment for the dwelling of this retribution body is precisely the "land" (kṣetra). This is because one contemplates the principle of the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa).
Because it is the fruit and retribution obtained by giving rise to true outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava*), it is called "actual" (*bhūta*).

Because the physical and mental fruits obtained from causes that lack fixed retribution constitute a dwelling place where the dependent retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*) is unimpeded and sovereign, it is called "fruit-retribution.
It may also be termed the "Land of Actual Retribution without Obstruction. Regarding the "Land without Obstruction," a single world encompasses all worlds as one.
All worlds are likewise thus; this is called the Ocean of Worlds and is also called the Inexhaustible Treasury of Worlds.
According to the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), by entering this world from the first stage (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*), there are seven kinds of purity:
first, purity of single essence (*ekatva-viśuddhi*), wherein all Buddha-lands are one Buddha-land and one Buddha-land is all Buddha-lands; second, purity of mastery (*vaśitā-viśuddhi*)... all.
1. Purity of the land, which is equal and pure; 2. Purity of the three adornments, wherein all Buddha-lands are adorned with supernatural powers and fully endowed with radiant marks;
3. Purity of enjoyment, which is free from all afflictions and achieves the path of purity;
4. Purity of the dwelling place, where immeasurable beings of wisdom completely fill that location; 5. Purity of the cause.
This is entering the Buddha’s supreme, wondrous, and impartial realm (7). "Fruition purity" means manifesting according to the inclinations of the minds of all sentient beings.
The first five [perfections] constitute the fulfillment of the essence; they possess essence, characteristics, and function.

The sixth clarifies the perfection of the cause, and the seventh is the fulfillment of the fruition. According to the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), this occurs from the First Abode (Prathamavihāra) upward.

Question: From which sutra is it said that the *sambhogakāya* (Real Reward Land) arises? Answer: The *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* (Renwang Banruo Jing) states: "The three levels of worthies and the ten stages of sages dwell in the fruit-reward;
one should know that they take this fruit-reward as their land. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:
"Furthermore, this Sahā world is level and even, and all these bodhisattvas dwell therein. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Dharmatā..."
The Buddha-body preaches the Dharma for the Dharma-body Bodhisattvas; in that land, even the names "Śrāvaka" and "Pratyekabuddha" do not exist.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* clarifies the Indra-net world, and the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* clarifies the Flower-King world.
These sūtras and śāstras all clarify that the land of fruition possesses unobstructed characteristics. Fourth is the Constantly Quiescent Light [Land].
"Land" refers to the principle of the *tathatā* (suchness) Dharma-realm illuminated by the supreme wisdom of wondrous enlightenment; this is termed a "land.

However, because the *dharmatā* (nature of phenomena) of the Mahāyāna is the very nature of true quiescent wisdom, it differs from the principle of the partial truth of "emptiness as annihilation" found in the Two Vehicles.
Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The emptiness of the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) is called wisdom. This sutra also says: "If..."
To know that the nature of ignorance is itself clarity—this is the meaning of the Land of Constant Quiescent Light (*nitya-prabhāsvara-ābhāsa-kṣetra*).

It is so called because it is the dwelling place of the inconceivable meaning and the supreme wisdom of wondrous enlightenment. The dwelling place of the Dharma-body is also called the Dharma-nature Land (*dharmatā-kṣetra*);
yet, while True Suchness and Buddha-nature are neither body nor land, they are spoken of as body and land.

To speak of lands while being detached from the body is both a single dharma and a dual meaning. The *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The accumulation of wisdom is the penetration of *vijñapti-mātra*;
thus one grasps the Pure Land. It is not a physical form; it is the primary essence, not an ornamentation. Question:

From which sutra or śāstra does the term "Land of Constant Quiescent Light" (*nitya-prabhāsvara-kṣetra*) originate? Answer: The *Ratnaketuparipṛcchā-sūtra* (Renwang bore jing) states: "The three stages of the Sages... [and so forth].
The ten sages abide in the retribution of their fruits, while only the Buddha alone dwells in the Pure Land.
This sutra states: "As one's mind is pure, so is the Buddha-land pure"; the ultimate limit of mental purity is reached in the Buddha.
The *Samantabhadra-dhyāna-sūtra* states: "Śākyamuni is named Vairocana, pervading all places; the dwelling place of that Buddha is called the Constantly Quiescent Light."

This is the meaning of that. Question: Various sutras and treatises explain the four lands (catur-bhūmi) in a scattered manner as you have described; why then do we not see the names of the four lands appearing together in a single passage within any sutra or treatise? Answer: The number of sutras and treatises that cover this matter is originally not many, and those who study them are likewise not fully comprehensive. Why must there be no textual evidence for the four lands appearing together? It is just like [the following example]: *The Mahāyāna-saṃparigraha-śāstra* states: "The *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* says: 'If one wishes to know the Buddha’s lifespan, one should look at the lifespan of the Tathāgata Vairocana. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: 'The lifespan of the Tathāgata Akṣobhya is immeasurable. Now, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* refers to the Land of Ultimate Bliss (Sukhāvatī), while the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* refers to the Land of Utmost Bliss (Abhirati). These two sutras each mention one land, yet they do not state that these two lands are distinct from one another. Furthermore, the *Śrīmālā-devī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* speaks of the "Pure Land of the Tathāgata," and the *Brahmajāla-sūtra* speaks of the "Pure Land of the Buddha. These two sutras each mention one land, yet they do not state that these two lands are distinct from one another. Moreover, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* speaks of the "Pure Land of the Tathāgata," and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* speaks of the "Pure Land of the Buddha. These two treatises each mention one land, yet they do not state that these two lands are distinct from one another. Furthermore, the *Mahāyāna-saṃparigraha-śāstra* speaks of the "Pure Land of the Tathāgata," and the *Mahāyāna-abhidharma-samuccaya-śāstra* speaks of the "Pure Land of the Buddha. These two treatises each mention one land, yet they do not state that these two lands are distinct from one another. Therefore, although the names of the various lands appear separately in different places, it cannot be said that they are not identical. This is precisely the same principle as the present case.* ||| This is the meaning of that. Question: Various sutras and treatises explain the four lands in a scattered manner as you have described; why then do we not see the names of the four lands appearing together in a single passage within any sutra or treatise? Answer: The number of sutras and treatises that cover this matter is originally not many, and those who study them are likewise not fully comprehensive. Why must there be no textual evidence for the four lands appearing together? It is just like [the following example]: *The Mahāyāna-saṃparigraha-śāstra* states: "The *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* says: 'If one wishes to know the Buddha’s lifespan, one should look at the lifespan of the Tathāgata Vairocana. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: 'The lifespan of the Tathāgata Akṣobhya is immeasurable. Now, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* refers to the Land of Ultimate Bliss (Sukhāvatī), while the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* refers to the Land of Utmost Bliss (Abhirati). These two sutras each mention one land, yet they do not state that these two lands are distinct from one another. Furthermore, the *Śrīmālā-devī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* speaks of the "Pure Land of the Tathāgata," and the *Brahmajāla-sūtra* speaks of the "Pure Land of the Buddha. These two sutras each mention one land, yet they do not state that these two lands are distinct from one another. Moreover, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* speaks of the "Pure Land of the Tathāgata," and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* speaks of the "Pure Land of the Buddha. These two treatises each mention one land, yet they do not state that these two lands are distinct from one another. Furthermore, the *Mahāyāna-saṃparigraha-śāstra* speaks of the "Pure Land of the Tathāgata," and the *Mahāyāna-abhidharma-samuccaya-śāstra* speaks of the "Pure Land of the Buddha. These two treatises each mention one land, yet they do not state that these two lands are distinct from one another. Therefore, although the names of the various lands appear separately in different places, it cannot be said that they are not identical. This is precisely the same principle as the present case. ||| This is the meaning of that. This sutra states that the answer to the householder’s son was given by distinguishing the Buddha-land through four meanings;

why then could this not be its intended meaning? The sutra says: "One takes up the Buddha-land according to the beings to be transformed; one takes up the Buddha-land according to the beings to be disciplined;
one takes up the Buddha-land according to how various beings should enter the Buddha's wisdom through such a land; and according to various beings..."
Regarding the four points—namely, by which land one should be born to give rise to the roots of a bodhisattva—these correspond perfectly to the four lands;
however, since the terminology differs, the Buddha’s intention is difficult to fathom. These shall be explained individually below when we enter the text.

Question: Since this sutra has not yet clarified the opening of the provisional to reveal the real (*kai-gen ken-jitsu*), how can it clarify that those of the two vehicles are born in the land of remaining traces (*uyōdo*)?
Furthermore, this sutra states: "The Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, yet sentient beings each understand it according to their own kind.
How could this hinder the simultaneous horizontal understanding (*hyōge*) of both the Two Vehicles and the Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching?

Nor would it obstruct the unimpeded horizontal and vertical understanding (*hyōjū no ge*) of the Bodhisattvas of the Distinct and Complete Teachings. Question: The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* clarifies that there are ten kinds of Buddha-lands.
Question: Do these four types of lands encompass all [Buddha-fields]? Answer: No. Why? Because they encompass only ten lands.
Furthermore, some say that while the sutra clarifies twenty-seven grades of Buddha-fields, the land of Amitāyus Buddha is merely the sixth grade of pure land;
thus, if one looks at the text, the four lands do not exhaustively encompass them all. Question: If that is so, why does it not rely on the *Avataṃsaka* (Flower Garland)?
This clarifies the meaning of the ten grades of pure lands and even the twenty-seven kinds of Buddha-lands taught [in this scripture]. Answer:

Generally speaking, although there are scriptural passages that facilitate the explanation of these matters by correlating them with the four teachings (*catur-yāna*), the number of items is so great that it is difficult to establish a correspondence between the broad and the concise meanings;
thus, the underlying intent is difficult to perceive. Third, regarding the clarification of the causes for cultivating the Buddha-land: this scripture is not...
However, while the primary retribution (正報) is explained in terms of its fruit (*phala*), the secondary environment (*niśraya*)—the land—is likewise explained in terms of its cause (*hetu*).
The "cause of the support" (*niśraya-hetu*) refers precisely to the cause of the Buddha-land;

therefore, in his response to Ratnākara, the Buddha explains the cause of the support by means of seventeen horizontal primary causes and explains the cause of the support of the land by means of thirteen vertical primary causes. Since there are thus four [categories of] lands...

One must first clarify the four kinds of causes. Generally speaking, it is explained that the causes of the vows and practices of the Bodhisattvas of the four teachings are able to evoke the fruits of the four kinds of Buddhas;
based on these causes, they evoke the four lands. However, if one examines this minutely, there are not without some minor difficulties.
Now, returning to the analysis according to the four teachings: first, the Bodhisattvas cultivate the provisional vows of the three teachings.

The practice of cultivation is truly the single cause of the teaching of vows and conduct for the sake of accomplishing sentient beings—whether they be of the four types of beings, or those who have not yet severed the conditions of the realm within, or those who have severed the conditions but not yet exhausted them.
When a Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood within this realm, these four types of practicing beings come and dwell together in the land; there, they cultivate the four types of understanding and practice.
As for the causes, there are two: first, the Bodhisattva cultivates the four practices of skillful means and reality, thereby accomplishing the four types of sentient beings;
second, through the accomplishment of the expedient contemplative practices for these four types of sentient beings, he severs all fetters within the realm of existence.

When the Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood in a land of residual defilement (*sopadhiśeṣa*), the four types of sentient beings come together to be born in that land, where they cultivate the causes of both the Separate and Perfect Teachings.
Third, if a bodhisattva cultivates the causal practices of both the Separate and Perfect Vows and achieves them,

such that within the realm of sentient beings the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) are exhausted and they are able to sever the ignorance (*avidyā*) beyond the realm, then when this bodhisattva attains Buddhahood in a land of retribution,
those sentient beings of the Separate and Perfect Teachings who have established the causes for the outflow-free *dharmatā* will come to be born in that land.
This is the cultivation of the causes for the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao). Fourth, as for the cause of cultivating the vows and practices of the Perfect Teaching:

when the cause reaches its limit and the fruit is fulfilled, the Way is perfected in wondrous enlightenment, and one dwells in the Land of Eternal Quiescent Light. This is the same for all sentient beings of the Perfect Teaching who receive this teaching;

if they cultivate the perfect causes of vows and practices to their ultimate perfection, they shall likewise dwell in the Land of Eternal Quiescent Light, just as the Buddhas of the ten directions do.
Profoundly still like empty space, without increase or decrease, it serves as the cause for constantly manifesting the four lands to bring sentient beings to maturity.
It draws in four types of beings to dwell together in the Buddha-land; through the cause of cultivating vows and practices, the fruit of Bodhi is realized.
This "Land of Co-residence in Eternal Quiescence" endures until the end of the future, just as is clarified in the "Life Span" chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
The fourth section clarifies that the visions of Buddha-lands differ. This sutra states:

"For example, when the various devas eat from the same precious vessel, the color of the rice varies according to their respective karmic retributions. Yet, when it comes to discussing the lands of all Buddhas, they are all like empty space;
since one cannot even say they possess anything, how could there be any visible differences? If one does not perceive such characteristics, [how can one speak of difference?]

That which is visible is that the Buddha-lands are not identical; they possess ten levels of entry, and the explanations in the text below regarding the differences in the color of the food should be distinguished accordingly.
Question: The Sūtra states that the various devas eat from the same precious vessel, yet the color of the food differs according to their karmic retribution.

Is this necessarily the case that there is one substance seen differently due to different perceptions, or is it that there are different substances and one perception? Answer: This should be analyzed through four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
First, regarding the distinction between different natures and different views: one perceives this Sahā world as defiled and Amitābha’s land as a pure land;
thus, one sees it as defiled here and pure there. Second, regarding different natures and a single view:

for instance, in the *Sahā* world and [Sukhāvatī], although the natures of defilement and purity differ, the bodhisattvas of both the Round and the Gradual Teachings perceive them using their divine eyes, yet they do so based solely on a single remaining earth. Third.

Fourth, the difference between distinct objects and distinct perceptions: for example, when Śāriputra saw this land as defiled while Śikhin saw it as pure, both perceived the same single *sāvaśeṣa* (remaining) land, yet they saw it differently as either pure or impure.
Fifth, the identity of object and identity of perception:

this refers to the Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas with the three types of mind-made bodies (*manomayakāya*). These five kinds of persons have all exhausted the fetters within the realms (*dhātu*).

Question: When one is born in another land, the lands perceived therein are no different [from those perceived here]. What is the intention behind explaining that a single substance is revealed by means of "other lands"?

Answer: Because those of the Three Vehicles alike, through the path of ineffable ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), give rise to true outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), the five aggregates they manifest in the lands they receive are, for the time being, identical; therefore, it is said that they are real. Question:

This sutra uses the analogy of various devas eating from the same precious vessel yet perceiving differences in the color of the rice, asking whether this is due to the color itself being unobstructed while the vision is obstructed, or whether both the color and the vision are obstructed and thus perceive differences.

The answer is that this should be analyzed through four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*): first, there is the case where both the color and the vision are obstructed; this refers to the defiled and the pure.
There are two other points where what is seen differs between the two lands: Second, regarding obstructed matter versus unobstructed vision:
while the *dharmakāya* bodhisattvas rely on unimpeded divine eyes such that both defiled and pure aspects of the two lands are entirely unobstructed matter;
Third, regarding unobstructed matter versus obstructed vision: this refers to the world-system of Indra’s net.
Regarding the two types of sentient beings—those with defilement and those who are pure—there are two kinds of lands they perceive: those with obstructions and those without obstructions.
The perception of unobstructed form and the absence of obstruction refers to the lands perceived by those dwelling in the stages of the Three Sages and Ten Saints within the Land of Retribution.
Question: This sutra states that when various devas eat from identical precious vessels, they perceive differences in the color of the food. What does this mean?

Question: Is there a difference between seeing that which has material substance (*sapratigha*) and seeing that which lacks material substance (*apratigha*)? Answer: This should be analyzed according to four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*): 1.
If one considers the defiled and pure lands, as well as the remaining lands of true recompense (*vipākabhūmi*), all are instances of seeing differences within that which has material substance. 2.

There is the case of seeing differences within that which has material obstruction (*sapratigha*), while that which lacks material obstruction is precisely what Bodhisattvas perceive by relying on the Buddha’s wisdom; in these three lands, all are eternally quiescent.

Third, regarding the luminous land: when there are three kinds of unobstructed form and one perceives them as having substantial obstruction, this is precisely the perception of the distinct substances of the three lands by sentient beings within the Land of Eternal Quiescent Light. Fourth, regarding the absence of substantial obstruction:
when one perceives the land that lacks substantial obstruction, this is the pure vision of the Dharma-nature, which is the pure Buddha-land of the minds of the Buddhas of the ten directions.
The *tathatā* (suchness), the impartial *dharmadhātu*, and the eternally quiescent land of light are formless and without substance.

Thus, these twelve brief instances have been set forth to show the differences in the vision of Buddha-lands. If one were to investigate exhaustively the characteristics of the lands manifested through karmic response, they would indeed be immeasurable;
yet though they are immeasurable, they are ultimately non-existent, for they are like empty space, and therefore pure.
The name "householder emptying his room" signifies that all Buddha-lands throughout the ten directions are entirely empty.

Fifth, the clarification of those who attain rebirth is explained in two parts: first, a general explanation of rebirth with respect to the four lands; second, a specific explanation of rebirth with respect to the four lands.
Regarding the first, the general explanation of rebirth with respect to the four lands, it is also termed "attaining rebirth."
It is also called "coming to be born here," as clarified in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*. If one receives birth by going from this land to that land, it is called "transmigration" (*wang-sheng*);
if one receives birth by coming from that land to this land, it is called "coming to be born" (*lai-sheng*).
The same applies to the next two lands; they differ only in being viewed horizontally or vertically. The Land of Constant Quiescent Light is beyond...
"Birth" refers to that which cannot be described as coming or going; there is only the possibility of coming to the three lands, but no possibility of going away from them.
Second, specifically clarifying rebirth by means of the four lands, there are four parts: first, clarifying rebirth in defiled and pure lands.

There are two lands, the defiled and the pure. Regarding taking birth in a defiled land, it is through the moisture of the delusions of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi- and bhāvanā-kleśa*) that these delusions moisten evil karma.

The delusions that produce birth in the four evil destinies moisten wholesome karma, whereby one is born among humans or devas. If one clarifies the matter of the birth of the noble ones of the Three Vehicles:
although a *srotāpanna* has severed the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava*), they have not yet severed the nine grades of the contemplative delusions (*bhāvanā-āsrava*) of the desire realm;

these contemplative delusions moisten their birth among humans and devas for seven more times. A *sakṛdāgāmin*, moreover, has three grades of delusions moistening their existence in the desire realm, whereby they still return once more.
The Anāgāmin who, due to the moisture of afflictions regarding the form and formless realms, is reborn in those two realms;
the Bodhisattva of the Shared Teaching up to the sixth stage who has not yet exhausted the afflictions of the desire realm and is thus reborn;

and the one of the Distinct Teaching in the Ten Abidings who has not yet exhausted the pervasive afflictions and is thus reborn—these may all be understood as being similar to the third fruit. Regarding the Perfect Teaching, [up to] the fifth [stage]...

From the stage of the *śrāvaka* disciple up to those who have newly entered the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), as long as their pervasive delusions (*sāmānya-kleśa*) are not yet exhausted, their rebirths may likewise be understood as being similar to those of the three fruits;
these are all actual rebirths in the Land of Common Dwelling (*sahā-loka-dhātu*).

As for those who come by means of expedient power (*upāya*), they are either *āryas* of the Three Vehicles who, having exhausted the delusions within the realms, come from the Land of Expedient Means (*pariṇāmanā-bhūmi*) by virtue of their vows, or they come from the Land of Retribution (*vipāka-bhūmi*).
The Land of No Obstruction and the Land of Constant Quiescent Light share the same function; they should come to be born in this defiled land of common residence.

Next, it is explained that if ordinary beings were to truly be born in the Pure Land, there would be no four evil realms; rather, they would be born among humans or devas through the moistening of good karma by the afflictions of views and thoughts.
As for those who are born as sages—whether born through the provisional or the real—their categories can be understood from what precedes.

Second, it clarifies that those who attain rebirth in the Land of Remainder—namely, those of the Three Vehicles who equally perceive the primary truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and have exhausted the four abidings (*catur-vāsana*)—all attain rebirth and receive the Dharma-nature body (*dharmatā-kāya*).

Furthermore, those Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas of the Tripiṭaka Teaching, as well as those of the Three Vehicles in the Shared Teaching who have exhausted both views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), all go there to receive birth.
This also includes Bodhisattvas of the Ten Practices in the Distinct Teaching and those of the Perfect Teaching.

Those at the final stage of the ten stages of faith (daśa-śraddhā) are forever separated from the ocean of suffering in the triple world and all attain rebirth in the *sopadhiśeṣa* (with remainder) lands;
this is because these cases refer to actual rebirth. As the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states:

"The death and birth of transformation (*pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa*) cannot be severed by the two vehicles or by bodhisattvas of great power who possess the three types of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*); therefore, they merely attain rebirth in the *sopadhiśeṣa* lands."
Question: Regarding the Dharma-nature body, what are the three kinds of mind-made bodies? Answer: First is the mind-made body produced by the correct reception of samādhi.
This likely refers to the vehicle of Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching who equally enter the tranquil concentration of true emptiness;
thus the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says that because śrāvakas have a predominance of meditative power, they do not see the Buddha-nature. Second is the mind-made body through awakening to the Dharma-nature.

The "mind-made body" (manomaya-kāya) likely refers to a Bodhisattva of the Separate Teaching (pratyeka-yāna), who, although having realized the dharma-nature of partial emptiness, is aware of the dharma-nature of the Middle Way.

The "three types of mind-made bodies of non-action" likely refer to a Bodhisattva of the Perfect Teaching (ekayāna), who contemplates the non-action of the Four Truths of the Middle Way and perfectly subdues ignorance.
Regarding these three, they are all called "mind" because—[the text continues:]—they have not yet... [end of fragment].

When one gives rise to true cultivation and conditional cultivation, these are still based on intentional mental activity (*manasikāra*) with ignorance as the condition and untainted karma (*anāsrava-karman*) as the cause;

thus, one immediately attains birth in the Dharma-body. Question: According to the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, the three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*) all exist within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), and they should be born in the land of retribution (*vipākabhūmi*).
How is it possible that they are born in the land with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-bhūmi*)? Answer: This is explained according to the ten stages of the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavasthāna-śāsana*).
The three types of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*) are categorized as being born in the land of retribution.

If one classifies them according to the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*), the three types of mind-made bodies correspond precisely to those Bodhisattvas of the three teachings who have severed all afflictions within the realm;

they are thus identical in being born in the Land of Remainder (*śeṣabhūmi*). Those who come by means of provisional power are actually born in the Land of Constant Quiescence and Radiance (*nityapraśāntaprabhāsvara-bhūmi*), which transcends the [Land of] Reward (*vipākabhūmi*).

It is evident that the Dharmakāya should come to be born in the Land of Further Existence (*sopadhiśeṣa-bhūmi*). Regarding those who come to be born in the Land of Unobstructed Retribution of the Threefold Knowledge (*trividyā-phala*):

if it concerns the Land of Co-residence (*sahabhūmi*), those who have exhausted all pervasive afflictions (*āvaraṇa-kleśa*) and eliminated ignorance (*avidyā*)—namely, those at the first stage (*bhūmi*) of the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-śāsana*) and the first dwelling (*vihāra*) of the Perfect Teaching (*pūrṇa-śāsana*)—are all able to attain rebirth therein, up to and including the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*). This is the fourth clarification.
If the Constant Quiescent Light Land (*nitya-prabhāsvara-kṣetra*) is ultimately and eternally quiescent, it is neither arising nor non-arising; how, then, could there be going forth or coming forth?

If one clearly distinguishes the Constant Quiescent Light Land, within the Ten Stages of the Patience of Quiescent Extinction (*śānti-nirvāṇa-akṣānti*), there are two births, and within the Ground of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi-bhūmi*) of the Patience of Quiescent Extinction, there is one birth.
Some say this refers to the beginning of the Perfect Teaching (*pūrṇa-yāna*).

Even those dwelling in the stage of "partial penetration" (bhāga-bheda) who have destroyed ignorance and perceive the principle of the Buddha-nature possess the sense of "partial birth" (*bhāga-janman*), continuing thus up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Because they are still constrained by the retribution of the *pariṇāmi-ka* death and rebirth resulting from residual ignorance, it is said that they "dwell in the fruit of retribution.
Since the Subtle Enlightenment (*miao-jue*) has eternally exhausted [all traces], it is said that "one person dwells in the Pure Land. The preceding forty-one [stages]...

If the ground is a land of retribution, it is called the "land born of retribution"; if one partially perceives the principle of true quiescence, it is called the "land born of the eternally quiescent light.

Question: In the stage of shared existence with segmented birth (*paricchinna-saha-bhava*), one must exhaustively sever the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāva-kleśa*) and discard the retribution body before being born into the Land of Remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-bhūmi*).
Should one not likewise exhaustively sever the distinct afflictions of views and thought and discard the transformation body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*) in order to be born into that Land of Remainder?
Question: Does the *sambhogakāya* (recompense body) arise only within the *vipākabhūmi* (land of retribution)? Answer: Not so.

Although the coarse, segmented retribution and the obstructive afflictions (*kleśa*) have been exhausted and must be abandoned, if there remains a residual retribution, one moves from cause to effect as specific delusions are successively destroyed;

this is indeed the true *vipākabhūmi*. Question: When the *saṃbhogakāya* receives birth, does the *dharmakāya* (constant, quiescent light) also receive birth? Answer: Since... [the text here is incomplete].
Question: If it is called "eternally quiescent," how can it undergo birth? Birth is movement; how, then, can it be named eternally quiescent? Answer:

How can you say above that birth is the land of eternal quiescent light? Answer: In the land of retribution (*vipākabhūmi*), there is the discussion of boundaries regarding birth. When wisdom is generated and one perceives the Truth, that Truth is itself non-birth.
This is precisely the meaning of the principle of "non-birth as birth. Question: If it is "not birth" yet "birth," then it should also be called "not [birth]."
The constant answers are likewise so; why is this? Because ultimate, eternal quiescence is precisely non-arising and non-non-arising.
Abiding in the forty-one stages of quiescence is precisely non-arising and non-non-arising, and neither-constant-nor-unconstant.
Sixth, clarifying the differences in the teachings expounded across the four lands, there are four points; the first clarifies the teaching in the defiled and pure lands.
First, it clarifies the differences in the teachings expounded in the land of impurity and purity; second, it clarifies the differences in the teachings expounded in the land of remaining defilement;

third, it clarifies the differences in the teachings expounded in the land of unobstructed retribution; and fourth, it clarifies the differences in the teachings expounded in the land of eternal quiescent light.

Regarding the first point—clarifying the differences in the teachings expounded in the lands of defilement and purity: within the Land of Common Abode for Ordinary Beings and Sages, there are two types, namely, the defiled and the pure. First, the defiled [land].

Regarding the "earth" (the stage of the *śrāvaka*): when the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) are heavy and the faculties are either sharp or dull—those with sharp faculties respond to the sudden teaching of the Mahāyāna, like the rising sun first illuminating the high mountains;

whereas those with dull faculties, burdened by the heavy five turbidities, are first taught the Tripiṭaka, then the Vaipulya and Mahāprajñāpāramitā, and gradually tamed through skillful means until, at the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and *Mahāparinirvāṇa*, they finally hear the Perfect Teaching and perceive their Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*).
This reveals the secret treasury. Second, regarding the two pure lands:
