although the Pure Land of Flower Light is not an age of evil, because of its original vow, it teaches the Three Vehicles; thus, it likewise possesses both sudden and gradual teachings. Question:

If even a pure land can reveal the gradual teaching, why was the Bodhisattva of Fragrant Accumulation so astonished? (The answer seems to be missing. Second, explaining that there are [gradual teachings].
Regarding the differences in the teachings expounded in other lands: practitioners of the Three Vehicles who have exhausted their fetters all attain rebirth there;

however, within this context, there is no lack of distinction between those of sharp and dull faculties. According to the principles of the Tripiṭaka Teaching and the Two Vehicles of the Shared Teaching, both are considered dull;
for the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* clarifies that Arhats are dull in receiving the Dharma-nature body because they take a circuitous route toward the Buddha-way.

The Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) benefit those of the Two Vehicles; the Bodhisattvas of the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao) enter the provisional (jia) and benefit those of the Shared Teaching;
the Bodhisattvas of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) benefit those of the Distinct Teaching.

Although the Tathāgata teaches only the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) therein, without further opening up the expedient means of the Three Vehicles, within that One Vehicle there is nonetheless no lack of provisional distinctions and the Great Teaching.

Riding upon the true, perfect Mahāyāna to respond to two conditions: if one clarifies the revelation of the provisional to manifest the real, although there is no opening of the provisional [teachings] of the Tripitaka or the Shared Teaching, there is the opening of the provisional of the Distinct Teaching to manifest the reality of the Perfect Teaching.
Therefore, the Lotus Sūtra clarifies that Arhats are born in that land to seek the Buddha’s wisdom and obtain hearing of this sūtra; only then...
By means of the Buddha-vehicle, they attain extinction (*nirvāṇa*); the retribution of the three types of supernormal knowledge (*trividyā*) is free from obstruction.
Since those who preach the teachings differ, yet all have shattered ignorance, those who are reborn there possess a single root-nature; it is the Great Straight Path, without further detours.
In that land, the Buddha teaches only the One Perfect Teaching (*ekakalpa-deśanā*). This is the teaching spoken in the Land of Constant Quiescent Light (*nityapraśāntaprakāśa*).

Regarding the differences in teaching: if one speaks from the perspective of the ultimate *dharmadhātu* of constant tranquil light (*nitya-śānta-prabhāsa-kṣetra*), there is no speaking and no showing; beyond the letter *tā*, there are no words that can be spoken.

Yet, when it is said that "the Dharma is taught," this refers to the fact that the Dharmakāya is itself the *dharmadhātu*, which eternally and universally provides silent support to all sentient beings—this is what is meant by "the Dharmakāya preaching the Dharma.
If, however, one distinguishes between the two based on the *dharmadhātu* of constant tranquil light as a result of retribution (*vipākaphala*), [the distinction is as follows].

Regarding the differences in the various explanations of the Dharma: the teaching of the four unconditioned truths (*asaṃskṛta-satya*) refers to the teachings expounded in the land of unobstructed fruition and retribution;
the teaching of the single truth of reality (*eka-tattva-satya*) refers to the teachings expounded in the Land of Constant Tranquil Light.

The two lower lands may be understood through this same classification. Seventh, regarding the clarification of the four types by means of contemplating the mind: the fundamental nature of the mind...
Coming, all is ultimately empty and quiescent; yet sentient beings are for the most part inverted, with few being non-inverted.
Through the conditions of ignorance, they give rise to good and evil—this is precisely the dharma produced by causes and conditions. It is emptiness, it is the provisional, and it is the Middle Way.
This Way is the realm of causes and conditions, of good and evil; it is the land where ordinary beings and sages dwell together. Why is this so?

Contemplating this good and evil: the evil mind that is contemplated is precisely the defiled land (*saṃkliṣṭa-kṣetra*), while the good mind that is contemplated is precisely the pure land (*pariśuddha-kṣetra*).

If one understands that the phenomena of causes and conditions are illusory—whether by analyzing phenomena into emptiness (*prabheda-śūnyatā*) or by realizing the essence of phenomena as emptiness (*dharmatā-śūnyatā*)—and contemplates the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), then that ultimate realm is the land with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-bhūmi*). Knowing that emptiness is not [inherently] empty, one does not...
Taking emptiness as witness, one also knows that the Middle Way is neither cause nor fruit; yet it is both cause and fruit, for all lack a fixed nature.
If one realizes that cause and fruit are without obstruction, this is precisely the land of unobstructed fruition.

Although there are differences in entering and emerging through the skillful means of emptiness and the provisional, the source of the mind of ignorance is itself Buddha-nature. If [one realizes] ignorance...
Nature itself is clarity; this is the Land of Constant Quiescent Light. Therefore, this sutra says: "According as the mind is pure, so is the Buddha-land pure.
The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* says: "If you wish to purify a Buddha-land, you should purify your own mind.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "Immeasurable worlds all arise from the conditions of the mind; all phenomena enter into the One."
Regarding the eighth section, "The Path of Hair" (*mārga*), those who interpret this sutra through the meaning of the Buddha-land (*buddhakṣetra*) do so according to three points:
first, the general introduction; second, the general exposition of the main teaching; and third, the explanation of the dissemination. First, regarding the general introduction:

the Tathāgata joined his palms and manifested the [pure] lands as a portent precisely to symbolize the teaching on the Buddha-land. Thus, Ratnākara expressed his praise, saying: "I now pay homage to the World-Honored One."
This small canopy appears within it as my three-thousandfold world-system;

because Ratnākara deeply understands that the canopy is intended to be joined, and because he wishes to preach on the Pure Land, after his praise is finished, he immediately questions the Buddha regarding the causes and conditions of the Buddha-land. The description of the manifested auspicious signs truly signifies the intention to preach on the Buddha-land.
Second, explaining the general introduction to the formal discourse, there are three sections of the scriptural text: first, the single room.
Externally two, internally three; exiting the room, one general [category]. Regarding the external three and a half sections:

in the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*, the Buddha was requested to explain the causes and effects of the Buddha-land (*buddhakṣetra*). The Tathāgata answered concerning the causes and effects of the Buddha-land by pressing the earth with his toe to manifest a pure land, thereby enabling all sentient beings to obtain the benefits of the Mahāyāna.
He then restored the land to its original state for those seeking the vehicle of the śrāvaka.

This provides the benefit of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). If one does not understand the meaning of the Buddha-land as the *niśraya-pratisthā* (the supporting environment), how could one recognize the profound purport of this chapter of the sutra?
Next, regarding the "Expedient Means" (*Upāya-kauśalya*) chapter:

for the sake of kings and elders, it expounds the two types of contemplation—the analytical and the essential—and exhorts them to seek the primary cause for the fruit of Buddhahood; if the supporting cause is perfected, then all lands will be complete.
If a king or elder has not severed the karmic bonds within their realm, they will be reborn in a Pure Land of Co-residence;
if they have severed the karmic bonds within their realm, they will be reborn in a Land of Remainder. When one attains Buddhahood, beings of these two types come to be born in that land.
Next, in the "Chapter on Disciples," the refutation of the ten great disciples and five hundred arhats intends to demonstrate the severing of the realms.
If the collection of external conditions reaches the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, one severs the delusions of differentiation and is immediately born into the land of retribution;

subsequently, at the time of attaining Buddhahood, three types of sentient beings come to be born in that land. Next, in the "Chapter on the Universal Bodhisattvas," the four great bodhisattvas and eight thousand bodhisattvas are rebuked:
if one severs the ignorance and afflictions of the dharma-realm, one is then born into the Land of Eternal Quiescent Light. Hereafter...
When one attains the state of a Buddha of ultimate wondrous enlightenment, beings of a single type are born in that land.

Regarding the second point, concerning the textual passages of the six chapters within the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*: when Mañjuśrī visits Vimalakīrti in the city of Vaiśālī to inquire after his illness, Vimalakīrti manifests the emptiness of his room.
He explains that this manifestation of the room’s emptiness occurs because the lands of the Buddhas of the ten directions are empty. Is this not indeed the correct [explanation]?
The first section, "Manifesting the Buddha-land," accords with the meaning of the Tathāgata’s teaching on the Buddha-land; it demonstrates that the Buddha-land is the fruition of the Dharma-body.

Next, the section "On the Inconceivable" universally manifests inconceivable matters—such as Mount Sumeru entering a mustard seed—which are all the sovereign and unimpeded nature of the Buddha-land as the environment (the *niśraya-vipāka*).
Finally, the section "Observing Sentient Beings" universally shows that the goddess dwelling in her chamber for twelve years is identical [to the Buddha].
Vimalakīrti resides in the Land of Constant Quiescence precisely to assist in manifesting the Buddha-land;
therefore, it is said that the pure lands of the Buddhas of the ten directions are constantly manifested within this room. Next, regarding the "Chapter on the Universal Path to Buddhahood":

practicing upon what is not the path and thereby attaining the universal penetration of the Buddha-path is precisely to manifest all pure lands within impure lands. Thus, Vimalakīrti spoke these verses:
Although it is known that the lands of all Buddhas and sentient beings are empty, one constantly cultivates the pure land to transform and guide all classes of beings.
Next, in the "Chapter on Entering the Dharma-Gate of Non-Duality," each of the bodhisattvas speaks of entering the dharma-gate of non-duality;
this is intended to shatter the ignorance regarding the two aforementioned lands and enter the land of retribution, abiding in the land of eternal quiescence. Next...
The *Gandhavyūha-parivarta* (Chapter on the Fragrant Accumulation) manifests this chamber as the pure land of Universal Fragrance in contrast to the defiled land of Sahā;
this serves as the scriptural proof for the five chapters within the chamber that accord with the Buddha’s teaching on the two lands of purity and defilement for bodhisattvas.

Furthermore, the two chapters concerning exiting the chamber—namely, the *Bodhisattvacaryā-parivarta* (Chapter on Bodhisattva Practice), where Vimalakīrti supports the great assembly in his palm and returns them to the Āmra Garden—complete this section.

The Buddha extensively expounded various Buddha-lands to Ānanda, further clarifying the essential meaning. If one does not understand the text of this chapter with precision, how could one distinguish it?
Next, the section on the Akṣobhya Buddha Chapter corresponds to the manifestation of lands outside the hall, which serves as a proof for the Tathāgata’s teaching of various lands;
its meaning is clear. Those who hear this sūtra and attain the Way will be twice as many as before.

Regarding the two chapters on the "Circulation" (Prakāśana)—the "Dharma-pūjā" chapter and the "Devānām-indra-pratijñā" chapter—the former involves the Devānām-indra’s vow to transmit the sutra and the Tathāgata’s seal of approval;
this is precisely for the purpose of circulating the essence of inconceivable liberation and the core doctrine of the causes and effects of the Buddha-land.
The "Entrustment" (Parīndanā) chapter is the Tathāgata’s formal entrustment to Maitreya and Ānanda.
This chapter ensures that the *Acintyavimokṣa-dharmaparyāya* and the causes and effects of the Buddha-lands explained above shall continue to circulate without interruption.
Regarding the explanation of this chapter (this is the fourth major section at the beginning of the scroll): "Chapter" (*pin*) takes "classification" as its meaning;
when the categories of meaning within the scriptural text are similar, later generations have grouped them into a single segment and designated it a "chapter."

However, the title of this chapter should properly be "Introduction Chapter" (*Nidāna-parivarta*); that it is called the "Buddha-land Chapter" (*Buddhakṣetra-parivarta*) is because it is named after its primary discourse.
Question: Since this chapter contains both an introduction and a main discourse, why is the title designated solely by the "Buddha-land" of the main discourse?
Answer: This is not a valid question. If you were to designate it according to the introduction, you would again have to ask why the introduction is not used instead.
In this "Chapter on the Correct," we now explain that other sūtras are not without similar examples.

For instance, in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, the first half of the chapter is the introduction (*nidāna*), while from the point where it says "Addressing Śāriputra" onwards, the latter half is the main exposition (*samyag-deśanā*). If using the introduction to title the chapter is permissible, what harm would there be in doing so?
If you do not allow this sūtra’s introductory section to receive the name of the main exposition, then I likewise do not allow it.

The first half of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* constitutes the introduction (*nidāna*), while the subsequent half constitutes the main body (*samyak-pravacana*). Yet, the title of the chapter uses the term "Introduction" (*nidāna*) to designate the whole.

Question: If this is so, one should properly use the title "Introduction" for that section. Answer: The *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* also employs the introduction and the formal teaching within the same chapter;

this too would present a difficulty [if we were to restrict the title strictly]. Furthermore, these chapters were established by later scholars; their intentions differ, and they are not the work of the Buddha himself.

That which has been composed here is not something that Ānanda lacked the capacity to definitively uphold; although this sutra does not explicitly designate the "Preface Chapter" (*Nidāna-parivarta*) as the first, the meaning of the preface is perfectly evident, and its significance must be explained in advance.
The meanings of the preface are manifold; now, I shall briefly provide a comprehensive explanation using three points:
first, a brief explanation of the meaning of the preface; second, clarifying the universal and the particular; third, applying it to the contemplation of the mind. First, the brief explanation.

Regarding the meaning of "preface" (*nidāna*), it is briefly explained through three senses: first, the preface takes "sequence" as its meaning; second, the preface takes "basis" or "source" as its meaning;
third, the preface takes "narrative exposition" as its meaning. First, regarding the preface as having the sense of "sequence":
when composing a literary work, the initial section is called the preface. Herein, these six meanings constitute the teaching of the Buddha’s sutras.

First, it is called the "Introduction" (xu) because it serves as the head or beginning. Second, the Introduction is defined by the sense of "reliance" (youjie): the Great Sage’s teaching must rely upon certain conditions;
thus, he manifested auspicious omens to inspire joy in the minds of sentient beings, saying that "the Way arises from joy," and by relying on this, he was able to deliver his teachings.
Third, the Introduction is defined by the sense of "narrating" (xushu).

Since the sentiments of the people have already given rise to admiration and longing, yet the Sage’s intent is difficult to fathom, the assembly has turned their hearts toward him without knowing where to direct them.
Therefore, it was necessary to borrow the titles of high positions; perhaps a disciple, or a manifested Buddha or Bodhisattva, would first provide a description.

Once the doubts of the multitude were thus dispelled and they knew where to find the source of their devotion, only then could the teaching be delivered; hence it is called a "Preface" (*xu*). Now, I shall clarify this.
Regarding the six meanings at the beginning of each sutra, these constitute the sequence of the introductory framework (*nidāna*).

Specifically, the manifestation of the land is the sequence of the "basis" (*upaniṣad*), while the seven-syllable verses of the *Ratnakūṭa* expressing praise constitute the sequence of the "introductory narrative" (*upodghāta*). Question: Do all sutras possess these three sequences? Answer: This matter is not fixed;
there are cases where they are complete and cases where they are incomplete. Some may possess only two meanings, and some may possess only one. All [sutras] are thus accounted for.
This constitutes the introductory section (*nidāna*). Question: Since the characters used to explain the various introductions differ from one another, how can they all be employed together here?
Answer: If one follows the distinctions found in written characters, there is such differentiation; however, the intent of the sutra unifies these three meanings.
Since they are already fully prepared for common use, there should be no hindrance to employing the character "order" (*xu*) [here].
First, it clarifies the four reliances, meaning reliance on the meaning and not on the words. Second, it clarifies the general and specific [introductions].

This involves binding the preceding three sections into two: the general introduction and the specific introduction. The first six points, beginning with "Thus have I heard," constitute the general introduction;

the sequence of manifesting auspicious signs and the sequence of the narrative together constitute the specific introduction. As for what is called "general," at the beginning of all sutras, the six meanings universally serve as the opening.
Regarding the distinction between the General Preface (*tongxu*) and the Specific Preface (*biexu*):

the former refers to the initial manifestation of auspicious signs by the assembly, while the latter refers to the various ways in which the preface describes the circumstances, each serving to manifest different meanings; hence it is called the "Specific Preface. Question:

Why are these two—the General and Specific Prefaces—different? Answer: As explained previously, the titles of all sutras must necessarily include both general and specific elements; this is now [the case] because...
Regarding specific names, there is a specific preface and specific verbal teachings; regarding general names, there is a general preface, and all are spoken by the Buddha.

This extends even to clarifying the general and specific principles based on the preceding practices; because of these general and specific [principles], the meaning of the two prefaces—the general and the specific—is established.
Question: If one follows the two prefaces, the general and the specific, from the perspective of both the specific and the general...
Question: When establishing names, the sequence is such that the specific comes first and the general follows; how can the general come first and the specific follow? Answer:

Regarding the convenience of establishing names, it should be such that the specific comes first and the general follows; regarding the convenience of the sequence, it should be such that the general comes first and the specific follows.

Furthermore, when clarifying the meaning through a single path, it is also the case that the specific comes first and the general follows. Why is this so? It is because, for instance, as for the manifestation of auspicious signs... [by] means of... [the specific precedes].
Based on these six points mentioned prior to the discourse on the past, it is evident that the Tathāgata uttered these words only as he was about to enter parinirvāṇa;

therefore, we know that the prologue preceding the main body of the sutra is intended to inspire faith in the disciples of the present, while the prologue following the sutra is intended to engender faith in the disciples of the future. Question: If this is so, when the Buddha was [still in the world]...
Question: If the *Sūtra on the World* (*Shijing*) lacks a prologue at the beginning, it cannot be called a *sūtra*. Answer:

Although the specific prologue was not yet expounded prior to it, when the Buddha preached the Dharma, it was already inherently possessed by him; therefore, it is entitled a *sūtra*. Third, regarding the contemplation of the mind (*guanxin*), there are two types of prologues:
the general and the specific. The mind itself is the general, while contemplation is the specific. Through this mind and contemplation, the one [truth] is accomplished.
Because it encompasses all Buddha-dharmas, contemplating the mind is the initial gateway for entering the Path; it is that by which one relies [upon the Path]. Question:

If this is so, and if contemplating the mind is taken as the "fishing net" (a provisional means) for entering the Path, would it not be a contradiction to treat it as the meaning of both the general and specific prefaces?

Answer: It is for the sake of convenience in establishing the name. Thus, while one speaks of "contemplating the mind," the convenience of practice is precisely "mind-contemplation. This follows the same principle as what was stated previously.

The meaning of the matter is now clear. Regarding the previous question: since the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) clarifies the contemplation of the mind (*guanxin*) in various places, I fear that if one were to enter the text [of the sutra] again in this manner, it might disrupt the integrity of the scriptural teachings.
Answer: Those who expound the scriptural teachings do so fundamentally to instruct people in entering the Way.
For the worthy ones who cherish the Way, there is contemplative practice (*guanxing*) at every turn; how could they seek out the sacred scriptures without [engaging in such practice]?

For one who practices contemplation, it is sufficient that the skillful exposition is appropriate; it does not merely avoid harm, but also achieves both the literal meaning and the underlying principle.
Since contemplative wisdom and discernment are thereby attained, how could there be the fault of causing confusion or disorder?
*Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra Commentary*, Fascicle One.
Commentary on the Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra, Scroll Two (from "Thus Have I Heard" to "The Āmra Grove").
Fifth, the clarification of entering the main text. Now, in explaining the general and specific prefaces, there are two points:

first, the explanation of the six meanings of the general preface, beginning with "Thus have I heard"; second, the explanation of the specific preface, such as the manifestation of auspicious signs. First, the explanation of the six meanings of the general preface.

These six meanings collectively serve as the introduction to all the various sutras; furthermore, they must be distinguished according to two further senses: first, a general explanation, and second, a specific explanation.

Regarding the general explanation: "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) is the characteristic feature of the Buddha’s teaching when he instructs Ānanda and the other great disciples to enter the Dharma.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "When the Buddha was about to enter nirvana, Ānanda..."
Because the fetter of craving had not yet been severed, his mind was submerged in an ocean of sorrow. Aniruddha said to Ānanda, "You are one who protects the Dharma of the Buddha.
If you have any doubts regarding future matters, consult and resolve them at once. Why remain in an ocean of sorrow like an ordinary worldly person?
Ānanda, having attained the power of mindfulness and the Way, recovered from his despondency and regained his composure.
There were four matters for inquiry: first, after the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha, how should we practice the Path?
Second, who shall serve as our teacher? Third, how should we dwell together with the ill-spoken Caraka?

Fourth, what words should be placed at the beginning of the Buddha’s sūtras—whether during his present lifetime or after his passing—to instruct Ānanda on practicing in reliance upon the four foundations of mindfulness?
The *Dharmapada-vinaya-sūtra* is your Great Teacher; you should practice your bodily and verbal actions in this manner.

If Chanda commits verbal misconduct, he should be disciplined according to the Brahma-punishment (*brahma-daṇḍa*). If his mind becomes supple, he should further be taught the *Nandika-kātyāyana-sūtra*, whereby he will immediately enter the Path.
This is the treasury of the Dharma-jewels accumulated by me over three great *asaṃkhyeya*-kalpas; it is the first [instruction] to be followed.

To state: "Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha was in such-and-such a direction, in such-and-such a country, at such-and-such a location, in a grove of trees"—this formula is not unique to my own Dharma; it is likewise placed at the beginning of the sutras of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
To know these six meanings of "Thus have I heard" is what constitutes the General Preface (sādhāraṇa-nidāna).

All sūtras invariably place this at their beginning; this meaning is also called the "Introductory Preface of the Bequest" (*parindanā-nidāna*). It is the Tathāgata’s final instruction, established as the opening of the sūtra.
It is also called the "Preface Prior to the Sūtra," for all Buddhas of the three periods of time must necessarily place these words at the beginning of their sūtras.
Question: Why are such words as "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) placed at the beginning of the sūtra? Why are they called "harsh words"?

Question: Since the Buddha taught the Brahma-faring (brahmacarya) for bhikṣus, and since those who abide by the Prātimokṣa within the immeasurable Buddha-dharma all attain entry into the Path, why does he command them to cultivate only the four foundations of mindfulness? Answer:

The sūtras employ such expressions as "peaceful" and so forth in order to sever doubts and encourage faith; furthermore, they serve to authenticate the Buddha’s own words, distinguishing them from those spoken by his disciples.

Because it is taught in sixteen aspects, and also to establish the profound faith of practitioners, and also to refute the scriptures of outsiders, the beginning of the text marks the head of the teaching with the two characters *ā* and *u*. *Ā-u* refers to auspicious signs;
[here] it refers to the faults of heterodox and deviant matters, such as those fully refuted in the *Śata-śāstra*, for various reasons such as these.
It is because the Buddha’s initial establishment of the teaching was based on these six principles. As for the case of the harsh-spoken Ānanda who taught the Dharma of Brahmā:
Ānanda, relying on his own royal lineage, had left the household life while the Buddha was still in the world; he treated the bhikṣus with contempt and did not follow the laws of the Saṃgha.
When the time came for the communal rites of the Sangha, he mocked them with a laugh, saying they were like fallen leaves gathered together by a whirlwind.

In one place, what is being discussed? Even after the Buddha had passed into *parinirvāṇa*, [the practice] was not changed. The Buddha ordered that the *brahma-daṇḍa* (brahminical penalty) be established;
"banishment" (*pabbājana*) refers to expulsion. It is also called the *brahma-daṇḍa-dharma*. As for the method of punishment: a separate altar (*maṇḍala*) is established.
Those who have committed offenses according to the law are made to enter this altar. No other *brahmans* may speak with them. If [their] mind...
For those to be tamed, he preached the *Nata-kātyāyana-sūtra* to cause them to leave behind existence and non-existence;

for those to be taught the Middle Way, he preached [the teachings] whereby they immediately enter the first fruit (*srotāpanna*). This is the intent behind the fact that this school clarifies the "neither existent nor non-existent" gate within the Tripiṭaka Teaching as distinct from the other three gates.
Regarding the instruction that the bhikṣus abide by the *Prātimokṣa*, [it is as follows: *Pā*...
*Vinaya* (Luo-ti-mu-xie) is translated here as "Preserving Liberation" (*bao-jietuo*), also as "Recompense Liberation" (*bao-jietuo*), and also as "Liberation Everywhere" (*chu-chu-jietuo*).

Question: Since the *Vinaya* clarifies matters such as eating only at the proper time and wearing robes according to the rules—many of which appear to be non-essential or secondary matters—how can it be called "Preserving Liberation"?
Answer: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The Buddha taught the *Vinaya* in order to ensure that the Buddha-dharma endures for a long time."
One should not seek for [an ultimate] reality; to seek for reality is to give rise to false views.
At present, because the monastic community does not keep the precepts in mind, I fear that the Buddha-dharma will not abide for long.

Regarding your question as to why, when the gates of the Daoist path to Buddhahood are immeasurable, one is instead instructed to cultivate the Way by relying solely on the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*): I answer that if one departs from these four...
If one practices generosity while mindful of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), one merely attains great wealth; by observing the precepts, one is reborn among humans or devas;
through the pure precepts and pure conduct of the ascetic practices (*dhūta*), one attains meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and is reborn in the Brahma heavens according to the level of dhyāna;

and through extensive learning and preaching the Dharma, one gains worldly wisdom and eloquence, and in future lives will again obtain the retribution of intelligence. However, if these are conjoined with the foundations of mindfulness, they can then destroy the four [inverted views].
If one practices various wholesome dharmas with a mind free from aversion, there is nothing that is not the Path. Question:

The Śrāvaka sūtras state that one must rely on the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) to cultivate the Path, whereas the Mahāyāna teachings speak of entering the Path by contemplating non-arising (*anutpāda*).

Is it necessary for the Mahāyāna to employ the contemplation of "attaining something" (*upalambha*) via the four foundations of mindfulness? Answer: The Mahāyāna possesses the four foundations of mindfulness of non-arising. What [could there be] else?

Regarding the distinctions among the stages, there is the entry into the path through the Mahāyāna’s correct contemplation of non-arising. Although the Buddha's teachings are immeasurable, they do not transcend the "half" and "full" [teachings].
The *śrāvaka* sūtras speak of the four foundations of mindfulness characterized by arising and ceasing; this is the "half-character.

The Mahāyāna speaks of the three kinds of foundations of mindfulness—non-arising, immeasurable, and unconditioned; this is the "full-character. The "half-character" refers to the former, while the "full-character" refers to the latter.

That is to say, the four "withered" characters are the four "flourishing" ones; through these withered and flourishing [characters] between the twin trees, one attains the vision of Buddha-nature and abides in Great Nirvana—this is called the Dharma-realm of all Buddhas.

One should know that beyond the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), what other superior methods for entering the Path exist in either the Mahayana or Hinayana? Therefore, the Buddha’s final injunction was for his disciples to rely upon this.
The four foundations of mindfulness are the path of cultivation. Second, the detailed explanation of the general introduction:

regarding these six meanings, while the traditional commentaries mostly employ five meanings, we now employ six. The six meanings are: first, "Thus" (*evam*); second, "I have heard" (*śrutam*); third, "at one time" (*ekasmin samaye*);
fourth, "the Buddha was dwelling" (*bhagavān viharati sma*); fifth, "the location"; and sixth, "those who heard together. Regarding "Thus":

The beginning of encouraging faith; "I have heard" means that I personally received these words from the sound [of the Buddha's voice]; "at one time" refers to the moment of being moved by the teaching;
"Buddha" refers to the Lord who appears to transform beings; "place" refers to the location where the sutra was heard;

"those who heard together" serves as testimony that this is not a personal fabrication or a mistaken transmission. These six meanings follow one another precisely for the purpose of exhorting others toward the attainment of Buddhahood.

Those who see and hear [this teaching] in future generations will have their doubts stilled and their faith increased; thus, the merit of benefiting oneself and others is accomplished and the Way is realized.
Such is what is called "the beginning of encouraging faith. This intention lies in encouraging faith, and since all six meanings serve to encourage faith, they are placed at the outset;
therefore, it is called "the beginning of encouraging faith."
Thus it is.
According to this, there are three points: first, a general clarification of the meaning of "thus" (evam). The intention of "thus" is to encourage faith;

that is, the Tathāgata understands according to the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) and teaches according to the true nature of phenomena, such that what he has taught is truthful and must certainly be trusted and followed. (*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*)
It is said: "The great ocean of the Buddha-dharma can be entered through faith and crossed by means of wisdom. Such a person possesses the characteristic of faith.
Furthermore, "thus" is a term for wholesome faith. One who lacks faith says, "This matter is not thus," while one who has faith says, "This matter is thus.
A person with such faith can enter the Buddha-dharma and attain the four fruits of the śramaṇa.

Those who lack faith, even if they have left the household life, shaved their heads, donned the dyed robes, and studied various sūtras—being able to debate and provide answers—they remain empty-handed within the Buddha-dharma and gain nothing at all. Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Such [teachings] demonstrate to people the Dharma of non-contention; the Buddha preached with a mind free from dependence, and the disciples received it with a mind free from attachment."
Therefore, one is able to attain liberation; thus it is said that this is not as the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) teach.

This is because those who speak do so with a mind of attachment to views, and those who listen receive it with a mind of grasping and clinging. They engage in strife in the present life and, upon death, enter hell;

how could this be called "thus"? As a verse in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "Because of their own love for and attachment to their own dharma, they disparage the dharmas of others, even though they uphold [their own]."
Furthermore, practitioners of the precepts do not escape the suffering of hell. Moreover, many Dharma masters of antiquity have frequently said, "It is thus" (*evam*);
this "thus" is "according to principle" (*yathā-artha*). It is "according to principle" because it is skillfully explained, and it is "it is" (*iti*) because there is nothing that is not so.

Second, regarding the explanation according to the teachings (*śāsana*), we now clarify that while the four inexpressibles are beyond description, they manifest as four teachings in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings.
The four teachings each have four such aspects: first, the suchness of the arising and ceasing through causes and conditions; second, the suchness of causes and conditions as emptiness;
third, the suchness of causes and conditions as provisional names; and fourth, the suchness of causes and conditions as the Middle Way.
Regarding the first, the suchness of the arising and ceasing through causes and conditions: in the past, the Buddha taught at Vārāṇasī that the five aggregates both arise and cease together.

When the neighbors and others heard this teaching, they immediately attained enlightenment. Furthermore, those seeking the path of the śrāvaka within this Sūtra realized that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are impermanent;
they attained the fruit of arhatship and the purity of the Dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣur-viśuddhi*).

This demonstrates that leaving the household life and donning the dyed robes is not in vain, for one can thereby attain the four fruits of the śramaṇa. Second, it clarifies that causes and conditions are themselves empty.
This is as explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*: the three vehicles equally perceive the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) through the path of ineffable speech that severs afflictions.
This sutra refutes Kātyāyana’s [view] by clarifying five points; when two hundred bhikṣus heard this teaching, their minds attained liberation.
This is precisely what demonstrates to people the dharma of non-contention (*araṇa*). Thus, the provisional designation [of phenomena] arises from three causes and conditions.
As the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings* states: "The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Ocean*, and *Emptiness* proclaim that Bodhisattvas undergo cultivation over successive kalpas.
This sūtra also says: "One receives all sensations by means of non-reception.

If a Bodhisattva hears such an exposition, they attain the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgajñatā*), enter the stage of a Bodhisattva, and come to know the faculties of sentient beings. These are the four causes.
Regarding the Middle Way being thus, as stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the Buddha appears in the world because of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena;
the manifested Buddhas (*nirmāṇa-buddha*) likewise appear in the world because of the true reality of all phenomena. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* says:
"The meaning of the true reality of all phenomena has already been explained for you. In this sūtra, each of the bodhisattvas speaks of entering [the path].

Regarding the gate of the two marks: if a bodhisattva hears such an exposition, they immediately perceive the Buddha-nature, open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and abide in inconceivable liberation.
Because the Buddha-dharma contains these four kinds of meanings, the beginning of all sutras establishes "Thus" (*evam*).
In the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, within the sudden teaching, there is the section on causes and conditions and provisional names.
The Path is of two kinds: thus, in the Śrāvaka sūtras of the Tripiṭaka teaching, there is only the arising and ceasing of dependent origination;
thus, in the various Vaipulya Mahāyāna sūtras, all four kinds are possessed;
thus, in the Mahāprajñāpāramitā, excluding arising and ceasing, three kinds are possessed; and thus, in the Lotus Sūtra, there is only the Middle Way within dependent origination.
The single reality-mark (*tathatā*) is thus; likewise, the Great Nirvāṇa clarifies that the Buddha-dharmadhātu also possesses these four kinds of *tathatā*.
This sutra is likewise a Vaipulya Mahāyāna teaching on "clarified butter" (*ghṛta*) that is indeterminate, possessing all four kinds of *tathatā*, as evidenced by the scriptural passages cited above.
Since this sutra already possesses the four kinds of *tathatā* at its very beginning...
He sets forth these words. A question is asked: "If principle is non-dual, how can there be four such [teachings]?
He replies: "All dharmas are ultimately ineffable; they are neither provisional nor real. Since even 'one suchness' does not exist, how much less could there be four?
Yet, because they are provisional, three are taught; and because they are real, one suchness is taught."

When both the provisional and the ultimate are fully elucidated, there are four such [principles]. Regarding the third point, the clarification of the meaning of "thusness" through the contemplation of the mind, this refers to the three contemplations clarifying the four suchnesses.
As previously cited from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*: "If one wishes to know the mind of the Tathāgata, one should contemplate the mind of sentient beings;
if one sees the mind of the Tathāgata, one sees the mind of sentient beings. It is like breaking [a single vessel into many].
A single mote of dust contains the sūtras of the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system.
The mind produced by the causes and conditions of a single moment of ignorance in sentient beings is endowed with these four kinds of principles.

If one contemplates that the mind arises through causes and conditions and undergoes birth and extinction, entering from the conventional into emptiness, this is the principle of "birth and extinction. If one contemplates the causes and conditions of the mind...

The essence of emptiness is provisionally entering emptiness; this is the true truth of emptiness (*śūnyatā-satya*). Thus, if one contemplates the causes and conditions of the mind and realizes that emptiness is not [inherently] empty, one enters the provisional without obstruction;
this is the conventional designation (*prajñapti*). Thus, if one contemplates the causes and conditions of the mind, it is the single ultimate truth (*eka-bhūta-artha-satya*);
Buddha-nature is precisely the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*). This is what is meant by the fourfold suchness (*tathatā*) as fully contained within the contemplation of the mind.
Regarding this principle, a question is asked: "If contemplating the mind is itself the possession of these four aspects, then one should be a Buddha or a Bodhisattva.

The answer is: "One must employ the distinction of the 'six stages of realization' (*ṣaḍ-bhūmi*) to prevent the error of overstepping one's station, giving rise to *adhimāna* (arrogance), or falling back into the ranks of the poor by failing to recognize one's own worth—like counting someone else's jewels while being denied one's own share."

"I have heard" (evam mayā śrutam). Because this refers to the Dharma personally heard by the disciples such as Ānanda, it is called "I have heard. Now, the interpretation is also presented according to three intentions:
first, a general explanation; second, a specific explanation according to the teachings; and third, an explanation according to the contemplation of the mind. First, the general [explanation].
The commentator Ānanda personally received the Buddha’s oral instructions; therefore, he says, "I have heard.

The reason for this is that if one transmits what was heard from another, there is often much that is false or erroneous; whereas if one speaks according to one's own mind, how could it necessarily accord with the principles of reality?

Now, since he has personally heard the Buddha’s teaching, it is trustworthy. Thus, the multitude of sentient beings receive it with acceptance, leaving no room for doubt. — *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Dazhidu lun)

The treatise states: "It is said that 'I' exists because it conforms to worldly convention; it is said that 'I' hears because it conforms to worldly convention. Regarding those who say "I" exists in accordance with worldly convention:

since those who have attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) and those on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) would otherwise fail to sustain the Buddha-dharma and benefit sentient beings, they conform to worldly convention by speaking of an "I.

This is appropriate for the external world in order to remain in harmony with the mundane without dispute, while internally not contradicting the reality of the Dharma; thus, they are able to transmit the scriptures and bring about benefit.
This matter is like using gold coins to buy copper coins and selling them; such is the nature of buying and selling, and people do not find it strange.

Because of this conjunction, it is called "hearing": when the faculty of the ear is unimpaired, the sound is within the range of audibility, and the intention to hear arises, then the auditory consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*) is produced through the conjunction of the object, the sense-faculty, and the mental state.
Subsequently, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is able to differentiate the various things heard. Thus, it is due to this conjunction that hearing occurs.

"Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*): Ānanda and others were internally possessed of keen faculties of hearing, while externally they received without omission the Buddha’s eightfold voice and clear eloquence; therefore, it is called "Thus have I heard. Question:

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that Ānanda was born on the night the Buddha attained the Way, and that he did not appear until twenty years had passed after the Buddha’s enlightenment. How is this so?
From that time on, when the Buddha preached the sūtras, Ānanda did not hear them;
because the Tathāgata was about to enter nirvana, Ānanda was obscured by Māra and likewise could not hear [the final teachings]. How then can it all be titled "Thus have I heard"?
The answer is given in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: "When Ānanda was about to compile the Dharma-piṭaka, he joined his palms toward the Buddha at the time of the Nirvāṇa..."
While seated in the *paryaṅka* posture, he spoke in verse: "When the Buddha first preached the Dharma, at that time I did not see [him].
Thus it was heard by successive transmission even as far as Vārāṇasī. Regarding this "heard by successive transmission," there are two interpretations. First, the *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states:
"Ānanda practiced the meditation of non-forgetfulness (*asaṃpramoṣa-dhyāna*) and attained the Buddha’s *bodhi-samādhi*. By the power of this samādhi, he himself..."
It is called "I heard" because one was able to seek out the Buddha’s words as they were transmitted in succession until they reached Vārāṇasī, and thus heard and retained them all.
A second interpretation states that it is called "I heard" because the Buddha sequentially taught the sūtras that Ānanda had not previously heard, continuing until they reached Vārāṇasī.
How is this known? It is because Ānanda’s original vow was to serve as the Buddha’s attendant.

Regarding the mastery of hearing and retaining the Buddha’s sutras, as clarified in the *Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish*, Ānanda was originally a householder in a previous life who, by virtue of offering food, made a vow to become a disciple capable of hearing and retaining the teachings.

Furthermore, the *Sutra on Repaying Kindness* explains that Ānanda requested four vows from the Buddha; three of these vows are as described in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, while the fourth vow concerns the sutras spoken by the Buddha.
To those who have not yet heard it, I request that you explain it further. The Buddha granted their wish, and for those who had not heard it previously, he explained it again.
That which was transmitted by Ānanda consists of eighty-four million fascicles, all of which begin with the words "Thus have I heard.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* clarifies that when the Dharma-piṭaka was compiled, Upāli and others each ascended a high seat and all proclaimed, "Thus [have I heard]."
I have heard that it is not necessarily the case that all [instances of] "Thus have I heard" (evam mayā śrutam) were spoken by Ānanda. Question:

Does Ānanda merely say "Thus have I heard" when compiling the Sūtras of the Hīnayāna, or does he also say "Thus have I heard" when compiling the Mahāyāna sūtras? Answer: There are differing interpretations.
Some say that Ānanda only says "Thus have I heard" when compiling the Hīnayāna; as for the Mahāyāna sūtras, they were compiled by Mañjuśrī.
It was compiled by Maitreya and other great bodhisattvas, and thus it is called "Thus have I heard.
Furthermore, another interpretation states that Ānanda did not merely compile the Hīnayāna, but also compiled the Mahāyāna sūtras spoken in common with the two vehicles;
for this reason, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* was entrusted to Ānanda, and this sūtra is likewise so. As for those [sūtras] spoken not in common with the two vehicles, they are the Great [Vehicle].
The Bodhisattvas also compiled [the teachings], and it is further said that Ānanda likewise compiled the Mahāyāna sūtras not shared with the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha).
As the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* states, there are three Ānandas: first, Ānanda the Worthy; second, Ānanda the Retainer;
and third, Ānanda the Ocean. Now, if one refers to Ānanda the Worthy, he was the one who heard and retained the teachings of the Tripiṭaka; [Ānanda] the Retainer was...
Ānanda, the Ocean-like One, is one who hears and upholds the Mahāyāna teachings spoken in common with the two vehicles;
he is one who hears and upholds the Mahāyāna sūtras spoken not in common with the two vehicles. Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says:

"As soon as Ānanda heard the Buddha bestow his prediction, he immediately recollected the dharma-treasuries of immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of past Buddhas, just as he has now heard them, and he also recognized their origins."
How could my vow not be sufficient to fully uphold the teaching of even a single Buddha? Second, the specific explanation of "I heard" (*evaṃ mayā śrutam*) consists of two points:
first, clarifying "I" (*aham*) according to the four teachings; second, clarifying "heard" (*śrutam*) according to the four teachings.

Regarding the first—clarifying "I" according to the four teachings—there are likewise four different types. First, clarifying "I" according to the *Tripiṭaka* (Śrāvaka) Teaching: based on the [Sāṃmitīya]...

In the *Pañcavastuka*, it is taught that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) truly lack a self (*ātman*), existing as nothing more than a name. According to the explanation of the Dharmaguptaka school, there is a "provisional self" (*prajñapti-ātman*).
What the Vātsīputrīya school clarifies is that the self resides within the fifth "inexpressible basket" (*avaktavya-piṭaka*).

Although such explanations differ regarding the self, they all serve to refute the externalist's conception of a substantial spirit-self (*puruṣa-ātman*) or primordial nature (*prakṛti*); this is the meaning of my teaching on the "provisionally named self."

Second, regarding the explanation of the self (*ātman*) according to the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-śāsana*): as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states, "The nature of form is like the nature of the self;
the nature of the self is like the nature of form. Thus, the self exists only as a mere word, and form also exists only as a mere word; both the self and form are like illusions and transformations.

Third, regarding the explanation of the self according to the Distinct Teaching (*pratyeka-bhāṣita-śāsana*): it defines the self solely by the meaning of sovereignty (*vaśitā*). One is skilled in knowing this.
To see [reality] without obstruction—this "absence of obstruction" is precisely the meaning of the self (ātman).

Furthermore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* clarifies that the consciousness which distinguishes between self and other is also called the "consciousness resembling a self"; this is the explanation of the meaning of the self according to the Separate Teaching (Pratyekabuddha-yāna).
Regarding the explanation of the self in the Perfect Teaching (Ekayāna), the Middle Way Buddha-nature is itself the meaning of the self. As the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states:
The Buddha sometimes speaks of a self and sometimes speaks of non-self; within the Buddha’s True Dharma, there is neither self nor non-self.
This sutra states that "self" and "non-self" are non-dual, which is the true meaning of non-self.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra states that within the dharma of non-self, the meaning of the true self is taught. It further says: "Self and non-self..."

The nature is non-dual; this non-dual nature is precisely the true nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). This true nature is the true self (*ātman*) within the twenty-five realms of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*).

While the first three teachings clarify the "self" as a provisional self, that which is called the "true self" within the teaching of non-self refers to the true, ultimate self clarified by the Perfect Teaching (*vimalakīrti-samantabhadra-yāna*). Because the self is distinguished according to each teaching, it is said: "I heard."

Question: If that is so, why does the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* state, "The self is spoken of in accordance with worldly convention"? Answer: The explanations of the self in the three teachings are all in accordance with [sentient beings'] dispositions;
is this not precisely speaking of the self in accordance with worldly convention? The explanation of the self in the Perfect Teaching is none other than Buddha-nature.
This self of Buddha-nature is the primary truth (*paramārtha*) and is not in accordance with worldly convention. The explanations of the three teachings...

When I hear [the teaching], this is discussed in terms of the faculty of hearing (*śrotra-indriya*). The Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) clarifies that "I" is precisely "hearing"; by pointing to the nature of form (*rūpa-dharmatā*), it explains the True Self (*bhūtātman*).

Apart from the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), there is no separate ear capable of hearing. One may understand how the various scriptures possess more or fewer instances of the "I" by applying the four teachings (*catur-yāna*).

Second, regarding the meaning of "hearing" as clarified through the four teachings, it is as follows: *Note: The original text appears to be a commentary on the Tiantai doctrine of the "True Self" (Zhengwo), specifically linking the subject of "I" to the auditory faculty and the ultimate nature of reality.*
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* clarifies that there are four types of the meaning of "hearing": first, hearing hearing; second, not-hearing hearing; third, hearing not-hearing;
and fourth, not-hearing not-hearing. Based on these four meanings of hearing, it is likely that the four teachings differ in their explanation of the meaning of hearing.
The Tripitaka Teaching corresponds to the meaning of "hearing hearing," as it uses the small birth to give rise to the great birth.
Therefore, it is called "the arising of arising. Now it may also be said that "a small hearing accomplishes hearing," and thus it is called "hearing-hearing. Question:
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* clarifies that "the arising of arising" refers to the continuous succession of the twelve links of dependent origination;
why, then, can you now use the category of "small arising" to explain the meaning of "hearing-hearing"? Answer: [As follows:]...
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* commentary explains that "birth" possesses two meanings; however, we do not adopt [the first] here.
Regarding the clarification of "the birth of birth" (*jāti-jāti*) in terms of practice, we only take up the meaning of "the birth of birth" as it clarifies the principle of arising and ceasing.

If one were to clarify "the birth of birth" by means of the continuous succession of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), this would be inconvenient for the sages who hear the meaning of the sutra. Why is this so? Because of the Tripiṭaka...

Having taught the various practitioners the meaning of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) as the process of successive births, [the teaching] is already subverted;

there remains only the retributive body (*vipākakāya*), wherein the eight phases [of a Buddha’s life] arise from the conjunction of sense organs and their objects, and thus it is called "hearing. Second, the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*) is precisely "hearing what is not heard":

hearing that is like a dream or an illusion is the pointing to emptiness while speaking of hearing; this is termed "hearing what is not heard. Third, the Distinct Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*) is precisely...
Regarding the meaning of "hearing what has not been heard," one attains mastery over the dharmas that have been heard; this is why it is called "hearing what has not been heard. Why is this so?

At the time of death according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), that which was heard dies and yet is born again as hearing. This refers to the *śrutadharā-dhāraṇī* (dhāraṇī of retaining what is heard), by which one is able to retain whatever is heard with mastery.
Furthermore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "That which possesses objects (*saviṣaya*) is the consciousness that should be experienced (*vijñeya*). This is precisely [the point].

The Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao) of the Mahāyāna clarifies the meaning of "hearing. The Perfect Teaching (Yuan-jiao), however, is precisely the meaning of "neither hearing nor not hearing," for in the Buddha-nature of the Great Parinirvāṇa, the characteristics of hearing are exhausted.
Question: If there are no characteristics of hearing, how can one speak of "hearing"? Answer:
If the characteristics of hearing were entirely exhausted such that nothing at all could be heard, then when the Buddha dwells in Great Nirvāṇa, he would likewise never hear anything.
All sounds throughout the ten directions of the Dharma-realm are as clarified in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* regarding the merit of the faculty of hearing:

at the initial stage of "semblance-hearing," one hears the hundred-fold auspicious marks of countless Buddhas throughout the ten directions preaching the Dharma for sentient beings, and is able to hear and uphold it all;
how much more so when attaining the stage of "Dharma-Cloud" and partially realizing the true mark of hearing, whereby one hears everything throughout the ten directions.

The Buddha-dharma is able to sustain both like clouds; through the wondrous realization of hearing marks (*śrutalakṣaṇa*), one ultimately exhausts all sounds within the entire Dharma-realm and hears them all at once. Thus, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* says:
"If one knows that the Tathāgata never preaches the Dharma, this is called being fully endowed with much learning (*bahuśruta*). This sutra also says: "As for those who listen to the Dharma..."

There is neither hearing nor attainment; now, by means of the four teachings, the meaning of "hearing" is clarified. According to various sutras, the extent of what is heard can be categorized as more or less, as previously understood.
Question: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* clarifies that in the Buddha-dharma there is no self, but only names, which accord with worldly convention and are free from contention.
Why, then, do you now differentiate the four teachings to clarify that the conceptions of self differ? If this were so, it would mean that a self actually exists.
He replied: "If there were definitely a self, how could the four teachings distinguish it differently? If there were definitely no self, how could the sutras contain these differing explanations?

If one does not permit such distinctions, not only will the Buddha’s skillful means and teaching gates be destroyed, but each of the doctrines of those who lack faith will also be undermined. As for what is called the five aggregates..."
In truth, there is no self, but only names; it is by means of these names that one may understand this.
Since the Dharmaguptaka school already posits a provisional self (*prajñapti-ātman*), how could they not employ the names of individuals? I have heard that they do not accept a provisional self.

Furthermore, since the Vātsīputrīya school speaks of a fifth "inexpressible treasury" (*avaktavya-puṇḍarīka*) which possesses a self, how can you claim they do not accept this self? I have heard this and thus I take it as such.

Regarding the name "I heard": this is a question concerning the universal application of the teachings. Since it is clear that all things are illusory transformations (*māyā-nirmita*), why should I not employ the "illusory self" (*māyā-ātman*)?
When I hear [the teaching], I employ the names of several people; such mutual expectations and disputes lead to mutual loss.

Third, regarding the interpretation of "I heard" through the contemplation of the mind: the three contemplations (*trividha-bhāvanā*) distinguish the four teachings, and "I heard" is categorized accordingly.
Thus it may be known through careful investigation.
At that time, this was precisely when the fourfold assembly was moved by the teaching and attained the Way; this also serves as an auxiliary factor for accomplishing such [attainment].

Because it is for the sake of generating faith, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The times and directions are all established for the purpose of generating faith. Now, in explaining "one time" (*ekasamaya*), there are three intentions:

first, a general explanation; second, a specific explanation according to the teachings (*śāsana*); and third, an explanation according to the contemplation of the mind (*citta*). First, regarding the general explanation:

the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says that numbers, time, and so forth are truly non-existent, as they are not subsumed within the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), or elements (*dhātu*). They exist merely in accordance with...

In worldly convention, there is no fault in speaking of "one time. The heading of this chapter states that the moment the fourfold assembly was moved by the teaching and attained the Way is called "one time";
this refers to a long duration as being a short duration, hence it is termed "one time.

If discussed comprehensively, the entire period from the beginning to the end of the teaching gate through which the fourfold assembly is moved—whether long or short—is all called "one time," which is to say, it binds together many times into one.
A "short period" (*śvāsakṣaṇa*) refers to a single moment, as stated in the *Śīlaskandha-vinaya*: "The spring equinox lasts for four months, which constitutes one period.

Although the spring equinox actually comprises many moments, they are collectively bound together and designated as a single period. Regarding the "short period" that clarifies the attainment of the Way:

when teaching is delivered according to the capacity of the audience, those who hear the teaching enter [the path] immediately; this is like the single *kṣaṇa* of the patience regarding suffering (*duḥkhadharma-jñānakṣānti*). This is explained in terms of a short period.

For the time being, we shall now clarify "one time" (*ekakāla*) by summarizing both its long and short durations. This refers to the entirety of a single period of teaching, meaning that the preaching of the Dharma throughout a complete cycle constitutes a single temporal event.
Analyzing this further, there are briefly five points: first, clarifying "one time" in terms of the spiritual capacities of sentient beings;

second, clarifying "one time" in terms of the Buddha’s teaching; third, clarifying it in terms of the synthesis of capacity and teaching; [fourth, in terms of the temporal duration of the teaching]; and fifth, in terms of the ultimate realization of the goal.
First, regarding the "one time" (*ekakāla*) in terms of attaining the Way: it clarifies that the one time refers to the five [aspects] concerning Ānanda’s hearing of the sūtra.
Second, regarding the "one time" in terms of the manifestation of a single capacity: as for "one time," when the capacity for mundane goodness manifests, this constitutes a long duration;

when the capacity for supramundane goodness manifests, this constitutes a short duration. In total, both these long and short durations are "one time. Third, regarding the "one time" in terms of the Buddha’s preaching of the teaching.
To clarify "one time" (ekakāla): when the provisional teachings employ the three *siddhāntas* to initiate instruction, this constitutes "many times";
when true wisdom employs the *paramārtha-siddhānta* to initiate instruction, this constitutes "few times. In sum, both these many and few are designated as "one time.
Third, regarding the harmony between the teaching and the capacity (*yogyatā*) to clarify "one time": the provisional teaching accords with the worldly roots of goodness.
That is to say, when the teaching for a long period of time is combined with supramundane roots of goodness, it is because it is combined with the teaching for a short period of time;
thus, as it does not abide in two periods, it is called "one period. Fourth, explaining "one period" in terms of the fourfold assembly attaining the Way:
if one attains a mundane way, this constitutes many periods; if one attains a supramundane way, then...
Whether it be a short duration or this entire span of time, all are designated as "one time. Fifth, regarding the designation of "one time" based on Ānanda’s hearing of the sutra:
when the Buddha preached the sutra for a long or short duration, it was precisely at the time Ānanda heard the sutra;
because his hearing was not at a different time, it is called "one time. Furthermore, through the Buddha-awakening samādhi attained by Ānanda, he [perceived] the sutras he had not previously heard.
Because one attains the power of samādhi to hear and enter it, hearing within samādhi is called "at one time" (*ekasamaya*).
Furthermore, it is explained that the Buddha’s re-explanation for Ānanda constitutes the time when Ānanda hears the sutra; thus, it is called "at one time.
Second, explaining "at one time" in terms of the teachings (*yōkyō*) means distinguishing the four kinds of "one meaning" according to the Four Teachings. First, regarding the Three [Teachings]...
The *Treatise on the Causes and Conditions of Arising and Ceasing* clarifies that "one time" (*ekakāla*) also possesses the five meanings of "one time.

It either employs the time according to worldly convention or the time as a provisional designation based on dharmas; it holds that there is no separate time apart from dharmas, and thus defines it as "one time.
Second, regarding the Shared Teaching (*pṛthagjana-śāsana*), "one time" also possesses the five meanings of "one time," as follows: [text continues]
The "one time" (*ekakāla*) of dreams also possesses the five meanings of "one time" as clarified in the Three Separate Teachings (*pṛthagupadeśa*).
It overcomes the inversion regarding "one time," enabling one to discern and enumerate all dharmas and to perceive the events of the three periods of time without obstruction.

The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* clarifies that the "consciousness of number" (*saṃkhyājñāna*) subsumes the incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*), while the "consciousness of time" (*adhvajñāna*) subsumes the three periods of time.
If one considers this "single moment," it is also the single moment of the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavahāra*), which likewise possesses the fivefold meaning of "single moment.
However, the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya*) specifically explains "single moment" by means of the inconceivable *dharmatā*, wherein all things enter into a single moment.
As this sutra clarifies, for a Bodhisattva dwelling in the inconceivable liberation, seven days constitute one eon (*kalpa*), and one eon constitutes [a single moment].
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* explains that sixty minor kalpas are like the duration of a meal; the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* explains ten "all-encompassing" [kalpas] and so forth.
By means of these, it clarifies that "one time" (*ekakāla*) is precisely the meaning of "one time" in the Perfect Teaching (*yāna*).
If one uses the four teachings to clarify "one time," one should understand that the presence or absence of "one time" across various sūtras is analogous in this way. This is the third [point].

Regarding the meaning of "contemplating the mind as a single moment": it refers to the principle that the mind arises and ceases through causes and conditions. When the mind is in a state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one is able to know the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of worldly phenomena;

thus, within a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*), the eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*) is opened, and one is able to perceive the principle of arising and ceasing—this is why it is called "a single moment.
If, however, it is not a concentrated mind, but rather a brief, sudden flash of insight where one perceives the principle, this is what was previously considered.
Later, when one realizes that conceptualizations and inverted thoughts exist, although a mind of understanding arises, it cannot see the principle because it is not simultaneous.
Furthermore, regarding the contemplation of the mind, "simultaneity" is clarified: when entering the contemplation of the provisional from the true, the eye of wisdom opens;
when entering the contemplation of the provisional from the empty, the dharma-eye opens; and when practicing the correct contemplation of the Middle Way, the Buddha-eye opens—all at once.
When this concentrated mind suddenly awakens for even a brief moment, one immediately perceives the principle of the true, singular, ultimate reality;
this is called "simultaneous" (yīshí). Thus it is said:
"The Buddha is present."
The Buddha is indeed able to speak thus; as the Master of Transformation, he also serves to assist in establishing the credibility of what is heard.
Why is this so? Because the ninety-six kinds of teachings spoken by others are based on false views and inversion, and are therefore insufficient grounds for taking refuge in them.
As for that which is spoken by the sages of the Three Vehicles, since they still occupy positions that are not ultimate, [their words require further validation].

Furthermore, what has been taught is not yet ultimate; now it is clarified that the Great Enlightenment is teacherless, luminous, and realized instantaneously, such that what is spoken is truly authentic.
From this point on, those who hear the sutra will have their minds delighted and satisfied. This section also contains three points: first, a general clarification of the Buddha’s dwelling;

second, a classification of the different dwellings of the Buddha according to the teachings; and third, an explanation of the dwelling through the contemplation of the mind. First, the general [clarification].
Regarding the clarification of the meaning of "Buddha": the ancient term *buddha* means "the Awakened. One who awakens oneself and awakens others is called a Buddha.
As the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* clarifies the term *buddha*, it says "the Knower. What dharma does he know?
With wisdom, he knows the number of future and present sentient beings and non-sentient things, as well as all dharmas—whether they are permanent or impermanent.

Because he attained clear and perfect awakening beneath the Bodhi tree, he is called "Buddha. He is endowed with the ten titles; he is also called the "Omniscient One" (Sarvajña) and the "Kalaviṅka Buddha. His virtues are immeasurable, and his supreme names are likewise immeasurable. I shall not explain them all here now. As for the term "dwelling" (sthita), it is merely another name for "abiding. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Four... [The text continues as follows: The Buddha is called "Tathāgata" because he has come from suchness (*tathatā*) and gone to suchness. He is called "Arhat" because he has destroyed all afflictions and enemies. He is called "Samyaksaṃbuddha" because he has perfectly awakened to all phenomena. He is called "Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna" because he is perfected in knowledge and conduct. He is called "Sugata" because he has gone well and departed well. He is called "Lokavid" because he knows the world. He is called "Anuttara" because there is no one superior to him.

He is called "Puruṣadamyasārathi" because he is the charioteer who tames those to be trained among men. He is called "Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām" because he is the teacher of gods and humans. He is called "Bhagavat" because he possesses the six qualities of sovereignty. These are the ten titles. Furthermore, because he possesses the wisdom that knows all things without exception, he is called the "Omniscient One. Because his voice is like the song of the kalaviṅka bird, he is called the "Kalaviṅka Buddha. His merits are boundless, and thus his supreme names are also boundless. I do not explain them in detail here. What is meant by "dwelling" is simply a synonym for "abiding. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "Four... [End of excerpt].
The various bodily postures of sitting, lying, walking, and standing are called "abiding. There are four kinds of abiding: first, the celestial abiding;
second, the Brahma abiding; third, the noble abiding; and fourth, the Buddha abiding. The celestial abiding consists of three things:
generosity, ethical discipline, and a virtuous mind; therefore, it is called the celestial abiding. The Brahma abiding consists of dwelling in the four dhyānas and the four immeasurable minds.

The four formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) are the noble dwellings (*āryavihāra*), which consist of abiding in the principles of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), as well as the Four Noble Truths and the twelvefold chain of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
The Buddha-dwellings (*buddhavihāra*) are the immeasurable samādhis such as the Śūraṅgama and all the Buddha-qualities such as the ten powers (*daśabala*).
Just as the Dharma attained by the Buddha, he dwells therein out of compassion for sentient beings.
Regarding the second distinct explanation of the meaning of the Buddha’s dwelling (*vihāra*) by way of the teachings— namely, the differences clarified through the four *yānas*—
the detailed analysis of the meaning of the Buddha according to these four *yānas* is already briefly contained in the *Xuanshu*.
However, for the sake of transforming sentient beings of four types of faculties, there are likewise four modes of manifesting signs, just as at the time of his initial enlightenment.
The arising of the Way, the turning of the wheel of Dharma, and the entry into parinirvāṇa all manifest through the four teachings with differing bodily forms and characteristics.
Regarding the differing bodily forms manifested at the initial attainment of enlightenment, as clarified in the *Suvikrāntavikramī-paripṛcchā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*,

when the Tathāgata first sat beneath the Bodhi tree and attained perfect awakening, he sometimes manifested sitting upon grass, sometimes manifested sitting upon celestial robes, and sometimes manifested occupying a precious throne.

Alternatively, [the Buddha] now appears in the midst of empty space; this is the initial Perfect Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi) manifesting various forms in response to conditions and adapting to beings.

This represents the fact that the characteristics of the merits of the manifest Buddhas, as clarified by the four teachings, are not the same. Next, to clarify the differences in the physical manifestations when turning the wheel of Dharma:
if one expounds the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra’s perfect and sudden teaching, then both great and small marks are manifested.

When turning the Dharma wheel of the Four Noble Truths regarding the arising and ceasing of the body as being like that of a deer in the Deer Park, he manifests in the form of an old bhikṣu, divested of his jeweled ornaments.
When preaching the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras, he manifests either as the noble and distinguished form within the gate or as an image covered in dust and dirt outside the gate.
When preaching the Mahāprajñāpāramitā, he likewise manifests as the noble and distinguished form within the gate.
The physical body and the various marks of the Buddha’s bodies appear because of the doubts of sentient beings; thus, he manifests an eternal body and emits an eternal light.
If he preaches the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, he manifests only marks of supreme majesty; if he preaches the *Nirvāṇa*, he fully manifests the four types of bodily forms.

These matters are identical to those in the Vaipulya [sūtras] regarding the manifestation of bodily forms. This briefly clarifies the differences in the manifestations of bodily forms as they are transformed and displayed.
These various bodies manifested in response to conditions—how could they be limited to merely manifesting four types of physical forms?
For now, speaking generally according to the differences between the Four Teachings, I have briefly described these four modes of manifestation.

Next, to clarify the different ways the four types of bodies manifest upon entering *nirvāṇa*, the *Xiǎngfǎ juéyì jīng* (Sūtra on Resolving Doubts Concerning the Semblance Dharma) states: "When the Tathāgata was about to enter..."
At the time of the *nirvāṇa*, the great assembly saw the Buddha in some cases as having the appearance of a śramaṇa;

in others, they saw him with the majestic marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) of sublime dignity; in others, they saw him seated upon a precious lotus flower preaching the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground;
and in yet others, they beheld his body manifesting like empty space, without boundaries or surface. Is this not a sign that the work of expounding the four teachings has already been completed?

He manifested this sign as he was about to enter *nirvāṇa*. Since this sutra is subsumed under the Vaipulya teachings and was preached while residing in the city of Vaiśālī, the manifestations of the Mahāyāna Vaipulya that he could display must likewise appear in accordance with the conditions of sentient beings' karmic responses.
Thus, in this sutra, the son of an elder, Ratnākara, spoke in verse to offer praise, saying: "Each person beholds the World-Honored One standing before them."

Thus, regarding the supernatural powers and the unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), those who perceive them each see different manifestations of the Buddha’s body and marks according to the capacities of the four teachings.
Question: Do the roots of goodness (*kuśala-mūla*) of the four teachings, as perceived according to conditions, necessarily accord with the distinctions previously set forth? Answer:

Generally speaking, the principle lies in the responsive perception of capacities according to conditions. However, if one considers it from the perspective of their obstructions, it can be said that what is seen is inferior.
