If one speaks of the mind being constantly abiding while arising from ignorance and craving through various forms of illumination and liberation, yet considers this to be the mind’s constant abiding—wherein the illumination of tranquility and the maturation of contemplative liberation appear as objects of light without the marks of entering or exiting—this is not ultimate abiding.

If, however, one does not engage in such conceptualization, then within the liberation of tranquil illumination, the Dharma-body manifests; it is tranquil yet eternally illuminating. This is [ultimate abiding].

This refers to the ultimate mind that dwells in constant tranquility; because these bodhisattvas have all attained the inconceivable, quiescent, and illuminating ultimate dwelling, it is said that their minds dwell constantly in unimpeded liberation.
Next, regarding the contemplation of the mind, there is a distinction based on the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*):

if distinguished by their specific characteristics, all three contemplations constitute the path of non-obstruction (*ānantaryamārga*) for severing [afflictions] and the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) for realization.
Ultimately abiding in the single mind and the three contemplations constitutes the constant abiding of the mind in unimpeded liberation.
*Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra-bhāṣya*, Fascicle Three;
*Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra-bhāṣya*, Fascicle Four (from "Mindfulness and Concentration" through "Together with Thirty-two Thousand People").
"Mindfulness, concentration, dhāraṇī, and eloquence are uninterrupted.
Second, the praise of the virtue of wisdom has three distinct parts: first, a general praise of the virtue of wisdom; second, a specific praise of the virtue of wisdom;

and third, a praise of the stages that explains its fulfillment. Regarding the first, the general praise of the virtue of wisdom, this refers precisely to mindfulness, concentration, and dhāraṇī. If...
While other sutras generally praise the virtues of samādhi and dhāraṇī, this [text] praises the mindfulness-concentration (smṛti-samādhi) and the total-holding (dhāraṇī);
thus, it praises the very virtues of the samādhi-dhāraṇī. By means of these two, the chapter of praise is established.

"Mindfulness" refers to the Buddha-mindfulness samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*) and various other samādhis; when a bodhisattva attains this Buddha-mindfulness samādhi, the Buddhas of the ten directions...
It is constantly present before one and is also called the King Samādhi. Upon entering this samādhi, all samādhis enter into it.

Why is this? Because whether it be the fundamental dhyānas, the liberations (vimokṣa), the bases of mastery (abhibhvāyatana), the nine successive attainments (anupūrvavihārasamāpatti), the lion’s stretch (siṃhavijṛmbhita), or the leap-over (vyutkrāntaka), these are all conventional-samādhis that contemplate the Four Noble Truths, the twelve links of dependent origination, and emptiness.

The signless (*animitta*) and the wishless (*apraṇihita*), as well as the nine kinds of great dhyānas such as the samādhi of the true nature (*svabhāva*), and the hundred and eight samādhis including the *pratyutpanna* (one-practice), the *śūraṅgama*, and others, are all samādhis of the ultimate truth of the Middle Way.
The *Ratnarājasūtra* states: "If one attains the samādhi of the three truths, one immediately enters the King Samādhi of the Bodhisattva."

Because when one enters this samādhi, all samādhis enter within it and the Buddhas of the ten directions all appear before one, we know that the "Samādhi of Admiration and Recollection" is an expression for the virtues of all samādhis. To distinguish them according to the four teachings:
if one analyzes the conventional to enter the ultimate, this is the Samādhi of the Two Truths as clarified in the Tripiṭaka Teaching; it is named solely in reference to the two truths.
If the essence of the King Samādhi enters the ultimate from the conventional, it is the Two Truths Samādhi of the Shared Teaching;
it is called the King Samādhi by way of the Two Truths. If one enters the Middle Way from the fundamental conventional truth, it is the Three Truths Samādhi of the Distinct Teaching;
it is called the King Samādhi by way of the Three Truths. If one enters the Three Truths with a single mind in a perfect manner, it is the Perfect [Teaching].

The teaching on the Samādhi of the Three Truths and the Samādhi of the Vidyārāja: the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* presents a divergent interpretation, and the point where it differs from the *Samādhirāja-samādhi* lies herein.
If one approaches this from the perspective of contemplating the mind, it constitutes the three contemplations;

by contemplating the three truths and cultivating the Samādhi of the Three Truths, the King-like Samādhi is spontaneously accomplished—this may be understood as a matter of course. As for "total retention" (*dhāraṇī*), it is precisely...
Praising the virtue of *dhāraṇī*: this term means "able to hold" and "able to restrain.

It is called "holding" because it maintains all wholesome dharmas so they are not lost, and it is called "restraining" because it prevents all unwholesome dharmas from arising. It is also called "total retention" (*saṃdhāraṇa*) because it ensures that all wholesome dharmas are not lost.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* clarifies three *dhāraṇīs*: the first is the *āvartanī-dhāraṇī*.
Second is the *śata-sahasra-koṭi-parivarta-dhāraṇī*, and third is the *dharma-nirghoṣa-upāya-dhāraṇī*. Regarding the *parivarta-dhāraṇī*, "parivarta" means "to revolve.
Through the contemplation that enters emptiness from the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), one is able to revolve the contemplation;

by entering emptiness from the conventional, one turns away from and destroys all views and attachments within and beyond the realms, thereby attaining entry into the ultimate truth of emptiness (*paramārtha-satya*). If one were merely to destroy [them]...
The "dhāraṇī within the realm" refers to the dhāraṇī of the Shared Teaching (Sādhāraṇa-yāna), which, through single-mindedness, completely breaks through both the realms within and without.
The "hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of revolving dhāraṇīs" refers to the dhāraṇī of the Perfect Teaching (Vipula-yāna);

that is, entering from emptiness into the provisional (the false), revolving and discerning to enter the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) within the realm and the conventional truth without the realm, revolving to break through the sands of dust [of delusions].

The dharani of the ignorance within and beyond the realms reveals the Buddha-dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. If one were to separately destroy the ignorance beyond the realms, it would be the dharani of the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddha*);
however, now, with a single mind, to completely destroy the ignorance both within and beyond the realms is precisely the dharani of the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya*).
As for the "Dharani of Skillful Means of the Dharma-Sound," this refers to the two contemplations serving as skillful means.

If one can explain how to enter the Middle Way of the Supreme Truth (paramārtha-satya), entering the Middle Way by gradually severing ignorance, this is the dhāraṇī of the Separate Teaching (pratyekabuddha-yāna).
If, without severing ignorance, one enters the Middle Way in a single mind through perfect realization, this is the dhāraṇī of the Perfect Teaching (ekayāna).
What is called the "Dhāraṇī of Skillful Means of Dharma-Sound" refers to attaining this dhāraṇī.
He understands all speech and sounds, and is also able to preach the Dharma with a single voice so that sentient beings may each attain understanding according to their own kind.
When a Bodhisattva attains these three *dhāraṇīs*, they enter the *anāvaraṇa-dhāraṇī* (unimpeded *dhāraṇī*) and become fully endowed with all *dhāraṇīs*.
Question: This sutra praises the *dhāraṇīs* of those in their final birth (*caramabhavika*). Why then is this explained in terms of the beginner’s stage?
Answer: The initial aspiration and the ultimate state are fundamentally not distinct. Subsequently, the mind enters the three truths without obstruction;
its breadth is vast and its subtlety extreme, while its depth reaches the very source. This is precisely the unobstructed *dhāraṇī* of a Bodhisattva in his final birth (*caramabhavika*).
Question: Do Bodhisattvas of the Tripitaka stage possess *dhāraṇīs*? Answer: For example, King Śibi attained the *dhāraṇī* for protection through taking refuge.
Nuns, you should know that there are also various minor *dhāraṇīs*. If even a Wheel-Turning King can attain them, how much more so a Bodhisattva?
Question: Do the Śrāvakas attain minor *dhāraṇīs*? Answer: For those of the Two Vehicles who enter *nirvāṇa*, *dhāraṇīs* are not required.

Regarding the cultivation of *dhāraṇīs* through the contemplation of the mind, they are easily understood by analogy with the Three Contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*); there is no need for further detailed analysis.
" Eloquence" (pratibhāna) refers to the four types of analytical eloquence (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* clarifies seven types of eloquence;

the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra* clarifies twenty types; and the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* clarifies forty types. This praise of the power and function of samādhi and dhāraṇī must be explained through the four teachings (*catur-yāna*) to clarify the meaning of eloquence.
First, regarding the Tripiṭaka: if one distinguishes the names of the Four Truths of arising and ceasing, [the following applies].

If one is unhindered regarding the Dharma, this is the unimpeded analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*). If one is unhindered in discerning the meaning of the Four Truths of arising and ceasing, this is the unimpeded analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*).

If one thoroughly understands that the languages of the six realms of existence differ and can likewise speak in those same tongues to explain the words of the Four Truths of arising and ceasing without impediment, this is the unimpeded analytical knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*). If one... [weighs...]

The roots depend upon the arising of phenomena, which cannot be described; yet, by employing the four *siddhāntas* to accord with the capacities of beings, one preaches without end—this is the unimpeded eloquence of joyful speech (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).
Eloquence is the ability to discern and clarify; it is like using honey to assist medicine, making it easy for those who take it.

Using literary expression to assist the Way is how one transforms and guides through practice. Regarding the *Tongjiao* (Common Teaching), it is based on non-arising (*anutpāda*); regarding the *Biejiao* (Distinct Teaching)...

In terms of the immeasurable Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya*) and the classification of the Unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*), it can be understood that what is called "uninterrupted" means inexhaustible.

The analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*) and the analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*), when taking suffering and its origin as their objects, involve the inexhaustible knowledge of the disease. The analytical knowledge of phenomena and the analytical knowledge of meaning, when taking the path and cessation as their objects, involve the inexhaustible knowledge of the medicine.

The analytical knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*) and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*) involve the inexhaustible and inexhaustible administration of medicine according to the disease.

This is the meaning of non-extinction. Furthermore, from the discourse on arising and ceasing, one develops the discourse on non-arising; from the discourse on non-arising, one brings forth the discourse on the immeasurable;
from the discourse on the immeasurable, one brings forth the discourse on the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*). As for the discourse on the unconditioned, it is like the wind in the sky:
because there is no obstruction when preaching the Dharma, it is said to be "uninterrupted. One cultivates these four discourses by means of the three contemplations applied to the mind.
The general interpretation may be understood accordingly.
[The Buddha] is fully endowed with generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, and the power of skillful means.

This second section separately praises his merit of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*). Furthermore, from meditative concentration and wisdom, the seven perfections (*pāramitā*) are opened up; from meditative concentration downward, four are opened up, while from wisdom, [the remaining three] are opened up.
The term "distinct" (*bie*) is used because it opens up the provisional means (*upāya*).

If one correlates the ten *pāramitās* with the ten stages (*bhūmi*), the opening up of meditation (*dhyāna*) produces power and vows, while the opening up of wisdom (*prajñā*) produces skillful means (*upāya*) and knowledge (*jñāna*).

If one distinguishes them according to the four teachings (*catvāraḥ śāsana-dharmāḥ*), the practice of giving (*dāna*) up to skillful means (*upāya*)—each performed in accordance with the four kinds of Four Truths (*catuḥ-satya*)—constitutes the four teachings.
What is clarified here is that although there are four distinct types, ranging from giving (*dāna*) and ethical discipline (*śīla*) up to skillful means (*upāya*), it is said that none are lacking.
This is the meaning of *pāramitā*. The meaning of *pāramitā* is translated as "the completion of the task" and also as "reaching the other shore.
Thus, the perfection of giving is precisely the completion of the task and the reaching of the other shore; this applies likewise up to skillful means.
Since it is likewise so, it is said that there is nothing not fully possessed; this is precisely the seven *pāramitās*.
To clarify the seven degrees (*pāramitās*) by means of the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*):

if one contemplates that the mind arises and ceases through causes and conditions—being simultaneously empty, provisional, and middle—one does not perceive stinginess or giving, nor holding precepts or violating them, nor anger or forbearance, nor diligence or indolence, nor concentration or distraction.
One does not perceive the foolish or the wise, nor the skillful or the clumsy; ultimately, these do not exist at all.

Yet, one is able to skillfully discern from stinginess and generosity up to skillfulness and clumsiness, understanding them with crystalline clarity; this is precisely what it means to be fully endowed with nothing lacking.
This leads to the attainment of the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) which is characterized by non-apprehension.

Regarding the subsequent three sections that praise and establish this stage: the term "attainment" (*dai*) signifies reaching [this state], while "non-arising" (*buqi*) means that the afflictions, birth-and-death, and all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*)—both within and outside the realms—cease to arise.
Because there is no longer any movement of thought, one attains ultimate quiescence.

This is called the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); it is also the great patience regarding non-birth (*mahā-anutpāda-kṣānti*) and is termed the patience of quiescent extinction (*śānta-nirodha-kṣānti*).

As for what is called "non-attainment," it does not mean that there is absolutely nothing to be attained; rather, one takes non-attainment as attainment. Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"One takes non-attainment as attainment; by this, one attains non-attainment. Furthermore, in the *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* (Renwang jing)...
The *Sūtra on the Five Patiences* and the *Necklace Sūtra on the Four Patiences*, though differing in their presentation, both clarify the patience of quiescence (*śānti-kṣānti*).

Within this patience of quiescence there are superior and inferior levels: the "diamond-like mind" (*vajropama-citta*) is termed the lower patience, while the stage of Buddhahood (*buddha-bhūmi*) is termed the upper patience.

If one distinguishes the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*) and separately establishes the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), it may further be divided into three grades: lower, middle, and upper.

Now, since this sutra praises his virtues as being "adjacent to the fruit" (*phala*) while also stating that he has "attained" it, one should know that he has attained the lower, middle, and [upper] patiences (*kṣānti*).
If we distinguish the four types of patience according to each of the four teachings: in the Tripiṭaka Teaching, there is originally no such text;

however, if we establish them based on the meaning, they can also be divided into four patiences: first, the *vīrya-kṣānti* (patience of subduing) during the first asaṃkhyeya kalpa; second, the [patience] during the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa... [text continues].

The three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* constitute the patience of conformity (*anulomikī-kṣānti*); planting the marks for a hundred eons and subduing delusions so they do not arise constitutes the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);

severing the fetters through the thirty-four moments of mind is called the patience of extinction (*nirodha-kṣānti*). In the Shared Teaching (*pāryāya-śāsana*), the stage of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi*) is called the patience of subduing (*vinaya-kṣānti*), and the stage of nature (*gotra-bhūmi*) is called the patience of conformity;
from the wisdom and abandonment of the *srotāpanna* up to the ninth stage is called the patience of non-arising.

The *jīngēn* (patience toward beings) of the ten stages is called "like a Buddha" and is named *jìmò* (extinction); the Separate Teaching’s iron wheel of the ten faiths is named *fùrěn* (patience of subduing);

the thirty minds are named *shùnrěn* (patience of compliance); from the first stage to the ninth stage is named *wúshēng rěn* (patience of non-arising); and the tenth stage, the diamond mind, is named *jìmò rěn* (patience of extinction).
In the Perfect Teaching, the five ranks of disciples are named *fùrěn* (patience of subduing), and the iron wheel of the ten faiths is likewise so named.

The purification of the six sense organs is the initial stage of *anulomikī-kṣānti* (conformity patience); from the first through the ninth stages it is called *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (non-arising patience);
and at the tenth stage, the diamond-like mind, it is called *nirvāṇa-kṣānti* (extinction patience).

Generally speaking, from the initial mind of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) upward, these are also termed *vinaya-kṣānti* (subduing patience), *anulomikī-kṣānti*, *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*, and *nirvāṇa-kṣānti*. Therefore, the *Renwang jing* says: "From..."

From the initial arousal of the mind (*prathamacittotpāda*) up to the *Vajraśekhara*, all are termed "Patience of Subjugation" (*vinaya-kṣānti*); this is the intended meaning of the names Samantabhadra and Bhadramukha. Question: In the subsequent passage praising the virtues of Vimalakīrti, it is stated only that he has attained "patience of non-arising" (*anutpāda-kṣānti*). One should know, therefore, that the "patience of the non-arising of dharmas" (*anutpatti-dharma-kṣānti*) is nothing other than the patience of non-arising. Why, then, is the "patience of the non-arising of dharmas" here explained by means of "quiescence" (*śānti*)? Answer: [The patience of non-arising refers to the realization that] dharmas do not arise; the patience of quiescence refers to the fact that, because they do not arise, they are inherently extinguished. Thus, the former is the cause and the latter is the result. Furthermore, the patience of non-arising is the stage of the Bodhisattva, while the patience of quiescence is the stage of the Buddha. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Moreover, the term "non-arising" is used as a designation for the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), whereas "quiescence" is used as a designation for the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Consequently, there is no fault in explaining the patience of the non-arising of dharmas through the gate of quiescence. This is why the *Mahāyāna-abhidharma-samuccaya-śāstra* states: "The patience of the non-arising of dharmas is the patience of quiescence. It is also said: "The patience of the non-arising of dharmas is the patience of quiescence. This is because, since dharmas do not arise, they are fundamentally quiescent. Thus, the two are one in essence but differ in their designations. Therefore, there is no error in using the term "quiescence" to explain the patience of the non-arising of dharmas. Regarding the teaching that the fruit arises from the cause as "the patience of non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), if we take the general meaning, "non-arising" is merely another name for "quiescence" (*śānti*).
Thus, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* speaks of "nirvāṇa," while this sūtra speaks of "dharmas being fundamentally unborn and now non-extinguished.
If this is the case, the patience of quiescence is precisely the patience of non-arising; what room is there for doubt? If, however, [we consider it] in terms of...

When one practices contemplation with single-mindedness through the three contemplations on the three truths such that delusions do not arise, this is precisely the cultivation of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Therefore, the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "One wears the robe of the Tathāgata"; for the "robe of the Tathāgata" is the mind of gentleness and forbearance.
Having already been able to turn the irreversible wheel in accordance with [the truth], one skillfully understands the characteristics of phenomena and knows the faculties of sentient beings.

Regarding these two points that extensively praise the transformation of others, there are further two parts: first, clarifying the internal possession of the methods for transforming others; second, correctly clarifying the methods for transforming others.

Regarding the first—clarifying the internal possession of the methods for transforming others—there are further three parts: first, clarifying the internal possession of the methods for transforming others... [and so forth].

The Dharma has two aspects: first, clarifying the external requisites for transforming others; second, providing a general explanation of both internal and external requisites for transforming others.
As explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, possessing internal wisdom is called "power" (*bala*), while employing external conduct without timidity is called "fearlessness" (*vaiśāradya*).

If internal wisdom is not clear and external deportment is not complete, one will have fear when among the assembly; how then could one subdue others? Only when both internal and external factors are fully prepared can this be achieved.
This is sufficient to transform sentient beings. First, clarifying that one internally possesses the methods for transforming others: this means one has already attained the capacity for compliance.
There are three kinds of compliance: first, compliance with the Buddha; second, compliance with the principle; and third, compliance with the faculties and conditions of sentient beings.
The Buddha turns the wheel of the Four Noble Truths for sentient beings in four ways; the Bodhisattva turns it in accordance with the Buddha, which is precisely compliance with the Buddha.
The principle of the three truths—the arising and ceasing of dependent origination—is simultaneously empty, provisionally existent, and the Middle Way.

Because one explains and speaks in accordance with this principle, it is said to be "in accord with principle. Although the faculties and natures of sentient beings are manifold, they do not exceed four types;
because one responds to their capacities without error by employing the four *siddhāntas*, it is called "in accord with sentient beings. Furthermore, if one speaks in accordance with principle...
This compliance with true wisdom and compliance with the teaching for sentient beings is compliance with provisional wisdom;

this compliance with the Buddha’s various skillful means of appearing and disappearing is compliance with both provisional and real wisdom. What is now called "compliance" (anuloma) possesses these three meanings.
Regarding the turning of the non-retrogressive wheel of Dharma: the fourfold Four Noble Truths constitute the essence of the wheel, while the four *siddhāntas* constitute its function of turning.
The Wheel of Non-Retrogression consists of four types: first, the Wheel of Non-Retrogression in Matters, which turns the Four Truths of Arising and Ceasing;
second, the Wheel of Non-Retrogression in Stages, which turns the Four Truths of Non-Arising and Non-Ceasing;
third, the Wheel of Non-Retrogression in Practice, which turns the Immeasurable Four Truths; and fourth, the Wheel of Non-Retrogression in Mindfulness, which turns the Unconditioned Four Truths.

If, according to the Threefold Canon (Tripitaka) teaching on the four truths of arising and ceasing, one considers the stage of non-retrogression in terms of the Bodhisattva’s practice, the Tripitaka teaching clarifies that this stage of non-retrogression does not involve the severance of fetters; rather, it is defined by five matters:

not being born in the four evil realms, not receiving a female body, not being born in borderlands, having all sense faculties complete, and attaining the knowledge of past lives. One who possesses these five matters is so named.

For those who are *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive), this refers to non-retrogression in terms of the objective state (*vastu*). If following the Shared Teaching (*pāryāya-śāsana*), from the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) upward up to the stage of Arhat, it is called non-retrogression in terms of rank and position (*avasthāna*).
From the seventh ground onward, engaging with existence to transform sentient beings while practicing various deeds is called non-retrogression in terms of practice (*caryā*).

On the eighth ground, where the path and contemplation flow together, it is called non-retrogression in terms of mindfulness (*smṛti*). If following the Distinct Teaching (*pratyeka-śāsana*), it is at the ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*).

In the Ten Abodes, there is non-retrogression of position; in the Ten Practices, there is non-retrogression of practice; in the Ten Dedications, there is non-retrogression of cultivation at the first thought-moment;
and in the Ten Stages, there is partial realization of non-retrogression of thought. As for the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), the one mind possesses the three types of non-retrogression:

in the First Abode, the Dharmakāya does not fall into the common or distinct stages, which is called non-retrogression of position; the one mind possesses all practices, which is called non-retrogression of practice.

To enter the flow of the Dharma moment by moment is precisely what is meant by "non-retrogression in mindfulness. To explain this according to the three contemplations of specific characteristics (*biphasa*):

through the contemplation of entering emptiness from the conventional, one attains non-retrogression in the stage of cultivation; through the contemplation of entering the conventional from emptiness, one attains non-retrogression in practice;

and through the correct contemplation of the Middle Way, one attains non-retrogression in mindfulness. If one were to judge the three types of non-retrogression based on these three contemplations, this interpretation would still be somewhat remote; therefore, we now proceed based on...

To practice the three contemplations within a single mind, correctly contemplating the Middle Way, so that one does not regress during the stages of cultivation and does not regress in the practice of simultaneously illuminating the two truths,
naturally flowing into the ocean of *sarvajñā*— this is called "non-retrogression through mindfulness.

To "skillfully understand the characteristics of dharmas and know the faculties of sentient beings" means that skillfully understanding the characteristics of dharmas is to understand them according to their true nature (*dharmatā*), while knowing the faculties of sentient beings is...
This consciousness is skilled in understanding the medicinal dharma of the fourfold Four Noble Truths and thoroughly knows the illnesses of the four types of sentient beings;

by using these to transform others, it is absolutely free from the error of mistaking their capacities. Among the ten powers, the power of the possible and the impossible is precisely the characteristic of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, the power of knowing superior and inferior faculties is precisely the knowledge that the faculties of all sentient beings are [as they are].
This is the perfection of internal power. To clarify the four kinds of suffering and its origin according to the four teachings, these are the "roots";
the four kinds of path and cessation are the "dharmic characteristics.
Thus, the great assembly attains fearlessness.

This constitutes the second clarification: the external requisites for transforming others. Because he covers the ten dharma realms with unconditional great compassion (*nirālamba-mahāmaitrī*), it is said that he "shades the great assembly.
Furthermore, the term "shading" implies transcendence; because he penetrates the four kinds of Four Noble Truths and surpasses all things, he is able to shade them.
One who attains fearlessness is able to benefit others through compassion, merit, and wisdom.
Because it is all-encompassing, it is said that "attaining fearlessness" is precisely the explanation of the external application of the dharma of being without timidity or fear.
One cultivates one's mind through merit and wisdom;

this is the general explanation of the three types of supernormal knowledge (*vidyā*) regarding the internal and external methods for transforming others, which consists of three parts: first, the explanation of the absence of fear within the inner mind.
Fearlessness in two ways: first, explaining fearlessness in outward application; second, concluding the establishment of fearlessness. Regarding the first, explaining fearlessness in the inner mind:
being endowed with the two adornments, one is able to roar the lion’s roar. This explains the accomplishment of fearlessness in the inner mind.

"Mind" refers to the intrinsically pure mind (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara-citta*), which is also the *dharmakāya*. Because merit and wisdom are able to manifest this intrinsically pure mind, [one is fearless].
It is said that by cultivating the mind, one uses it to adorn the intrinsically pure nature of the mind;
this is precisely to possess the two adornments, which adorn the Dharma-body. The four teachings clarify the three provisional and one real aspects of merit and wisdom;
by cultivating the mind through these provisional and real aspects combined, the mind becomes fearless.
First, regarding the adornment of the body with marks and signs, his physical form is supreme, having abandoned all worldly ornaments.
Second, regarding the external application of the fearless dharma, he is honored by various physical forms and objects, as elucidated by Kātyāyanīputra regarding the karma of the thirty-two marks;
this is shared with the worldly wheel-turning kings and Brahmā kings.
There are those who possess minor merits; what is there to marvel at in that? Therefore, it is not called "foremost.
If one follows the Shared Teaching (*pāryāya-śāsana*) and cultivates the thirty-two marks with a mind corresponding to emptiness, this is cultivation based on the Truth of Reality (*satyārtha*);

since the principle of the marks has not yet reached its ultimate limit, these marks are not foremost. As for the marks clarified in the Distinct Teaching (*pratyeka-śāsana*), they involve the cultivation of conditions to manifest the Real, and the cultivation of conditions to cultivate the marks.
Since the marks and embellishments resulting from causal cultivation are characteristics of the cognitive hindrances, they are not the primary [marks].
As for the marks and embellishments clarified in the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), when the Dharma-body is manifested, the marks and embellishments are fully perfected. Thus, the Lotus Sūtra says:

"Profoundly penetrating the characteristics of sin and merit, universally illuminating the ten directions, the subtle and wondrous pure Dharma-body possesses the thirty-two marks. The Dharma-body exists.
Ordinary beings have no means by which they can recognize these wondrous marks;

therefore, in order to manifest these marks, the *saṃbhogakāya* displays the white tuft of hair (*ūrṇā-kośa*) to symbolize the principle of the Middle Way, and displays the deep blue eyes (*abhinīla-netra*) to symbolize unconditional great compassion (*nirālamba-mahākaruṇā*).

Since the remaining marks likewise each possess their own symbolic significance, one should know that these marks are precisely the thirty-two marks of the *dharmakāya*. [This concludes] the section on physical form and appearance.
The first is the color of the *dharmatā*. The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Sublime color is serene and eternally abiding;
it is not subject to the transformations of birth, old age, sickness, and death. This sublime color is the foremost among all colors;
therefore, it can manifest the images of the ten *dharmadhātus*, just as a wish-fulfilling jewel does. The color of the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) represents the truth.
Regarding the true nature of form (*rūpa*), within the principle of true form, it is foremost that the color of the Buddha’s body is supreme among all manifested forms.

This refers to the relinquishing of all worldly ornaments; this tradition explains the primary marks and secondary signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*). It does not mean the relinquishing of worldly clothing or decorative finery;
for if one were to relinquish these, even those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) and non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) would be capable of doing so—what then would be worthy of praise?

Regarding the present statement on "renunciation": according to the Tripiṭaka Teaching, a Bodhisattva renounces the finery of humans and devas and cultivates the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) over a hundred kalpas to adorn themselves as a vessel for Bodhi. According to the Shared Teaching, a Bodhisattva renounces the mind that grasps at existence;
for to cultivate the marks and signs with a mind that grasps at existence is merely worldly adornment. Thus it is said, "Great Wisdom."
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* refutes the marks [of a Buddha] accumulated over a hundred kalpas, stating: "If one views me by means of form, such a person follows a deviant path.
In the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), Bodhisattvas abandon the empty mind within the realm and cultivate the marks and signs through conditions outside the realm;
this is the cultivation of marks and signs. In the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), all that is cultivated both within and outside the realm is merely worldly adornment.
Since all that is excellent is entirely subsumed within the relinquishing of the dharma-body, and when the true aspect is revealed, it manifests of itself;
therefore, it is said that his marks and signs adorn the body and his physical form is supreme. How could this be the same as the false cultivation of causes to adorn the body with marks and signs?
"The fame and reputation are loftier than Mount Sumeru.
This concludes the following three points, which consist of two intentions: first, concluding the external; second, concluding the internal.
Regarding the conclusion of the external: "the fame and reputation are loftier than Mount Sumeru" constitutes the accomplishment of the external fearlessnesses.
The merit of the Bodhisattva’s external transformation pervades the ten dharma-realms; because his name stands high above all things, it is said that his loftiness exceeds Mount Sumeru.

Furthermore, the distinct and common teachings clarify the ten stages (*bhūmi*) as being like the ten jewel mountains, while the distinct and common teachings clarify the Buddha as being like Mount Sumeru.
Now, the stage of the ten grounds in the Perfect Teaching surpasses those of both the distinct and common teachings.
Because it clarifies the fruit of Buddhahood, it is said to surpass Mount Sumeru. Furthermore, Mount Sumeru is stable, vast, and lofty;
the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is likewise immovable, its principle supreme and unsurpassed. Because wisdom possesses the power to manifest this principle, it is said to surpass Mount Sumeru.
Deep faith is firm and solid like a vajra.
Second, this establishes the internal dharma of fearlessness. There are two kinds of faith: first, faith through hearing; second, faith through realization.
When distinguished according to the four teachings, each has its own stages. Here, we distinguish these two types of faith solely according to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao). If...
The disciples of the five ranks hear and believe exclusively; they believe in what dharma? They believe in the principle of the inconceivable threefold virtues (*triguṇa*).

As for the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) and the purification of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya-viśuddhi*), these are also matters of hearing and believing, yet they also attain a semblance of realized belief (*sādṛśya-sākṣāt-kriyā-śraddhā*).

From the first stage of the abiding in the resolve for enlightenment (*prathama-cittotpāda-vihāra*) upward, there is both hearing and believing, as well as true realized belief. At the stage of Buddhahood (*buddha-bhūmi*), there is only realized belief. Now [I shall explain].
Since these great bodhisattvas occupy high positions and their two types of faith are perfectly deep, it is said that their profound faith is firm and solid;
this means that the two types of faith cannot be thwarted or destroyed by any internal or external conditions. It is likened to a vajra to illustrate profound faith, for the vajra has two meanings:
first, its sharp edge penetrates to the ultimate limit; second, its substance is so solid that it withstands all things.

That which cannot be diminished and which benefits by penetrating to the ultimate limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) refers to the internal convergence of the two types of faith—faith through hearing and faith through realization—and the utility of concentration and wisdom, which exhaustively reach the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Its substance is firm such that no phenomenon can obstruct it;

this is like how true wisdom and the two types of faith cannot be damaged by the conditions of afflictions or birth-and-death. This praises the internal possession of the qualities for transforming others.
The Jewel of the Dharma shines universally.

This section explicitly clarifies the transformation of others; from here down to "and the range of mental activity," there are three distinct parts: first, emitting light and preaching the Dharma to clarify the transformation of others;
second, correctly preaching the Dharma to clarify the transformation of others; third, teaching the methods for progressive cultivation to transform others. First.
Regarding those who emit light and preach the Dharma to transform others, there are again two parts: first, the explicit explanation of emitting light and preaching the Dharma;

second, the explanation through deep entry into dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) to substantiate the emission of light and the preaching of the Dharma. The first part, the emission of light and preaching the Dharma, consists of three sections:
first, the emission of light; second, the preaching of the Dharma; third, the explanation and praise. As for the emission of light: this explains and substantiates the transformation of others.
This is the Jewel of the Dharma, the treasure that gives rise to all wholesome dharmas through the Bodhisattva’s compassion and wisdom conditioned by the principle of the three truths.
As for "universal illumination," it is because he enters the Samādhi of Emitting Light and the Samādhi of Universal Radiance that he is able to illuminate universally.
If there are ordinary beings who should be delivered by means of worldly wholesome dharmas, he then enters the world.
The Samādhi of the Truths emits the light of mundane wholesome dharmas to illuminate beings, causing them to leave behind all suffering and attain mundane happiness.

If there are those who should be liberated by means of supramundane wholesome dharmas, he immediately enters the Samādhi of the Ultimate Truth and emits the light of mundane wholesome dharmas to cause them to attain the fruits of the paths of the Two Vehicles. If there are those who should be liberated by means of the supreme, supramundane wholesome dharmas...
"Crossing over" means immediately entering the Samādhi of the Middle Way and emitting the supreme, supramundane wholesome dharmas;

"illumination" means opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and entering the stage of a Bodhisattva. Therefore, both the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and the *Saṃghāṭa Sūtra* state that the Buddha possesses a light named "Non-Miserliness.
If he emits this light to illuminate sentient beings, they are able to abandon miserliness and practice giving.
Up to the six perfections, all matters are likewise. In the *Avalokiteśvara-sūtra*, it says: "He universally radiates pure light to extinguish the darkness of ignorance.
In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, he first emits light from his limbs and joints, and subsequently emits light from his pores;
when this touches the bodies of sentient beings, the blind regain their sight and the deaf regain their hearing—such are the various worldly benefits.
Furthermore, it can cause them to attain the Way and resolve upon Bodhicitta. It is like fishing with a net:

those who are not caught by the first cast are netted again later; or like a light: those whose light has not yet reached them are reached when the light is emitted again. Thus, all who possess the conditions for connection receive benefit and enter the Way.
It is the same for a Bodhisattva entering the Way: they emit light that universally illumines the ten dharma realms.

Sentient beings all obtain benefit and enter the Way. Furthermore, if one emits a single ray of light to cease and eliminate stinginess, or another ray to eliminate anger, this is the intent of the Separate Teaching (biejiao) and is not called "universal illumination" (puzhao). Furthermore, if one emits rays of light of the Two Truths, it likewise is not called "universal.
Now, these Bodhisattvas are able to emit the perfect light of the Middle Way (zhongdao), which universally illuminates; they emit only this.
A single light illuminates all places, causing each to obtain benefit according to their capacities and enter the Way; therefore, it is called the "illumination of the Dharma Jewel.

Question: How can this light destroy evil and give rise to goodness? Answer: It is like when the smoke from medicinal incense touches one who suffers from illness—the pain is immediately removed and the body attains peace and happiness.
When the emitted light touches the body, it destroys evil and gives rise to goodness in exactly the same way.
Thus, because light issues from all roots of goodness, it removes all suffering of sentient beings who come into contact with it;
furthermore,
it rains down ambrosia.
These two clarify that the rain of Dharma is nectar (*amṛta*). Nectar is the wondrous medicine of the devas; by consuming it, one attains peace and happiness and does not die.

The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "The true nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is called the celestial nectar; it enables those of the three vehicles to equally attain the noble path, nirvāṇa, and eternal bliss.
This nectar of the true nature is of two kinds: first, the true nature of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Among these two, for sentient beings who should be delivered by means of the True Truth (*satyadharma*), he rains down the nectar of partial truth;

the three vehicles alike attain the *nirvāṇa* of the "transformed city. If there are those with the perfect capacity for the Mahāyāna, he rains down the nectar of the Middle Way and the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*);
thus they open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, perceive the Buddha-nature, and abide in Great *Nirvāṇa*. Therefore, the Dharma...
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "The Buddha’s impartial teaching is like a rain of a single flavor, yet it is received differently according to the dispositions of sentient beings;
these bodhisattvas’ preaching of the Dharma of ambrosia is likewise in every respect."
Among all vocal sounds, they are foremost in their subtle and wondrous quality.
These three types of clairvoyance explain the praise of raining down the rain of ambrosia; for what reason can these bodhisattvas preach the Dharma-rain of ambrosia?
It is because they possess subtle and wondrous vocal sounds, such as those described in the Lotus Sūtra regarding the clarity of the tongue.
If one wishes to pervade the trichiliocosm with a single word through the merit of the sense faculties, one can achieve this at will;
even an Iron-Wheel-turning Bodhisattva is capable of such a feat, so how much more so for a Bodhisattva in his final birth?

Why should he not be able to fill the sentient beings of the ten Dharma-realms with wondrous sounds, so that each may understand according to their kind, universally receive and practice [the teaching], and thereby obtain its benefit?
Regarding "the most subtle and supreme": from the Buddha downward, no speech or sound within the entire world can surpass it;
furthermore, because it is understood as being the very voice of the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena), it is called "the most subtle and supreme."
Entering deeply into dependent origination.
Second, explaining the entry into dependent origination to establish the emission of light and the preaching of the Dharma has two parts:
first, explaining the entry into dependent origination to praise the virtue of wisdom and establish the emission of light and the preaching of the Dharma; second, severing all false views.

The following section praises the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*) to explain and establish the emission of light and the preaching of the Dharma. The subsequent section praises the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*) to explain and establish the emission of light and the preaching of the Dharma.

The reason why [the Buddha] is able to emit light and preach the Dharma to benefit others so profoundly and universally is precisely because his wisdom is able to penetrate deeply into dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
There are two kinds of dependent origination: first, the dependent origination of saṃsāra; second, the dependent origination of liberation (*mokṣa*).
The dependent origination of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) is precisely ignorance (*avidyā*), the twelve links of dependent origination, and all of birth and death.
The dependent origination of liberation is precisely the wisdom that contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination, giving rise to all the Buddha-dharmas of liberation.
Now, to clarify "deeply entering dependent origination" means deeply entering the twelve links of dependent origination; thus, the dependent origination of birth and death is itself perfected.

Because it explains the conditions of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states that there are four types of contemplation regarding the twelve links of dependent origination.
If one enters deeply into them, one attains the supreme wisdom and clearly perceives the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*). Why is this so?

If one contemplates the arising and ceasing of the twelve links of dependent origination, this is the method by which the Bodhisattvas of the Tripitaka subdue their faculties and bring them to fulfillment.

If one has not yet practiced the Six Perfections, it is not called "deep entry. If one contemplates the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination and realizes emptiness to sever the delusions within the realm of desire, this is the Bodhisattva of the Shared Teaching (Sādhāraṇa-yāna), who likewise is not yet called "deep entry.

If one contemplates the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination and knows that emptiness is not [mere] emptiness, entering into the provisional (the conventional) to shatter the sands-of-Ganges of ignorance both within and without the realms, one attains entry into the Middle Way and shatters the ten [stages].
The single grade of ignorance belongs to the Bodhisattvas of the Separate Teaching (biejiao), who are not yet called "deeply entered" [into the truth].

Only the Bodhisattvas of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) practice the perfect contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination with a single mind. From the first dwelling (*bhūmi*), they give rise to the true vision of the Middle Way;

reaching the stage of the "near-enlightened" (*sui-chu*), they shatter the forty-one grades of ignorance, at which point they are called "deeply entered into dependent origination. These Bodhisattvas have not only entered the ten [stages], but...

Regarding the two types of dependent origination—primary retribution and environmental support—the former involves deeply penetrating the dependent origination of the world as primary retribution, whereby one knows the causes and conditions by which worlds are formed and the causes and conditions by which worlds are destroyed.
Since one is already able to penetrate dependent origination deeply, one is thus able to expound the nectar of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of causes and conditions;
the meaning and intent of this "deep penetration" are also clearly evident.
Having severed all false views regarding the two extremes of existence and non-existence, they are free from any remaining habitual tendencies.
These two verses praise the virtue of severance and explain that the one who emits light and preaches the Dharma universally pours down nectar;

because he himself is free from the darkness of delusion, he can universally emit light to illuminate the darkness of sentient beings, and because he himself is free from bondage, he can rain [down the Dharma].
The Ambrosia that liberates sentient beings from bondage and severs all false views regarding the two extremes of existence and non-existence:
there are two kinds of false views. First, those within the realm (*dhātu*); second, those outside the realm.

Regarding the first, the sixty-two views and various other false views all belong to the dualistic views of existence and non-existence. Regarding the second, there are likewise various [views] outside the realm.
The various views are likewise all comprised within the two views of existence and non-existence.

Now, all views within the realm of conditioned phenomena belong to the extreme of existence, while all views outside the realm of conditioned phenomena belong to the extreme of non-existence. Therefore, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

"Ordinary beings have [the view of] existence, and those of the Two Vehicles have [the view of] non-existence; the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas is neither existent nor non-existent—the Middle Way of Right View. As for the Buddha:
Because its nature shatters the two extremes of existence and non-existence as well as all false views, it is said to "sever all false views regarding the two extremes of existence and non-existence.

Furthermore, another interpretation states that through the correct contemplation of the Middle Way, one shatters the two extremes of existence and non-existence regarding both the ultimate (paramārtha) and the conventional (saṃvṛti).

Upon reaching the pinnacle of the Vajra-peak, when wisdom is perfected, the essence of the Middle Way manifests, and only then are the delusions concerning the three truths completely exhausted. Thus it is said.

Regarding "having no further residual habits": in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), from the first stage (*chuzhu*) up to the Cloud of Dharma (*fayun*) stage, although all views of existence and non-existence have been perfectly severed, residual habits (*xi*) still remain.

Upon reaching the Stage of Equal Enlightenment (*dengque*), one enters the Gate of the Double Profundity and re-cultivates the practices of ordinary beings for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas.
Because the realization of principle is clear and habitual tendencies are extremely subtle—like a faint wisp of smoke—it is so named.
There are no further residual habits remaining, just as when a *śroṇa* of salt is thrown into a great river, it no longer has a salty taste.

Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "The two views of existence and non-existence are extinguished without remainder; this is the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena as taught by the Buddha.

Question: This cannot be so. Answer: If one merely explains the cessation of the two views of existence and non-existence within the realm of conditioned existence (*saṃsāra*), how could [the ultimate truth] be attained?

To explain this passage: furthermore, if one were to interpret the meaning according to the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*) of the *Dilun* school—whereby upon attaining the stages (*bhūmi*), one leaves behind the obstacles of the ordinary person’s marks of self (*ātmagrāha*) and severs the two views of existence and non-existence—how could such an interpretation possibly account for this text? Question: What fault is there in this? Answer:

In the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings (*tongjiao*), all false views and the two extremes of existence and non-existence are severed precisely at the initial realization of the Path (*darśanamārga*). How, then, could [the Separate Teaching] be applied here?

This praises the virtues of one in the stage of "near-attainment" (the Bodhisattva on the verge of Buddhahood). According to the Separate Teaching (Pṛthagdharma), upon ascending to the first bhūmi, one perceives the Buddha-nature and severs the delusions of dualistic views—namely, the extremes of existence and non-existence—which are false views outside the [three] realms;
these are all empty. How could this possibly be used to explain the passage praising the virtues of one in the stage of near-attainment?

The *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* states: "In the ninth bhūmi, one severs the habit-energy of views; in the tenth bhūmi, one severs the habit-energy of craving. The *Dìchí lùn* (Śīlaparivarta-śāstra) [states the same].
The statement that "one leaves behind all views and enters the pure, purified dhyāna" refers here to the stage of Vajra-like Perfect Enlightenment;

now, according to the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra*, this scriptural passage is explained as follows: the interpretation of the cessation of delusions according to our school’s use of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) becomes even more distinct.
He expounds the Dharma with fearlessness, like the roar of a lion.
Second, regarding the correct exposition of the Dharma and the praise of transforming others: from this point down to "exceeding measure," all are praises of his preaching of the Dharma.

First, two similes are presented together to praise the accomplishment of transforming others; subsequently, one general praise is offered for the merit of transforming others. There is no [other] [omission].
Regarding the measure, the initial analogy speaks of the "lion’s roar. A lion’s roar refers to definitive teaching;

definitive teaching means proclaiming that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature. As for what is called "fearlessness in expounding the Dharma," "expounding" means extensively, and because the mind is free from timidity, it is called fearlessness. These bodhisattvas are able, regarding the four [fearlessnesses]— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly.

The standard list of four fearlessnesses (catur-vaiśāradya) in Mahāyāna Buddhism consists of: fearlessness in claiming perfect enlightenment, fearlessness in declaring the exhaustion of outflows, fearlessness in explaining the obstacles to the path, and fearlessness in teaching the path leading to the cessation of suffering.*
It may be said that by employing the four *siddhāntas* to respond to conditions, one extensively gives rise to the four teachings.
This is like the lion’s roar, which is a metaphor for expounding the nectar-like Dharma of the true reality (*dharmatā*) and attaining fearlessness.
Just as when a lion roars, it not only has no fear of birds and beasts, but can also cause fragrant elephants to lose their dung and flying creatures to fall, so too do these Bodhisattvas.
In expounding the Dharma of Ambrosia, he is not only without fear or weakness of mind toward all celestial Māras, non-Buddhists, and sentient beings;
he also causes the celestial Māras to lose their attachment to their foul discourses, causes the non-Buddhists to fall from their prideful adherence to views,
and causes the afflictions of attachment and views in all sentient beings to be extinguished.
His preaching is like a thunderclap.
This is compared to the rain of the nectar-like Dharma, which can cause the growth of wholesome qualities. The *Śāstra* fully sets forth four types of Dharma-preachers;

the thunder is a metaphor for extensive learning (*bahuśruta*), while the rain is a metaphor for beautiful conduct (*sucarita*). These are found in detail in the treatise itself. Here, we clarify that thunder is used to signify the awakening from hibernation.
The rain moistens all that lives; now he shall proclaim the rain of ambrosia.
He strikes with the thunder of the eightfold voice to awaken those slumbering in the two extremes and false views, causing the sprouts of all roots of goodness to bud and open.

Because the roots of goodness of all practitioners produced in their past lives thus bud and flourish—whether they be the three types of grass, the two types of wood, or those born from the single ground—he is said to "preach the Dharma."
It is like the roar of thunder.
"Immeasurable" and "having transcended measure"—these two phrases collectively praise the immeasurable merit of transforming others. These are the supernormal powers and wisdom of these bodhisattvas.
The light emitted by wisdom and the teaching of the Dharma transform sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions in measureless and limitless numbers;
they cannot be reckoned even by the number of asaṃkhyeya. That which has "exceeded measure" means that those who are transformed and delivered are inexpressible.
Furthermore, that which is "without measure" refers to those who practice through the seven kinds of skillful means, whom the wisdom of analytical deliberation is unable to measure.
Furthermore, that which exceeds this measure cannot be known by the inconceivable wisdom of those below the tenth stage of the Perfect Teaching (Eonkyō).
Like a sea captain who gathers the treasures of all dharmas, he thoroughly understands the profound and subtle meaning of all phenomena and well knows the capacities of sentient beings.
The destinations of coming and going, as well as the mental activities—these three constitute the methods for cultivating others.
Although the merit of Bodhisattvas in transforming others is great, until they have realized the ultimate fruit, they must still cultivate these methods for transforming others;
this is precisely how Bodhisattvas enter the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi-bhūmi*).

For hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, one enters the Gate of Profound Mystery (*chongxuanmen*) to cultivate the practice of transforming others. Regarding this "Gate of Profound Mystery," the *Dichijing lun* (*Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra*) states:
"The power of entering, abiding, and arising in dhyāna, and returning from relinquishment to enter dhyāna again.

"Entering" refers to entering all dharma-gates from the state of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*) up to the higher stages (*bhūmi*). "Arising-power" refers to [the power] from the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) regarding all dharma-gates.
Regarding "arising and entering to abide in all dharma-gates": this means that by abiding in a single dharma-gate, one immediately abides in all dharma-gates.
Regarding "leaving and re-entering": this refers to practicing again for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas.

Therefore, in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, Maitreya praises the bodhisattvas from the lower direction, saying: "They skillfully enter, exit, and abide for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions [of kalpas]."
Having attained a hundred million samādhis and great supernormal powers, he has long cultivated the Brahma-faring and is well-versed in practicing all wholesome dharmas in their proper sequence.
Skilled in question and answer, he is a jewel among men. He gathers the jewels of the many teachings like a sea-captain;
for such a captain not only leads others into the sea to gather treasures, but also obtains them for himself.

When Bodhisattvas lead sentient beings into the ocean of birth and death, they do not merely cause those beings to obtain the treasure of the Buddha-dharma and then attribute the merit of this transformation to themselves;
rather, by entering the Gate of Profound Mystery, the benefit of the Dharma is likewise vast, immeasurable, and boundless. Therefore, this sutra says:
"If one does not enter the great ocean, one cannot obtain the priceless jewel. Thus, a Bodhisattva does not enter [the ocean] without entering the vast sea of afflictions.

One cannot obtain the jewel of all-knowledge; yet, a Bodhisattva in the stage of succession (the "Successor" Bodhisattva) enters the Gate of Profound Mystery and, through the retribution of countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, performs the deeds of ordinary beings, thereby emitting light and preaching the Dharma to benefit sentient beings.
One who thoroughly understands the profound and subtle meaning of all dharmas is a Bodhisattva who has entered the inner adornment of wisdom within the Gate of Profound Mystery.
"Progression" (*vṛddhi*) is another name for "penetrating understanding" (*prajñā*). "All phenomena" (*sarvadharma*) refers to all phenomena within the ten dharma-realms.
Regarding the meaning of "profound and subtle": because the principle of the two truths and three truths of the phenomena within the ten dharma-realms is extremely deep, it is called "profound.
Because the three virtues (*triguṇa*) are neither vertical nor horizontal, it is called the "subtle" meaning. [This is] excellent.

"Knowing the destinations where sentient beings go and come, as well as the movements of their minds"—these two phrases clarify that the Bodhisattvas enter and abide in the gate of the double mystery (*chóngxuán mén*), thereby advancing their external perception of the faculties and conditions of the sentient beings they transform.
These Bodhisattvas have attained the true divine eye and constantly abide in samādhi; they do not perceive the death and rebirth of sentient beings through dualistic characteristics.
"Going from death there to being born here" is called "coming to the destination. This refers to knowing that causes can lead to effects;
it is the cause of wholesome and unwholesome karmic conditions leading to the fruit of receiving retribution—whether good or ugly.

Furthermore, regarding the mental activities performed, one uses the Knowledge of All Modes (sarvajñajñāna) to know the causal roots of habitual practices in past lives, as well as the roots produced by the three types of grasses, two types of trees, and the single ground.

Their natures are different. The three types of grass and two types of trees represent the three vehicles of the *Tripitaka*, the *Shared*, and the *Distinct* teachings—the seven kinds of roots of goodness of the provisional means.

That which is produced from the ground represents the roots and conditions of the *Perfect* teaching. Having previously clarified the application of medicine, we now clarify the diagnosis of the illness;
once one recognizes both the medicine and the illness, one can administer the medicine according to the illness. Thus, it is known that this refers to those dwelling in the heavy [afflictions].
The virtue of the Mysterious Gate (Xuanmen) in transforming others becomes increasingly profound and vast.
It approaches the peerless, sovereign wisdom of the Buddha.

Third, regarding the praise of virtues based on the proximate fruit (*phala*), this passage has three distinct parts: first, praising one’s own practice; second, praising the transformation [of others].

The other three [verses] provide a general explanation, forming one praise of his own practice (*sva-caryā*). This is further divided into two: first, a praise of the wisdom-virtue (*jñāna-guṇa*) of his own practice;
second, a praise of the abandonment-virtue (*prahāṇa-guṇa*) of his own practice. Regarding the praise of the wisdom-virtue of his own practice, it is further divided into two.

First, the general praise of the wisdom-virtue of his own practice refers to the sovereign wisdom (*vibhu-prajñā*) of the Buddha, who is "unequaled by any equal" (*asama-sama*). As for "unequaled by any equal":
The Buddhas of the ten directions have no equal; because he now equals the Buddhas of the ten directions, he is called "unequaled with the unequaled" (*asamasama*).

Furthermore, explaining this according to principle: the principle of true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) has nothing that can equal it, while the Buddha’s knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), being perfectly consummate, is able to equal the principle of true reality;
therefore, he is named "unequaled with the unequaled. Even though one who has attained the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) of the Perfect Teaching has already...

Although one who has truly seen the principle and attained the peerless Dharma still possesses forty-one grades of ignorance and remains distant from wondrous enlightenment—thus not being called "adjacent to the fruit"—if one considers it in relation to the Buddha or the principle, they are nonetheless not distant.
Because the Bodhisattva of the Vajra-mind is near both to the Buddha and to the principle, he is described as "equal to the unequaled.
Regarding the meaning of "equal to the unequaled," four interpretations are made according to the Four Teachings.
These may be understood through analysis.

Regarding the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities, there are two distinct ways of praising his own practice and wisdom, as explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. First, it says: "The Bodhisattva..."
Secondly, it is said that Bodhisattvas partially attain the Buddha’s powers (*bala*), fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*).
They are like the moon on the fourteenth day, while the Buddha is like the moon on the fifteenth day; they are thus adjacent to one another.
If one explains the powers and fearlessnesses according to the Four Teachings, as in the *Tripiṭaka* [Teaching], the ten powers and fearlessnesses are all explained in the same manner.

The Mahāyāna teachings on the *Abhidharma* (Vibhāṣā) explain the "unshared dharmas" (*āveṇika-dharma*) by establishing them as a distinct set of teachings; therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* critiques the *Abhidharma*, stating:
"Since the names 'powers' (*bala*) and 'fearlessnesses' (*vaiśāradya*) are identical to those in the Mahāyāna's unshared dharmas, how can they be established separately?

Now, we merely distinguish their similarities and differences based on whether they involve the abandonment or suppression [of afflictions]; this difference in name and meaning does not constitute an obstacle. As for the Shared Teaching (*pāryāya-yāna*), it relies on the illumination of the two [truths].

One should know that in the *Dìbā dìfēn* (The Stages of the Eight Truths), from the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward, one partially attains the ten powers (*daśabala*), the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and so forth;
reaching the tenth stage, the ten powers and other dharmas thus obtained are called "near to the Peerless" (*anuttara-samāsa-nikaṣa*).
In the Perfect Teaching (*yánjiào*), this applies from the first abiding (*prathama-vihāra*) upward.

The *Sūtra of the Lotus of the Wondrous Dharma* (*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*) clarifies that at the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), one attains the ten powers (*daśa-bala*) of the Tathāgata, such as the knowledge of what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñāna*), as well as the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) and the unshared qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*).
It states that reaching the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*) constitutes being close to the Buddha’s powers, fearlessnesses, and unshared qualities;
this is a praise of the wisdom and virtue of the neighboring fruit (*sāmantaka-phala*). As previously stated, [this refers to] the Buddha’s mastery (*vaśitā*).
Because within the Buddha-wisdom of the wise there is no ignorance, they possess ultimate mastery;
although Bodhisattvas still possess ignorance, it is like a wisp of smoke as they are about to attain Buddha-wisdom. It is for this reason that they are praised.
"It closes the gates to all evil destinies.
This praises the virtue of severance in one's own practice. Regarding the "gates to evil destinies," although there are many such destinies, they do not exceed two types:

those arising from conditions (*pratyaya-samudaya*). For Bodhisattvas who have realized emptiness through the general teaching, they close the gates to the evil destinies that arise from conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta*). Specifically, [the text continues:]...
This teaches that Bodhisattvas perceive the non-empty closing of the gates to the evil realms caused by the accumulation of unconditioned conditions;
because these Bodhisattvas perceive the source of the Middle Way within the Buddha-nature, they are able to close all gates to the various evil realms.
Alternatively, this may be understood as praising the transformation of others, whereby they close the gates to the evil realms for all sentient beings.

He manifests birth within the five destinies to appear as a Great King of Physicians who skillfully cures all ailments; according to the disease he provides the medicine, enabling it to be taken and practiced.
These two points praise his transformation of others. If one includes the asuras, this refers to the manifestation of his body within the six destinies.

If, according to the Tripiṭaka Teaching, it is explained that [bodhisattvas] manifest bodies in the five destinies through vows to be born amidst fetters, or by employing supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) within defiled or pure lands to transform sentient beings;

or if, according to the Shared Teaching, it is explained that those in the seventh stage sever the fetters within the realm of desire and, supported by their remaining habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), vow to be born in the five destinies to manifest their bodies and likewise employ supernatural powers to transform beings; or if, according to the Distinct...
The Teaching (Tripitaka Vehicle) clarifies that from the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward, one should give rise [to the fruit] without needing to rely on the cultivation of habits.

The Complete Teaching (Perfect Teaching) clarifies that from the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*) upward, one attains the single body and immeasurable bodies—the pure and wondrous Dharma-body—which is tranquil yet responds to all things;
this is precisely the power of the twenty-five samādhis permeating and giving rise to the twenty-five states of existence. This is called "giving birth to the five paths."
Regarding the phrase "manifesting his body" and the subsequent statement that he "is born in the five realms to manifest his body":
this refers to the Bodhisattva of the Stage of Succession (Upapadya-bhūmi), whose Dharma-body attains the twenty-five samādhis. Internally, these break through the twenty-five obstacles;

externally, they involve the subtle and compassionate influence of kindness upon all evil destinies, responding to the capacities of beings to manifest throughout the ten directions and receive bodies within the five realms to benefit sentient beings.

He also acts as a Great King of Physicians to treat the various ailments of sentient beings. This clarifies that once [the Bodhisattva] has been born into the five realms, his intention lies in benefiting others;
"benefiting others" specifically refers to treating the diseases of the karmic afflictions of sentient beings.

Furthermore, it can be explained that in contrast to the "Small Physician," the Bodhisattvas of the three vehicles and those Bodhisattvas of the lower stages of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) are all "Small Physicians. Now, these various Bodhisattvas...
He is called the Great Physician; he is also able to manifest the eight phases of attaining enlightenment as the Great King of Physicians to cure all diseases.
"Curing all illnesses" refers to treating all afflictions and unwholesome karmic diseases both within and outside the realms.

"Prescribing medicine according to the illness" means responding to the capacities of beings by employing the four *siddhāntas* to preach the medicinal Dharma of the four teachings, thereby enabling practitioners to take and apply it.

When sentient beings hear the Dharma and practice it, they are able to sever the afflictions both within and beyond the realms, thereby attaining the liberation of the noble paths of the two vehicles, Great and Small.
They fully accomplish immeasurable merits and purify all immeasurable Buddha-lands; there are none among those who see or hear them who do not [attain benefit].

"Whatever one does for the benefit of others shall not be in vain"—this is a general explanation that establishes the praise of the proximate fruit (*pratyupabhoga-phala*). "All immeasurable merits are accomplished" explains the fulfillment of the merit of one's own practice;
"all immeasurable Buddha-lands are purified" explains the fulfillment of the merit of transforming others.
Those who see or hear [the Buddha] will all receive benefit. The Dharma-body is neither form nor sound, yet it responds according to the capacities of beings.
When it manifests form or sound, it is invariably for the purpose of benefiting sentient beings;

because there is a karmic affinity, those who see the form or hear the sound immediately obtain both worldly and world-transcending benefits. Whatever actions are performed are never in vain. "Tang" (唐) means empty or in vain.
The term "discarded" (*qi*) also means "lost. Interpreting this according to one's own practice: as the mind proceeds, it spontaneously accords with reality;
because it will certainly become a superior cause that brings about its fruit without fail, it is said that its merit is not discarded in vain.
Interpreting this in terms of transforming others: although sentient beings may not yet enter the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the ultimate standpoint), they do not lose the three [other standpoints].

Because the benefit of generating the mind of awakening (*cittotpāda*), turning toward [the Dharma], and giving rise to good while destroying evil is complete, it is said that its merit is not wasted;
that the merit of transformation returns to oneself is likewise not lost.
In this way, they are fully endowed with all such merits.
Third, the conclusion summarizes these praises of merit: "All these Bodhisattvas have fully accomplished the merits praised above.
If one were to select phrases from the Northern and Southern versions to assign them to specific stages in praising their virtues, how could it be said that all Bodhisattvas [possess them]?
The principle of "accomplishment" (chengjiu) naturally accords with the interpretations of each school. Furthermore, another explanation states: the merits of a Bodhisattva are immeasurable;

the praise offered above consists merely of these dozens of items. To praise them by category as being immeasurable is to acknowledge that they are fully accomplished, such that they cannot be described in their entirety.
Their names were Bodhisattva Equal Contemplation, Bodhisattva Unequal Contemplation, and Bodhisattva Equal-and-Unequal Contemplation.

Regarding the fourth section on the cumulative names of those who heard the teaching together: although their superior virtues have been praised, if their specific names are not explicitly revealed, one will not know who they are;
therefore, fifty-two bodhisattvas are briefly set forth here to serve as witnesses to those who heard the teaching and to encourage faith.
The meaning is established as follows: if one were to explain this according to the four teachings, the details would become excessively numerous;

therefore, I shall briefly explain the names based on the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*), which is sufficient to understand the general principle. Regarding "equal contemplation" (*samadarśana*), it refers to entering the Middle Way from the two [lower] contemplations, for this is non-dual equality;

hence it is called equal contemplation. As for the Bodhisattva’s "unequal contemplation," it refers merely to the distinct observation of the two truths through simultaneous illumination (*dvayasatyasamprativedha*).
Because there are immeasurable distinctions, he is named the Bodhisattva of Unequal Contemplation (*Asama-darśana*).

"Equal" (*sama*) and "unequal" (*asama*) refer to the Middle Way within correct contemplation, which simultaneously illuminates the two truths: illuminating the Middle is called "equal," while illuminating the two truths is called "unequal.
By combining essence and function, he is named the Bodhisattva of Equal and Unequal Contemplation. All of this must be distinguished by means of the six stages of identity (*liu ji*).

Thus, there is no confusion or intermixture. That all sentient beings are themselves the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) constitutes the "identity-in-principle" (*liriji*) contemplation of a bodhisattva.
If, upon hearing the name "true reality," one knows for oneself that it is precisely the principle of true reality, this is the "identity-in-name" (*mingzij*) contemplation of a bodhisattva.
If one contemplates the Middle Way and attains unimpeded penetration, this is...
The Bodhisattva of Equal Contemplation at the Stage of Practice (*pratipatti*) is one who, having given rise to a semblance understanding, attains the purity of the six sense faculties;

this is called the Bodhisattva of Equal Contemplation at the Stage of Semblance. The Bodhisattva of Equal Contemplation at the Stage of Partial Realization of Truth from the First Abode (*prathamābhūmi*) upward is one who has given rise to true illumination.
One who illuminates to the ultimate source of the true reality (*dharmatā*) is called a Buddha of Equal Contemplation.
