Furthermore, these so-called "Equal Contemplation Bodhisattvas" (*samadarśana-bodhisattva*) are those at the ultimate stage of partial realization (*pradeśa-prativedha*), who are adjacent to the state of ultimate perfection (*niṣṭhā-gata*).
Therefore, they are called "Equal Contemplation Bodhisattvas. They are not "Unequal Contemplation," nor are they "Equal-and-Unequal Contemplation," and so on, up to the class of Mañjuśrī.
One must deeply penetrate this meaning; one must not, upon merely hearing that "contemplating the mind" (*citta-darśana*) is the goal, immediately become confused and conflated.

One who possesses overweening pride acts as a *caṇḍāla* among bodhisattvas; if one does not accept these words, it means one lacks faith in the definitive teachings (*nītārtha*) of all Mahāyāna sūtras.
The Bodhisattva King of Sovereignty over Samādhi, by means of the threefold contemplation within a single mind, is able to contemplate the nature of the mind; this is called "supreme samādhi.
Having attained this supreme samādhi, he achieves mastery over all true and conventional meditative concentrations, just like a king.
The Bodhisattva Dharmeśvara,

through single-minded threefold contemplation, correctly contemplates the three truths; his mind is free from obstruction, and he possesses mastery over all phenomena within the ten realms of existence.

The Bodhisattva Dharmalakṣaṇa [represents] the manifestation of the dharma-characteristics of the three truths of all phenomena within the ten dharma-realms through the single mind and the three contemplations.
The Bodhisattva Prabhālakṣaṇa...
The light of wisdom from this single-minded threefold contemplation can manifest the true reality (*dharmatā*).
Bodhisattva Guangyan (Light Adornment):
the wisdom-light of the single-minded threefold contemplation adorns the Dharma-body.
The Bodhisattva Mahāvyūha, with single-mindedness, contemplates the nature of the mind through the threefold contemplation; that nature is vast and expansive like empty space.
Because the object is great, wisdom is great; this great wisdom adorns the Dharma-body.
As for the Bodhisattva Ratnakūṭa:

with single-mindedness he practices the threefold contemplation, correctly observing that although the nature of the mind is empty, it is fully endowed with the dharma-treasures of the myriad practices;
because these are accumulated, he is named Ratnakūṭa (Treasure Accumulation).
As for Bodhisattva Prajñākūṭa,
when his single-minded threefold contemplation accords with the *dharmatā*, it is the accumulation of the four types of eloquence (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*).
As for Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi...
The completion of the three contemplations of mind constitutes the hand that possesses the jewels of both provisional and ultimate wisdom;
thus, he is the Bodhisattva Jewel-Seal Hand.
With the seal of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa-mudrā*), he seals the hand of wisdom consisting of the three contemplations within one mind.
The Bodhisattva Constantly Raising the Hand represents the mind of right contemplation seeking the fruit of Buddhahood with the hands.
The Bodhisattva Constantly Lowering the Hand...
The hand of wisdom of the three contemplations is the unconditioned great compassion that transforms sentient beings below.
The Bodhisattva Samantabhadra dwells in the mind of right contemplation and takes pity upon sentient beings.
The Bodhisattva Nandendriya:
through correct contemplation, he attains the Tathāgatagarbha, his heart filled with great joy like a pauper finding a treasure trove.
The Bodhisattva Nandarāja.
Through the threefold contemplation in a single mind, one attains the true Middle Way; with the joy of the Dharma, one is as sovereign as a king.
Bodhisattva Bianyin, through the threefold contemplation in a single mind, discerns the sounds of various regions throughout the dharma-realm, penetrating them all within a single mind.
It is an obstruction.
As for the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha:
if one contemplates the nature of the mind as being like space, having no accumulation whatsoever, it is then called a "garbha" (storehouse).
Bodhisattva Grasping the Precious Torch:
with single-mindedness and the threefold contemplation, he wields the precious torch of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment to illuminate and reveal the source of the mind.
Bodhisattva Jewel Courage.
By correctly contemplating the nature of the mind, one perceives the treasure of all dharmas; thus, within the realm of birth and death, the mind possesses courage.
This is the Bodhisattva Treasure-Viewing.
By employing the three contemplations within a single mind, one contemplates the treasure of wisdom and clearly perceives the Buddha-nature.
As for the Bodhisattva Imperial Net:

it is like the Dharma-net of a sovereign king, which is immeasurable. Through the single mind and threefold contemplation, one contemplates the principle of the Three Truths, fully possessing the net of all immeasurable dharmas.
This net ensnares all afflictions and sentient beings.
Regarding the Bodhisattva Mingwang (Net of Light):

as stated in the *Siyi jing* (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi-sūtra), "bright light constitutes the Dharma-net"; and in the *Dazhidu lun* (Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra), it is said that emitting light forms a net, using the analogy of a fisherman casting a net.
This refers to the single mind and the threefold contemplation (*sankuan*) wherein one contemplates the luminous net of the mind.
The Bodhisattva of Objectless Contemplation,
with single-mindedness, contemplates through the threefold contemplation that causes and conditions are ultimately unobtainable; seeing neither the contemplating subject nor the contemplated object,
the essence of true cultivation manifests as objectless, thought-free, and eternally observing within stillness.
The Bodhisattva Jñānasaṃcaya possesses the accumulation of all wisdom through the three contemplations with a single mind.
The Bodhisattva Ratnavijaya.
The Jewel of Supreme Contemplation surpasses all jewels of the world.
The Bodhisattva Heavenly King, through correct contemplation, manifests the ultimate reality (paramārtha); having attained the ultimate reality, he possesses sovereignty like a king.
The Bodhisattva Huaimo (Destroyer of Māra):
the mind of correct contemplation can destroy the two extremes and the eight māras.
The Bodhisattva Diande (Light-Virtue).
When one concentrates the mind on the three contemplations, the true insight that realizes the principle arises swiftly, and the three contemplations are immediately perfected;
it is like seeing the path at once when lightning flashes in the night.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Sovereign King.
Through the threefold contemplation of the single mind, one attains the nature of true self and achieves sovereignty over all phenomena, like a king.
Regarding the Bodhisattva Adorned with the Marks of Merit:
through the threefold contemplation of the single mind, one is able to embody the myriad virtues; the marks of these myriad virtuous merits adorn the Dharma-body.
The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda,
through the correct contemplation of the Middle Way, attains the Buddha-nature and achieves the Siṃhanāda Samādhi.
The Bodhisattva Garjitasvara.
Observing the mind, one perceives the Middle Way; his vast learning and sublime conduct are like the thunderous roar that startles all those hibernating in the ice of the two extremes.
This is the Bodhisattva Sound of Colliding Mountains.

Just as when two mountains strike one another, the sound pervades the four directions, so too does the correspondence between the object and wisdom of correct contemplation give rise to the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
The Gandhahastin Bodhisattva,
through correct contemplation, is free from the stench of afflictions and is able to bear the burden of all beings.
The Bodhisattva White Fragrant Elephant:
He correctly contemplates the fundamental nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), which is originally devoid of any dark or evil influence, giving rise instead to pure and wholesome dharmas.
Because his five-part body emits fragrant incense, he is named "White Fragrance. He gives rise to all forms of loving-kindness and compassion, bearing the burden of all beings like a white elephant.
It is like an elephant.
The Bodhisattva Constantly Diligent correctly contemplates diligence and perceives the true permanence of the dharma-nature, thereby accomplishing the four right efforts of non-action.
The Bodhisattva Never-Despising correctly contemplates emptiness and non-emptiness, not dwelling in the one-sided emptiness of the conjured city of rest.
The Bodhisattva Wondrous Birth.
Contemplating that the mind is unborn, all phenomena are unborn; this is the wondrous birth of Prajñā.
The Bodhisattva of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra contemplates that the mind possesses the causes of merit and wisdom, which adorn the Dharmakāya.
Regarding Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra* states: "By contemplating the heart-vessel and focusing the mind on a single point, one will immediately behold Avalokiteśvara.
As for Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva...
The accomplishment of right contemplation subdues the enmity of Māra and restrains all heterodox teachers.
Regarding the Bodhisattva Brahmajāla:
the Sanskrit name signifies the pure net of right contemplation and the pure Dharma-net for all sentient beings, both internal and external.
The Bodhisattva Ratnadanda (Precious Staff).
Contemplating the mind as being endowed with merit and wisdom constitutes the staff; by relying on this Dharma-treasure staff, one advances toward the fruit of Bodhi.
It is also said that sentient beings rely on this staff to enter the Middle Way.
The Bodhisattva Asaṃjñeya,
through single-minded threefold contemplation, attained the wisdom of the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa), such that no dharma of the mundane or supramundane worlds could surpass it.
Bodhisattva Arraying the Land:
"With single-mindedness, observe that when the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure.
Bodhisattva Golden Topknot:
The attainment of the wisdom of the true mark through the threefold contemplation with a single mind is called "Golden Topknot" (Suvarṇacūḍa), which signifies provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*);
because it adorns the head of the mind, it is called the "Golden Topknot.
This refers to the Bodhisattva Maṇicūḍa.

The threefold contemplation in a single mind is precisely the wisdom of the true reality (dharmatā), as clarified in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* regarding the bright pearl within the topknot of a wheel-turning sage king.
Maitreya Bodhisattva—
This refers to Maitreya, who through the single mind and threefold contemplation attains unconditional compassion (*nirālambana-maitrī*), like a magnet attracting iron.

As for the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, if he perceives the Buddha-nature through the single mind and threefold contemplation, he is endowed with the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*) which are neither vertical nor horizontal; therefore, it is called "sublime" (*miao*).

The Virtue is likewise: when these Bodhisattvas cite a single contemplation gate (*vipaśyanā-mukha*) to specifically designate their name and lead sentient beings to take refuge in their hearts—if each person were to possess all contemplation gates, then their names would be mutually interpenetrating;
this is what is meant by "equality of names," "equality of words," and "equality of dharmas. One who can understand it in this way will, within the mind of right contemplation, behold [the truth].
Because all Buddhas are one, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:
"If there are those who can believe what you have spoken, they shall see me, as well as you and the assembly of bhikṣus, along with all the bodhisattvas. What does this mean?
The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* says that the Tathāgatas of the ten directions share a single Dharma-body; they are of one body and one wisdom-power.
Fearlessness is likewise so; thus, what has preceded was an explanation by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas based on the contemplation of the mind. Question:

How can ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) employ this contemplation of the mind to explain the meaning of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas? Answer: This very sutra states: "Where should one seek the liberation of all Buddhas?
One should seek it within the mental activities of all sentient beings. If one clings merely to the literal text...
"To seek the liberation of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas apart from words and the mind is like clutching a stone and throwing oneself into a deep abyss,
or wandering at night without a lamp.
Such were the thirty-two thousand people [who spoke thus].

This is the fifth major section, which concludes by asking whether all these bodhisattvas are necessarily in the stage of the ten grounds (*daśabhūmi*) as equal-enlightened ones (*samyaksambuddha*) in their final birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*).
The answer is: the masters of the North say they range from the first ground to the tenth;
the masters of the South say they are in the eighth, ninth, or tenth grounds. Furthermore, there are masters who cite the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*) as an analogy.

It is said that they are all in the stage of the "place of succession" (the bodhisattva stage immediately preceding Buddhahood). Now, I say this is not so. Since the preceding clarification of "original and trace" has already determined their relative status, it is unfathomable;
why then must one definitively judge them?
*Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra-vyākhyā*, Fascicle Four.
Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra Commentary, Scroll Five (From "Furthermore, there were ten thousand Brahmā kings" to "his eyes never for a moment left [him]").
Furthermore, ten thousand Brahmā kings, such as Śikhin and others, came from the other four continents to the place where the Buddha was to listen to the Dharma.

The following section is the third [part], which distinguishes the assembly of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and clarifies that the various devas, the eight classes of supernatural beings, and the fourfold assembly all heard this sutra together, thereby serving as evidence to prove that the transmission of the scripture is not erroneous.
Within this group, it is not that there are no noble ones (*ārya*) of either the Great or Small Vehicles;

however, the discussion is conducted from the perspective of the majority. Furthermore, they are designated as "ordinary beings" in contrast to the aforementioned assembly of noble ones. Regarding this:
There is the real and there is the provisional. If one follows actual karma and afflictions to undergo birth, this is the real ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
If a Dharma-body Bodhisattva dwells in the twenty-five samādhis to shatter the twenty-five states of existence and manifests birth through responsive traces, this is the provisional.
This scripture praises the Bodhisattva above, saying: "He enters the five paths of rebirth to manifest his body"—this is precisely that meaning.
It is also said that "because sentient beings are ill, the Bodhisattva is also ill"—the meaning lies here.
Therefore, regarding those among the eight classes of devas and the fourfold assembly who sat in the audience and heard the sutra, one should apply a fourfold analysis (*catuṣkoṭi*).
As it is stated by the side in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: "To be lax regarding the precepts is not called laxity; rather, to be lax regarding the Vehicle is what is called laxity."
There are many ways to explain this; here, we shall adopt one perspective to interpret this sūtra passage by means of a fourfold classification:

first, both morality (*śīla*) and the vehicle (*yāna*) are urgent; second, morality is lax while the vehicle is urgent; third, morality is urgent while the vehicle is lax; fourth, both the vehicle and morality are lax.
Generally speaking, regarding all wholesome dharmas and all contemplative practices, both morality and the vehicle are involved.
Those who obtain these precepts all obtain this vehicle (*yāna*). Now, to distinguish separately between the precepts (*śīla*) and the vehicle:

from the three refuges, the five precepts, the ten wholesome paths, and the eight fast-day observances, up to the monastic discipline (*vinaya*) and even the discipline concomitant with meditative concentration (*samādhi-sahaja-śīla*), which can restrain body and speech and prevent the fruits of the evil realms—obtaining the name of "human" or "deva" is what is called the "precept-vehicle.
As for the "vehicle," it refers to either the understanding produced upon hearing the sutras or the wisdom of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*).

Investigating the Four Truths and the principle of the arising and ceasing—and the non-arising and non-ceasing—of the twelve links of dependent origination, the wisdom that can destroy afflictions and transport one out of the three realms is called a "vehicle" (*yāna*). Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:

"Virtue with signs does not move or emerge; virtue without signs can move and emerge. However, there are distinctions between coarse and subtle regarding precepts, and likewise distinctions among vehicles.
Regarding the distinction between the Great and the Small, the clarification of this meaning now consists of two parts: first, the profound explanation; second, the commentary on the scriptural text.
The profound explanation is briefly divided into seven points.

First, clarifying the differences in the urgency of the vehicle (*yāna*) versus the precepts (*śīla*), and the differing encounters with the Buddha. Second, clarifying the two aspects of faith and the Dharma...
Chapter Three: The Faculties of Practice; Chapter Four: Clarifying the Faculties of the Two Vehicles, Great and Small; Chapter Five:
Clarifying the Faculties of the Gradual and Sudden Approaches to Hearing the Dharma; Chapter Six: Clarifying the Bodhisattva’s Manifestation as an Ordinary Person;
Chapter Seven: Clarifying the Contemplation of the Mind; Chapter Eight: Clarifying the Transformation of Others.

First, clarifying that the relative urgency of the precepts (*śīla*) and the vehicle (*yāna*), as well as the difference in encountering a Buddha, constitutes the formal explanation of the preceding four lines:

1. Clarifying those for whom both the precepts and the vehicle are urgent: - When the precepts are urgent, one receives the retribution of humans or devas; by further practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one gives rise to the "concentration-bound precepts" (*samādhi-samvara*) and receives the body of a Brahmā.
- When the vehicle is urgent, one sees a Buddha and attains the Way. This refers to the various devas and the fourfold assembly in this sutra.

This assembly has gathered for this very purpose: that while their adherence to the precepts may be lax, their pursuit of the Great Vehicle is urgent. Because their practice of the precepts is lax, they have committed transgressions and were born in the three evil realms;
yet because their pursuit of the Vehicle is urgent, they have encountered a Buddha and heard the Dharma, thereby attaining the Path of the Sages today.
This is why dragons, spirits, yakṣas, asuras, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and so forth, all come to hear the Dharma; such is the intent. And so on...
When the Mahāvaipulya Dhāraṇī was being preached, Vasu emerged from hell and came together with various sinners to listen to the Dharma;

furthermore, the multitude of hungry ghosts also came to listen to the Dharma. When the Buddha preached the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, all manner of spirits, ghosts, birds, beasts, and so forth came as well.
Moreover, when the Buddha emitted light during the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* (Great Chapter), those in hell immediately attained liberation.

Those who cast off their bodies as hell-beings and are reborn in the six heavens of the desire realm to descend and listen to the Dharma all did so because, in the past, their practice of the precepts was lax while their pursuit of the Mahāyāna was urgent.
Question: Since the three evil realms are difficult places, how can one attain the Way there? Answer: Because they are few, it is said that they do not attain it;
it does not mean that they absolutely cannot attain the Way. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "It is like a human body having..."
Although the man with the black mole is not called a "black man," it is not that he lacks blackness.

If one is urgent regarding the precepts but lax regarding the vehicle, one will obtain the status of a deva or human and receive various rewards of pleasure; yet if one is lax regarding the vehicle, one will not encounter a Buddha or hear the sutras.
Even if one were to encounter a Buddha and hear the sutras, one would still not enter the Path—just as the thirty trillion households in Śrāvastī did not [attain liberation].
The passage "Seeing the Buddha" refers to the thirty thousand billion households who, though they saw the Buddha, did not come to hear the Dharma.
The phrase "the devas of the higher realms" refers to those who, being attached to celestial pleasures, do not come to hear the Dharma; this is precisely what is meant.

The statement that during the Zhou dynasty the Buddha appeared in the world, such that stars fell like rain yet the people of this land could neither see the Buddha nor hear the sutras, all conveys this same meaning. (4)
It is clarified that if both the precepts (*śīla*) and the vehicle (*yāna*) are lax, one falls into the three miserable realms (*apāya*).

If the vehicle is lax, one fails to see the Buddha or hear the sutras, wandering through birth and death without end. Second, it clarifies that the root-natures (*gotra*) of the two practices—faith (*śraddhā*) and Dharma (*dharma*)—are different;
this consists of two points: first, the root-nature of faith-practice (*śraddhā-carita*); second, the root-nature of Dharma-practice (*dharma-carita*). First, the root-nature of faith-practice:

This refers to that which is accomplished through the cultivation of the merit of hearing-wisdom (*śrutamayī-prajñā*). These individuals are all those from the past who were learned, having received, upheld, recited, heard, and expounded the teachings.
Within this category, there are four types: first, those for whom both the precepts and the vehicle are urgent;

they obtain the bodies of humans or devas, see the Buddha, hear the sutras, and enter the Path of the Sages. Second, those for whom the precepts are lax but the vehicle is urgent; they receive birth as dragons or spirits.
First, when the conditions for meeting a Buddha and hearing the sutras are equal, one may likewise enter the Path of the Sages.

Second, when the precepts are urgent but the vehicle is slow, although one may be born among humans or devas and enjoy the pleasures of the five desires, one will not meet a Buddha, hear the sutras, or enter the Path.

Third, when both the precepts and the vehicle are slow, one will be born in the three evil realms, failing to meet a Buddha or hear the Dharma, thus wandering through birth and death and sinking into the ocean of suffering.
There is no limit to this. Those who study the meaning [of the teachings] today must certainly grasp this intent:

those whose faculties are rooted in the practice of the two dharmas achieve wisdom through the cultivation of habitual practice; these are precisely the practitioners of seated meditation and contemplative conduct from the past.

The distinctions between gain and loss regarding the fourfold classification of the vehicle and the precepts can be understood by analogy with the faculties of those whose practice is based on faith; however, these belong only to those of sharp faculties.

There is a distinction in that some, having heard only a little, are immediately able to observe and penetrate [the truth]. Those who practice seated meditation and contemplation must also take this deeply to heart.

Third, explaining the differences between the capacities of the Great and Small Vehicles: this refers back to the two types of capacity—those following faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and those following the Dharma (*dharmānusārin*)—each of which has different capacities of Great and Small.
This constitutes two parts: first, those who follow by faith; second, [those who follow by Dharma].
The nature of the faculties for those who practice according to the Dharma is twofold and distinct: first, the nature of the faculties for those who practice through faith in the Mahāyāna;
second, the nature of the faculties for those who practice through faith in the Hīnayāna. Regarding the first, the practitioner of faith in the Mahāyāna faculties:

in the past, they heard the Mahāyāna; being urgent regarding both precepts and vehicle, their urgency regarding the precepts led them to be born among humans or devas, and their urgency regarding the vehicle led them to hear the Mahāyāna once again.
Regarding those who attain awakening through hearing, the gains and losses of the remaining three phrases are of a different category than the preceding case, as can be known.

Next, for those of the śrāvaka lineage who are practitioners by way of faith: in the past, they were urgent regarding both the śrāvaka precepts and the vehicle; being urgent regarding the precepts, they were reborn among humans and devas;

being urgent regarding the vehicle, they again heard the śrāvaka teachings and attained awakening through hearing. The gains and losses of the remaining three phrases are of a different category [from this]. This may be understood.
Knowing the two types of clear understanding, one should know that the natures of the faculties for practicing the Dharma also differ between the Great and Small Vehicles;
the four permutations regarding the relative laxity or urgency of the precepts and the vehicle can be understood through the category of those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*).

However, the distinction lies in the fact that those with sharp faculties who practiced contemplation in the past have few [scriptural] hearings and personally contemplate the realization of principle (*tattva*). Fourth, clarifying the differences in the natures of sudden and gradual faculties consists of two parts.

First, it clarifies that within each of the two practices of the Mahāyāna, there are those of sudden-rooted capacity; second, it clarifies that within each of the two practices of the Hīnayāna—faith and dharma—there are those of gradual-rooted capacity.
First, regarding the clarification that within each of the two Mahāyāna practices of faith and dharma there are those of sudden-rooted capacity, this is divided into two parts.
The first clarifies the sudden-rooted capacity of the Mahāyāna practice of faith: if, from immeasurable kalpas past, one has heard...

If one upholds, recites, explains, or transcribes Mahāyāna sūtras, and if both the vehicle (*yāna*) and the precepts (*śīla*) are urgent, one will immediately be reborn among humans or devas as Śakra or Brahmā;
encountering Vairocana, one hears the teachings of the seven locations and eight assemblies and enters the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*).
This is like the rising sun first illuminating the high mountains. If the precepts are lax while the vehicle is urgent, one may fall into the three evil paths and receive the body of a nāga.

Even for spirits, asuras, mahoragas, wind and rain deities, and others who hold the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), if they hear the teaching of the seven locations and eight assemblies from Vairocana, they will awaken to and understand the Mahāyāna and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

If their observance of the precepts is strict while their progress on the vehicle is slow, yet they receive the bodies of humans or devas and encounter Vairocana to hear the teaching of the seven locations and eight assemblies, [they shall likewise attain awakening]; however, if both their vehicle and their precepts are lax, [they shall not].
Falling into the three evil realms, they fail to encounter a Buddha to hear the teachings of the seven locations and eight assemblies; thus they transmigrate through birth and death without end.

Next, it clarifies those of the Great Vehicle who possess sudden faculties—namely, those who formerly studied the Great Vehicle and practiced seated meditation, cultivating the three contemplations in one mind through the provisional-middle-middle-provisional contemplations, and whose practice of the precepts was urgent.
The fourfold categories of gain and loss regarding the "relaxed" [practice] can be understood by analogy with the Mahāyāna faith-practice (*śraddhā-carita*);

however, those of sharp faculties who have heard but little are able to personally observe and penetrate [the truth], which results in a distinction. Second, to clarify the two types of faith and dharma-practice for those of gradualist dispositions in the Hīnayāna:
first, the person of gradualist disposition through faith, who, lacking the capacity for sudden enlightenment, is not included [among the sudden practitioners].

The teaching of the *Avataṃsaka* regarding the seven locations and eight assemblies was established because those with the karmic conditions for gradual enlightenment were able to hear the Tripiṭaka, the Vaipulya, the Mahāprajñāpāramitā, and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* sūtras.
However, one must distinguish between the four permutations of the urgency or laxity of the precepts and the vehicle (*śīla-yāna*), as there are differences in the attainment or failure of practice.
To know this beforehand is like the metaphor of the "poisonous drum" clarified in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. If...
When the sound of the poison drum is heard, those near die and those far away also die.
"Those near die" is a metaphor for hearing the teachings of the *Avataṃsaka*, seeing the Buddha-body at the outset, and immediately accepting it with faith to enter the wisdom of the Tathāgata.

"Those far away also die" is a metaphor for those whose faculties and conditions lead to gradual enlightenment: they initially cultivate the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), distancing themselves from the Buddha-way, and subsequently hear the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā sutras.
If one reaches the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and *Nirvāṇa*, all have already attained the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata;
this is illustrated by the analogy of hearing the sound of a poison-drum, where even those at a distance die. That the flavors arise from one another is precisely the intended meaning here.
That upon this inconceivable seat of liberation there are devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings as the assembly of fellow listeners is, namely:

Regarding those who are urgent in both precepts and vehicle, urgent in precepts but slow in the vehicle, or slow in both precepts and vehicle—do these also possess the karmic conditions for the two practices of faith and Dharma?

Furthermore, among those with the two types of root-natures—those for whom both precepts and vehicle are urgent, and those for whom precepts are slow while the vehicle is urgent—who encounters a Buddha and hears the sutras to attain the Way?

Question: Are there also those whose precepts are urgent but whose vehicle is slow, or whose precepts and vehicle are both slow, who likewise possess the karmic conditions for the two practices of faith and Dharma?
When asked about attaining the Way, he replied: "If one encounters a Tathāgata, it serves as the causal condition for both the vehicle (yāna) and the precepts (śīla) to be urgent.
If one does not encounter a Buddha and hear the sutras, it nonetheless serves as the causal condition for both the vehicle and the precepts to be urgent within the True and Semblance Dharma periods.
Therefore, as the Tathāgata was about to enter nirvana, he left this bequest: 'Abide by the Prātimokṣa and dwell in the four foundations of mindfulness.'"
The practice of the Path and the entrustment for its circulation are both causes and conditions for making faith, conduct, and the vehicle equally urgent.

Question: If it is only the case that they serve as causes and conditions for making the precepts and the vehicle equally urgent, how can there also be the causal conditions for those whose precepts are lax while their vehicle is urgent?
Answer: The Buddhas and Tathāgatas employ the path of peace and security to act as these causes and conditions.

However, because the karmic defilements of sentient beings are deep and heavy, although they may uphold the Great Vehicle and practice seated meditation and contemplation, they are unable to purely maintain the Brahma-precepts.
This constitutes the causal condition for a "slack vehicle and urgent vehicle" disposition.

Even though their precepts are slack and they fall into the three evil realms, if in the future they encounter Maitreya and the thousand Buddhas appearing in the world, they will hear the teachings of both the gradual and the sudden, and thereby attain [liberation].
Regarding "entering the Way," the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "One who is lax regarding the precepts is not truly called lax. This is precisely its meaning.

One who is lax regarding the Vehicle (*yāna*) is indeed called lax. Although one may be born among humans or devas and enjoy the pleasures of the five desires due to being strict regarding the precepts while lax regarding the Vehicle, once that karmic fruit is exhausted, they will continue to transmigrate through birth and death. Therefore, one must not be lax regarding the Vehicle.
This is what is meant by being "slack. Therefore it is said: "It would be better to die as Devadatta and enter hell than to be born in heaven and enjoy the pleasures as Udraka Rāmaputra.
Devadatta originally attained the stage of *uṣmagata* (warmth), yet through his evil karma he fell into hell;
upon emerging and regaining a human body, he became a Pratyekabuddha, possessing such sharp intelligence and wisdom that he surpassed Śāriputra and Udraka Rāmaputra.
Although Fu attained rebirth in heaven, once his heavenly merit was exhausted, he fell back into the three miserable realms, transmigrating through the flow of birth and death without end.

Fifth, it clarifies that Bodhisattvas manifest traces in accordance with ordinary beings in order to meet those with whom they have a karmic connection and go together to the Buddha’s presence to hear the sutras.
Dharma-body Bodhisattvas abide in twenty-five samādhis, while sentient beings abide in twenty.
When the five sense organs are stimulated, one should accordingly receive the bodies of the twenty-five realms of existence.

If one receives a body within the four evil destinies, it is due to the power of the roots of goodness of the stainless samādhi, the non-retrogressive samādhi, the mind-joy samādhi, and the samādhi of joy;

thus, one assumes a body in the four destinies to lead those whose precepts are lax but whose aspiration for the Vehicle is urgent, so that they may practice both the path of faith and the path of the Dharma.

When sentient beings of the two vehicles—great and small—and of sudden or gradual capacities come to hear the Śākyamuni Buddha’s teachings of both the gradual and the sudden, he provides the causal conditions for them to enter the Way;
if their discipline and vehicle are both lax, he acts as the cause and condition for them to become both urgent.

Next, by dwelling in the twenty-one samādhis, such as the Illusion-like Samādhi, through the power of his roots of goodness and compassion, he receives [the offerings of] the twenty-one kinds of humans and devas.

As the one who guides those whose practice of both precepts and vehicle is urgent, as well as those who believe in both the sudden and gradual teachings of the Great and Small Vehicles, all beings come to hear these two teachings—sudden and gradual—in order to attain entry into the Way.

Second, for the sake of those who are urgent regarding the precepts but slow regarding the vehicle and thus cling to the pleasures of devas and humans, this serves as the causal condition for them to cultivate the practice where both precepts and vehicle are urgent. Now, at this inconceivable Dharma-seat...
Among the eight classes of beings and the fourfold assembly, there are Dharma-body Bodhisattvas who manifest in the bodies of these eight classes and fourfold assemblies;
this is precisely that meaning. Sixth, regarding the contemplation of the mind:

if a person’s contemplative practice—whether of the Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna—is such that both the vehicle and the precepts are urgent, they shall in the future receive the body of a human or deva and attain the sight of Maitreya and hear his teaching.

If one’s practice of the Dharma is lax while their vehicle is urgent, they will receive a body in the three evil realms in the future, yet they shall behold Maitreya and hear the Dharma to enter the Way.
If one’s practice of the precepts is urgent while their vehicle is lax, they will receive a body among humans or devas in the future, but they will not behold Maitreya;
even if they were to behold him, being attached to pleasure and negligent, they would be unable to draw near. If both the precepts and the vehicle are lax, [the same applies].

In the future, they will fall into the three miserable realms and never encounter a Buddha or hear the sutras; even if they were to see or hear them, they would ultimately be unable to resolve their minds toward enlightenment.

If they cannot practice seated meditation and contemplative cultivation, nor engage in recitation, lecturing, or exposition, then the nature of their roots for faith-practice and the relative urgency or laxity of their observance of the precepts and the vehicle can be known. Seventh, regarding the transformation of others: if one practices contemplative cultivation...
When one is proficient in seated meditation and preaching, one should observe the mental activities [of others].

By using these four points to discern gain and loss, one will clearly perceive that the karmic conduct of those being transformed differs; thus, their future suffering or happiness, their ascent or descent, and their success or failure in entering the Path will be known exactly as they are.
One should guide them with this intention. Second, the commentary on the scriptural text follows.
Regarding the assembly of ordinary beings, there are four parts: first, the assembly of Brahmā devas; second, the assembly of Śakra devas;
third, the assembly of the eight classes of beings; and fourth, the assembly of the four divisions of followers. First, concerning the ten thousand Brahmā kings:
"Brahmā" is an Indian term translated here as "Leaving" (li) or "Pure Conduct" (jingxing). The Brahmā King is the sovereign of the Sahā world and dwells within the First Dhyāna.

Question: The Abhidharma states that from the second dhyāna upward there is no dharma of speech, and thus no establishment of a king. Yet the *Āṭānāṭiya-sūtra* (Yingluo jing) clarifies that each successive dhyāna has its own Brahmā King.
Now, it is said that these [higher realms] merely add the cultivation of the immeasurable minds (*apramāṇa-citta*), and because their retribution is superior, they act as kings;
however, they possess no governing authority. In the first dhyāna, because there is vitarka and vicāra as well as speech, there is a presiding leader.
He thus became the lord of the Sahā world. This was due to his past practice where both precepts and vehicle were urgent;

because his observance of the precepts was urgent, he attained the first dhyāna, and by further cultivating the four immeasurable minds, he was born in the Brahma Heaven as its king, leading all the Brahmas of the first dhyāna to come and listen to the Dharma.
If a Bodhisattva manifests such traces, it is the White-colored Samādhi and various other samādhis.

Due to the influence of the power of ignorance, one is born in the Brahma Heaven of the First Dhyāna; there, through transformation, he leads the various Brahma assemblies to come and listen to the Mahāyāna.
As for Śikhin, this translates as "Fire" or "Fire-Head," and it is also said to translate as "Conch-Crest";
because the flesh-tuft on his crown resembles a conch shell, he is named "Conch-Crest. Considering the introduction to the *Lotus Sūtra*, it is likely that he belongs to the Second Dhyāna.

Regarding the phrase "the kings and others," this refers to those who attained the third and fourth dhyānas. These were all individuals from the past who were equally diligent in both the precepts (*śīla*) and the vehicle (*yāna*).

Because they were diligent in the precepts, they attained the second, third, and fourth dhyānas; by cultivating the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), they were reborn in the heavens according to their meditative states.
However, because they were diligent in the vehicle, they have come to hear the Dharma. If these are Bodhisattvas manifesting as traces...

This refers to abiding in the *yuganaddha-samādhi* (the samādhi of the pair) to produce the *dvitīya-dhyāna-ghoṣa-svara-samādhi* (the thunder-sound samādhi of the second dhyāna), producing the *tṛtīya-dhyāna-varṣa-samādhi* (the rain-showering samādhi of the third dhyāna), and producing the *caturtha-dhyāna* to lead the various Brahmā assemblies to come and listen to the Dharma. Question: For what reason do they come from other four-continent worlds?
Answer: Because the upper realms dwell in the vast expanse of space, their place of origin is difficult to know; thus, one uses the lower to infer the upper.
Knowing that he was about to arrive, it was said that he had come from another of the four continents.
Furthermore, twelve thousand Śakras also came from other of the four continents and took their seats in the assembly.
This second section clarifies that Śakra is Śakradevendra, the lord of the gods dwelling on earth.
"Śakradeva" is translated as "Capable of Action" (Nengzuo). Regarding this Śakradevendra: after the parinirvāṇa of the previous Buddha Kāśyapa, there was a stūpa that had fallen into ruin.
A certain woman resolved to repair it, and thirty-two other people likewise gave rise to the aspiration.
Those who assisted in the restoration of the stūpa and those who performed the merit of restoring the stūpa became the thirty-two lords of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Those who assisted in the restoration became the thirty-two auxiliary ministers; when the number of sovereign and ministers are combined, they are called the Thirty-three Gods (*Trāyastriṃśa*).

These celestial emperors and their retinues were all those who, in the past, were diligent in both morality (*śīla*) and spiritual practice (*yāna*), and who further cultivated pure acts of giving and various merits.
Therefore, having been born in that heaven, because their practice regarding the vehicle was swift, they have come together to this assembly.

The provisional manifestations of the Bodhisattvas, as well as the Heavenly Emperor and his retinue, are all born in that heaven through the熏 (perfuming) of the *Durjayasamādhi* (Unconquerable Samādhi); they have come to lead the various devas attached to pleasure to listen to the Dharma.
As for those who have come from the other four continents, these four continents possess only one [such being].
"Lord of Devas, since there are now twelve thousand [deities], it is said that they have come from the other four continents.
Question: "The superior devas of the upper realms are very numerous; for what reason are Brahmā and Śakra singled out? Answer:
"Brahmā is the first heaven of the Form Realm (rūpadhātu) and is the lord of the Sahā world; therefore, he must be singled out. Furthermore, he is the one who invited the Buddha."

The Lord who turns the wheel of Dharma is also a *dānapati* (patron) of the Buddha; therefore, he is specifically identified first. Furthermore, the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the higher realms of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

The Heavenly Emperor (*Śakra*) is the lord of the gods dwelling on earth in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); he too requested that the wheel of Dharma be turned and is likewise a *dānapati* of the Buddha.
Furthermore, other deities of great majesty and power— gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas,
kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and so forth— all came to the assembly.

This is the third section concerning the eight classes of beings (*aṣṭa-devanikāya*). Since the significance of these eight classes is extensively related to many matters, they will not be fully analyzed here;

rather, I shall explain them according to the text of this sūtra. Regarding the "eight classes" and the other gods of great power (*mahānubhāva*), the term "great power" applies universally to all eight classes;
it is spoken of by taking the most eminent among them, yet all of them possess great power. The deities explained above are merely those who have appeared.
Brahmā, Śakra, and the gods of great power in the realms of desire and form, along with their retinues, have all come to this assembly.

Now, furthermore, those from the entire Desire Realm—namely, the Four Heavenly Kings, as well as the kings and their retinues of the Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmita-vaśavartin heavens—have all come together with their followers to hear the Dharma. As for the Form Realm...
The four dhyānas are also where the five Śuddhāvāsakāyika deva kings and their retinues reside;

because they all previously practiced both the precepts and the vehicle with urgency and further cultivated dhyāna, they were born in those heavens. Because of their urgency regarding the vehicle, they come together with their retinues to listen to the Dharma.
If Bodhisattvas manifest through expedient traces in these heavens, they abide in the Immovable Samādhi (Acalasamādhi) and give rise to the four heavens.
The King’s Samādhi of Heavenly Joy gives rise to the blue Samādhi of the Yāma Heaven;
the yellow Samādhi gives rise to the Tuṣita Heaven; the red Samādhi gives rise to the Nirmāṇarati Heaven;
and the Mirror-like Samādhi gives rise to the five classes of Anāgāmin Heaven—all in order to invite these devas to come and listen to the Dharma. He asked:

Question: Why do Bodhisattvas not come from the Heaven of No-Thought (asaṃjñisattva) or the four formless realms (ārūpyadhātu)? Answer: The Heaven of No-Thought belongs to the non-Buddhists (tīrthika).

Although Bodhisattvas may dwell in the Samādhi of Emptiness-like-Quiescence (śūnyatā-samādhi) and be born in that heaven, it is explained from the perspective of the majority: because their past discipline was intense while their vehicle was lax, most do not come.
As for the Bodhisattvas in the four formless heavens, they dwell in the Samādhi of Non-obstruction (anāvaraṇa-samādhi) and are born in the realm of space (ākāśa).
Those who dwell in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness arise from the Samādhi of Constant Abiding; those who dwell in the Sphere of Nothingness arise from the Samādhi of Joyful Abiding;

and those who dwell in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception arise from the Samādhi of Self-Abiding. They are also born in those heavens, but because they are formless (*arūpin*), they do not come to listen to the Dharma.

Even if they were to come, being formless, they could not be seen nor perceived through sensory function; thus, their status as fellow-hearers is established by inference. As it is said: [text fragment].
Because these various devas have not yet attained such discernment, they are specifically referred to as "devas" here. As for the *nāgas*, they belong to the animal realm;

their primary retribution (*pratyaya*) is that of snakes, while their secondary environment (*upādāya*) consists of palaces made of the seven treasures that resemble those of the devas. They are also able to transform themselves into extremely handsome human forms.

In the past, they were lax in their observance of the precepts but zealous in their practice of the vehicle [of cultivation]. Due to this laxity in the precepts, they fell into the state of a *nāga*; however, because of their generosity, they obtained such excellent rewards.
Because their karmic retribution resembles that of the devas and their resolve is swift, they come with their retinues to listen to the Dharma;
for example, when the bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita preached the Dharma to four nāgas, they closed their mouths and moved away, yet upon hearing the Dharma, they immediately attained awakening.
Bodhisattvas dwelling in the *avaivartika-samādhi* are born into the nāga realm to lead all nāgas to hear the Dharma. Gods (*deva*) and yakṣas both belong to the realm of ghosts (*preta*).

"Yakṣa" is translated here as "light and swift. There are three kinds of yakṣas: first, those on the earth; second, those in the void; and third, those in the heavens who serve as attendants to the devas.
These all fall into the realm of ghosts and spirits because they were lax in their observance of the precepts while being impetuous in their practice [of the Way].

Due to their evil and poisonous nature, they receive the body of a yakṣa. Because they practiced a small amount of giving, they also have a slight karmic fruit: [the possession of] carriages and horses.
Because of their past generosity, they are able to fly through the air; because of their swift progress, they are able to come with their retinues to listen to the Dharma.
If a bodhisattva’s tracks are identical [to theirs], it means they dwell in a mind that delights in samādhi and acts as a spirit, ghost, or yakṣa to lead them to come and listen to the Dharma.
Gandharva is translated here as "Fragrance-Body" (xiāngyīn); these are deities who soar upon the mountains and skies. Is this not so?
Those who consume wine, meat, and fragrances require only the fragrance to sustain the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

It is further said that these are the banners of the Lord of Heaven, the abodes of the gods of inverted pleasure (*viparīta-rati*) who dwell upon the ten jeweled mountains. They manifest various extraordinary forms and ascend to heaven to perform music;

because they were fond of watching performances and listening to music in past lives, their discipline was lax, and they fell among the ghosts and spirits. These musical deities are the fruit of their giving, resembling the gods of the heavens. [The Asuras...]

"Rao" (羅) is an old term meaning "no wine," or it refers to one whose body is large; because he gathered flowers from the four continents to brew wine in the ocean, it did not succeed, hence he is called "No Wine.
It is also translated as "Non-God" (Asura); although this deity's retribution is most excellent and ranks as a peer to the various devas, he is nonetheless not a deva.
Furthermore, it is translated as "Not Handsome"; he only produces daughters, while his father, Śacīpati, is handsome.
Because his brothers and kinsmen were all ugly, he is said to be "not upright. Some say that while the men are ugly, the women are upright;

because this deity was jealous of others who possessed beautiful women in the past, he receives a retribution of constant fear. This is also a case of being lax in the precepts but urgent in the vehicle (*yāna*).
Being lax in the precepts leads to falling among the asuras, yet because one is urgent in the vehicle, one listens to the Dharma. The Bodhisattva dwells in joy.
One should give rise to the *muditā-samādhi* (samādhi of joy) to draw them forth and cause them to listen to the Dharma. *Garuda* is translated here as "Golden-Winged Bird";

this belongs to the realm of animals (*tiryagyoni*). Furthermore, because in the past their discipline was lax while their aspiration for the vehicle was urgent—due to lax discipline they fell into the conduct of a *garuda*, and due to practicing generosity there is a wish-fulfilling jewel beneath their necks; they take dragons as their food.

Because their vehicle is swift, they are able to come and listen to the Dharma. When Bodhisattvas abide in the Samādhi of Non-retrogression, their traces are identical to those of rebirth, and they are drawn forth to listen to the Dharma.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "The Dharmakāya is a garuḍa; the four bases of psychic power are its feet, and compassion is its bright, pure eye.
Abiding at the tree of all-knowledge, the Bodhisattva-garuḍa king [soars] amidst birth and death."
To seize and place gods, humans, and nāgas from within the great ocean upon the shore of nirvāṇa—this is the Dharma-gate of the Golden-Winged Bird (Garuda) of the Non-Retrogression Samādhi.

One should know that the Dharmakāya abides in all samādhis, and that the various Dharma-gates of the nāgas, devas, asuras, and others may likewise be understood by analogy with the Golden-Winged Bird.
*Kiṃnara* is translated here as "Doubtful Deity" (*Yishen*) or "Head."
Above them are the various devas with horns, whose divine retribution for playing stringed and wind instruments is slight; these are the gandharvas.

They too, in the past, were lax in their observance of the precepts but zealous in their practice of the vehicle, delighting in music, and thus were born into the realm of ghosts and spirits as musical deities.

Having cultivated merit to a small degree, they possess a meager karmic fruit; yet because they were zealous in their practice of the vehicle, they come to hear the Dharma. Bodhisattvas abide in their minds, delighting in samādhi.
They are born there to be drawn forth to hear the Dharma. *Mahoraga* refers to the serpent deities, also called earth-dragons;
they are legless, belly-crawling spirits who are the guardian deities of worldly shrines. They receive the wine and meat offered by people, which all enters the serpent's belly.

These beings also have lax discipline while being "swift" in their karmic momentum; they violate the precepts, are deceitful and full of anger, practice little in the way of giving, and are greedily addicted to wine and meat.

If one’s precepts are lax, one falls among the ghosts and spirits; many wrathful insects enter their bodies and devour them. By practicing a little generosity and humility, one receives offerings from others.

[The text] frequently mentions wine and meat; when one encounters a Buddha in a state of urgency and hears the Dharma, the Bodhisattva dwells in a mind that delights in samādhi and manifests this body to lead [beings] to listen to the Dharma.
Thus it is explained for each of the eight classes of beings, one by one.

Regarding the two practices of faith and dharma, the distinctions between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, and the different capacities and conditions of those who follow the sudden or gradual approaches, can be understood from what precedes.
All the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās came together to the assembly.
This is the fourth [section] concerning the fourfold assembly. The term *bhikṣu* contains three meanings, as explained previously. *Bhikṣuṇī* means "woman.

According to a sutra, they are called "male famine-removers" (*pindapātika*) and "female famine-removers"; *upāsaka* and *upāsikā* are translated as "pure-faith male" (*qingxin shi*) and "pure-faith female" (*qingxin nü*).
They are also called "virtuous-dwelling male" (*shan su nán*) and "virtuous-dwelling female" (*shan su nü*), or alternatively, "meritorious men" (*xun shi*).

Although the daughter of the Kṣatriya clan lived as a householder, she observed the five precepts and severed sexual desire; because men and women did not sleep together, she is called "Good Sleeping" (Sunakṣatrā).

This interpretation cannot be definitively applied. These were her past causal practices: being diligent in both the precepts (śīla) and the vehicle (yāna), she was born into the human realm due to her diligence in the precepts, and having encountered a Buddha through her diligence in the vehicle, she heard the Dharma and became a disciple of the Buddha to study the Path. Question: What is meant by this?

Question: The fourfold assembly is already fully equipped; since both the precepts and the vehicle are urgent, for what reason are there those who seek to leave the household life but are not permitted to do so? Answer:
There are some whose minds delight in tonsure and who take pleasure in the flavor of the Buddha-dharma, yet whose bodies and minds both feel weary [of the world];

therefore, when they encounter a Buddha, they leave the household life and realize the Way. There are also those who, though they delight in the Buddha-dharma, do not feel weary of or desire to leave their physical forms; therefore, even when they encounter [a Buddha], they do not [leave].
When the Buddha was at home, he realized the Way; as a Bodhisattva, he dwelt in the Sunlight Samādhi, Moonlight Samādhi, Illusion-like Samādhi, and Mirage Samādhi.

He manifested in the four continents to serve as the fourfold assembly of disciples for the Buddhas, leading all ordinary beings to become members of the fourfold assembly, to hear the Dharma, and to enter the Path.

At that time, the Buddha was surrounded by a respectful assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands who were listening to his teaching of the Dharma. From this point down to the seven-character verses constitutes the second section, the specific introductory narrative (*nidāna*). The description of the manifested auspicious signs (*prātihārya*) expresses that he specifically intends to preach this sūtra, distinguishing it from other sūtras. This section itself is divided into two parts: 1. [The manifestation of the auspicious signs. (The text continues: At that time, the World-Honored One was seated upon a lion throne at the foot of a great jeweled tree in the center of the *Sahā* world, surrounded by a great assembly of bodhisattvas. At that moment, the Buddha emitted a great light from between his eyebrows, which illuminated all the worlds throughout the ten directions. In every direction, there appeared hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of buddha-lands, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, all filled with various jeweled trees. Beneath each jeweled tree sat a buddha, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary characteristics, emitting a great light that illuminated the worlds of the ten directions. Furthermore, within those lands, there were no hells, hungry ghosts, animals, or the realms of asuras; nor were there mountains, rivers, oceans, or the sun and moon. There were only bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, all sitting beneath jeweled trees and listening to the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma. At that time, the Buddha emitted a great light from his mouth, which shone upon the crown of the heads of all the bodhisattvas and śrāvakas. Having illuminated them, the light returned and entered the Buddha’s mouth. Then, the World-Honored One addressed the venerable Mahākāśyapa: "Kāśyapa, do you see these hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of buddha-lands, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, appearing before you? Kāśyapa replied to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, I see them. The Buddha said: "Kāśyapa, these buddha-lands are all pure and free from defilement. However, because sentient beings are attached to their own views, they perceive these lands as impure. Kāśyapa, it is as if there were a man who, having traveled through the southern regions, saw a great pond. Seeing it, he thought to himself: 'This water is so clear and pure that even if one were to cast a hair into it, it would not be disturbed. At that time, there was a leper whose body was covered in sores and oozing pus, who came to the side of the pond and looked down into the water. Because of the filth on his own body, he perceived the water as turbid and foul. Kāśyapa, what do you think? Is that water truly turbid and foul? Kāśyapa replied: "No, World-Honored One. That water is naturally pure and clear; it is only because of the filth on the leper's body that he perceives it as turbid. The Buddha said: "Kāśyapa, it is the same for sentient beings. Because they are attached to their own views, they perceive the pure lands of the Buddhas as impure. Kāśyapa, it is like a man who, having traveled through the northern regions, saw a great river. Seeing it, he thought to himself: 'This river is so deep and vast that even a large elephant could not reach its bottom. At that time, there was a blind man who came to the side of the river and looked down into the water. Because of his blindness, he perceived the river as shallow. Kāśyapa, what do you think? Is that river truly shallow? Kāśyapa replied: "No, World-Honored One. That river is naturally deep; it is only because of the man's blindness that he perceives it as shallow. The Buddha said: "Kāśyapa, it is the same for sentient beings. Because they are attached to their own views, they perceive the profound Dharma of the Buddhas as shallow. Kāśyapa, it is like a man who, having traveled through the eastern regions, saw a great mountain. Seeing it, he thought to himself: 'This mountain is so high and steep that even a great bird cannot fly over it. At that time, there was a cripple whose legs were broken and who came to the side of the mountain. Because of his crippled legs, he perceived the mountain as low. Kāśyapa, what do you think? Is that mountain truly low? Kāśyapa replied: "No, World-Honored One. That mountain is naturally high; it is only because of the cripple's condition that he perceives it as low. The Buddha said: "Kāśyapa, it is the same for sentient beings. Because they are attached to their own views, they perceive the lofty Dharma of the Buddhas as low. Kāśyapa, it is like a man who, having traveled through the western regions, saw a great palace. Seeing it, he thought to himself: 'This palace is so magnificent and grand that even a great king cannot surpass it. At that time, there was a poor man who came to the side of the palace. Because of his poverty, he perceived the palace as small. Kāśyapa, what do you think? Is that palace truly small? Kāśyapa replied: "No, World-Honored One. That palace is naturally grand; it is only because of the poor man's condition that he perceives it as small. The Buddha said: "Kāśyapa, it is the same for sentient beings. Because they are attached to their own views, they perceive the magnificent Dharma of the Buddhas as insignificant. Kāśyapa, it is like a man who, having traveled through the northern regions, saw a great city. Seeing it, he thought to himself: 'This city is so vast and prosperous that even a great sovereign cannot equal it. At that time, there was a beggar who came to the side of the city. Because of his status as a beggar, he perceived the city as desolate. Kāśyapa, what do you think? Is that city truly desolate? Kāśyapa replied: "No, World-Honored One. That city is naturally prosperous; it is only because of the beggar's condition that he perceives it as desolate. The Buddha said: "Kāśyapa, it is the same for sentient beings. Because they are attached to their own views, they perceive the flourishing Dharma of the Buddhas as withered. Kāśyapa, it is like a man who, having traveled through the southern regions, saw a great field. Seeing it, he thought to himself: 'This field is so lush and abundant that even a great harvest cannot surpass it. At that time, there was a man who had lost his eyesight and came to the side of the field. Because of his blindness, he perceived the field as barren. Kāśyapa, what do you think? Is that field truly barren? Kāśyapa replied: "No, World-Honored One. That field is naturally fertile; it is only because of the blind man's condition that he perceives it as barren. The Buddha said: "Kāśyapa, it is the same for sentient beings. Because they are attached to their own views, they perceive the fertile Dharma of the Buddhas as barren. Kāśyapa, it is like a man who, having traveled through the western regions, saw a great forest. Seeing it, he thought to himself: 'This forest is so dense and thick that even a great wind cannot penetrate it. At that time, there was a man suffering from a chronic illness who came to the side of the forest. Because of his illness, he perceived the forest as sparse. Kāśyapa, what do you think? Is that forest truly sparse? Kāśyapa replied: "No, World-Honored One. That forest is naturally dense; it is only because of the sick man's condition that he perceives it as sparse. The Buddha said: "Kāśyapa, it is the same for sentient beings. Because they are attached to their own views, they perceive the dense Dharma of the Buddhas as sparse. Kāśyapa, it is like a man who, having traveled through the northern regions, saw a great jewel. Seeing it, he thought to himself: 'This jewel is so precious and rare that even a great king cannot obtain it. At that time, there was a man of low birth who came to the side of the jewel. Because of his low status, he perceived the jewel as worthless. Kāśyapa, what do you think? Is that jewel truly worthless? Kāśyapa replied: "No, World-Honored One. That jewel is naturally precious; it is only because of the low-born man's condition that he perceives it as worthless. The Buddha said: "Kāśyapa, it is the same for sentient beings. Because they are attached to their own views, they perceive the precious Dharma of the Buddhas as trivial. Kāśyapa, it is like a man who, having traveled through the
From the time the Buddha granted [the request] until the end of the long prose section is called the "Introductory Section on the Arising" (Nidāna).
From the point where the son of the elder finishes speaking the verses is called the "Introductory Section on the Narration.

As for "arising," it means manifesting signs to specifically indicate the intention to preach this sutra; since "manifesting" takes the sense of bringing forth, and he was about to preach the inconceivable Dharma-body of liberation.
Because this is the essence of the Buddha-land and the core principle of cause and effect,
three auspicious omens appear to signify the intention to expound the inconceivable Dharma-body of liberation and the three kinds of pure lands that serve as its basis. First,

the manifestation of the majestic and sublime *vairocana-kāya* (body of universal manifestation) signifies the intention to expound the essence of the Dharma-body of true-nature liberation, and also signifies the intention to expound the [intrinsic] nature.

The pure true realm, the eternal tranquil land of light, is represented by the two sons of elders offering five hundred jeweled canopies which, through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, merge into a single canopy.

This further symbolizes the intention to preach the Dharma-body of perfect retribution, wherein the various causes have been fully gathered and synthesized into a single reality of wisdom and liberation.
It also symbolizes the intention to preach the perfectly pure land of actual retribution. Third, the manifestation.
The Buddhas of the three thousandfold world-systems preaching the Dharma all appear within the canopy;
this is the boundless great function that manifests the desire to preach the *upāya* (expedient means), the liberation of the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body). Question:

How is it known that this manifests the *vairocana-kāya* (special majestic body) to signify the desire to preach the inconceivable ritual, the true nature, and the liberation of the *dharmakāya* (truth body)? Answer: As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*: [as in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*].
The sutra clarifies the exalted special body (*viśeṣa-kāya*) by using the metaphor of Mount Sumeru reflecting in the ocean, such that no other mountains can equal it;

this sutra is likewise so. Furthermore, in the *Lotus Sutra*, it is explained that when a wealthy elder resides in a city, his majesty and virtue are uniquely sublime, causing the impoverished son to flee in alarm;
this refers to the Tathāgata manifesting the exalted special body to preach the *Avataṃsaka* teachings for those of inferior capacity.
Because he was capable of this, he avoided [the king] from afar; he immediately cast off his jeweled necklace and donned tattered, soiled garments.

This was to manifest as an old bhikṣu in order to preach the teachings of the Tripiṭaka. After passing beyond this stage, with minds that accorded with one another in faith, they entered and exited without hindrance.
He manifested the body in tattered garments and then appeared in a majestic and dignified form—this is the manifestation of the *vairocana-kāya* (the Body of Sovereign Excellence).

This refers to the teaching of the Vaipulya scriptures: the elder manifests his majestic form within the house and commands the impoverished son to take charge of the family property—this is the manifestation of the *vairocana-kāya* (the body of supreme marks).
Furthermore, it refers to Subhūti being commanded to turn the wheel of the teaching by expounding the *Prajñāpāramitā* for the sake of all bodhisattvas;
moreover, it refers to the gathering of kings, ministers, and retinues within the house to formally establish the relationship between father and son.

"By nature you are truly my son, and I am truly your father"—this was precisely when the Lotus Sūtra manifested the Honored One’s Universal Body (*vairocana-kāya*) to bestow predictions of enlightenment upon the śrāvakas.
First, he was seen from afar and avoided; next, he entered and exited without hindrance; then, he took charge of the various goods;
finally, the natural bond of father and son was established. Thus, the noble Elder Śreṣṭhin appeared four times, adorned with his jeweled necklaces.
The adornment of the body is entirely a metaphor for the supreme, extraordinary body of the Honored One Śākyamuni;

its immeasurable and boundless radiance and form are all intended to manifest the teaching of the Dharma-body of true reality (*dharmatā*). This sutra is a Vaipulya teaching, wherein entering and emerging are without difficulty:
though he emerges from a thatched hut and sees an old garment, once he enters the house, he beholds [the splendor].

The Elder Āmrapālī—the Elder Āmrapālī is none other than the present Buddha—surrounded by a multitude of immeasurable beings, manifested his supreme and extraordinary body (*vairocana-kāya*) and asked:
"How is it known that he manifests this supreme and extraordinary form to signify the preaching of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*)?
He replied: "The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: 'I adorn my body with marks; its radiance illuminates the world. No... [text continues].
The *Dàpǐn jīng* (Mahāvaipulya Sūtra), which was expounded for the sake of those honored by the multitude, states: "The true reality (*yathābhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all dharmas is itself the Buddha;
because the true reality of all dharmas has no going, this sūtra also says: 'Contemplate the true reality of the body; contemplating the Buddha is likewise. Question:
How can this further express the Pure Land of Tranquil Light (*śāntaprabhāsa*)? Answer: Since this sūtra already...
Since taking the Buddha-land as the primary principle already manifests the Dharma-body of pure wisdom, does it not also manifest the land of the pure object?
The Dharma-body is itself the Pure Land; apart from the body there is no separate land, and apart from the land there is no separate body.
However, since True Suchness and the Real Mark are neither wisdom nor objects—yet are spoken of as wisdom and objects, and neither body nor land—yet are spoken of as body and land...
That which is manifested in the body is precisely the manifestation of the Buddha-land; therefore, the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"When wisdom practices the penetration of *vijñapti-mātra*, one thus grasps the Buddha-land. It is not a physical form, for its primary substance is not ornamentation, yet it is the ornamentation [of the land].
This sutra says, "As the mind is pure, so the Buddha-land is pure. Since this expresses the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the true mind, is it not an expression of the eternal?
The Land of Tranquil Light (*śāntaraśmi-kṣetra*) merely expresses the meaning of the body, which generally accords with the previous explanation;
whereas the *Samantaprabhā-sūtra* expresses the meaning of the land specifically, correctly indicating that what is about to be explained is the Buddha-field (*buddhakṣetra*). Question:

When the canopies are joined to manifest the land, how is it known that this expresses the lands of both the retribution-body (*vipākakāya*) and the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*)? Answer: Five hundred small canopies combine to form one great canopy; does this not express the assembly?
These causes combine to form one great fruit; this "great fruit" is precisely the *dharmakāya* of perfect retribution (*pūrṇavipāka*).

Where there is a *saṃbhogakāya*, there must be a *saṃbhogakṣetra*. Therefore, this sutra states: "When a Bodhisattva practices such deeds as *dāna* and attains Buddhahood, sentient beings such as these come to be born in that land.
Question: This clarifies the attainment of the Way by the *nirmāṇakāya*; how can it serve as proof for the existence of the *saṃbhogakṣetra*?
Answer: Because the *saṃbhogakāya* (recompense body) is perfected, there is the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body), which is established according to the realm.
Regarding the introductory section on the manifestation [of the Buddha], it is divided into two parts. First, clarifying the Buddha’s manifestation of his body, which has three distinct sections:

first, the Buddha preaching the Dharma for the great assembly; second, the illustration by means of a simile; third, the application of the simile. Regarding the first, the Buddha preaching the Dharma for the great assembly: "Majestic and most venerable... [and so forth].
Regarding the manifestation of the form-body of the Honored and Victorious One that preaches the inconceivable Dharma-body of liberation:
at that time, the Buddha was respectfully surrounded by an assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands who he taught the Dharma. This assembly consisted of four types:
first, the "initiating assembly," such as Ratnakūṭa, Mañjuśrī, Maitreya, and others, who mutually inspire one another.

Second, the responsive audience (anugraha-parṣad), which includes those in this land and other lands, such as Dharma-body Bodhisattvas, provisional manifestations, devas, nāgas, the eight classes of beings, and the fourfold assembly.

Third, the audience according to their capacity (yathābhavyatā-parṣad), who derive benefit upon hearing the teaching, such as the five hundred elders whose precepts and vehicle were both urgent, those whose precepts were lax but whose vehicle was urgent, and the devas, nāgas, the eight classes of beings, and the fourfold assembly. Fourth, the conclusion.
Regarding "conditioning the assembly," it means acting as the condition for the pores [of those present] to receive moisture, so that they may gradually attain future understanding;

this refers to those for whom the vehicle of morality is urgent while the vehicle [of wisdom] is slow, or for whom both morality and the vehicle are slow—namely, the eight classes of devas and nagas and the fourfold assembly.

These four categories encompass all assemblies. "Respectfully surrounding" clarifies that the internal spiritual capacity has been awakened; "surrounding" refers to the act of encircling [the Buddha].
The four sides are completely surrounded; this represents a city with four gates through which one enters to see a sovereign ruler.
The four gates move according to the turning of the Buddha’s teachings, representing the seeing of the inconceivable true nature, the Dharma-body of liberation.
As for the one who preaches the Dharma: formerly, Master Shangtong questioned the Tripiṭaka Master Changshen, who said, "When the Buddha was in the world..."

Question: What kind of Dharma did he preach to the immeasurable great assembly? Answer: He preached the *Samantaprabhā-sūtra*. "Universal Collection" (*samanta-prabhā*) refers to that which is subsumed within the Vaipulya teachings.

The reason it serves as the introduction to this present sutra is that while that [previous] scripture explains the causes and effects of the primary retribution (*vipāka*), this [present] scripture explains the causes and effects of the Buddha-land as the secondary environment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
Since the primary retribution necessarily possesses its basis, it serves as the introduction. This is, for example, like...
First the *Anantārthika* (Infinite Meanings) is spoken, followed by the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* (Lotus of the True Dharma); thus, the *Anantārthika* serves as the introduction (*nidāna*).
It is like Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, manifesting within the great ocean.
These two parables illustrate [the teaching]. As for "Mount Sumeru," this is translated as "Peaceful Brilliance" (*An-ming*) or "Exalted Height. What does it mean?

To "delight in loftiness" is also to "delight in greatness. This metaphor refers to the Buddha’s body of true recompense (*sambhoga-kāya*) and the sublime, extraordinary body (*vairocana-kāya*), for it reaches the pinnacle of the ultimate reality (*dharmatā*).
Thus, it is said to "delight in loftiness"; because its merit and wisdom pervade the entire *dharmadhātu*, it is said to "delight in greatness.

As for the manifestation at the great ocean, this reveals that those in the fourfold assembly who have a karmic affinity with this seat possess roots of goodness through the four gates; it also reveals all [beings].
The ocean of birth and death of sentient beings is like a mountain rising majestically from the vast blue sea, yet it can emerge in splendor beyond the sea.
The Buddha does not dwell in birth and death, nor does he abandon birth and death. Because he does not dwell in birth and death, he is as high as a mountain;
because he does not abandon birth and death, his reflection appears in the great ocean. Although the seawater is not the four colors of blue, yellow, white, or crystal, [it reflects all things].

The waters reflecting the jewels on the four sides of the mountain thus possess four kinds of colors on those four sides. This clarifies that the minds of sentient beings are not [limited to] the four gates;
the Buddha, through the skillful means (*upāya*) of *siddhānta*, teaches the four gates so that the minds of good and evil are extinguished.
When one understands that the fundamental nature is identical to the Dharma, there is no further divergent understanding regarding the teaching of the four gates.
He sits peacefully upon a lion throne of various jewels, surpassing all the assembled multitudes who have come.
These three combined serve as a metaphor: "sitting peacefully upon various jewels" represents the principle of the myriad virtues of the *dharmatā*;
the "fearless lion throne" represents the emptiness (*śūnyatā*) of all phenomena; thus, the fearless emptiness of the myriad virtues constitutes the throne. His physical form is majestic and sublime.
The majesty being commensurate with the precious throne is an analogy for how true wisdom, subtle and wondrous, corresponds with all virtues, fearlessness, and the principle of emptiness.

This union is compared to Mount Sumeru; its eclipsing of the entire assembly of those who have come is an illumination of how the teaching of the Mahāyāna eclipses the false understandings of the multitude, such that they collectively achieve the single Great Vehicle understanding. This is precisely...
