It obscures the four gates of all false views and likewise obscures the understanding of the four gates of the Hīnayāna, so that the understanding of the four gates of the Mahāyāna—the Buddha-dharma—is fully realized.
This serves to harmonize and illuminate the analogy of the great ocean.
At that time, in the city of Vaiśālī, there was the son of an elder named Ratnākara, who, together with five hundred sons of elders,
came to the place where the Buddha was carrying seven-jeweled parasols; they prostrated themselves at his feet and each offered their own parasol as a collective offering to the Buddha.
These two clarifications regarding the elder’s son offering the parasol are threefold: first, the elder’s son offers the parasol to signify the cause for its manifestation;
second, the Tathāgata joins the parasols to manifest an auspicious omen; third, the great assembly beholds this omen with joy.
This manifested sign represents these three meanings. Why is this so? Because when the elder offers the parasols and the Tathāgata joins them into one—

The dedication of compassion cultivated within the causal stage toward the fruit of Buddhahood to become non-referential compassion (*anālambana-maitrī*) signifies the realization of the perfect retributive *dharmakāya*;
it also signifies the manifestation of the pure land as the environment (*niśraya-vipāka*). This demonstrates that the primary tenet of this sutra is the cause and fruit of the Buddha-land.
Furthermore, the manifestation of all lands therein represents the pure land of the fruition stage, while the manifestation of all responsive lands represents...

The power and function of this sutra are further seen in the Buddhas of the ten directions preaching the Dharma, which signifies that in every responsive land there must be a Buddha as a transformative master.
That the great assembly rejoices means that upon hearing of the inconceivable liberation, the spiritual capacity for the Buddha-land has been awakened;
they will certainly receive great benefit and thus generate joy in anticipation. Therefore, it is known that these manifested signs secretly indicate the very emergence of this sutra.
Because this serves as the basis for the introductory narrative, a separate preface is provided to elucidate it. Regarding the offering of the parasol by the son of an elder, there are three points:
first, to clarify that the son of the elder came together with his peers; second, to clarify his reverent devotion; and third, to clarify the act of offering the parasol.
As for the first point—clarifying that the son of the elder came together with his peers—the city of Vaiśālī is explained in detail as previously stated.
Because it symbolizes *nirvāṇa*, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Pure dharmas constitute the city; contemplative wisdom forms the walls;
supreme gnosis is the multi-storied pavilion; shame and remorse are the deep moat; the three gates of liberation are the entrances;

right mindfulness is the defense; the four paths are the straight road. By traveling upon them, one exits the realm [of saṃsāra], erects the unsurpassed Dharma banner, and utterly destroys all [afflictions]."
Māra now [realizes that] the luminous nature of purity and nirvāṇa is like a city; it is neither the son of the elder nor the Tathāgata, the son of the elder.
Because the Tathāgata dwells together in this city, he is called the "son" in terms of the cause and the "Buddha" in terms of the fruit.

The fundamental nature is neither cause nor fruit, yet cause and fruit depend upon the fundamental nature; in meaning, they are the same as a city. This explains the meaning of the name Ratnakūṭa (Jewel Accumulation). As for the explanation of the names and meanings: [text continues].
The previous account of the five hundred sons of elders may be understood through its numerical significance;

it represents either the Dharma-gates or the roots of goodness of the five kinds of spiritual lineages (*gotra*). Since there are one hundred within each of the five lineages, this constitutes five hundred kinds of roots of goodness.
Because these are all causes, they are all referred to as "sons. As for the canopy of the seven treasures, it symbolizes the cultivation of the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*).

To cease birth and attain true understanding of the real mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is called the "seven treasures. To give rise to compassion by traversing the various dharmas is termed the "canopy" (*chattrā*).
"Canopy" takes the sense of covering; it signifies the compassionate mind that provides shelter and protection for all sentient beings.

Those who come to the Buddha’s presence do so because, through the conditions of practicing the traversal of dharmas, their compassion is dedicated toward the fruit, becoming the perfected canopy of great non-referential compassion (*anālambana-mahāmaitrī*).
Second, "the reverent one" bows his head to the feet to manifest the ritual of respect; this signifies the superior wisdom of the cause connecting to the inferior wisdom of the fruit.
Third, "offering the parasol" refers to making offerings because the cause possesses the meaning of providing the resources that bring about the fruition.
By the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, he caused all the precious canopies to merge into a single canopy that completely covered the trichiliocosm.

This was the second manifestation: the Tathāgata merged the canopies to display an auspicious sign, universally indicating his intention to preach the inconceivable Dharma-body and pure land of liberation;
specifically speaking, he manifested this inconceivable phenomenon precisely to indicate his desire [to speak].
The explanation of the causes and conditions for the Pure Land of Receptive Retribution (依報淨土) as a Buddha-land consists of two parts:
first, clarifying the convergence of the canopy; second, manifesting the actual appearance. First, regarding the clarification of the covering of the three thousandfold world-system:

the five hundred sons of elders each presented [a jewel], which symbolizes that each has cultivated their own cause; that these converge to form a single canopy symbolizes the attainment of a single, perfect fruit. Since...
When there is a true cause capable of inducing a true fruit, one attains a Buddha-land; this refers to the dependent fruit attained through the inducement of the Buddha-land by its cause.

As for the statement that it "pervasively covers the three thousandfold world-system," this signifies that the essence of the single fruit is none other than unconditioned great compassion, which universally covers the Dharma-realm.
Regarding the primary retribution, the Buddha has already explained it in the *Samantaprabhā-sūtra*; what is discussed here is...
The manifestation of signs correctly indicates the intent to explain the dependent retribution lands that universally encompass the Dharma-realm;
thus, the vast and long characteristics of this world all appear therein.

Second, regarding the clarification of the actual manifestations, there are two parts: first, the manifestation of the lands, and second, the manifestation of the various Buddhas preaching the Dharma.

First, regarding the manifestation of the world’s vast and long characteristics: below this, the actual manifestation of the signs of the *niśraya-vipāka* (retributive environment) lands consists of four parts:
first, the manifestation of the land’s vast and long characteristics; second, the manifestation of the ten mountains; third, the manifestation of the great oceans and rivers;
and fourth, the manifestation of the sun, moon, and celestial palaces. First, the manifestation of the land’s vast and long characteristics directly symbolizes the *niśraya* (support) of the land.
It is called "broad" because it extends horizontally across a hundred billion worlds, and "long" because it reaches upward to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*);
alternatively, it is explained as being "broad" because it spans the ten directions horizontally, and "long" because it reaches the limits of the four lands vertically.
Furthermore, within this trichiliocosm, there are all the Sumeru Mountains, Snowy Mountains, Mucilinda Mountains,
Mahāmucilinda Mountains, Fragrant Mountains, Jewel Mountains, Gold Mountains, Black Mountains, Iron Ring Mountains, and Great Iron Ring Mountains.
The manifestation of the ten mountains likely symbolizes the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*).
The manifestation of the great ocean, rivers, streams,
and springs likely symbolizes the world of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha-loka*).
Furthermore, the sun, moon, and stars, as well as the celestial palaces of the devas, the palaces of the nāgas, and the palaces of all the honored deities, all appeared within the precious canopy.
The four [palaces] appearing below—the sun, moon, and celestial palaces—may perhaps represent the receptacle world (bhājana-loka).
The four types of appearances appearing above likely represent the four kinds of worlds. That these four worlds appear within the canopy signifies that...

Having explained the primary retribution (*vipāka*), he is about to explain the secondary retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*). The secondary retribution of the world is that upon which the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of sentient beings and the physical world (*bhājana-loka*) depend.
Question: Since it currently manifests as the appearance of the insentient (*nirveditaka-lakṣaṇa*), how can it represent the sentient?
Answer: When the Buddha wishes to expound all Mahāyāna sūtras, has the manifestation of signs ever not been like this? If it were to conform to the world of sentient beings...
The five aggregates and the vessel-world (bhājana-loka) are not unclear; however, because the Buddha’s intention is difficult to fathom, let us set this matter aside for now.
Furthermore, the teachings of all the Buddhas of the ten directions also appear within the precious canopy.

These two clarifications manifest all Buddhas and their preaching of the Dharma. If one speaks of the *niśraya-vipāka* (retributive environment) of a Buddha-land, there must necessarily be sentient beings who rely upon it;
since there are sentient beings who can be transformed, there must accordingly be the Buddha’s transformation and guidance of them.
Thus, within the center, the Buddha is manifested and the preaching of the Dharma is manifested. Because four Buddhas dwell in four lands, they are all termed "Buddha-lands."
At that time, the entire great assembly, beholding the Buddha’s supernatural power, marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence;
with palms joined, they paid homage to the Buddha and gazed upon his venerable countenance, their eyes never for a moment turning away.
This section on the three types of assemblies beholding the auspicious signs and rejoicing contains three distinct parts, the first of which is the praise.

1. To exclaim, "This is unprecedented! constitutes the offering of verbal action (*vākkarman*), for he says that such an unprecedented omen—the manifestation of the joined canopy—has never appeared since time immemorial, signifying the Buddha’s intent to describe the characteristics of his buddha-field. 2.

To join one's palms and pay homage to the Buddha constitutes the offering of physical action (*kāyakarman*). 3. To gaze up at the Honored One’s countenance constitutes the offering of mental action (*manaskarman*). Thus it is said.
Because these auspicious omens appear, one will certainly hear the teaching on the inconceivable Buddha-land;
because one will attain the purification of the three karmas and the inconceivable transformation of the three wheels, as well as such immeasurable merits, the joyful mind arises in anticipation.
This is why the three karmas are all extended in offering. However, the manifestation of these omens is primarily intended to inspire and stir the sentiments of sentient beings.
Since the sentiments of the people have already been inspired with reverence and admiration, the Great Sage must now proceed to respond to conditions by preaching the Dharma;
thus, this preface of joy and respect serves to further deepen the meaning of our intimacy. *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra-vyākhyā*, Fascicle Five.

The son of the elder Ratnākara then spoke in verse before the Buddha, saying:
This second, distinct introduction describes the prologue. The manifestations of the Great Sage are difficult to fathom;

were it not for Ratnākara’s sublime and brilliant wisdom, who could know what they signify? Desiring to inspire the assembly at that time, Ratnākara spoke thirty-six lines of verse in praise to make them understand that these auspicious omens manifested to indicate the teaching on the *Buddhakṣetrapraṇidhāna* (Vows for the Buddha-field) and the analysis of faith and understanding.
His eyes are pure, long, and wide like blue lotuses.
Regarding these thirty-six lines of verse that praise and extol [the Buddha], there are two distinct parts:
first, seventeen lines that describe the reasons for the manifestation of the proclamation; second, nineteen lines that formally describe the manifestation of the auspicious omens.
Regarding the reasons for expressing this in the preceding table, there are two parts: first, nine lines describing the praise of the *sambhogakāya* (enjoyment body) as the proximate cause;
second, eight lines describing the praise of the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) as the remote cause.
As for what is called the "superior *sambhogakāya*," it refers to the physical body, its marks and signs, and its radiance manifested when teaching the Mahāyāna to bodhisattvas.

The "excellent response" (śubha-nirmāṇa-kāya) refers to that which possesses manifest majesty and excellence; by seeking this excellent response, one immediately attains the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

As for the "inferior response" (hīna-nirmāṇa-kāya), it refers to the physical manifestations shown when teaching the Tripiṭaka for the sake of Śrāvakas; these are inferior, and by seeking such an inferior response, one does not perceive the Dharma-body.
Thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "The elder immediately removed his jeweled necklace and put on worn-out, soiled garments..."

With dust covering his body, he appeared as though possessed by fear. He asked: "For what reason is the *saṃbhoga-kāya* (the superior response-body) near, while the *nirmāṇa-kāya* (the inferior response-body) is distant?
He replied: "The *saṃbhoga-kāya* is near because it is that which preached the *Saṃnipāta-sūtra* on this very seat; since it manifests such auspicious signs, it is near.
The *nirmāṇa-kāya* is distant because it is that which formerly preached the Tripiṭaka teachings; its presence depends on remote conditions, and thus it is distant."
Yuan You asked: "The accounts of the three inferior vehicles within the Tripiṭaka are naturally matters of the past;
how can they serve as the distant causes for this sutra? Yuan You replied: "The Lotus Sutra states: 'For twenty years you were constantly made to remove excrement;

after this period had passed, our minds came to accord with one another through mutual trust, and you entered and left [the house] without difficulty. Therefore, at the present time, together with all the śrāvakas..."

In expounding the Mahāyāna sūtras, he manifests a superior *nirmāṇakāya* (response body). The appearance of the canopy and the manifestation of auspicious omens serve as signs that he is about to preach on the Buddha-lands (*buddhakṣetra*).

One should know that this is because the inferior response body of the past is made to yield, and the superior response body of the present is manifested; the manifestation of omens serves as the sign of this emergence. Thus, it constitutes the "remote cause.
Regarding the nine lines of verse that describe and praise the manifestation of omens, there are two parts: first, the initial two lines provide a brief praise of the superior response body.

The physical form and voice of the Dharma-body provide two kinds of benefit; this is followed by seven lines of verse that extensively praise these superior benefits of the physical form and voice of the Dharma-body.

Now, here we briefly and extensively praise these two benefits of form and voice, both of which describe what the Buddha previously taught to the fourfold assembly in the *Samantavyūha-sūtra* regarding the Middle Way and the causes and effects of the primary retribution (*pratyaya-vipāka*). How is this known? It is because the subsequent verses praise it by stating: "He preached..."
Dharmas neither exist nor do they not exist; they arise through causes and conditions. Regarding the preceding two lines, which praise the benefit of form and sound, there are two parts:
the first line praises the benefit of form, and the second line praises the benefit of sound.
The first phrase praises the merit of physical appearance (*rūpa*), and the second phrase praises the merit of the mind (*citta*). Therefore, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* says:
The Buddha-nature is both form and non-form. Why is it called form? Because it is the diamond body (*vajrakāya*) and because it is said to possess the thirty-two marks.
Why is it non-form? Because the ten powers and four fearlessnesses are dharmas that are not form.
Now, the first phrase praises the merit of form; praising it in terms of the eye is precisely one aspect of the thirty-two marks of the diamond body.
Regarding "marks" (lakṣaṇa): although the parts of the body are many, that which is most honored is the head; and although the parts of the head are many, that which is most essential is the eyes.

Thus, by praising the superior, one encompasses the inferior; citing the eyes serves as the praise. Although the wisdom and merits such as the ten powers (daśabala) and the fearlessnesses (vaiśāradya) are numerous, praising the mind encompasses them all without exception.
Therefore, citing these essentials, one praises both form (rūpa) and mind (citta). As for what is called "the eyes":
This is another name for the eye; the eye presides over the liver, and when the liver is moved by compassion, the eyes shed tears.
Thus, praising the eye is itself praising great compassion. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that Prajñā is the Mother of Buddhas, while Great Compassion is the mother of Prajñā.
Therefore, it is based on these characteristics that the merit of form (*rūpa*) is praised. Question: Does the Dharma-body also possess characteristics? Answer: [The answer follows].
It is said: "This refers to the supreme response-body (nirmāṇakāya) manifesting the Dharma-body. By seeking this characteristic of the eye, one attains the Dharma-body Buddha-eye;

'The subtle and wondrous pure Dharma-body possesses the thirty-two marks. However, 'eye' is a general name; when distinguished according to its function..."

There are five eyes: first, the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*), which sees coarse material forms; second, the heavenly eye (*divya-cakṣus*), which sees subtle material forms that are the results of causes and conditions;
third, the wisdom eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*), which sees both coarse and subtle forms as well as the principle of partial truth regarding the mind;

fourth, the Dharma eye (*dharma-cakṣus*), which sees all phenomena as conventional truths consisting of the causal conditions of coarse and subtle form and mind, expressed through provisional names; and fifth, the Buddha eye (*buddha-cakṣus*), which sees the Middle Way and the perfect, true Buddha-nature.
Principle can also simultaneously illuminate both coarse and subtle causes and conditions, as well as phenomena and principle;
now, based on the four teachings, it is clarified that there are four distinct types of Buddhas, and the meaning of the five eyes is likewise distinguished into four different types.
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* clarifies that Subhūti, the Tathāgata possesses the fleshly eye, up to and including the Buddha-eye. [The Buddha said: "Not so, Subhūti."
He addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the Tathāgata possesses the fleshly eye, up to and including the Buddha-eye.

'cultivated' (xiū) means long, and 'broad' (guǎng) means wide. Because the five eyes perceive objects with vertical depth and exhaust their ultimate source, they are called 'cultivated.'"
It is called "vast" because it extends horizontally throughout the entire dharma-realm. Regarding the phrase "like a blue lotus," the literal explanation is as follows:

"His eyes are pure, long, and wide, like blue lotuses. Now, I shall briefly analyze the five eyes and provide a commentary on the phrase "eyes are pure."
"Long and wide like a blue lotus" means that its significance differs from that of the fleshly eye.

Horizontally, it sees the ten directions within and beyond the realms. Thus it is called "broad. It is pure and stainless, like the sands of the Ganges and the countless names [of dharmas]. Therefore, it is like a blue lotus. As for the Dharma-eye being "long and broad like a blue lotus": vertically, it sees the fourfold Four Truths within and beyond the realms; thus it is called "long. Horizontally, it sees the ten directions within and beyond the realms. Thus it is called "broad. It is pure and stainless, like the sands of the Ganges and the countless names [of dharmas]. Therefore, it is like a blue lotus. As for the Dharma-eye being "long and broad like a blue lotus": vertically, it sees the fourfold Four Truths within and beyond the realms; thus it is called "long. Horizontally, it sees the ten directions within and beyond the realms. Thus it is called "broad. It is pure and stainless, like the sands of the Ganges and the countless names [of dharmas]. Therefore, it is like a blue lotus. As for the Dharma-eye being "long and broad like a blue lotus": vertically, it sees the fourfold Four Truths within and beyond the realms; thus it is called "long. Horizontally, it sees the ten directions within and beyond the realms. Thus it is called "broad. It is pure and stainless, like the sands of the Ganges and the countless names [of dharmas]. Therefore, it is like a blue lotus. As for the Dharma-eye being "long and broad like a blue lotus": vertically, it sees the fourfold Four Truths within and beyond the realms; thus it is called "long. Therefore, it is like a blue lotus. As for the Dharma-eye being "long and broad like a blue lotus": vertically, it sees the fourfold Four Truths within and beyond the realms; thus it is called "long. Horizontally, it sees the ten directions within and beyond the realms. Thus it is called "broad. It is pure and stainless, like the sands of the Ganges and the countless names [of dharmas].
