Entering into all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), these phenomena are all truly profound and vast. Previously, the primary cause (*hetu*) was explained as that which evokes the Buddha’s *dharmakāya*;
now, the dependent cause (*pratyaya*) is clarified as that which evokes the Buddha’s land (*buddhakṣetra*). Regarding giving (*dāna*), there are five kinds: first, the giving of worldly matters;
second, the giving by those of the Three Piṭakas, the Two Vehicles, and Bodhisattvas; third, the giving by Bodhisattvas who follow the common teachings...
Bestowing upon the four types of Bodhisattvas of the Separate Teaching; bestowing upon the five types of Bodhisattvas of the Perfect Teaching.
Regarding worldly matters of giving, there are six kinds, namely the six paths of giving:

first, if one commits the ten evil deeds, violates the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts, or destroys the Triple Gem—as in the case of Devadatta who transformed Ajātaśatru—[this constitutes such giving].
If a worldly king bestows wealth as a reward for those bhikṣus who have plotted rebellion, or if one who has broken the precepts and committed evil acts is able to practice giving—
such forms of giving lead to rebirth in hell after death and are called "hellish dāna. Second, if one commits the ten non-virtuous actions,
breaks the precepts, and is full of anger, yet practices giving, they will later fall into the realm of dragons, where their dependent retribution consists of palaces made of the seven treasures.
Giving that resembles the karmic retribution of a celestial being, yet results in entering the scales and flesh of a serpent or insect, where the body suffers itching and heat from shifting sands,
or giving obtained through breaking precepts, arrogance, or intimidation— such as when one later receives the body of a *garuḍa*— is called the "giving of animals. Furthermore,
the three types of action and the ten unwholesome paths, including breaking precepts, flattery, poison, and unrighteousness [constitute such giving].

If one gives material gifts while receiving the retribution of a yakṣa, or if one breaks the precepts, is deceitful and fraudulent, is addicted to wine and meat, and harbors much anger and resentment, giving such illicit material gifts constitutes *dāna* for a mahoraga; this is what is called the "giving of ghosts and spirits.

Fourth, if one maintains the precepts slightly but is jealous and harbors resentment, yet performs many meritorious deeds, one will fall among the asuras by the power of their environmental retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*).
Those who resist and oppose the heavens will experience many terrors as their primary retribution;

this applies even to Gandharvas, Kinnaras, and others whose giving is characterized by flattery and insincerity, and who, while fond of music, are able to practice charity and show respect—all such beings are categorized within the realm of ghosts (*preta*).
If one opens the classification to six realms, they are categorized within the realm of asuras. Fifth, if one upholds the ten [precepts]...
If one maintains the five precepts and practices giving for one's own sake with a frivolous mind, a narrow mind, or a restricted mind, this is the *dāna* of the Vaiśya or Śūdra.
If one maintains the precepts with a sincere and earnest mind and gives wealth acquired in accordance with the Dharma, this is the *dāna* of the householder (*gṛhapati*).

If one maintains the precepts, delights in the Path, and respectfully gives what one has extensively studied, this is the *dāna* of the Brāhmaṇa. If one maintains the precepts with reverence... [text continues]
To give with a heart of reverence and compassion, being able to relinquish one’s own wealth and also teaching others to cultivate merit—such is the *dāna* of a Kṣatriya king.

These various forms of giving are all the *dāna* of humans. Sixth, if one practices the superior grade of the ten wholesome paths, maintains the precepts with meticulous care, listens to the Dharma with respect, practices kindness and charity, is filial and obedient, offers flowers, incense, and continuous lamps, and honors precious objects in accordance with the Dharma and with purity.
Generosity consisting of material wealth and merit is all *deva-dāna* (giving to the gods), as clarified in the Vinaya Piṭaka.

For instance, it is recorded that a young boy who worked for hire made a vow to be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven after providing offerings to the Saṅgha, and the Buddha confirmed his rebirth there.

Observing the precepts more subtly, up to the practice of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) with a mind of renunciation, results in birth in the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*); such giving is called *bhāvanā-deva-dāna* (giving through cultivation). It is thus with these and other such cases.

First, it is explained that all acts of giving are worldly matters, and thus the retributions for the fruits of giving differ. Second, regarding the *dāna* (generosity) of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas of the Tripiṭaka:

they contemplate the impermanence of causes and conditions and employ the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) such as the faculty of discernment (*pravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*) and the faculty of relinquishment (*tyāga-saṃbodhyaṅga*). By sacrificing their bodies, lives, and wealth, they attain the path of the Two Vehicles.
For example, when a monk serving as the administrator (*sthavira*) of an āraṇya monastery suddenly encountered a band of thieves who required someone to perform a spirit-exorcism ritual...
They burst into the monastery intending to seize the Elder and the Second Elder, wishing to take their bodies as ransom;
this continued down through the ranks until they reached the last novice, who also begged for his life as ransom. The bandits said, "The sun is setting and we must depart in haste;
why delay? The novice then spoke a verse to the bandits, saying: "My years are but three or five; my flesh is fat."
Furthermore, when one offers what is crisp and delicious as a sacrifice to the gods, the gods receive great joy;

when a thief steals much wealth and returns to provide for his wife and children, he never fears the local officials nor leaves the marketplace. When other thieves hear of this, they rejoice and go to offer sacrifices to the gods.
A *śrāmaṇera*, however, contemplates impermanence with single-mindedness, his mindfulness continuing in uninterrupted succession; thus, even as the blade is placed upon his neck, it falls away.
However, when the thief realized that the Arhat had attained the Way and that his own neck was no different from the one being cut, he was greatly startled and asked why this was so.
The śrāmaṇera immediately ascended into the void and manifested the eighteen transformations; he then preached the Dharma for the thieves.

Out of a sincere heart, he took their place in death, and they now attained realization of the Way. Upon hearing this, the entire band of thieves all gave rise to the aspiration for the Way and sought to leave the world.
All such [giving] as these are the *dāna* of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).

If a Bodhisattva’s *dāna* involves relinquishing body, life, and wealth while contemplating impermanence (*anitya*) and making vows of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), such as King Śibi offering his own body to replace that of a pigeon with a heart free of regret—this is called the *dāna* of the body.
Regarding the fulfillment of the causes and conditions for relinquishing life, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* clarifies the stage of the causal ground (*hetubhūmi*) of Śākyamuni and Devadatta.
Each served as a leader of a herd of deer, and all the herds were gathered together in one place. While the king was out hunting, he surrounded this herd of deer.
Śākya, the deer-king, gave rise to this thought: "We have followed one another for a long time; why must we all die at once?
He then ran swiftly toward the king, while arrows flew from all four sides like rain. The king said to his attendants, "Stop! Do not shoot!"

"The deer have come to seek refuge with me; there must be a profound purpose behind this. When the deer arrived before the King, they prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet and knelt for a long time, addressing the King:
'We are fortunate to have been born within Your Majesty's kingdom. Now that we are surrounded and captured, how could we dare offer any excuse?

However, Your Majesty’s food supply is not great, and now the lives of all these deer are to be extinguished at once. We beg that you grant us release, so that on each day one deer may be dispatched [to provide your meal].'"

The deer were used to supply the kitchen so that fresh meat was never lacking; yet, all at once they died, and not only would our lineage be severed, but it is also feared that the King’s need for fresh meat will likewise be difficult to satisfy.
The King agreed to their words, and they returned to their dwelling place.
Both herds of deer were thus preserved in safety, and each day one deer was designated to provide the kitchen with its meal. It was now the turn of a deer from the herd of Devadatta to be selected.
A doe had recently given birth to two fawns; she was taken to the kitchen, and subsequently, the two fawns died from lack of milk.
Thereupon, the doe went to her king, prostrated herself with her head at his feet, and wept as she recounted her own impending death without regret.

She said only this: "I think of my two children; since they have been deprived of nursing, their death is certain beyond doubt. I pray that Your Majesty will extend your compassion and wait for the time when the next offspring is born."
"Since I am able to sustain myself and dare not refuse death, Tāṭaka, the deer king, became greatly enraged and said, 'Death is your lot;
who shall I send to replace you? The doe immediately thought to herself, 'My king lacks compassion and does not grant me mercy.
She then joined that herd and went to where the Śākya deer king was, prostrated before him, and with great sorrow recounted the aforementioned matter concerning her king."

Since you do not show compassion or pity, I beg the King to devise a plan for our sake to preserve the lives of my two children. Śākya, the Deer King, immediately gave rise to a compassionate thought;
after reflecting for a long time, he replied to the mother deer: "Within your own herd, someone should die in your stead. How much more so for me?
If this matter were not within my lot, it would be fitting for my own body to take its place, so that you and your children may survive."
"Your life may be spared; you may return to that herd to raise these two young ones. Thereupon, the Deer King went at once to the kitchen.
When the kitchen attendants saw that the deer’s body was magnificent and robust, they did not dare to slaughter him and reported this to the Great King. The King sent for him to be summoned.
Once the Deer King had arrived, he prostrated himself and stood kneeling. The King then asked, "The other deer are already exhausted, yet you have come?"
Then the deer knelt and replied, "By Your Majesty’s compassionate grace, our herd has become increasingly numerous and flourishing.
However, there is one doe in that herd who has recently given birth to two fawns; as they have no substitute, they have come to seek refuge with me.
I reflected that unless I take their place, how could they survive? Therefore, I have come to serve as their substitute."

The King’s cook prepared a meal for the Great King, who was greatly astonished and marveled; he immediately replied to the deer, saying, "You have the form of a deer, yet you possess human compassion and benevolence.
You shall take the place of that dead deer-king; now you may return, and I shall release all the other deer.

Such various causes and conditions of the Bodhisattva giving up his life are called the perfection of the *dāna* of giving up life. As for the fulfillment of the three kinds of material giving, it is like Prince Sudāṇa, who always delighted in [generosity].
The giving of his two sons to a Brahmin without any regret in his heart, as well as his various other acts of charity, are fully recorded in that sutra;
this is called the fulfillment of the Bodhisattva’s perfection of the Dana-paramita of material giving within the Tripitaka.

Regarding the Dana of the Bodhisattva who masters the teachings of the Three Super-knowledges (Traividya): if one realizes that the three factors—the giver, the recipient, and the gift—are all empty, then...
Arising great compassion like a magical illusion out of pity for sentient beings, one relinquishes body, life, and wealth; this is called the *dānapāramitā* of the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*).

Regarding the *dāna* of the Bodhisattva in the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*) of the Four Ming [Masters]: although they know that the three factors [giver, gift, and recipient] are empty, they do not abide in emptiness.
Entering into the provisional as an illusory transformation, they practice various forms of giving, relinquishing body, life, and wealth like flowers.

The *Śrīmālā-sūtra* speaks of ten kinds of giving, while the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* clarifies nine kinds of giving. Regarding the *dāna* (generosity) of a Bodhisattva in the Perfect Teaching (*paripūrṇa-yāna*), the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states:
"One who gives away their body [attains] an end to birth and death equal to that of the limit of existence;

being free from old age, sickness, and death, they attain the indestructible and eternally abiding. Giving up one's life and giving away wealth likewise results in an end to birth and death equal to that of the limit of existence; being free from old age and sickness, one attains [the same]."
It is indestructible and eternally abiding. Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* clarifies that the Tathāgata’s giving (*dāna*) is the Great Parinirvāṇa;

the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* clarifies that the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) is precisely the Buddha-nature; and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* clarifies that the perfection of giving is precisely the Mahāyāna because it is ungraspable.
It further states: "All dharmas tend toward the perfection of giving"—this is the tendency toward the unconditioned.
Since even the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) cannot be apprehended, how could there be any "going" or "not going"? A later passage in this sutra states:

"Giving is the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), for one does not hope for recompense. Thus, giving is the primary cause for attaining the fruit of *bodhi*; by relying on this cause, one realizes a pure land.
Of the four types of giving mentioned previously, three are provisional while the last is real. This refers to the Bodhisattva himself.

Practicing skillful means and bestowing gifts, as well as teaching others to do so, praising them, and rejoicing in their practice—when such a person later attains Buddhahood, sentient beings who are capable of relinquishing all five aggregates will come to be born in that land.

If one attains Buddhahood in a defiled land, then those from the three evil paths will also come to be born there; if it is a pure land, there are only humans and devas, and matters concerning the four teachings of the wholesome.

If one can renounce sentient beings [to come] and be born in that land, or if there is another land where a Buddha has attained enlightenment and possesses only the four teachings to exhaust the conditioned causal accumulation (*saṃskṛta-pratyaya-samudaya*) so that sentient beings come to be born in that land;

or if it is a land of fruition (*vipākabhūmi*) where a Buddha has attained enlightenment and possesses only the two teachings of the Distinct (*bhedaka*) and the Perfect (*vaipulya*), whereby they perceive the Middle Way Buddha-nature and exhaust all unconditioned causal accumulations (*asaṃskṛta-pratyaya-samudaya*). All are capable [of this].

When one abandons sentient beings to be born in that land—such as the Land of Constant Quiescent Light—at the time of attaining Buddhahood, there is only the perfect teaching’s contemplation of the Middle Way, wherein the conditioned accumulation of causes and conditions is severed and exhausted; thus, all sentient beings who can be abandoned come to be born in that land.
Therefore, it is said that "all sentient beings who can be abandoned" come to that land. The various meanings of the four lands are, in essence, the nature of the direct mind.

Observing the precepts is the pure land of a bodhisattva; when the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, sentient beings who have fulfilled their vows by practicing the ten paths of wholesome action will come to be born in that land.

Furthermore, there are five kinds [of observing the precepts]: the first is observing the precepts through formal characteristics, which pertains to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*); the next four kinds are [the remaining types of] observing the precepts.
This refers to the four teachings which clarify the four kinds of right speech, right action, and right livelihood; all are termed "maintaining the precepts.
A full explanation of these matters would be too extensive, but one should know that the first four are provisional precepts while the last one is the real precept.

When a Bodhisattva practices these themselves, teaches them to others, rejoices in them, and praises them, then at the time of their subsequent Buddhahood, the fivefold ten wholesome paths will fulfill the vows of sentient beings who come to be born in that land.

The ten wholesome actions of the nation are precisely right action, right speech, and right livelihood. By aligning one's teachings with clear vows, because the precepts (*śīla*) are pure, all various virtues are able to arise;
since everything sought is realized as a fruit, it is called "fulfilling vows.
The various meanings of coming to be born throughout the four lands can be understood through the principle of the direct mind.
Patience is the pure land of a bodhisattva; when the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, sentient beings adorned with the thirty-two marks come to be born in that land.
Furthermore, patience is of five kinds: first, patience regarding worldly matters, such as that of ordinary people; the remaining four types of patience are [as follows].
Distinguishing the four provisional and one real [teachings] according to the fourfold teaching:

the Bodhisattva’s own practice and transformation of others, the praise and sympathetic joy [therein], and at the time of attaining Buddhahood, the five kinds of thirty-two marks soften sentient beings so that they are born in his land;
like the Wheel-Turning King, Śakra, and the various devas of the upper realms, all possess the thirty-two marks, and even Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas likewise do.
Regarding the marks: next, the four teachings differ in their four types of cultivation for the thirty-two marks, all of which take forbearance as the foundation.

The four types clarify the cultivation of the marks; having previously praised his virtues and explained his relinquishing of finery, the brief analysis of the classes of beings born in the four lands can now be understood through a straightforward mind.
Diligence is the pure land of a bodhisattva; when the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, sentient beings who have diligently cultivated all merits come to be born in that land.

Some masters say that diligence has no separate essence other than being designated in relation to various practices, while others say it is that which enables the accomplishment of those various practices.
There is a distinct essence of diligence which is fivefold: first, the diligence of phenomena, which refers to ordinary persons;
the remaining four types of diligence each pertain to the eight kinds of diligence within the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma). These eight kinds of diligence are:

the diligence of the four right efforts (samyak-prahāṇa), the faculty of diligence, the power of diligence, the factor of enlightenment of diligence, and the right diligence—these constitute the eight. In the Tripitaka Teaching, these are the eight kinds of diligence regarding arising and ceasing.

The eight kinds of diligence of the *Anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* in the Shared Teaching; the eight kinds of immeasurable diligence in the Distinct Teaching; and the eight kinds of unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*) diligence in the Perfect Teaching.
These four types of skillful means and one type of reality are cultivated by the Bodhisattva for self-purification, for teaching others, and for praising and rejoicing in [the merits of others].
When he later attains Buddhahood, he diligently cultivates all five kinds of merit, and sentient beings come to be born in his land. Thus are the four lands distinguished.
The distinctions and various categories of meaning can be understood through the straightforward mind.
Meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is the pure land of a bodhisattva; when the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, sentient beings whose minds are collected and undisturbed come to be born in that land.

Meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) is also of five kinds: first, worldly meditative concentration, such as the four *dhyānas* and four formless attainments (*ārūpya*) acquired by ordinary persons;

second to fifth, the four types of meditative concentration corresponding to the four teachings, each of which contains eight kinds of concentration within its respective set of fourfold paths of practice—namely, the concentrations of the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), the faculties (*indriya*), the powers (*bala*), and the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) and right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*)—up to the nine successive liberations (*anupūrva-vimokṣa*).
The various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) are all forms of meditative absorption (*samādhi*). Of these, the first four are provisional while the last one is real.

When a Bodhisattva practices them themselves, teaches others, praises them, and rejoices in them, they will, upon attaining Buddhahood, cause sentient beings who have gathered their minds without distraction through the four teachings and five types [of practice] to be born in his land.
The four lands and their various categories can be understood through a straightforward mind.
Wisdom is the pure land of the Bodhisattva; when the Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, sentient beings of right concentration come to be born in that land.

Wisdom consists of the eight kinds of wisdom found within the four types of *dharmapada* (path factors) elucidated in the Four Teachings—namely, the wisdom of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*), the power of wisdom (*prajñābala*), the factor of enlightenment of investigation (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*), and right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*). Of these, the former four are provisional (*upāya*), while the latter one is real (*bhūta*).

When a Bodhisattva, having practiced for themselves and transformed others, and having offered praise and rejoiced in merit, attains Buddhahood, five kinds of beings with right determination (*samyaktva-niyata*) come to be born in that land.
This "right determination" does not refer to the right determination of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), but rather to the "determination group" (*niyata-rāśi*) among the three groups.
Those who receive the four teachings and each enter the stage of the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) within the inner path are all of the determination group. They come [to that land].
The birth in the four lands and the various categories of meaning can be understood through the direct mind (*ṛju-citta*). Question:

If this is so, how can the wisdom of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) enter the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*)? Answer: Even the mundane right view (*laukika-samyag-dṛṣṭi*) enters and emerges from the stage of right determination;
it may also be described as being included therein.

The four immeasurable minds are the pure land of a bodhisattva; when the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, sentient beings who have perfected loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity come to be born in that land.
There are eight kinds of "threefold clear knowledges" (trividyā) which, in relation to the practice of transforming others, purify the land; this is merely a preliminary explanation.

Since the Bodhisattva first resolved to attain enlightenment, he has always been conjoined with great compassion (*mahāmaitrī*); how could there be the practice of the six perfections without the function of transforming others?
These eight sections concern the primary cause for attaining the fruit of Buddhahood; because the causal basis gives rise to the Buddha-field, they describe the practice for purifying the Pure Land.
Furthermore, the four immeasurable minds (*apramāṇa-citta*) also have five types, the first of which is the objective condition (*vastu-pratyaya*).
The four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*) are cultivated by ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) to attain birth in the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) as Brahmā Kings.

Within each of the Four Teachings, there are respectively four immeasurable minds: in the Tripitaka Teaching, they clarify the immeasurable minds that take conditioned phenomena of arising and ceasing as their object;

in the Shared Teaching, they clarify the immeasurable minds that take the dharma of non-arising as their object; and in the Distinct Teaching, they clarify the immeasurable minds of the *ālayavijñāna* beyond the realms, which are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

The Dharma-dharmas, the conditions for the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), the perfect teaching that clarifies the Middle Way Buddha-nature, and the unconditioned compassion, joy, and equanimity—just as a magnet attracts iron—are the four immeasurable minds of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*). Of these, the former four are provisional while the latter one is real.

Through these, the Bodhisattva practices for self-cultivation and transforms others by means of praise and sympathetic joy; when they subsequently attain Buddhahood, there are five kinds of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).

Through compassion, joy, and equanimity toward sentient beings, they come to be born in that land. The distinctions between the four teachings and the four lands regarding the various meanings of being born there represent the direct mind.
The four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) are the pure land of the Bodhisattva; when the Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, sentient beings who are encompassed by liberation come [to that land].

Born in that land, these four methods of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) are not practiced by ordinary beings or those of the two vehicles; rather, there are simply four types, which correspond to the four different sets of four integrations elucidated in the Four Teachings.
Among these, the former three are provisional (*upāya*), while the latter one is real (*bhūta*); this is the Bodhisattva [method].
Having practiced it oneself, taught it to others, praised it, and rejoiced in it, when one later attains Buddhahood, there will be four kinds of liberated beings who come to be born in that land.

Regarding those who come to be born through liberation: by means of the Bodhisattva’s four methods of attraction (*saṃgraha-vastu*), they gather sentient beings in order to lead them into the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Therefore, all the beings thus gathered possess the cause for liberation. Thus, there are four [types] who come to be born.
The land and its various categories of meaning can be understood through the direct mind (*ṛju-citta*).

Skillful means (*upāya*) is the pure land of a bodhisattva; when that bodhisattva attains buddhahood, sentient beings who possess unimpeded skillful means regarding all phenomena come to be born in his land.
Skillful means (*upāya*) are not practiced by ordinary beings or those of the two vehicles; there are only four kinds of skillful means, which are the four teachings (*catur-yāna*).

Each of these four teachings possesses three types of skillful means: first, the skillful means of self-cultivation; second, the skillful means of self-cultivation for transforming others; and third, the skillful means of transforming others.
Furthermore, each of the four teachings has three further skillful means: first, the skillful means of refuting phenomena (*dharma-pratikṣepa-upāya*).

First, the establishment of the two [types of] skillful means; second, the skillful means of teaching others; third, the skillful means of practicing oneself and teaching others, followed by praising and rejoicing in [their practice].

Subsequently, at the time of attaining Buddhahood, all skillful means will be unimpeded. Sentient beings who come to be born in that land—whether they are born in the four lands or belong to various other categories—can be known through their straightforward mind.

The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are the bodhisattva’s pure land; when the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, sentient beings who practice the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path will come to be born in that land.

Regarding the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*), these do not apply to ordinary beings or those of the two vehicles; their full details are as clarified in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning).
There are four types of the thirty-seven factors, meaning that the explanations provided by the four teachings differ, which constitutes the four kinds of thirty-seven factors.
[The first three] are provisional, while the one is real. Regarding the Bodhisattva’s own practice and transformation of others, there follow the praises and sympathetic joy.
When he attains Buddhahood, there will be four kinds of practitioners of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment who come to be born in his land;
those from the four stages [of the śrāvaka], as well as other categories of beings, can be known by their straightforward minds.
The mind of dedication is the pure land of the bodhisattva; when the bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, he obtains all fully perfected merits.
Regarding the "land" (*kṣetra*):

the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) is like sound entering a horn. There are four types, which correspond to the four teachings (*catur-yāna*) clarifying the four distinct modes of dedication by the bodhisattvas.
These consist of the three provisional and one real [teachings], wherein the bodhisattvas—whether practicing for themselves or teaching others—perform their respective dedications.
After praising and rejoicing, when one attains Buddhahood, sentient beings who possess the four kinds of perfect merit will come to be born in that land.
Because one dedicates one's own merit to sentient beings so that their virtues are never incomplete, those who are born there have all their merits made fully complete.
One should also say that sentient beings who wish to practice dedication will come to be born in that land; otherwise, there would be fear [of failure].
The text is merely abbreviated; the rebirth in the four lands and other related categories can be understood through a straightforward mind.

It is said that the removal of the eight difficulties constitutes the pure land of a bodhisattva: when a bodhisattva attains buddhahood, there shall be no three evil realms or eight difficulties in his land.

The eight difficulties (*aṣṭāv akṣaṇāḥ*) are: first, the three evil realms, which constitute the first three difficulties; fourth, the difficulty of being born in Uttarakuru; fifth, the difficulty of being born in the long-lived heavens;
sixth, the difficulty of being blind, deaf, or mute; seventh, the difficulty of possessing worldly wisdom and eloquence;

and eighth, the difficulty of being born before or after a Buddha. Regarding these, there are two types: first, the eight difficulties within the realm (*dhātu*), which constitute the difficulties for the first two teachings. Second...
The eight difficulties outside the realms (*dhātu*) refer to the difficulties of the latter two teachings; regarding Bodhisattvas, these are explained according to the four teachings.
Excluding these two kinds of eight difficulties, one should further distinguish them in the chapter on Subhūti.

When a Bodhisattva has personally eliminated [these difficulties] for themselves and praised and rejoiced in [the elimination of] others, at the time they attain Buddhahood, their land will be free from the three evil states and the eight difficulties. This should be analyzed according to the four lands (*bhūmi*).
The distinctions between the meanings of "having difficulties" and "being free from difficulties" are manifold and difficult to fully analyze.

To maintain one's own observance of the precepts without censuring the deficiencies of others is the pure land of a bodhisattva; when that bodhisattva attains buddhahood, there will not even be the name of "violating prohibitions" in his land.
According to the four teachings (*catur-yāna*), there are likewise four types of "self-restraint without censuring others.

These should be distinguished by means of four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*): first, not self-restraining while censuring others; second, self-restraining without censuring others; third, self-restraining while censuring others;
fourth, neither self-restraining nor censuring others. The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "Suppose there were three sons..."
"One who dies by the staff has but one son remaining; he must certainly be strictly disciplined. How can you fail to censure him at all?
However, if one lacks evil intent within and will surely benefit others, this statement regarding 'not censuring' does not mean that there is no censure or reproach whatsoever.
Rather, it means that the Bodhisattva perceives the capacities of these four types of sentient beings without error; therefore, the Bodhisattva practices and teaches accordingly."

After praising and rejoicing in others, when one attains Buddhahood, sentient beings who previously lacked the capacity for the teachings, whose actions were contrary to principle, or who had broken the precepts will come to be born in that land;
those born in the four lands and other such categories can be understood through their straightforward minds.
The ten wholesome paths of action are the bodhisattva’s pure land. When the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, sentient beings will not have their lives cut short prematurely;

they will possess great wealth and practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*); their speech will be truthful and always gentle; their retinues will never be separated from them and will be harmonious, resolving disputes through goodness; their words will invariably be beneficial;
and they will be free from envy and anger, possessing right view—such beings will come to be born in that land.

The ten wholesome actions are of two kinds: first, the ten wholesome actions of restraint (*saṃvara-kuśala*); second, the ten wholesome actions of practice (*caryā-kuśala*). This present intent concerns the ten wholesome actions of restraint.
Furthermore, it is clarified that the ten wholesome actions are also of five types: first, the ten wholesome actions of phenomena (*vastu-kuśala*), which are practiced by ordinary worldlings;

the latter four types clarify the ten wholesome actions by distinguishing them according to the Four Teachings, including the Bodhisattva’s own practice, teaching others, and praising [them] accordingly.
That one’s life is not cut short after attaining Buddhahood is the non-killing of sentient beings; that one possesses great wealth is the non-stealing of sentient beings;
that one practices the holy life (*brahmacarya*) is the non-lustfulness toward sentient beings; that one’s speech is truthful is the non-lying toward sentient beings;
and that one always uses gentle words is the non-harsh speech toward sentient beings and their retinues.
Those who do not abandon the harmonizing of disputes are beings free from double-tongued speech;
those whose words are invariably beneficial are beings free from frivolous speech. Being without envy is being free from covetousness.
Envy is indeed a defilement of anger, yet it is explained here in terms of covetousness because envy exists by virtue of covetousness. Being without anger is...
Not being angry with sentient beings and possessing right view are precisely the roots of goodness that prevent delusion; these are the qualities by which sentient beings come to be born hereafter.

Hereafter, the four types of sentient beings who practice the ten wholesome paths according to the four teachings will be explained in relation to their rebirth in the four lands and other meanings, which can be understood by looking directly at the nature of their sincere minds.
Thus, the Bodhisattva Ratnakūṭa, according to his straightforward mind (*ṛju-citta*), is able to initiate practice.
These two [verses] clarify the cultivation of the Pure Land; there are thirteen sections that clarify the causes for accomplishing the Pure Land.

Above, from the "straightforward mind," seventeen lines were cited horizontally to clarify the practice of cultivating the Pure Land; now, returning to the "straightforward mind," [the text continues].
The mind is vertically clarified, progressing from the shallow to the deep to form the causes for the Pure Land. This verticality encompasses all preceding practices;
there is not a single dharma that is not cultivated vertically. To speak of the horizontal is to know that the vertical exists, and to speak of the vertical is to know that the horizontal exists.
Horizontal and vertical mutually support one another, vast and lofty, without obstruction. Every single practice reaches the adamantine mind, and the mind is pure.

Thus, regarding the purity of the Buddha-lands, there are three sections: first, a classification according to the four teachings; second, an analysis based on the contemplation of the mind; and third, an exegesis of the scriptural text.
Regarding the first, the classification according to the four teachings, the explanation of the thirteen passages is as follows:
why is it that the Tripitaka [teaching] does not clarify the purification of the Buddha-land? It is because the Śrāvaka sūtras do not clarify the ten [stages].
How could the Buddha, at this stage, discuss reaching various lands to cultivate the practice of purifying buddha-fields?

If one were to say that he does, it would result in the same doubt as that of Śāriputra. Since there is no teaching regarding the purification of buddha-fields [in this context], then there is neither the practice nor the person;
why then should it be discussed? As for the two teachings—the general and the specific—since they both contain the teaching on purifying buddha-fields, one must treat them broadly.

Discussing this, it consists of three points: first, an explanation according to the Shared Teaching; second, an explanation according to the Distinct Teaching; and third, an explanation according to the Perfect Teaching.
Regarding the first, the explanation according to the ten stages (*bhūmi*) of the Shared Teaching: the "straight mind" corresponds to the stage of seeing (*darśana-bhūmi*).

Prior to this, one has not yet manifested the truth and is thus termed "crooked. Having attained the stages, one manifests the truth and perceives reality, thereby becoming free from all crooked views; hence the name.

By means of this straightforward mind (*ṛju-citta*), one enters the second stage (*dvitīyā bhūmi*). Because one is able to practice these seventeen phrases throughout the second stage, it is called "the practice of application" (*prayoga-prasthāna*).
Through this practice of application, one enters the third stage. Because both understanding and practice advance together in the third stage, it is called the "profound mind" (*gambhīra-citta*).
By virtue of this profound mind, one attains entry into the fourth stage. In the fourth stage, as both phenomena and principle (*dharma-naya*) are practiced together, then [one attains] self-...
The term "tiao-tiao" (harmonizing) means "subduing"; because of this subduing, one enters the fifth stage (*pañcamī-bhūmi*).
Since in the fifth stage both phenomena and principle are subdued, and one is able to practice according to the teachings, one enters the sixth stage.

In the sixth stage, one is able to give rise to the mind of dedication (*pariṇāmanā-citta*) toward all wholesome dharmas; by dedicating these toward the fruit of Buddhahood for the sake of sentient beings, through this dedication—
Upon entering the seventh stage (*bhūmi*), one possesses the skillful means (*upāya*) to cultivate one's own practice and transform others, thereby attaining entry into the eighth stage.
In the eighth stage, one is able to cause the path and contemplation to flow together (*dvayam samavahitaṃ vahati*), and can also teach and subdue sentient beings everywhere.

Once sentient beings are subdued, the Buddha-land (*buddhakṣetra*) becomes pure; once the Buddha-land is pure, one attains entry into the ninth stage. In the ninth stage, one is able to expound the Dharma.

Because the purity of the Dharma-teaching is itself the purity of wisdom, the ninth stage is called the Stage of Excellent Wisdom (*Sādhumatī-bhūmi*), as it possesses the forty kinds of eloquence (*pratibhāna*).
By means of the purity of wisdom, one enters the tenth stage; since the tenth stage is the purity of the mind, all merits are purified.
Beginning from the "straight mind" and concluding with the final verse, it says: "If you wish to attain a pure land, you should purify your own mind."

"When the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure. This passage, drawn from the *Ten Stages* (Daśabhūmika), serves to establish the "vertical" practice of mutual support for purifying the Buddha-land within the Shared Teaching (Pāryāptika-yāna).
Second, regarding the explanation according to the Distinct Teaching (Pratyeka-yāna), there are two different intentions concerning the thirteen passages of the sutra in relation to the Ten Stages:
first, from the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), one awakens to the true vision of the Middle Way Buddha-nature. That is to say—

The name "straight mind" (*ṛjukacitta*) refers to that which breaks through ignorance and departs from the crookedness of the two extremes; this can be understood through the general teaching (*pāryāyika-yāna*) from the second stage (*bhūmi*) up to the tenth stage.

The distinction lies only in the fact that the general teaching perceives the partial truth (*prādeśika-satya*), whereas the distinct teaching (*vaiyāvṛtya-yāna*) perceives the perfect truth (*pariniṣpanna-satya*).

Next, according to the *Ratnaketu-dhāraṇī-sūtra* (Renwang jing), there are fourteen types of *prajñā*; one must further employ these to explain the vertical characteristics (*ūrdhva-lakṣaṇa*) of this sūtra.
Regarding the meaning of that sutra, it takes the thirty minds collectively to correspond with the three types of *prajñā*.
If this is so, then the "direct mind" (*ṛju-citta*) corresponds directly to the ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*). Why is this? Entering into the *prajñā* of principle is called an "abode.

Although one has not yet seen the perfect ultimate truth (*pariniṣpanna-tattva*), one has already seen the partial ultimate truth (*ekadeśa-tattva*), thereby destroying the four grave delusions. By correctly cultivating the Middle Way, a semblance-understanding (*pratirūpa-bodhi*) arises; this is called "direct."

The "mind" (*citta*) corresponds to the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*); these ten practices are precisely the meaning of cultivation. The "deep mind" (*adhyāśaya*) corresponds to the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*);
by entering into principle, it enables both understanding and practice to become profoundly deep; thus, the sutras describe the ten dedications as the "profound and vast mind.

"Subduing" (*vinaya*) corresponds to the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*); because one gives rise to the true Middle Way at this stage, where the path of contemplation and the path of observation flow together, it receives the name "subduing."
The second stage corresponds to practicing as taught; the third stage corresponds to dedication; the fourth stage corresponds to skillful means;
the fifth stage corresponds to maturing sentient beings; the sixth stage corresponds to purifying the buddha-field; the seventh stage corresponds to purity in preaching the Dharma;

the eighth stage corresponds to purity of wisdom; the ninth stage corresponds to purity of mind; the tenth stage corresponds to purity of all merits; and Equal Enlightenment corresponds to [the purity of]...

The latter phrase states that "if the mind is pure, then the Buddha-land is pure. If one takes the preceding and succeeding stages of the grounds into account, and bases this on the fourteen types of *prajñā* in relation to the various phrases arranged vertically, the number of phrases is complete.

Although some expressions may not explicitly name the meaning of each ground, there is no point at which the interpretation of the underlying intent fails to apply. One should provide an explanation according to what is appropriate for the person being taught.
There is no error. Regarding the explanation of the thirteen passages according to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) in three sections:

although the preceding [explanation] relied upon the meaning of distinct stages, there was still something remaining. How could it be that the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*) consists merely of the merit of "subduing without remainder"?
If these were fully possessed, then not only would the single name "Subduer" (*dānta*) be partial; how could "Subduing" alone be appropriate?
This designation refers to a teaching that is not yet perfected; we shall now not rely upon it.
Instead, we shall distinguish the vertical depth by correlating all fourteen phrases with the stages of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao), thereby clarifying the horizontal breadth.

What is the intended meaning of stating that these fourteen phrases are already fully present within the mind of the first stage (prathamabhūmi)? It is because, having already perceived the principle through the copper wheel [of the third dhyāna], they are complete therein.
Is the destruction of ignorance not the direct mind? Is the single mind endowed with the ten thousand practices not the practice of cultivation?
Is the moment-to-moment flow into the ocean of *sarvajñā* not the profound mind? Is the perfect elimination of the five abodes not the taming of the self?

Is the correspondence between understanding and practice, such that speech and action are non-dual, not acting according to one's words? Is the constant dedication of merit to all sentient beings for them to together head toward the Sublime not the ultimate goal?
Is awakening not the dedication [of merit]? Is the perfection of the provisional and the real not the skillful means?

Is it not by attaining the Tathāgata’s single body and infinite bodies that one can, within the land of common cohabitation, teach and transform beings through the color-body of Samantabhadra? Is this not the accomplishment of sentient beings?
If one achieves the path by purifying the land and the four teachings are received, such that sentient beings come to be born in that realm—is this not the purification of the Buddha-land?
The land is pure, for it proclaims the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) with a single voice to meet the capacities of beings; is this not the purity of the Dharma?
The wisdom that serenely illuminates is pure; is this not the purity of wisdom? The true mark of reality is the true mind, untainted like space; is this not the purity of the mind?

When the one mind is fully endowed with the myriad practices and merit and wisdom are perfected, is this not the purity of merit? Since the primary retribution is thus pure, so too is the environment.
The retribution is also pure, identical to that of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas; seeing the Dharma-nature, one dwells within the Indra-net and enters the *śāntaprabhāsa* (tranquil light).

Is this not the purity of the Buddha-land? One should know that within the mind of the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*), when it is profoundly established vertically, these fourteen phrases and immeasurable phrases exhaust the source of the mind, encompassing everything without exception. Therefore, the first gateway of the letter "A" is complete.
The forty-one letter-gates of the feet also fully possess the letter-gate of *a*. One should know that if discussed vertically, they penetrate through to the future limit;
if explained horizontally, all gates are simultaneously complete, as previously clarified regarding the seventeen dharmas and all phenomena.
This includes the initial arousal of the mind, correct practice, lateral transformation, and the accomplishment of the two pure lands for the benefit and welfare of sentient beings.

Because all [qualities] are not fully present within the initial mind alone, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "At the moment of first generating the bodhicitta, one immediately attains perfect enlightenment.
The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states: "One attains the Tathāgata’s single body that is an infinite body.

Since the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) already encompasses both the transverse and vertical phrases regarding the purification of Buddha-fields, its meaning is thus; the remaining forty-one stages are likewise the same.
This is the same analogy of the fifteenth-day moon found in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* cited previously.

Second, to clarify the vertical explanation of the thirteenfold dharma-gates based on contemplating the mind (*citta-vipaśyanā*), which mutually support one another in cultivating the causes for the Pure Land:

the single mind of the three contemplations (*ekacitta-trivipaśyanā*) observing the Middle Way Dharma-nature is precisely the "straight mind" (*ṛju-citta*). This single thought-moment inherently and simultaneously possesses the preceding seventeen [dharma-gates].
The practice of purifying the Buddha-land is precisely to follow one’s straightforward mind;

thus, through the mutual support of phenomena and principle, one can enter the profound Dharma-realm. By means of the profound mind, the unwholesome intentions regarding phenomena and principle are subdued.
With the mind thus subdued, whatever Dharma is taught, one is able to act in accordance with those teachings. Because [this] exists...

"Wholesome conduct" means turning back the wholesome deeds one has performed and dedicating them as a gift to sentient beings. Since one can dedicate and bestow these upon sentient beings, one is able to cause sentient beings to sever evil and cultivate goodness.
Because sentient beings sever evil and cultivate goodness, the Buddha-field becomes pure.

Because the Buddha-field is pure, the objective realm is pure; because the objective realm is pure, the teaching of the Dharma is pure; because the teaching is pure, the nature [of the Dharma] is revealed; and thus there is internal wisdom.
Wisdom then attains increased brilliance; because the inner mind’s wisdom is luminous and pure, all merits are entirely purified.
Such instances as these are all the purification of the Buddha-land through contemplating the mind. Therefore, a sutra says: "If one wishes to purify a Buddha-land, one should purify one's own mind;
according to the purity of the mind, so too is the Buddha-land pure. This is the vertical cultivation.
These fourteen phrases clearly represent the internal stage of contemplating the mind, and are thus termed the "stage of contemplative practice" (*kan-gyō-ji*). Therefore, the *Lotus Sūtra* states:

"One should know that such a person has already proceeded toward the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and is seated beneath the tree of enlightenment, close to perfect awakening (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

If one's meritorious practice becomes pure and mature, the Buddhas of the ten directions will provide secret empowerment, whereby one immediately attains entry into the "iron wheel" stage, which corresponds to the thirteenth mental state of the "semblance" stage (*sō-zui-shin*).
From the stage of similarity, one enters the thirteen mental states of partial realization of reality within the Copper Wheel [Bhūmi].
Therein, one spontaneously performs the benefit of self and others and establishes karmic connections with sentient beings in the two lands.

If, upon entering the Copper Wheel, there are sentient beings to be transformed who are to be liberated through the form of a Buddha, one immediately manifests the body of a Buddha and expounds for them the gradual, sudden, indeterminate, and secret Dharma-gates.
To transform and subdue sentient beings so that they enter the Buddha-wisdom, one arouses the roots [of merit] and takes up a buddha-field.

If it were not thus, for what reason would the first stage (prathamabhūmi) involve the accomplishment of the path through the eight signs? Although it is generally said that one contemplates the mind, in reality, this is the meaning of the truly pure buddha-field.
This is the teaching of definitive meaning (nītārtha); if it differs from this, it is mostly mere words.
Next, there is nothing other than the vertical to manifest the distinct, and nothing other than the circular to manifest the horizontal.

For example, without the sun one cannot establish the moon, and without the moon one cannot count the days; the sun and moon depend upon each other to form a single year, and even up to hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands, and millions of years.
Now, when the vertical and horizontal depend upon each other, the meaning of "high" and "broad" is revealed. That which is neither vertical nor horizontal is yet the vertical.

Yet, it is horizontally arranged like the letter *i* of the world, and Śiva’s three eyes; one should know that the meaning of the Pure Land exists by depending upon the secret treasury of the three virtues (*triguṇa*).

If one speaks of the three bodies (*trikāya*) and the three virtues, this refers to the primary retribution (*pratyaya-vipāka*); if one speaks of the three lands or four lands, this refers to the environmental retribution (*adhiṣṭhāna-vipāka*).
The way in which the primary and environmental retributions mutually constitute one another can be understood from this. Third, to clarify the exegesis of the scriptural text:

Following that straightforward mind (ṛju-citta), one is able to initiate practice; this straightforward mind is precisely the attainment of the eightfold straightness of the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*) within the Middle Way of the aforementioned Perfect Teaching (*paripūrṇa-yāna*) contemplation.
Having attained this straightforward mind, one is then able to fulfill all practices;

therefore, it is called "initiating practice. It is also said that having attained this straightforward mind, one is able to carry out the seventeen kinds [of practices] previously explained as the horizontal manifestation of all [dharmas].

Because it is a gateway to practice, it is said that according to one's upright mind (*ṛjukacitta*), one is able to initiate practice; according to the initiation of practice, one attains the profound mind (*gambhīracitta*). The upright mind is precisely understanding (*adhimukti*), and the initiation of practice is practice (*pratipatti*). Understanding guides practice, and practice supports understanding. Understanding [is the cause] and practice is the fruit. Understanding is the seed and practice is the harvest. Understanding is the root and practice is the trunk. Understanding is the flower and practice is the fruit. Understanding is the cause and practice is the result. Understanding is the beginning and practice is the end. Understanding is the internal and practice is the external. Understanding is the primary and practice is the secondary. Understanding is the essence and practice is the function. Understanding is the principle and practice is the phenomenon. Understanding is the realization and practice is the cultivation. Understanding is the awakening and practice is the application. Understanding is the wisdom and practice is the conduct. Understanding is the liberation and practice is the means. Understanding is the goal and practice is the path. Understanding is the destination and practice is the journey. Understanding is the light and practice is the illumination. Understanding is the clarity and practice is the manifestation. Understanding is the stillness and practice is the movement. Understanding is the depth and practice is the breadth. Understanding is the source and practice is the flow. Understanding is the foundation and practice is the edifice. Understanding is the vessel and practice is the content. Understanding is the master and practice is the servant. Understanding is the sovereign and practice is the subject. Understanding is the guide and practice is the follower. Understanding is the teacher and practice is the student. Understanding is the father and practice is the son. Understanding is the mother and practice is the child. Understanding is the origin and practice is the continuation. Understanding is the beginning and practice is the completion. Understanding is the first step and practice is the final stride. Understanding is the initial aspiration and practice is the ultimate fulfillment. Understanding is the seed of enlightenment and practice is the tree of enlightenment. Understanding is the dawn of the Dharma and practice is the full day of the Dharma. Understanding is the entry into the gate of reality and practice is the mastery within that gate. Understanding is the opening of the treasury of the Dharma and practice is the utilization of its contents. Understanding is the grasping of the truth and practice is the application of that truth. Understanding is the seeing of the Buddha-nature and practice is the realization of that nature. Understanding is the hearing of the Dharma and practice is the realization of the Dharma. Understanding is the serving of the Sangha and practice is the harmonizing with the Sangha. Understanding is the purification of the mind and practice is the purification of conduct. Understanding is the cultivation of wisdom and practice is the cultivation of merit. Understanding is the transcendence of the world and practice is the benefit of the world. Understanding is the departure from suffering and practice is the cessation of suffering. Understanding is the attainment of nirvana and practice is the path to nirvana. Understanding is the perfection of the paramitas and practice is the fulfillment of the bodhisattva path. Understanding is the realization of the non-arising of dharmas and practice is the manifestation of the unceasing activity of the Dharma. Understanding is the emptiness of all phenomena and practice is the skillful means within that emptiness. Understanding is the signlessness of all phenomena and practice is the compassionate response to sentient beings. Understanding is the wishlessness of all phenomena and practice is the dedication of roots of goodness. Understanding is the equality of all dharmas and practice is the differentiation of means. Understanding is the non-duality of subject and object and practice is the engagement with the manifold world. Understanding is the non-conceptualization of dharmas and practice is the non-abiding in cessation. Understanding is the non-attachment to dharmas and practice is the non-rejection of the mundane. Understanding is the non-grasping of dharmas and practice is the non-abandoning of sentient beings. Understanding is the non-clinging to dharmas and practice is the non-falling into the two extremes. Understanding is the non-discrimination of dharmas and practice is the non-confusion regarding the distinctions between dharmas. Understanding is the non-obstruction of dharmas and practice is the non-hindrance in the performance of deeds. Understanding is the non-differentiation of dharmas and practice is the non-contradiction of the teachings. Understanding is the non-deception of dharmas and practice is the non-failure in the vows. Understanding is the non-delusion of dharmas and practice is the non-wavering in the resolve. Understanding is the non-inversion of dharmas and practice is the non-deviation from the path. Understanding is the non-perverted view of dharmas and practice is the non-erroneous application of the means. Understanding is the non-mistaken cognition of dharmas and practice is the non-contradictory realization of the fruit. Understanding is the non-confusion regarding the nature of dharmas and practice is the non-erroneous manifestation of the power of the Dharma. Understanding is the non-obscuration of the light of wisdom and practice is the non-extinguishing of the lamp of the Dharma. Understanding is the non-obstruction of the eye of the Dharma and practice is the non-blinding of the eye of sentient beings. Understanding is the non-defilement of the mind and practice is the non-corruption of conduct. Understanding is the non-turbidity of the ocean of the Dharma and practice is the non-stirring of the waves of affliction. Understanding is the non-agitation of the mountain of the Dharma and practice is the non-shaking of the stability of the mind. Understanding is the non-distraction of the samādhi and practice is the non-interruption of the continuity of concentration. Understanding is the non-dissipation of the power of mindfulness and practice is the non-loss of the objects of recollection. Understanding is the non-forgetfulness of the Dharma and practice is the non-abandoning of the teaching. Understanding is the non-decline of the roots of goodness and practice is the non-retrogression in the accumulation of merit. Understanding is the non-regression in the stage of the bodhisattva and practice is the non-falling back into the stages of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha. Understanding is the non-abandoning of the great vow and practice is the non-ceasing of the work of salvation. Understanding is the non-separation from the Buddha and practice is the non-failing to see the Buddhas. Understanding is the non-separation from the Dharma and practice is the non-failing to hear the Dharma. Understanding is the non-separation from the Sangha and practice is the non-failing to serve the Sangha. Understanding is the non-separation from the bodhisattvas and practice is the non-failing to associate with them. Understanding is the non-separation from the perfections and practice is the non-failing to fulfill them. Understanding is the non-separation from the bodhipakṣa-dharmas and practice is the non-failing to cultivate them. Understanding is the non-separation from the powers and fearlessnesses and practice is the non-failing to manifest them. Understanding is the non-separation from the marks and minor signs and practice is the non-failing to adorn the body. Understanding is the non-separation from the pure lands and practice is the non-failing to purify them. Understanding is the non-separation from the transformation of sentient beings and practice is the non-failing to mature them. Understanding is the non-separation from the turning of the wheel of the Dharma and practice is the non-failing to propagate the teaching. Understanding is the non-separation from the ultimate nirvana and practice is the non-failing to enter the city of peace. Understanding is the non-separation from the Tathāgata’s knowledge and practice is the non-failing to realize the wisdom of the Buddha. Understanding is the non-separation from the Dharma-body and practice is the non-failing to manifest the form-body. Understanding is the non-separation from the realm of reality and practice is the non-failing to pervade all worlds. Understanding is the non-separation from the nature of all dharmas and practice is the non-failing to accord with the true nature of things. Understanding is the non-separation from the equality of all Buddhas and practice is the non-failing to honor them equally. Understanding is the non-separation from the non-duality of samsara and nirvana and practice is the non-failing to transcend both while dwelling in neither. Understanding is the non-separation from the non-arising of all dharmas and practice is the non-failing to manifest the arising of all dharmas for the sake of sentient beings. Understanding is the non-separation from the non-existence of all dharmas and practice is the non-failing to establish the existence of all dharmas through skillful means. Understanding is the non-separation from the emptiness of all dharmas and practice is the non-failing to manifest the non-empty through compassion. Understanding is the non-separation from the signlessness of all dharmas and practice is the non-failing to manifest signs for the sake of those to be converted. Understanding is the non-separation from the wishlessness of all dharmas and practice is the non-failing to make wishes for the benefit of others. Understanding is the non-separation from the non-self of all dharmas and practice is the non-failing to take up the burden of self for the sake of others.

When the aspects of practice are perfected—like having both eyes and feet complete—one reaches the Cool Lake; this is called the "profound and vast mind," which is why it says, "one then attains the profound mind.
As that profound mind develops, the will becomes subdued.

Once the practice of understanding is profound, one is able to harmonize the delusions of both principle and phenomena. The delusion of principle is precisely the ignorance that is confused about the Middle Way;
the delusion of phenomena is the confusion regarding the phenomena of the Dharma-realm within the Two Truths.

If, from the very first moment of generating the mind of enlightenment, one enters the Middle Way and simultaneously illuminates the Two Truths, then thought after thought is quiescent, flowing spontaneously.
Entering the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge) enables one to subdue both the delusions of phenomena and principle; as the *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* states:
"From the first generation of the bodhicitta until reaching the Vajra-peak, all are termed 'Patience of Subduing' (*vinaya-kṣānti*); this is what is meant by the subduing of the mind."
If one tames the mind according to one's will, then one acts as taught.
If the mind is not tamed, though the mouth speaks of emptiness, the practice remains within existence; however, if the mind is tamed, this fault does not arise.
Whatever is spoken is not merely for the sake of meeting the capacities of beings to benefit them; rather, when the inner mind is pure, one is able to act exactly as taught.
When one's actions accord with one's words, the roots of merit and virtue are accomplished.
By practicing according to what has been taught, one is able to dedicate [merit].
Having internally accomplished various wholesome merits, one dedicates these roots of goodness toward the fruit of Buddhahood, and further dedicates this...
It is skillful to establish [benefits] for sentient beings; if there were no superior goodness, what would there be to dedicate?
It is like a sound that can enter a horn: if the sound within were not soft and resonant, how could one speak of the distance to which the sound entering the horn would reach?
According to that dedication, there is skillful means (*upāya*).
Having dedicated one's own practice, one is able internally to dedicate it toward the fruit of Buddhahood and externally to bestow it universally upon all sentient beings;
because one is thus able to be skillful, able to dismantle [delusions], able to establish [the truth], and able to deliver sentient beings with artistry, it is said that "there is skillful means."
According to their expedient means, they bring sentient beings to maturity.

Since these expedient means are skillful, their refutations and establishments are likewise skillful. Through skillful refutation, they are able to subdue sentient beings; through skillful establishment, they are able to gather in the multitudes.
Subduing them ensures that all evils are forever severed; gathering them ensures that all virtues are universally assembled. If [the multitude]...
The arising of the two virtues of cessation and practice within the four teachings constitutes the completion of the two merits of wisdom and severance;
this is precisely the formation of the primary retribution’s cause and effect.
As one brings sentient beings to fulfillment, the Buddha-land becomes pure accordingly.

If the categories of sentient beings are the Pure Land of a Bodhisattva, then the primary retribution of these beings—consisting solely of wholesome deeds and devoid of evil—and their secondary retribution—their environment—are pure.
When the primary retribution results from the cultivation of wholesome causes, the Buddha-land becomes adorned;
when the land is thus pure and adorned, the Buddha-land is purified.
As the Buddha-land is pure, so is the Dharma taught pure.
If one teaches the Dharma in a defiled land, it is like an elder holding a refuse basket; thus, in accordance with conditions, one preaches the harsh and urgent Dharma.
As in the case of the Pure Name (Viśuddhanāman), when the bodhisattvas who came from the Fragrant Accumulation Land (Gandhavyūha) were told that the beings of this land require subduing.
As the purity of the teaching of the Dharma increases, so does the purity of wisdom.
If the fundamental teaching of the Dharma accords with the capacities and conditions of sentient beings and is pure, then the resulting wisdom of the Bodhisattva will likewise be pure.
It is like a fierce wind that causes the sound of bells to grow great; or as when there is immediate discourse in the world for those who possess sharp faculties.
Those of wisdom and merit who come to hear his preaching of the Dharma will find their wisdom opened and understood beyond their expectations,
and their eloquence will become unimpeded.
As their wisdom becomes pure, so too does their mind become pure.
When the wisdom of one who expounds the Dharma advances, the defilements of delusion gradually dissolve and the mind becomes increasingly manifest;
this is precisely the meaning of the purity of the mind.
As the mind becomes pure, all merits and virtues become pure accordingly.
With a straightforward mind, one cultivates all merits with complete purity and without attachment;
this is how all merits become pure.
Therefore, Ratnākara, if a bodhisattva wishes to attain a pure land, they should purify their own mind; as the mind becomes pure, so shall the land.
"The Buddha-field is pure.
This is the final summary of the essential points clarifying the causes for purifying the Pure Land.

When it says, "If one wishes to purify the land, one should purify one's own mind," it clarifies that from the "direct mind" (*ṛju-citta*) onward, there are thirteen phrases; although their names and meanings differ, they are [in essence] correct.

The intent is that all are pure minds; as for the statement "according to the purity of one's mind, so is the Buddha-land pure," this refers to the four types of minds elucidated by the Four Teachings.
When these four kinds of minds are pure, the four kinds of Buddha-lands are all pure. Furthermore, these four kinds of minds are in fact just one:
the intrinsically pure mind (*prakṛti-viśuddha-citta*). When this intrinsically pure mind is pure, it is simply one.
All Buddha-lands are entirely pure. From the first thought of enlightenment, the Bodhisattva purifies the mind through the Four Noble Truths;

the first three are provisional, while the last one is the ultimate reality. When delusions regarding phenomena and principle are eliminated, the primary retribution immediately attains the fruit of Buddhahood, and the secondary retribution attains the Land of Constant Quiescent Light, which is ultimately pure.
Through the convergence of these four conditions, the defilements of sentient beings are removed.

Because their pure minds differ in the manner of their coming to evoke the response, they each perceive either the defiled or the pure Constant Quiescent Light Land (*nitya-prabhāsvara-ābhāsa-kṣetra*).
This is, for example, like the gods who eat from the same precious vessel; according to their respective karmic retributions, the color of the rice appears different. The meaning lies here.
At that time, Śāriputra, empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, had this thought: "If it is said that when a bodhisattva’s mind is pure,
the buddha-field is pure, then when our World-Honored One was originally a bodhisattva, was his intention not pure that this buddha-field is so impure?"
This second section concerning the arising of doubt in Śāriputra has two distinct parts: first, explaining the cause for the arising of doubt; second, explaining the nature of the doubt itself.
Regarding the cause for the arising of doubt: it is because he received the Buddha’s spiritual power that doubt arose.
The specific circumstances regarding Śāriputra will be briefly presented in the "Chapter on Disciples," where it is shown how the Tathāgata’s spiritual power was bestowed upon Śāriputra.
Although this sutra was addressed to those of small capacity, Mahākāśyapa— being foremost in wisdom among those of the Hīnayāna and revered by all the śrāvakas—
suddenly conceived a doubt. Immediately, all the śrāvakas likewise gave rise to doubt,
wondering whether within the Mahāyāna Vaipulya there are inconceivable secret matters and inconceivable secrets.
The "matter" refers to the fact that within this defiled land there exists a pure land. Śāriputra’s Small Vehicle perspective was unable to accord with his capacity;
thus, he raised doubts, which necessarily required the Buddha’s power to harmonize with the minds of sentient beings—hence, he "relied upon the Buddha’s spiritual power.

If it were as in the *Lotus Sūtra*, where the Great Vehicle is revealed and the far-reaching truth made manifest, clarifying that all śrāvakas secretly maintain the practices of bodhisattvas, how could he not have been able to accord with his capacity?
This gives rise to doubt. Second, to clarify the nature of this doubt: one doubts the Buddha’s answer to Ratnākara that "the mind being pure, the buddha-field is pure.
Because one clings to the teachings of the former Tripiṭaka, doubt arises.

In the teachings of the former Tripiṭaka, it was taught that bodhisattvas practice for three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* and equally attain the fruit of Buddhahood and a buddha-field. How can it now be said that if the bodhisattva’s mind is pure, then the [buddha-field] is pure?
Regarding the fact that Śākyamuni Bodhisattva alone lacks a pure land while others do: this must be because when he was a bodhisattva, his mind was not pure.
If the mind is not pure, how can one attain Buddhahood? If the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure; how then could the Buddha-land be defiled and evil?
Because such contradictions give rise to doubt, those who have not yet dared to ask may do so out of self-deprecation. I now venture to ask.

"Perhaps fearing that I might fail [to ask], I venture to inquire; yet, as the Tathāgata perceives all with his transcendent vision, he naturally knows the proper time to resolve the doubts of the great assembly.
For this reason, though I have been reflecting on it, I did not dare to pose the question.
The Buddha, knowing his intention, immediately addressed him, saying: "What do you think? Are the sun and moon not pure? Yet the blind—"
[This] is not seen.
Below this, the third section clarifies the text that resolves the doubts of Śāriputra; it has three distinct parts: first, the Buddha cites the sun and moon and questions Śāriputra;
second, Śāriputra responds by relying on the facts; third, the Buddha answers by providing a combined explanation through analogy. First, citing the sun:
The analogy of the moon and sun represents the Pure Lands of the True and the Responsive.

Just as the palaces of the sun and moon are composed of various jewels and their light can illuminate the four continents, so too within those solar and lunar palaces there are celestial sons who represent the two lands of the True and the Responsive;

these are composed of the Dharma-jewels of myriad virtues and can constantly illuminate the sentient beings of the four lands, serving as the locus for the Dharma-bodies of the True and the Responsive.
Furthermore, it is like the mutual dependence of the two practices of the Real (zhen) and the Conditional (yuan).

Just as the sun and moon depend on each other to bring all things to fruition and illuminate everything, so too are the Real and the Conditional. If the Conditional is not established, the Real is not manifested;
if the Real is not manifested, the Conditional is not established. Because the Real and the Conditional are joined, there are thus four kinds of Pure Lands that eternally exist of themselves.
Although it shines forth clearly, the blind do not see whether it exists or does not exist; because the accumulation of karmic obstacles obstructs the five eyes, they are unable to see.
