As for "entering brothels," this refers to manifesting the act of entering them; he demonstrates the faults of desire by explaining that the nine orifices constantly flow with foul, exposed impurities, thereby causing others to know that desire is evil and unwholesome.
If the mind of desire ceases, the four roots of goodness [will arise].
The four dharmas that give rise to lustful defilement are also termed "sexual misconduct.

If one demonstrates and understands the faults of craving and attachment, and does not cling to them, the mind becomes pure and one attains entry into the inconceivable four lands. Therefore, a sutra says: "First, one uses the hook of desire to entice;
subsequently, one guides the person with the Dharma."
He enters various wine shops and is able to establish his resolve.
His entering wine shops is a manifestation of his traces; as for his own resolve, there are thirty-six faults in alcohol:

if ordinary people drink it, their spirits become clouded, they lose their way, and their superior resolve collapses entirely. A Great Being (Mahāsattva) is able to establish his own resolve and cause others to do so as well.

"Zhi-zhi" (aspiration-aspiration) refers to the four kinds of bodhicitta; that the aspiration is indestructible is precisely the inconceivable liberation and the non-retrogression that serves as the cause for the four kinds of pure lands.
Furthermore, wine represents afflictions and the tavern represents the five aggregates.

Ordinary persons drink both grain-based wine and the wine of afflictions; the followers of the Two Vehicles drink the wine of emptiness and signlessness. The followers of the Two Vehicles... [are thus described].
Because one does not vomit up this wine, one gives rise to the perception of impermanence regarding the Buddha-nature; thus the Sūtra says:

"Holding the vessel of the *śūnyatā-samādhi*, one is intoxicated by the signlessness (*animitta*) of Prajñā. In the Shared Teaching (*paryāya-yāna*), one is identical to the Two Vehicles; in the Distinct Teaching (*viśeṣa-yāna*), one has not yet seen the Middle Way—this too is intoxication.
To state the essential point: all afflictions (*kleśa*) that cause delusive intoxication are collectively termed "wine."
Although Bodhisattvas further enter into all afflictions, they employ those afflictions as the work of a Buddha;
just as one may drink a thousand measures of wine without becoming intoxicated or confused, it is said that they are able to establish their resolve.
If [the Bodhisattva] is among householders, he becomes the most honored among them and preaches the supreme Dharma for them.
This section below praises the noble one's virtuous power; through the skillful means of verbal secrecy (*vākkarmopāya*), he benefits sentient beings.

In discussing the Great Being (*mahāsattva*), there is no fixed distinction between high and low, as he manifests everywhere; yet here, the text specifically cites those who are honorable and eminent to fulfill the purpose of praising his virtues. Thus it says, "The Great Being."
Virtue serves as a model for all things and thus occupies the foremost position among the multitude. Now, when it is said that he is among the elders, he is the most venerable of elders;
as a world-renowned elder, each member of his village community harbors superior virtue and thus considers himself noble.
Yet, because the Great Being’s manifest traces as an elder possess virtues exceeding theirs, he is honored by them. [For this reason,] he preaches the Dharma for them.
Regarding the "Supreme Dharma" (Jingfa): first, he expounds the conventional supreme dharma so that all may submit;

subsequently, he accords with the four capacities [of sentient beings] to expound the supreme dharma of the four teachings. Having been honored as their master, he transforms those below by means of those above, leading them through compliance and obedience into the lineage of the inconceivable liberation and the Pure Land.
If he is among householders, he is the most honored among householders and severs their greedy attachments.

Regarding those who are honored among householders: in foreign lands, a householder possessing one hundred million in wealth is called a lower householder, while one possessing up to ten billion is called a superior householder.
In this land, those whose domestic virtue is long-established are called householders; it is feared that this person is such a one.
Those who possess great wealth and property are called *gṛhapati* (lay householders). Vimalakīrti constantly kept their pursuit of wealth and profit in mind;
though he manifested the traces of a superior virtue by possessing immeasurable riches, his giving was inexhaustible. Thus, he was honored by the *gṛhapatis*.
Accordingly, to suit the four different capacities of those beings, he preached the four teachings and the methods for practicing *dāna* (generosity), so that they might become free from greed.
He enters the inconceivable liberation and the pure land.
If he is among the kṣatriyas, he is honored as the most eminent among them and teaches through patience.
"Li" (利) is translated here as "royal lineage"; the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* translates it as "lord of the fields. In the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, his traces manifest compassion.

Because the excellence of patience is supreme, it is made the object of veneration; those who teach through patience do so because the Kṣatriyas possess sovereign power and much self-indulgence and majesty, and thus they are taught patience.
The root-natures of the Kṣatriyas are also of four kinds, and the four teachings respond to their conditions.
Through various forms of loving-kindness and patience, they are led to enter the lineage of the inconceivable liberation and the pure land.
If he is among the Brahmins, he is the most honored among them, having eliminated their pride.
"Brahmin" (婆羅門) is translated here as "one of external intent," meaning those who have inherited from generation to generation a superior and excellent external learning;
it is also translated as "Pure Conduct" (淨行), meaning one whose pure name manifests traces to demonstrate peerless excellence in learning and conduct, such that none can surpass him.

For this reason, they are held in high esteem; it is because their pride has been removed. Among the Brahmins, there are those who, relying on their own learning and pure conduct, look down upon others.
However, upon encountering the profound learning and superior Dharma of Vimalakīrti, their pride naturally collapses.

Yet, as their faculties and dispositions differ, they do not fall outside of four types; according to the four teachings, the Dharma is preached to them as appropriate, so that each may abandon their pride.
This is the resonance and legacy of entering the Pure Land of inconceivable liberation.
If one is among the great ministers, one should honor them as the most venerable and instruct them with the True Dharma (*saddharma*).
As for those who are the most venerable among the great ministers, each has their own specific domain of responsibility; regarding that which they oversee...
The "Luminous and Pure Name" (*Vimalanāman*) is so called because it demonstrates luminous penetration; thus, all are honored.

"Teaching by means of the True Dharma" (*Saddharmadeśanā*) indicates the true dharma of the supreme and wondrous methods of governance for all ministers. Furthermore, the way of a minister must be the correct path to assist the sovereign;

those who are treacherous and sycophantic are transformed so that they become sincere and loyal. However, the root-natures (*indriya*) of all ministers do not exceed four types, which act according to conditions.
By preaching the fourfold Dharma of the Four Noble Truths to cause others to enter the inconceivable liberation and the four lands,
he establishes the station of the Dharma King.
If he is among princes, he is the most honored among them, demonstrating loyalty and filial piety.
Among princes, the Honored One Vimalakīrti is preeminent; because he is profoundly learned, filial, and possessed of supreme virtue, he is revered by all princes.
To instruct them in profound filial piety, [the Buddha taught that] as princes, one must be filial as a son and sincere as a minister.
However, since the dispositions of princes differ, the four teachings are expounded according to what is appropriate for each, and thus the four aspects of the Buddha-dharma are taught.
To cultivate the way of sincerity and filial piety as the children of the four kinds of Dharma Kings, practicing in accordance with the four teachings, is filiality;
to disregard one's own body and life in order to propagate the four teachings is loyalty.
These four kinds of sincere filial piety are the seeds for entering the inconceivable liberation and being reborn in the four lands.
If one is among the inner officials and is the most honored among them, they shall transform and govern the palace women.
According to the laws of foreign lands, those who have been true and upright for seven generations, who have never committed sexual misconduct, and who possess virtue are taken as inner officials;
they are entrusted with entry into the palace to manage internal affairs, and the ruler regards them as intimate and essential confidants, keeping their counsel secret.

Furthermore, Vimalakīrti manifested the traces of purity by demonstrating that he was not subject to lust; because his virtue was supreme and beyond reproach, he was held in the highest esteem among all the palace eunuchs.
As for his transformation of the palace women: since these women were externally constrained by prohibitions, they often gave rise to internal deviant thoughts.
If such perverse and improper thoughts were to persist, they would destroy the four kinds of roots of goodness. Thus, the Great Being (Mahāsattva) employs the four teachings to respond to them.
The Master preached the fourfold Eightfold Path so that they might attain right view and enter the lineage of the inconceivable;
this is the cause for being reborn in the four lands.
If one is among the common people, he causes them to become honored among the common people and to give rise to the power of merit.

Among the common people, those who are honored have little karmic reward, while those of low birth are constantly despised and unable to reach the heights; yet they dare to admire those of superior station.
Although a Great Being (Mahāsattva) manifests the appearance of a particular caste, his virtue is lofty and honored, and he is able to show universal love to all subordinates.

Thus, the common people feel profound gratitude and redouble their respect for him. This causes them to arouse the power of merit, as the common people are always humble and lowly, yet follow [his example].
Because their root-natures differ, he teaches the four vehicles, explaining that through the power of the merit of practicing charity and giving,
one shall be born in the Pure Land and attain the fruit of supreme excellence.
If they are among the Brahmā gods, he instructs them with superior wisdom as the most honored one within the Brahmā heavens.

Among the eighteen Brahmās who are honored within the Brahma-heaven, although they frequently enter the four dhyānas and the four immeasurables with much attachment to their flavors, their entry is not profound or pure;

thus, their names and traces merely indicate these various dhyānas. However, because [the Buddha] contemplates, refines, perfumes, and cultivates them to enter deeply into the boundless, he is instructed by all the Brahmās.
For those of superior wisdom, he explains the pure dhyāna and the stainless dhyāna.
The supreme wisdom of the skillful means for entering, abiding in, and emerging from [the path] consists merely of the various natures of the Brahma-faculties;

according to the conditions of those to be guided, the four teachings are expounded accordingly as the supreme wisdom of the fourfold Four Noble Truths, leading them into the inconceivable liberation of the Buddha’s four lands.
If he appears among Śakra as the most honored among the Śakras to demonstrate impermanence—

wherein that most honored one among the Śakras, the god Śakra, is attached to pleasure and immersed in delusion, unaware that he is sinking into the net of desire— then Vimalakīrti, who is free from desire,
pure, and sublime, and who is revered by the Lord of Devas, explains impermanence for him, so that the Lord of Devas may preserve himself.

The Great Being (Mahāsattva) Nityapriya constantly preached for them the fifteen contemplative gates on impermanence (*anitya*), as clearly explained in the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
However, because the spiritual faculties (*indriya*) of Śakra differ, the four teachings (*catuḥ-deśanā*) preach different aspects of impermanence according to the needs of those to be converted.

In the Tripiṭaka Teaching, the clarification of impermanence involves arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*), which possesses a fixed characteristic; in the Shared Teaching, impermanence is likewise explained.
All are like illusions and transformations; in the Separate Teaching (Biaojiao), from the stage of the Vajra back down, all are impermanent.

In the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), all dharmas tend toward impermanence, and there is nothing that does not pass through this tendency. These four types of teaching on impermanence serve as gateways to lead one into the inconceivable liberation of the Buddha’s Four Lands (Four Dhātu).
If one dwells among the World-Protectors (Lokapālas), who are honored as the most venerable among them, one protects all sentient beings.
These Honored Ones among the World-Protectors, the Four Heavenly Kings, reside upon the four terraces halfway up Mount Sumeru;
each presides over two classes of spirits and deities, ensuring they do not harm the people of the four continents. Thus, the traces of a Great Being manifest compassion and protection.

Furthermore, because beings surpass even the World-Protectors (Lokapālas), they are honored and protected by the World-Protectors. As for those who protect all sentient beings, the faculties (indriya) of the Four Heavenly Kings differ;

therefore, the Great Being (Mahāsattva) preaches the Dharma for them so that they may give rise to four kinds of fourfold great vows (caturvidha-catuḥ-praṇidhāna) to protect those sentient beings who possess the roots of goodness (kuśalamūla) of the Four Noble Truths (catuḥ-satya).
Within each of the Four Noble Truths, there are the four [vows] corresponding to the wisdom of the Four Noble Truths, and these are present within each of the Four Heavenly Kings.

Seeing and contemplating [the truths] are subsumed under the two classes of spirits; when these two types of spirits do not disturb the various wholesome mental factors, they are protecting all sentient beings.
By responding to conditions through the teaching of the four *yānas*, they protect the True Dharma arising from the four kinds of the Four Truths so that it does not decline.
When the four kinds of roots of goodness are thus preserved, one enters the inconceivable and is born in the Pure Land.
"Kong" means "to transmit.
The Elder Vimalakīrti benefits sentient beings through such immeasurable skillful means (*upāya*).
This is the third section, which establishes these skillful means; he dwells in Vaiśālī, and this pertains solely to the skillful means of Vimalakīrti’s three karmas.

To assist in manifesting inconceivable liberation and the Buddha-land, which pervades the ten directions and the ten dharma-realms, how could it be limited merely to the thirty-five matters mentioned above?
Such are the immeasurable benefits. A question is asked:

Regarding the title "World-Honored One" (Bhagavān) now mentioned, does it mean that he is honored because his single body enters into all bodies, or should it mean that he is honored because he takes birth in each and every place?
Regarding this, he replied: "All possess these types of meanings. For example, as in the Universal Gate (Samantamukha), various bodies are manifested;
now we specifically take up the swift arising of the teaching. Through the traces of a single body, the Elder is able to skillfully employ all [means];

wherever he manifests himself, there is no one who does not respectfully receive him, and there is no sentient being whose capacity is opened and transformed who does not receive benefit. One should know that such things do not apply to the Dharma-body of the Elder."

Because he manifests objects through the conditions of karma, he will thus manifest as a householder; though his body is fundamentally free from illness, he relies upon the pretext of illness to give rise to the teaching for the sake of sentient beings.
Therefore, it is necessary to first describe the preceding expedient means as a prelude. Up to this point, the conclusion is established:

from the fundamental [state], he descends to manifest traces, revealing the expedient means of the fundamental [nature] through causes and conditions, appearing in form and using sound to benefit sentient beings.
Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra Commentary, Scroll Nine;
Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra Commentary, Scroll Ten (Part Two of the Chapter on Expedient Means):
He manifests illness through expedient means.
From here down to the conclusion of the chapter on entering the room, there are eight and a half fascicles of sutra text that constitute the second major section.

This section concerns Vimalakīrti’s skillful means of feigning illness to manifest the teaching, assisting the Buddha in propagating the transformation [of beings], leading them into inconceivable liberation, removing the defilements of their karmic offenses, enabling them to see pure lands, and introducing them to the four realms so as to perfect the practice for attaining a pure buddha-field. Now...
The clear exposition of the name "Skillful Means" and the pretext of illness are intended for four purposes: first, to transform kings, ministers, and subjects;
second, to inspire the class of disciples; third, to inspire the class of bodhisattvas; and fourth, to inspire the "Inquiry into Illness" chapter.
Regarding the first purpose—to transform the king, ministers, elders, and householders—it is because he pretexts illness that the king, elders, and others [are moved].
I have come to offer my condolences; therefore, I shall use this occasion of my physical ailment to address you with words of rebuke and exhortation for your own convenience.
If you can give rise to a mind weary of worldly pleasures, you will immediately be able to sever all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and cultivate the myriad practices (*sādhana*).

This constitutes the seed-germ for entering the inconceivable liberation, and it is the cause for attaining birth in the Pure Lands of the Shared Residence (*sahabhū*) and the Land of Residual Existence (*śeṣa*). Second, this serves to inspire and arouse [the disciple].
Regarding the "Chapter on the Disciples": if the Tathāgata did not manifest illness, he would have had no reason to summon his disciples for questioning.

If the disciples had not received this summons, how could they have recounted the matters of their past reprimands? Thus, today all those of the Two Vehicles may hear together of their past stagnation in the Lesser Vehicle and their subsequent reprimands;
and when those who cling to the Lesser Vehicle and delight in the Lesser Vehicle hear this, they will abandon their attachment.

It is with great care that this subdues [the mind] and inspires longing for the Mahāyāna; in the near term, it serves as the means for entering the chamber and hearing the inconceivable causes and conditions for the formation of *sarpis* (clarified butter);
in the distant term, it serves as the precursor to the ripening of *mantha-sarpis* and *ghṛta-maṇḍa* (ghee-cream) through the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* and *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* sūtras.
It is also a virtuous condition for the arising of the land of *vipākaphala*. Third, regarding its function of initiating the Bodhisattva stage: if one does not rely upon...
If the sick Bodhisattvas had not been summoned, how could they have each related their past experiences of being rebuked?
Thus, today, the Bodhisattvas of the Tripiṭaka Teaching, the Shared Teaching, and the Distinct Teaching may all have their attachments and stagnations regarding expedient means broken down;
together they shall rejoice in the Perfect and Sudden Way, achieving entry into inconceivable liberation and the excellence of purifying Buddha-lands.
As for the fourth reason for initiating the "Inquiry into the Illness" chapter: if one did not feign illness, by what means could Mañjuśrī have been summoned?
Having received the command, Mañjuśrī entered the chamber to inquire after the illness and discuss the Way.

He extensively developed and enlightened sentient beings, causing the fame of the disciples to resound throughout the three thousandfold world system, and advancing the Bodhisattvas toward the practice of the three contemplations so they might enter the inconceivable liberation.

The realization of the Way is the cause for purifying the Buddha-land. These four intentions all arise from relying upon illness; since illness is not substantially real, it is called a "skillful means" (*upāya*). The power of skillful means is entrusted to the preaching of the Dharma, which properly belongs to the benefit of sound. Now, to clarify the intention behind Vimalakīrti’s reliance on illness to give rise to the teaching, there are four points; the general outline of the scriptural text is as follows: [The text continues with the four points: 1. To manifest the principle that the body is empty while the mind is not. 2. To manifest the principle that the mind is empty while the body is not. 3. To manifest the principle that both body and mind are not empty. 4. To manifest the principle that both body and mind are empty. By means of these four principles, he manifests the four kinds of purity. Because these four kinds of purity are the causes for purifying the Buddha-land, they are explained here. Furthermore, the four kinds of purity are the causes for attaining the four wisdoms. Because these four wisdoms are the causes for purifying the Buddha-land, they are also explained here.

Thus, the four kinds of purity and the four wisdoms together constitute the eight aspects of the pure land. This is the meaning of the four intentions. The first three intentions are the causes for purifying the land through the practice of the path; the fourth intention is the cause for purifying the land through the fruition of the path. These four intentions all arise from relying upon illness. Since illness is not substantially real, it is called a "skillful means. The power of skillful means is entrusted to the preaching of the Dharma, which properly belongs to the benefit of sound. Now, in clarifying the intention behind Vimalakīrti’s reliance on illness to give rise to the teaching, there are four [points], and the scriptural text provides a general judgment of them as a whole.
This is divided into two sections. First, from here down to the end of the "Bodhisattva" chapter, there are two and a half chapters;

these constitute the teaching given outside the chamber, which clarifies the methods of reprimand and subjugation. Second, from the "Mañjuśrī’s Inquiry on the Illness" chapter onward, there are six chapters concerning entry into the chamber;
these constitute the teaching given inside the chamber, which clarifies the methods of guidance and reception. Because subjugation is followed by reception, it causes [sentient beings] to...
The True Dharma shall abide for a long time; that which is called "the True Dharma abiding for a long time" is precisely abiding in the inconceivable liberation.
Within the act of subduing (*nigraha*), there is not a lack of gathering (*saṃgraha*); within the act of gathering, there is not a lack of subduing.

However, this is discussed in terms of what predominates, such that there may be secondary or primary aspects. Now, regarding the text on subduing outside the chamber, it is divided into three parts. First:
The first half of the chapter clarifies the subduing of sentient beings within the realm who are conditioned by the accumulation of the conditioned;

the second chapter concerns the subduing of sentient beings who are conditioned by the accumulation of the unconditioned; and the third chapter concerning Bodhisattvas concerns the subduing of those whose accumulation is conditioned by their own essential *dharmadhātu*.
Question: Is there a difference between being conditioned by the unconditioned and being conditioned by one's own essence?
Answer: There are Mahāyāna masters whose explanations differ. What is said here is that although the names are distinct, the essence of the delusion is not different.

The two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) give rise to clinging toward the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) due to being deluded regarding their own nature; because they cling to the unconditioned, they correctly take the unconditioned as a condition for the arising of [afflictions].

They are called Bodhisattvas because they also give rise to the arising of conditions for the unconditioned due to being deluded regarding their own nature; however, the Bodhisattva observes and destroys this.

Although the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) has no accumulation through conditions, as long as these delusions have not been exhausted, they remain attached to the substance and are separately designated by the name "accumulation through conditions of its own substance.
This is like ordinary beings who, being deluded regarding reality, give rise to conditioned accumulations;

even though practitioners who perceive reality have severed [the afflictions of] views and discursive thought (*vitarka*), because they are not yet exhaustive, they still possess the designations of greed and anger toward the truth, as well as the taints of the form realm and the formless realm. Question: *Note: The term "delusions" (*moha*) here refers to the underlying ignorance that persists despite the partial realization of truth.*

Question: If a practitioner of the Śrāvaka vehicle has not exhausted the conditioned accumulation of conditions (*saṃskṛta-pratyaya-samudāya*) and, though seeing the Truth, still possesses delusion, they are said to "not take the Truth as their object" and are thus called "conditioned accumulation by way of self-nature" (*svabhāva-pratyaya-samudāya*).

Why then can a Bodhisattva, who has not exhausted the unconditioned accumulation of conditions (*asaṃskṛta-pratyaya-samudāya*) and sees the Truth, be separately designated by the name "conditioned accumulation by way of self-nature"?

Answer: The vision of the Truth by those of the Two Vehicles is merely the principle of emptiness (*śūnyatā-tattva*); this principle of emptiness is not the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Therefore, it is not the same.

Having attained the name of "Bodhisattva" as an established self-substance, because the Bodhisattva perceives the true reality—that this very Dharma-body is eternally present—one may separately establish the name based on the conditions of its accumulation.
Since the Bodhisattva’s delusions are yet unknown and not fully understood, they must be suppressed.
Now, it is explained that this half-chapter of the sutra contains four intended meanings, the first of which is the correct elucidation of skillful means (*upāya*).
1. Manifesting Illness; 2. Explaining the Visits and Inquiries of Those Who Came to See Him; 3. Explaining the Causes for Preaching the Dharma; 4.
Explaining the Benefits Gained by the Assembly at That Time. First, regarding "Manifesting Illness": The Sūtra states that he manifested illness through skillful means.

Although Vimalakīrti’s Dharma-body is free from illness, he manifested this same illness [as others]. This signifies that the Dharma-body is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and possesses nothing [of the nature of illness].

Taking the causal accumulation of suffering as a condition, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, he manifests through skillful means the afflictions of the cause and effect of conditioned phenomena belonging to ordinary persons;
furthermore, he shares the afflictions of the cause and effect of unconditioned causal accumulations common to the Two Vehicles;

and he likewise shares the afflictions of the causal accumulation of the dharma-realm within his own being, which pertains to Bodhisattvas. Question: How is this known to be so? Answer: [As follows:]...
It is said that a later passage in this sutra states: "The illness of a bodhisattva arises from great compassion;
because sentient beings are ill, I am also ill. If sentient beings were free from illness, then I too would be free from illness. A questioner asks:

Since Vimalakīrti’s manifest traces reside within the human realm, he may share the same physical ailments as ordinary people; yet, internally, he demonstrates the practice of the bodhisattva path. Is this not the case?

Question: Since the Bodhisattvas possess the disease of the accumulation of conditions for their own physical bodies—and this is not the case for the Two Vehicles—how can they be the same as the Two Vehicles regarding the disease of the accumulation of conditions for the unconditioned?
Answer: Vimalakīrti dwells in the inconceivable; he manifests in whatever form is necessary to deliver those who should be saved by the bodies of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
How could he not manifest that same illness? Furthermore, [this refers to] the Bodhisattvas of the Manifestation (Pratibhāsa) Teaching.
The Buddha’s own body manifested this illness of the conditioned arising of the unconditioned; this illness is the same as that of the two vehicles.
Regarding the meaning of manifesting illness (and so forth), it shall be fully analyzed in the "Inquiry into the Illness" chapter.
Because of his illness, the king, ministers, elders, householders, brahmins, and other princes,
along with thousands of other officials and attendants, all went to inquire after his health.

This is the second inquiry regarding his illness. Since Vimalakīrti is honored by all beings and possesses the qualities praised as before, and furthermore, since there are no commoners or officials who do not receive his grace, how could one not go now that he is ill to inquire after him?
Therefore, the kings, ministers, and subjects have all come to inquire about his illness; indeed, the multitude who have come to inquire about his illness is countless thousands.

All these people were spiritual friends with whom Vimalakīrti had karmic affinities in the present life; because they had formed wholesome conditions through the four teachings in past lives, their spiritual capacities were stirred and moved, leading them to seek his presence.
Relying on the occasion of inquiring after his illness as a catalyst, they all came to pay their respects and inquire after him.
In the past, Vimalakīrti used his own physical illness as an occasion to expound the Dharma extensively.
This is the third point: if he did not manifest illness, there would be no means to rebuke the various noble families; even if they were to come, there would be no cause for his censure.
Furthermore, it is difficult to explain how he could pass over others' bodies to speak of faults when Vimalakīrti himself was in the same situation.
Since they possess bodies and are subject to illness, and as I too am subject to illness, how could they possibly be exempt from it?

Therefore, by means of my own illness, I have extensively expounded upon the faults and afflictions of the body to inspire in them a sense of weary detachment (*nirveda*) and to exhort them to seek the fruit of Buddhahood.

Furthermore, there are two distinct aspects to preaching the Dharma on account of illness: first, explaining the gate of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-mukha*) through weary detachment, which carries the meaning of admonition; second, exhorting them to seek the state of a Buddha.

The body itself is the meaning of exhortation. The reason there are these two kinds of teaching is that the contemplative practice of wearying detachment is the instruction to sever evil, while the exhortation to seek the Buddha-body is the encouragement to produce goodness;
through this, one enters the inconceivable and accomplishes the karma for the Pure Land. Furthermore, if one were to merely exhort weary detachment...
One may distance oneself from severing evil without being exhorted to seek Buddhahood, or one may fear the world and fall into the two stages (*dvibhūmi*).
If one falls into these two stages, according to what is elucidated in this sutra and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, one becomes a person whose faculties are ruined;

however, according to what is elucidated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, one merely takes a circuitous route toward the Buddha-way. Now, regarding this chapter, the gate of contemplation is manifold.
This is the contemplative gateway common to the teachings of the Tripitaka. How is this known?

For instance, the analogy of the *dharmatā* being like a plantain tree is the teaching of the Tripitaka, whereas the analogies such as illusions and dreams represent the intent of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-śāsana*).
"Venerable sirs, this body is impermanent, lacking strength, lacking power, and lacking solidity; it is a nature that quickly decays and cannot be relied upon.
This is the first contemplation, which explains the practice of contemplation by means of censure to induce weary detachment. Other masters provide a fivefold interpretation.
There is a master who uses the five aspects of impermanence (*anityatā*) to explain this passage, clarifying its meaning through two gates and briefly enumerating five types.
First, regarding the teaching based on the two paths of insight (*darśana-mārga*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*): how is this known?

Because the initial explanation of suffering and the following four aspects precisely pertain to the path of insight, while the subsequent explanation of the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) pertains to the path of cultivation; thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains the ten [aspects].

The first three contemplations illustrate the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*); the fourth illustrates the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*); and the final three contemplations represent the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*).

Now, I exhort all people to seek the fruit of Buddhahood; there is no need to speak of the final three contemplations. Second, to clarify the teaching according to the two types of foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*):
if one speaks of the four aspects under the category of suffering, these are the "foundations of mindfulness as intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva-smṛtyupasthāna*); if one speaks of [the other truths]...

Pure contemplation (*śubha-vipaśyanā*) is precisely the common application of mindfulness (*sāmānya-smṛtyupasthāna*). Regarding the three knowledges (*trividyā*), they are explained in terms of two types of practice:
if one speaks of the four [foundations] below suffering, this is the practice of wisdom (*prajñā-carita*); if one speaks of impurity (*aśubha*), this is the practice of conduct (*caryā-carita*).

Regarding the four knowledges, they are explained in terms of two types of contemplation: if one relies on the four practices below suffering, this is the contemplation of reality (*bhūta-vipaśyanā*); if one speaks of impurity, it is...
This is the contemplation that attains liberation. Regarding the five sciences (*pañcavidyā*), they are explained in terms of the two paths: the primary path and the auxiliary path.

If one speaks of the four aspects below suffering (*duḥkha*), this refers to the primary path; if one speaks of impurity (*aśubha*), this refers to the various meditative concentrations such as the nine notions (*navasaṃjñā*), the liberations (*vimokṣa*), and the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
In this manner, through these various dual gateways, he extensively provides instruction, guidance, benefit, and joy for all people.
Now, the Pure Name (Vimalakīrti) addresses these two extremes for the sake of those who have come to inquire after his illness and preach the Dharma;
his intent is manifold, but five points are briefly set forth: first, to cause those who hear the Dharma to cultivate contemplation with weary detachment and seek the Unsurpassed Way;
if the conditions of their accumulation [of karma] are not yet severed, this constitutes the cause for being reborn in either a defiled or a pure Buddha-land in a future life.
1. If the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) that take the two realms as their object are severed, one will immediately attain rebirth in a *sopadhiśeṣa* (with remainder) land.

2. If one can direct the mind toward the Buddha’s wisdom, it shall be just as seen by Śaṅkhakuñjara; thus, the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-sūtra* clarifies that through the power of repentance, karmic obstructions are gradually eliminated, and one perceives the pure and wondrous land within this very body.
3. If one realizes the principle of true non-arising (*bhūtānutpāda*), [one attains liberation].

Through patience, one immediately attains rebirth in the land of fruition; through the inconceivable liberation of the five stages of dwelling, one is able to accomplish the maturation of sentient beings and the purification of Buddha-lands.
When all conditions have ripened and one sits at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), one takes up a Buddha-land according to the beings to be transformed.
By feigning illness, he preached these two types of contemplative practices as skillful means for benefit; this is a brief understanding.
The general meaning is as follows: now, regarding the four aspects of the suffering of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), first we explain impermanence through the gate of existence (*yōmon*).
A sutra states: "This body is impermanent. This means that the body exists by gathering three factors; the body is merely a provisional name (*prajñapti*).

Because these three factors are impermanent, one says the body is impermanent; there is no separate body apart from them. That the body is constituted by these three factors is like [the example of] the great...

The *Saṃyukta Āgama* states that at the stage of the *kalala*, there are three factors: first, life; second, warmth; and third, consciousness. The inhalation and exhalation of breath are termed "life.
That which is neither putrid nor decomposed is designated as "warmth. Within this [embryo], the mental faculty is called "consciousness.
The integration of these three factors is named the stage of the *kalala*, continuing thus until birth, through the prime of youth, and into old age.
All these are sustained by karma, wherein the three factors arise and cease in an uninterrupted succession.

Ordinary beings do not understand this and falsely grasp at the characteristics of the body, giving rise to perceptions of permanence and various afflictions. Unaware that their vital breath will be severed and the three factors will separate, they are struck with terror and sorrow, sinking into the sea of suffering.
Their entire life passes in vain; though they may feel regret upon reaching the Yellow Springs, what can they do?
Now, the virtuous friend Vimalakīrti has taught that the body is impermanent in order to shatter the perversion of regarding it as permanent. Why is this so?

If one considers the body to be formed by the gathering of the three factors [wind, heat, and consciousness], then when the breath ceases, that which was calculated as "life" is extinguished. If the breath departs and does not return, the body becomes like rubble;
how then can life be preserved? It is only because the vital warmth sustains the water, and the moisture of the water permeates the earth [of the body] that life appears to persist.

The deluded claim that this body is permanent; yet fire arises from conditions and, when those conditions disperse, the fire is extinguished, and the body then becomes putrid and rotten—how could it possibly be permanent?
Bound by karma, the deluded consciousness shifts through different realms in each moment, while the "self" is said to be eternally sovereign.
If the rope of karma is severed, the mind immediately takes rebirth and the body dissolves and perishes. One should know that these three matters are thus.
All things are impermanent. If one awakens to this fire of impermanence that burns the world, even the *sabhāga-rūpa* (the body as the primary fruit of retribution) cannot be preserved;
how much less so the *vibhāga-rūpa* (the external world as the secondary support), which has no bearing on human affairs?

If one can thus awaken to coarse impermanence, one will be able to relinquish all conditioned phenomena. If one contemplates subtle impermanence, when the mind is settled in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one perceives the principle of impermanence.

Entering the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga) immediately is called *srotāpanna*; whether it be wisdom (*jñāna*) or abandonment (*prahāṇa*), this is the Bodhisattva’s acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*).

According to the *Abhidharma* (Vibhāṣā), when the meaning is clarified through the gate of existence (*bhāvavāda*), the subtle principle of impermanence (*anityatā*) is seen; this is the Path of Seeing.

According to the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, when the meaning is clarified through the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), one enters emptiness by means of the subtle impermanence; only then is it the Path of Seeing. Now, as for what is said here...

The Gate of Existence clarifies the meaning that skillful cultivation of impermanence can destroy the two views of self-existence (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), thereby entering the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*).

This refers to the sixty-two views—namely, the view of existence, the view of non-existence, the view of both existence and non-existence, the view of neither existence nor non-existence, the view of equality, and so forth—as well as all other views.
If one knows that these are all entirely impermanent, one will be able to perceive the principle and sever them.

This refers to the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava*). By deeply contemplating impermanence (*anityatā*), one not only severs these views but can also sever the delusions of thought (*bhāvanā-āsrava*).

Therefore, the Buddha said that by skillfully cultivating the perception of impermanence, one can sever attachment to the realm of form (*rūpa-rāga*) and attachment to the formless realm (*arūpya-rāga*). When the Sūtra says "there is nothing strong," it is to establish the meaning of impermanence;
for if the three bases (*trivastu*) upon which conventional designations depend were strong, then neither arising nor ceasing could take place.
One who is subject to transition and thus possesses birth, cessation, and the change of impermanence should know that the substance of these three factors is weak and the body lacks strength.
As a sutra says, "those who lack power," this also serves to establish impermanence.

If the three factors upon which the provisional name "body" depends possessed power, they would be able to resist the birth and cessation of conditioned phenomena; yet because of these three factors— [the body] is unable to do so.
Because it lacks the power to resist the arising and ceasing of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), it is transformed by the nature of conditioned arising and ceasing;
thus, one should know that this body is powerless. As the Sūtra says, "There is nothing solid," for the essence of these three things all lacks a fixed nature.
If there were a fixed nature, that nature would truly be like a vajra; how could it then be subject to conditioned arising?

That which is altered and destroyed by cessation is impermanent. Now, because this body of conventional designation lacks intrinsic nature due to the conditions of the three factors and is not independent, it is conditioned and subject to alteration and destruction by arising and cessation; one should know that this body has no solidity.
For example, when the Arhats wished to compile the Dharma-piṭaka, they first recited a verse, saying: "Impermanent."
The *Vajramati-bhañjana-ārya-mahāparvatarāja-sūtra* states: "The nature of rapid decay is this provisional designation of a body, which relies upon three factors;
these three factors are weak and inferior, easily destroyed and subject to sudden collapse. One should know that this body is of the nature of rapid decay.
The sūtra further states: "It is not to be trusted. This is the concluding phrase that refutes attachment. [These refer to] this body and these three things.
If there were permanence, constancy, strength, power, solidity, and indestructibility, then one might calculate things as permanent.

However, since karma is exhausted without appointment with anyone, one cannot guarantee that an exhaled breath will meet an inhaled breath; one cannot guarantee that what is about to enter the mouth remains upon eating;

and one cannot guarantee that a preceding thought remains for a succeeding thought. Whatever actions are performed, none can be guaranteed. Why is this so? Because one perceives the world as it truly is.
A person passes away in an instant without realizing it; how can they falsely reckon that things are permanent?
Believing in this deluded sentiment, they excuse themselves, commit evil, do not cultivate the Way, and do not perform meritorious deeds.
"O virtuous ones, this body is suffering, it is affliction, and it is the gathering place of all diseases; thus, the wise do not rely upon it.
This is the teaching according to the gate of contemplation on suffering. It specifically clarifies suffering through three phrases. As the Sūtra says:
"It is suffering because it is impermanent. Why is this so? If the body is constituted by three things, all three things are entirely impermanent.
That which is constantly being cut—the body as a provisional designation—is itself suffering.
This body, composed of these three factors, being afflicted by the three sufferings, the four sufferings, and the eight sufferings, is what constitutes suffering. As the Sūtra says:
"To be tormented" means that the body as a provisional designation, composed of these three factors, is tormented by the nine provocations and various external conditions.
Being afflicted by objects is "distress" (*upāyāsa*). That is to say, internal suffering is "suffering" (*duḥkha*), while external suffering that comes to press upon one is "distress.
Furthermore, the initial suffering is "suffering," and its repeated and incessant pressing is called "distress. As the Sūtra says, "the gathering place of all maladies":
the three factors in combination are termed the body; these are breath and warmth, which are material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) consisting of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
On a large scale, there are four hundred and four illnesses gathered within this body and mind.
There are four divisions of afflictions (*kleśa*), and from these four divisions of afflictions, eighty-four thousand illnesses of affliction arise.

Thus, all such illnesses of form and mind are gathered within the body that is a mere provisional designation (*prajñapti-sat*); therefore, it is said that "it is the locus where all illnesses converge. Furthermore, it acts for the sake of those who suffer.
Suffering (*duḥkha*) refers to the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), because there is no relaxation or haste, and because there is no lightness or heaviness;

thus it is called suffering. "Action as affliction" refers to the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*); because adverse conditions afflict and destroy pleasant sensations (*sukha-vedanā*), it is called affliction.

"Being like a disease" refers to the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*); since the body itself consists of the four [primary] sufferings, it is further burdened by the sufferings of the four hundred and four diseases; therefore, it is so described.

Question: Since the general suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) has four distinct aspects and the specific suffering of suffering also has four distinct aspects—and since the specific suffering of suffering is, in fact, these same four types of suffering—why is illness specifically designated as the "suffering of suffering"? Answer:

Because the suffering of birth already oppresses one, the suffering of death has not yet arrived, and the suffering of old age is slight, it is in relation to the suffering of illness that the "suffering of suffering" is explained. Furthermore...
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* speaks of "relying on illness" as a pretext for the sake of [explaining] the suffering of illness. The Sūtra says, "That which is not relied upon by the wise.

This concludes the meaning of suffering. If one can carefully and precisely observe that the provisional body possesses three aspects and clearly perceives that there is not even a moment of pleasure—that is what constitutes being "wise. If these three aspects are all subject to the three types of suffering...
Since suffering is not a single instance of pleasure, nor is there even a moment of pleasure that can be maintained or relied upon,
the *Śrī-sūtra* (Ruiying jing) states: "Therefore, the sage constantly regards the body as a source of affliction,
whereas the fool cherishes it until death, never reaching satiety."
This body is like a mass of foam, incapable of being grasped or rubbed; this body is like a bubble, unable to endure for long;
this body is like a mirage, born from craving and thirst; this body is like a plantain tree, having no solidity within;
this body is like an illusion, arising from perversion; this body is like a dream, a false perception; this body is like a shadow, appearing through the conditions of karma. This body...

This body is like an echo, dependent upon various causes and conditions; this body is like a floating cloud, changing and perishing in an instant; this body is like lightning, not abiding for even a single thought-moment.

These ten similes are precisely intended as analogies for the practice of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). There are two approaches to their interpretation: first, they are treated collectively and individually.

Explaining the two aspects of the common characteristics: first, regarding the classification into specific and general, the first five similes are specific similes for the five aggregates (*skandha*), while the subsequent five similes are general similes for the five aggregates.
How is this known? According to the explicit texts of the Sūtras and Śāstras, it says: "Contemplate form as like a mass of foam;
contemplate feeling as like a bubble; contemplate perception as like a mirage; contemplate mental formations as like a plantain tree; contemplate consciousness as like an illusion."

Regarding "form" (*rūpa*), the five subsequent analogies below—since there is no explicit textual correlation for them individually—should be understood as collectively illustrating the emptiness of the body.

Question: Do these five analogies correspond specifically to the five aggregates (*skandha*)? To which teaching do they definitively belong? If they belong to the Tripiṭaka Teaching (*Tripiṭaka-yāna*), one should not say that the mirage illustrates perception (*saṃjñā*) and the illusion illustrates consciousness (*vijñāna*).

If they belong to the Shared Teaching (*Sādhāraṇa-yāna*), one should not say that foam illustrates form and bubbles illustrate feeling (*vedanā*). [If they were the latter,] how could they illustrate reeds and plants?

The analogy of the plantain tree is used as a response; the four teachings of the Vaipulya (fangděng) all employ various analogies for the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), yet there is no doubt regarding this.

However, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that within the Śrāvaka sūtras, there are occasions where the Dharma-nature is taught through analogies such as being like an illusion for those of sharp faculties.

This is merely discussed from the perspective of the majority; each teaching gate has its own primary followers. Furthermore, the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* sometimes reiterates what preceded it.

Question: The two teachings explain that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are the primary subject, and the six metaphors and ten analogies illustrate the five aggregates up to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).

If these ten metaphors, whether taken individually or collectively, all illustrate the emptiness of the five aggregates, what is the intention behind not correlating them with the formation of a provisional body based on the five aggregates, but instead frequently correlating them with the formation of a provisional body based on the three factors? Answer: This... [The text continues: ...is because the three factors are the most fundamental basis for the arising of the provisional self, whereas the five aggregates are a more complex synthesis of various phenomena. Furthermore, the three factors—name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), and contact (*sparśa*)—are the immediate conditions for the manifestation of the deluded mind and the grasping of a self.

By focusing on these three factors, the text emphasizes the mechanism by which the false sense of self is constructed from the very beginning of existence. Thus, while the five aggregates encompass the full scope of phenomenal reality, the three factors serve as the specific lens through which the illusion of a personal identity is established. This distinction allows the teaching to penetrate the root of delusion rather than merely describing its outward manifestations.
Furthermore, the Buddha has at times taught that two factors constitute the provisional body, namely name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*);
or he has taught that three factors constitute the provisional body, which is what is used here; or he has taught that five factors constitute the body, namely the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*);

or he has taught that six factors constitute the body, namely the six bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*). These various combinations and divisions all appear in the sūtras and śāstras, following [the specific context].
Establishing these [analogies] based on conditions and adapting them to the capacities of beings ensures that there is no loss of principle.

The frequent use of three matters here is for the purpose of clarifying the various gates of dhyāna-contemplation and for their practical convenience. Next, I shall provide a general explanation: all ten of these analogies illustrate the emptiness of the body.
Although other sutras use the first five analogies to represent the five aggregates individually, this sutra states that all ten analogies apply to the [body].
This body is not distinguished from the previous five analogies for the five aggregates; therefore, it cannot be explained separately as either specific or general as was done previously.

Here, we simply provide a general clarification of these ten analogies, showing that many illustrate the emptiness of the provisional name (prajñapti) of the body, while some also illustrate the emptiness of dharmas.
Within these ten analogies, five belong to the Tripiṭaka Teaching, five belong to the Mahāyāna Shared Teaching, and one belongs to the Distinct Teaching.
The Master explains that this chapter employs the contemplation gates of the Tripiṭaka Teaching and the Shared Teaching as the means for preaching the Dharma to various people;
its intent lies in using both the "clumsy" and "skillful" methods to sever the conditioned arising of the outflows within the realms.
The five similes—like a mass of foam, like a bubble, like a plantain tree, like a cloud, and like lightning—are the similes of the Small Vehicle Tripiṭaka Teaching. (5)
For example, regarding the analogies common to the Mahāyāna *pāṭha* (teaching), they are like a mirage, like an illusion, like a dream, like a shadow, and like an echo. Question:
How is this known to be so? Answer: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* contains this distinction, as explained in detail previously. Question:
Regarding the analogies such as "a mass of foam" found in the *Tripiṭaka* teachings, how does their meaning differ from the meaning of the Mahāyāna analogies such as "a mirage"?
The distinct response regarding the Tripiṭaka Teaching uses analogies such as a mass of foam and so forth: the material substance of this world exists, yet it is merely empty and unsubstantial;
it is easily analyzed into emptiness. Because people do not know that the physical body is empty, these analogies are employed.
As for what is clarified in the Mahāyāna through analogies such as a mirage and so forth: although they appear to exist when seen by the eye, they are in reality non-existent and subtle.
The empty and subtle substance of formless matter is used as an analogy for all coarse and subtle matter that possesses substance;
it signifies that all dharmas that possess a substantial nature are empty. Question: Since all dharmas are empty, how can emptiness be used as an analogy for emptiness? Answer:

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that the emptiness which is easy to understand is used as an analogy for the emptiness which is difficult to understand; therefore, ten analogies and ten similes are employed.
Question: The analogies such as "a mass of foam" and so forth also apply universally to those of the three vehicles;
for what reason are the analogies such as "a mirage" and so forth not called universal teachings of the Mahāyāna, even though they likewise serve as analogies for those of the three vehicles?
Answer: The analogies such as "a mirage" and so forth are not only for the sake of the three vehicles; they are universal.
Furthermore, because it can encompass both the *pṛthagjana* (separate), *vaipulya* (expanded), and *pariniṣpanna* (perfect) [teachings], it is that which is employed in the *Mahāyāna-sūtras*.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-śāstra* states: "Based on the *ālayavijñāna*, eight similes such as illusions and dreams are taught. The similes of the mass of foam and the bubble are not like this;
how could they be considered equivalent? My current explanation of the ten similes concerns only the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), which fully applies to both arising and phenomena (*dharma*).
In the Tripiṭaka teachings, the analogy of emptiness mostly illustrates the emptiness of persons and rarely illustrates the emptiness of dharmas;
whereas in the Mahāyāna teachings, analogies such as a mirage and so forth illustrate the emptiness of persons and simultaneously illustrate the emptiness of dharmas.

That the illustrations in these two teachings are presented in a mixed manner without clear distinction is precisely because they observe the capacities of sentient beings to benefit them accordingly. As the Sūtra says: "This body is a collection of foam."
That which can be grasped and rubbed is like a mass of foam formed by the impact of flowing water; this foam gradually grows and perishes in an instant.
To the observer, it seems as if there were something to grasp, yet upon closer inspection, it has no reality. This body is likewise so:

through the successive flow of ignorance, volitional formations, and consciousness, it takes hold of the other—namely, the yin and yang constituents—and through the conjunction of these three factors, a body is formed, called the *kalala*.
"Rāmi" means that when one uses wisdom to examine and illuminate [reality], one does not perceive a fixed, substantial bodily form;

there are only three things, like a handful of foam—where there is no foam, there is only water. This analogy illustrates the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), but it has not yet clarified the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
As the Sūtra says regarding "like a bubble": when an upper drop of water meets lower water, a bubble arises; thus, it is the upper water... [that forms the bubble].
With water as the cause and conditions, bubbles arise, floating and flowing for a long time before perishing in an instant;
or they are destroyed immediately upon contact with other objects. To those who observe them from the outset, they are called "bubbles. The body is also like this:

with ignorance, formations, and consciousness as causes, and the physical constituents of the parents as conditions, there is the arising of the three matters (the three elements). The body is also like a *kalala*.
The consciousness that comes and goes gradually increases; when its conditions are exhausted, it dies and perishes, or it dies and perishes through injury by another.
One who lacks wisdom claims that this body exists as something distinct from these three factors. Upon careful examination, there is no separate body apart from these three factors.
As the Sūtra says, "It is like a mirage": a mirage arises in the wilderness when sunlight and wind interact, appearing as the form of flames.

One with impaired vision perceives it and conceives the notion that it is produced from water; yet when one seeks it with careful scrutiny, not only is water unobtainable, but the flame itself is also non-existent.
This body is likewise so: stirred by the winds of various karmas and the deluded thoughts of the light of mental consciousness, it seizes upon the constituent parts of others;
through the conjunction of these three factors, the *kalala* develops and grows in an uninterrupted succession, driven by the defilement of craving.
One thoroughly discerns that the body is wisdom; one fully realizes that not only is the body unattainable, but these three things are also empty.

Therefore, it is said to be "like a mirage. Thus, the analogy of the mirage clearly reveals the principle of the emptiness of both arising and dharmas, which is entirely different from analogies such as the mass of foam.
As the Sūtra says: "This body is like a plantain tree; within it there is no core."
From the moment the plantain tree is born, its leaves wrap one over another until the core, where there is ultimately no reality; this body is also like this.
From the initial stage of the *kalala* onward, these three things are all false and hollow, and there is no perception of a "body. Why is this?
Because it does not rot or decay; the three great elements form the skin, flesh, and bone-marrow, each having ninety-nine layers.

Upon examination, this illusory body cannot be found: within the continuity of inhalation and exhalation, throughout hundreds of thousands of breaths, the body cannot be found in each individual breath;
within the successive arising and ceasing of momentary consciousness, throughout immeasurable moments, the body cannot be found in each individual moment.
Since there is no separate body apart from these three factors, one knows [it to be non-existent].
The physical form is empty both internally and externally, like a plantain tree that has no core. As the Sūtra says:
"This body is like an illusion, arising from inversion; it is like a magician who, using illusory arts, conjures various objects such as monkeys, rabbits, and horses.
When outsiders see them, they all take them to be real. The magician of ignorance uses the illusory arts of the *saṃskāras* to conjure [existence]."
By performing these three things, one perceives the signs of the *kalala* stage through to birth, maturity, old age, and death within the external body, and grasps them as being fixed and real.
However, if one knows that ignorance does not arise, then the grasping for a self-body and these three things are all non-existent, like an illusion or empty space.
As the Sūtra says: "This body is like a dream, a false and delusive vision; it is seen because of the absence of [intrinsic reality]."

Just as one whose mind is obscured by ignorance lies prostrate in this sleep and perceives the body traveling elsewhere—only upon awakening does one realize the dream was real—so too, when the mind-nature is obscured by ignorance, the dharma-body is in a state of quiescence that is like lying down;

from there, deluded formations arise, and through the conjunction of the three factors, one enters the womb. This process, beginning with the *kalala* stage and continuing through growth until old age and death, is like a dream.

Within this, one sees that the body reaches everywhere; yet upon observing the mind and attaining awakening, one knows that all that is perceived—the body and the three objects—is empty and non-existent, for it is like a dream.
As the Sūtra says: "This body is like a shadow, manifested from karmic conditions.
When there is an object that obstructs light, a shadow appears; when the object changes, the shadow changes; and when the object moves, [the shadow moves].
When the movement of shadows is obscured by the light of principle and wisdom through the karma of ignorance, then the three factors combine;
the *kalala* retribution-body and the shadow-body, as well as the karma-body and the distinct retribution-body, fluctuate and are not identical from birth until death.

If one knows that all things produced by the karma of ignorance are ultimately empty—like shadows—even the three factors that constitute the retribution-body are likewise so. Thus it is said in the Sūtra: [The three factors are like a shadow].

To say that this body is like an echo, belonging to various causes and conditions: just as an echo arises when sound is produced by the striking together of two things and there is an empty valley, so too is the body;
it arises through the sound of ignorance and karmic formations.
Within the empty valley of the mother’s womb, these three factors harmonize, and the kalala—the provisional body—comes into correspondence. Thus, it belongs to various causes and conditions.
This [body] has ignorance and karma as its causes and the empty valley of the mother’s womb as its conditions.
Born from these causes and conditions, it is not self-made, not made by another, not both, and not without cause. Therefore, it is said to be "unborn. That which is unborn is like an echo and empty.
Furthermore, just as there is sound because the lips, tongue, teeth, palate, throat, and the *udāna* wind touch the body in seven places, so too is this [body].

Sound arises from conditions, yet sound cannot be apprehended; the body belongs to the aggregates, yet the body cannot be apprehended—it is like an echo. Question: The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* clarifies eight similes, each with its own specific correspondence. What is the intention of this sutra in using five similes all to illustrate that the body is empty? Answer: First, it clarifies the distinctions between the Shared (Tongjiao), the Complete (Yuanjiao), and the Perfect (Yuan) teachings; the primary intent lies precisely here. If one considers the Shared and Complete teachings: 1. The Shared Teaching regards the body as empty because it is subject to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). 2. The Complete Teaching regards the body as empty because it is subject to the five aggregates (*skandha*). 3. The Perfect Teaching regards the body as empty because it is subject to the six sense bases (*āyatana*). 4. The Shared Teaching regards the body as empty because it is subject to the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). 5. The Complete Teaching regards the body as empty because it is subject to the eighteen realms (*dhātu*). 6. The Perfect Teaching regards the body as empty because it is subject to the threefold nature (*trisvabhāva*). 7. The Shared Teaching regards the body as empty because it is subject to the two truths (*satyadvaya*). 8. The Complete Teaching regards the body as empty because it is subject to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). 9. The Perfect Teaching regards the body as empty because it is subject to the three non-natures (*triniḥsvabhāvatā*).
