The five, six, eight, and ten similes taught all apply universally;

for instance, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* clarifies that everything from form (*rūpa*) up to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) is like an illusion or a transformation, and this sutra likewise applies these universal similes.

As for the distinct application of the eight similes, this represents the intent of the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavahāra*), just as the four virtues are individually matched with the four samādhis to refute the four types of people.
The ultimate meaning of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) is that all things are ultimately inexplicable. As a sutra says: "This body is like a floating cloud, changing and perishing in an instant.
A cloud emerges from a dragon; it is also the arising of yin and yang vapors that transform into various different colors.

Seen from afar, it appears to exist, yet when looked at closely, it is not there. Ignorance (avidyā) and volitional formations (saṃskāra) are the parents—the dragon—whose union of yin and yang vapors gives rise to the three [realms].
Regarding the provisional designation of the *kalala* body, from its birth until its growth, there are various activities;
if one observes it from afar, the appearance of a body exists, yet if one approaches it with noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*), the appearance of a body cannot be found.
To say that it changes and perishes in an instant refers to the Tripitaka Teaching’s entry into emptiness (*śūnyatā*) by way of impermanence (*anitya*). As the Sūtra says: "This body is like..."

Regarding the statement that "lightning does not abide for even a single moment," some say it is light produced when a dragon sleeps, while others say it is light produced by the friction of two stones striking together;

this light is so rapid that it immediately extinguishes. The precise meaning of lightning remains unexplained. However, when ignorance (*avidyā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) rely upon the union with another’s physical constituents, the three factors form the *kalala* body;
because the light of this body is impermanent from moment to moment, lightning is said to be swift.
This extinction is emptiness; this analogy further clarifies the intent of entering emptiness through impermanence.
This body has no master, being like the earth; this body has no self, being like fire; this body has no life-span, being like wind;
this body has no person, being like water; this body is not real, for the four great elements constitute its home; thus, the body is empty.
Being free from "I" and "mine," this body is insentient like grass, wood, tiles, or pebbles; it is devoid of agency and is driven by the force of the wind.
Fourth, because it is without a master, [the text] clarifies the absence of self through eight points, examining it according to six types of phenomena.
This refutes our sixteen views. The first five sections examine the absence of self (*anātman*) with respect to the four great elements;
the next two sections examine the absence of self with respect to the element of space; and the final section examines the absence of self with respect to the element of consciousness.
Question: What is the distinction between the practice of non-self and the practice of emptiness? Answer: There are four points regarding this lack of fixed determination: first, sentient beings...

The so-called "emptiness of the aggregates" (skandha-śūnyatā) and the "non-self" (anātman) refer to the internal absence of a person (*pudgala*), because phenomena (*dharma*) lack sovereignty and are therefore non-self.
The two [remaining] aggregates are called "empty of sentient beings" (*sattva-śūnyatā*) and "non-self," because the aggregates are merely phenomena and not a sentient being;
they are thus called "empty of sentient beings" and "non-self" in contrast to the sixteen types of views (*ṣoḍaśa-dṛṣṭi*). All three are called "empty" in the same manner as the arising of phenomena.
The two [types of] emptiness refer to the meaning of emptiness; the four [types of] non-self refer collectively to the meaning of non-self.

In this sutra, the gate of emptiness is extensively clarified through the two types of emptiness—emptiness of persons and emptiness of phenomena—whereas the clarification of non-self here is primarily focused on the non-self of phenomena.
Question: Since the previous explanation of the practice of emptiness involved two teachings with different ways of entering emptiness, may the practice of non-self likewise be so?
Regarding the two non-answers, although the text is one, it can serve two purposes. Why is this so? For instance, if one says that there is no master, taking the earth as an analogy:
if one analytically breaks down the earth and does not perceive a master, this is the gate of the contemplation of non-self (*anātman*) according to the Tripiṭaka Teaching.

If one realizes that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is like the self and that the nature of the self is like the nature of phenomena—such that the nature of phenomena is ultimately identical to the self—[this is another use].
"Non-existence" refers to the fact that dharmas are ultimately non-existent; this is the Mahāyāna gate of contemplation on non-self according to the universal teaching (*pāṭha-sāmānya-śāsana*).

Regarding the first five sections, they are divided into two parts: first, examination by specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), and second, examination by general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
The four great elements constitute these four [sections]. As the Sūtra says: "This body has no master; it is like the earth. This specifically concerns the element of earth (*pṛthivī-dhātu*).
To clarify the absence of self (*anātman*), I shall now provide two explanations: first, refuting the views of outsiders; second, clarifying the meaning through internal contemplation.
1. Refuting the Outsiders: The outsiders maintain the following view: "If one says there is no soul (*ātman*) within the body, how can it be that one is able to carry light or heavy burdens?
To refute this internally, [the text] states: "The earth is also capable of bearing up mountains and peaks; could it therefore possess a soul?"

Next, regarding the explanation based on internal contemplation: according to the *Abhidharma*, sentient beings are designated as provisional names (*prajñapti*) while the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*) is a substantial dharma (*dravya-dharma*);
according to the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, the earth element is also a provisional name while the four subtle particles (*catur-aṇu*) are substantial dharmas.

Now it is explained that although there is a distinction between the provisional and the substantial, they are both subsumed under the contemplation of the non-self (*anātman*) within the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), just like the earth element itself.

These [four elements] are composed of the four subtle particles (*paramāṇu*). If one subtle particle is the master, then the other three are also masters; if one is not the master, then the other three are also not masters.

One should know that there is no master. If the internal earth element is composed of the four subtle particles and lacks a master, then the external earth element composed of the four subtle particles likewise lacks a master.
If both the internal and external lack a master, then this body consists of these three things [the three elements].
How could that which is produced have a master? If there is no master, it is because it is *anātman* (selfless). Therefore, it is said that this body has no master, being like the earth.
Furthermore, the *Avalokiteśvara-bodhisattva-samantamukha-parivarta-sūtra* says: "The earth has no solid nature.

If the earth were to exist, would it exist as having its own-nature (*svabhāva*), another-nature (*parabhāva*), a common-nature (*sāmānyasvabhāva*), or a causeless-nature (*ahetusvabhāva*)? One must examine which of these four it conforms to.
If one asserts that "one nature" is real while all else is false, this constitutes the meaning of "rigidity" (kaṭhina) and the meaning of "substantiality" (svabhāva).

If, upon examining the four natures, one finds them to be unobtainable and thus maintains that "this ground is non-existent" while all else is false, this likewise constitutes rigidity and substantiality.
If, regarding the ground, one holds it to be both existent and non-existent...
That which is true and all else is false speech is precisely the nature; it is the master.
If one perceives that "this is" or "this is not," this is true and all else is false speech; it is precisely the nature; it is the master.
If one harbors conceptual attachment toward these four propositions, that itself is the nature. The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "All these..."
If sentient beings take up signs with their minds, they become attached to a self, a person, a being, or a life-span.

If they take up the sign of dharmas, they likewise become attached to a self, a person, a being, or a life-span. If they take up the sign of non-dharmas, they also become attached to a self, a person, a being, or a life-span.
If one does not grasp at these four positions, this is the contemplation that the earth has no quality of solidity; if there is no actual solidity, then...
Because it is without a master and without a self, this body is said to be masterless, like the earth. A sutra states: "This body is without self, like fire. This is also explained in two ways.
First, regarding the refutation of the views of outsiders: outsiders postulate the existence of a divine self (*ātman*). How do they know this?
They observe that the body can move east and west and produce sounds; therefore, they know [it has a self].
Regarding the claim that there is a "divine self" (ātman) within, an internal refutation states: We refute those two propositions by means of the single principle of fire. Why is this?
Fire burns wild grass and is likewise able to move freely in all directions; thus, it too would be a divine self.
Furthermore, when fire burns bamboo and wood, it produces various sounds; thus, it too would possess a divine self. Next, explaining by means of internal contemplation: fire is...
That which is composed of two atoms lacks a fixed nature; this absence of nature is precisely the absence of fire.
Likewise, this body is composed of name-and-form (nāmarūpa) and thus lacks a fixed nature; this absence of nature in the body is precisely the absence of self (ātman).
Furthermore, the heat of the various afflictions within this body is fire; if external fire is without self, internal fire is likewise without self. Again, please [explain].
The *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra* states: "Great fire arises from causes and conditions; if it arises from conditions, it is without reality and without self.

This refutes intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and, by extension, the four logical positions (*catuskoṭi*), as can be understood through the analogy of the earth. The sūtra further states: "This body is without life-force (*jīva*); it is like the wind.
This is explained through two types of refutation: external and internal. Regarding the refutation of outsiders (*bāhya*), those who postulate a self (*ātman*) say:
How is this known? If there were no self, how could there be the continuous succession of inhalation and exhalation without interruption?
An internal opponent objects: "Inhalation is merely the characteristic of wind; external wind has no life-force (*jīva*). How then can internal wind be the life-force?
Next, regarding the explanation through internal contemplation: because the characteristics of wind strike against one another, it is light, empty, and free, moving without obstruction within.
What constitutes life-span? The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states: "The inhalation and exhalation of breath are called life-span.
If one contemplates these inhalations and exhalations, there is no accumulation in their emergence, no dispersion in their departure; they come without a path and go without a track.
Like the wind in space, they cannot be apprehended. Since the wind itself is not life, how could the breath be life? Furthermore...
The *Avalokiteśvara-bodhisattva-sūtra* states: "The nature of wind is unimpeded. Now, regarding the fourfold contemplation of wind:
if one says that wind has a nature such that the fourfold conceptualization can be obtained, this is a characteristic of obstruction and one cannot enter the Way.

If, through the fourfold contemplation of wind, wind is found to be unobtainable, this is non-obstruction; because it is non-obstructive, it is the entry into the limit of reality (*tathatā*). Thus one contemplates.
The three matters of the body are not the life-span because they are like the wind; therefore, it is said that this body is without life, being like the wind.

The Sūtra says: "This body has no person," which is like water. Regarding the obstruction of the external person by means of the element of water, the internal contemplation and understanding first clarify the refutation of the person.
The externalist calculates that there is a self, which is the person. How is this known? If within the body...
"How can water, being without a spirit, bestow compassionate grace and moisten what lies below by conforming to the shapes of objects? An insider refutes this, saying:
'I see that when one seeks water, it can flow down and moisten, conforming to the squareness or roundness of its vessel; yet water has no spirit and no person.

And yet you [the spirit] can bestow grace and moisten things in accordance with their forms—this too lacks both spirit and person. Now, to clarify the understanding of internal contemplation: water is composed of the three subtle elements (*trimaṇḍala*)."

That which is produced has no fixed nature, nor does it have the nature of non-existence; thus, the body composed of the three elements—water and so forth—has no fixed nature, nor does it have the nature of non-existence.
Since there is no body, there is no person; therefore, it is said that this body is "without a person," being like water.

Furthermore, another interpretation is as follows: it is like a small child who sees a reflection in the water and says, "There is a person in the water," and then enters the water to search for them.

A person can ultimately never be found. Among the three factors [of the body, sensation, and mind], the ordinary person gives rise to the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), asserting that the body is the person.
Through deep contemplation of these three factors, one does not perceive the characteristics of a body, and thus there is no person. Furthermore, as the *Sutra of Invoking Avalokiteśvara* states:

"The nature of water does not abide; for that which abides is obstructed by the squareness or roundness of a pond, and thus it abides—it is not that the nature of water itself possesses the quality of abiding."
Now, examining persons is also like this: one obtains the designation "person" in accordance with various phenomena, yet there is no fixed nature.

If one examines water through the four propositions (*catuskoṭi*) and finds it to have a nature and to possess attachment, this is the meaning of "abiding. If one examines water through the four propositions and finds it to lack a nature and to be without attachment, this is "non-abiding.
Because it is non-abiding, there is entry into the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). As a sutra says: "This body is not real... (the fourth [proposition]).
"This is the general refutation of my teaching on the non-existence of the self (*anātman*) by means of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
If one were to provide an interpretation for refuting the calculations of outsiders (*bāhyaka*), their calculation would state:

"If there were no real, substantial divine self (*ātman*) within the body, then since we currently see the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*) residing in dependence upon the body, we know that a real divine self exists. The insider refutes this, saying: "Presently..."
The body, which is the locus of the six sense organs, rests upon the four great elements; there is no separate self (ātman) upon which it can depend.
If one explains this according to internal contemplation, the name "body" is a single entity, yet each individual body should not reside in four locations as a dwelling place for a self.

If a single great self were to dwell [in them], then the other three great elements would lack the provisional designation of "body. If they do exist [as bodies], then there would be four bodies. Thus, the relationship between the self and the body is either one of identity or one of separation.
Regarding the four lines of inquiry: because one cannot find the body when examining it within the four great elements, the body does not exist.
If the body is not found in reality, then the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is destroyed; once the view of a self is destroyed, the sixteen types of speculative views are all destroyed.
As the Sūtra says: "This body is empty, being devoid of 'I' and 'mine. This is the second [section], which explains the destruction of the body by means of the element of space.
The practice of the non-self (*anātman*) is as follows: if one understands it as the refutation of "persons," [one considers that] outsiders reckon there is "mine" (*ātmīya*).
If there were no self (*ātman*), how could there be anything that belongs to "mine"? If there were no self, how could there be real possession of lands, people, and things?
If one perceives reality, one should know that the "self" is likewise an internal person. [The opponent] objects: "If that is so, then 'possession' is the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*)."
I, too, should be empty, just as the space within the body is empty; because the various kinds of external emptiness and all external space are that which is emptied, I am also empty.
If one explains this in terms of internal contemplation, it is precisely by means of the various kinds of emptiness that the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is destroyed.
Since the body is a provisional name for the four great elements and derived matter surrounding empty space, apart from space, there is no such thing as a body.
If the body is empty both internally and externally, it is not called "body" or "life. Examining the body by means of the element of space (*ākāśa*), the body cannot be apprehended;
thus, the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is destroyed. Once the view of a self is destroyed, one is free from "I" and "mine.

As the Sūtra says, "This body is insentient, like grass, wood, tiles, or pebbles"—this is the third examination, which destroys the notion of a knowing consciousness and explains the practice of non-self (*anātman*).
If one interprets this as refuting the non-Buddhist view, they might say: "If there is no self (*ātman*) within the body, how can one perceive such matters as the seasonal shifts of the four times?

The Buddhist proponent refutes this, saying: "Just as grass, trees, tiles, and pebbles likewise follow the transformations of the yin and yang seasons at each moment, it appears as though there is cognition, yet it is not the cognition of a self. Although the present body possesses cognition, [it is likewise]."
Grasses, trees, tiles, and rubble possess no conscious awareness. Furthermore, the non-Buddhists (bāhyaka) reckon that within the body there is a self (*ātman*), and that this self causes cognition.
To refute this, one asks: "If it is the self that causes cognition, then who causes the self to cognize? Ultimately, what need is there for the self to be caused [to act] by another self?
If there is no self to cause it, then there is no cognizer; it would be just like grasses, trees, tiles, and rubble. If one were to rely upon [this argument],...
Regarding the internal contemplation of the seeds of consciousness (*vijñāna-bīja*): why is this so? Because the three factors—body, life-force, and warmth—constitute the person;

that which is aware is simply consciousness (*vijñāna*). If one were to claim that consciousness is capable of knowing, [this is untenable]: past consciousness has already ceased, and because it has ceased, it cannot know.

Present consciousness does not abide for even a moment; since there is no time when it pauses, it cannot know. Future consciousness has not yet arisen, and because it has not yet arisen, it cannot know.
How could this consciousness possibly possess knowing? If one seeks knowing throughout the three periods of time, it cannot be found;

since there is no separate knowing apart from the three periods of time, it is said that this body is without knowing, like grass, trees, tiles, or pebbles. The Sūtra says: "This body is without agency;

it is turned by the power of the wind. Next, regarding the movement of the wind, I shall assist in completing the refutation of the existence of agency in consciousness to explain the practice of non-self.

Furthermore, regarding the refutation of the non-Buddhist (bāhyaka) interpretation: because the non-Buddhists postulate a self (ātman/puruṣa) within the body, they are able to grasp, act, and perform all manner of activities.
The Buddhist (ādhyātmika) refutes this, saying: "This is not something produced by the body; it is all driven by the power of wind (vāyu).
If one explains this according to internal contemplation of the mind, then within the deluded mind, various objects arise depending upon the wind.
The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states: "There is a wind that can move upward and a wind that can move downward. If one contemplates the upward-moving wind, the mind is drawn up by it;
if one contemplates the downward-moving wind, the mind is drawn down by it. All activities performed through its movement follow the mind.
If the pathways of this wind are not unobstructed, then the hands and feet will not function according to the mind."
Although there is mindfulness, movement arises from nowhere; it is like a person pulling a stiff bolt, where various actions are performed by the shadow of the mechanism.
If the stiff rope is severed, the hand has nothing to pull. One should know that all these are the workings of wind.
Now, observing this dependence on wind, it does not arise of itself, nor does it arise from another. That which is without arising is emptiness; emptiness is empty.
Since one cannot even possess this body composed of the three elements, and the body itself cannot be apprehended, who is it that acts?
This body is impure, filled with filth and evil.
This is the second teaching on the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), which destroys lustful desire and contemplates the five lower fetters (*pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*).
If one follows what was previously explained regarding the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), this constitutes the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

If contrasted with what preceded it, it refers to attaining liberation through the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and practicing the various auxiliary paths of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). This is not fixed;

if the preceding stage was the illumination of the Path of Seeing, these are its skillful means (*upāya*); if the illumination occurred simultaneously, these are the auxiliary paths. Now, speaking from the perspective after the Path of Seeing, this is contrasted with cultivation.

Regarding the Path: if a Bodhisattva enters the Path of Seeing and advances toward the various antidotal meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), they first employ these four perceptions (*saṃjñā*) to destroy the afflictions of the Desire Realm.
If six grades [of afflictions] are severed, one becomes a Sakṛdāgāmin;

if this wisdom-severance constitutes the Bodhisattva’s *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (receptivity to the non-arising of phenomena), then if all nine grades are exhausted, one becomes an Anāgāmin. Whether by wisdom or...

This is the Bodhisattva’s *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*. Now, to clarify that the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) serves as the antidote to the four perceptions (*saṃjñā*), the scriptural text briefly conveys this meaning. The four perceptions are: first, the perception of impurity; second, the perception of the impurity of food;
third, the perception of the world as unsatisfactory; and fourth, the perception of death. As the Sūtra says: "This body is [impure]..."
That it is filled with impurities, filth, and evil is precisely the perception of impurity (*aśubha-saṃjñā*).

Next, the sutra says that although one provisionally relies on bathing, clothing, and food, this is the perception of the impurity of food (*āhāre pratikūla-saṃjñā*). Next, the sutra says that this body is a calamity, afflicted by one hundred and one diseases, and is like a dilapidated well;
this is the perception of the world as being not worth delighting in (*lokānabhirati-saṃjñā*). Next, the sutra says that this body is without...

The certainty that one must die is precisely the perception of death (*maraṇasaṃjñā*). Next, the mention of "like a venomous snake" and so forth is a general analogy for the meaning of the preceding four perceptions.
Furthermore, if this scriptural passage establishes four points regarding the arising of suffering:
first, from the impurity of the body up to its reliance on food and clothing, this constitutes the suffering of birth; next, it speaks of "a hundred and one calamities."
"Affliction by illness" refers to the suffering of illness; next, "like a well on a mound" refers to the suffering of old age;

next, "one must inevitably die" refers to the suffering of death; and finally, the analogies of the poisonous snake and so forth collectively illustrate the four types of suffering mentioned in the preceding four lines.
Furthermore, there are two ways of explaining these four sufferings: one is to state them as they arise—namely, birth, old age, illness, and death.
This explains the four sufferings according to principle (*li*), which belongs to the practice of wisdom (*hui-xing*); this is as fully explained previously.

If one explains the four sufferings according to phenomena (*shi*), this constitutes the practice of cultivation (*xing-xing*). The four sufferings elucidated in this section of the sutra refer to the four sufferings of phenomena.
The sutra says: "This body is impure and filled with foulness," which refers to the five kinds of impurity. If...
If one perceives this impurity by following the breath, it is the meditation door of the sixteen special excellences (*ṣoḍaśa-viśeṣa-dhyāna-mukha*).
If one perceives impurity by contemplating the breath, it is the meditation door of universal clarity (*samantaprabhāsa-dhyāna-mukha*).

If one perceives this impurity through mental visualization, it is the various doors such as the nine notions of repulsiveness (*navasaṃjñā-vipaśyanā*), the liberations (*vimokṣa*), and the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*). Furthermore, that which is said to belong to the suffering of birth refers to the five kinds of impurity.
Excluding ultimate impurity, the remaining four types are all the suffering of birth.
This body is like empty space; though it is provisionally sustained by bathing, clothing, and food, it inevitably returns to decay and extinction.
This is the contemplation on the impurity of food. The reason for this is that once food enters the belly, it decomposes into excrement, urine, fat, flesh, and pus;
the nine orifices and the pores constantly discharge impurities. Although one bathes, filth continues to emerge from the pores;
and even if one adorns the body with clean and fine garments, they become soiled in an instant.
One wears a body and clothing that are foul, stinking, and impure; even when clean, they quickly decay. Food and drink are inherently impure;

once entering the mouth and mingling with saliva, they become like vomit. Upon reaching the interior of the abdomen, they turn into excrement, urine, pus, and blood, nourishing thirty-six substances—all of which are impure.
These fill the belly and flow out from the nine orifices and all the pores of the body as foul-smelling places.
"Abominable things all arise from food and drink; this contemplation on the impurity of food breaks those who crave it.
As for what is said to belong to the suffering of birth: birth entails these afflictions, and the wise, observing them, see them as suffering.
This body is a calamity, afflicted by one hundred and one ailments; this body is like a dilapidated well, pressed down by old age.
These two sufferings of illness and old age constitute the internal world of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of sentient beings.

Because there exists within it such phenomena that are to be loathed and feared, it belongs to the world and is characterized by the perception of its lack of delight. It is simply because the primary retribution of the internal body itself is not delightful.
Therefore, all things within the land of retribution—the people and objects—are not to be delighted in.
A sutra says, "This body is a calamity," meaning that various disasters and manifold sufferings of illness arise from the body; one should know that the body is the locus of calamity.
A sutra says, "One hundred and one afflictions of illness": when the four great elements are out of harmony, one hundred and one illnesses are stirred up.
The four great imbalances of the causes of illness arise from the body; these various sufferings of illness all afflict the body, which constitutes calamity and misfortune.
The textual division of the four sufferings explains the suffering of illness as a matter of fact.
The Sūtra says: "This body is like a well by a mound, pressed by old age. If one forms the four perceptions, their clear meaning still pertains to sentient beings within [the internal realm]. Five.

The world of the aggregates (*skandha-loka*) is not to be delighted in because it is oppressed by old age; if one explains the meaning based on the four types of suffering, this precisely refers to the suffering of old age.
Master Kumārajīva said: "The 'dilapidated well' refers to a ruined well. Formerly, there was a man who had committed an offense against the king.
The man fled, and the king ordered a drunken elephant to pursue him. Terrified and in haste, the man threw himself into the air."
A man found a gourd vine at the edge of a well; grasping it with his hand, he noticed venomous snakes below spitting poison toward him.
Beside him were five poisonous serpents that further sought to harm him, while two rats gnawed at the vine until it was on the verge of breaking.
A great elephant stood above him, also intending to seize him. The man was in extreme peril and suffering, filled with the greatest terror. Above him—
At one time there was a single tree with drops of honey falling into its mouth; because of the taste, it forgot its fear of the mountain well and death.
The intoxicated elephant represents impermanence (*anitya*); the poisonous dragon represents the evil realms (*durgati*); the five venomous snakes represent the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*);

the decaying grass represents the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*); the white and black rats are metaphors for day and night; the drops of honey represent the pleasures of the five desires (*pañca-kāma-guṇa*). Having obtained the honey—
The metaphor of "dropping [the honey] while forgetting one's fear" illustrates how sentient beings obtain the honey of the five sensual desires and do not fear suffering.
This body is without permanence and must inevitably die;

this is precisely where the teaching on the perception of death is applied. To clarify the meaning through the four types of suffering, this refers specifically to the suffering of death. As the Sūtra says:
This body is without fixed duration; composed of three elements and sustained by the power of karma, it lacks any permanent characteristic.

Through the convergence of causes and conditions, it is provisionally united, yet when these causes disperse, the body perishes. One may die suddenly, or be harmed by another, or finally die when one's own karma is exhausted.
From birth through to old age and death, there is no fixed time for its arrival; it may come due to illness.
Even Shang Lao reached his end through the natural process of death; Pengzu lived for eight hundred years but ultimately perished; and the immortals died in mid-air.
One should know that within the mountains and seas, one cannot escape this death; there is neither noble nor base, and neither the foolish nor the wise can avoid it.
Therefore, the Sūtra says that death is the inevitable end. As the Buddha asked the bhikṣus: "How do you cultivate the perception of death? There is [a method].
A bhikṣu joined his palms and said, "I cannot guarantee that this body will last for seven days.

The Buddha’s intention was to encourage the cultivation of the perception of death. Furthermore, another bhikṣu joined his palms and said to the Buddha, "I do not dare to believe that this body can last for six days.
Another said he did not believe it would last for five days; another said three days; and another said two.
Some said they would practice for one day; some said for half a day. The Buddha said, "All of these are practicing with indolence.
Regarding those who cultivate the perception of death, some said, "I cannot guarantee that my exhalation will be followed by an inhalation. The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent!
This is truly cultivating the perception of death. If one can thus skillfully cultivate the perception of death, before long one shall attain liberation and nirvana."
Furthermore, this body is like a venomous snake, like a hostile thief, and like an empty village; it is a composite formed by the aggregates, elements, and sense bases.
This collectively illustrates the previous four perceptions, stating that "the body is like a venomous snake" and "like an empty village," both of which are to be feared.
One should fully and clearly form the perception that the world is not to be relished.
If explained according to the four types of suffering, it means that this body in its entirety is like a venomous snake or a hostile thief—something not to be relished.
This is what the *Vena-viṣa-sūtra* (The Sutra on the Venomous Snake) clarifies, and it is also fully expounded in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. Now...
This briefly outlines the essential points. As the Sūtra says: "The 'venomous snake' is like a venomous snake in the world kept in a single basket;

each acts in opposition to the others and does not accord with one another. This is intended to clarify that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) of the body act in mutual opposition, just like the worldly venomous snakes, having no distinction between them.
Furthermore, it is like a worldly venomous snake which, though nurtured by a person, becomes enraged when [the time is right].

Furthermore, these [four elements] sting and kill people; they do not recognize the kindness of their nourishment. Since the four great elements are what sustain the body for the practitioner, one ought to repay their kindness.
Yet, when these four elements go awry, they inflict injury upon the person's wholesome qualities.

They cause the practitioner to fall into the ocean of suffering in the future, being no different from a venomous snake; therefore, they are called "venomous snakes. As the Sūtra says, they are like hostile bandits.

Just as bandits seize people's wealth and harm their lives, so too do the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*) within the body of a practitioner plunder their wholesome wealth and sever their life-force of wisdom;
they are no different from worldly bandits. A sutra says: "It is like an empty village;
an empty village is originally desolate and devoid of things, yet it does not give rise to human defilement. This clarifies the contemplation of the six sense faculties.
This emptiness and absence of a self-soul means that even this flavor does not give rise to defilement in people; one contemplates it as being like an empty village.

Because Bodhisattvas of the four teachings, when their contemplation of the Real reaches its ultimate limit, realize the four kinds of Buddhahood, it is said that they "arise from the Real. As the Sūtra says, "arising from non-heedlessness," if one follows the four teachings: 1. **In the Tripitaka Teaching:** Non-heedlessness refers to the practice of the three trainings (*triśikṣā*) through the cultivation of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharma*). 2. **In the Shared Teaching:** Non-heedlessness refers to the cultivation of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) through the realization of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). 3. **In the Distinct Teaching:** Non-heedlessness refers to the cultivation of the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*) through the realization of the emptiness of dharmas (*dharma-śūnyatā*). 4. **In the Perfect Teaching:** Non-heedlessness refers to the cultivation of the unconditioned Four Noble Truths through the realization of the Middle Way. When a bodhisattva employs wisdom to contemplate reality, their deluded thoughts regarding conditioned phenomena are immediately termed the "state of heedlessness" within the bodhisattva stage.
Now, when the bodhisattvas of the four teachings employ wisdom to contemplate principle, their minds continue in succession without abandoning great compassion;
this is called "non-heedlessness. This non-heedlessness is precisely what manifests the characteristics of *avaivartika* (non-retrogression), because of this mind.
Because the mind is quiescent and naturally flows into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), it is said to be born from non-negligence.
From such immeasurable pure dharmas, the body of the Tathāgata is born.
This is the extensive category of exhortation. Such categories of practice within this dharma-gate of merit are immeasurable;
here, the *Vimalakīrti* cites thirteen articles as the basis for exhortation. All those various pure dharma-gates are not limited to these alone;

they must all rely on the aforementioned wisdom of insight (*vipaśyanā*) and calm abiding (*śamatha*), the practice of the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), and the realization of the true path through actual contemplation, serving as aids for attaining liberation.

Skillfully applying the mind to cultivate all aspects of the Path constitutes the meaning of the fulfillment of causes and the perfection of fruits for each respective stage of the Bodhisattvas of the Four Teachings.
All these merits give rise to the body of the Tathāgata. When he preaches with a single voice, sentient beings understand according to their own kind;
this "understanding according to their kind" refers to the categories of cause, fruit, and practice elucidated by the Four Teachings.
The various distinctions— neither provisional nor real, the three provisional and one real, and the four *siddhāntas* that respond to capacities and benefit beings so that all may receive,
practice, and obtain their benefit— are such that if a student can carefully grasp the intent of the two types of teaching from the first five sections,
and initially aspire to realize the fruit by practicing the cause, then the words of this sutra will not have come in vain.
"O virtuous ones, those who wish to attain the Buddha-body that severs all the illnesses of sentient beings should resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This is the third exhortation. Since you know that the merit of the Buddha-body is thus, it is like [relying on] various superior causes."
If you now wish to aspire to the fruit, you must practice the cause; why stop as before? The resolve of a Great Being who seeks self-benefit must necessarily be for the benefit of others.
Now, Vimalakīrti has taken up illness to assist the Buddha in manifesting the teaching; thus, it is for the benefit of others.
Now, if all of you gentlemen can aspire to practice the cause, you should likewise follow the example of the Buddha and Vimalakīrti in order to sever the illnesses of all sentient beings. (1)

Regarding the curing of all illnesses of sentient beings, as clarified previously: there are the illnesses of conditioned causes, conditions, habits, and fruits for ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and Bodhisattvas of the Six Perfections;
the illnesses of both conditioned and unconditioned causes, conditions, habits, and fruits for those of the Two Vehicles and Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-śikṣā*);
and the illnesses of the causes, conditions, habits, and fruits of the *dharmadhātu* itself for Bodhisattvas of the Distinct and Perfect Teachings (*bhinnayāna* and *vimalakīrti-yāna*).

Now, each of the four teachings, according to its respective understanding, should serve to eliminate [afflictions] and seek the unsurpassed path; this constitutes the fulfillment of the other's intention.
In this way, the Elder Vimalakīrti taught the Dharma as was appropriate for those who had come to inquire after his illness, [benefiting] countless thousands.
All people gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This is the fourth instance of the assembly gaining benefit during the time of illumination.

Vimalakīrti, according to the differing capacities of those who came to inquire after his illness, responded to conditions through teachings that employ both the gates of prohibition and exhortation, utilizing the four *siddhāntas* to reach the faculties of the four types of disciples.
Because what is taught is without error, it is said that "the Dharma is preached according to what is appropriate.

As the Sūtra says, "causing immeasurable sentient beings to all resolve upon Bodhicitta," since the faculties and conditions of these beings differ according to the four teachings (*catur-yāna*), there are likewise four ways in which they resolve upon Bodhicitta.
According to these four types, immeasurable paths of the Bodhi-mind are each developed; this is precisely what is meant by "attaining [it] universally."

Receiving and practicing [these teachings] to obtain their benefits constitutes the power of the unshared dharmas (*āveṇika-dharma*). Regarding the meaning of the bodhicitta according to the four teachings:

it arises from the four kinds of Four Noble Truths and gives rise to four kinds of compassion and the four great vows. This is as clarified in the *Xuan-yi* (Profound Meaning) of the Four Teachings regarding the four modes of generating the bodhicitta.

This chapter follows the "Chapter on Expedient Means" (*Upāya-paṭala*) and is intended to refute [the notion of] unconditioned causes and conditions and to manifest [the true nature of reality].
The teaching on the Tathāgata’s purification of the Buddha-land through the inconceivable liberation of the Dharma-body has many intended meanings;
how could it be fathomed by ordinary sentiments? Now, I shall briefly explain the textual meaning of this chapter using three points:
first, to clarify the purpose of this chapter’s appearance; second, to provide a brief explanation of the term "disciple"; third, [to explain] the entry...
The first section of the commentary on the text: This chapter follows immediately after the "Expedient Means.

The Great Sage, out of compassion, desires to enable sentient beings to attain the inconceivable Dharma-body of liberation as their primary retribution (*vipāka*), and the pure Buddha-lands as their secondary retribution (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

However, the transformation of beings must necessarily occur through those with whom they have a karmic affinity. Thus, the Bodhisattva Vimalakīrti has long been associated with these beings here in this land of patience (*kṣānti*).
Having bound himself to the supreme karma of Bodhi, he already knew the Buddha’s intention;

previously, on account of his illness, he had extensively preached various teachings for the sake of all people, thereby fulfilling the inconceivable doctrine of liberation and the Buddha-land. Now, lying again upon his bed in silent contemplation, his mind was set upon the Tathāgata’s great compassion.
He thought that if the Buddha were to summon his disciples to inquire after him, he would certainly take his leave of the past.

The matter of the reprimand and censure serves to manifest and establish the Tathāgata’s teaching on the inconceivable path of liberation and the sublime Dharma of the causes and conditions for purifying a Buddha-land.
Now, to clarify the purpose of this chapter, five points will be briefly set forth: first, to reveal the supreme wisdom of Vimalakīrti;
second, to cause the fourfold assembly to abandon the Lesser Vehicle and aspire to the Great Vehicle; third, to... [text continues].

1. To manifest the supreme wisdom of Vimalakīrti: if he were to command his disciples to inquire after his illness, they would inevitably recount his past being rebuked as their excuse; when the present assembly hears this wondrous Dharma, they will immediately give rise to an unfathomable reverence for Vimalakīrti. 2. To establish the Pure Land: by means of the power of skillful means, he transforms the five turbidities into the five virtues, thereby establishing the Pure Land.

3. To refute the Lesser Vehicle: he refutes the two vehicles and establishes the teaching of the *Sūtra of the Clarified Butter* (Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda). 4. To seal and authenticate the sūtras: he seals and authenticates the first [sūtra]. 5. To manifest the supreme wisdom of Vimalakīrti:

if he were to command his disciples to inquire after his illness, they would inevitably recount his past being rebuked as their excuse; when the present assembly hears this wondrous Dharma, they will immediately give rise to an unfathomable reverence for Vimalakīrti.

Their thoughts of reverence increase all the more; if deep faith arises from within, they are then fit to hear the teaching on the inconceivable liberation and the pure Buddha-lands spoken in the inner chamber.
Second, in order to cause the fourfold assembly to abandon the Lesser Vehicle and aspire to the Great Vehicle:
if one is a Śrāvaka who has realized the fruits, yet is unable to turn their mind toward the Great Vehicle by themselves—just as [the Elder] Ghoṣila...

Originally, lotuses do not grow on dry land; yet, although the fourfold assembly of śrāvakas who have not yet entered the stage of certainty (samyaktva-niyāma) delight in the Hīnayāna, upon now hearing how each of the disciples recounted the matters of their past rebukes, they will surely resolve to train in the Mahāyāna.
It is as when the Buddha preached the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*: there were śrāvakas who had not yet entered [the stage of certainty].
In the state of correct realization, he relinquished the robes he had received and offered them as an act of worship to the Tathāgata;
immediately, he gave rise to the mind of the Mahāyāna, whereupon the Buddha emitted light and conferred upon him a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).

This was also a universal opening of the Mahāyāna path for the fourfold assembly, benefiting immeasurable beings. Why is this so? It is because when Vimalakīrti rebuked the disciples in the past, those who heard it at that time—
It is not as much as the case when Upāli was rebuked, where the minds of those two bhikṣus attained purity;
nor is it as much as when Ānanda was rebuked, where ten thousand Brahmās resolved upon Bodhicitta.

Furthermore, it is not as much as the benefit derived from this Dharma assembly, wherein the great multitude, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, have all heard and known [the teaching], and the benefit therein must logically be immeasurable; therefore, it is necessary [to record it].
He commanded his disciples to each recount the events of being rebuked.

Third, regarding the manifestation of the Buddha-land, it is intended to show that the manner in which those of the Two Vehicles were rebuked in the past is identical in intent to the present teaching on the clarity of the Buddha-land.
How is this known? Because sentient beings fail to see the Pure Land due to their own transgressions, as Śāriputra himself described what he saw.
That which was impure is now called "pure. In the past, he caused them to abandon the fault of clinging to the Lesser Vehicle, leading each to despise the small and aspire to the great;
thus, their wholesome roots were secretly awakened. Now, they have attained a seat within this Mahāyāna assembly.

By receiving the Buddha’s spiritual power, they behold the pure land and hear this teaching, such that their sentiment is identical to that of the five hundred who previously entered the inner chamber and heard the secret [teachings].
Through this discourse on contemplation, the worlds of Lamp-King (*Dīparāja*), the land of Fragrant Accumulation (*Gandhavyūha*), and the realm of Akṣobhya are all manifested before one's eyes.
Fourth, in order to manifest and perfect the *Sūtra* of the Clarified Butter (*Navanīta*) teaching:

for instance, when the Sudden Teaching was first opened, only those with great capacity awakened to the Way; those with inferior faculties and heavy defilements were not permitted to hear it, as they lacked the Way therein.

It is like milk: the Tripitaka Master next employs skillful means to open the way for those of inferior faculties, who, upon hearing the teachings of the Sūtras, sever their views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), transcend the state of ordinary beings, and become sages—this is precisely the meaning of "transforming milk into curd.
Next, they hear the accounts of how Great Beings of the past rebuked and admonished them; these are now all fully recounted, even unto their entry [into the path].

The sounds of remorse and lamentation fill the three thousandfold world system; this is like when small ice and stagnant frost begin to melt and the seeds of faith gradually transform—this is comparable to the production of *ghṛta* (clarified butter).
Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "After this, their minds will accord with one another in mutual trust, and they will enter and exit [the teachings] without difficulty.
When they reach the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, it transforms into mature *ghṛta*, and they enter the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

That "nirvāṇa" is precisely the attainment of *amṛta* (the essence of clarified butter) is a reiteration of the reason why those rebuked [by Vimalakīrti] entered his room and produced *ghṛta* (butter).

Question: If each of the five hundred [disciples] recounted their own past instances of being rebuked to manifest the virtue of Vimalakīrti as the reason for entering his room and producing *ghṛta*, then this must belong to the introduction (*nidāna*) and not to the formal discourse (*samyag-vyākhyāna*). Answer: [As follows:]...
It is said that the "Clarified Butter" (*sarpis*) of realization is not necessarily restricted to those Śrāvakas who have entered the inner chamber;
rather, there may be those who, having previously heard the various Vaipulya sūtras, have already attained the state of "Clarified Butter," as was the case with Aṅgulimāla when he was rebuked.
Or perhaps there were those who had already attained the state of "Clarified Butter" at the time they were rebuked in the past, or who hear it again now.
Regarding those who maintain that the "produced ghee" (jāta-sarpiḥ) is attained only upon entering the chamber,
or that it is attained only after the subsequent exposition of the various Vaipulya Mahāyāna sūtras through refutation and censure—

how can it be definitively established that the "entry into the chamber" constitutes the introductory section (*nidāna*) of the "produced ghee"? If it were the case that the "produced ghee" consists merely of the introductory section itself...
The introductory section consists of entering the room and returning from the Āmra grove to explain the reasons for the two chapters; this entry into the room also constitutes the introduction.

The fifth part serves to seal and finalize the scripture: if Vimalakīrti had merely moved according to the capacities of beings and rebuked them wherever he went, then he would have simply dismissed his teaching;
it was only because he was commanded to send his disciples to inquire after his illness that each of them recounted their experiences again.

Regarding the question asked yesterday concerning the refutation [of the Śrāvakas], how could it be that the great assembly heard it together while the Tathāgata remained silent, thereby establishing it as a definitive sūtra for the benefit of the fourfold assembly throughout the three periods of the True, Semblance, and Final Dharma? Question:

In this chapter, how many contemplations (*vipaśyanā*) are employed in the refutation of the Śrāvakas' three contemplations, and how many teachings (*upadeśa*) are employed in the four teachings? Answer: This chapter fully employs all three [contemplations].

The contemplation of merely "striking" refers to the contemplation of analyzing the provisional to enter emptiness; it properly employs the Mahāyāna Three Teachings to strike at the Tripiṭaka Teaching.

Clarifying the Sequence of Questions and Answers. First, a brief explanation of the meaning of the term "disciple" (śrāvaka):

Now, the teacher possesses the capacity to mold and perfect, while the student possesses the virtue of endowment through their resources. As for the resource of abandoning one’s father to follow a teacher, it is a matter of reverence.
The Master is like a father, and the disciple is like a younger brother; thus the Master said, "Hui dwells with me as a father, and I dwell with Hui as a younger brother.

Now, when the disciples of Śāriputra receive instruction from the Buddha, this is the ritual of teacher and disciple, which corresponds to what is called being a "disciple" (śrāvaka) here in this land. A question was asked: "The Buddha is all..."
The Compassionate Father of all sentient beings, for all sentient beings are the children of the Buddha; as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:

"Now these three realms are all mine, and the sentient beings therein are all my children. This, then, is not established according to the Confucian system of revering one's elders and treating juniors as one's own children.
[Question: Answer: Buddhist scriptures have two meanings; some are based on...
Names are established based on principle, yet they naturally follow worldly convention as their designation. As the *Lotus Sūtra* states: "When I was a crown prince, Rāhula was my eldest son;
now that I have attained the Buddha-way, he receives the Dharma and becomes my Dharma-son.
This is precisely clarifying the meaning by way of principle: both the mundane and the supramundane are father and son. If one were to clarify the meaning according to worldly convention...
This is just as the Master said: "Seeking the gates of the Buddha-dharma, all follow worldly conventions with a mind free from contention;
because they do not contradict the true Dharma, there is no fault in explaining the disciples according to external meanings. Question: If that is so, then all worldly people are disciples.
Why then do you single out the Śrāvakas? Answer: Generally speaking, it is indeed as you say. However, speaking specifically:

Although a person living at home may occasionally come to receive the Way, since their physical form dwells within the mundane net of worldly affairs—serving parents and sovereign—they cannot constantly attend upon [the Buddha] morning and night or always receive sustenance and instruction from the World-Honored Buddha. A Bodhisattva, always cherishing the benefit of sentient beings, responds whenever there is an opportunity;
how could they remain exclusively by the Buddha’s side to receive sustenance and perform service? Thus it is said: "Sound."
Having heard [the Dharma], they renounced the household life and followed the Buddha as his inner retinue;
furthermore, from hearing arose understanding, whereby they fulfilled the meaning of being disciples through the complete perfection of both phenomena and principle (*dharma* and *artha*).

Furthermore, in the *Śrāvaka-sūtras*, five kinds of "sons of the Buddha" are explained, but it is not said that there are Bodhisattvas who obtain the five fruits, nor is it said that there are Bodhisattvas; therefore, [they are called] "disciples."
The name "disciple" (*śrāvaka*) belongs primarily to those of the Śrāvaka vehicle; however, in the Mahāyāna, it is mostly the Dharmakāya Bodhisattvas who are designated as "sons of the Buddha.
Here, following the conventions of the Śrāvaka sūtras, the term "disciple" is established for the sake of naming, because this designation is widely accepted by the world;
thus, the title of the chapter is marked by the word "disciple. Second, the specific explanation of the ten disciples: the *Daśa-śrāvaka-sūtra* clarifies the ten great [disciples].
The sequence of the disciples varies considerably; here, I shall distinguish ten disciples according to the order established by this very sutra.
This sequence largely accords with the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* in its intention of clarifying the three capacities of the roots, differing only in that Kātyāyana is placed after Pūrṇa.
Thus, when the Tathāgata, as the sovereign king of the Dharma-path over the trichiliocosm, first opened the Three Piṭakas—
The Teachings must rely on Dharma-ministers and assistants to transform sentient beings together;
because these ten great śrāvakas each possess superior excellence in one of the ten virtues, they each preside over a specific dharma to assist the Buddha in transforming all sentient beings.
Śāriputra is foremost in the wisdom of the Buddha-dharma; second, Maudgalyāyana is foremost in the supernormal powers (ṛddhi); third, Kātyāyana...
1. The ascetic (dhūta) Śāṇakavāsin was foremost in ascetic practices; 2.
Subhūti was foremost in the practice of emptiness and the samādhi of non-contention; 3. Pūrṇa was foremost in eloquence and preaching the Dharma;
4. Kātyāyana was foremost in exegesis and debate; 5. Aniruddha was foremost in the divine eye; 6. Upāli was foremost in...
First, Rāhula is foremost among those who uphold the Vinaya; second, Ānanda is foremost among those who practice secret conduct and maintain the precepts;
third, Ānanda is foremost among those of great learning and dhāraṇī-retention. This section explains the causes, conditions, merits, and meanings of these ten disciples;
when entering the text, these shall be briefly clarified. Although each of the ten disciples possesses ten virtues, they each excel in different areas.
"Long-suffering follows that which is long-suffering," this is the first designation based on preeminence. A question was asked:

"If each of the ten virtues possesses its own particular excellence, and one is designated as foremost based on that specific excellence—for instance, Śāriputra’s supernormal powers and his mastery of robes, while Maudgalyāyana exerted all his supernatural might to pull at this robe, causing the entire trichiliocosm to tremble, yet he could not move the hem of the garment."
"Regarding your robe-belt, Maudgalyāyana reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
'When the Buddha enters meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), Śāriputra does not hear his name; when Śāriputra enters meditative concentration, Maudgalyāyana does not hear his name;
when Maudgalyāyana enters meditative concentration, none of the other Arhats hear his name. If this is so, how can Maudgalyāyana be called one who possesses supernatural powers (*abhijñā*)?"

Question: First, if Maudgalyāyana’s supernormal powers (ṛddhi) were not uniquely superior, and the other eight disciples did not each necessarily possess their own specific excellence, how is this explained?
Answer: This principle may involve unique superiority, or it may not involve unique superiority.

Not involving unique superiority is as when Maudgalyāyana’s supernormal powers do not surpass those of Śāriputra; this is a case of relative superiority and inferiority. [An example of] relative superiority and inferiority is as with Subhūti...
When it comes to preaching emptiness, Śāriputra finds it difficult to question;

yet, when the merits of the ten great disciples are analyzed and discussed, their physical forms may not necessarily possess superior qualities over one another. It is because each possesses a particular excellence among their ten virtues that they are called "foremost.
However, since the Tathāgata is the Dharma King, those appointed as his Dharma Ministers are like the great ministers of a worldly state.
Although there are various talents, the eight seats and the ministers each have their own specific jurisdictions and cannot be confused or overstepped.
Although the ten disciples’ virtues may overlap, some being superior and others inferior, no single person can alone shoulder two duties;
therefore, the ten virtues are divided and assigned to eleven [positions]. They assist the Buddha in proclaiming the ten types of teaching gates, so as to lead sentient beings...

Out of reverence and aspiration, it is necessary to bestow upon him the title of "Foremost in Virtue," so that all sentient beings may each, according to their faculties and conditions, find a point of focus for their minds;
though they each assist in proclaiming the Buddha’s teachings, they ultimately converge upon the One Way.
Third, regarding the general correspondence with the ten mental factors (*caitasika*), the *Abhidharma* verses of the Tripiṭaka Teaching state: "Perception, desire, contact, and wisdom."

The mental factors of mindfulness, reflection, and liberation, as well as the attention directed toward the object and the concentration on that object, are the "universal" (mahābhūmika) dharmas that support the mind-king.
They give rise to all the various mental factors, just as a kingdom has ten ministers who together assist a single sovereign.
If the ruler and his ministers together practice what is not the Way, then all the people within the realm will likewise commit evil.
When ruler and minister assist one another to practice upright governance together, all the people within the realm will possess the Way.

Now, when sentient beings have a mind-king accompanied by the ten mental factors (caitta), if they contemplate what is unwholesome, then immeasurable unwholesome afflictions and mental factors will arise;
if the mind-king and the ten factors support one another to contemplate what is wholesome, then immeasurable wholesome states will arise.
Merit and wisdom arise from the mental factors (*caitta*). Furthermore, the mind-king (*cittarāja*) is the teacher, and the ten mental factors are the ten disciples.
If the teacher and disciples together perform evil, they transform all people to become evil;
if the teacher and disciples together perform good, they transform all people to cultivate goodness. This applies to both the mind-king and the ten mental factors.
It is also like this; therefore, this sutra says: "The assembly of disciples' afflictions are turned according to their will.
Now, all sentient beings possess the mind-king and the ten mental factors (caitta-dharma).

If they encounter celestial Māras, non-Buddhists, or discourses on craving and views, they immediately give rise to various afflictions and transmigrate through birth and death, as if serving an evil ruler or an evil minister.
This is the transformation brought about by evil teachers and evil disciples. Now, the Buddha is the Dharma King and the ten disciples are the Dharma Ministers;

they are thus the teachers of the True Dharma and the disciples of the True Dharma. By practicing through wisdom and performing the practices of the True Dharma, they transform sentient beings together.

The mind-king possesses the ten supernormal powers, and the mental factors (caitta-dharmas) likewise do so. If sentient beings believe and accept this, and practice through the cultivation of wisdom, [they shall be transformed].

That is to say, when the various afflictions (*kleśa*) of the "View-Theory" (*dṛṣṭi-prasaṅga*) are extinguished, one accomplishes all the immeasurable wholesome mental factors (*citta-saṃskāra*) of the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

If sentient beings believe, accept, and practice these practices, they immediately shatter all the unwholesome mental factors of the celestial Māras, birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), and [affliction], thereby accomplishing the immeasurable wholesome mental factors of the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). Furthermore, regarding these ten...
Numbers are themselves dharma-gates through which one can fully enter nirvana. Initially, the number ten serves as the seed;
by practicing from this point, one eventually achieves the Way, just as a tree with a trunk as thick as an embrace begins from a tiny sprout.
Now, the Dharma King wishes to teach all sentient beings through the doctrines of the "Half" and the "Full"; therefore, he must first act in accordance with their inclinations and desires.
This sutra says: "First one uses the hook of desire to entice, and later leads them into the Buddha-way.

Now, as each of the ten disciples propagates a single dharma, people gather according to their kind and things divide into groups; following their respective inclinations and desires, each employs a specific dharma-door to gather them as followers.
Although each presides over a single dharma-door, how could it ever not be complete with all ten?

Regarding the virtue [of the ten mental factors], whenever any one of the ten mental factors arises, all ten arise accordingly; although they function under the designation of a single factor, in reality there are ten factors.
Fourth, as for the specific correspondence with disciples: first, the mental factor of perception (*saṃjñā*) corresponds specifically to Pūrṇa.
Pūrṇa’s perception was particularly strong, and he entered the Path through perception; therefore, he is called "The One of Perception" (*Saṃjñin*).
It is heard that among the disciples, he was foremost in preaching the Dharma. As for why this is so, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states:

"One who has realized real dharmas through consciousness and grasps conventional names through conceptualization—Pūrṇa, because his application of conceptualization and enumeration is clear, is able to distinguish names and characteristics;
thus, with unimpeded eloquence, he is the foremost among those who preach the Dharma. Furthermore, there are various conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).
Those who delight in preaching the Dharma and entering the Path took Pūrṇa as their teacher.

The reason for this was that the Buddha’s virtue is so revered that one must not rashly question or disturb him; thus, those who were newly trained each followed their own inclinations and went to serve him.
Later in this chapter, it says: "There were two bhikṣus who had violated the precepts; they did not dare to question the Buddha, so they went to Upāli..."
Upāli is precisely that person. As we see today in the world, it is always thus: those who delight in the Vinaya draw near to a Vinaya master;
those who delight in dhyāna follow after a meditation master; and those who delight in the meaning [of the teachings] draw near to a Dharma master.
Therefore, it is said: "The Vinaya is conjoined with dhyāna, and dhyāna is conjoined with this [Dharma]; this is what gives rise to the Tathāgata."

The teaching of entering the Way through the four types of withered and the four types of flourishing flowers is the instruction for entering the Path by means of the *chanda-skandha* (the aggregate of desire). It is because [the Buddha] wished to match it with Mahākāśyapa;
Mahākāśyapa must have been one whose *chanda-skandha* was particularly strong, as he entered the Path through the power of his wholesome desire (*kuśala-chanda*).

Thus, among all the disciples, he was foremost in the practice of *dhūta* (ascetic purification). The reason for this is that the *chanda-skandha* is the root of all wholesome dharmas, and Kāśyapa had severed [all unwholesome desires].

To have one's aspirations for worldly glory set upon the essential joy of renunciation and to delight in mountains and forests is the arousal of wholesome desire and the abandonment of worldly evil desires.
If there are sentient beings who delight in the dhūta practices and enter the Path, Kāśyapa immediately gathers them in as his followers through the dharma-gate of the dhūtas,
manifesting the Tathāgata’s four types of withering and four types of flourishing through the dhūta practices.
Regarding the teaching for entering the Path, the *Saṃprayukta-ābhidharma* (or *Saṃyukta-āgama*) frequently addresses Kātyāyana;
it is likely because Kātyāyana was particularly adept at this category of analysis, as he would immediately arise to investigate and examine the principles of meaning in order to enter the Path.

Thus, among the Śrāvakas, he was foremost in the exposition of doctrine. This is because his questions and answers proceeded back and forth, mutually engaging one another, like a debate held within a private chamber.
He was inexhaustible, unhindered, and unobstructed; because he had cultivated the joy of debate (*vāda-rati*) with particular intensity, he was able to act in this way.
If there were sentient beings who delighted in debating doctrines to enter the Path, Kātyāyana would go to them as their teacher.

He then used the Dharma-gate of debating doctrines to attract them as his followers, desiring to manifest for them the Tathāgata’s four types of "withering" and four types of "flourishing" regarding the entry into the Path through debate.
Regarding the teaching on the mental factor of wisdom (*prajñā-saṃskāra*): it was taught in contrast to Śāriputra, for Śāriputra was preeminently skilled in the mental factor of wisdom;
because he entered the Path through the mental factor of wisdom, he is the foremost in wisdom among all the śrāvakas and a great general of the Wheel of Dharma.

This reveals the teaching on entering the Path through the four types of "withering" and the four types of "flourishing. Regarding the teaching on the mental factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃskāra*): it was taught in contrast to Upāli. As for Upāli—
When this mindfulness (*smṛti*) is particularly strong, one uses mindfulness to uphold the Vinaya and enter the Path; among all the Śrāvakas, Upāli was foremost in upholding the Vinaya.
The reason for this is that to create conditions for recollection and to maintain it without forgetting is what is called "mindfulness.
Upāli, through his body and speech, weighed the gravity of matters in response to circumstances without any lapse of memory; thus, he was supreme in upholding the Vinaya. If there were a multitude...
Those who give rise to the desire for joy and enter the Way through the Vinaya-piṭaka immediately go to rely upon him;

Upāli then takes them as his followers by means of the Dharma-gates of the Vinaya-piṭaka, manifesting the Tathāgata’s teaching on entering the Way through the four types of austerity and the four types of prosperity within the Vinaya-piṭaka.
As for Cunda and Rāhula, Cunda likely entered the Way through the predominance of reflection (*cintā*), while Rāhula entered the Way through the practice of secrecy (*rahasya*).
Among all the śrāvakas, he is foremost in secret practice. Why is this so? Because the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) consists of the mental factor of volition (*cetanā*).
If volition is sharp and one cultivates various ascetic practices while concealing one's merits, one is supreme among those of secret practice.
If sentient beings delight in the secret practice of upholding the precepts, they shall take refuge in and follow Rāhula’s Dharma-gate of Secret Practice.

He gathers them in and causes them to practice the "counting of thoughts" (*vitarka-gaṇanā*) so that they may enter the Way and manifest the secret practices of the Tathāgata’s Half- and Full-teachings.
Regarding the "counting of liberation" (*vimokṣa-gaṇanā*), it corresponds to Subhūti; Subhūti should be understood as one who specializes in the counting of liberation.

By employing this method of counting, he cultivates the liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣa*) and enters the Way; thus, among all the Śrāvakas, he is foremost in understanding emptiness. No [other] is his equal.
The Samādhi of Non-contention is serene and solitary, transcending all and not competing with external things.

If there are sentient beings who delight in the liberation of emptiness and enter the Way through non-contention, Subhūti follows and instructs them accordingly. He leads them into the Way by means of the Dharma-gate of the liberation of emptiness, taking them as his followers;
thus he assists the Buddha in widely proclaiming the Dharma of the emptiness of both decay and flourishing.

The gate is the teaching for entering the Path. To apply the mind to objects and practice counting is directed toward Anuruddha. Anuruddha must have been exceptionally sharp in his capacity for recollection and counting;
because he lost his physical eyesight, the Buddha instructed him to cultivate this practice of counting to develop the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) and thereby enter the Path.
For this reason, among the Śrāvakas, he is foremost in the divine eye. This is because, in cultivating the divine eye, one must necessarily...
One must abide with the mind focused on an object, taking the signs of the sun, moon, and starlight as the basis for cultivation to develop the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).

If sentient beings delight in cultivating the divine eye to enter the Path, Nalakalīra taught the method of cultivating the divine eye by using the recitation of numbers to continue the mind upon external objects;
he gathered them as his followers to assist in manifesting the Tathāgata’s celestial powers regarding decay and flourishing.
The teaching on entering the Path through the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-āyatana*) concerns the meditative count (*samādhi-gaṇanā*). It was directed toward Maudgalyāyana;

Maudgalyāyana must have possessed an especially strong and sharp faculty for concentration (*samādhi*), and by cultivating this count, he entered meditative absorption and advanced on the Path. For this reason, among all the Śrāvakas, he is foremost in dhyāna-concentration.
Why is this so? Because ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) all possess this meditative count; were it not for concentration, they would fall headlong from level ground.

Because sentient beings are unable to practice it, they do not attain profound concentration. Maudgalyāyana, this enumeration clarifies that by cultivating it extensively, one attains profound dhyāna and mastery over the supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*).
If there are sentient beings who delight in meditative concentration and supernormal powers as a means of entering the Path, they should all draw near to such a person to receive instruction.
Maudgalyāyana, by means of this Dharma-gate of meditative concentration, he leads sentient beings into [the Path].

The *Daoshu* (Exposition on the Path) clarifies the Tathāgata’s teachings on entering the path through the four types of austere and the four types of flourishing meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*).
It was specifically composed for Ānanda; Ānanda was indeed one who possessed a powerful and sharp capacity for receiving and retaining what he heard, thereby entering the path.

For this reason, among all the *śrāvakas*, he was foremost in extensive learning and total retention (*dhāraṇī*). As for why it is called the *Daoshu* in four fascicles, it is as follows: [text continues].

The "aggregate of sensation" (*vedanā-skandha*) refers to the mind associated with pain and other [feelings]; here, it is generally termed "sensation" because its essential meaning is that of experiencing (*anubhava*).

Therefore, this aggregate clearly receives and maintains the Buddha-dharma, just as a complete vessel holds water. For those sentient beings who delight in extensive learning and enter the Path, they rely upon Ānanda;
since Ānanda possesses great learning and total retention (*dhāraṇī*), he serves as their retinue, leading them to enter through the aggregate of sensation.
The Way of Attaining Buddhahood: Withering and Flourishing, Hearing and Retaining—Entering the Path of the Teaching. Fifth, explaining the Twin Trees:
Although the preceding section clarified withering and flourishing, the phrasing was brief and the meaning not yet fully manifest.

This refers to the ten disciples collectively assisting the Tathāgata to adorn the teachings of the Half- and Full-Equipped Vehicles—the four instances of withering and the four of flourishing—thereby leading sentient beings into the Middle Way, enabling them to see the Buddha-nature and abide therein.
The Great Nirvāṇa is precisely abiding in inconceivable liberation; this is the meaning of entering nirvāṇa between the twin trees.
If it is as elucidated in the Tripiṭaka—contemplating impermanence to shatter the four inversions of permanence and so forth—it adorns the four withered aspects to guide and receive sentient beings.
Within each of these enumerations, one fully cultivates the four *siddhāntas* to gather and embrace all beings, whether according to their circumstances or...
Whether through the gathering of worldly desires, or by following people, or by following remedies, or by following the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*),
one gathers sentient beings according to their skillful means to assist the Dharma King and accomplish the teaching of the "half-letters" (*ardhakṣara*) for the benefit of all.
If one person performs the gathering through the four *siddhāntas*, then ten people constitute forty kinds of adornment.
From "withered" up to "five hundred," there are two thousand [terms] that adorn the four types of withered [trees]. Question:
If ten people correspond to the number ten, and five hundred correspond to what dharma? Answer: What the Dharma King has taught must have a specific reason.
Now, having seen the Dharma-gate transmitted by five hundred people, one must not recklessly attempt to imitate it; if one seeks its meaning...
If one were to provisionally explain this principle by counting each [factor] as one, there would be ten; ten tens make a hundred, and since each of those tens has ten, that constitutes a hundred.
When these are applied to the five sense faculties (*pañcendriya*), they constitute five hundred.

Furthermore, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* clarifies that five hundred bhikṣus each spoke of the cause of the body, all of which pertain to the "half-letters" (*ardhākṣara*)—the distinctions of entering the Path through the four types of withered austerity. Next...
It is explained that the ten disciples correspond to ten kinds of Dharma gates to assist the Buddha in propagating the full-character teachings.

Because sentient beings were unable to endure them, he employed the power of skillful means to establish the four "withered" (ku) teachings. These ten disciples are all Mahāsattvas of the Dharma-body;
they secretly conceal their bodhisattva practices while outwardly manifesting as śrāvakas. Since the Tathāgata has entrusted [this task]...
