When he was born in the royal palace, ten disciples also emerged according to their conditions. Once the Tathāgata had practiced the Way under the tree, his disciples likewise studied heterodox paths;
all were clever and possessed sharp intelligence, serving as teachers of external paths. Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says:
"I originally adhered to false views and served as a teacher to various Brahmins. The World-Honored One, knowing my mind, uprooted my heterodoxy and preached the Nirvāṇa.

The reason Pāṇini was chosen as his teacher was that he was easy to subdue. Once the Tathāgata had attained the Way, Pāṇini immediately came to take refuge and received the teaching of the four *kārikās*.
Since his master had submitted, his disciples followed the wind of his example and all entered the Dharma-gate of the four *kārikās* and the *ardhamātrikā* (half-syllable) teachings.
After this, their minds accorded with one another in mutual trust; the Buddha then desired to preach the Mahāyāna.

Because his coming and going are without hindrance, Vimalakīrti rebukes the Hinayana and censures the various followers of the Two Vehicles, causing them to rejoice in the Great [Vehicle] and loathe the Small.
These disciples bow their heads and accept this reproof, demonstrating that they occupy a station inferior to his; this is the "anvil.
The Great Being’s censure and rebuke serve as the "hammer," together maturing the vessels of sentient beings so that the Great Matter may arise and be manifested.

The Tathāgata, through his skillful means and secret teachings, causes all sentient beings to feel shame for the Lesser Vehicle and aspire to the Great, so that they may open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, attain eternal bliss, and enter the Dharma-gate of the *maṃtra* (full letter).
All of this is accomplished by means of the ten disciples, who, through ten kinds of Dharma-gates, mutually manifest and assist one another in accomplishing the Buddha-work.
A detailed explanation of the meaning of the five flavors is found in the *Lotus Sūtra*; it is not [the subject] of this [text].
The *Sūtra* does not fully clarify the intended meaning. Furthermore, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* clarifies that the four honored ones adorned the twin trees;
it should likewise have specified all ten persons. However, it mentions only six and omits the other four because that sūtra was intended to refute the six heterodox teachers (*ṣaṭ-tīrthika*).
Since those six teachers took perverse views and sought to destroy the twin trees, the sūtra specifically names these six people to adorn the twin trees, rather than including all ten.
The reason for this is that all sentient beings possess the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and ten mental factors (*caitasika*), which constitute the three kinds of Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*).
How is this known? The mind-king is the direct cause of Buddha-nature (*zhengyin foxing*); the factor of wisdom (*prajñā*) is the revealing cause of Buddha-nature (*lioyin foxing*);
and the remaining nine factors are all the conditional cause of Buddha-nature (*yuan-yin foxing*). These three kinds of Buddha-nature are clearly and perfectly present.

Because they are frequently obscured by afflictions (*kleśa*), they are unable to give rise [to the path]; therefore, the Tathāgata, together with his ten disciples, uses the hammer and anvil to strike away and eliminate these various afflictions.

He brings them to maturity like clarified butter (*ghṛta*) through skillful means, causing them to enter the Dharma-gates of the "Half" and "Full," opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*), and manifesting the three kinds of Buddha-nature (*trividhabuddhadhātu*) to enter the secret treasury of the three virtues (*triguṇaguhya-kośa*). Now, we shall distinguish the ten disciples in relation to these ten [afflictions].
The Mind-Numbered (Citta-saṃkhyā) Vairocana Tathāgata, together with the Mind-King (Citta-rāja), brings about both partial and complete benefits for sentient beings;

this meaning is crystal clear from antiquity to the present. Since this meaning has not been clarified, how could one know that the intent of my disciple was to support and perfect the teaching of inconceivable liberation?
Sixth, regarding the clarification of the birth in the land of retribution, there are the ten great disciples.

Using these ten gates to assist in adorning the twin trees of the Buddha, when those sentient beings to be converted achieve the four types of "withered" arhats and enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, they are immediately reborn in other lands to receive the *dharmatā-kāya*.
This is because such persons have dull faculties, as their path toward Buddhahood is circuitous. Now, in contrast to Vimalakīrti, this is like the hammer and anvil being brought together.

Thereupon, one enters the four ranks of honor; upon reaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, one opens the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, thereby attaining the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and entering the first stage of the Bodhisattva path (*prathama-cittotpāda-vihāra*).

At the time of death, one is not reborn in a land of residual existence, but is instead born in the Pure Land of Fruitional Reward, the World of the Lotus King, as an attendant of Vairocana, hearing only the Perfect Teaching.
It is said that their minds are extinguished and they naturally flow into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge). Seventh, regarding the clarification of purifying the Buddha-land:
these ten disciples use ten dharma-gates to adorn the twin trees, which is precisely the accomplishment of sentient beings and the purification of the Buddha-land.
This continues until the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, where the Buddha bestows predictions upon these ten disciples; [at that time], they had not yet...
When he attains Buddhahood, all the sentient beings he transforms will dwell in ten kinds of Dharma-gates and be reborn in his land.
Furthermore, the causes cultivated by these transformed beings—the four types of withering and the four types of flourishing—are used to subdue sentient beings and purify the Buddha-land;
when he becomes a Buddha, such beings as these will all likewise be reborn in that land.

Furthermore, if one were to examine this sutra’s teaching as a whole and clarify its intent, it is merely to reprove the śrāvakas and praise the bodhisattvas who dwell in inconceivable liberation, sport with supernormal powers, and purify buddha-fields. It states that those of the two vehicles have forever severed these roots;
they are ruined individuals who are no longer capable of enduring the five desires. For this reason, Kāśyapa uttered his lamentation and remorse.

His voice resounded throughout the three thousandfold world-system; now, taking the intent of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* as my standard, I shall speak regarding the bestowal of predictions upon Śāriputra, Mahākāśyapa, Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra, and others.
[The Sūtra] states that "the path you practice is the bodhisattva path," and further says that those who have few desires and loathe birth-and-death are truly purifying their own buddha-fields.
Thus, when one reasons according to this principle, it becomes clear that Vimalakīrti’s rebuke and refutation of the ten great disciples was based on this very point.
The five hundred arhats are all those who have perfected the roles of hammer and anvil as śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;

through their successive efforts, they have all become causes for the purification of Buddha-lands. This is the disciple’s reiteration of the intent of the "Chapter on Assisting the Establishment of the Buddha-land," which has remained thus from antiquity until the present—who has truly known it?
Eighth, regarding the clarification of contemplating the mind: now, let us examine this interpretation.
This is also the contemplation of the mind. Why is this? The practitioner possesses the ten categories of the mind-king (*citta-rāja*).

The mind-king is the Tathāgata; the mental factors (*caitasika*) are the disciples. However, for sentient beings, these ten categories of the mind-king arise incessantly throughout the succession of moments, day and night, as immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings.
All phenomena that are not the mind-king are the retinues of the māras and demons. The mind-king...
If the ten numerical categories are correct, then all dharmas are correct. Furthermore, those practitioners of the Way at this time must skillfully grasp this meaning.
If they cultivate wisdom, they should simply give rise to the mental factor of wisdom within, contemplating and discerning through it;
thereby, they will develop the wisdom of both the partial and the complete, benefiting themselves and transforming others, just like Śāriputra adorning the twin trees. If...

When practicing meditative concentration, one should single-mindedly cultivate and investigate the inner mind, repeatedly refining the concentration until one attains entry into various profound *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (half- and full-) meditative absorptions and gains mastery over the supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*).
Thus, one may personally transform oneself and others, becoming equal to Maudgalyāyana in adorning the twin trees.
If one wishes to practice the *dhūta* austerities, one should instead give rise to wholesome desires within the mind and repeatedly shake off transgressions from one's conduct in deep mountains.
Purifying oneself while transforming others is identical to Mahākāśyapa’s adornment of the twin śāla trees.
Thus, each of the ten disciples, through their respective mental activities, accomplished the transformation of beings; each of their practices reveals that they arose from the mind.
If one can contemplate the nature of the mind with clarity, this is precisely seeing the Buddha-nature and abiding in Great Nirvāṇa, which is identical to being a Tathāgata.
The twin *śāla* trees are fully adorned. If one observes with a mind of clear practice, seeing the Mind-King is the Dharma-King, and the mental factors (*caitta*) are the great disciples;
the meaning of the adornment of the twin trees is as if seen with one's own eyes.

How could the *Guānxīnyùyì mìshù* (Commentary on the Secret Meaning of the Contemplation of the Mind) exhaustively describe the mind? Ninth, the critical analysis of the sequence of inquiries regarding the illness.
Question: Why does the Tathāgata not first dispatch the bodhisattvas, but instead first dispatches the śrāvakas? Answer:

If he had first dispatched the bodhisattvas and each of them had declared their inability [to proceed], the śrāvakas would have looked upon the precipice and retreated, thereby losing the five hundred dharma-gates.
By first commanding the śrāvakas, if they decline, then the five hundred dharma-gates will all be sealed with approval.

It can be established that the sequence of the sutra is such that the Bodhisattva was sent immediately after [the Buddha’s passing], thereby fully completing the account of the Dharma previously taught by Vimalakīrti.
Question: If one discusses the order of seniority, Ānanda should have been sent first. Answer:

Although each of the ten great disciples presides over a specific dharma-gate, even though Śāriputra was first commanded, he was not capable of it; thus, among the others, there were those who were mutually qualified.
"Those under his charge must be sent away so that no fault may arise.
At that time, the elder Vimalakīrti thought to himself: "I am currently bedridden with illness; will the World-Honored One, in his great compassion, not deign to show me mercy?"
The third section, the entry into the text for explanation, consists of two parts: first, explaining Vimalakīrti’s silent contemplation; second, explaining the Tathāgata’s dispatching of questions.
Regarding the first, Vimalakīrti’s silent contemplation, there are two intentions: first, his own reflection on being bedridden with illness; second, his reflection on the Tathāgata’s intent.
As for Vimalakīrti’s own reflection on being bedridden upon his couch, this refers to the initial stage of his self-reflection on his illness.
However, since the Pure Name (Vimalakīrti) occupies the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), how could he have any illness?
That he conceived the thought of being ill was precisely because he wished to rely upon illness to give rise to the teaching; thus he gave rise to this thought.

Now, "conceiving the thought" is explained as the Dharma-body abiding in the position of the three virtues at the stage of Equal Enlightenment, wherein "conceiving the thought" represents *prajñā* (wisdom) and "illness" represents... [the remainder of the sentence is missing from the source].
Liberation is represented by the bed; this refers to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), which is the three virtues neither vertical nor horizontal, like the letter *i* in the world.
Why is this so? The Dharma-body is precisely the intrinsically pure mind: when hidden, it is called the Tathāgatagarbha; when manifest, it is called the Dharma-body.
This is liberation as true nature (*tathatā*). As for the meaning of "lying down" representing Prajñā, it is like a person...
"Sleeping" refers to the cessation of all weariness, afflictions, and worldly activities. The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Who attains peaceful sleep?
It is the Buddhas, who constantly dwell in the samādhi of contemplating emptiness; their body and mind are tranquil and unmoving.

Now, having perfected the cultivation of causes by contemplating emptiness through Prajñā, all conditioned practices have come to rest. Because the principle of original purity is revealed, this state is designated as "sleeping."
Clarifying the meaning of *prajñā* is precisely the liberation through true wisdom (*prajñā-vimukti*).

To swiftly manifest the liberation through skillful means (*upāya-vimukti*) means that when *prajñā* accords with the principle of true nature, there arises great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) without conditions that does not abandon sentient beings;
because the body is permeated by compassion, one is able to manifest illness through skillful means. As the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* says: "The Buddhas discipline sentient beings."
The state [of being free from defilement] is called liberation. Because sentient beings are afflicted, Vimalakīrti manifests illness through skillful means;
he harmonizes with the light of the world yet remains untainted by its dust. This is precisely the pure liberation of skillful means. Question:

For what purpose did Vimalakīrti intentionally conceive of his own illness? Since it is the Dharma-body, how could prajñā and great compassion give rise to illness to manifest identity with the multitudes?
Bound by the afflictions of birth, his urgent desire to benefit sentient beings has not yet been manifested; thus, harboring inner frustration, he expresses his reflections.
As the Sūtra says: "World-Honored One, with your great compassion, will you not deign to show pity?
This is the second point, clarifying that Vimalakīrti remained silent because he required the Tathāgata to inquire after him. Vimalakīrti abides in the stage of causes.
I still grieve for sentient beings, wishing to uproot their suffering arising from the three types of conditions, and thus manifest illness myself.
At the stage of the Tathāgata’s fruition, great compassion without object constantly desires to bestow upon sentient beings the bliss of Great Nirvāṇa; moreover, your own name is exceedingly pure.
How could you not show me pity? If you send someone to inquire after me, I shall be able to describe my state of illness myself. If this meaning were made manifest, [it would be so].
When the three conditions converge, the afflictions of sentient beings regarding cause and effect are healed;
thus, the illness of the one with whom he has a karmic connection—Vimalakīrti—is also healed. Is this not truly in accord with the Tathāgata’s great compassion that bestows happiness?
The Buddha, knowing his intention, immediately addressed Śāriputra: "Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness.
This constitutes the second instance of the Tathāgata dispatching someone to inquire, which has two meanings: first, the Buddha knows the mental reflections of Vimalakīrti;
second, he dispatches him to go and inquire. As the sutra says, "The Buddha knew his intention," which refers to the wisdom of quiescent illumination that perceives Vimalakīrti from afar.
The intention of feigning illness arises from great compassion for those who lack such conditions; thus, he manifests illness for the sake of all sentient beings.
The wise can understand this, just as a wise person knows that a snake has no feet. As the Sūtra says:
"Śāriputra, go to Vimalakīrti and inquire after his illness. This is the second instance of the Buddha dispatching someone to visit and inquire, making two [instances].
First, he commands ten disciples; second, he commands five hundred śrāvakas. Now, regarding the command to the ten disciples, we shall follow the text and establish ten sections.
The first is the command to Śāriputra, which itself consists of two parts: first, the Buddha’s command;
second, Śāriputra’s respectful refusal on the grounds of his inability. As for why Śāriputra is commanded first: Śāriputra is the Buddha’s...

The attendant on the left was the foremost in wisdom among the assembly of śrāvakas; renowned for his high virtue and profound dignity, there were none, whether internal or external, who did not pay him respectful homage.

Although Vimalakīrti, though a layman, was diligent in practice, possessed thorough mastery of the Buddha-dharma, and had attained spiritual awakening with such eloquence that it was difficult to respond to him in debate, Śāriputra was therefore first commanded to convey the message and inquire after his health. This was solely due to the karmic conditions involving Śāriputra.
It is so vast that it is difficult to explain in full; I shall now speak of it briefly. Śāriputra is translated here as "Body-Son" (Shenzi).
The reason for this is that his mother’s name was Śārī; this is translated as "Body.
Because this woman was intelligent, virtuous, and possessed a beautiful physical form, people of the time gave her the name "Body," and *putra* means "son. Thus, he is called Śāriputra.
This was born from her body and received its name from its mother; thus it was called Śāriputra. When the mother was pregnant, she suddenly experienced an auspicious dream:
she saw a man clad in armor, holding a vajra-pestle in his hand, who shattered all the mountains and then stood beside one mountain. Upon waking, she immediately related this dream to her husband.
The master of exegesis, Mādhavaśa, explained his husband’s words as follows: "You shall have a child;
that which you bear will surely be male. His body shall be clad in armor—this child will certainly possess profound virtue.
He who holds a vajra-pestle in his hand is one who is intelligent and possesses great wisdom. He who shatters all mountains is one who shall become a great [being]."
When the Master of Treatises had refuted all opposing doctrines and was standing by the side of a mountain, he found one person whose mind was so subdued that he became his disciple.
His mother, from the time she conceived him, possessed extraordinary spiritual wisdom;
when she engaged in debate with her elder brother, Mahākoṭṭhila, she always excelled him, while her brother was constantly defeated since she had been pregnant with him.
This "stagnation" refers to the child’s wisdom permeating its mother. Upon his birth, when he reached the age of eight, he ascended the seat of debate;
among the masters of logic in the kingdom of Mathurā, there was none who did not express astonishment. By the age of sixteen, he was peerless in the debates of the great kingdoms.
He became friends with Maudgalyāyana, and together they served Sañjaya as their teacher.
Yaśas, whose intelligence surpassed that of all other heterodox teachers, together with Maudgalyāyana, each had their own disciples.

Having heard that the Tathāgata had appeared in the world to teach and transform the three Kāśyapa brothers and their thousand disciples, all of whom had become arhats, Yaśas immediately conceived faith from afar and sought out the Buddha’s location. On the road, he encountered Uruvilvākāśyapa.
When the verse on the Three Truths was preached, Śāriputra immediately attained the nectar of immortality and realized the fruit of Srotāpanna;
he then returned and spoke it for Maudgalyāyana, who only after hearing it three times attained the nectar of immortality and realized the fruit of Srotāpanna.

The two of them, each accompanied by their own disciples, went together to the place where the Tathāgata was, left the household life to practice the Way, and Śāriputra became an Arhat seven days later.
Because he was a great general intent upon turning the wheel of Dharma for the Buddha, while still on the stage of training, he traveled through the three piṭakas for seven days;
having attained unimpeded mastery of all dharma-gates, he then severed his fetters and realized arhatship.
Thus, among the ordained śrāvaka disciples, he is foremost in wisdom. This is why, from the time of his conception...
One of superior intelligence and wisdom desired to convert all clever heterodox practitioners (tīrthikas) to become his disciples;

later, encountering the Buddha and leaving the household life to become an arhat, he led all those clever heterodox practitioners to become disciples of the Buddha, causing them to study under the "half-letters" to manifest the teaching of the four types of withered trees. Now, he is rebuked in silence by Vimalakīrti.
However, it is not known which interlocutor intended to cause those disciples who study the "four withered" teachings to feel inward shame and inferiority,
so that they might revere the wisdom-teachings of the "four flourishing. When it comes to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* spoken before the Buddha—
specifically the *Dapin jing* (Large Sutra)— spoken to Śāriputra— it causes all the śrāvakas to believe in and understand the "full-lettered" wisdom of the four flourishing.
As for Wisdom (Prajñā), at the Lotus Sūtra, he first received the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision from Śāriputra as one destined for the prophecy of becoming the Buddha Flower-Light;

all śrāvakas, the eight classes of beings, and the fourfold assembly likewise had their Buddha-knowledge and vision opened, and they joyfully praised him, each speaking in unison with a verse, saying:
"O Greatly Wise Śāriputra, you have now received the Honored One's prophecy. I...
Others are likewise; they shall certainly attain Buddhahood, becoming the most honored and unsurpassed among all worlds.

This is because they have fully awakened to the true understanding of the four glories. Thus, in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, when the Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda asked the Buddha, "Who is able to adorn the twin śāla trees?
the Buddha replied, "O Śāriputra of great wisdom, it is precisely [those who have attained this realization]."
Regarding that person, there are certain Dharma masters who claim that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is a teaching of impermanence. They argue:

"Śāriputra, the Tathāgata entered parinirvāṇa three months after [the preaching of this sutra]; since you did not hear the teaching of the twin trees within the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, how could this [person] be one who adorns the twin trees?
You should know that it was at the time of preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* that they received [this prediction].
The record of the eight classes of beings and the fourfold assembly attaining simultaneous understanding through Śāriputra is precisely the manifestation of the meaning of the Twin Trees.
This passage probes the intent of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; such an intent had not yet been revealed in the various Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā teachings.

For this reason, when the Buddha sent [Mañjuśrī] to inquire after Vimalakīrti’s illness, he first addressed Śāriputra; if Śāriputra were to recount his past being rebuked by him, [the purpose would be fulfilled].
This further clarifies the four glories and fulfills the meaning of the aforementioned benefit.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, I am not fit to go there to inquire about his illness.
This is the second instance of Śāriputra respectfully declining the mission; the scriptural text contains four meanings: first, [the meaning of] Śāriputra...
1. The respectful refusal; 2. The reason for the inability; 3. The specific matters of the inability; 4. The conclusion of the inability.

First, regarding the respectful refusal of the inability: it is precisely because he was previously rebuked and did not understand the meaning of those words that he is unable to accept the command to go inquire after his illness.
Why is this? I recall that in the past, while sitting in meditative seclusion beneath a tree in a forest, Śāriputra spoke of his inability [to endure the Buddha’s teaching].
This was the second reason Śāriputra described his incapacity, namely, because he was sitting in meditative seclusion beneath a tree in the forest.

Regarding "sitting in meditative seclusion" (*pratisaṃlayana*), some teachers explain it as having the meaning of "withdrawing and ceasing," just as a tortoise can hide its six limbs within its shell.

Māra cannot cause harm because when one sits in meditative seclusion (*pratisaṃlayana*), the six consciousnesses and the six sense objects are withdrawn, such that even external Māras cannot afflict them;

thus it is called "withdrawal" (*saṃkṣepa*). Now, to clarify: the term "seclusion" (*yàn*) means "peaceful stability. One peacefully abides in the various dhyānas, up to and including abiding in the cessation of perception and feeling (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
By stilling external toil and fatigue, which resemble the Dharma of Nirvāṇa, one establishes this within the mind and personally realizes the cessation of perception and feeling.
Therefore, it is called "sitting in repose.
At that time, Vimalakīrti came and said to me, "O Śāriputra, it is not necessarily this kind of sitting that constitutes sitting in repose.
This is the third section, which correctly describes the reprimand; it consists of three parts: first, a general reprimand; second, a specific demonstration of true sitting in repose.

Regarding the statement that "sitting and forming the seals of the three fetters" constitutes meditative seclusion (*yànzù*), the initial general reproach says it need not be sitting to be considered meditative seclusion.

This is not entirely a denial [of sitting], nor does it intend to mock those who dwell in remote places. What kind of meditative seclusion did Śāriputra practice that he was rebuked by the Great Being?
If one considers the meaning of the subsequent passages in light of this, it is mostly based on the Tripiṭaka and the "half-words" teaching (*bànzìjiào*).
To enter the various dhyānas and the samādhi of cessation while being unable to advance toward the Buddha’s wisdom is to sit in meditation with the "full letter" [of conventional truth].

Since there are six faults in entering the various dhyānas and the samādhi of cessation [in such a manner], it is criticized as "unnecessary. "Unnecessary" (*abuddha*) is merely another name for "not of definitive meaning" (*neyārtha*).
If one sits in meditation through conceptual deliberation, that is "unnecessary"; if one sits in meditation without conceptual deliberation, [it is necessary].
"Sitting" refers to the *Abhidharma* (Abhidharmakośa), which clarifies that the cessation of non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) occurs in thirteen locations.
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* clarifies that the emptiness of mind occurs in two locations.

Now, regarding the Three Vehicles of the Tripiṭaka Teaching, there are five locations where practitioners enter the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*), each differing in how they attain entry. The first is the fundamental [dhyāna].

1. Entering the meditative absorption of cessation by relying on the *samāpatti* of clear and pure meditation; 2. Entering the meditative absorption of cessation by relying on the meditation of the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*); 3.

Entering the meditative absorption of cessation by relying on the meditation refined through the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*); 4. Entering the meditative absorption of cessation by relying on the meditation of the "lion’s bound" (*siṃhavijṛmbhita*) and "perfumed" (*vāsita*);

5. Entering the meditative absorption of cessation by relying on the meditation of "leaping over" (*vyutkrāntaka*). The first [method] is from the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, while the latter four are from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Śāstra*.

This chapter of the sutra was produced by the Meditation Master of Mount Nanyue. It follows the fundamental Pure Dhyāna exactly: one who enters the extinction samādhi practices the Contemplation of Penetrating Clarity.
First, in the first dhyāna, one contemplates form as being like foam; in the second dhyāna, one contemplates form as being like clouds;
in the third dhyāna, one contemplates form as being like shadows; and in the fourth dhyāna, it is like a reflection in a mirror. Next, one extinguishes form and takes up emptiness. However—

With single-minded focus, one takes emptiness as an object, and so on, up to taking the cessation of perception and feeling (*nirodhasamāpatti*)—which is the breaking of even non-perception—as an object.
Although there are no coarse afflictions (*kleśa*), ten kinds of subtle factors are still present; these subtle factors are themselves afflictions and the cause of birth and death.

When a disciple of the Buddha realizes that these are not noble dharmas (*āryadharma*), they are able to extinguish them, as well as the mind capable of extinguishing them and its mental concomitants (*caitasika-dharma*). Therefore, it is called the "attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling."

This explains the entry into the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) through the fundamental pure dhyānas. Next, regarding the entry into the meditative absorption of cessation through the contemplation of the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*):
one contemplates the impurity of the internal and external body as white bones emitting light, thereby entering the first liberation.

Through the two spheres of mastery (*abhibhv-āyatana*), one extinguishes the afflictions of the second dhyāna; at that time, one no longer perceives forms such as foam, clouds, or reflections in a mirror, but [perceives only]...

Contemplating the pure form-sphere (*rūpāyatana*) as the object of the third dhyāna, because it is pure, one purifies the eight forms and extinguishes the afflictions of the third dhyāna through the flowing light, thereby accomplishing the fourth dhyāna, the four bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and the eight bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*).

If one then extinguishes the perception of form and takes emptiness as the object, at that time, by deeply contemplating emptiness through the concentration on the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), one turns away from it with detachment and does not revert; this is called "infinite space."

The liberation through dwelling (*āyatana-vimokṣa*) is likewise, extending even to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). At that time, one knows that even in neither-perception-nor-non-perception there are still the four aggregates (*skandha*) and ten kinds of subtle afflictions (*kleśa*).
By deeply contemplating and detaching from these attachments, one advances in the cultivation of the cessation of sensation and perception (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha*).

At that time, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is further designated as "liberation through turning away" (*parāvṛtti-vimokṣa*). If one turns away from and ceases all mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitasika-dharma*), one realizes it through bodily witness (*kāyasākṣin*).
The cessation of feeling and perception (*vedanā-saṃjñā-nirodha*) is precisely the liberation through the abandonment of feeling and perception (*saṃjñā-vedayita-vimokṣa*).

In the causal stage, it is called "liberation" (*vimokṣa*); when the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*) arises and the remaining delusions of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are completely exhausted, this liberation then shifts its name to "deliverance" (*vimukti*).
If one speaks of the fruit within the cause, liberation may also be termed "deliverance"; if one speaks of the cause within the fruit, deliverance may also be termed "liberation."
Setting aside the previous [view], it is now judged that the "back-slippages" (*prātimokṣa*) are not themselves liberation.

An *anāgāmin* who relies on the eight back-slippages to enter the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*) still cannot be called "liberated. If these were indeed liberation, they would have to be Arhats;
how then could they still be *anāgāmins* who have realized [only] the body-witness (*kāyasākṣin*)? This is explained by clarifying the entry into cessation (*nirodha*) in terms of the back-slippages.
Regarding the third point, entering the cessation attainment (*nirodha-samāpatti*) through the purification of the nine successive meditations (*navānupūrvavihāra-dhyāna*):
although one may have previously entered cessation through the liberations (*vimokṣa*), this requires deliberate mental application and a specific resolve to enter;
it is not spontaneous. Now, having mastered the purifications of the liberations, one proceeds from the first dhyāna...
Entering sequentially until reaching the state of non-perception, one then enters the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) spontaneously and without interval; this is easy.
However, upon emerging, it is like a sleeping person awakening. Fourth, regarding entering the meditative absorption of cessation through the "lion’s bound" (*siṃhavijṛmbhita*) meditation:
whereas in previous practice one could only enter sequentially, here it is clarified that one not only enters sequentially but [proceeds directly] until...

Emerging from the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) in immediate succession—progressing step-by-step from the attainment of cessation up to the first dhyāna—is characterized by mastery and a meditative power that is increasingly superior in its uninterrupted flow.
Fifth, regarding the practice of "leaping" (*vyutkrāntaka*) in the cultivation of dhyāna:

although one has previously been able to enter and emerge from these states with mastery and without interruption, one has not yet been able to leap into them or leap out of them; it is now, in this [practice], that such occurs.

One who transcends the dhyānas can leap from the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) into the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), and upon arising from that cessation, leap back out of the Sphere of Nothingness;
this is like the leap of a lion of yellow hue. This is called skillfully entering, emerging, abiding, and arising within hundreds of thousands of samādhis.
The power of this concentration is the greatest. Now, regarding these five kinds of dhyāna, we shall clarify how the five flavors arise in succession.

The fundamental supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), clarity, and pure dhyāna are like milk; the liberations (*vimokṣa*) are like curd; the nine successive attainments (*anupūrva-samāpatti*) are like fresh butter;
the *vaiśāradya* (mastery) is like matured butter; and the *vyutkrāntaka-dhyāna* (leap-over meditation) is like clarified butter (*ghṛta*).

This leap-over meditation is supreme, capable of fully possessing such merits as the knowledge of vows (*praṇidhi-jñāna*), the samādhi of non-contention (*araṇā-samādhi*), the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), the three types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*), the six supernormal powers, and the eighteen transformations (*vikurvaṇa*), up to the pinnacle.
Among all dhyānas, the "summit" (mūrdhan) is the most supreme;

it is not only the fourth dhyāna that possesses the summit dhyāna, but all others do as well, even extending to the point where the transcending entry (*vyutkrāntaka-samāpatti*) within all dhyānas is called the summit. Question:

For what reason are there further five distinctions—namely, the fundamental (*maula*), the cultivated (*parikarman*), the refined (*anuloma*), the purified (*viloma*), and the practiced (*abhyasta*)—within the fundamental dhyānas? Answer: It is like the process of refining [gold].
The initial penetration of the skin is like soaking it in water; the subsequent liberation (*prahāṇa*) is like scraping away the hair;
the sequential concentration (*anupūrva-samādhi*) is like penetrating the brain; and the leaping-over (*vyutkrāntaka*) is like softening it by fumigation.

This differs from the explanations of the *Śaikṣa* school regarding fumigation and refinement (as detailed in the commentary). If a Śrāvaka Arhat attains the leaping-over, he is named a Mahānāga-citta.
"Tranquil and supple" refers to the fact that within the matters of the Three Vehicles, meditative concentration (dhyāna) reaches its ultimate limit here.

Since Śāriputra was already a great Arhat, he was at that time roaming among the groves practicing these various dhyānas and entering the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) to still all weariness and toil.
Upon arising from this meditative concentration, he was rebuked by the Great Being (the Bodhisattva) because he was unable to proceed toward the wisdom of the Buddha.
Having transcended these various dhyānas, he suddenly avoids the clamor of the world to sit in quietude within the forest and enter into the various meditative absorptions (dhyāna-samādhi).
Therefore, Vimalakīrti rebukes him, saying "it is not necessarily so. This rebuke does not mean that he cannot proceed toward the Buddha-wisdom;
for if one were not foremost in wisdom, how could one enter the various dhyānas and attain the ultimate? Furthermore, the phrase "not necessarily so" is not [a denial of his attainment].
To completely eliminate [the former] does not necessarily mean that this constitutes the ultimate; for what reason?

The meditative concentrations attained by Śāriputra, as explained above, are the "half-syllable" (*ardha-akṣara*) concentrations of the four types of withered meditation, and not the "full-syllable" (*pūrṇa-akṣara*) ninefold great meditations—the profound cave of *mahāparinirvāṇa* concentration known as the "Eternally Quiescent Samādhi. Therefore, it is said:
It is not necessary.
Now, as for "sitting in quietude," it means that one does not manifest body or mind within the three realms; this is what constitutes sitting in quietude.
This is the second clarification, specifically showing that true sitting in quietude is precisely the inconceivable entry into the various dhyānas and the cessation-concentration (nirodha-samāpatti).

Regarding these six kinds of methods for sitting in meditation (*yansuo*), according to this scriptural passage, there are three pairs: first, clarifying true sitting in meditation by means of the two dharmas of essence and function;
second, clarifying true sitting in meditation by means of the two dharmas of dharma and mind; and third, clarifying true sitting in meditation by means of the two dharmas of cause and effect.
Regarding the first, that which concerns essence and function, it is further divided into two parts, the first of which clarifies—
To clarify the true nature of "sitting in meditation" (yansuo): the Sūtra states that not manifesting body or mind within the three realms constitutes sitting in meditation.
Śāriputra did not enter the aforementioned various dhyānas or the meditative absorption of cessation by means of pursuing the Buddha’s wisdom;

rather, he had to abandon clamor and rely on a quiet place in the forest, straightening his body and withdrawing his thoughts, before he could attain meditative absorption. This, then, pertains to the three realms.

Within this, relying on the body and mind as they manifest according to desire, one enters the various dhyānas; if one enters the samādhi of cessation, there is a fixed period for entering and emerging.
When the body is like wood or stone and the mind is like extinguished ashes, this is the manifestation of the body.

When the mind is like extinguished ashes yet there is still a fixed period for entering and emerging, this is the manifestation of the mind. Although these are called "leaving behind clamor," they are not yet permanent.
If one extinguishes [the mind] and then again manifests signs to cause others to marvel, how can there be true extinction?

One who truly sits in meditation approaches the Buddha-wisdom; accordingly, they enter the nine kinds of great dhyānas as well as all the various dhyānas attained by the two vehicles, even entering the inconceivable and the inconceivable extinction-samādhi at will. They need not avoid clamor.
Sitting quietly and upright, one collects the mind to manifest signs so that beings may see, hear, know, and perceive;

this is precisely what it means to manifest body and mind without being within the three realms. Therefore, the latter part of this sutra says: "Practicing dhyāna while remaining amidst desires, causing the minds of Māras to become confused and disordered.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva knows that all sentient beings are the very mark of nirvāṇa and cannot be [further]...
Regarding "extinction," the *Siddhārthabuddhi-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states: "All sentient beings are within the samādhi of extinction; I, too, am precisely the samādhi of extinction.
How could there be a samādhi to be sought elsewhere apart from this? This is called attaining the Buddha-wisdom by realizing that all things are themselves the samādhi of extinction.
Not straightening the body is called the non-manifestation of the body; not directing the thoughts is called the non-manifestation of the mind. Thus, both body and mind are non-manifesting.

Being in the same world, one does not conflict with the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*); although one enters this absorption of cessation, it does not hinder one’s dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*).

Since there is no fault of mental movement regarding entering or emerging from concentration, and one is further freed from the error of manifesting signs within the triple world (*tridhātu*), such entry into concentration is true *pratisaṃlayana*.

Furthermore, once a Dharma-body Bodhisattva has received the body of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-kāya*) and departed from the triple world, they abide within that body of the nature of phenomena.
To enter the various meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) while not manifesting body or mind within the triple world (*tridhātu*)—this is true "sitting in meditation" (*pratisaṃlayana*).

If one discusses this from the perspective of ultimate principle, all sentient beings in the triple world are already in the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), for Śāriputra himself was unaware of this.

However, if explained according to conventional phenomena, within the *dharmatā-kāya* of the supreme meditative absorption, there is definitively no body belonging to the triple world; yet even Śāriputra still possessed such a body.
Since one cannot truly be said to be seated in meditative repose while possessing a body and mind within the three realms, he remained silent.

This point is similar to when Śāriputra answered the novice Sūtaśaya, who asked: "Can one enter the attainment of cessation in the realm of form? Śāriputra replied: "The World-Honored One has taught that one cannot enter the attainment of cessation in the realm of form.
Because of this doubt, the novice came to the Buddha’s presence to inquire about it. The Buddha replied: "If [one were to enter it] in the realm of desire..."

"One who has previously cultivated the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) obtains the form (*rūpa*) of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) upon entering it; one who has not previously cultivated it in the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*) cannot enter the attainment.
You, a mere small bird, how can you contend with and revile the great dragons and garuḍas?

Now, by this, it is made clear that Śāriputra did not know that there is a body outside the realms that can enter the attainment of cessation; this was also the fault of the śrāmaṇera, who remained silent here."
This passage criticizes Śāriputra for not knowing the true essence of *pratisaṃlayanā* (seated meditation) and demonstrates that true essence.

If one cultivates the three contemplations within a single mind, this constitutes training toward the Buddha-wisdom and giving rise to the six kinds of *pratisaṃlayanā*. This can be deeply understood through reflection;
there is no need for a detailed, point-by-point correspondence here.
To manifest various dignified postures without arising from the meditative concentration of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is true "sitting in meditation.

This passage demonstrates an inconceivable and supreme function; by stating that one manifests various dignified postures without arising from the concentration of cessation, it satirizes those who enter the concentration of cessation as being useless, for Śrāvakas enter such concentrations only because they have formed a mental intention to emerge from them at a specific time.

When entering into meditative absorption (*samādhi*), one cannot manifest the four dignified postures (*īryāpatha*). For example, when Kāśyapa entered absorption, he was unable to perform his own daily duties;
it was only after Maitreya arose from his concentration that the eighteen transformations were manifested.

Thus we know that when those of the Two Vehicles enter absorption, they have no utility for themselves and provide no benefit to others; as worldly people say, "This object is useless, so discard it."
If the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) of the two vehicles were useless, they would likewise lack substance, as they are merely concentrations of cessation that can be conceptualized;
therefore, they are disparaged as being unnecessary. Now, because the inconceivable concentration of the Mahāyāna is useful, it possesses substance.

Thus, by means of the Bodhisattva’s inclination toward the Buddha-wisdom, one enters the inconceivable concentration and is able to manifest [the world] without arising from the concentration of cessation.
The majestic deportment of the ten dharma realms is like the lute of an asura, which follows the melodic tones produced by others;

when a bodhisattva emerges from the extinction samādhi, they can manifest all manner of majestic deportments according to the capacities of sentient beings. While entering meditative absorption here, they manifest their forms throughout the ten directions;
while sitting in repose elsewhere, they walk and stand in this place. Since you śrāvakas have entered meditative absorption and made such a formal commitment, why do you not likewise take a vow?

The vow to permeate meditative concentration so that the karmic responses of sentient beings do not arise, yet to manifest various dignified demeanors within this concentration, stems precisely from not seeing the inconceivable true nature.

Because of the absence of the *praṇidhāna-pāramitā* (perfection of aspiration), one cannot manifest the four dignified demeanors across the ten dharma-realms within the cessation concentration (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
Since this concentration is useless, it is not valued by beings; therefore, it was previously criticized.
It is not necessary. Furthermore, when the Dharma-body enters meditative concentration, it is not like this:

although it lacks a body subject to birth and death within the three realms, the Dharma-nature body—by proceeding toward Buddha-wisdom and entering various dhyānas and inconceivable cessation-concentrations (*nirodha-samāpatti*)—is able to manifest the ten dharma-realms and the four modes of deportment within the three realms, such that there is no phenomenon whatsoever that it does not demonstrate.
This is what is called the inconceivable, ultimate, and true meditative seclusion (*pratisaṃlayanā*).
To manifest the affairs of an ordinary person without abandoning the dharmas of the Path—this is meditative seclusion.
This is the second [point], which, by means of a pair concerning the mind and the dharmas, rebukes the clumsiness of that mind and those dharmas, asserting that it is not true meditative seclusion.
Therefore, the previous reproach stated that this was not necessarily so; the text contains two points: first, a reproach based on the Dharma.

If Śāriputra were to emerge from the truth and enter into the mundane world, he would then be able to conform to the movements and conduct of ordinary beings. If he did not relinquish the various *dhyānas* and the *nirodha-samāpatti*, how could he expect to emerge from meditative absorption?
One should know that this would mean abandoning the dharmas of the Path and becoming identical to the dharmas of ordinary beings; thus, he would be an ordinary person.

Regarding the noble Dharma, there are two things that must not be abandoned. It is not so for the Bodhisattva; because they aspire to the wisdom of the Buddha, they know that the ordinary and the Buddha-Dharma are non-dual and without distinction.
How could one abandon the path of the Dharma to further enter the path of the Dharma?
This is precisely to practice within what is not the path in order to penetrate the Buddha-path. If one cannot penetrate through what is not the path, how can one be called [a practitioner]?

For the sake of the Way, the Bodhisattva must first attain the wisdom of the Buddha before being able to not abandon the dharmas of the Way while manifesting the affairs of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
"Dharmas of the Way" refers to the practice of wisdom and the practice of the path as elucidated in the Four Teachings.

"Affairs of an ordinary person" refers to the unwholesome matters of the three karmas, the wholesome matters of the three karmas, the matters of the three unwholesome roots, and the matters of the three wholesome roots.

Regarding "matters" (*vastu*): it is as previously praised concerning Vimalakīrti, such as the twenty-nine matters of immeasurable skillful means, including how he "though appearing as a layman, upholds the pure monastic discipline of a *śramaṇa*," and so forth. Regarding "matters":

the *dharmakāya* eternally abides in *samādhi*, yet without abandoning any of the practices of the Path, it manifests throughout the three realms, universally conforming to all ordinary things; and within that ordinary body...
Having attained mastery of the Buddha-way and entered the King Samādhi, all other samādhis are entirely contained within it;
yet he does not abandon such dharmas of the path, manifesting the affairs of ordinary people to lead sentient beings into the inconceivable liberation of the Buddha’s pure land.
This is precisely the ultimate, true sitting in meditation. It is with this that he ridicules the clumsiness of their [the practitioners'] dharmas.
Therefore, he previously rebuked him, saying it was unnecessary.
"The mind does not dwell within, nor does it dwell without; this is called sitting in meditation.
This [passage] concerns the mind and rebukes it, stating that the mind neither dwells within nor dwells without. This refers to Śāriputra and—
When followers of the Two Vehicles enter meditative concentration (*samādhi*), their minds abide within; when they emerge and possess a distracted mind, they abide in external objects.

When practicing the dhyāna of contemplating principles, the mind abides within; when practicing the dhyāna of contemplating purity, the mind abides without. When entering the cessation of perception and feeling (*nirodhasamāpatti*)—a state resembling *nirvāṇa*—the mind abides within;
when emerging from the cessation of perception and feeling, the mind abides without. Thus, the mind depends on the internal and external as it enters and emerges.
What is called "tranquil stillness" (*yanji*) if it is subject to the faults of agitation and dispersion? Therefore, the previous censure stated that it is not necessary [to seek it elsewhere].

Now, the Bodhisattva, by means of the wisdom directed toward Buddhahood, contemplates the Middle Way and the *dharmatā*; even *nirvāṇa* and *saṃsāra* are not perceived. Where could the internal or external mind abide?

Since all phenomena have ceased, within both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and emergence from it, as well as within agitation and dispersion, where could the internal or external mind abide? It has no place to be.
If there are two extremes, there is agitation and distraction, and thus it is not true *pratisaṃlayanā* (seated meditation). Therefore, it is said that a Bodhisattva need not [act in such a way];

rather, by darkening the mind within the *dharmatā*, one is neither distracted nor attached. When the mind is free from agitation and distraction, this is the inconceivable, ultimate, and true *pratisaṃlayanā*.
This passage criticizes the clumsiness of having the mind dwell upon a support, which is not true *pratisaṃlayanā*.
To practice the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment without being moved by any views is to sit in meditation.
This third pair, concerning the dharma of cause and effect, demonstrates true sitting in meditation and rejects that which is not true sitting in meditation.
Furthermore, "stillness" constitutes two aspects. What is now called "being unmoved by various views" is a critique of their deviance;

it is not true *pratisaṃlayanā* (secluded meditation). Being unmoved by various views is itself the cause of true *pratisaṃlayanā*. Now, based on this, one should analyze it through four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*):
there are those who are moved by views yet do not cultivate the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; there are those who [are unmoved] regarding views... [and so forth].
Neither being unmoving nor practicing the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, one may naturally be moved by various views while practicing the thirty-seven factors;
or, naturally being unmoved by various views, one may practice the path-factors (*mārga-aṅga*).

If one is moved by various views yet does not practice the path-factors, this is like the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) who cling to the view of existence, or even abandon existence to grasp at non-existence.
The sixty-two views, being neither existent nor non-existent, are like avoiding empty space;
yet though they may abandon all views in their desire to attain *nirvāṇa*, they do not know how to cultivate the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.

Therefore, in the *Subhadra Sūtra*, the Buddha let out a lion’s roar, declaring that because they lack the Eightfold Noble Path, they certainly cannot possess the four fruits of the *śramaṇa*. Regarding all [these views]...
Regarding those who hold views yet do not cultivate the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment: these are outsiders who give rise to views;

if they claim that their own position is true and all else is false, they cling to them with unyielding fixity, like grasping at empty space, and they likewise do not know how to cultivate the path-factors.
Regarding those who are moved by various views yet practice the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment: these are the followers of the Two Vehicles within the Tripiṭaka Teaching.

When one arises with the four views, one immediately knows that these are the two views of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), which are defiled causes and conditions for the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).

Because they are impermanent and fluctuating, they are called "movement within views. One who cultivates the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśadbodhipākṣikadharma*) contemplates these two views of self-identity and extremes;

through the four applications of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*) regarding the five aggregates, one destroys the four inversions (*viparyāsa*) and gives rise to the four right efforts (*catvāri samyakprahāṇāni*), the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), and so forth.

Because the powers (*bala*), the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and the path-factors (*mārgāṅga*) constitute the stages of *ūṣmagata*, *mūrdhan*, *kṣānti*, and the entry into the dharma-sphere, as well as the vision of the outflows-free (*anāsrava*) state, they are called the "cultivation of the thirty-seven factors.
Thus, the Mahāyāna Sūtra says: "Regarding those who contemplate the stage of *ūṣmagata*, there are seventy-three people; among my disciples there are such, but among the outsiders there are none.
This applies equally to Śāriputra and all those of the two vehicles. Cultivating the thirty-seven factors in this manner constitutes *samādhi* through quiet sitting (*yañsǎ*).

Therefore, he rebukes him, saying that it is not necessarily so. A bodhisattva who cultivates the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment while remaining unmoved by various views knows that the sixty-two views are themselves bodhi;

because they neither grasp nor reject them, it is said that one who cultivates the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment while remaining unmoved by various views observes the two views of self-identity and extremes as defiling the five [aggregates].
When practicing the four foundations of mindfulness in private: observing that the nature of form is neither defiled nor pure is the foundation of mindfulness of the body;

observing that the nature of sensation is neither suffering nor pleasure is the foundation of mindfulness of sensation; observing that the nature of mind is neither permanent nor impermanent is the practice of the foundation of mindfulness of mind;
and observing that the nature of the two aggregates of perception and formations is neither self nor non-self is the practice of the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena.
This is the distinct contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness. As the *Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:

"The dharma-nature of form, the dharma-nature of sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—the Bodhisattva, by inclining toward the wisdom of the Buddha, contemplates the dharma-nature of form as neither defiled nor pure;
this is the ultimate contemplation of purity. Contemplating the dharma-nature of sensation as neither suffering nor pleasure is Great Nirvāṇa. Contemplating the mind as..."

That which is eternally neither impermanent nor permanent is the Dharmakāya’s true permanence. Contemplating that the two aggregates of perception (*saṃjñā*) and mental formations (*saṃskāra*) are neither self nor non-self constitutes the eight masteries of the self.
This is the cultivation of all modes [of knowledge].

The four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), and the diligent exertion therein constitute the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*). Entering meditative concentration with tranquility constitutes the four bases of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*).

The fulfillment of these five kinds of dharmas is precisely the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) in their superior function of advancement; the warding off of all afflictions is the five powers (*pañcabala*).
Once power is established, the ability to discern, harmonize, and balance meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) constitutes the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*).

To perceive the Middle Way and the principle of Buddha-nature, and to proceed along the path with tranquil security, is the Eightfold Noble Path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*). This is the inconceivable ultimate.

This is true *pratisaṃlayanā* (seated meditation). This [previous statement] was a critique of the clumsiness of practicing the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment while being moved by various views.
"To enter *nirvāṇa* without severing the afflictions (*kleśa*)—this is *pratisaṃlayanā*."
This explains true *samādhi-sitting* by way of its fruit, censuring Śāriputra’s deviation in taking the fruit of the extinction-attainment (*nirodha-samāpatti*) as the goal of the two vehicles.
When Śāriputra first met Aśvajit and attained the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*), he severed the delusions of view;

within seven days, he entered the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) and exhausted the five lower-tier fetters (*pañcāvara-bhāgīya-saṃyojana*), the five upper-tier fetters (*pañcordhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*), and all the active afflictions (*anuśaya*) of the three realms. This is what is meant [by the fruit].

If one cuts off afflictions and enters *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, such that when this retributive body perishes, both body and wisdom are exhausted, this is equivalent to entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* by cutting off afflictions.
This also consists of four propositions: first, neither cutting off nor entering, which refers to ordinary beings and the *śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha* bodhisattvas of the Tripitaka;
second, cutting off and entering, which refers to those of the Two Vehicles who have attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
Furthermore, there are three types of bodhisattvas: those of the Separate Teaching (Pratyekabuddha-yāna), who sever [the afflictions] but do not enter [nirvāṇa];

those of the Shared Teaching (Śrāvaka-yāna), who sever them and do enter; and those of the Perfect Teaching (Ekayāna), who do not sever them and yet enter. Therefore, the very nature of lust, anger, and ignorance is itself liberation.
All sentient beings are the very mark of nirvāṇa and cannot be further extinguished. If the dharmic nature of greed, hatred, and ignorance fully possesses all the Buddhas...
The Dharma is such that afflictions are not to be severed; this means that without severing ignorance and craving, one gives rise to clarity and liberation.

If Śāriputra and those of the two vehicles sever their delusions to enter nirvāṇa, it is like breaking through a wall to escape, yet fearing the cycle of birth and death, they cannot employ afflictions to perform the work of a Buddha.
If a bodhisattva proceeds toward the wisdom of a Buddha, [they do not act thus].
Having severed [the afflictions], one enters [nirvāṇa] like a person who has attained supernatural powers (abhijñā) passing through a wall without the wall being able to obstruct them.
This means that one still employs the afflictions themselves as the work of a Buddha; this is called "entering nirvāṇa without severing the afflictions.
According to another interpretation, because the afflictions are themselves emptiness, there is no need to sever them. If that were so, Mount Sumeru could enter a mustard seed.

At that time, there would be no mustard seed into which it could enter. If one says that the mustard seed is empty, then ultimately it is Mount Sumeru that enters the emptiness, not the mustard seed entering its own existence;

such would be the error. If one contemplates the nature of afflictions (*kleśa*) and finds it remains entirely unbroken, yet is able to enter *nirvāṇa* without moving, then the nature of the mustard seed is neither large nor small; being small does not obstruct the large, for it is capable of containing Mount Sumeru.
The nature of this Great Sumeru is neither large nor small; the large does not obstruct the small, for it can enter the smallness of a mustard seed.
Although it is said that it enters, its original location remains unmoved; although it is said that it does not enter, it truly enters the mustard seed—this is inconceivable.
The principle of entering nirvana without severing the afflictions is identical to this: this is true sitting in meditation, which rebukes Śāriputra’s notion of severance.
It is not necessary to enter into what is not true *pratisaṃlayanā* (secluded meditation).
If one can sit in this manner, it is approved by the Buddha.
This is the third point establishing the meaning of true *pratisaṃlayanā*. If Śāriputra can thus proceed toward the wisdom of the Buddha, he will achieve it.
These six kinds of sitting in seclusion constitute ultimate sitting in seclusion; they are what has been certified by the Buddha.

How could one dare to criticize them, saying they are not necessary? It is simply because Śāriputra was unable to sit in seclusion in this manner within the forest, but instead relied on the four teachings for the withered [trees], and thus [the Buddha] previously criticized him, saying it was unnecessary.
"At that time, World-Honored One, having heard these words, I remained silent and ceased speaking, unable to offer a reply; therefore, I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness.
This is the third instance where Śāriputra concludes his speech by stating his inability [to respond]. "Hearing these words and remaining silent" does not mean he did not understand them.
The characteristics of the Dharma raise six points to rebuke and contrast them with the intended meaning, showing that they are not necessarily required.
Not understanding these matters is like being deaf; being unable to provide a response is like being mute—it is not that one lacks ears or a tongue.
Since there are such instances of failing to comprehend, how could one be fit to transmit the instructions and go there to inquire? Therefore, I am not qualified to visit him.

Question: If one adopts this standard for inquiring after illness, how does it differ from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, which clarifies that the śrāvakas sitting in the assembly were like the deaf and the mute?

From the perspective of principle, this approach refutes the wisdom and karmic activities of the two vehicles’ stage of no-more-learning, leading them into inconceivable liberation and causing them to be born in the Pure Land of fruition;
furthermore, it also becomes a cause for purifying a Buddha-land. Question.
It is asked: Śāriputra rebuked [Maudgalyāyana] by means of the category of wisdom (*prajñā*), being foremost in wisdom yet employing meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to do so;

Maudgalyāyana rebuked [Śāriputra] by means of the category of concentration, being foremost in dhyāna-concentration and the supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāda*) yet employing the wisdom of preaching the Dharma to do so.

What is the meaning of this? The answer is: A sutra states, "There is no wisdom apart from dhyāna, and no dhyāna apart from wisdom. Master Yuan (Daoyuan) wrote in the preface to the *Chanjing* (Dhyāna Sutra): "Without dhyāna there is no wisdom; without wisdom there is no dhyāna. This is the intent.
It is said that without wisdom, meditation cannot deepen its stillness; without meditation, wisdom cannot exhaust its illumination.
If Śāriputra possessed profound meditation, he would have attained great wisdom; since meditation is not remote from wisdom, wisdom likewise does not extend beyond it.

Therefore, he used meditation to rebuke [the Buddha], yet as this sutra later shows, one approaches the Buddha’s wisdom by means of "sitting in quietude" (*yañzan*); since he did not rely upon the Buddha’s wisdom, [his practice was incomplete].
As for his sitting in meditative seclusion amidst those four splendors, his intention lay in this:

if Maudgalyāyana had deeply cultivated dhyāna-concentration and attained supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), how could it be that his powers failed him when he preached the Dharma according to his own inclinations rather than in accordance with the faculties and conditions of his listeners?

Since his preaching was erroneous, one should know that his concentration was shallow and his supernormal powers lacked discernment; thus, his purpose in going there to reprimand him through his concentration lay in this.
Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra, Scroll Eleven;
Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra, Scroll Twelve (The Chapter of the Disciples, Part Two).
The Buddha addressed Mahāmaudgalyāyana: "Go to Vimalakīrti and inquire after his illness."
This section consists of two parts: first, the Buddha’s command for Mahāmaudgalyāyana to inquire after his illness;
second, Maudgalyāyana’s respectful refusal on the grounds of his own incapacity. As for why the Buddha commanded Mahāmaudgalyāyana:

since Śāriputra had already declined on the grounds of incapacity, and because Maudgalyāyana was foremost in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), the Buddha commanded him next. "Mahāmaudgalyāyana" is his family name; it is originally... [text ends].
His original name was Kolita; because his parents had no children, they requested [a son] from a *kolita* tree and named him after it.
Furthermore, in the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa* (The Scripture on Inquiring After Illness), Maudgalyāyana is translated as "radish" (*laifuken*);
his father liked to eat this food, and thus the child was named after it. In Paramārtha’s Tripiṭaka Master’s translation of the *Aṣṭādaśanikāya-śāstra*, it is translated as "hú."
Beans were the preferred food of the immortals of antiquity; they subsequently adopted this as their clan name.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana was the son of a high minister; not only was his lineage noble, but his wisdom and virtue were also profound.

Śāriputra became his friend precisely because he was so highly esteemed and possessed such virtue. The karmic conditions for his renunciation of the world alongside Śāriputra have already been briefly related above.
It is clear that because Maudgalyāyana studied according to the sequence of meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), he became foremost in *dhyāna-samādhi* and supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāda*).
All those among the fourfold assembly who delighted in *dhyāna-samādhi*, supernatural faculties, and entering the Path took him as their teacher and sought deeply into his ultimate aim.
Maudgalyāyana led them into the Path through the dharma-gate of the sequence of meditative absorptions; this precisely manifests the "four kinds of withered meditation" (*caturvidha-śuṣka-dhyāna*).

Although he was one who practiced the teachings of meditative concentration, he was rebuked by Vimalakīrti in order to cause him to abandon the "four types of withered learning" and to despise the small while aspiring toward the Great.
Now, when the Tathāgata commands Maudgalyāyana to inquire after his illness, if Maudgalyāyana recounts the events of his past rebuke,
the meaning of the "four types of flourishing" will gradually become manifest, thereby fulfilling the significance of the five kinds of benefits.
Maudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, I am not fit to go there to inquire after his illness.
This second submission of inability to go contains four points in its text: first, the formal submission of inability;
second, the explanation of the reasons for this inability; third, the detailed account of the reprimand he received; and fourth, the conclusion regarding his previous life as a householder.

When my preaching of the Dharma was subsequently rebuked by Vimalakīrti, I did not know how to respond at that time; how, then, could I have been fit to transmit the intent of the Tathāgata? Why is this so?
I recall that in the past, when I entered the great city of Vaiśālī, while among the lanes and alleys for the sake of various [beings]...
The layperson (*gṛhapati*) preaches the Dharma.
This is the second reason for being incapable [of attaining realization], namely, preaching the Dharma to a layperson in the lanes and alleys.
"Lanes and alleys" refers merely to the narrow, winding paths of village neighborhoods; alternatively, it may symbolize the principle of being severed by ditches and passages.
It is not the Great Straight Path. As for those who preach the Dharma to the laypeople (*gṛhapati*), these laypeople are precisely the eight hundred wealthy householders.
Regarding those who preach the Dharma, there are teachers who explain it as having words; they preach the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions as dharmas with characteristics (*sanimitta*).
I fear this is not so, for the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions belong to the vehicle of humans and devas (*manuṣya-deva-yāna*), and are not [the Mahāyāna].
The teaching on entering the Way through the principles of the Truths is now clearly explained;

for the most part, these refer to the intent of entering the Way in the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) by analyzing phenomena to enter emptiness according to the gates of the Tripitaka teachings. How is this known? By comparing it with what precedes and follows, all the reproaches directed at the śrāvakas are made in contrast between the "half" and the "full.
Furthermore, if one examines the text of the reproach itself, it must be so.
At that time, Vimalakīrti came and said to me, "O Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when preaching the Dharma to lay householders, you ought not to preach as you have just done.
This is the third account of being rebuked in the past; regarding this passage, there are three points, the first of which is a general summary.
[Section on] Rebuking (2): A Specific Rebuke (3). The Layman hears the Dharma and gains benefit (1). First, the general rebuke:

"One should not speak as you, Venerable Sir, have said. This is the general rebuke. The use of different characters for "inappropriate" (*bùdāng*) also indicates that it is inappropriate according to the characteristics of the Dharma and its underlying conditions.
Now, to clarify the general rebuke, there are three types of what is inappropriate. The first rebuke concerns Maudgalyāyana.

Regarding the four points of what is inappropriate: first, it is inappropriate for the Dharma-characteristics; second, it is inappropriate for the faculties and conditions; third, it is inappropriate for the Buddha-mind;

and fourth, it is inappropriate for the Dharma-characteristics themselves. First, regarding being inappropriate for the Dharma-characteristics: since Dharma-characteristics are themselves empty, how can one speak of "entering emptiness by breaking down and analyzing ditches and alleys"?

This deviates from the Dharma-characteristics and is therefore inappropriate according to principle. Second, regarding being inappropriate for the faculties and conditions: the person before you possesses the faculties and conditions for the Mahāyāna and must be taught [the Mahāyāna].
Regarding the Mahāyāna Dharma, it is like placing foul food in a precious vessel; not only does one fail to attain the Great Way, but one also loses minor benefits.
This is what is meant by "not being appropriate for the faculties and conditions. Third, regarding "not conforming to the Buddha’s intention":

the Buddha’s original intention was for the great causal conditions [of the Mahāyāna], but because sentient beings could not endure such matters, he had no choice but to receive them with the Small Vehicle. Now that there is the Great [Vehicle]...

The capacity [of the listener] should immediately prompt the teaching of the Great [Vehicle]; this is the Buddha’s fundamental intention. Why, then, suddenly use the Small Vehicle to transform those with great faculties?
This does not accord with the Buddha’s mind. Thus, there are three kinds of "inappropriateness" (*abhabba*);

by summarizing these three meanings to censure [the teaching], it is said that it is "inappropriate," as in what you have said, O Venerable One. However, although Maudgalyāyana was foremost in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), he spoke only in brief.

The reason for the "Dharma-rebuke" (*dharmotsarga*) is precisely that one's power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) is shallow and one's vision of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) is not clear.

It is like water that has not yet become limpid, wherein the reflection of a pearl does not appear; or like a minor concentration (*kṣudra-samādhi*), where the observation of another person's faculties (*indriya*)—whether sharp or dull—is not clear, resulting in the failure to grasp the capacity of the listener.
To rebuke the shallowness of the Dharma-exposition is to rebuke the insufficiency of one's meditative concentration.
This meaning is fully analyzed and examined in the chapter on Śāriputra.
Now, one who preaches the Dharma should preach it in accordance with the Dharma.
From this point onward is the second section, the specific reprimand, which contains three points; that is, the application of the Mahāyāna.
The three teachings are distinct; this refutes Maudgalyāyana’s three points of impropriety. Herein are three pairs:

first, externally explaining according to the characteristics of dharmas and internally understanding according to the characteristics of dharmas—this is the Mahāyāna teaching of universal penetration (*tongjiao*).
By [explaining] emptiness and thereby rejecting non-emptiness, it refutes Maudgalyāyana’s unreasonableness in his exposition of the Dharma. Second, the pair: externally one should realize...

To know and see that one’s faculties and conditions are internal and wholesome, thereby attaining freedom from obstruction, is to employ the Mahāyāna of the Separate Teaching (Pṛthagvidha-yāna) to refute Maudgalyāyana’s teaching that [the Dharma] does not accord with faculties and conditions and thus fails to attain the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid). As for the third pair:

to externally show compassion for sentient beings while inwardly mindful of repaying the Buddha’s grace is to employ the Mahāyāna of the Perfect Teaching (Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra) to refute Maudgalyāyana’s teaching.

His intentions were not in accord with the Buddha’s mind. A Bodhisattva can employ these three teachings of the Mahāyāna to preach the Dharma, which is precisely preaching in accordance with the Dharma.
Maudgalyāyana was unable to use these three teachings of the Mahāyāna to preach the Dharma for the lay devotees;
therefore, he now refutes the errors of his exposition of the Tripiṭaka teaching, so that they may rely upon the Mahāyāna as it truly is.
Regarding the exposition of the characteristics of the Dharma, we shall now proceed with the first exhortation: "One should explain according to the Dharma. This passage contains two meanings:

first, it correctly clarifies that one should explain according to the Dharma; second, it clarifies that one should interpret according to the Dharma. Now, regarding the section on explaining according to the Dharma, there are three points:
first, the heading that provides a general exhortation; second, the detailed explanation; and third, the conclusion. The Sūtra says: "Now..."

The one who preaches the Dharma should preach it in accordance with the Dharma; this is the heading that provides a general exhortation, urging that one preach in accordance with the Dharma as clarified in the Mahāyāna teachings regarding the three kinds of emptiness of the essential nature of phenomena (*dharmasvabhāva*).
“Dharmas have no sentient beings, because they are free from the defilements of sentient beings.
