Seeing forms through the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*) is precisely what constitutes the true divine eye. As the Sūtra says: "Constantly abiding in samādhi, one sees all Buddha-lands."
Not perceiving through dualistic marks—this is the second characteristic of the true divine eye.
As for what is called "always abiding in samādhi," it means always abiding in the King Samādhi, as well as the Śūraṅgama and other various samādhis;
it is also to always abide in the Great Parinirvāṇa, the eternal tranquil concentration, and the deep cave of dhyāna-concentration. This is such that all sentient beings...
The characteristics of the *nirodhasamāpatti* (attainment of cessation) do not arise in this samādhi. The Sūtra states that "seeing all Buddha-lands" means seeing them as eternally quiescent;
it is like a bright mirror that does not move or pure water that has no waves, wherein all myriad forms naturally appear.
The Sūtra states that "one does not rely on dualistic marks" means not producing conditioned marks, unlike the Brahma Kings, non-Buddhists, or Śrāvakas who possess conditioned phenomena.
The manifestation of signs refers to the divine eye supernormal power (*divyacakṣur-abhijñā*);
it is not the signless state, nor is it the signless state of the unconditioned, partial truth attained by the Two Vehicles, wherein there is a profound lack of vision.

Furthermore, "not by means of two signs" means that the true divine eye of the Middle Way is not the dual signs of the two truths—conventional and ultimate—but rather, by transcending these two signs, it is able to illuminate everywhere.
The four kinds of Buddha-lands, the three types of sentient beings, their deaths and rebirths, and both the primary and secondary retributions all appear within the King Samādhi;
this is precisely the True Heavenly Eye. Question: These two types of True Heavenly Eyes are elucidated in the Four Teachings;

under which teaching are they subsumed? Answer: If it is neither partial nor complete, but perceives both the partial and the complete simultaneously, it is the Complete Teaching (the Perfect Teaching).

Regarding the teaching on the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), it was asked: "If the divine eye attained by the Buddha through the path of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*) is called the 'true divine eye,' then by what other name is the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*) designated? The answer was:

"Now, when one takes the seeing of the Middle Way as the basis for the arising of the divine eye—seeing the coarse and subtle forms of the lands of the ten directions and the dharma-realm of the ten directions—that is the divine eye. As for the Buddha-eye..."
This treatise establishes the perfect vision of the Dharma-realm of the three truths; when analyzed according to their respective meanings, there is no confusion or error.
How much more so is this the case for the five eyes, such as the divine eye, which remain perfectly distinct from one another?
As clarified in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, the Tathāgata possesses the fleshly eye up to the Buddha-eye; this meaning should be fully distinguished, setting aside other matters.
Having deeply grasped this meaning, what hindrance could the divine eye pose to the four eyes?
Thereupon, the Brahma King Śuddhāvāsa and his retinue of five hundred Brahmās all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
after prostrating at the feet of Vimalakīrti, they suddenly vanished.
This is the fifth section, clarifying the passage on the Brahma King’s generation of the bodhicitta. It consists of two parts:

first, the actual clarification that the Brahma King and his retinue all generated the bodhicitta; second, the clarification of their paying respects and departing. Regarding the first part, concerning the Brahma King and those Brahmās who generated the mind:
although they had previously heard what the Nāga [Vinaya] Master taught, they did not yet discern the principle of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, because they lack the ability to universally perceive all Buddha-lands, they cannot cause the Brahmās to develop deep faith and resolve for Bodhicitta.

However, when the true reality of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) clarified by the Mahāsattva is revealed—vastly exceeding the scope of their own divine eyes and in accordance with the Mahāyāna faculties and conditions of the Brahmās—they all resolve for Bodhicitta.
This is according to the Perfect Teaching (*Vipula-yāna*).
If the aspiration is generated in a semblance manner, it constitutes entry into the stage of the ten faiths of the Iron Wheel;

if it is a genuine generation of the aspiration, it constitutes entry into the first abode of the Copper Wheel. The second [section], on repaying kindness and paying respect, is not manifested, as per the text.
Therefore, I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness.

This is the fourth reason for my inability; Ānanda reflects upon himself that in the past, when he was a Brahmā King, he preached the divine eye, yet was rebuked by the Great Being and did not know how to respond—how could I possibly bear to carry out the Tathāgata’s command to go and inquire after his illness?
Thus ends the fourteenth fascicle of the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra-bhāṣya*.
Fascicle Fifteen of the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra-bhāṣya* (The Fifth Part of the Chapter on Disciples).
The Buddha said to Upāli, "Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness.
This is the eighth instance of the Buddha commanding Upāli; the text also contains two parts:
first, the Buddha’s command to inquire after his illness, and second, Upāli’s respectful refusal on the grounds that he is incapable. The reason the Buddha commanded Upāli next was because...
Among the śrāvaka disciples, Upāli was foremost in upholding the Vinaya; "Upāli" is translated here as "Foremost" (or "Head"), and in another sense as "Transformation-Born.
This person feared that [beings] might enter the Path through the counting of thoughts.

The reason for this is that within the two piṭakas of the Tripiṭaka teachings—the Sūtra and Abhidharma—there are some teachings spoken by the Buddha himself, while others were spoken by his disciples.
Whether it be teachings given by emanations, devas, or rishis according to their capacities, once they are authorized by the Buddha, they constitute Sūtra.
As for the Vinaya precepts, each and every one was established by the Buddha himself; they serve to maintain the True Dharma and constitute his inner retinue.
One must contemplate and uphold these so as not to forget them. If the power of mindfulness is strong, there will be no [forgetting].

Furthermore, regarding omissions: if one upholds the precepts and wields the Vinaya without focused mindfulness and clear discernment of what is light and what is grave, then many transgressions will occur and one's actions will be deviant and erroneous.
Therefore, the Buddha taught the bhikṣus to constantly cultivate the six recollections at dawn;

if the power of mindfulness is strong, one will not forget and no transgressions will occur, ensuring that one's actions are free from error. Thus, one attains the highest mastery in upholding the Vinaya.
Furthermore, Upāli, wishing to reveal the Tathāgata’s treasury of the Half and Full Precepts,
first uses the four types of withered *vinaya* of the Lesser Vehicle to lead sentient beings into the Buddha’s True Dharma, so that they may uphold the precepts without deficiency,
without breach, without perforation, without admixture, in accordance with the Path, and without attachment; these six kinds of purity are thereby perfected.
The four fruits of the Hīnayāna are the adornment of the four types of austere Vinaya-piṭaka. Next, wishing to manifest the four types of flourishing precepts praised by wisdom—
the precept of mastery, the precept of fulfillment, the precept of accordance with meditative concentration, and the precept of purity through realization—

the Buddha now commands Upāli to inquire after the illness [of Vimalakīrti], so as to use Vimalakīrti’s censure and refutation to cause the fourfold assembly to despise the small and aspire to the great.

If one recounts the matter of being struck by the lute in the past, it further elucidates the Tathāgata’s fourfold treasury of majestic precepts and fulfills the meaning of the five kinds of benefits previously mentioned.
Upāli said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness."
This is the second section, the formal declination of inability, which consists of four parts: (1) the formal declination of inability; (2) the explanation of the reasons for this inability;
(3) the formal narration of the matter for which one was rebuked; and (4) the conclusion establishing the inability. Regarding the first, the formal declination of inability:
it is because in the past, when explaining the characteristics of the Vinaya, my judgments were not clear, and thus I was [reproached by] the Pure [Sangha].
How could one named Hacheqi (Aśvajit) be worthy of transmitting the Tathāgata’s intent?
I recall that in the past, there were two bhikṣus who had violated the disciplinary rules and felt ashamed; they did not dare to ask the Buddha, so they came to question me, saying:
"O Upāli, we have indeed violated the disciplinary rules and feel truly ashamed; we do not dare to ask the Buddha, but pray that you will explain it to us."
Having been freed from the fault of doubt and regret, I then provided them with an explanation according to the Dharma.
This is the second account of the reasons for their incapacity, which consists of two parts: first, the two bhikṣus' violation of the precepts and their subsequent doubts;

second, [the fact that] my explanation of the characteristics of the Vinaya for those two bhikṣus did not accord with reason. The text itself contains two sections: the first concerns the two bhikṣus’ transgression of the precepts and their inquiry. Second... [The text continues].
The first [point] concerns the explanation of the Dharma for one or two bhikṣus who have transgressed the precepts and seek instruction.

Regarding the gravity of the offenses committed by these two bhikṣus, this has not yet been definitively determined. If they were minor offenses, how could it be that they did not dare to ask the Buddha?

If they were grave offenses, there would be no provision for repentance in the Vinaya regarding such heavy crimes; alternatively, perhaps these were merely the preliminary stages (upāya) to a grave offense.
The Master once saw it stated in a sutra: There was a bhikṣu lying down in an araṇya when his organ became erect.

A woman gathering firewood saw him, and her desire being aroused, she committed an act of unrighteousness. The bhikṣu woke up from his sleep and, fearing he had committed a primary pārājika offense, was filled with doubt and fear.
Furthermore, there was another bhikṣu who, out of anger toward this woman, wished to strike her; the woman fled in terror and fell into a pit and died. The bhikṣu [was likewise filled with remorse].
His mind was filled with doubt and fear that he might have violated the precept against taking life;

consequently, out of shame and reverence for the World-Honored One, he did not dare to inquire himself, but instead requested Upāli to resolve his doubts. This clarifies the intent behind the ten great disciples assisting the Tathāgata to propagate the ten dharma-gates.
As the Sūtra says: "I shall then explain it to him according to the Dharma"—this is the second [point].
To "explain clearly" means to explain as clarified in the Vinaya; that is, to explain the various bases of offenses according to the rules, judging their gravity or lightness.
Alternatively, it refers to teaching the procedures for the assembly’s *karmavācanā* (formal acts) to eliminate [offenses], each in accordance with what is clarified in the Vinaya;
therefore, it is said that he "explains in accordance with the Dharma."
At that time, Vimalakīrti came and said to me: "O Upāli, do not further increase the offense of these two bhikṣus.
This is the third [section] correctly describing the matter of being rebuked; the text consists of two parts: first, the correct description of Vimalakīrti’s rebuke;
second, the clarification of how the minds of the two bhikṣus attained purity. Regarding the first, the description of Vimalakīrti’s rebuke:"
The text contains seven points: first, a formal censure; second, an exhortation to directly eliminate [the offense]; third, providing an explanation;

fourth, citing the Buddha’s words as proof; fifth, interrogating Upāli; sixth, entering into the true nature through the three provisional designations (*prajñapti*) to analytically sever and eliminate [the offense];

and seventh, concluding that this constitutes being foremost in upholding the Vinaya. Regarding the first, the formal censure: if one repents according to the principle of the mind, then [the offense] does not exist.

The affairs of the Saṃgha concerning the accumulation of transgressions are complex and their characteristics are manifold; as the Sūtra says, "Do not further increase the offenses of these two bhikṣus.
Since offenses arise from deluded conceptualization (vikalpa), one must eliminate such conceptualization for them.
Upāli forcibly distinguished the characteristics of the offenses for the two bhikṣus, stating which were light and which were heavy; it should be done in this manner.
This method of *karmavācanā* involves engaging with worldly affairs, thereby increasing one's deluded thoughts and discriminations;
because this gives rise to heavy remorse, it obstructs meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*, *dhyāna*), thus further increasing the offenses of the two bhikṣus.
One should directly eliminate it without disturbing the mind.
This is the second point of Pure Name’s exhortation: to directly eliminate it without disturbing the mind.

If one observes the nature of offenses as pure, delusive thoughts will naturally cease; this is what is meant by elimination. By not relying on phenomenal characteristics, the mind becomes non-existent.
The reason why such disturbances arise is that offenses originate from the mind and are extinguished back within the mind. If there is an offense, there is necessarily a mind;
if there is no offense, there is no mind. If one contemplates the mind and finds it ultimately ungraspable, then the characteristics of offense are not seen.
Since the offense cannot be found, it is directly eliminated without disturbing the mind—this is the meaning.

Furthermore, it is now clarified that there are three kinds of repentance through which transgressions are extinguished: first, ritual repentance (*vidhi-pratikramaṇa*), which removes and extinguishes transgressions of the unmanifested precepts;

this is the method of clear repentance according to the Vinaya. Second, repentance by contemplating signs (*nimitta-pratikramaṇa*), which removes and extinguishes natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*);

this is clear repentance according to the gateway of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Third, repentance by contemplating non-arising (*anutpāda-pratikramaṇa*), which removes and extinguishes the root of delusive thoughts.
This fundamental offense is to be repented through the gateway of wisdom. Furthermore, the offense of violating non-manifest action (*avijñapti*) obstructs morality;

the nature-offense (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) obstructs meditative concentration; and the root-offense obstructs wisdom. Through a single method of repentance, these offenses are extinguished. Regarding the extinction of the offense of violating non-manifest action:

as clarified in the Vinaya, there are methods for repenting offenses such as the various *karmans* of discipline (*śikṣāpada*). If one performs this rite, it is accomplished and the offense is extinguished.
Because the transgression of the non-informative (avijñapti) offense does not extinguish the natural offense (prakṛti-sāvadya), the *Mahā-śāstra* states:
"For example, if a bhikṣu cuts down plants or trees and thereby deprives living beings of their lives, these two offenses belong to the same category;

although one may perform the ritual confession (*vidhi-pratideśanā*) to extinguish the transgression of the non-informative offense, the guilt for cutting down plants and the guilt for depriving living beings of their lives are not extinguished. Even though one has transgressed the non-informative offense..."

Regarding the extinction of offenses: this does not merely mean their eradication; for if one engages in ritualistic proliferation and disrupts the practice of dhyāna-concentration, it constitutes an obstruction to entering the state of non-arising (*anutpāda*), which is to disturb the mind.

As for the repentance of the two contemplations (*dvividha-vipaśyanā*), as clarified by the practices taught in the various Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras, one perceives the signs of the extinction of offenses.
The Bodhisattva Precepts state: "In repentance, if one sees light, flowers, or seeds..."
If one perceives auspicious signs (*lakṣaṇa*), the transgression is immediately extinguished; yet if no auspicious signs are seen, even though one performs repentance, there is no benefit.

If auspicious signs are seen, not only is the transgression of non-action (*avijñapti-pāpa*) extinguished, but the transgression of nature (*prakṛti-pāpa*) is also extinguished—though the fundamental transgression (*mūla-pāpa*) is not.
If the mind moves due to grasping at signs, the "water of the mind" will remain turbid; how then could the jewel appear? This, too, is to disturb the mind.

Regarding the third, the Repentance of Non-arising (*anutpāda*): when this contemplation is perfected, it can eliminate the offenses of fundamental delusion, just as when the roots of a tree are pulled out, the branches and leaves wither of their own accord.
The *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-bhadracaryā-praṇidhāna-sūtra* states: "The ocean of all karmic obstructions arises from false conceptualization;
if one wishes to repent, sit upright and contemplate the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), and all offenses will vanish like frost."
The sun of wisdom, when exposed, is able to eliminate [obscurations] without the need for laborious ritual acts or the entanglements of grasping at signs;

this is precisely the meaning of not disturbing the mind. Question: If that is so, why do various sutras state that repentance must involve generating profound shame, remorse, and fear, followed by reform and separation [from faults]?
How can you now say that ritual acts and the grasping of signs are unnecessary? Answer: People... [text fragment]

There are two types: first, those of dull faculties; second, those of sharp faculties. If a person of dull faculties commits a transgression, their mind is heavy [at the time of the act], yet light at the time of repentance.

Because a light mind cannot eliminate a heavy transgression, for such a person, one must cause them to give rise to intense shame, remorse, and fear, and perform the rite of transformation through the method of taking signs. If it is a person of sharp faculties, they directly and correctly contemplate.
The root of the transgressions of the mind’s delusive thoughts is inherently extinguished; when remorse does not arise, one has exhausted the old and does not create the new.
This is precisely to eliminate [transgressions] directly without disturbing the mind. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"If a person can repent for their transgressions, once repented, do not worry further. In this way, the mind is peaceful and happy; one should not constantly dwell upon them, even if they have arisen."

If one repeatedly regrets it, the arrow of remorse enters the heart, causing pain that cannot be extracted; there will be sorrow and suffering in the present life, and after death, one will enter hell.
Furthermore, if one clings to the existence of this transgression, the transgression becomes increasingly heavy; if one does not cling to the transgression, the transgression gradually lightens.
If one can perceive the principle of the nature of phenomena at its root, all transgressions are immediately extinguished. This is called the direct path.
Thus, when it is extinguished, one does not disturb the mind.
Why is this? Because the nature of that offense is neither within, nor without, nor in between.
This is the third explanation. The Sūtra says: "The nature of that offense is neither within, nor without..."
As for those who are in between, the nature of their offenses is fundamentally empty and ultimately non-existent;

although they may create offenses through deluded thoughts, if they contemplate that offenses are empty, they are then offenseless. Why is this so? If offenses were existent, they would possess a fixed nature.
If they possessed a fixed nature, they could not escape three locations: first, the internal, which is one's own mind; second, the external, which is...
Regarding the three external objects, the two intermediate states are precisely the mind and object uniting to produce sin together.
Now, if we examine whether [sin] exists internally, it would mean that self-nature itself is the sin; if that were so, one would always possess sin even before confronting an object.
Yet, as we clearly observe, no sin arises when one has not yet confronted an object. How, then, could it exist within?
If intrinsic nature does not exist within, and one claims that transgression exists without, then "without" refers to objects and others.
Since others are of an external nature, if transgression were inherent in that other-nature, it would belong solely to them; what concern would it have for oneself?
If transgression is not fixed as being either in the internal mind or in external objects, but rather arises when the internal and external combine, then it must be co-arisen.

If guilt arises simultaneously [with the action], there are two faults: namely, the existence of both self-nature and other-nature. If there were such self-nature and other-nature, then these two faults would arise together.
If that were so, then just as when one cuts down grass and trees, the person within would have guilt, the external grass and trees should likewise have guilt.
If you claim that the intermediate space is the knife, then the knife should have guilt, as should the person and the grass and trees.
Both are without fault; one should know that fault does not arise from both together nor exist in the interval between them.

Furthermore, it is explained that fault is not within, for it does not reside in the six internal faculties (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*); it is not without, for it does not reside in the six external objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*);

it is not in the interval between the two, for it does not reside in the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*). If the eighteen realms (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*) are fundamentally empty by nature, then there is no fault.
If the nature itself does not even exist, how could there be sin? Furthermore, sin arises from the mind.
When one contemplates the mind, it is seen that the mind is not self-born, not born of another, and not born of both; thus the mind is neither within, nor without, nor in between the two.
As it is with the mind, so it is with the defilements of sin, and so it is with all phenomena. Therefore, this is the Universal Worthy Contemplation.
The Sūtra says: "Contemplate that the mind is no-mind; dharmas do not abide in dharmas. My own mind is naturally empty, and there is no master of sin or merit.

All dharmas are thus non-abiding and indestructible. To perform repentance in this manner is called the Great Repentance, the Adornment Repentance, the Sinless Repentance, and the Repentance that Destroys the Consciousness. When practicing this repentance, the mind is like...
In every thought-moment, Śrotapāṇi beholds Samantabhadra Bodhisattva and the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Of the two previous interpretations, both are somewhat coarse in their contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) and do not accord with the text of this sutra;

the latter interpretation is precisely what is required and perfectly accords with the words of the Buddha cited by Vimalakīrti below. If one can contemplate in this way, one will perceive the offenses and see the offenses.
That which is "non-arising" refers to the contemplation of non-arising as a repentance; this means to directly eliminate [faults] without disturbing the mind.
One can thus see that Vimalakīrti’s intention in his previous reproaches and challenges was explained by this very point.
As the Buddha has taught: "Because the mind is defiled, sentient beings are defiled; because the mind is pure, sentient beings are pure.
The mind is neither within, nor without, nor in between. As it is with the mind, so it is with the stains of transgression; so it is with all phenomena—they do not transcend suchness."
This is the fourth [section], which cites the Buddha’s own words as evidence to resolve the doubts of Upāli.
The reason for this is that Upāli thought to himself: "The Vinaya was personally spoken by the Buddha’s own mouth; I shall judge according to this—what fault could there be?
Now, why would this Great Being not accept it simply because he cites the Buddha’s words? However, the Buddha’s words are of two kinds.
There are two kinds of speech: first, words of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), and second, words of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*).
How could one cling to words of provisional meaning while failing to accept words of definitive meaning? This was also done to clarify the faith of the two bhikṣus by citing the Buddha’s own words.
If Upāli were to harbor doubts and attachments, thinking that such a judgment contradicts the Buddha’s words, [it would not be so].
In the Buddha’s Vinaya, it is asked: "With what intention did you act? If one acts with a defiled mind, whether the deed is light or heavy, it is entirely a transgression;
how can you say there is no offense? The Great Being then cited the Buddha’s words:

"Because the mind is defiled, sentient beings are defiled. One should know that offenses arise from the mind. If one perceives the mind, then because sentient beings exist and are defiled, [offenses] likewise exist.
If one knows that sin is empty of mind, this is the purity of mind; the purity of mind is the purity of sentient beings; the purity of sentient beings is the absence of sin.
This means that the knowing mind and the known object are both not located within, without, or between the two.
This is the state of no-mind. If there is no mind, one does not even perceive a mind; how, then, could there be defilement? Therefore, the Sūtra speaks of "sin."
The same applies to defilements and likewise to all phenomena; none transcend suchness (*tathatā*).

As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states, when a bodhisattva practices *prajñā*, they do not perceive any phenomenon that exists outside of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); "phenomena" (*dharma*) is simply another name for suchness.
“Upāli, when one attains liberation through the characteristic of the mind, is there still any defilement? “I say, no.
Vimalakīrti said, “The same is true for all sentient beings: the characteristic of their minds is without defilement.”
This is the fifth interrogation, which consists of three parts: first, the question by the Mahāsattva; second, the answer by Upāli;
third, the Mahāsattva’s reaffirmation of those words as being of the same nature as the stainless characteristic of true emptiness. Initially, the sutra states:
"When Upāli attained liberation through the characteristics of the mind, was there any defilement? This question to Upāli analyzes phenomena through contemplation.
"When the mind enters into the partial truth (*tathyatā*), is there still defilement? Upāli replied, "No.
[The Buddha] continued, "By means of the analytical observation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*), when one perceives the truth of the mind, that true mind is devoid of any mark of defilement.
Vimalakīrti said, "The nature of the minds of all sentient beings is likewise free from defilement. This is the manifestation of the three types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*). Mahā...
The Dharma-body of the Mahāyāna teachings clarifies that the mental characteristics of sentient beings are identical to emptiness; within this emptiness, there is likewise no defilement.
O Upāli, it is only deluded thought (*vikalpa*) that is defilement, while the absence of deluded thought is purity. Inversion is defilement, while the absence of inversion is purity.
Grasping at a self is defilement, while not grasping at a self is purity.
This is the sixth section, which clarifies the entry into emptiness by means of the three provisional designations (*prajñapti*) through analytical discernment and elimination.

Regarding the three provisional designations: first, the provisional designation of causal formation; second, the provisional designation of continuity; and third, the provisional designation of relative dependence.

These are the three provisional designations elucidated as the essence within the Mahāyāna, by means of which one enters into emptiness. Therefore, the subsequent text employs analogies such as illusions and dreams to discern the characteristics of these provisional designations.

In this way, even through the provisional (prajñapti), one may enter the perfect reality. This is in contrast to the analysis of the three types of provisional constructs used to enter reality as taught in the Tripiṭaka Teaching.

The reason for this is that the three types of provisional constructs clarified in the Tripiṭaka Teaching employ the provisional constructs according to conventional sentiment (*sāṃvṛti-prajñapti*) to enter reality, whereas the three types of provisional constructs clarified in the Mahāyāna employ the provisional constructs according to principle (*dharmatā-prajñapti*).
Entering the Truth by means of the three provisional [teachings] has already been fully analyzed in the preceding *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) of this sutra;
it shall not be recounted again here. This section, however, distinguishes between the two types of *vinaya* for extinguishing offenses:

Upāli employs the *vinaya* of expedient means that is "clumsy," whereas Vimalakīrti employs the *vinaya* of expedient means that is "skillful. The text consists of three parts: first, the preceding...

1. Clarifying that the substance [of phenomena] enters emptiness through the provisional nature of causal formation; 2. Clarifying that the substance enters emptiness through the provisional nature of continuity; 3.

Clarifying that the substance enters emptiness through the provisional nature of mutual dependence. If one sees that these three types of provisional natures enter emptiness, they are immediately the True and the Middle, and thus there is no aspect of transgression;
this is the Mahāyāna Vinaya, which directly eradicates and extinguishes [offenses]. Regarding the first [section], the text on "causal formation" consists of three parts.
Now, to explain specifically how the conditions of ignorance establish the provisional nature of causes:
Ignorance is precisely the defiled five aggregates, which can constitute a "provisional person" through the establishment of causes; this is the "provisional establishment by causes.

Ignorance is precisely perversion (*viparyāsa*), and perversion does not exceed three types: namely, perversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*), perversion of mind (*citta-viparyāsa*), and perversion of view (*dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa*).
The inversion of these three is precisely ignorance as a causal condition, which can establish the three provisional designations and the three aggregates.
When these three inversions and the three aggregates correspond with the mind-king, there arise all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) and the defilements of transgression.

If one can thoroughly understand that the three inversions do not arise of themselves, nor do they arise from another, nor do they arise from both together, nor are they without cause—this is non-arising; and where there is non-arising, there is no [self].
The cessation of the mind is without fault; this refers to the attainment of the provisional through the cause of the essence, thereby clarifying the elimination of cessation.
The Sūtra says: "Upāli, conceptualization is defilement; the absence of conceptualization is purity. This clarifies that conceptualization is inverted;

inversion is precisely the attainment of the provisional through the cause. Discussing defilement in terms of the provisional, the essence of the provisional is emptiness, and thus conceptualization does not arise.
Because there is no stain of transgression, it is said that the absence of deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is purity. The Sūtra states: "Inversion is defilement;
non-inversion is purity. This clarifies that the mind is inverted. "Inversion" refers to the conventional designation based on causes (*hetu-saṃvṛti*);

it is spoken of as a conventional designation. The substance of this conventionality is itself empty. When inversion does not arise, there is no stain of transgression; therefore, it is called non-inversion.
This is precisely purity. As the Sūtra says: "To grasp at a self is defilement; not grasping at a self is purity.

To grasp at the view of a self is itself the self; this inversion is established as provisional based on causes. Referring to this provisional [self], one speaks of the substance of defilement. Since this provisional [self] is empty, it is "not grasping at a self.
If one does not grasp at a self, then there is no fault or defilement; therefore, it is said that "not grasping at a self is purity."
Furthermore, Upāli, all phenomena arise and perish without abiding, like an illusion and like lightning.
These two clarifications explain the entry into emptiness by means of the conventional continuity of substance; "like an illusion" is a metaphor for this continuity.
Phenomena are merely provisional designations; yet, as long as their continuity persists, there is still fault.

If the nature of this continuity does not arise from itself, nor from another, nor from both together, nor without cause, then one enters the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*). Thus, one no longer perceives the characteristics of faults, and the false stains of transgression naturally extinguish themselves.
The analogy of lightning is used to illustrate how the arising and ceasing of continuity occurs with such rapidity. [Question: As for...
Question: The teaching of the Tripitaka uses lightning as a metaphor; how can it serve the purpose of entering the Mahāyāna? Answer:

Although the metaphor of illusion has already been explained to show that continuity is unreal, its meaning regarding extreme rapidity has not yet been made manifest. Therefore, the metaphor of lightning is borrowed here to reveal this sense of rapidity.
All phenomena do not wait for one another; they do not abide for even a single thought-moment.
All phenomena are false perceptions, like dreams, like mirages, like the moon reflected in water, like images in a mirror—they arise from deluded conceptualization.
These three types of knowledge (*vidyā*) are essentially empty through mutual dependence. There are two kinds of mutual dependence: first, mutual dependence between knowledges at different times;

second, mutual dependence between knowledges at the same time. This discussion concerns mutual dependence in terms of different times, which is why it says, "down to not abiding for even a single thought-moment.
Furthermore, if one examines mutual dependence through the four propositions—self, other, both, and neither—it too cannot be found.
Because one enters into emptiness, it is said that all views of mutual dependence are false and illusory.
Furthermore, from the passage "all dharmas are illusory views" onwards, this may serve as a general analogy for how the three provisional designations (*tri-prajñapti*) constitute all dharmas;
since all dharmas are ultimately non-existent, any conceptual differentiation of the three provisional designations to constitute all dharmas is entirely a false and illusory view. Therefore...

The Sūtra says: "Like a dream, a mirage, water, or the moon [reflected in water], they arise from deluded thought (*vikalpa*). If one realizes that these three types of provisional existence are empty, then deluded thought will not arise;
when the mind is free from transgression, it is pure. Therefore, regarding the term "purity" mentioned previously, one should simply eliminate [delusion] directly.
One who knows this is called one who upholds the Vinaya; one who knows this is called one who has a good understanding.

This is the seventh point establishing the upholding of the Vinaya. Now it is clarified that the true intent of the sūtras and precepts spoken by the Buddha was originally intended for sentient beings to sever evil and enter the Path.
If one deeply grasps the Buddha’s intent, knowing what is light and what is heavy, one will skillfully employ the sūtras.

If one observes the precepts with the ability to respond to circumstances and discern how to eliminate material offenses so that others may enter the Path, this does not contradict the Buddha’s teachings;
it is truly to uphold the Vinaya. As the Sūtras state, "He who knows this is called one who well understands. The Vinaya is the means for weighing lightness and gravity;

knowing the characteristics of lightness and gravity, one realizes they are all like illusions and transformations. Thus, one who well understands lightness and gravity enters into the absence of lightness and gravity.
The non-repetition of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) and nirvāṇa is precisely the Vinaya of skillful mastery and profound understanding.
Thereupon, the two bhikṣus said: "How sublime is this wisdom! It is beyond the reach of Upāli; though he was supreme in upholding the Vinaya, he could not explain it."
This is the second section clarifying how the minds of two bhikṣus attained purity.
Regarding this text, there are three points: first, the two bhikṣus praise Vimalakīrti; second, Upāli submits and recounts his sincere realization;
third, the minds of the two bhikṣus attain purity and they resolve to attain bodhicitta. The two bhikṣus praise Upāli’s clumsy methods of deliverance and... [they] revere... [him].
Because there is a distinction between the skillful deliverance of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* and the clumsy skill of upholding the Vinaya,
the text praises the superior wisdom [of Vimalakīrti] and laments that Upāli’s clumsy method of upholding the Vinaya is insufficient. As the Sūtra states,

"Upāli is foremost in upholding the Vinaya yet cannot explain it," meaning that Upāli is merely able to uphold the teachings of the Tripiṭaka and is preeminent in clarifying the Vinaya, but he lacks the ability to expound upon it.
This is my judgment regarding the preaching of the Vinaya according to the capacities of beings through the Mahāyāna’s general, distinct, and perfect teachings.
I replied: "Since the time of the Tathāgata, no śrāvaka or bodhisattva has been able to restrain his eloquence in joyful exposition;
such is the brilliance and penetration of his wisdom."
This was the praise offered by the two bhikṣus, Upāli and Kṣemadatta, who were both satisfied and humbled.
Since the time the Tathāgata entered parinirvāṇa, there has been no śrāvaka or bodhisattva capable of restraining his eloquence in joyful exposition;
even those who practice the three teachings are unable to restrain the Vimalakīrti’s skillful and ultimate eloquence in joyful exposition. As the sutra says of him:
When wisdom and clarity reach such a state, it constitutes the embodiment of the Dharma and the vision of principle;

one illuminates the capacities of beings with distinct clarity, recognizes their ailments and identifies the appropriate remedies, and administers medicine according to the ailment, attaining unimpeded mastery.
At that time, the doubts and regrets of the two bhikṣus were immediately dispelled, and they gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, making this vow:
"May all sentient beings attain such eloquence as this."
This refers to the bhikṣus possessing the three types of supernormal knowledge (traividya) generating the bodhicitta.

When the Sūtra states that "at that time, the two bhikṣus' doubts and regrets were immediately eliminated," "doubt" refers to the elimination of doubt regarding the offenses of sexual misconduct and killing;
"regret" refers to both the regret for having committed an offense and the intensified regret of Upāli, which was likewise eliminated. They then generated the bodhicitta, as distinguished previously.
I made this vow, saying: "May all beings attain such eloquence; may they obtain the unimpeded eloquence of the Mahāyāna, just like this Great Being.
Therefore, I am not fit to go to him to inquire after his illness.
"This is because I am bound by the four fetters and am incapable," Upāli thought to himself. "I am a clumsy practitioner who merely upholds the Vinaya;
in the past, I was unable to eliminate the offenses of two bhikṣus, which led to my being rebuked by this Great Being.
Since that time, I have been deferential and respectful, and thus I am unfit to transmit the Tathāgata’s intent and go to inquire after his illness."
The Buddha said to Rāhula, "Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness.
This is the ninth instance of the Buddha commanding Rāhula to inquire after his illness. The text also consists of two parts: first, the Buddha's command to inquire after his illness;
second, Rāhula’s respectful refusal on the grounds of his own inadequacy. The reason he was commanded next is that...
Among the Śrāvaka disciples, he was foremost in secret conduct. Rāhula was the son of the Buddha when he was a Bodhisattva;
he is also called Lóuyún, which translates as "Covering Obstruction" (Āvaraṇa). Because he remained in his mother’s womb for six years without emerging, he was named Covering Obstruction.
The *Nidāna-sūtra* clarifies that because he blocked a mouse hole in a previous life, he now receives this retribution.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* clarifies that in the past, Rāhula was a king who went out to visit a rishi.

Becoming absorbed in pleasure, he forgot for six days until he remembered and went out to see the rishi. Because the rishi had remained outside for six days and was distressed, [Rāhula] stayed in the womb for six years;
thus he was named Āvarṇa (Covered/Obstructed). There is also a translation that says "born in the palace. When Prince Siddhārtha wished to leap over [the city walls],...
In the city, the renunciant pointed his finger at his consort’s belly and said, "Six years hence, you shall give birth to a son.

Yaśodharā then became aware that she was pregnant. The people of the country all suspected that because the Crown Prince had renounced the world while the Great Consort remained in the palace, how could she have become pregnant?
They wondered if it were not due to illicit relations. Later, the Buddha and King Śuddhodana together verified this for the Great Consort.
The son of a son is born from the mother’s womb; for this reason, he is named "Womb-born" (*garbha-ja*).
Furthermore, the *Adbhuta-dharma Sūtra* clarifies that King Śuddhodana and his kinsmen, believing the Prince was not their own offspring, had him burned in a pit of fire.

Yaśodharā, having sworn an oath, entered the flames while holding her child, and she emerged cradled by a lotus flower; both mother and child remained safe and sound, while the King and [his kin]... [were struck with wonder].
Only then did the kinsmen and ministers believe that he was indeed the son of the Crown Prince. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* clarifies that Yaśodharā had been suspected;
she waited until after [Rāhula] was born, and upon seeing him, she realized he resembled his father, whereupon the King’s doubts were extinguished and his affection for her redoubled.
Rāhula must have entered the Path through frequent reflection; therefore, he was foremost in secret practice (*guhyacaryā*).
Furthermore, in order to manifest the Tathāgata’s teachings on the secret practices of the Half and Full [Vehicles], he first demonstrates the four types of austere secret practices.
First, he leads the fourfold assembly who delight in secret practices into the Way of the Half-Syllables (*ardhakṣara*).
Thus, the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "Rāhula’s secret practices—only I can know them; he manifests as my eldest son to demonstrate this."

Next, for the sake of all sentient beings, [the Buddha] wishes to reveal the four secret practices (*rahasya-caryā*) and demonstrate the acceptance of the Pure Name (*Vimalakīrti*), thereby causing sentient beings to despise the small and aspire to the Great.
Now, the Buddha commands those who inquire after his illness to have Rāhula recount the events of his past being rebuked;
this will once again manifest the teaching gate of the four secret practices, thereby accomplishing the five kinds of benefits mentioned previously.
This is the meaning.
Rāhula addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, I am not capable of going there to inquire after his illness.
This is the second instance of declining on the grounds of incapacity; the text consists of four parts: first, the formal declination of incapacity; second, the description... [text continues].

Regarding the reasons for his inability [to comply], there are three parts: first, the account of his previous life; second, the description of being rebuked by Vimalakīrti; third, the conclusion that he is unable [to act]. First, concerning his respectful refusal due to his inability:
this is because in the past, when he was the son of a householder, he preached on the merits of renunciation and was subsequently rebuked and defeated by Vimalakīrti;
how then could he possibly be fit to transmit the intent of the Tathāgata?
Why is this? I recall that in the past, the sons of the elders of Vaiśālī came to where I was, prostrated themselves in salutation, and asked me:
"O Rāhula, you are the son of the Buddha; having renounced the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch to leave the household life and pursue the Way, what are the benefits of such renunciation?"

This is the second [section] explaining the reasons for being incapable [of renunciation], concerning how [the Buddha] was rebuked in the past when teaching the merits of renunciation to the sons of elders.
Regarding this text, there are two parts: first, the sons of the elders inquire about the merits of renunciation;
second, Rāhula answers. First, to clarify the inquiry of the sons of the elders: if the Buddha were a householder, he should have acted as follows...

Since a Wheel-Turning Sage King, having renounced the world, attains Buddhahood, and even if Rāhula had remained at home, he would have attained the fruit of a Golden-Wheel Sage Emperor—the most supreme among men—and guided others through the ten wholesome paths of action, his merit would have been immeasurable;
yet, suddenly renouncing the world, he remains alone for his own sake. What benefit is there in this? It must be because he has profound insight that he asks this question.
I then, in accordance with the Dharma, explained for him the merits and benefits of renouncing the household life.
This is the second clarification regarding Rāhula’s response concerning the explanation of the merits and benefits of renunciation.

There is a teacher who says that this is clarified in the *Xiányú jīng* (Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish) as a comparison of the merits and benefits of renunciation for various types of people; however, I maintain that this is not so. It is extensive.
Regarding the question of Rāhula’s merit from leaving the household life: how could it be a matter of discussing the amount of blessings gained by saving others?

It must have been for the sake of explaining the teachings of the Tripiṭaka, clarifying that by leaving the household life one attains the ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*), the three samādhis, the three insights (*trividyā*), the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*), and other such supramundane merits, including the transcendence of birth and death and the attainment of both *sopadhiśeṣa* and *nirupadhiśeṣa* nirvāṇa.

"Is his virtue not equal to that of a Wheel-Turning King? Yet, once the retribution for the fruits of birth and death is exhausted, there is no end to his wandering through the three realms of existence.
At that time, Vimalakīrti came and said to me, "Rāhula, you should not speak of the merits of leaving the household life."
This is the third section, which correctly describes the matter of being rebuked; it consists of five parts: first, the formal rebuke; second, the explanation thereof;
third, the extensive demonstration of the merits of leaving the household life; fourth, the conclusion regarding true renunciation; and fifth, the exhortation to the elders.
Regarding the passage from the *Ekottarika-āgama* (specifically the section on the reprimand) which states that the benefits and merits of leaving the household life (*pravrajyā*) were not spoken of:
as for why Vimalakīrti reprimanded [Śāriputra] for not speaking of the benefits and merits of leaving the household life, there are three reasons.
First, since Rāhula was foremost in secret practice (*guhyacaryā*), how could he have spoken of the benefits and merits of leaving the household life? If he had spoken of them...
If merit is simply that which manifests itself, what is meant by "secret practice"?

Second, [the Buddha] praises the narrowness and inferiority of the merit of those who have left home in the Lesser Vehicle, noting that it does not correspond to the roots and conditions of the sons of elders for the Great Vehicle.

Third, if one were to speak of the merit of leaving home through outward appearance and robes, since these sons of elders each possess their own obstacles, they would be unable to obtain this merit of leaving home through outward appearance and robes.
Because Rāhula spoke of the merits of renunciation while possessing these three faults, he was rebuked by Vimalakīrti, who said that one should not preach for such a person.
Why is this? Because there is neither benefit nor merit; this is what is meant by saying that the conditioned dharmas of renunciation can be spoken of [only in that limited sense].

"Benefit and merit belong to the householder; as for those who have left the home life, they practice the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), and within the unconditioned dharma there is neither benefit nor merit.
This is the second explanation. According to the teachings of the Tripiṭaka, if one is able to conceal [one's faults], there will be precept, concentration, and wisdom.
To keep one's unconditioned merits secret so that others do not perceive them is called "secret practice. Now, when the Great Being rebukes this, there is both a factual and a principled dimension.
As for the factual dimension of the rebuke: if it were indeed a secret practice, he should not have personally declared the benefits of his renunciation to the sons of the elders.
If he says it was spoken for the benefit of sentient beings and not for himself, [the following applies].

Regarding the first point, concerning the manifestation of the benefits and merits of leaving the household life: since one does not know the faculties and conditions [of others], if one speaks without it acceding to their capacity, what benefit is there?
Second, regarding the refutation based on principle: the Sūtra states that there is neither benefit nor merit in this being "leaving the household life.
Now, we clarify that unconditioned dharmas are themselves space and Buddha-nature; if space and Buddha-nature possess no merit, [how can there be such things as benefit or merit]?
To see the Buddha-nature is to abide in Great Nirvana and depart from the home of birth-and-death within the two extremes; this is true renunciation.

If one sees the Buddha-nature as being like empty space and attains the Great Nirvana of the Three Virtues, then there is nothing accumulated, which is called a "treasury" (garbha) and is termed true esoteric practice.
This is the manifestation of the four types of flourishing [practice] in contrast to the four types of withered esoteric practice.
Honor is the practice of secret conduct. The Sūtra states that among conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), it can be said that there is benefit and merit.

This refers to Harakūṇa (Haraka), who, by perceiving the partial truth (*ekadeśatattva*), achieved wisdom and the severance of afflictions; yet these still belong to conditioned phenomena and possess both benefit and merit.

Since they are conditioned, one cannot thereby escape the cycle of death and rebirth characterized by transformation (*pariṇāma-vaśavarti-jarāmaraṇa*). How, then, can this be called "leaving home" (*pravrajyā*)? Therefore, [the Great Nirvāṇa...]
The *Pāṇḍava-sūtra* states: "That which is empty is birth-and-death; that which is not empty is Great Nirvāṇa. The sūtra further says:
"Now, those who have left the household life do so for the sake of the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). Within the unconditioned dharma, there is neither profit nor merit.

This was said to Kātyāyanīputra to rebuke his mindset regarding leaving the household life. Indeed, the fundamental purpose of one who has left the household life is to depart from the house of birth-and-death and seek the Truth.

Regarding the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharma that is truly unconditioned, as stated in the following passage: "The Buddha-body is unconditioned and does not fall into the categories of numerical reckoning.
If one has not yet escaped birth and death and yet abides in the conditioned, this aspiration for renunciation is incorrect.

The reason for this is that those of the Hīnayāna perceive the Truth and attain the *saṃkhyā-nirodha* (cessation through counting) or the *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa with remainder), which they claim to be unconditioned.

If one has not yet seen the Middle Way through the clear meaning of the Mahāyāna, and merely severs ignorance and specific delusions, this remains the conditioned dharma of *parināmika-jarāmaraṇa* (transformation death).

If, however, one sees the Buddha-nature of the Middle Way and abides in Great Nirvāṇa, severing ignorance and specific delusions along with *parināmika-jarāmaraṇa*, this is indeed the true unconditioned dharma; it is the equal and true Dharma-realm.
Because the Buddha does not "save" sentient beings, it is said that within the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharma there is neither benefit nor merit.
Thus, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The śrāvaka saṃgha is called the conditioned saṃgha;

the bodhisattva saṃgha is called the unconditioned saṃgha. A questioner asks: When Vimalakīrti rebuked Rāhula, he used the unconditioned precisely to refute the conditioned; yet, is the unconditioned merely...
Question: How can one speak of the "function" (*yòng*) regarding the principle of the Buddha-nature of empty space?

It is said that the Mahāyāna’s true secret practice breaks Vimalakīrti’s (Lóuyún) un-true secret practice. Answer: Since Rāhula is attached to conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta*), all his secret practices are conditioned.
Now, Vimalakīrti first brings forth the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) to break them; once the true unconditioned is realized, it is as follows:

Having obtained the wish-fulfilling jewel, there is nothing that cannot be possessed; therefore, what was previously described as the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is followed by a detailed explanation of the merits of renunciation.
These are all practices that embody every merit within the true unconditioned dharma, which is precisely the meaning of "true secret practice" (*rahasyacaryā*).
Rāhula, for one who has gone forth, there is no "that" and no "this," nor is there anything in between;
being free from the sixty-two views, he abides in nirvāṇa, which is accepted by the wise and is the sphere of practice for the noble ones.
This is the extensive explanation of the merits of Mahāyāna renunciation given by the Three Knowledges (Traividya) to Rāhula;
that is to say, to be fully endowed with all practices within the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharma is called "true secret conduct" (*rahasyacaryā*). This text consists of two parts:

first, clarifying the merits of one’s own practice; second, clarifying the merits of transforming others. Regarding the first, the merits of one’s own practice, this refers to right contemplation (*samyagdarśana*).
The Middle Way shatters the Lesser Vehicle’s notion of unconditioned nirvana situated between this and that shore. Why is this so?
In the Śrāvaka sūtras, nirvana is clarified as the far shore, saṃsāra as this shore, and afflictions as the middle current;
yet in the Mahāyāna, both "this" and "that" shores, as well as the middle current, are all considered "this shore. If a Bodhisattva contemplates the Middle Way, they attain the truth.

When one is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), one does not perceive self, other, or the middle; with a nature like empty space, one directly perceives the Buddha-nature and abides in Great Nirvāṇa—this is called true unconditionality.

As the Sūtra says, "Abiding in Nirvāṇa apart from the sixty-two views," if a Bodhisattva correctly contemplates the Middle Way and attains true unconditionality, they not only depart from the sixty-two views within the realm of desire and form, but [transcend them all].
Furthermore, because it is free from all views outside the [true] realm, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra* explains "pure dhyāna" (*viśuddha-dhyāna*) by stating:
"Pure dhyāna is that which is free from all views. This is precisely its meaning. The Sūtra says:

"One who abides in nirvāṇa"—if one contemplates the Middle Way, one sees the Buddha-nature and dwells in the city of primordially existing nirvāṇa, the secret treasury of the three inconceivable virtues.
The Dharmakāya, Prajñā, and Liberation are neither vertical nor horizontal, like the letter *i* in the world;
as the Sūtra says, "that which is received by the wise and practiced by the sages," this cites the fruit to establish the cause. Wisdom belongs to the Omniscient One;
although there is nothing [ultimately] received, the mind is in profound accord with the principle of the Middle Way and the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), and this is termed "receiving."
Furthermore, the sutras state that "the sphere of the noble ones" refers to the Middle Way and the true mark (*dharmatā*), for this is precisely the sphere traversed by the noble ones.
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "The Great Vehicle of the Perfection of Wisdom is the path from which the Buddha has come.

Moreover, that which is received by the wise is the contemplation of the Middle Way for the sake of realizing the fruit; the sphere of the noble ones is the contemplation of the Middle Way for the sake of cultivation.
The Middle Way is neither cause nor fruit, yet it is able to accomplish the myriad practices and meritorious virtues of the Mahāyāna causes and fruits;
this is precisely the true practice of secrecy (*guhyacaryā*).
It subdues all Māras, crosses over the five destinies, purifies the five eyes, attains the five powers, establishes the five faculties, and does not afflict others.
Being free from all various evils constitutes the second clarification of the Mahāyāna’s merit of renouncing the world and transforming others; this passage contains two points:

first, subduing the various māras, which is the refutation of the discourse on craving (*tṛṣṇā-vāda*); second, crushing the various non-Buddhists, which is the refutation of the discourse on views (*dṛṣṭi-vāda*). However, [the former] is merely craving...
There are two kinds of views: first, the views of craving within the realm [of desire], which are the followers of Pāpīyān and the six heterodox masters;
second, the views of craving outside the realm, which belong to the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*).
When the sutras speak of "subduing all māras and delivering those in the five paths," this refers precisely to the merit of subduing māras and transforming others through the single illumination.
Regarding the "subduing of Māra," the *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra* clarifies that by attaining the Bodhisattva path, one destroys the Māra of afflictions;
by attaining the Dharma-nature body, one destroys the Māra of the aggregates (*skandha-māra*); by attaining the Bodhisattva path and the Dharma-body, one destroys the Māra of death;
and by attaining the Immovable Samādhi, one destroys the Māra of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin devas. The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* clarifies that there are eight kinds of Māras.
Regarding what are called permanence, bliss, self, and purity: the first four māras—impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity—are the internal māras;
the latter four māras are the external māras. Now, concerning the former four māras of affliction and so forth:
if the four māras of affliction and so forth arise based on [the misconceptions of] permanence, bliss, self, and purity, they constitute the four internal [māras].
If Māra arises from the four [perversions]—impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity—such as the afflictions and so forth, these are the four Māras outside the realm.
When a Bodhisattva correctly contemplates the Middle Way and attains the true unconditioned dharma, they destroy the eight inversions;

this is the destruction of the eight Māras through one's own practice. If, for the sake of sentient beings, one explains that the Middle Way is neither existent nor non-existent, this is the transformation of others.
To destroy the four Māras, such as the Māra of Permanence and so forth, is to demonstrate that the Middle Way is not non-existent;

because this very act destroys the four Māras, such as the Māra of Impermanence and so forth, it is said that he "subdues all Māras. As for "delivering those in the five destinies," sentient beings in the five destinies are all the retinues of Māra;

if a Bodhisattva, through the power of the roots of goodness of his benevolence and compassion, is born within the five destinies and manifests his body to engage in their common affairs, [he delivers them].
By preaching the Dharma, one is able to deliver those in the five paths and the six realms; by opening the six realms, one emerges from the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*).
When a Bodhisattva contemplates the Middle Way and simultaneously illuminates the two truths, they immediately attain the Samādhi of the Three Truths and accomplish the twenty-five samādhis.

By means of the ten stages of destroying the twenty-five states of existence, one is able to deliver those within the five paths of the realm of desire and those outside the realm of form and formlessness.

Regarding the hearing of the three kinds of mind-made bodies of the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta, the Sūtra says that for a Bodhisattva to purify the five eyes, they must cultivate the true unconditioned by means of single-minded, perfect contemplation of the three truths.

When contemplating the coarse objects of the conventional truth to destroy all evil karma, it is called "purifying the flesh eye. When contemplating the subtle objects of the conventional truth to destroy all distracted minds, it is called... [the divine eye].

If the pure celestial eye contemplates the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and destroys the afflictions of view and thought within the triple world, it is called the pure wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*).

If it contemplates the conventional truths (*saṃvṛti-satya*) of both the internal and external worlds and destroys the ignorance as vast as the sands of the Ganges, it is called the pure dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*).

If it contemplates the Middle Way, simultaneously illuminating the two truths, and perfectly eliminates the views and thoughts and ignorance of the entire dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), this is the pure Buddha-eye.

Regarding the "Eye," the Sūtra states that one who attains the five powers (pañcabala) purifies the five eyes and thereby attains the five powers—namely, the five powers among the fourfold sets of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma).

Why is this so? If one contemplates the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), entering it through both the analytical and the substantial methods, one purifies the eye of wisdom (prajñā-cakṣus) and thereby attains the five powers of arising-and-ceasing (utpāda-nirodha) as well as the five powers of non-arising (anutpāda).
If one enters the contemplation of the conventional from emptiness, the pure Dharma-eye immediately attains the five powers of measurelessness;
if one contemplates the Middle Way, perfectly illuminating the Dharma-realm, the pure Buddha-eye immediately attains the five powers of non-action.
The first three sets of five powers are provisional, while the final set of five powers is real. As the Sūtra says: "The Bodhisattva establishes the five faculties."

Knowing that the equal Dharma-realm is like space—neither provisional nor real—one is able through skillful means to accomplish the five powers of both the provisional and the real, thereby transforming the four types of sentient beings and causing each to give rise to the five faculties; this is precisely what is meant by "establishing the faculties of sentient beings.
As the Sūtra says, "not troubling others," the Bodhisattva employs the four *siddhāntas* to respond to these four [types of beings].
By planting the roots of goodness in sentient beings according to their specific conditions without error, one avoids the fault of destroying the roots of goodness of others;

this is truly what is meant by "not disturbing them. As the Sūtra says, "being free from various evils," the Bodhisattva spontaneously accomplishes the four kinds of five powers (*pañcabala*), whereby they are able to leave behind all various evils both within and outside the realms, and are able to establish the four kinds of five faculties (*pañcendriya*) in sentient beings.
Doubt, wrong thoughts, indolence, distraction, delusion, and all other unwholesome afflictions—
these are precisely what cause sentient beings to be separated from various evils.
It crushes all heterodox paths, transcends provisional names, emerges from the mire, and is without attachment, without "mine-ness," and without anything received.
"Without disturbance, harboring joy within, protecting the minds of others, following meditative concentration,
and remaining free from all faults— this is the second [point], which clarifies the merit of transforming others by means of subduing non-Buddhists.
As the Sūtra says, "subduing all non-Buddhists" refers to subduing the six masters within the realm, the ninety-six types of non-Buddhists, and the heterodox teachers outside the realm.
The Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are those who follow the Shared Teaching of the Bodhisattvas. Why is this so?
Because when a Bodhisattva correctly contemplates the Middle Way and attains true unconditionedness (*asaṃskṛta*), they are able to personally destroy the two extremes of the non-Buddhists.

If, for the sake of sentient beings, they preach "it is not existent," they subdue the non-Buddhists within the realms; if they preach "it is not non-existent," they subdue the non-Buddhists outside the realms. This is why...
If one’s mental activity transcends all that lies outside of principle, then all such things are external paths;

to subdue them and cause them to enter the Middle Way is the accomplishment of the merit of transforming others. As the Sūtra says: "Transcending conventional designations, both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are merely conventional designations.
If a Bodhisattva contemplates the Middle Way and attains true unconditionedness (*asaṃskṛta*), then the mind transcends these two.

The "extremes" are mere conventional designations (*prajñapti*). If one explains to sentient beings that [the extremes] do not exist, it causes those within the realm to transcend the conventional designation of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) according to worldly truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

If one explains that they are not non-existent, it causes those outside the realm to transcend the conventional designation of the "transformed city" (*nirmāṇa-pura*)—that is, *nirvāṇa*—according to ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). As the Sūtra says: "One who emerges from the mud is a Bodhisattva."
Correctly contemplating the Middle Way is precisely to emerge from the mud of the two kinds of afflictions—view-based and thought-based—both within and beyond the realms.
If one preaches "non-existence" for the sake of sentient beings, those within the realms emerge from the mud of view-based and thought-based afflictions;
if one preaches "non-non-existence" for the sake of sentient beings, those beyond the realms emerge from the distinct delusions of view-based and thought-based afflictions.

Regarding the "mud of affliction," the Sūtra states that there is no "attachment" (*saṃyoga*). Here, "attachment" refers to karma; because afflictions such as craving moisten karma, it is called "attachment.
When a Bodhisattva correctly contemplates the Middle Way, they are able to sever the karma of the two extremes—namely, [the extremes of] existence and non-existence.

If, for the sake of sentient beings, one teaches that things are not existent, one severs the attachment to the karma and afflictions within the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*). If, for the sake of sentient beings...
To say that it is not non-existent is to sever the fetters of karma and afflictions beyond the realms. The Sūtra says, "There is no 'mine'":
if a Bodhisattva correctly contemplates the Middle Way, they perceive neither a self nor anything belonging to a self within or beyond the realms.
If one speaks of "non-existence" for the sake of sentient beings, it is to destroy the notion of "mine" within the realms; if one speaks of "not non-existence," it is to...

The *Sūtra on Destroying the "Mine" Outside the Realm* states that "there is nothing to be received"; this means that within the Bodhisattva’s correct contemplation of the Middle Way, one does not accept the two extremes.
If, for the sake of sentient beings, one explains that [the self] does not exist, it means that sentient beings within the realm do not grasp at nirvāṇa.
The sūtra states that "there is no disturbance"; this means that within the Bodhisattva’s correct contemplation of the Middle Way, there is no distraction or movement toward the two extremes.
Regarding these disturbances: if one were to preach to sentient beings that things do not exist, it would destroy the disturbances of objective clinging within the realm of conditioned existence;
if one were to preach that they are not non-existent, it would destroy the disturbances of conceptualizing true emptiness outside the realm of conditioned existence.
Therefore, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states: "Sentient beings with minds distracted by emptiness are not its proper domain. The Sūtra says that those who harbor joy within are Bodhisattvas.
If one contemplates the Middle Way as simultaneously illuminating the two truths, one immediately attains the joy that is the factor of enlightenment known as "joy.

If one explains the Middle Way and the two truths, along with the four factors of enlightenment including joy, to sentient beings, and if those sentient beings attain these four forms of joy, the Bodhisattva rejoices in the sentient beings' attainment of the four joys;
this constitutes the immeasurable mind of joy (*muditā*), which is inwardly harboring joy.

Furthermore, the Sūtra says that "to protect the intentions of others" means to observe the faculties and conditions of the four types of sentient beings and preach the Three Truths using the four *siddhāntas*.
Not to conflict with the minds of these four types of sentient beings is precisely what it means to protect their intentions.

The Sūtra states that a Bodhisattva who follows meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), if they observe the Middle Way and simultaneously illumine the two truths, enters the Samādhi of the Three Truths and abides in the Great [Vehicle].

In the profound cave of *nirvāṇa* meditative concentration, one is able to manifest various dignified postures (*īryāpatha*) without arising from the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), preaching the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings—just as the lute of the *asura*s causes all sentient beings to attain the three truths (*trisaṃdhi*), the three samādhis, and all meditative concentrations.
As the Sūtra says regarding "being free from all faults": if a bodhisattva contemplates the Middle Way, there is no longer anything within the realms (*dhātu*).

The faults of the two kinds of afflictions pertaining to the external realm are thereby eliminated, resulting in the three types of infallibility, the three types of non-protection, and the three karmas that follow wisdom.
Through inconceivable transformations of the three wheels, one transforms all sentient beings within and without the realms;
there is no longer any fault of harming others, impairing their faculties, or mismatching their capacities, and one is thus able to cause all sentient beings to transcend the realms.
This is the fault of regarding the internal realm as external.
If one can act in this way, that is true renunciation.
This is the fourth discourse on the True Renunciant, which states: "If one can act in this way, that is precisely within suchness."
To realize the true state of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*) and to possess all merits for both self-cultivation and the transformation of others—this is precisely it.

Thus, the single mind is fully endowed with the myriad practices (*sarvacaryā*), just as a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*) contains all treasures; this is the fourfold flourishing of true esoteric practice.
As the Sūtra says, "Those who are truly renunciant" correctly contemplate the Middle Way, which is the emptiness of space and the Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*).
To attain true unconditionedness (*asaṃskṛta*) and thereby emerge from the twenty-five states of existence of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*),

as well as to emerge from the houses of all Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching— that is, to emerge from the houses of both the ultimate and conventional truths (*satya*) and from the house of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa—
is therefore called "leaving home" (*pravrajyā*).
Thereupon, Vimalakīrti said to the sons of the elders, "You all should together go forth into homelessness within the True Dharma.
Why is this? Because a Buddha appears in the world but rarely.
This is the fifth passage in which Vimalakīrti encourages the elders to go forth; it consists of four parts. First, Vimalakīrti...
1. Exhorting the Elder to Leave Home; 2. Each of the Elder’s Sons Respects Their Departure Due to Obstacles;
3. Vimalakīrti Re-exhorts Them to Generate the Bodhicitta; 4. Clarifying the Elder’s Sons’ Generation of the Bodhicitta.

Regarding the first point, "Vimalakīrti exhorting the elder to leave home," this means exhorting him to cultivate the Middle Way and Right Contemplation in order to seek true unconditioned liberation.
It is the home of birth and death at the extremes; therefore, it is called "pure. It says to you: "Within the True Dharma, you should seek to go forth into homelessness.

The True Dharma is precisely the True Dharma of the Middle Way. If you can all contemplate this principle together, you will all be able to escape from the home of birth and death at the two extremes.
The Sūtra asks: "Why is this so? Because a Buddha appears in the world is difficult."
If a Buddha appears in the world, one may hear the Dharma of the Middle Way and the unconditioned;
if no Buddha appears in the world, how could one hear it for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas?

Since the Buddha-Dharma of the true mark of the Middle Way is so difficult to encounter and hear, having now encountered and heard the True Dharma, how can one fail to contemplate and practice it to transcend birth and death within the two extremes?
...the home of such people.
The sons of the elders said, "Householder, we have heard the Buddha’s words: one may not go forth into homelessness if one's parents do not permit it.
This was the second [reason] why the sons of the elders each declined, citing obstacles that prevented them from shaving their hair, changing their attire, and leaving the household life.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* fundamentally exhorts one to contemplate the Middle Way and seek the true unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

However, this son of a householder had not yet grasped this meaning and thought that the exhortation was merely to shave his head and leave the household life. Therefore, he spoke with a sense of obstruction, saying:

"I have heard the Buddha teach that if one's parents do not permit it, one cannot leave the household life; this is what is prescribed by the Buddhist precepts," as fully set forth in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.
Vimalakīrti said:
"In this way, you should immediately resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
this is true renunciation, and this is true full ordination."
This is the exhortation to the practice of contemplative renunciation by Vimalakīrti, who possesses the three types of supernormal knowledge.
There are four propositions regarding the meaning of renunciation: first, neither body nor mind has renounced; second, the body has renounced but the mind has not;
third, the body has not renounced but the mind has—this is precisely renunciation through contemplative practice; fourth, both body and mind have renounced.
The householder Vimalakīrti then exhorted them again, saying, "If you would simply resolve to attain Bodhicitta, this would be as good as kindling the fire.
[This refers to] the Buddha’s regulation that if one's parents do not permit it, one may not change one's dress or shave one's head to leave the household life;
yet Vimalakīrti already knew of this matter, and therefore he said it was acceptable. However, each of these sons of the elders possessed their own Mahāyāna contemplative practice.

The reason the purity of roots of goodness is so named is that it exhorts one to resolve upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, to cultivate right contemplation, and to seek true non-action (*asamskṛta*).
This immediately leads to exiting the house of birth and death within the two extremes.

Since the precepts arise from the mind, if the bodhicitta is resolved, the goodness of the Bodhisattva precepts arises simultaneously with that mind; therefore, it is said that this constitutes "complete fulfillment."
At that time, all thirty-two sons of the elders resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This refers to how these sons of the elders from the four directions, following the exhortation of Vimalakīrti, all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed path and generated the bodhicitta;
the meaning of this is fully explained as previously set forth.
Therefore, I am not fit to go there to inquire after his illness.
