This is the fourth section, concluding that Rāhula is incapable [of this task]. Reflecting upon my own past, when I preached to the sons of the elders on the merits of renunciation, the words and meanings were coarse and shallow;
they were neither words of true, esoteric practice, nor were they worthy of the [Vimalakīrti’s] long [discourse].
Since this son’s faculties and conditions have already been rebuked and broken by Vimalakīrti, how could he possibly be capable of transmitting the Tathāgata’s intent?
The Buddha said to Ānanda: "Go to Vimalakīrti and inquire after his illness."
This is the tenth instance of the Buddha commanding Ānanda to inquire after his illness; the text also consists of two parts:
first, the Buddha’s command to inquire after his illness, and second, Ānanda’s respectful refusal on the grounds of his own incapacity.

The reason the Tathāgata next commanded Ānanda to inquire after his illness was that, among the śrāvaka disciples, Ānanda was foremost in erudition. Furthermore, Ānanda was the Tathāgata’s own cousin.
This is translated as "Joyful" (Pramudita). Regarding why it is named "Joyful," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* clarifies that there are three causes and conditions for receiving this name:
first, receiving the name from one's original vow; second, parents bestowing a name; and third, receiving a name based on what others perceive.
Receiving the name from one's original vow and being named "Joyful" refers specifically to the causal stage of Śākyamuni Buddha.
When the Earth was a potter, he encountered the past Buddha Śākyamuni; at that time, there was an attendant named Ānanda who possessed the power of hearing and retaining all teachings.

The potter then made a vow, saying: "May it be that when I attain Buddhahood in the future, my name shall likewise be Śākya, and my attendant who possesses the power of hearing and retaining all teachings shall likewise be named Ānanda.
Furthermore, from lifetime to lifetime since then, Ānanda has continued to make this vow.
He was named "Joy" (Nanda) because he became the Buddha’s attendant;

he is called Joy because when the Tathāgata was about to attain enlightenment, the Demon King, filled with jealousy and wrath, raised eighteen billion ghost-soldiers and demonic hosts to harass the Bodhisattva.
Because the Bodhisattva’s mind remained upright, the demonic army retreated and was destroyed, and he [the boy] then arrived at the presence of Śuddhodana.
The King spoke, saying: "Last night, as your son was about to attain the Way, he was thwarted by Māra;
he has now passed away. The King and his retinue were all filled with grief and suffering. The gods of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven immediately informed the King, saying:
"Your son has attained Perfect Enlightenment; there is no need for sorrow or distress. The King remained in doubt and dispatched a messenger to investigate; the messenger returned.
When it was reported that the Crown Prince had already attained perfect enlightenment, the King, his retinue, and all the subjects within the realm were filled with great joy.
Shortly thereafter, King Droṇodana received news that a son had been born; the King rejoiced once more.
Since this child was born at a time of such joy, he should be given a name; thus he was named Nanda. This was the name his parents gave him: Nanda.

Furthermore, he received the name Ānanda from those who saw him; because he had cultivated compassion and kindness throughout successive lifetimes, as a karmic reward he obtained a physical form with the primary and secondary marks that were so upright and majestic that all who saw him could not help but feel love and respect, giving rise to a heart of joy. Therefore, he was named "Joy" (Ānanda).
Thus, when the Dharma-treasury was being compiled, the various Arhats spoke in verse to praise Ānanda, saying:
His face is like the pure full moon; his eyes are like blue lotuses. The waters of the great ocean of the Buddha-dharma flow into the body of Ānanda.

Because Ānanda has entered the Path through the faculty of hearing, when he hears the Tathāgata preach the Dharma, it is like water held in a perfect vessel, without any loss or leakage. He is a member of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body retinue.

In order to manifest the teachings of the Great Sage regarding the entry into the Way through both the "Half" and "Full" vehicles of extensive learning, he first used the "withered" (ku) form of extensive learning to lead the fourfold assembly into the Way.

Next, in order to manifest the teachings on entering the Way through the "flourishing" (rong) form of extensive learning, he showed Vimalakīrti’s reprimand and refutation so that all sentient beings might come to despise the small and aspire to the Great. Now, the Buddha commands—
This causes the messenger of inquiry, Ānanda, to recount the past incident of being rebuked,
thereby further elucidating the teaching on the four glories of much learning (*bahuśruta*) entering the Path, which fulfills the meaning of the five kinds of benefits mentioned previously.

I respectfully decline, for in the past, when I begged for milk on behalf of the Tathāgata, I was struck with a whip yet offered no reply;
how could I dare transmit the Buddha’s sacred command to go there and inquire after his illness?
Why is this? I recall that in former times, when the World-Honored One suffered a slight ailment that required cow’s milk, I immediately—
Holding his almsbowl, he went to the gate of a great brahmin’s house and stood there.

This is the second account of the reasons for his inability [to teach]; because the World-Honored One had a slight ailment that required cow’s milk, he went with his bowl to beg for it, and was therefore rebuked.
Why is this so? For the Tripiṭaka teachings clarify only the arising [of phenomena].

The Body-Buddha (*kāya-buddha*) is the true Buddha; it is not said that there is a Dharma-nature Body-Buddha (*dharmatā-kāya-buddha*). The Buddha of the three bodies and three virtues is the Birth-Body Buddha (*janma-kāya-buddha*).
Because the Birth-Body Buddha dwells in *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana with remainder), he still possesses a retribution-body (*vipāka-kāya*).

Consequently, there are occurrences such as the golden needles, the horse-barley, hunger, thirst, cold, heat, and illness. For this reason, when his body was slightly ill, he required cow’s milk, which Ānanda did not [provide].
Knowing that there is a Buddha of the three bodies within the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), it is said that the *sāvaśeṣa-nirmāṇakāya* (the body with remainder) truly having an illness is real;
thus, his begging for milk while holding an alms bowl is [an instance of] the "half-letters" (*ardhākṣara*).

Those who possess much learning but have not heard of the merits of the *dharmakāya*—that its adamantine essence is eternally abiding and profoundly serene—are like those who were struck by this [criticism].
At that time, Vimalakīrti came and said to me, "Ānanda, why are you standing here at dawn holding your alms bowl?
I replied, "Householder, the World-Honored One has a slight ailment; I have come here because he requires cow's milk."

This is the third section, which correctly describes the incident of being rebuked; it consists of three parts: first, an inquiry into Ānanda’s intention in requesting [milk]; second, the actual rebuke; and third, the clarification of Ānanda’s shame. Regarding the first, the inquiry into the intention for requesting milk, there are two parts: first, Vimalakīrti’s question, and second, Ānanda’s answer. First, the reason why Vimalakīrti asks Ānanda: *The Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra*, fascicle 2, translated by Kumārajīva, "Chapter on the Parable of the Physician. At that time, the Licchavi Vimalakīrti addressed the Venerable Ānanda: "Venerable Ānanda, why do you go to the house of the Licchavi lady Gautamī to beg for milk? Ānanda replied: "Good man, the Buddha has fallen ill with a wind-disorder (*vāta-vyādhi*). The World-Honored One has instructed me to go to the house of the Licchavi lady Gautamī to beg for milk, so that he may take it and be cured of his illness. Vimalakīrti said: "Venerable Ānanda, do not say such things. Why? Because the Tathāgata is free from all sicknesses and afflictions. Furthermore, the Tathāgata is the Great Physician King who cures the illnesses of all sentient beings. How could he himself have an illness? Moreover, the Tathāgata is the King of Medicine, whose body is like a diamond (*vajra*), indestructible and unbreakable. How could he have an illness? Furthermore, the Tathāgata is the King of the Dharma, whose body is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), the body of liberation, the body of reality (*dharmatākāya*), and the body of non-arising. How could he have an illness? Furthermore, the Tathāgata is the King of Truth, whose body is the truth-body (*satyakāya*), the body of reality (*tattvakāya*), the body of non-duality, and the body of non-differentiation. How could he have an illness? Furthermore, the Tathāgata is the King of Non-attachment, whose body is the body of non-attachment, the body of non-obstruction, the body of non-bondage, and the body of non-entanglement. How could he have an illness? Furthermore, the Tathāgata is the King of Non-retrogression, whose body is the body of non-retrogression, the body of non-decline, the body of non-extinction, and the body of non-perishing. How could he have an illness? Furthermore, the Tathāgata is the King of Non-defilement, whose body is the body of non-defilement, the body of non-taint, the body of non-outflow (*anāsrava-kāya*), and the body of non-corruption. How could he have an illness? Furthermore, the Tathāgata is the King of Non-birth, whose body is the body of non-birth, the body of non-arising, the body of non-origination, and the body of non-production. How could he have an illness? Furthermore, the Tathāgata is the King of Non-death, whose body is the body of non-death, the body of non-passing away, the body of non-extinction, and the body of non-perishing. How could he have an illness? Regarding the repeated prohibition and the refutation of Ānanda’s two types of slander, the Sūtra says: "Stop, stop, Ānanda! Do not speak thus.

Because there are two instances of "stop," it serves to stop these two types of slander. As for the two types of slander: first is the slander of exaggeration (*samāropa*), and second is the slander of deprecation (*apavāda*).
Regarding the slander of exaggeration: the Tathāgata’s true *dharmakāya* is fully endowed with the perfection of cessation (*nirodha-guṇa*) and possesses nothing [that is not already complete].
If one were to say that there is a cause of suffering and a fruit of suffering within the fruition itself, this would be to slander the Dharma-body by superimposing unwholesome dharmas upon it.
Second, as for the slander of diminution: the Tathāgata’s true Dharma-body is perfectly endowed with the virtues of wisdom;

yet, one might claim that because various wholesome qualities are not yet sufficient, the fruit of bliss is not perfected, and that there still remains illness and affliction. This is [the second type of slander].

This refers to the two types of slander: diminution and exaggeration. Now, when Ānanda says that the Buddha’s body has a slight ailment, this constitutes both the slander of exaggeration and the slander of diminution.
The first "Stop, stop, Ānanda" is to cease the slander of exaggeration; the second "Stop, stop, Ānanda" is to cease the slander of diminution.
Therefore, it is said: "Stop, stop, Ānanda; do not utter words of these two slanders."
The body of the Tathāgata is a diamond-like essence; all evils have been severed and all virtues are universally assembled. How could there be any illness?
How could there be any affliction?
This is the second [point] revealing that the Tathāgata’s body is a diamond-like essence, which first stops Ānanda’s two types of slander so that he may not...
Having spoken these words, Ānanda could not fathom the profound intent behind the repeated injunctions.
This is because Vimalakīrti manifested the Tathāgata’s vajra-body to counteract the teachings of the Tripiṭaka, which clarify the Buddha of the birth-body (*janma-kāya*). As the Sūtra states:
"The body of the Tathāgata is the essence of the vajra; the essence of the vajra is the Dharma-body, the eternal body. Therefore, it is by means of the vajra that [this is revealed].
As for the analogy: the diamond essence is firm and its function is sharp and penetrating to the ultimate limit.
Its firmness of essence is a metaphor for the *dharmakāya*, which cannot be invaded by delusions or the cycle of birth and death, remaining eternally present and unchanging.

Its sharpness of function is a metaphor for the wisdom-virtue of the *dharmakāya*; the great *prajñā*’s illuminating activity is fully equipped to reach everywhere. Its penetration to the ultimate limit refers to—

To illustrate this by means of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*): when the perfection of the virtue of severance reaches its ultimate limit and all obstacles are severed within the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), this is precisely liberation and *nirvāṇa*.
Thus, these three virtues—the Dharma-body and so forth—are neither vertical nor horizontal, like the world-characteristic letter "I" (*ī*).
Therefore, the *Vajra* is used as a metaphor for the Dharma-body. As the Sūtra says, "All evils have been severed and all virtues universally assembled," "all evils have been severed" refers to...
That which means the severance of both views and afflictions within and without the realms, and the universal gathering of all wholesome dharmas, is precisely Mahāprajñāpāramitā.
That it can lead all myriad virtues to merge in the principle of the Middle Way, reaching ultimate perfection and consummation, is the Dharma-body;
thus the three virtues of wisdom and severance are fully complete. The meaning of this perfect consummation is clearly manifest. As the Sūtra says: "What illness could there possibly be? When...
What affliction could there be? If all evils have been exhausted, then there is no bitter fruit; what illness could there be?
If all virtues are universally assembled, one attains ultimate, eternal bliss; what affliction could there be?

This [explanation] from the Tripiṭaka teaching refers to the "illness" because it concerns the wisdom and severance of the *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (body with remainder). If [one follows] the Mahāyāna teaching, it refers to the ultimate...
Ultimately, the Dharma-body possesses clear wisdom and severance; because the Dharma-body has no suffering, it has no illness.

That Ānanda spoke of having illness and affliction is precisely a twofold slander. However, the traditional exegesis of the teachings of the four periods or five periods sometimes states that the *Prajñā* [sūtras] still belong to the Buddha’s eighty-year career, while this sūtra is a Vaipulya teaching, claiming it is identical to the *Śūraṅgama*.
To clarify that the Buddha’s lifespan is seven hundred asaṃkhyeya kalpas, yet not accept the present explanation of the ten disciples,
merely to manifest the teachings on decline and prosperity— how could this possibly reconcile the text of this sutra?
"Hush, Ānanda! Do not slander the Tathāgata; do not let other people hear such coarse words.
Do not let the devas of great majesty and power, nor the bodhisattvas who have come from the pure lands of other directions, hear these words.
Ānanda, even a universal monarch (cakravartin) obtains freedom from illness through his meager merit; how much more so the Tathāgata, whose assembly of immeasurable merit is universally supreme?"
Ah, how remarkable! These three points establish two types of denial (*apavāda*). According to this text, there are two: first, establishing the denial of diminution (*apavāda-apakarṣa*);

second, establishing the denial of augmentation (*apavāda-adhyāropa*). Regarding the first, which clarifies the establishment of the denial of diminution: this text uses the Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*) as its proof.
The meaning is made manifest. When the Sūtra says, "Go silently, Ānanda; do not slander the Tathāgata," the phrase "go silently" means to restrain Ānanda from words of disparagement, hence "silently.
"Go" is an exhortation to depart. Since the true body of the Tathāgata has no illness, why trouble him by begging for milk?
Therefore, he is told to go. If one were to say that the Tathāgata has an illness, that would be... [illegible].
This increases slander. When the Sūtra says, "Do not let heterodox persons hear these coarse words," it is because those of external paths harbor divergent views;

if such heterodox persons were to hear that the Tathāgata is ill, they would immediately claim that although the Buddha practices goodness, his rewards for good deeds remain coarse and incomplete, and that he still suffers from illness and affliction.
How would this differ from ordinary worldly people? It only serves to increase their sin of false slander.
Do not speak in such a way that the devas of great majesty and power, or the bodhisattvas who have come from other pure lands, should hear these words.
For the devas of great majesty and power, their minor wholesome karmic rewards result in freedom from illness;

likewise, for all sentient beings in other pure lands, their minor wholesome karmic rewards result in freedom from illness. Yet, if they were to hear Ānanda say that the Buddha is ill, [they would be deeply distressed].
This was deeply strange and difficult to comprehend. The Sūtra states that even a Cakravartin King, possessing but meager merit, still attains freedom from illness;
for a Cakravartin King, throughout three lifetimes, practices the ten wholesome paths, both performing them himself and teaching others to do so.
If such meager merit can still result in freedom from illness, how much more so for the Tathāgata, who has gathered immeasurable merit and is universally supreme? Thus it is said.
Having practiced the Mahāprajñāpāramitā for immeasurable kalpas, leading the myriad practices and attaining the ultimate truth of principle, one realizes the eternal bliss of Nirvāṇa;

how could such a person have illness? To say they have illness would mean their merit has diminished, which would be no different from the lands of a Wheel-Turning King, where sentient beings are merely gods of great majesty—would this not be a great loss?
"Go, Ānanda! Do not cause us to suffer such humiliation. If the non-Buddhist brahmins hear these words, they will think:
'What kind of teacher is this? Being unable to cure his own illness, how can he claim to cure the illnesses of others?
You must depart quickly and in secret so that no one hears you."
This constitutes the second point of the *Saṃyuktāgama* Sūtra on the Refutation of Exaggerated Blame, which states: "Go, Ānanda! Do not cause us to suffer such shame.
The intent of this reproach is as follows: if one were to say that the Tathāgata has illness, it would constitute an exaggerated blame.

To say that the Dharma-body, which is without illness, has illness is like saying that if there is a fruit of illness, there must necessarily be a cause for that illness; and the cause of illness is none other than evil.
If those with wholesome afflictions were like those with sickness and evil—namely, evil persons—how could they together take this as their teacher?
Since Ānanda is already a practitioner, he should not feel shame before his fellow practitioners; yet, had he spoken such words, it would have been to shame the fourfold assembly of Bodhisattvas.
Therefore, it is said: "Do not cause us to suffer such shame. As the Sūtra says:
If the non-Buddhist brahmins hear these words, they will think: "What kind of teacher is this?
Being unable to save oneself from one's own illness, how can he save others who are ill? This would mean that the teacher and his disciples are equally subject to disgrace.
Furthermore, it would cause those with increased false views to commit the grave sin of slander; such a thing must not happen.
Therefore, I urge you to depart secretly and swiftly so that no one hears of it;
for if others do not hear of it, this matter of shame will not be made public and you will avoid disgrace. To let others hear of it would only increase the sin of inciting their slander.
Ānanda, you should know that the bodies of all Tathāgatas are the Dharma-body, not bodies of thought or desire. The Buddha is the World-Honored One who has transcended the three realms;
the Buddha’s body is without outflows, for all taints have been exhausted. The Buddha’s body is unconditioned and does not fall within the realm of numerical categories.
How could such a body as this have any illness?

This is the fourfold layered explanation (*catuḥkoṭika-vyākhyāna*), which is the method of layered exposition: [the Buddha] refutes Ānanda’s view that the Dharma-body is without illness and his attachment to the idea that the birth-body (*janma-kāya*) has illness;
by speaking thus, he avoids the two fallacious views of exaggeration and depreciation.
Regarding this, there are four passages in the sūtra through which one should know that the Tathāgata’s body is the Dharma-body and not a body of thought or desire.

The explanation of the Dharma-body as being "severed from the merit of cessation" means that volition (*cetanā*) is precisely "action" (*saṃskāra*) and desire (*chanda*) is precisely "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*), among all such afflictions.

If afflictions were to conjoin with action, they would moisten karma and lead to rebirth; however, within the realm of the Dharma-body, both internal and external karma and afflictions have already been severed.
Therefore, it is said to be a "body that is neither volition nor desire. The reason for providing this explanation is precisely to refute the Tripiṭaka [teaching].

The *Sūtra on the Abiding in Nirvāṇa with Remainder* states that the Reward Body Buddha (*saṃbhogakāya*) still possesses minor ailments because he remains within the realm of the fruits of karma and afflictions;
yet, if one clings to this and asserts that [the Buddha] truly has illness, it constitutes the slander of exaggeration. The Sūtra says:

"The Buddha, the World-Honored One, transcends the three realms. This explains that the Dharma Body (*dharmakāya*), the wisdom-virtue of Great Prajñā, transcends the conditioned existence of birth and death (*bhavasaṃskāra*).
The two types of *yì* (transformation) exist beyond the three realms; how could there be the illness of the *saṃbhogakāya* within the realms?

This refers precisely to the breaking of the *piṭaka* teaching regarding the Buddha’s remaining birth-body (*sopadhiśeṣa-kāya*), which is still a human body within the realms and therefore possesses illness.
If one insists that he has illness, it constitutes a slanderous denial of the Sūtra, which states: "The Buddha’s body is without outflows (*anāsrava*); all outflows have been exhausted."

This is a further detailed explanation: because the Buddha’s Dharma-body has exhausted the two kinds of threefold outflows—those within the realms and those outside the realms—it does not fall into the two kinds of birth and death.
How could there be illness, which is the fruit of outflows within the realms?
This refutes the view that the Buddha residing in a "body of remaining birth" according to the Tripiṭaka Teaching still possesses the retribution of outflows.
If one has a slight illness and holds this [teaching] while claiming that having an illness constitutes an increase in slander, the Sūtra says:

"The Buddha’s body is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and does not fall into any numerical categories. This is a further explanation that the Dharma-body’s wisdom-virtue is unconditioned, eternally serene, neither a conditioned phenomenon within the realms (*dhātu*), nor a conditioned phenomenon outside the realms;
it is thus devoid of the two kinds of phenomena consisting of the provisional combinations of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*). How could this be so?
There exist within the realm the numerical dharmas of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*) that constitute karmic retribution; based on these, there is minor illness.

That is to say, according to the Tripiṭaka Teaching, even a Buddha who has manifested a physical body (*janmakāya*) and dwells in *nirvāṇa* with remainder still possesses the numerical dharmas of the aggregates, elements, and bases of karmic retribution;
because he relies upon these, he has illness. If one clings to this [interpretation] and asserts that [the Buddha] has illness, then [that claim] is established.
The passage from the *Dūṣaṇa-sūtra* stating, "In such a body as this, what illness could there possibly be? is a summary [of the preceding].
Since the Dharma-body is characterized by wisdom and the abandonment of defilements (*jñāna-prahāṇa*), and these four faults do not exist therein, how could it have illness?

By refuting Ānanda’s interpretation—which takes the intent of the Tripiṭaka teachings to mean that the birth-body Buddha (*janma-kāya-buddha*) has illness—one falls into two types of slander. The previous commentary on the chapter concerning Subhūti clarified the nature of such slander.
The meaning of "Buddha" is thus clarified here.
At that time, I, the World-Honored One, truly felt ashamed, thinking: "Could it be that, being close to the Buddha, I have misunderstood what was heard?
This is the third section, clarifying Ānanda’s internal sense of shame; according to the text, it consists of two parts, the first of which is the actual clarification.
Ānanda felt shame and remorse because he heard two voices in the air that consoled and exhorted him. First, it clarified Ānanda’s shame and remorse:

from time immemorial, he had considered himself a man of great learning (*bahuśruta*) who retained teachings without error; yet now, having been rebuked by the Great Being, he realized he had incurred the fault of dual slander.
This was a profound humiliation for both himself and his teachers, and thus he harbored shame and remorse within. Furthermore...
He thought to himself: "Though I am close to the Buddha, his sincere words cannot be dismissed as trivial;
it must be that I have misheard them, which is why I have been rebuked by this Great Being.
Immediately, he heard a voice from the air saying: "Ānanda, it is as the layman says; however, it is only because the Buddha has appeared in this world of five turbidities."
"Manifesting this Dharma, he practices the way of delivering sentient beings; Ānanda, take the milk and do not feel ashamed.

This is the second instance of light. Having heard the voice from mid-air, which was harmonious, penetrating, and consoling, Ānanda felt deep shame and remorse, fearing the sin of slandering the two [parents]. Therefore, the voice from mid-air explained and comforted him.
The voice from the sky must be the voice of the Dharmakāya of Vairocana, as clarified in the *Samantabhadra-darśana-sūtra*.
The Sūtra states that "it is as the householder says," meaning that Vimalakīrti preaches the Dharma;

since this body is fully endowed with wisdom and the severance of afflictions (*jñāna-prahāṇa*), it has no illness and does not need to beg for milk. This is the preaching of true wisdom, and its words are not false.
Furthermore, a sutra states: "It is solely for the sake of appearing in this world of five turbidities that the Buddha manifests these practices to deliver sentient beings.

The five turbidities are: first, the turbidity of the eon; second, the turbidity of afflictions; third, the turbidity of sentient beings; fourth, the turbidity of views; and fifth, the turbidity of lifespan.
If the Buddha appears in this evil world of the five turbidities to deliver disciples of dull faculties who are śrāvakas, he manifests as an inferior response-body."
Because he conforms to the ways of the world, his manifest illness is the teaching of expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).
Now, for the sake of converting the brahmins, it was necessary to take milk as a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*); thus, there is no need for weariness or shame.

This is the meaning of the difference between the true body (*dharmakāya*) and the response body (*nirmāṇakāya*): although the *dharmakāya* in its fundamental state (*mūlabhūmi*) is without illness, in its traces (*vyañjana*), the response body manifests illness through skillful means (*upāya*).
If one who benefits beings understands this intention, how could begging for milk constitute the two types of slander? There is no need for shame or remorse.
Such is the wisdom and eloquence of the World-Honored One Vimalakīrti; therefore, I am not fit to go to him to inquire after his illness.
This is the fourth point establishing that Ānanda was incapable [of this task]. Vimalakīrti, reflecting upon his own Mahāyāna erudition and eloquence, had previously rebuked and censured him;
at that time, Ānanda did not know how to respond. How could he possibly be fit to transmit the Tathāgata’s intent and go to inquire after his illness?
Thus, each of these five hundred great disciples spoke to the Buddha regarding their own past causes and conditions, recounting the words spoken by Vimalakīrti,
and all said, "We are unable to go to him to inquire after his illness."

This is the second major section. Since the original text of the *Sūtra on the Second Summoning of the Five Hundred Great Disciples to Inquire about Their Illness* is concise, it has not been translated here in full.
If all five hundred were rebuked by Vimalakīrti, it would mean that these five hundred bhikṣus had each entered the Path based on the teachings of the Tripiṭaka;
Vimalakīrti, in turn, used the five hundred Mahāyāna dharmas to respond to them.
The teachings that refute, suppress, differentiate specific characteristics, and reveal the principles of decay and flourishing have already been expounded by Master Men;
since their texts were not transmitted to this land, how could one possibly apply one's mind to interpreting them?
Commentary on the Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra, Scroll Fifteen;
Commentary on the Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra, Scroll Sixteen (The Fourth Chapter: Bodhisattvas, Part One).
This chapter follows the "Chapter on Disciples" and constitutes the third [section], which serves to refute the dharma-realm as having an intrinsic nature.

The purpose for the arrival of this chapter is manifold, as it teaches how the inconceivable Dharma-body of liberation, manifested through the gathering of conditions, accomplishes the purification of the Buddha-land of a Tathāgata;
how could this be measured by ordinary intellect? Now, I shall briefly provide an exegesis of the textual meaning of this chapter using three points:
first, to explicitly clarify the purpose for the arrival of this chapter; second, to briefly explain the [meaning of] Bodhi...
The Third Section on the Meaning of "Sat" (薩), Part One: Explanation of the Text.

This chapter follows the Chapter on the Disciples because the Great Sage, the Dharma King, desires to enable sentient beings to attain the inconceivable *dharmakāya* as their primary retribution (*pratyaya-vedanīya*) and liberation, and to establish pure Buddha-lands as their secondary retribution (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
Therefore, he previously commanded his great disciples, each of whom recounted their own inability [to fulfill this task].

Because the śrāvakas rely on the teachings of the Tripiṭaka, they all take partial truth as their realization and are entirely obstructed by the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) due to the conditions of their accumulation [of merit and knowledge].
Consequently, each declined when previously summoned, and were all rebuked by Vimalakīrti; how could they possibly be capable of transmitting the intent of the Tathāgata?

Since the bodhisattvas do not take partial truth as their realization and do not remain obstructed by the unconditioned due to the conditions of their accumulation, the [Tathāgata] next commands them.

However, although Bodhisattvas do not stagnate in the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) through the gathering of conditions, they still suffer from the affliction of having a self-substance through the gathering of conditions within the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
For this reason, in the past, Vimalakīrti rebuked them all;

this indicates that what is elucidated by the three teachings is entirely expedient means, and that the true reward of the inconceivable Dharmakāya has not yet been revealed—the meaning of the truly pure Buddha-land as the objective environment (niśraya-pratisthāna).
Because [the illness] was not yet cured, each of the bodhisattvas declined, stating they were unable to convey the Tathāgata’s intent to go inquire after his illness.
Now, to clarify the purpose for the arrival of this chapter, there are briefly five points: first, to manifest the inconceivable, supreme wisdom of Vimalakīrti;
second, to transform the gates of skillful means (*upāya*); third, to support the teaching on the Buddha-land; and fourth, to subdue [those who are arrogant].

The Bodhisattva dwelling in the practice of skillful means, in order to enter the gateway to the Great Vehicle, the Lotus Sūtra, and Nirvāṇa, must perfect the five seals through these five intentions.
Although the names and numbers of these five roughly correspond to those in the "Chapter on the Disciples," their meanings differ and must not be indiscriminately conflated.
The first is for the purpose of manifesting the inconceivable and supreme wisdom of Vimalakīrti.
Although the great disciples mentioned above recounted being rebuked by Vimalakīrti without offering a response, their wisdom and realization as śrāvakas transcend the three realms;
yet, since they belong to the Hīnayāna and their merit and wisdom are narrow and shallow, how could they suffice to fully manifest the divine wisdom of Vimalakīrti?
It would be like competing in strength with a small child—it would not be considered a feat of prowess. For this reason, he next commanded the four great bodhisattvas and the other great ones...

The Master ordered [the disciples] to go inquire after his illness; if they all reported that he was unable to bear it, then the entire assembly would hear that Vimalakīrti’s wisdom and virtue were so lofty and far-reaching as to transcend all others, such that there would be none who did not give rise to reverence in their hearts and none who did not submit.
If Mañjuśrī were then commanded to enter the room to discuss the Way, everyone would receive the great benefit of the Dharma. This intention seems to be for the sake of those within the room.

The preface consists only of the remaining four meanings, all of which are the main exposition; since this is discussed according to the majority of cases, they cannot be classified as belonging to the preface.
As for the second point previously analyzed in various places—that it serves as a "teaching-gate of expedient means for turning"—this is also the meaning of "turning contemplation.
Why is this so? If one is a bodhisattva of dull faculties, this constitutes "turning the teaching"; this is precisely...
Those who practice through faith are those of dull faculties; if they are bodhisattvas of sharp faculties, they are practitioners who transform their contemplation of these dharmas.

Regarding this, there are two parts: first, clarifying the meaning of transforming the teaching; second, clarifying the meaning of transforming the contemplation. First, regarding the meaning of transforming the teaching:

because the Buddha perceived that bodhisattvas of dull faculties were unable to hear the teaching for entering the Buddha-way through the perfect [round] approach, he opened up the provisional [square] approach.

He then instructed the gatekeeper to welcome and guide these bodhisattvas who had practiced various skillful means; having been matured by those dull faculties, they were now capable of hearing the Perfect Teaching (Vimalakīrtinirdeśa) to enter the Path.

Now, wishing to turn them away from the teachings of skillful means, he caused the bodhisattvas who had practiced various skillful means to each be rebuked and humbled by Vimalakīrti in their past lives.
Now, wishing to turn them toward the provisional [truth] through the reality of the ultimate, this must be done again.

The account of universally causing [the news] to be heard and known, followed by the command for the various bodhisattvas to go and inquire after his illness, consists of three distinct types of successive instruction (*parāvṛtti*).
First, the turning of the provisional teachings of the Tripiṭaka; second, the turning of the provisional teachings within the *Prajñāpāramitā* of the night of attaining the Way;
and third, the turning of the provisional teachings within the *Avataṃsaka*. Regarding the first, the turning of the provisional teachings of the Tripiṭaka: it is as follows—
There are two meanings: first, gradual transformation; second, sudden transformation. Regarding gradual transformation:
for bodhisattvas of dull faculties, the initial teaching is the same as the five flavors taught to the śrāvakas, yet there is a slight difference in terms of the persons involved. Why is this so?
Because the three vehicles study the Tripiṭaka together; when the two vehicles sever their fetters, they become "curd," and thus both the teaching and the person are curd.
The Bodhisattva’s subduing of the fetters through the *śrāvaka* teachings is like curd; these people are still like milk. Regarding those who undergo sudden transformation:

*śrāvakas* cannot undergo sudden transformation within the Vaipulya (*fangděng*) teachings, whereas those of keen faculties among the Bodhisattvas of the Tripiṭaka teachings can immediately undergo sudden transformation within these Vaipulya teachings by entering the Dharma-gate of non-duality. This is precisely what is meant by "indefinite" [lineage].

The intent of the teaching is like fresh butter mixed with poison that kills when ingested. Second, regarding the teaching on the transformation of skillful means as clarified in the *Rātriprātihārya-prajñāpāramitā*:
the *Rātriprātihārya-prajñāpāramitā* is itself the Buddha; from the night of his attainment of the Way until his entry into *nirvāṇa*, he constantly preached the *prajñā*.
If this teaching were contained within the Tripiṭaka, it would have been taught for the sake of those of sharp faculties and thus kept secret.

If Esoteric Buddhism were not included within the Three Baskets (Tripitaka) and were instead heard separately by the various Bodhisattvas, it would constitute an "indeterminate teaching" (aniyata-vinaya).
However, this very [teaching] originated from the Deer Park and expounds the Prajñāpāramitā, fully clarifying the three types of wisdom (*trividya*).
Within this, there are three kinds of Bodhisattvas; the first two kinds of Bodhisattvas are those who receive the Prajñā and the skillful means (*upāya*).
Regarding the teaching gates, the *Vimalakīrti* employs the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) to refute and correct.

If it refutes a Bodhisattva of the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*) who dwells in "all-knowledge" (*sarvajñatā*) yet perceives the Middle Way, this is like poison arising within fresh butter that kills the person.

If it refutes one who has received the *Prajñāpāramitā* of the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*) and attained the "knowledge of the categories of phenomena" (*dharmajñāna*), such that they are able to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, this is "matured."

If one suffers from the poison of ignorance and kills others, yet possesses the Prajñāpāramitā and cultivates the omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) of the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*), then there is the need for refutation or no need for refutation.
That which does not require refutation is precisely one who has deeply grasped the meaning of the Perfect Teaching;

such a person neither clings to views of arising nor gives rise to the craving for the Dharma that obstructs the Path. Therefore, there is no need for refutation. For this reason, it is necessary [to distinguish between these cases].
Although those who criticize [the Bodhisattvas] have received the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao), they fail to grasp its true intent;
because their views arise from literal speech, they occasionally give rise to attachment to the Dharma that accords with the Path. Since such faults exist, they are rebuked by Vimalakīrti.

If the mind opens and awakens to enter the Dharma-gate of non-duality, it is like the "supreme cream" (tíhú) in which poison has been introduced, killing the person. This refers to the third type of Bodhisattva.

If one receives the *Huayan* [Avataṃsaka] through its provisional (*upāya*) and distinct (*vyatireka*) teachings, and cultivates the path with the seed-wisdom of the stages (*bhūmi-jñāna*), yet remains biased and attached, one will be rebuked by Vimalakīrti.
Even if the mind attains awakening, it is like consuming matured butter that has been poisoned—the poison will manifest and kill.

If one receives the *Huayan* through its perfect (*pariniṣpanna*) teaching, then there is neither rebuke nor non-rebuke. By analogy, the gains and losses of receiving the perfect teaching of the *Prajñāpāramitā* can be understood in the same way.
Furthermore, one should know that regarding the four flavors [of the teachings], whether one has attained the intended meaning (*abhiprāya*) or not, both are subject to censure.
Why is this? Those who adhere to their practice and give rise to views have not attained the intended meaning and must therefore be censured.

Although they may equally follow the teachings and practices to sever delusions, these are not yet the reality (*tattva*); thus, they must be censured so as to lead them into reality. This applies if one receives the teachings of reality.
Those who have not attained the intended meaning must be rebuked; those who have attained it need not be rebuked.
If discursive views arise, or if attachment to the Dharma that accords with the Way arises such that one fails to accord with the principle, one must rebuke them.

If discursive views do not arise and attachment to the Dharma does not arise, one will naturally attain [the goal] without needing to be rebuked. Question: For what reason is this so? Answer: Because...

The previous submission regarding the provisional teachings (*upāya-śāsana*) states that since the teachings given to people are both discarded, it follows that neither [type of practitioner] can be subject to censure.

The latter submission concerns the Bodhisattvas of the Perfect Teaching (*pūrṇa-yāna*): for those who practice according to these teachings without abandoning them, and who have attained their realization, there is no need for censure.

This chapter explains that while the Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching (*sāmānya-yāna*) and the Distinct Teaching (*viśeṣa-yāna*) are consistently refuted and broken down, the Bodhisattvas of the Perfect Teaching are not.

Alternatively, [the text] may suggest that while the teachings of the preliminary expedient means (*upāya*) are criticized along with the illness, the subsequent reception of the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-dharma*) involves criticizing the illness but not the teaching. One must constantly keep this in mind; when you reach the passage below, do not harbor doubts.
Furthermore, if one follows the view that the *Prajñāpāramitā* was taught from the night he attained the Way...
If there are those with bodies belonging to the Shared Teaching (tongjiao), they should immediately attain the Way through the Two Vehicles. Question:
Must it be the case that the Bodhisattvas of Expedient Means (fangbian) are invariably subject to censure? Answer:

Since this teaching has not yet reached the level of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, and since some may still derive benefit from the expedient means, I fear it cannot be entirely discarded; it merely serves to reveal the true Mahāyāna.

Because the intention is clear, it is judged as before. Alternatively, it may be that the preliminary skillful means (*upāya*) teachings for bodhisattvas merely censure the illness but do not censure the dharma;
this requires further distinction. If one refers to the person practicing the path, then both the dharma and the illness are censured.
If, however, it concerns the dharma of skillful means, then this dharma is the dharma of the Tathāgata’s skillful means.

"If one intends to receive the Dharma from future generations, it is sufficient that those who came before have abandoned their illnesses; it is not strictly necessary that they abandon the Dharma. Question:

"The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is a teaching of the Perfect and Sudden (yuanton). How can it be that Bodhisattvas who study this teaching must still censure and rebuke others while transmitting the teaching?
Answer: "The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is like the rising sun, which first shines upon the high mountains. Those of sharp faculties [are like the high mountains]."

Since Bodhisattvas have already attained awakening therein, why would they need to break through it? However, those among the deities seated there whose faculties are inferior still require the guidance of the Separate Teaching (Pṛthagdeśanā).
This Separate Teaching does not depart from the true intent of the *Avataṃsaka*;

rather, it must be criticized and corrected so that they may return to the ocean of the perfect and sudden Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) of the *Avataṃsaka*. Or, even if they have heard the *Avataṃsaka*...
If one clings to the teachings of the Perfect and Sudden as literal truth and gives rise to verbal views, one will not attain awakening;
therefore, it is necessary to use censure to lead them into the ocean of the Huayan Dharma-realm.

Thus, the censure and critique by Vimalakīrti was intended to eliminate the stagnation of those who have missed the true meaning of the Huayan, rather than to censure the wheel of the Dharma of the Sudden Teaching itself. Question: Furthermore, the sutra says: [The remainder of the text follows...]
From the night he attained the Way until the night of his parinirvāṇa, the Buddha constantly preached the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra. The Buddha answered Kāśyapa:
"Since I attained the Way, Bodhisattvas from the ten directions have come to inquire about this meaning.

Among them, there must also be Bodhisattvas who, despite their skillful means, have not yet fully understood it; why then do they not express this intention? He replied: "Although such an intention exists..."
Since there is no explicit textual evidence to suggest that from the very moment he first attained the Way he preached a Nirvana distinct from the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Prajñāpāramitā*,
it would follow that there must have been practitioners who clung to expedient means or were stalled in the Perfect [Teaching], and were thus rebuked by Vimalakīrti. If, on the other hand,
these [texts] are merely alternative names for the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Prajñāpāramitā*, then the previous clarification regarding his censure and rebuke would already encompass this meaning.
He also asked: "Is the Prajñā taught from the night of attaining the Way simply another name for the Avataṃsaka, or should it be understood as having a distinct subject matter?
He replied: "If one consults the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra, it clarifies that there are two kinds of Prajñā:
first, that taught in common with those of the Two Vehicles; second, that not shared with the Two Vehicles, such as the Prajñā taught in the *Acintya-sūtra*."
According to this text, it appears that *Avataṃsaka* is likely an alternative name for *Prajñāpāramitā*. Furthermore, a verse in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* praising *Prajñā* states:
"If one contemplates the Buddha, *Prajñā*, and *Nirvāṇa* according to the Dharma, these three are of one characteristic;
in reality, there is no difference between them. Thus, while *Avataṃsaka* derives its name from "Great Vaipulya Buddha," *Prajñā* is likewise derived from [the same source].
Wisdom is designated by the term "reception" (*vedanā*), while Nirvana is named according to liberation (*vimukti*).

If one follows this treatise, there is no logical fault in the fact that the three sūtras have different names in different schools; it is also not an impediment for the three sūtras to be merely different names for a single school.
Since no explicit textual evidence from the sūtras or śāstras has been seen regarding their identity or difference, they cannot be definitively adjudicated. Question: From... [text continues].
Question: Before the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*’s critique and censure, there should also have been various Vaipulya teachings;
since bodhisattvas who received these teachings were hindered by attachments, Vimalakīrti’s critique and his subsequent turning of the teaching—why does this intention not appear therein? Answer:

Because it cannot yet be definitively determined whether such matters existed or not, they are not separately set forth. Second, it clarifies the benefit of the dharma-practice for those who turn [the teaching] into contemplation.

When a person of keen faculties dwells within the gates of contemplation according to their respective skillful means, if they hear a Great Being censure various bodhisattvas, they immediately shift their contemplation.

Such a person, having heard the teachings of the Tripitaka, or having heard the teaching on Prajñā given by the Buddha at night after his attainment of the Way, or having heard the skillful means and distinct teachings of the *Avataṃsaka*, immediately gains faith, understanding, and awakening. However—
According to their respective understandings, they still relied on expedient contemplations and interpretations, remaining biased and failing to see the true Path.
When they heard the Great Being rebuke the various bodhisattvas, their minds suddenly opened and their intentions were liberated, and each attained entry into the Dharma-gate of non-duality.

Furthermore, if there are bodhisattvas who have heard the Tripiṭaka or attained the Way through it, yet upon hearing the teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā from that night onward, [their understanding is transformed].

Alternatively, upon hearing the teachings of the *Avataṃsaka*, one may immediately resolve to practice according to what little has been heard; this is still the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), like milk.
If one enters emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and gives rise to the true vision of principle, this is like curd.

If one proceeds from emptiness into the provisional (*upāya*) and perceives the conventional through the Dharma-eye, this is like fresh butter (*navanīta*). If one gives rise to an understanding of the semblance Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratibhāsa*), this is like matured butter (*ghṛta*).
If one gives rise to the true understanding of the Middle Way, that is the *amṛta* (clarified butter).
If, upon hearing the Great Being’s censure of the bodhisattvas’ initial resolve, one immediately awakens to and enters the Dharma-gate of non-duality, this is like poison in milk that kills.
If one enters the view of emptiness while claiming to have truly attained entry into the Dharma-gate of non-duality, this is like poison in curd that kills.
If one perceives the mundane and attains entry into the Dharma-gate of non-duality, it is like being killed by the poison of raw ghee;
if one attains entry into the Dharma-gate of non-duality through a semblance understanding of the Middle Way, it is like being killed by the poison of matured ghee;
if one perceives the true Middle Way and further enters the higher stages, this is the stage of clarified butter (*hṛdaya*).
That the poison was activated and killed the man was, in fact, the Great Being’s past act of striking the various bodhisattvas with hammers and anvils to perfect their bodhisattva practices.
At that time, each of them individually gained benefit; now, this great assembly all possesses the capacity to hear [this teaching].
Therefore, the Tathāgata next commanded the various bodhisattvas to inquire after his illness, and each recounted the matters of being struck in the past.

Thus, the great assembly at this gathering shall all partake in the benefit of the successive teaching and successive contemplation, just as they previously obtained benefit from the reproach [of Vimalakīrti];
it is for this purpose that he next commands the bodhisattvas to inquire after his illness.
Furthermore, in the past, the various bodhisattvas heard [the Dharma] in different places, and the benefit was not extensive; now, Āmra has gathered a multitude as vast as the sands of the Ganges.

The assembly surrounded the World-Honored One and together heard this reiteration, which brings immeasurable benefit. Since it was personally authorized by the Buddha, the meaning of the transmission of the teaching is finally established as definitive.

Question: If the Great Being rebukes the various bodhisattvas using only a single teaching, how can all of them be universally benefited? Answer: Even our Master [Confucius] said regarding the *Shijing* (Book of Poetry): "The Odes are the foundation for the cultivation of character. If even the teachings of the sages can transform people through a single principle, how much more so the Dharma of the Tathāgata? It is like the case of the *Yuefu* (Music Bureau) songs: though they are but one melody, they move the hearts of the multitude. Therefore, although the Great Being employs a single teaching, it is able to bring universal benefit. This is because the Dharma is inherently profound and vast; when applied with skillful means, it can respond to the capacities of beings and lead them to liberation. Thus, the single teaching is sufficient to encompass all. This is why the World-Honored One, having first delivered the *Prajñāpāramitā*, subsequently expounded the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Nirvāṇa*, and other sutras—each according to the specific needs of those to be transformed. Although the gates of the Dharma are diverse, their ultimate purpose is one. It is like the waters of the four great rivers: though their courses differ, they all flow toward the great ocean.

Therefore, we know that the single teaching of the Great Being is indeed capable of bringing universal benefit. Furthermore, the *Lotus Sūtra* states: "The Buddhas of the three times all rely on this one vehicle to deliver sentient beings. This confirms that the single teaching is the very source of universal salvation. Thus, the meaning of the transmission is fully established.

"Three hundred [sayings], one word summarizes them all. When the Great Beings (Mahāsattvas) employ the One Perfect Teaching (Ekayāna) to reprove and admonish those Bodhisattvas who are hindered by attachments to the provisional and the real, all of them derive benefit from the Single Path; how could there be any cause for doubt? Question:
"When the Great Beings reprove the Bodhisattvas, do they necessarily all obtain the benefit of the One Perfect Teaching? Answer: "Yes, they do."
Regarding the passage from the *Wǎngxún hāsìdà púsà wén* (The Text on Seeking the Four Great Bodhisattvas), it appears that all [the bodhisattvas] provide complete benefit;

however, since each bodhisattva describes their own text and none of them has yet crossed over [to liberation], how can one definitively judge this? Furthermore, as various Vaipulya sutras still retain elements of expedient means (*upāya*) and their clarifications of the meaning have not yet attained immediate identity with the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, how could it be permissible to claim that they entirely lack the expedient benefit of responding to the capacities of sentient beings? This is merely...

Third, regarding the manifestation of the teaching of the Pure Land: when rebuked in this manner, the bodhisattvas who have received the teachings of the provisional gates gather according to their conditions;

at the very point where they sever [delusions], their offenses are eliminated, hindrances are transformed, and their merit and wisdom increase and become luminous, such that they are capable of seeing the Pure Land.
Thus, upon entering the room, they see together that the room is empty, and they further behold the Pure Land of Lamp-King Buddha and the Buddha of Fragrant Accumulation.
Furthermore, according to the convergence of their respective conditions and the severance of their afflictions, beings are born in each of the three lands.
Moreover, as their merit and wisdom increase and clarify, and as they bring sentient beings to maturity, when they attain Buddhahood, all such beings come to be born in their land.
This accords with and completes the teaching on purifying the Buddha-land as expounded by the Tathāgata above. Chapter [Number].
Fourth, regarding those who are the heirs of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and the *Nirvāṇa* as gateways for entry:

as stated in the *Dharmadhātuprakṛti-śāstra*, "If a person of sharp faculties enters the *dharmadhātu* through the *Mahāprajñā*; if a person of middling faculties enters the *dharmadhātu* through the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*;
and if a person of inferior faculties enters the *dharmadhātu* through the *Nirvāṇa*—this is like treating raw ghee until it becomes matured."

Because *sarpis* (clarified butter) is produced from *dadhi* (curd), the *Prajñāpāramitā* constitutes the *ghṛta* (ghee) teaching; thus, through the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, one enters the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Because *dadhi* is said to be produced from *kṣīra* (milk), the *Prajñāpāramitā* is the *navanīta* (fresh butter);

because it becomes *ghṛta* in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, one enters the Dharma-realm within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Because *dadhi* is produced from *kṣīra*, [the teaching] reaches the state of *navanīta* at the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*.
Clarified butter reaches the stage of *sarpis* at the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and reaches the stage of *ghṛta* (the finest essence) at *Nirvāṇa*;
within this Great *Nirvāṇa*, one attains entry into the *dharmadhātu*. If it were not thus, one could not cause those of superior, middling, and inferior faculties to enter the *dharmadhātu*;
therefore, it is said that [this scripture] serves as the gateway for entering the *prajñā*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and *Nirvāṇa*. Question: Regarding this sutra...
Since it has already been clarified that one enters the inconceivable liberation, how can it not be clarified that one enters the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*)? The answer is:

What was explained above regarding the turning of the teaching and the turning of contemplation to enter the gate of non-duality (*advayadharma-mukha*) is none other than entering the *Avataṃsaka* Dharma-realm;

it is simply that those who have not yet realized this entry must wait until the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and the *Nirvāṇa* sūtras. Question: If that is so, then the Dharma-realm...
Question: With what intention was the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* (Nature Treatise) not explained [in detail], while the *Vaipulya* sūtras were?

Answer: The *Vaipulya* sūtras and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Great Chapter) are largely the same with minor differences. Because they are largely the same, explaining the entry into the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* is itself an explanation of the entry into the *Vaipulya*.

As for the minor differences, these are simply distinctions like those between fresh butter (*navanīta*) and clarified butter (*ghṛta*). Question: Previously, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (Lotus Sūtra) was explained for those of sharp faculties; now, regarding the *Dharmadhātu*...
Question: How can the *Xinglun* (Treatise on Nature) clarify that the *Dapin* (Large Perfection of Wisdom Sutra) is for those of superior faculties? Answer:
The preceding [discussion] judged according to the people of the Three Vehicles, whereas the *Xinglun* judges according to the One Buddha Vehicle. Question:

Previously, in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning), you judged the phases of the teaching by stating that the *Nirvana Sutra* and the *Lotus Sutra* are equally the "ghee" (*tíhú*). Why is it now possible for such a state to be reached only at the *Lotus Sutra*?
The Mature Ghee (Śṛta-ghṛta) replies: "Previously, in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning), you categorized the five flavors according to the teachings;

thus, the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* were certainly both assigned to the stage of ghee. Now, however, this categorization of the five flavors is made according to the persons [who receive them];
therefore, when reaching the *Lotus Sūtra*, there are those who are like mature ghee. He replies: "Such is the question. The fifth [section] serves to confirm the sūtra by clarifying the past."
Although the reprimands directed at specific individuals provided immediate benefit at the time, they were not authorized by the Buddha;

what was spoken by his disciples and bodhisattvas cannot be designated as "sūtra. Therefore, if he did not now command them to inquire after his illness, there would be no opportunity to recount the wondrous teachings of Vimalakīrti from the past.
For this reason, he next commanded the various bodhisattvas to inquire after his illness.
Each [of the four great bodhisattvas] recounts the events of their past rebukes;

this is what the Pure Name (Vimalakīrti) previously taught, which the great assembly heard together, was authenticated by the Tathāgata as a sūtra, and circulated for the benefit of future generations.

For these five reasons, it is necessary that the four great bodhisattvas and the other bodhisattvas be successively commanded to inquire after his illness. This is the second [section], the "Proper" [inquiry].
The "Chapter Explaining the Bodhisattva" explains the meaning of the term "bodhisattva" in full accordance with the previous explanation in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning).

However, the four teachings differ in how they clarify the bodhisattva: first, the bodhisattva as clarified in the Tripitaka Teaching arises from the Four Noble Truths of arising and ceasing to give rise to vows of compassion and resolve for bodhicitta;
for three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, they cultivate the six *pāramitās* of arising and ceasing.

1. The *Pāramitā* [teaching] subdues the afflictions within the realm of desire; through full maturity, one enters the stage of *avaivartika*. 2. The *Sāmānya-śāsana* (Shared Teaching) clarifies the meaning of the Bodhisattva:

by taking the four truths of non-arising as its object, one gives rise to compassionate vows, generates the bodhicitta, practices the six *pāramitās* of non-arising, and severs the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) within the realm of desire to enter the stage of *avaivartika*. 3. The Distinct [Teaching].

The Teaching of the Mahāyāna clarifies the meaning of the Bodhisattva: based on the immeasurable Four Noble Truths, one gives rise to the compassionate vow, generates the bodhicitta, practices the immeasurable Six Pāramitās up to the Ten Pāramitās, severs the ignorance as vast as the sands of the Ganges and the distinct delusions beyond the realm [of conditioned existence], and enters the stage of Avaivartika (non-retrogression).
This is the clarification of the meaning of the Bodhisattva according to the Fourth, Perfect Teaching.
Based on the non-conceptual (*anabhisaṃskāra*) Four Noble Truths, one gives rise to the compassionate vow, awakens the bodhicitta,

and cultivates the non-conceptual Six Pāramitās, up to the Ten Pāramitās, thereby perfectly severing the ignorance of views and thoughts within the dharma-realm and entering the stage of *avaivartika*.

The four teachings clarify that the stages of the bodhisattva’s awakening of the mind and their practice differ in both horizontal and vertical dimensions, and these are likewise fully contained herein.

As previously distinguished in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning), it is simply that the Great Sage, within the four [aspects of] the "inexpressible," employs the four *siddhāntas* because there are causes and conditions;
he accords with the different capacities and conditions—namely, the four types of seekers of the Buddha-way:
inferior, middling, superior, and the most superior—and thus teaches these four doctrines. The meaning of the Bodhisattva is likewise not the same in each. The first three are provisional (*upāya*).
If the latter one were the ultimate reality, it would not be both provisional and real;
yet, what is here called the "Bodhisattva Chapter" refers to the four great bodhisattvas and all other bodhisattvas who are the retinue of the Dharma-body of Śākyamuni Tathāgata.

These Tathāgatas have manifested in this land to respond to conditions and benefit sentient beings, displaying the four kinds of Buddha-bodies and preaching the Mahayana teachings of the four methods. They are the Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-body.
The Buddha likewise manifests four types of bodhisattvas according to the capacities of those who encounter him, so that they may serve as attendants to the Dharma King.
He guides and receives these four types of sentient beings with whom he has a karmic affinity, each of whom faithfully accepts and practices their respective skillful means.

When the path of contemplation of these three types of bodhisattvas has been somewhat perfected, the Tathāgata intends to transform their contemplation and lead them to study the Perfect Teaching (the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*).
In teaching the ultimate path of the Mahāyāna, if one does not first refute the teacher, the disciple’s dogmatic attachments will ultimately remain unalterable;
it is impossible for the Buddha himself to preach the teaching and for the bodhisattva to apply it to beings such that they suddenly change their tracks and alter their course on their own.
Such a thing is inconceivable. Since the Great Being Vimalakīrti has, from the outset, predominantly manifested as residing within the Perfect Teaching (Eka-yāna), [he proceeds accordingly].
Because they belong to the higher stages, they are able to reprove and admonish through various skillful means (*upāya*).

When Bodhisattvas of each successive higher stage cause their respective retinues—who abide in the teachings of skillful means and practice the bodhisattva path—to bend and submit, those retinues all fix their minds in inward humility, disparaging their own practices as not yet being the ultimate truth.
There is none among them who does not look up with admiration for the inconceivable, perfect, and true Great [Vehicle].

Some may have immediately given rise to the Bodhicitta of the Perfect Teaching (Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa), while others may have attained sudden enlightenment and entered inconceivable liberation, gaining the true patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). All such instances result from the skillful guidance of these four great Bodhisattvas and other Mahāsattvas;
now, as the Tathāgata commands you to inquire after his illness, each of you should recount your past experiences.
Regarding the matter of being rebuked: it was precisely at this time of great benefit that the assembly of the great multitude attained the five kinds of benefits previously mentioned;

therefore, it is called the "Bodhisattva Chapter. Question: Since the thirty-two thousand bodhisattvas were all at the stage of "neighboring the fruit" (sāmantaka-phala) and their status was no different from that of Vimalakīrti, for what reason were they all suddenly rebuked and refuted by Vimalakīrti? Answer: It is as follows:
Although the meaning has been briefly clarified, as there are many points, I shall now provide a concise explanation.
Some masters say that these bodhisattvas are the actual *anupūrvika-phala* (neighboring fruits), whereas the name "Pure" (*viśuddha*) refers to the provisional *anupūrvika-phala*, which is superior.
Other masters say they are equally neighboring fruits, as the *Renwang Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "The ten stages have three births; these bodhisattvas are the beginning."
The stage of "arising and abiding in arising" (sheng-zhu-sheng) is the position of the Pure Name (Vimalakīrti), which is the ultimate stage of birth; among all bodhisattvas, it is the most supreme.

Now, we shall provide a correct analysis and interpretation: both the bodhisattvas and Vimalakīrti possess both the fundamental (ben) and the manifested (ji), as well as the provisional (quan) and the real (shi). In terms of the provisional, they are identical; in terms of the real, they are identical.
They are merely great beings of the Dharma-body who have come together to assist the Buddha in manifesting the two aspects of the provisional and the real.

Teaching to bring sentient beings to fulfillment refers to these four great beings and all other bodhisattvas who, though having entered extinction, employ skillful means (*upāya*) to assist in establishing the provisional teachings, as seen in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* and the case of Aṅgulimāla, where the provisional reveals the ultimate to assist in establishing the ultimate teaching. "Provisional" is like the anvil and "ultimate" is like the hammer;

together they bring sentient beings to completion. If one discusses benefiting beings, both the provisional and the ultimate provide benefit; if one discusses the striking and stimulating [of realization], [the ultimate does so].
The striking of the mallet and the receiving of the anvil are both inconceivable matters;

that they together benefit sentient beings is something not even known by the followers of the Two Vehicles or the lesser bodhisattvas—how much less could ordinary people of the mundane world know the relative heights and depths of their fundamental and manifested traces?
A question is asked: "In the above, the ten disciples corresponded to the ten mental factors to jointly assist the Dharma King, thereby manifesting and perfecting the Half and Full Teachings."
The five hundred followers of the two teachings each spoke of the causes for the body’s attainment of the Way; Vimalakīrti refuted them all, and each had his own reason.
Now, what do these four great bodhisattvas represent? The answer is:

these four bodhisattvas are likely like the rain of four kinds of flowers in the *Lotus Sūtra*, which symbolizes opening, showing, awakening, and entering. Furthermore, the *Lotus Sūtra* clarifies the lower [capacities].
Just as they were about to leap forth, there appeared four great leaders who likewise manifested and revealed the stages of opening, showing, awakening, and entering;
from among the thirty-two thousand, only these four were selected, which should correspond to these four dharma-gates.

Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* clarifies that Rocana Buddha empowered four great bodhisattvas to expound the forty stages, beginning with Dharmamati, who spoke on the merits of the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*).
De-lin says that Vajradhvaja speaks of the ten practices, Vajragarbha speaks of the ten dedications, and [Vajragarbha] speaks of the ten stages;
if one searches for this meaning within the text of this chapter, it appears as though such an intention exists. How is this known?

For instance, when Maitreya is questioned, he proceeds solely toward the principle of the quiescent extinction of *tathatā* (suchness) to manifest bodhi; this is likely intended to open up the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*).

One should know that all sentient beings are the very state of Bodhi; this reveals the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*) and clarifies the characteristics of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) according to the Perfect Teaching (*ekayāna*).
Next, [the text] critiques the description of various *bodhimaṇḍas* by Vimalakīrti, fearing it might be taken as a mere representation of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

Vimalakīrti explains the meaning of all *bodhimaṇḍas*: first, that "all practices (*sarvacaryā*) are none other than the *bodhimaṇḍa*"—this is precisely what reveals the Buddha’s [knowledge and vision].

This is the knowledge and vision of the characteristics of the ten practices. Next, one rebukes and sustains worldly awakening, causing them to know that the suchness of the realm of Māra and the suchness of the Buddha-realm are identical, being one suchness without duality.
One realizes that the retinues of Māra all delight in the Buddha-dharma and cultivate the lamp of inexhaustibility;
this is to be unobstructed and unimpeded regarding phenomena and principle, able to transform the works of Māra into the works of the Buddha.

To enter the works of Māra through the works of the Buddha, so that good and evil are harmonized and both are mastered with sovereign ease—fearing lest one should attempt to awaken to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision—this is the characteristic of the tenth stage of Dedication (*daśamī pariṇāmanā*).
Next, it is said that by practicing generosity (*dāna*), one attains excellence:

being able to regard the high and low of the objective field as non-dual constitutes the gift of Dharma within the gift of material wealth; thus, within the gift of material wealth, one fully possesses all requisites.

To stand upon all dharmas, to revere the Tathāgata Duṣprasaha above and to succor beggars below, treating the two fields of compassion and respect as equal without distinction—this is precisely the assembly for the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*).
Fearing that this might be compared to the realization of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*), it is the characteristic mark of the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*).
Vimalakīrti’s rebuke contains many implications; with a single sound there are diverse interpretations—why must it necessarily correspond exclusively to the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpannayāna*)?
The four positions are merely a preliminary inquiry into the general meaning of the text; I fear it must be as such. Question:

If this is so, Maitreya is precisely the one who is next to attain Buddhahood (the *upapadya-parinirvāyin*); he ought to manifest the profound. How can he manifest the shallow? Answer: Because he is a Great Being and a Superior, he was specifically commanded [to appear] beforehand.
Furthermore, the Dharma’s principle requires that one proceed from the shallow to the profound; therefore, in response to Maitreya, it was necessary to open up the Buddha’s knowledge.
Furthermore, although these four stages are presented here in response to others, the primary intent does not lie in their relative depth or shallowness.
Why is this so? The Perfect Teaching clarifies that from the very first stage, all the merits of every stage are fully possessed;

thus, the initial opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is itself the revealing, awakening, entering, and realizing. This was taught in response to Maitreya to clarify the meaning of the "initial opening."

Guangyan (Radiant Adornment) reveals the initial manifestation of the meaning; Shizhi (Holding the World) reveals the initial awakening to the meaning; Shan-de (Skillful Attainment) reveals the initial entry into the meaning. These have no distinction of depth or shallowness, nor of priority or sequence; they are simply four aspects of the single, perfect stage of all-encompassing reality. Question: Is it not the case that by refuting Maitreya alone, one fully obtains the benefits described above—namely, the transformation of teaching and the transformation of contemplation? Answer: No. It is not so. Why? Because if one were to refute Maitreya alone, there would be no further benefit for others. Furthermore, if one were to refute Maitreya alone, it would mean that the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) has no power to transform sentient beings. Moreover, if one were to refute Maitreya alone, it would imply that the Buddha’s teachings are not yet complete. Therefore, it is necessary to refute Maitreya together with the other three bodhisattvas in order to manifest the ultimate, perfect meaning of the Dharma. This is why the text speaks of "the four bodhisattvas. If one were to refute Maitreya alone, it would fail to manifest the full scope of the Buddha’s transformative power. Thus, the refutation of Maitreya alone does not suffice to realize the aforementioned benefits of transforming the teaching and transforming contemplation. Therefore, the answer is "No. It is not the case that refuting Maitreya alone constitutes the aforementioned realization of the benefits of transforming the teaching and transforming contemplation. Why? Because the purpose of the refutation is to manifest the ultimate, perfect meaning of the Dharma through the collective realization of the four bodhisattvas.
