Therefore, the four means of integration (*catvāri saṃgrahavastūni*) are the site of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*), because they integrate sentient beings.

This is the second [point], clarifying the meaning of the site of awakening in terms of the practice of transforming others through the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*). The four immeasurables are precisely the mind that benefits others.
As the Sūtra says, "Loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is the site of awakening, because it integrates all sentient beings"; this refers to the bodhisattva at the initial stage.
Attaining true non-referential compassion (*anālambana-maitrī*) and departing from anger and affliction within the *dharmadhātu* reveals the true Dharma-body of compassion;
this is the meaning of the "site of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*). This compassion universally covers the *dharmadhātu*, which is equivalent to [the equality of] all sentient beings.

As the Sūtra says, "Compassion is the site of enlightenment," meaning that a bodhisattva at the initial stage dwells within non-referential great compassion, internally overcoming weariness and suffering—the Dharma-body of great compassion.

"Manifestation" (*khyāna*) is the meaning of the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*); although one dwells within the triple world, one rescues all sentient beings with a mind free from weariness or suffering.
"Joy" (*prīti*) is the site of enlightenment: when a bodhisattva at the initial stage attains true, objectless joy and the immeasurable mind, they shatter the maladies of the dharma-realm;
this lack of attachment to worldly pleasure reveals the true joy of the dharma-body, which is the meaning of the site of enlightenment.
Furthermore, rejoicing that all sentient beings are free from suffering and attain happiness is itself joy. As the Sūtra says:

"Equanimity is the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). When a beginner Bodhisattva dwells in the ground of emptiness and equality, they immediately shatter attachment and aversion to manifest the true, empty Dharmakāya;
this is the meaning of the site of enlightenment. Although one benefits all sentient beings, having no grasping or rejecting in the mind is itself love.

Regarding the statement in the sutra that "supernormal powers (abhijñā) are the site of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa)," this refers precisely to the transformative dharma. Upon first attaining the mind [of enlightenment], one achieves the purification of the six sense faculties (ṣaḍ-indriya-viśuddhi).

Through the supernormal power of mastery over the will (ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna-abhijñā), one destroys the karmic obstructions of the various faculties and penetrates the defilements of ignorance to reveal the true purity of the dharma-nature (dharmatā).
Thus, the six sense faculties themselves constitute the meaning of the site of awakening; this is the accomplishment of the six supernormal powers for the sake of transformation.

Regarding the statement in the sutras that liberation (*vimukti*) is the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), this is explained next because liberation accomplishes the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).
The *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra* states: "The Bodhisattva attains all dhyānas and is able to emerge from the liberations, bases of mastery, and bases of totality of the two vehicles.
If one of initial resolve enters the samādhi of the three truths, this constitutes twenty-five samādhis, excluding two.
Fifteenth, the manifestation of the afflictions of sinful suffering is the twenty-fifth; "I" is the meaning of the *bodhimaṇḍa*.
Because one can renounce the three realms through its causal power, one attains the eight liberations and the twenty-five samādhis.
The Sūtra says that skillful means (*upāya*) is the *bodhimaṇḍa*, which refers to the skillfulness in transforming others. This is because, from the beginning...
When the mind perceives the Middle Way, there is the skillful means of simultaneously illuminating the two truths;

by shattering the ignorance that is as vast as the sands of the Ganges, one reveals the various dharma-gates of skillful means—this is the meaning of the "site of enlightenment" (bodhimaṇḍa). It is the capacity for inconceivable transformation through the three wheels, manifesting the three mysteries to teach and transform all sentient beings with expedient skill.
The Sūtra says: "The four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) are the site of enlightenment. 4.
The "means of attraction" (saṃgrahavastu) refers to the methods employed as skillful means to transform sentient beings, which constitute the meaning of attaining the Way;
this is as explained under "skillful means," wherein one attracts sentient beings through generosity, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation, leading them to liberation.
Extensive learning is the site of awakening (*bodhimanda*), for one acts according to what has been heard. Subduing the mind is the site of awakening, for one correctly contemplates all phenomena.
The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are the site of awakening, for one relinquishes conditioned phenomena. The truths are the site of awakening, for they do not deceive the world.
Dependent origination is the site of awakening, for from ignorance through to old age and death, there is no exhaustion. All afflictions are the site of awakening...
The site of practice is the *bodhimaṇḍa* because one knows things as they truly are; it is the *bodhimaṇḍa* because one knows there is no self;
it is the *bodhimaṇḍa* because one knows all phenomena are empty.
This is the third illumination. A learned Bodhisattva of advancing practice, though able to practice for oneself, must still advance in the work of transforming others.
The *Xiuyao jing* states that "extensive learning (*bahuśruta*) is the site of enlightenment (*bodhimanda*).

For a bodhisattva who has first resolved to attain awakening, attaining true retention through hearing and hearing the Buddha-dharma of the ten directions destroys all darkness and delusion; thus, the manifestation of extensive learning is the meaning of the site of enlightenment, because one is able to practice according to what has been heard.
The sutra states that "subduing the mind is the site of enlightenment. The *Yingluo jing* states that this begins from the initial resolve.
Up to the *Vajraśekhara*, all are termed the "Patience of Subjugation" (*vinaya-kṣānti*). At the initial stage of contemplation, one fully subdues ignorance;

progressing to manifest the ultimate reality is the meaning of the "site of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*). The threefold contemplation within a single mind is the correct contemplation of all phenomena.

As the Sūtra says, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharma*) are the site of enlightenment. These thirty-seven factors consist of four kinds: three are provisional and one is real; they are for Bodhisattvas.

When the beginner attains the unconditioned (anabhisaṃskāra) thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, they are immediately able to eliminate the eight inversions and all delusive afflictions, revealing the five aggregates as the Dharma-nature and the Dharma-body, and through further cultivation, even attaining Great Nirvana; this is the meaning of the "site of enlightenment" (bodhimaṇḍa).
It involves abandoning the conditioned Four Truths within the realm, and also abandoning the conditioned Three Truths outside the realm. There is none [that is not abandoned].
The cessation of the truths (*nirodha-satya*) through non-action (*anabhisamskāra*) is precisely the true unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

As for "the truths are the site of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*), there are five subsequent sections below which constitute the objects of contemplation for the factors of the path (*mārga-pakṣa-dharma*). The Four Truths have four types: three are provisional (*upāya*) and one is real (*tattva*).
A bodhisattva at the initial stage uses the factors of the path to perceive these four types of Four Truths and sever the afflictions within the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).
Externally deluded regarding principle, all afflictions manifest the principle of the provisional and real Four Noble Truths; this is the meaning of the "site of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
To speak of the four kinds of Four Noble Truths is to not deceive the world. As the Sūtra says, "Dependent origination is the site of enlightenment.

Contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination reveals four kinds [of truth]: three are provisional and one is real. A bodhisattva at the initial stage is able to practice the path of non-action.

The chapter on contemplating the three paths of the twelve links of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) as the attainment of the three types of bodhi is precisely the meaning of the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
By contemplating dependent origination, one perceives the three types of Buddha-nature (buddhadhātu), which are inexhaustible.

As the Sūtra says, "All afflictions (kleśa) are the site of enlightenment," because a beginner Bodhisattva can employ the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣikadharma) to contemplate the three poisons without being defiled by them, thereby revealing the true Buddha within the false and illusory.
The Dharma is the meaning of the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). One is also able to know that both afflictions and Buddha-dharmas are ultimately empty.

A sutra states: "Sentient beings are the site of enlightenment. When a bodhisattva at the initial stage is able to employ the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) to contemplate the emptiness of sentient beings and does not perceive the marks of sentient beings, delusive confusion does not arise.
To see the true nature of sentient beings is to see the Buddha-nature; this is the Way.
Regarding the meaning of the "site" (*dharmapada*): if one does not perceive a fixed nature in sentient beings, then the non-duality of self and non-self is the true meaning of non-self.

As the Sūtra says: "All dharmas are the site of practice. A bodhisattva at the initial stage can employ the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) to contemplate the emptiness of all dharmas—such as the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*)—thereby destroying the delusions and inverted views within all dharmas.

It reveals that the five aggregates of the Buddha-nature attain five kinds of liberation; Nirvana is precisely the meaning of the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), and it also makes known that all dharmas and Nirvana ultimately return to emptiness.
Subduing pride is the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) because it is unshakable; the triple world is the site of enlightenment because there is nowhere to go;
the lion’s roar is the site of enlightenment because it is fearless.

These are the four [aspects] concerning the teaching on subduing pride that clarify the meaning of the site of enlightenment, for they represent the accomplishment of the bodhisattva’s contemplative practice.
It is capable of subduing the enmity of Māra. The Sūtra states that "subduing Māra is the site of enlightenment" (bodhimaṇḍa).

A bodhisattva at the initial stage of resolve can subdue the four māras, and even the eight māras. Seeing the suchness of the realm of Māra as the suchness of the realm of the Buddha is the true meaning of the site of enlightenment;
it means being able to dwell within the realm of Māra while subduing the mind of Māra, remaining unshakable. The Sūtra states that "the three realms are the site of enlightenment."
This refers to the meaning that a bodhisattva at the initial stage does not leave the triple world (*tridhātu*) nor cling to it;

by perceiving the three truths within the triple world, they realize the King of Samādhis and the twenty-five samādhis, whereby all Buddha-dharmas manifest—this is the significance of the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
One knows that the triple world is ultimately empty and that all phenomena have no destination. As the Sūtra says: "The Teacher..."
The lion’s roar is the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). To roar like a lion means to speak with certainty;

that a bodhisattva at the initial stage of mind can shatter doubts and delusions—that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature—is the meaning of the site of enlightenment, which is fearlessness in its ultimate sense.

The powers, fearlessnesses, and unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) are the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), for they are free from all faults; the three types of higher knowledge (*vidyā*) are the site of enlightenment, for they are without any remaining obstructions;
knowing all phenomena in a single thought-moment is the site of enlightenment, for it accomplishes all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
These are the five aspects of the powers (*bala*), fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*); they constitute the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).

When a bodhisattva at the initial stage achieves the ten kinds of power of knowledge (*jñāna-bala*)—as described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*—that is to say, by contemplating the single ultimate truth (*eka-tattva*), destroying ignorance, and attaining the powers, fearlessnesses, and unique true dharmas, this is the meaning of the site of enlightenment. The powers, fearlessnesses, and unique qualities are one’s own virtues.
Furthermore, transforming others without error is precisely the absence of all faults. As the Sūtra says, the "Threefold Knowledge" (trividyā) is the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa);

a bodhisattva at the initial stage of mind immediately attains the Threefold Knowledge, penetrating the phenomena and principles of the three periods of time without obstruction. As the Sūtra says, "The wisdom of a single thought-moment regarding all dharmas is the site of enlightenment";
this means that a bodhisattva at the initial stage of mind, upon perceiving the Middle Way, is able to simultaneously [realize both extremes].

Illuminating the two truths and shattering the three truths, the delusions of ignorance within the *dharmadhātu* are dispelled and true wisdom manifests; this is the meaning of the "site of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
At the initial stage, the accomplishment of the universal characteristic of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) also constitutes Buddhahood.
In this way, noble son, when a bodhisattva teaches and transforms sentient beings in accordance with the various pāramitās,
you should know that all their actions— from lifting a foot to setting it down— proceed from the site of enlightenment and abide within the Buddha-dharma.

This is the third formation of the *maṇḍala*. If one considers it in terms of the accomplishment of the aforementioned *pāramitās* by Vimalakīrti and his teaching and transforming of sentient beings—wherein every step he takes, whether lifting or setting down his foot, serves to eliminate falsehood and reveal the truth—this is precisely the coming from within the *maṇḍala*.

How could it be that he comes from a place of attaining the path under a Buddha? If one were to regard this as the initial arousal of the thought of enlightenment (*prathamacittotpāda*), [it would likewise be so].
A bodhisattva who abides in the initial resolve of understanding should teach and transform sentient beings through the various *pāramitās*, removing the false and manifesting the true;
with every lifting and placing of the feet, the wisdom of contemplation is ever-present before them—this is what it means to come from within the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).

This applies likewise to those in the thirty minds and the ten stages (*bhūmis*). If we consider those in the ten levels of faith, the purification of the six sense organs, or the disciples of the five ranks:

If one can constantly cultivate this contemplation of the mind to teach and transform sentient beings without losing mindfulness, then every lifting and placing of the feet constitutes coming from within the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), fully endowed with all Buddha-dharmas. As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states:
"One should know that such a person has proceeded to the site of enlightenment."
When this Dharma was being taught, five hundred devas and humans all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This refers to the time when the assembly attained benefit; five hundred devas and humans together, numbering five hundred, all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed path.
Therefore, I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness.
This is the fourth time I have respectfully declined, being unable to bear the task. Kāśyapa reflected that in the past he had been deluded regarding the true site of enlightenment;

it was only through the explanation provided by Mañjuśrī that he attained understanding. Since his spiritual wisdom is now weak and inferior, how could he possibly endure the mission of conveying the Tathāgata’s visit?
Inquiring after Illness.
*Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra-bhāṣya*, Scroll Seventeen.
*Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra-bhāṣya*, Scroll Eighteen (*Bodhisattva Chapter*, Part Three).
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Lokadhara, "Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness.
This is the third instance of the Buddha commanding Lokadhara to inquire after his illness; it consists of two parts: first, the Buddha’s command to inquire after his illness;

second, Lokadhara’s respectful refusal on the grounds of being unable to do so. As for why the Buddha commanded Lokadhara to inquire after his illness, it is because he had already emerged [from his previous state].

The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa is likewise a Mahāsattva of the Dharma-body who succeeds to the Honored One’s position. As for what is called "Holding the World" (*Lokadhara*), it means to lead, remember, and not forget; thus it is named "Holding the World. Its primary meaning is that of separation and distinction.

Because the true mind of the ultimate reality leads, remembers, and never forgets any phenomena, it is named "Holding the World. There are many interpretations of this term "holding," but they shall be briefly explained as follows: 1. **Holding by Means of Retention:** It refers to the power of retention (*dhāraṇī*) which holds all teachings and prevents them from being lost. 2. **Holding by Means of Sustaining:** It refers to sustaining the lives of sentient beings and preventing them from falling into the evil realms.

3. **Holding by Means of Upholding:** It refers to upholding the True Dharma so that it does not perish. 4. **Holding by Means of Guarding:** It refers to guarding the minds of sentient beings against afflictions and false views. 5. **Holding by Means of Non-forgetting:** It refers to the wisdom of non-forgetting (*asaṃpramoṣa-jñāna*) which clearly perceives all dharmas without confusion. These are the brief explanations of the various meanings of "holding."

There are five kinds of upholding (*dhāraṇī*): first, the upholding of prohibitions; second, the general upholding; third, the upholding of what is heard; fourth, the upholding of abiding; and fifth, the upholding of mastery.
Bodhisattvas of all four teachings possess these five kinds of upholding; however, three are provisional while one is real.

Now, regarding the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), the meaning of these five kinds of upholding is clarified as follows: First, the upholding of prohibitions: the Bodhisattva attains the true reality of the ultimate mark (*bhūtatathatā*).
First, the two *dhāraṇīs* that can illuminate and obstruct all afflictions, evil karma, and the retributive suffering of birth and death within the dharma-realm;
they sustain the merits of all myriad practices for the benefit of oneself and others, just as a perfect vessel holds water without any leakage.
Third, the *dhāraṇī* of hearing and retaining: whether it be the teachings of the Buddhas of the ten directions, or even those of the ten dharma-realms...
Fourth, "retention" (*dhāraṇī*) refers to being able to remember all words and phrases upon hearing them once, like a cloud holding rain without forgetting or losing it.

Fifth, "sustenance" (*parigraha*) refers to the unconditioned great compassion that bears the burden of delivering and liberating all sentient beings, vowing to protect and support them without ever abandoning them. Thus is the Bodhisattva.

From the initial aspiration, his mind is like space—neither partial nor circular—yet he is able to sustain both the provisional and the ultimate, up to the stage of Dharma-Cloud and Equal Enlightenment.
Sustaining the world while dwelling in the position of the Future Buddha, he maintains the five aspects of the provisional and the ultimate to their ultimate limit;
how could he not know that Pāpīyān had manifested as Śakra? It was merely to cause the assembly to realize that the realm of Māra is identical to the realm of the Buddha.

Because the suchness of one is non-dual with the suchness of all, he manifested ignorance in the past and allowed himself to be rebuked and subdued by Vimalakīrti, thereby causing sentient beings to awaken to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*).
"Opening" refers to the general demonstration, while "is" refers to the specific; the non-duality of the general and the specific is itself awakening.
This still pertains to the initial stage of the path; there is no need to seek it afar, for even the state of *samyaksaṃbodhi* is likewise so.
In this way, [the Buddha] first rebuked Maitreya and Guangyan; because they both held deviant attachments regarding the fruit, he criticized them by reference to the Bodhimanda.
Next, he rebuked Shizhi and Shan-de; because they both held erroneous conceptions regarding the cause, he criticized them by reference to the assembly where Māra offered his gifts.
Now, the Buddha next commands Shizhi to inquire after the illness of the sick man. He is the one to be questioned.
If one were to recount the events of being struck by the lute in the past, so that all bodhisattvas may recognize the deeds of Māra, awaken to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision,
and the great assembly may hear it together, this would fulfill the meaning of the aforementioned five kinds of benefits.
Lokadhara addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, I am not fit to go there to inquire after his illness.
This is the second instance of Lokadhara declining the mission; the text consists of four parts: first, the formal declination;
second, the explanation for the inability; third, the explicit clarification of the reasons for the inability; and fourth, the conclusion of the inability.
First, as for my inability to comply with your request, it is truly because in the past I failed to realize that Māra had assumed the form of Śakra and was being rebuked by Vimalakīrti;
how could such a person as I be fit to transmit the intent of the Tathāgata?
Why is this so? I recall that once, while I was dwelling in a quiet chamber...
This is the second section, explaining the reason for his inability [to teach], which concerns his failure to recognize that Māra had come in the guise of Śakra.
The text contains five points: first, his own account of formerly dwelling in a quiet chamber; second, his account of Māra coming in the guise of Śakra;
third, his own account of not recognizing Māra’s arrival and preaching the Dharma to him; fourth, Māra further employing women to cause distraction; and fifth, [the conclusion].
In his own humble and wondrous account, he states that he does not accept [offerings]. Regarding his former dwelling in a quiet chamber:
one who dwells in a quiet chamber, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, should do so desiring to avoid clamor and enter various *dhyānas* to progress in the cultivation of the Way. Dhṛtarāṣṭra is a Dharma-body Mahāsattva;
why would he need to enter the path through a birth-body? His traces are identical to those of a skillful-means Bodhisattva, serving as a model for sentient beings.
Because it was necessary to lead them in, I remained in a quiet chamber to demonstrate the practice of dhyāna-concentration.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān approached me with twelve thousand celestial maidens who resembled Śakra, playing lutes and singing;
together with his retinue, he bowed his head at my feet, joined his palms in reverence, and stood to one side.
This is the second account of Māra manifesting as Śakra coming [to the Buddha]. As for why Māra manifested as Śakra:
Śakra is a disciple of the Buddha who has already attained the Noble Path, and he is also the Buddha’s *dānapati* (patron). Therefore, he came to approach, consult, and receive instruction.
Since the World-Honored One was a renunciant bodhisattva, upon seeing a great *dānapati* arrive, he was obliged to offer him consolation and inquiry.
This obstructs and confuses [the path]; now, by means of the four types of bodhisattvas, we shall understand that the Maras are not uniform, and thus there are four kinds.
First, in the Tripiṭaka Teaching, it is clarified that the bodhisattva has not yet abandoned the Mara of afflictions (*kleśa-māra*) and the Mara of the aggregates (*skandha-māra*);

they merely observe and become aware of them through practice to suppress them, relying on this to cultivate the bodhisattva path. As for the Mara of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, if one attains supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), one can know them through intentional awareness (*manasikāra*).

The celestial Māra does not intentionally act [to hinder], nor does he know [the Bodhisattva’s intent]; even if he were to know, though he might use his supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) to subdue the celestial Māras, he could not yet destroy them permanently.
Only when [the Bodhisattva] reaches the foot of the Bodhi tree does he first subdue and destroy the *paranirmita-vaśavartin* celestial Māra;

after the Māra has retreated, the thirty-four moments of mind (*citta-kṣaṇa*) sever the fetters, and within this realm, all four types of Māras are completely exhausted. Second, the Exegesis of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*) clarifies bodhi...

When the Bodhisattva first enters and beholds the stage of seeing (*darśana-bhūmi*), he partially severs the Māra of afflictions (*kleśa-māra*) and attains the five factors of the Dharma-body (*pañca-dharma-skandha*).

He eliminates the Māra of the aggregates (*skandha-māra*) up to the sixth stage; although there are no longer active outflows (*anuśaya*) to moisten karma for future rebirth, he eliminates the Māras of the aggregates and death within the realm of desire.
Nevertheless, because he still possesses the power of his vows and accords with his practice, he takes birth within the realm of desire; thus, the aggregates and death cannot destroy the Bodhisattva.

Although one attains mastery over the supernormal powers on the seventh bhūmi of the path and can know the Māra of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods through focused attention (*manasikāra*), one cannot know them without such attention;
one can destroy them through focused attention, but cannot destroy them without it.

It is only upon reaching the foot of the Bodhi tree that one ultimately destroys the Māra of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods, severing him with the wisdom of a single moment of application (*ekakṣaṇa-samprayukta-prajñā*).
Since the habit-energies (*vāsanā*) are exhausted and there are no more habit-energies, vows cannot draw forth rebirth; this is the eternal exhaustion of the four Māras.

Third, the Separate Teaching clarifies that upon entering the ten stages (*bhūmi*) of the partial truth, one destroys the Māra of afflictions (*kleśa-māra*), the Māra of the aggregates (*skandha-māra*), and the Māra of death (*mṛtyu-māra*).

Upon attaining the ten practices (*caryā*), one gains mastery over supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); through intentional cognition, one knows the gods of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*), while through non-intentional cognition, one does not know them.
One is able to subdue [the demons] up to the first bhūmi, attaining a single body that is immeasurable in extent;

within the realms of a hundred buddha-worlds, the habitual tendencies of afflictions are exhausted, and the māra of the aggregates, the māra of death, and the māra of the sons of gods are all utterly destroyed.

Fourth, according to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), it is explained that a disciple of the five grades can perfectly subdue the four māras; if they enter the ten stages of faith, their six sense faculties become pure.

One who has completely severed the four māras does not even attend to the thought that a māra has arrived; this is a brief analysis of how the four teachings differ in their destruction of the four māras.

Regarding the eight māras—namely, permanence, bliss, self, purity, impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity—the Bodhisattvas of the Tripiṭaka Teaching have not yet eliminated them, but can only suppress the four māras;
it is only upon reaching the fulfillment of the thirty-four moments of mind that they are finally eliminated.

If, in the Shared Teaching (*pāṭha-sāmānya*), the stage of insight (*darśana-bhūmi*) is already able to eliminate the four demons of permanence, bliss, self, and purity; and in the Distinct Teaching (*bheda-śāsana*),

the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*) have already eliminated the four demons of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, while the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*) and ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) have already suppressed the four demons of impermanence and so forth,
and upon entering the [first] stage (*bhūmi-praveśa*), one has partially shattered the four demons of impermanence and so forth— then although the cause is impermanent, the fruit is [permanent].
This is always as the Buddha answered the Brahmin in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*. In the Separate Teaching (*pṛthagdeśanā*), the eight māras are all exhausted at the stage of Buddhahood;
in the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulyadeśanā*), they are already completely shattered from the first *cittotpāda* dwelling (*prathamacittotpādavihāra*).

The four māras within the realm are forever exhausted, and the four māras outside the realm, such as impermanence (*anityatā*) and so forth, are ultimately exhausted even in the final thought-moment. Next, the maintenance of the world (*dharaṇīloka*) is explained.

For what reason was he harassed by Māra? If we discuss one who upholds the traces of the world and manifests various skillful means (*upāya*) to teach those in the stage of the "Successor to the Throne" (*kumārabhūta*), then this is no small matter;
for one who knows that the teaching exists but the person does not, there is no need for further investigation.
However, because Dhṛtarāṣṭra followed the model of these various skillful means in his teaching, he manifested ignorance. There are three reasons for this being so.
These various skillful means teach Bodhisattvas that the suchness of the realm of Māra and the suchness of the realm of the Buddha are identical, equal, and non-dual;
the Buddha-realm is principle (*li*), while the Māra-realm is phenomena (*shi*).

Though these skillful means clarify that Bodhisattvas can enter true principle, they must not allow phenomena to obstruct principle or principle to obstruct phenomena. If one were to sever the fetters...
To avoid phenomena and enter into principle is like a person who, when afraid of non-human spirits, fails to realize that they are no different from the Buddha-realm;

such a person is then afflicted by Māra. The Great Being, however, realizes the non-duality of these two realms and, being free from acceptance or rejection, awakens to this and is thus able to subdue [Māra].
Second, all the various skillful means and teachings equally clarify the illumination of conditioned cultivation.

In stillness, there is entering and emerging from contemplation; if one applies the mind to contemplation, one immediately perceives the activities of Māra, but if one does not apply the mind, one does not perceive them.

In the true cultivation of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), there is no entering or emerging from contemplation, as one is always in samādhi, seeing all Buddha-lands without dualistic marks—tranquil yet constantly illuminating.
Since you, Jishi, are currently in stillness but have not yet entered contemplation, [you do not perceive them].
Because he directs his attention and shines his light upon it, he does not fail to recognize the Māra’s transformation into Śakra.
Because the Great Being is tranquil yet constantly illuminating, he is able to perceive it immediately. It is like a person practicing dhyāna in a deep mountain;

if they cannot distinguish between a human and a malevolent spirit, they must hang a large square mirror. Although the *māngmai* (phantoms) can deceive the human eye, they cannot alter their true form.

The manifestation of the original form in a mirror allows one to know its falsity; Māra is likewise able to deceive those whose cultivation is merely based on conditions and who have not yet entered meditative observation, preventing them from knowing [the truth].
However, he cannot deceive true practitioners of tranquil illumination who cultivate according to reality.

Third, although Bodhisattvas who rely on expedient means are able to enter observation and perceive the activities of Māra, or may be able to temporarily subdue him, [they are not yet free from his influence].
They are able to act with unimpeded mastery within their sphere of activity, just as a person who cannot discipline a wicked disciple abandons them and refuses to accept them,
whereas a skillful person does not abandon the wicked but employs skillful means to train and mature them until they become capable of service and are transformed into virtuous people;
the Bodhisattva of the Perfect Teaching (Vipula-yāna) disciplines Māra in the same way, not merely to subdue his evil mind, but...
Returning to the transformation of goodness can also cause others to give rise to the bodhicitta and realize the inexhaustible lamp, extensively transforming all beings.
While one’s own practice of the Buddha-dharma never diminishes, there is great benefit for immeasurable hosts of Māras.
Because Bodhisattvas who follow the teachings of expedient means lack these three meanings, they are disturbed by Māras. Now, Cīvara-dhara dwells in a quiet chamber.

Māra assumes the form of the Lord of Devas (Indra) with the intent to cause disturbance; the Sustainer of the World (the Buddha) remains unaware and enters meditative absorption because of this obstruction.

Just as the Buddha knows the capacities of people and manifests the Way to transform sentient beings, so too does Māra know those who are destined to attain the Way and comes to destroy them before their realization is complete.
I thought this was Śakra, and I said to him: "Welcome, Kauśika! Although you possess merit by right, you should not be self-indulgent;
you should contemplate the impermanence of the five desires and seek the root of goodness, cultivating the firm Dharma with respect to body, life, and wealth."
This is the account given by Traividya-dhara-loka, who described how in the past, when Māra arrived, he did not recognize him and preached the Dharma to him.
Dhara-loka exclaimed, "Welcome! because he did not know it was Māra, but took him to be Śakra, thinking that he had come with a virtuous mind seeking the sublime Dharma;
thus he exclaimed, "Welcome! Kauśika," for this was indeed Śakra himself in his human form.

Although one's clan name follows their original lineage and one may possess the merit to become a Lord of Heaven as a result of past blessings, such wealth and nobility must not lead to self-indulgence or negligence in the cultivation of the Path.
To tell Śakra that those who observe the impermanence of the five desires should seek the root of goodness is a mistaken teaching.
If it were merely for the sake of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna), one would simply take impermanence as the means of liberation.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* clarifies that the Heavenly Lord (Indra) was deeply attached to the five desires;

the Buddha, for his sake, expounded fifteen kinds of contemplative gates such as impermanence to destroy those desires. Once this was accomplished, he then commissioned him to teach the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Since it is stated that he was indeed the Heavenly Lord, [the Buddha] exhorted him to contemplate impermanence and leave desire behind, and to cultivate diligence regarding body, life, and wealth.
Regarding the three worldly jewels (*ratna*), there are five types: first, the three worldly jewels—compassion, patience, and refraining from using weapons or corporal punishment;
second, the jewel of the future body, obtained by giving food and drink to others; third, the jewel of the future life, obtained by releasing living beings and ceasing slaughter;

fourth, the jewel of future wealth, obtained through sincere giving. These are the retributions for the three worldly jewels. If one contemplates impermanence, [one transcends them] to reach the heavenly realms.
First, one must plant the firm karma for the future before long.

Second, regarding the Śrāvaka sūtras, those who cultivate the three kinds of firm dharmas—such as contemplating impermanence—attain the fivefold Dharma-body, the untainted life of wisdom, and the seven noble riches;
because these cannot be damaged or destroyed, they are called "firm. For the sake of sentient beings, Bodhisattvas cultivate all manner of meritorious virtues through the Buddha-dharma.

For one who does not begrudge body or life and has no sense of stinginess, the provisional reward (*huabao*) is the attainment of the three reliances (*san laojing*) within the mundane world, and the ultimate attainment is the fulfillment of the seven riches (*qichai*) through the fivefold dharma-body (*wufen fashen*). Regarding these three reliances:

if explained according to the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*), one contemplates that the fivefold dharma-body, the untainted life of wisdom (*wulou huiming*), and the seven noble riches are all empty, unarisen, and unceasing.
That which cannot be destroyed by afflictions, birth and death, celestial Māras, or external paths constitutes the three fortresses.

Fourth, regarding the three fortresses of the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavasthāna-śāsana*): ascending to the stages (*bhūmi*) and departing from the birth and death within the realms, whereby the *dharmakāya* manifests, is called the "fortress of the body," being the adamantine essence.
That the life-force of Prajñā-wisdom never ceases or perishes is called the "fortress of life."
The fact that the wealth of the myriad wholesome dharmas cannot be plundered or seized is precisely the "fortress of wealth.

When the Fivefold Perfect Teaching clarifies the three fortresses, it means that relinquishing body, life, and wealth makes them equal to the ultimate limit of birth and death; by being free from old age, sickness, and death, one attains the indestructible and eternally abiding state.
This is the convergence of all dharmas within body, life, and wealth, and it constitutes the three fortresses of the Three Virtues.

The World-Holder (Lokadhara) erroneously addressed the Lord of Devas regarding the three laws of confinement; as for the five kinds of meanings of these three confinements, it is not known for certain what he was referring to.
He then said to me: "Virtuous One, accept these twelve thousand women to serve as your attendants."
This is the fourth instance where Māra again offered a woman as a magical transformation. Having previously manifested as Śakra, he caused Dhṛtarāṣṭra to abandon his meditative sitting;

because [Dhṛtarāṣṭra] was unaware at that time, Māra now forcibly offers him a woman once more to severely obstruct and disturb him. Previously, when he manifested as Śakra, it was like a "soft thief" gaining entry;
now, by offering him a woman, he causes him to rise from his state of truth, allowing a "strong thief" to enter once again. This is how Māra acts.
The two thieves, the strong and the soft, harass and disturb one so that the concentrated mind is lost; while the world does not perceive it, one is thereby destroyed by Māra.
I say, Kausika, do not offer such unrighteous things to me, a śramaṇa son of the Śākya; this is not [proper].

"It would be appropriate for me [to accept]. This is the fifth science (*vidyā*) by which one sustains the world. [The donor] described his own strangeness in not accepting the girl, saying: "The girl is an object of unrighteousness (*adharma*); how could you forcibly have this gift? Therefore, I say that I do not require this unrighteous object. Śāriputra said: "I do not require it. The donor said: "If you do not require it, then take it back yourself. Śāriputra said: "I do not take it back. The donor said: "If you do not take it back, then let us go together to the Buddha and ask him about this matter. They went together to the Buddha and asked about this matter. The Buddha told Śāriputra: "Accept the girl; there is no fault in this. Śāriputra accepted her. The donor then gave her to Śāriputra as a wife. Later, she became pregnant. When the time came, she gave birth to a son. The boy grew up and eventually became a monk. He attained Arhatship and possessed the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*). He then returned to his former home and saw his mother. His mother said to him: "In the past, when you were in your mother's womb, you caused my body to suffer great pain. Why have you now come here? The son replied: "Mother, why do you speak such words? I am your son. His mother said: "How can you be my son? You are the son of a Brahmin. The son said: "Mother, I am indeed your son. His mother said: "If you are truly my son, then why did you not come to see me before? The son said: "Mother, I was born into the household of a Śākya, and I have renounced the world to become a monk. I have attained Arhatship and possess the six supernormal powers. I am now free from all suffering and abide in peace. Mother, you should rejoice. His mother said: "Son, if you have truly attained such a state, then please show me your miraculous powers. The son then displayed various transformations before his mother. His mother was filled with faith and joy, and she too renounced the world to become a nun. She soon attained Arhatship. Thus, through this account, it is shown that even those who were once objects of unrighteousness can, through the power of the Dharma, attain liberation.
