"This gate is for those of pure and simple Brahma-conduct; one should not accept such defiled conditions, as this is an unlawful offering.
Therefore, I say: 'This is not suitable for me.
Before he had finished speaking, Vimalakīrti arrived and said to me: "This is not Śakra; it is Māra who has come to harass you."
It is indeed so.
This is the third section, which correctly describes the incident of being rebuked; according to this text, there are eight points:
first, Vimalakīrti comes forth to awaken Lokadhara; second, Vimalakīrti approaches Māra and asks for his daughter; third, Māra becomes terrified and wishes to depart.
1. A voice in the sky exhorts him to relinquish the girl. 2. The Five Māras urge him to relinquish the girl. 3. The Great Being preaches the Dharma for the girl.
4. Māra begs for the girl. 5. The Great Being returns the girl. 6. Vimalakīrti arrives in person to awaken him.

Jie-shi (Dharmarakṣa) was unable to discern and awaken because he was under the influence of Māra’s illusions. This was truly due to his failure in causal cultivation, which led him to be ensnared by Māra’s illusions.
This is the realization of the Great Being. He awakens to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; not only does he awaken himself, but he also awakens others.
His tranquil illumination is perfectly bright; not only can he illuminate himself, but he illuminates all things.

Therefore, he was able to arrive before him and manifest the illusions and deceptions of Māra, demonstrating the right and wrong of the world. First, he showed that it was not Śakra; next, he revealed it to be Māra.
"Because he wishes to destroy the True Path, he merely says that he will trouble and obstruct you.
He then said to Māra, "These maidens may be given to me, for they are what I ought to receive.
This was the second instance where Vimalakīrti requested the maidens; this is why Vimalakīrti himself stated that they were what he ought to receive.
This involves two points: first, that Vimalakīrti is a layperson, so his accepting [the women] does not constitute an obstruction;
second, that the practice of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) is characterized by non-obstruction, wherein opposition or compliance, strength or gentleness, is nothing other than the Right Path.
Therefore, he did not consider the demon-maidens to be an obstruction, which is why he said, "As I am, they should be accepted."
Māra was immediately struck with fear and thought, "Vimalakīrti will surely trouble me. Desiring to vanish and depart, he tried to conceal his form, but he could not;
even by exhausting all his supernatural powers, he was unable to leave.

This describes how Māra, possessing the three types of supernormal knowledge (*traividya*), was terrified and wished to depart. The reason Māra was so terrified is fundamentally due to [Vimalakīrti’s] upholding [of the Dharma].
The worldly Mara, wishing to destroy others to establish himself, suddenly beheld Vimalakīrti and saw his own illusions and pretenses exposed.
Furthermore, realizing that Vimalakīrti’s spiritual power was no match for him and that he would inevitably suffer humiliation, he was struck with great terror and desired to vanish from sight.

Yet, though he could not vanish, even when he exerted all his supernatural powers, he still could not depart. For although Mara possesses supernatural power, how can it compare to the spiritual power of a Great Being of the Dharma-body?
Because he was restrained by the power of supernatural might, he could not go despite his utmost efforts.
Then, a voice was heard from the air saying, "Pāpīyan, give him your daughters, and only then may you depart."
This was the voice from the sky in the Four Clarities (*caturvidha-vidyā*) exhorting him to relinquish the girl.

Regarding the "voice from the sky," the ancient commentators of Guan and He explain that it was an emanation of a Māra-bodhisattva who, responding to the occasion, assisted in the transformation. They say: "You were just now about to bestow her upon the Holder of the World (*Lokadhara*);

now that Vimalakīrti requests her, how can you not give her? To give her does not contradict your original intention; only by doing so will she be permitted to depart. Alternatively, it may have been Vimalakīrti himself.
A voice arose in the air to subdue Māra; it was the voice of Śākyamuni’s *dharmakāya*, Vairocana, as clarified in the *Samantabhadra-sūtra*.
Out of fear, Māra bowed his head and yielded.

This was the fifth: the demoness Maṃśulī. Because the power of the demon king could not take her away by stealth, nor could he obtain her through empty threats, he further exhorted the demon king, saying, "If you do not surrender this woman, I fear you will suffer various humiliations.
Out of dread and having no other choice, the demon king then surrendered the woman.
At that time, Vimalakīrti said to the daughters of Māra, "Māra has given you all to me;
you should now all resolve to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. He then taught them the Dharma according to their respective capacities, causing them to give rise to the aspiration for the Way.
This is the sixth section, in which Vimalakīrti accepts the women and preaches the Dharma for them. He does so in order to subdue the minds of Māra and to bring benefit to the women;
thus, he must preach the Dharma. Regarding this text, there are two parts: first, exhorting the arousal of the bodhicitta, and second, exhorting the practice of cultivation.
These two are the essential dharmas of a Bodhisattva; the arousal of the mind is the very essence of cultivation.
This means that they are fully prepared to enter the cool pond of Nirvana. Therefore, Vimalakīrti first exhorted the women to resolve upon Bodhicitta.
As for "preaching the Dharma as appropriate," the Four Teachings clarify Bodhicitta;
according to their respective capacities and conditions, he employs the four *siddhāntas* to reach them, causing each to give rise to the aspiration for the Way.
He further said, "You have already resolved upon the path; there is the joy of the Dharma with which you may find self-delight, and you should no longer take pleasure in the five desires.

This constitutes the second exhortation to practice: since one has already generated the aspiration for enlightenment, if one does not practice, there is a fear that one might fall back again; therefore, it is necessary [to practice].
Exhorting the practice of the Bodhisattva’s joy in the Dharma serves as an antidote to the sensual pleasures of Māra’s palace;
regarding this, there are three parts: first, Vimalakīrti’s exhortation to practice the joy of the Dharma; second, the celestial maidens’ inquiry;
and third, Vimalakīrti’s response.
The celestial maidens then asked, "What is meant by the 'joy of the Dharma'?

This was the request made by these two enlightened celestial maidens. Although the maidens in the palace of Māra had experienced the pleasures of the five desires, they had never heard of the joy of the Dharma;
now that they had finally heard of it, they were unable to understand it and thus made this request.
He replied: "I delight in constantly believing in the Buddha, I delight in wishing to hear the Dharma, and I delight in making offerings to the Saṅgha.
This was the Pure Name (Vimalakīrti) answering the goddess to preach the joy of the Dharma, thereby shattering her attachment to the pleasures of the five desires.
What is called the joy of the Dharma has the desire for all wholesome dharmas as its root; if one possesses such desire and aspiration—

The mind is itself what constitutes happiness. Just as worldly people find joy in loving and cherishing their parents, relatives, and family estate, so too for a disciple of the Buddha, the Buddha serves as father, the Dharma as mother, and the practice of the path along with all spiritual kin replaces all material wealth.
That which is profound joy is precisely the supramundane joy of the Dharma. It is in this regard that [it is said].
The text consists of five parts: first, the constant joy of taking refuge in the Triple Gem; second, the joy of wishing to depart from the Truth of Origination;
third, the joyful contemplation of the Truth of Suffering; fourth, the joy of practicing the Truth of the Path; and fifth, the conclusion that establishes this as the joy of the Dharma.

If one can act in this manner, one will not only attain the joy of the Dharma within the causal stage, but after that, the attainment of the Nirvana of the Truth of Cessation is itself ultimate, eternal joy. Thus says the Sūtra.

Regarding the statement "delighting in always trusting the Buddha": since it was previously stated that he preaches the Dharma according to what is appropriate, the four teachings clarify that the Buddha accords with the inclinations of celestial women to give rise to faith and joyful affection;
this is precisely the joy of the Dharma (*dharmasukha*). Regarding the scriptural statement "delighting in wishing to hear the Dharma":

the four teachings clarify that the Mahāyāna Dharma is heard according to the mind’s delight in hearing; this is precisely the joy of the Dharma. Regarding the scriptural statement "delighting in making offerings": [the four teachings clarify...]
Regarding the Sangha, the four teachings clarify that making offerings according to one's inclination is itself the joy of the Dharma.
This joy consists in being free from the five desires;

this is the second clarification of the joy of being free from the Truth of Accumulation (samudaya-satya). Since accumulation ought to be abandoned, it is said that one should take joy in being free from the five desires.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* clarifies that the cause of all sufferings is rooted in craving; therefore, we know that the five desires are themselves the origin of suffering (*samudaya*).
Just as a person recovers from illness and attains peace and happiness, so too, by departing from the five desires, one attains the bliss of the Dharma.

The four teachings explain the departure from the five desires differently, according to what is employed based on one's past habitual tendencies. However, since [the teaching] first rebukes the heavens...
A woman who is attached to the five desires should extensively clarify her renunciation by means of the principles of the Tripiṭaka:
she should contemplate the five aggregates as enemies and thieves, contemplate the four great elements as venomous snakes, and contemplate the internal sense bases as an empty village.
This refers to the Threefold Knowledge (trividyā) which contemplates the Truth of Suffering; if one does not contemplate it as suffering, one will be afflicted by suffering.

How then could one attain the joy of the Dharma? Therefore, those who can contemplate suffering are not afflicted by it; they escape suffering and attain the joy of the Dharma through the wisdom of contemplation.
The contemplation of suffering according to the four teachings is employed according to the faculties and capacities of sentient beings.

"Delighting in following and protecting the resolve for enlightenment, delighting in benefiting sentient beings, and delighting in reverently making offerings to the Teacher—these are the four exhortations regarding the dharmas of the myriad practices of the Truth of the Path.
Within these texts, there are three meanings: first, the basis of practice; second, the correct practice;
and third, universal practice. Regarding the basis of practice, the sutra says: 'Delighting in following and protecting the resolve for enlightenment'—this is the exhortation."
When practicing virtue oneself, one must protect the mind of the Way; when the mind of the Way is secure and unimpaired, one finds joy in the Way itself, which is the joy of the Dharma.
As the Sūtra says, "rejoicing in benefiting sentient beings" is an exhortation to cultivate the Dharma of transforming others.
It is like parents who, seeing their child free from suffering and obtain happiness, also experience joy and delight. The Sūtra speaks of "rejoicing in reverence."
One who nurtures their teacher abandons their father to follow the master, thereby being able to perfect superior virtues;
revering the path of the Dharma and savoring its meaning to delight the spirit is itself the joy of the Dharma. To nourish and expand one’s sense of gratitude is likewise the joy of the Dharma.

Thus, while internally cultivating the path of self-practice and transforming others, externally there is the presence of an enlightened teacher to provide instruction; when these causes and conditions are fully present, [the path is complete].
To practice so that one's aspirations are fulfilled according to one's heart is the meaning of the joy of the Dharma.
One delights in practicing giving extensively, delights in firmly upholding the precepts, delights in patience and gentleness, delights in diligently accumulating roots of goodness,
delights in meditative concentration without distraction, and delights in stainless, luminous wisdom.
This is the essential summary of the collective practices of the six *pāramitās* as the correct conduct of these two bodhisattvas;

there are no bodhisattvas of the four teachings who do not practice this path to seek *bodhi*. However, because the gateways of their teachings differ, there arise the distinctions between the six *pāramitās* of arising-and-ceasing, non-arising, the immeasurable, and the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*).
This is fully explained in the "Chapter on the Buddha-land" (Buddhakṣetraparivarta) in the praise of the bodhisattvas.

The virtues and the practices for the Pure Land have been explained in brief. However, Vimalakīrti taught according to the needs of the occasion, allowing each of the heavenly maidens to follow their own conditions;
thus, they each attained the flavor of the path they delighted in, their spirits moistened and their minds satisfied.
The six perfections are all the joy of the Dharma.
They delight in the bodhicitta; they delight in subduing all māras; they delight in severing all afflictions (*kleśa*); they delight in purifying buddha-fields;

they delight in cultivating all meritorious virtues for the sake of accomplishing the primary and secondary marks; they delight in adorning the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*); they delight in hearing the profound Dharma without fear;

they delight in the three gates of liberation; they do not delight in improper times; they delight in associating with fellow students; and they have no aversion toward those who are not fellow students.

Delighting in overcoming resentment, delighting in protecting against evil associates, delighting in associating with virtuous friends, and delighting in a joyful and pure mind, one delights in cultivating the immeasurable factors of the path.
These constitute the two types of cultivation for the Bodhisattva who practices the three vidyās: first, the general; second, the specific. [The first is] the general.
This refers to the six *pāramitās*, which collectively encompass all practices; specifically, it refers to the distinct and universal practice of the myriad deeds.
What is clarified here is an exhortation for the celestial maidens to universally practice these deeds, briefly citing more than ten items to establish the meaning of "Dharma-joy.
As the Sūtra says, "rejoicing in the broadening of the bodhicitta" refers precisely to compassion and the four great vows.

Because it necessarily causes [the benefit] to be universal, it is called "vast. Furthermore, from the arising of compassion and great vows based on the Four Noble Truths of Arising and Cessation, up to the Unconditioned (anabhisaṃskāra) Four Noble Truths, this is the Bodhicitta becoming increasingly vast.
It is the mind of the Supreme Path that increases the joy of the Dharma. As the Sūtra says regarding "delighting in subduing all Māras," it is like achieving victory by pacifying an enemy.
The mind is then joyful. As the Sūtra says, "Joyfully severing all afflictions is like a disease being cured; this is the bliss of Nirvāṇa.
Regarding the Sūtra’s statement, "joyfully purifying Buddha-lands," the meaning of purifying Buddha-lands has already been explained previously:
it is like a worldly person's home being clean and pure, such that guests and hosts alike behold it with joy, delight, and pleasure. Regarding the Sūtra’s statement, "joyfully accomplishing..."

Regarding the cultivation of various merits through the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*): it is like a person who, seeing their own physical appearance to be upright and handsome while possessing inner virtue, feels immediate joy in their heart.

As the Sūtra says, "delighting in adorning the *bodhimaṇḍa*," the meaning of the *bodhimaṇḍa* according to the four teachings has been briefly explained as already analyzed in the *Śrī-raśmi-prabhāsa*.
Thus, when the false is removed and the true is revealed, and the false is extinguished so that the true is attained, one experiences delight.
Regarding "joy": the sutras state that those who delight in hearing the profound Dharma and do not fear it possess the four teachings. Each of these teachings possesses its own profound Dharma.
The Tripitaka Teaching and the Shared Teaching merely clarify the principle of partial truth within the realm of conditioned existence; they are not yet sufficient to be considered profound.

The Distinct and Complete Teachings clarify the perfect and true reality beyond the realm of conditioned existence; this is profound and difficult to fathom to the bottom. If one has a mind of fear, one will immediately become startled and suspicious.
If, upon hearing of suffering, one does not fear it but instead delights in, praises, and seeks it, one immediately attains a portion of true and eternal bliss.
The Sūtra states: "One delights in the three gates of liberation and does not delight in what is untimely. The four teachings clarify the three gates of liberation:

in the first two teachings, there is the timely and the untimely; "untimely" refers to the stage of the Two Vehicles, while "timely" refers to the stage of the Bodhisattva. Furthermore, regarding the preceding...

The Bodhisattvas of the two provisional teachings also practice the Middle Way and the true mark (*dharmatā*) within their contemplations of the Separate and Complete teachings, and cultivate the three gates of liberation;
this is indeed "timely. However, when viewed from the perspective of the Separate teaching in relation to the Complete, it is again "untimely," for the Complete teaching alone is the true time.
Why is this so? Because in all the various provisional teaching-gates, it is the time of practice, not the time of realization. If one wishes to attain...
Realization is always at the improper time; if one seeks it when it is the proper time, one immediately attains ultimate truth and achieves the three true liberations, which is true Dharma-bliss.
As the Sūtra says: "One should delight in associating with fellow students; toward those who are not fellow students, let the mind be free from resentment and obstruction.
The Four Teachings clarify that Bodhisattvas each have their own fellow students whom they should approach, practicing together in harmony and mutual encouragement.

To achieve a compliant mind is itself the joy of the Dharma. If one harbors resentment or obstruction toward ordinary beings, those of the two vehicles, or Bodhisattvas who are not fellow practitioners, one destroys the true joy of the Dharma.

If the mind is free from resentment and obstruction, and one can rejoice in others' merit to the extent that it surpasses their own, one will instead regain the Dharma-joy of sympathetic rejoicing (*anumodana*). As the Sūtra says: "One should take pleasure in protecting against evil."
If those who possess knowledge do not protect it, they will be able to destroy the joy of the Dharma;
if they can properly protect it, then harsh speech will not arise, and there will be no damage, so that the internal joy of the wholesome Dharma remains forever secure. As the Sūtra says:
"One delights in associating with spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), who can instruct, benefit, and gladden one, bringing about the wholesome dharmas of a person. The Sūtra says: "One delights..."
Regarding "joyful and pure mind," the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states: "As one truly knows through great knowledge, the movement of the mind reaches the ultimate mind;

therefore, it is called joy. As one truly knows through great knowledge, this is true Dharma-joy. The movement of the mind reaching the ultimate mind is called the pure Dharma-bliss. The sūtra further states:
"Delighting in the cultivation of immeasurable factors of the path" (mārga-pakṣya-dharma); there are four such [categories] according to the Four Teachings.

If the various factors of the path (*mārga-pakṣya-dharma*) are cultivated within the mind of a bodhisattva for the sake of transforming sentient beings, they are all called the "immeasurable factors of the path.

As for why the factors of the path are termed "Dharma-joy," the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states that through the untainted faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), and factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), one immediately attains immeasurable peace, stability, and happiness; if this is true even for those of the Two Vehicles, how much more so for a bodhisattva?

However, the analytical discernment of the immeasurable factors of the path (*mārga-pakṣya-dharma*) and the opening up of the meanings of the four teachings involve difficulties in discerning what is to be adopted and what is to be rejected;
this constitutes the Dharma-joy of a bodhisattva.
This is the fifth [point] that establishes Dharma-joy: if a bodhisattva possesses a mind of aspiration and desire, they shall cultivate such a path.
All dharmas are indeed the joy of the Dharma; it is simply that one category among the myriad paths of practice is being highlighted here.

If one cultivates with a mind of joyful aspiration, there is nothing that is not the joy of the Dharma. For instance, when one who practices the Way reads, recites, listens, studies, and sits in meditation, the mind experiences joy.
If the mind does not find joy and one forcibly constrains itself, then painful sensations will arise.
Thereupon, Pāpīyān said to the daughters, "I wish to return with you all to the celestial palace.
The daughters replied, "We have been granted this Dharma-joy by this layman; we find it exceedingly delightful and no longer take pleasure in the joys of the five desires.
Māra said, "Layman, you may release these women; to give away all that one possesses to others is the mark of a Bodhisattva."

This is the seventh clarification: Māra’s attempt to entice the women back to his celestial palace. This section consists of three parts: first, Māra’s attempt to entice the women back to his celestial palace;
second, the women’s delight in the joy of the Dharma and their refusal to follow him back; third, Māra’s request to Vimalakīrti for the women.
All of these may be understood according to the text.
Vimalakīrti said, "I have already relinquished them; you may take them away so that all sentient beings may fulfill their aspirations for the Dharma.
This is the eighth clarity: Vimalakīrti returns the māra-maidens. Regarding this, there are four parts: first, Vimalakīrti returns the māra-maidens; second... [text continues].
The women requested the Dharma and took their leave; Vimalakīrti preached the Dharma-gate of the Inexhaustible Lamp to the three pure ones.

The four women paid their respects and returned with Māra. Regarding the Great Being returning to the māra-maidens: the Great Being’s fundamental practice is always that of renunciation, specifically for the purpose of subduing Māra and benefiting sentient beings.
Since Māra had already been subdued, the women gave rise to the aspiration [for enlightenment], and he released them to return.
Furthermore, because the palace of Māra can be extensively transformed, he relinquishes it back to Māra so that all sentient beings whose Dharma-vows are fulfilled may return to Māra;
thus, Māra’s own vows are immediately fulfilled. For this reason, he established a vow that all who seek the Dharma shall attain the full fulfillment of their Dharma-vows.
Thereupon, the women asked Vimalakīrti, "How should we dwell in the palace of Māra?

This is the second clarification: the women wish to return and request the Dharma; as disciples who have changed their teacher, they must consult him for instructions regarding the matters of practice.
Vimalakīrti said, "Sisters, there is a Dharma-gate called the 'Inexhaustible Lamp'; you should study it.
As for the Inexhaustible Lamp, it is like a single lamp that ignites hundreds of thousands of lamps: the darkness is dispelled by all these lights, yet the light itself is never exhausted.
In the same way, sisters, when a single bodhisattva guides and instructs hundreds of thousands of sentient beings, causing them to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*..."
The bodhicitta does not perish within that resolve for enlightenment; rather, as one teaches the Dharma, all wholesome dharmas increase of their own accord.

This is called the "Inexhaustible Lamp. Although you dwell in the palaces of Māra, by means of this Inexhaustible Lamp, you cause countless sons and daughters of the gods to resolve upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. This is why [you are here].
Repaying the Buddha’s kindness also brings great benefit to all sentient beings.
This is the teaching of the Dharma-gate of the Inexhaustible Lamp for the sake of Pure Name.

Regarding the Inexhaustible Lamp Dharma-gate, bodhisattvas of the four teachings all possess it; however, there is a distinction between those that are ultimate and those that are not. If it pertains to the Tripiṭaka...
In the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*), one extinguishes the body and ceases wisdom to enter *nirvāṇa* without transforming others.

Although within the fruit there is an "exhaustible lamp," the transmission and transformation continue unceasingly during the causal stage; thus, even though one enters *nirvāṇa* upon reaching the fruit, the Buddha’s transformation continues through successive predictions of enlightenment.
This is the inexhaustibility of the exhaustible lamp. In contrast, the Distinct Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*) and the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya-yāna*) clarify true inexhaustibility.
A lamp refers to the wisdom that contemplates the Middle Way, which perceives all phenomena as being like space and thus inexhaustible;
this wisdom is likewise inexhaustible. This Dharma-lamp is itself inexhaustible, and its transformation of others is also inexhaustible.
For example, it is like two lamps: one has little oil and a small wick, while the other has much oil and a large wick; the one with much oil and a large wick [lasts longer].
The original lamp is inexhaustible, and the further transmission of other lamps is likewise inexhaustible.
Vimalakīrti transmits the Dharma-gate to others and causes hundreds of thousands to benefit and resolve their minds; yet, there is no diminution whatsoever in the original lamp.
Therefore, this is used as a metaphor: thus, those in darkness all attain illumination, and that light never ceases, so as to cause all beings [to do the same].
That sentient beings succeed to the lineage of the Dharma King is precisely how they can repay the Buddha’s kindness and benefit all sentient beings.
At that time, the goddess bowed her head at the feet of Vimalakīrti and followed Māra back to her palace, where she suddenly vanished.
The celestial maidens of the Fourth Dhyāna Heaven received the instructions, paid their respects,
and returned to their palace as described in the text. World-Honored One, because Vimalakīrti possesses such sovereign supernormal powers, wisdom, and eloquence,
I am not fit to go to him to inquire after his illness.

This is the fourth concluding statement on his incapacity. Vimalakīrti possesses such supernormal powers that he knows and perceives through tranquil illumination, and he has attained mastery in subduing Māra.
His wisdom and eloquence consist in preaching the Dharma for the māra-daughters and expounding the Dharma-gate of the Inexhaustible Lamp.
Holding the World, I reflect upon my own past and realize that I lack such qualities; how could I possibly be fit to transmit this?
The Tathāgata’s intention was to go and inquire after his illness.
The Buddha told the elder’s son Śrīgupta, "Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness.
This is the fourth instance of the Buddha commanding the elder’s son Śrīgupta; the text here consists of two parts: first, the Buddha’s command to inquire.
The two sons of the elder were well able to offer their respectful farewells, yet they could not bear [the illness]. Therefore, he next commanded those who were to inquire after his health.
"Well-acquired" (*Sujāta*) refers to one among the five hundred sons of the elders;
he was a *gṛhapati-bodhisattva* (householder bodhisattva) who manifested as dwelling in the position of a successor to the Buddha. He is called "Well-acquired" because "well" (*su*) is...
"Skillful attainment" (*śubha-lābha*) refers to attaining the principle through skillfulness; because one attains the principle with skill, it is called "skillful attainment.
Although the four teachings clarify the meaning of skillful attainment, their interpretations differ: first, the *piṭaka* teaching clarifies the meaning of skillful attainment for the two vehicles;

second, the śrāvaka attains the principle but cannot sever habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*); third, the pratyekabuddha severs habitual tendencies but not completely, which is not the meaning of skillful attainment; [and fourth], the bodhisattva...

It is not so; the intention lies in universal salvation. Because one attains the ultimate fruit where both principle and practice are perfected and both afflictions and habits are exhausted, it is called "attaining goodness.

Regarding the meaning of "attaining goodness" in the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao): while the previous Tripitaka Teaching clarifies the entry into emptiness by analytically deconstructing the conventional—a clumsy means of attaining the principle where all three vehicles fail to attain goodness—the Shared Teaching clarifies the realization of the true by embodying the conventional; this is the skillful means of attaining the principle.

All three vehicles are indeed "skillfully attaining" the principle of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). However, while the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) lack great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and skillful means (*upāya*), they attain the principle and immediately enter nirvāṇa;
thus, it is not called "skillful attainment. Bodhisattvas, having attained the principle, do not dwell in nirvāṇa but are able to extensively benefit all sentient beings.
They profoundly exhaust the source and reach the ultimate fruit of Buddhahood; because their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are completely exhausted, it is called "skillful."

Third, regarding the meaning of "attaining well" (*śubha-prāpti*) as elucidated in the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddhayāna*): while the Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇayāna*) correctly attain the partial truth (*ekadeśa-satya*), how could this be called attaining well?

Only by attaining the true [nature], dwelling neither [in samsara nor nirvana], cultivating the Buddha-dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and severing the distinct afflictions (*bhinna-kleśa*) of both views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-vicikitsā*) to perceive the principle of the Middle Way within the Separate Teaching can it be called attaining well.
Fourth, the meaning of attaining well as elucidated in the Perfect Teaching (*anuttarayāna*) is distinct.
If one teaches that a Bodhisattva practices contemplation based on conditions to sever the fetters, how can this be called truly attaining the Perfect Teaching?

Only when a Bodhisattva of the Perfect Teaching maintains the three observations within a single mind without severing the afflictions, yet possesses the five eyes to fully perceive the principle of the Dharma-realm,
such that every thought is quiescent and naturally flows into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), thereby accomplishing the ultimate *nirvāṇa* of the three virtues— only then is it truly good.
To attain the meaning is to have no attainment by which one might claim attainment; because one attains through this non-attainment, it is called "skillful attainment.
In the first three teachings, skillful attainment is explained as provisional (upāya); in the final, perfect teaching, skillful attainment is explained as real.

Now, the son of the elder understands that the meaning is neither provisional nor real, yet he is able to accomplish the skillful attainment of both the provisional and the real, and thereby transforms others.
Because these things benefit themselves and others, enabling them to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, they are called "well-attained.
Since this is the meaning, how could one fail to understand that the assembly for the gift of Dharma was rebuked by Vimalakīrti?

It must be that [the teaching] acts like a press or a hammer upon things to bring them to completion, in order to manifest their entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. How do we know this is so? Because he now summons all the bodhisattvas to inquire after his illness.
By taking the first three meanings of the Four Great Beings (*mahāsattva*), one may infer and reveal the first three meanings of the stages of opening, showing, and awakening for the beginner.

Now, designating them as "Good Attainment" (*Sudhāra*) is intended to reveal the path of entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*). The previous section on *Lokadhara* revealed the awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;

this section correctly clarifies the subduing of the realm of Māra. As such, it is no different from the Buddha-realm; this very identity is the meaning of the non-duality of phenomena and principle (*dharmatā*).
Now, to clarify that entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision means bestowing the Dharma-gift without before or after, all at once and equally—
this is precisely the non-dual yet dual path where the two streams of contemplation flow together, such that mind and mind naturally flow into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
Thus, when Vimalakīrti received the fine necklace and divided it into two parts, giving one part to the poor man...
The assembly where the Victorious Tathāgata bestowed a portion of his alms upon the lowliest beggar in the city represents the assembly of the Dharma-gift;
this still refers to the distant seeking of those at the initial stage of the path.

The assembly of seven days during which Vimalakīrti previously destroyed [the notion of] goodness and obtained material gifts was intended to address Bodhisattvas who have received the three teachings but have not yet entered the Middle Way that dualistically illuminates the two truths.
All such acts of giving constitute assemblies for non-Dharma-giving.

Now, as the Tathāgata has commanded that those who inquire after his illness should skillfully recount the matters of being rebuked in the past, when the great assembly hears this, all those bodhisattvas who have received the teachings on expedient means will feel shame and be humbled, thereby forming an assembly for seeking true Dharma-giving; this is precisely the fulfillment of the five aforementioned types.
This is the meaning of "benefit.
Śrīgupta addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I am not fit to go there to inquire after his illness.
This is the second instance of Śrīgupta declining and expressing his inability; the text consists of four parts, the first of which describes his declination.
I. The reason for being incapable of expounding; II. The actual account of being rebuked; III. The conclusion that he is incapable. First, regarding the submission of his inability:

it was precisely because in the past he held a great seven-day sacrificial assembly—a gathering characterized by unrighteous giving—that he was unable to lead sentient beings to the Path and consequently was rebuked by Vimalakīrti; how, then, could he be capable of transmitting [the Dharma]?
The Tathāgata has sent me to inquire after your illness.

Why is this? I recall that in the past, while at my father’s house, I established a great assembly for almsgiving to provide offerings to all śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and various non-Buddhist practitioners, as well as to the poor, the lowly, the destitute, and beggars, for a period of seven full days.
Day. This is the second account of the reason for being unable [to attend]:

on the day the great almsgiving assembly was established at his father’s house to provide offerings to all beings, the period having reached its conclusion, he did not know of the Dharma-giving assembly. What is called "his father’s house" refers to the Śākyas.

Because he obtained the ancestral dwelling where his forefathers had previously resided, it is called "his father's house. Regarding the one who established a great assembly for almsgiving, the ancient commentaries of the Guan and He schools explain:
"In that family, for generations, the ancestors held heterodox views and constantly maintained heterodox shrines to sacrifice to the spirits and deities.
For the lower sacrifices they used sheep; for the middle sacrifices they slaughtered oxen; and for the superior sacrifices they used human beings. Having fortunately attained [the Dharma],..."
This Bodhisattva transformed his father, turning him away from heterodoxy and leading him into the Right Path;

he brought an end to these heterodox sacrifices and exhorted him to practice the True Path and perform genuine *dāna*. His family became immensely wealthy, possessing an abundance of the four requisites;

therefore, they organized this great assembly to provide offerings to all—whether monastics or laypeople, followers of internal paths or external paths, as well as the poor and lowly—who came without discrimination.
The period required for this is seven days; however, the giving assembly itself is the Bodhisattva’s perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
One should distinguish the different modes of the perfection of giving according to the four teachings, which are as follows: First, the *Tripiṭaka* Teaching clarifies giving:
if one can relinquish all material wealth and even not spare one's own body or life, only then does the perfection of giving become complete, as in the case of Śibi.

The King substituted his own body for the pigeon, yet his heart felt no regret. Second, regarding the explanation of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) according to the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*):
if one is merely able to relinquish everything and does not spare even one's own life, this is simply giving, but not yet a "perfection.

If, however, one realizes that the three factors [the giver, the recipient, and the gift] are all empty, then whatever is bestowed is both giving and a "perfection. Third, regarding the explanation of the perfection of giving according to the Distinct Teaching (*pratyeka-yāna*), although...
To know that these three matters are all empty is the *dāna-pāramitā* (perfection of giving), yet it is not the *pāramitā* [in its ultimate sense].

If one can deliver others from specific delusions to Great Nirvana, and furthermore can discern that giving possesses immeasurable aspects for responding to capacities and delivering beings, this is both *dāna* and the *pāramitā*.
Regarding the clarification of the *dāna-pāramitā* in the Fourth Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*): even if one knows that while practicing giving one must break through specific delusions...
The practice of random giving has immeasurable varieties; this constitutes generosity (*dāna*) but is not yet the perfection (*pāramitā*).

Why is this so? Because it is not ultimate. If one knows that all phenomena (*dharmas*) tend toward generosity, then even "tending toward" is not found within generosity itself—how much less could there be "tending toward" or "not tending toward"? This is precisely the perfection of generosity. Why is this so?

Regarding *dāna*, one ultimately penetrates all dharmas. The first three types of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) are provisional and do not constitute the assembly for the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*);
the perfection of giving elucidated in the final, perfect teaching is the reality, which is precisely the assembly for the gift of Dharma.
Having skillfully attained these as expedient means, he manifested the practice previously explained: for seven days, he established a great sacrificial feast in his father’s house.
It is because he failed to comprehend the assembly on the ultimate perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) through the gift of Dharma as elucidated in the Perfect Teaching (*yāna*);
thus, the reason for his being rebuked by Vimalakīrti and found unfit lies herein.
At that time, Vimalakīrti entered the assembly and said to me, "O son of a householder, a great assembly of giving should not be like the one you have arranged;
it should be an assembly for the gift of Dharma. What use is this assembly of material gifts?"
This is the third section, "Sudeva’s Account of His Own Past Reproach. Regarding this text, there are six points: first, Vimalakīrti’s formal reproach;
second, Sudeva’s request for an explanation; third, Vimalakīrti’s brief discourse on the assembly concerning the gift of Dharma; fourth, Sudeva’s further request;
fifth, Vimalakīrti’s further extensive exposition on the assembly concerning the gift of Dharma; and sixth, [the conclusion].
In the Age of Clarity, the assembly gains benefit through one [teaching]. Regarding the "Reproach of Vimalakīrti":

although he reproaches those who possess the merit of material giving at a great assembly, this is because they do not know that within material wealth there is the Dharma; thus, it is not a true Dharma-giving assembly. For this reason, he first reproaches and later exhorts.
His initial reproach is that a gathering based on material giving is not called a "great assembly," because they do not perceive the Buddha within all material things.
How could the Dharma itself be called "great"? As for the subsequent exhortation, it is precisely the exhortation to practice the Great Assembly of the Dharma-gift (*dharma-dāna*).
If one can know that within material wealth all Buddha-dharmas are fully present, this is the Great Assembly of the Dharma-gift. It is asked:
Does the assembly of the Dharma-gift consist in preaching the Dharma, or does the assembly of the Dharma-gift consist in the full presence of [all dharmas] within material wealth?
When all dharmas are given as material gifts (*āmiṣa-dāna*), this is itself the assembly of the Dharma-gift (*dharma-dāna*). The answer states: there are two meanings.
First, according to various sutras and śāstras, it is generally explained that material things constitute material giving and the teaching of the Dharma constitutes the Dharma-gift;
this is the distinction between these two types of giving as elucidated throughout the four teachings. Now, we clarify the inconceivable, perfect, and universal [giving].
The Way of this path is not merely that preaching the Dharma is called the gift of Dharma;
rather, when one bestows upon sentient beings all Buddha-dharmas contained within material wealth, such material giving is itself the gift of Dharma.

For example, when the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati untied the many precious jewel necklaces from his own neck and gave them to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, it was said: "You should receive these as the treasure of the gift of Dharma."
The Jewel Necklace was not preached as the Dharma by Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva; rather, he merely bestowed the necklace and spoke of "Dharma-giving.
This must mean that because all Buddha-dharmas are fully contained within the necklace, bestowing the necklace is itself the gift of Dharma.
Thus, in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, during the assembly for the gift of Dharma, it is said: "Without before or after, one makes offerings simultaneously."
"All sentient beings" is what is called the assembly for the gift of Dharma. This is as was previously taught by Kāśyapa:

"If one gives a single meal to all beings, thereby making offerings to all Buddhas and the multitude of worthy sages, and if this is considered the assembly for the gift of Dharma, then what concern does preaching the Dharma have with being an assembly for the gift of Dharma?
Furthermore, Vimalakīrti accepted the fine necklace from Sudatta.
He divided it into two portions: one portion he offered to the Tathāgata Duṣprasaha, and the other portion he gave to the lowliest beggar in the city.

He said, "If a donor gives with an impartial mind to the lowliest beggar, regarding them as identical to the Tathāgata—the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*)—without making any distinction, acting out of great compassion and seeking no karmic reward, this is what is called being 'endowed [with the perfection of giving]."
The Dharma-giving (*dharma-dāna*) is clarified in this manner; furthermore, why would it be related to the teaching of the Dharma as being Dharma-giving?

Now, according to this sutra, the assembly for Dharma-giving—which clarifies that those who are "well-obtained" (*sukṛta*) through censure are precisely defined by the perfection of material giving (*āmiṣa-dāna*) as being all dharmas—is itself the assembly for Dharma-giving.
The reason for this is that material giving consists of form (*rūpa*) and sound (*śabda*).
The *Gandha-rasa-spraṣṭavya-mahā-varga-sūtra* states: "All dharmas tend toward form; this 'tending' does not transcend form, for even form itself is unobtainable.
How, then, could there be tending or non-tending? This applies likewise to sound, fragrance, taste, and touch.
If a bodhisattva penetrates the characteristics of these phenomena in this way, they will possess all Buddha-dharmas through their merit, compassion, and vows."
When one who has cultivated the merit and wisdom of this gift of wealth bestows it upon sentient beings, they receive its benefit according to their own capacity, just like placing poison in milk.
It is also like hearing the sound of a poisoned drum: not only those nearby perish, but even those at a distance die as well.
Such a gift benefits the recipients; not only for seven days, but all those who receive it together obtain this benefit.

All sentient beings likewise share equally in these benefits. Because [the donor] did not understand this principle regarding the seven-day assembly of giving (*dāna-pūjā*), Vimalakīrti rebuked his delusion, saying: "A great assembly of giving should not be conducted as you have arranged it.
He thus guided that act of giving so that it might become an assembly of the Dharma-gift (*dharma-dāna*), and exhorted him to perform such a gift of the Dharma.

Question: Why is this assembly of material giving (*āmiṣadāna*) established? Question: Is it only in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) that there is this assembly of Dharma-giving (*dharmadāna*), or do the three teachings also have such an assembly of Dharma-giving?
Answer: Bodhisattvas in the three teachings also apply their minds to contemplative practice (*guanxing*) within the context of giving, and thus they may possess this meaning;
however, it is not as universal as in the Perfect Teaching, and it emerges from the gates of the provisional (*fangbian*) teachings.

It is not necessarily the case that this matter is fully elucidated here; therefore, in the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), Vimalakīrti, wishing to manifest the entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and its unimpeded penetration,
uses his critique of Śāriputra as a skillful means to cause the assembly present at that time— those who had received the teachings of the provisional methods—
to realize that the Bodhisattvas’ giving of inconceivable wealth constitutes the perfection of the Dharma-giving dāna-pāramitā.
I said, "Householder, what is meant by a 'gathering for the gift of Dharma'?
This is the second clarification regarding why he was requested to speak on the gathering for the gift of Dharma. Why did you request him to speak?
Did you not know that preaching the Dharma constitutes the gift of Dharma? However, it is certain that Vimalakīrti’s intention was not merely this; there must be something else."
I am deeply perplexed as to why this is so; please explain it to me.
As for the Dharma-giving assembly, it is an offering made simultaneously to all sentient beings, without beginning or end; this is called the Dharma-giving assembly.

This is the brief answer of Vimalakīrti, who possesses the three types of clear knowledge (*traividya*), well-attaining the assembly for the gift of the Dharma. As the sutra says regarding the "assembly for the gift of the Dharma":
it has no before and no after. This refers to contemplating the objects of giving—wealth consisting of forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles—and seeing that all dharmas converge upon form;
that within form itself, the ten dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*) are fully present. This is what is called the "Dharma."
To give this dharma of form to others is to give all dharmas; it is like using a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*) to give to others—it is the giving of all treasures.

The recipient thereby obtains all treasures. Those who do not distinguish between the various jewels, the giver simply says "I give the jewel," and the recipient simply says "I receive the jewel. This is like the various skillful means (*upāya*) of the teaching.
Regarding "Saqishi zhu" (Sa-ji-shi-zhu): the giver of the jewel knows that all treasures are being given, and the receiver of the jewel knows that all treasures are being obtained;
this is like a Bodhisattva of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). Thus, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"There are two kinds of people who obtain great benefit and merit: first, those who give according to the Dharma; second, those who receive according to the Dharma. This is precisely the Dharma.

Regarding the assembly of giving where there is neither "before" nor "after": the "prior limit" refers to sentient beings of the six realms within birth and death (*saṃsāra*), while the "subsequent limit" refers to the four kinds of noble ones in *nirvāṇa*.
The Bodhisattva contemplates these three things as being identical and non-dual; both are the Middle Way.
That which is not birth and death is thus without a prior limit, and that which is not *nirvāṇa* is thus without a subsequent limit. Thus says the Sūtra.
To say that "simultaneously making offerings to all sentient beings" is called the assembly of the Dharma-gift means that the Middle Way is neither birth-and-death nor nirvana;
it can simultaneously illuminate birth-and-death, which comprises the sentient beings of the six realms, and it illuminates nirvana, which comprises the four types of persons.
This is the Bodhisattva who encompasses all sentient beings within the ten dharma-realms.
By bestowing a single color, all sentient beings are enabled to see the Middle Way;

this is precisely the great causal condition for the one great matter, intended so that all sentient beings may attain opening, showing, awakening, and entry. Therefore, it is said that "one bestows everything.
Furthermore, if sentient beings have not yet obtained this great benefit of equality, they each obtain the benefit of wholesome dharmas according to their respective faculties and conditions.
This is also the giving of all things; it is neither provisional nor ultimate, illuminating both types of giving simultaneously.

When the mind is tranquil and extinguished, one naturally flows into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge); this is the entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and it is called the assembly for the gift of Dharma.
What does this mean?
This is the assembly where Śubhavyūha has twice requested the Dharma-giving; it is for this reason that Śubhavyūha made his repeated request.
Vimalakīrti’s brief response was concise in expression yet profound and vast in meaning. Although it thus revealed the assembly for Dharma-giving, its significance remains...

His intention remained clear within his traces, yet he skillfully manifested as if not yet awakened, repeatedly requesting [instruction] so that the assembly of that time might all attain liberation and universally receive the benefit of the gift of Dharma.
That is to say: to give rise to a mind of loving-kindness through bodhicitta in order to save sentient beings; and to give rise to a mind of great compassion in order to uphold the True Dharma.
Arousing a mind of joy, one gathers wisdom and practices a mind of equanimity.

This is the fivefold purity of the "Renowned Name" (Vimalakīrti), which provides a comprehensive response by extensively explaining the thirty-two instances of the characteristics of the gift of Dharma within the assembly;
each of these dharma-gates is individually correlated with the [gift of] material wealth.
To discern the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*), one cannot be separated from material wealth;

if one were separated from wealth, then this would mean that within wealth there is no gift of Dharma, and thus the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) would not encompass all dharmas. Therefore, it is necessary to rely upon wealth to clarify all dharmas.
All dharmas converge in giving; this convergence does not exceed this. Why should it stop at merely thirty-two permutations? One should know this.

Briefly stated: if one clearly understands that all the riches of every practice are fully contained therein, and contemplates these riches as being complete with all dharmas, then when one gives these riches to others, all these contemplative methods depart along with the riches.
When the recipient receives these riches, they receive all dharmas; or they receive forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, and textures.
Contact and so forth merely cause that which is received to enter; thus, everything gains entry. It is like shooting an arrow smeared with poison at another person:
wherever it strikes, the poison enters, and once the poison is activated, it kills the body. The Bodhisattva is likewise:

by means of all observed phenomena, he causes them to enter into this "wealth. This wealth is called the gift of Dharma (dharma-dāna), and it follows the six sense faculties (ṣaḍ-indriya) of the person before him.
The Dharma of receiving offerings allows one to immediately enter [the path], as clarified in the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra:

just as poison placed in milk permeates all five flavors and can kill a person, when sentient beings receive these riches and subsequently infuse them with the contemplation of all dharmas, they transform them into roots of goodness.
Later, upon encountering a Buddha, their past virtues are awakened, and they immediately attain realization, just as the poison manifests its lethal effect.
Some people may attain awakening through milk, some through curd, some through fresh butter, some through clarified butter, and even through the ultimate essence (*sarpis*);
yet these can also kill. Thus, material wealth serves as a gift of Dharma when it kills the body of afflictions and gives rise to the Dharma-body of merit and wisdom.
If it is not like this, then giving material wealth provides only slight benefit in the present and nothing at all for the future.
Because the causes and conditions for entering the Way lie herein, wealth is not called the Dharma, nor does it carry the sense of the affliction of killing others.
Furthermore, just as medicinal incense cures all ailments wherever its fragrance reaches, so too does the perfect contemplation of the gift of wealth encompass all dharmas;
to bestow this upon sentient beings is itself the gift of Dharma. It is not merely preaching the teachings that constitutes the gift of Dharma. However—

fourth, on miscellaneous practices; and fifth, a conclusion forming the assembly of the gift of Dharma. this is the Bodhisattva’s aspiration to benefit and transform living beings. The Sūtra states: "That is to say, by means of bodhi, one gives rise to the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*). The aforementioned passage says:
Quiescence is bodhi. If one contemplates that all phenomena tend toward wealth and that wealth is ultimately quiescent, this is true bodhi;
it gives rise to unconditioned great compassion, which, like a magnet attracting iron, bestows the bliss of Great Nirvana.
As the Sūtra says, "One gives rise to the mind of great compassion in order to save sentient beings," for all sentient beings are [bound] by two things.

Sentient beings, deluded by extremes, sink into the ocean of suffering; if one contemplates this wealth as being free from the two extremes, one gives rise to unconditioned great compassion (*anālambana-mahākaruṇā*) to extract all beings from the suffering of birth and death within those two extremes.
As the Sūtra says, "By upholding the True Dharma, one gives rise to a joyful mind":
the True Dharma is the principle of the single, ultimate Truth (*ekābhisaṃbodhi-satya*). If one perceives this principle, one is fully endowed with all that is correct.
This Dharma enables sentient beings to leave behind the suffering of the two extremes, attain Great Nirvana, and achieve unconditional great joy.
As the Sutra says, "By gathering wisdom, one gives rise to the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*).

If one contemplates the three factors and perceives the Buddha-nature within emptiness—the principle of the Three Truths—one then gathers the three types of wisdom. There is neither giver nor receiver; one knows the four [truths].
The ineffable equality of the true Dharma-realm means that although the Buddha does not "deliver" sentient beings— yet uproots their suffering and bestows happiness—

his mind remains free from discrimination and harbors no sense of personal favor toward beings; this is precisely the arising of the great equanimity of non-conditioned compassion (*nirālamba-mahopekṣā*).
One arouses the dāna-pāramitā by gathering in those who are stingy and greedy; one arouses the śīla-pāramitā by transforming those who violate the precepts;
one arouses the kṣānti-pāramitā by means of the dharma of non-self; one arouses the vīrya-pāramitā by being detached from the marks of body and mind;
one arouses the dhyāna-pāramitā by means of the mark of bodhi; and one arouses the prajñā-pāramitā by means of all-knowledge (sarvajñatā).
This is the second assembly clarifying the Dharma-giving (*dharma-dāna*) through the correct practice of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*). As the Sūtra says:

"By gathering in those who are stingy and greedy, one gives rise to the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*). If one contemplates the three factors and perceives the Middle Way, one immediately departs from the two extremes.
To be neither stingy nor [excessively] generous is called true giving. In order to gather in the five kinds of sentient beings who are stingy and greedy, one gives rise to five kinds [of giving].
The four *dāna* (giving) and one *upāya* (skillful means) constitute the true *dāna*, which gathers in all sentient beings as previously praised in the virtues of Vimalakīrti.
Having briefly analyzed the words of the Sūtra, [it is shown that] by transforming those who violate the prohibitions, one gives rise to the practice of the *śīla-pāramitā*.

If one perceives the single Truth of Reality (*ekasatyatattva*), then forgetting both observance and violation is the true *śīla*. For the sake of transforming the five kinds of sentient beings, he manifests the violation of prohibitions.
Regarding the maintenance of the five kinds of *śīla*, the four provisional and one real [precepts] have already been explained in detail as in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*. As the Sūtra states:
"To give rise to *kṣānti* (patience) through the dharma of non-self," the Bodhisattva contemplates giving and thereby perceives the single reality of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Thus, regarding self and non-self as non-dual is true non-self; if one perceives true non-self, then there is no anger.
Forbearance that cannot endure [suffering] is true *kṣānti*. To transform sentient beings who harbor five kinds of anger, five kinds of *kṣānti* are initiated.
There are four expedient means and one reality, as distinguished previously. As the Sūtra says: "One gives rise to *vīrya* by being free from the marks of body and mind.

This means that when a Bodhisattva contemplates the three factors of giving (*dāna*), they perceive the single reality-Truth (*ekam tattvam*); thus, they do not perceive body or mind. If there were any marks, [they would not be real].
If there is no characteristic, then neither advancing nor being indolent is true *vīrya* (diligence).

This arises for the sake of transforming sentient beings who are indolent in five ways, giving rise to the five kinds of diligence. The four skillful means and one reality are fully explained as previously stated. The Sūtra says:

"To give rise to dhyāna by means of the characteristic of bodhi" means that when a Bodhisattva contemplates the three factors of giving (*dāna*) and perceives the single reality-truth (*ekasatyatattva*), that is itself quiescence (*śānti*).
Quiescence is bodhi; not perceiving the marks of concentration or distraction is true dhyāna-samādhi.

To transform sentient beings whose minds are distracted in five ways, five kinds of dhyāna-samādhi are initiated. These four provisional means and one reality are fully detailed as previously analyzed in the sūtra.

As for the statement that "one gives rise to prajñā by means of all-knowledge," it refers to the Bodhisattva’s contemplation of the three factors of giving; if one perceives the right path, [this constitutes the arising of prajñā].

That is to say, one does not perceive the distinction between the ignorant and the wise as being truly [different from] omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). Rather, in order to transform sentient beings who are deluded in five ways, five kinds of wisdom are established. These consist of four provisional means (*upāya*) and one reality (*bhūta*), as explained in detail previously. Question: When explaining the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*) by way of the four immeasurables (*brahmavihāra*), for what reason is only the "real" aspect taken up? Regarding the six perfections, the gift of Dharma is explained through both aspects because it encompasses both the cultivation of the path and the realization of its fruit. Since the gift of Dharma is the primary factor among the six perfections, it is explained through both the provisional and the real aspects. The four immeasurables (catvāry apramāṇāni) are based solely on what is inwardly harbored and unknown to others;

the six perfections (ṣaṭ pāramitāḥ), however, are intended to gather sentient beings, and since their dispositions are not uniform, both skillful means and reality must arise together. Furthermore, the explanation of the four immeasurables as representing reality already encompasses skillful means;
because they are hidden within and cannot be known by others, they are not explained in full detail here.

To transform sentient beings while arising in emptiness (*śūnyatā*), not to abandon conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) while arising in signlessness (*animitta*), and to manifest birth while arising in wishlessness (*apraṇihita*):
these three clarify the gift of Dharma by way of the three gates of liberation. As the Sūtra says: "To transform sentient beings while arising in..."
Regarding emptiness, when a bodhisattva contemplates giving and perceives the single ultimate truth, this is the samādhi of true emptiness.

To transform sentient beings and sever their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) regarding both internal and external realms, he establishes the four teachings to clarify the four kinds of samādhi of emptiness—namely, the three provisional means and the one ultimate reality.
As the sutra says: "Without abandoning conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), one gives rise to the signless (*animitta*). This refers to the Bodhisattva...
When Bodhisattvas observe that both extremes of giving are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), they perceive the True Path, which is the signless samādhi (*animitta-samādhi*).
To transform sentient beings, they preach the four teachings and give rise to four kinds of signless samādhi; these are the three provisional means and one reality. As the Sūtra says:
"Manifesting birth while arising as non-doers. Because the Two Vehicles have no karma and do not undergo birth, it is called "signless" (*animitta*).
Practicing the Bodhisattva contemplation of liberation, one perceives the gift as the single path of purity, free from the karma of birth and death within the two extremes;

this is the true Samādhi of Non-action. Through the power of the roots of goodness of compassion, one manifests birth for the sake of sentient beings, preaching the four teachings of non-action—three provisional and one real—and thus gives rise to non-action.
To uphold the True Dharma, they give rise to the power of skillful means; to deliver sentient beings, they give rise to the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*);

to respectfully serve all, they give rise to the method of removing pride; regarding body, life, and wealth, they give rise to the three steadfast dharmas (*tridṛḍhadharma*); within the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*), they give rise to the dharma of mindfulness;
regarding the six points of harmonious respect, they give rise to a mind of straightforwardness; in practicing wholesome dharmas, they give rise to a mind of pure livelihood and pure joy.
One gives rise to joy by drawing near to the worthy and holy; one gives rise to a mind of subduing by not hating others; one gives rise to a profound mind through the dharma of renunciation;

one gives rise to great learning by practicing according to the teaching; one gives rise to solitude through the dharma of non-contention; one gives rise to the inclination toward the Buddha’s wisdom; one gives rise to meditative seclusion;
one gives rise to the stages of practice to untie the bonds of sentient beings; and one gives rise to the possession of the marks and signs and the purification of the Buddha-land.
He gives rise to the karma of merit by knowing the mental inclinations of all sentient beings and preaching the Dharma according to their needs;
he gives rise to the karma of wisdom by knowing all phenomena without grasping or rejecting, entering the gate of the single characteristic;
he gives rise to the karma of insight by severing all afflictions, all obstructions, and all unwholesome dharmas; and he gives rise to all wholesome karmas through the attainment of omniscience.
Wisdom gives rise to all wholesome dharmas and all factors that assist the path to Buddhahood;

this constitutes the fourth [aspect], clarifying the gift of Dharma through various practices. As the Sūtra says: "To protect and uphold the True Dharma is to give rise to the power of skillful means.
When a Bodhisattva contemplates giving, if they perceive the Right Path, it is the very city-treasure of the True Dharma; for the sake of protecting this, [they practice giving].

Because of the Dharma, one gives rise to the expedient means (*upāya*) of the Three Vehicles; through the inconceivable transformation of the three wheels, one employs the four inexpressible functions and explains the Four Teachings by means of the four *siddhāntas*. This is precisely the exertion of the power of expedient means.

As the Sūtra says, "To deliver sentient beings, one gives rise to the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*)," for the Bodhisattva contemplates giving and perceives the Principle, desiring to deliver sentient beings by means of this Principle. Thus, it is the cause.
Generosity gives rise to the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*). As the Sūtra says, "By serving all with reverence, one gives rise to the dharma that eliminates pride.

When a Bodhisattva practices giving, they contemplate the recipient as being like a Buddha; by giving with a heart of reverence and love, they do not give rise to contempt or arrogance—this is precisely giving rise to the activity that eliminates pride.

Seeing that the one true reality (*ekasatyam*) of giving can give rise to the three steadfast dharmas as previously explained, the Sūtra states regarding the arising of the dharma of mindfulness within the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*):
when a Bodhisattva brings to mind the awakening to giving (*dāna-bodhi*), the one reality of giving is precisely the recollection of the Buddha;
the fact that the *dharmatā* of giving is eternal and unchanging is the recollection of the Dharma; and the union of wisdom with giving is the recollection of the Saṃgha.

The mindfulness of giving (*dāna-smṛti*) consists in being able to sever evil and give rise to goodness; this is the mindfulness of giving. The mindfulness of giving consists in being able to relinquish all dharmas;

this is the mindfulness of relinquishment (*tyāga-smṛti*). The mindfulness of giving consists in attaining birth in the heavens of causes, the heavens of purity, and the supreme Heaven of the Thirty-three (*trāyastriṃśa*);

this is the mindfulness of the heavens (*deva-smṛti*). These are merely general expressions of the Dharma; the objects of the six kinds of mindfulness are distinguished according to the four teachings.
To contemplate the various dharmas of provisional and ultimate reality without confusion is called "the dharma of giving rise to contemplation.
Regarding the arousal of a straightforward mind within the six points of harmonious respect (*ṣaḍ-ānulomikāḥ saṃvartanīyā dharmāḥ*):

when a bodhisattva practices giving, there are the four kinds of sixfold harmonies clarified by the Four Teachings—namely, sameness of body, sameness of speech, and sameness of mind through compassion; and sameness of giving, sameness of view, and sameness of precepts. These constitute the three [categories].
One practices *dāna* by unifying the provisional with the real; once one knows that the four [truths] are ineffable, one is able to give rise to a mind of sincerity and straightforwardness.

As the Sūtra says, "Practicing the wholesome Dharma gives rise to pure livelihood," meaning that when a Bodhisattva practices giving, they must abide in the correct and wholesome Dharma of the four teachings to give rise to the four kinds of pure livelihood.
These three provisional and one real [teachings] are all for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
This gives rise to a mind of wrong livelihood. The Sūtra says that with a pure and joyful mind, one draws near to the worthy and holy (*ārya*).
When a Bodhisattva practices giving and perceives the single Truth of Reality (*tattva*), their original nature is pure;

they attain true Dharma-joy and draw near to the worthy and holy ones revealed by the various skillful means (*upāya*)—those who are identical to those who have attained the Way—in order to benefit sentient beings. The Sūtra says: "One does not harbor hatred."
When a bodhisattva practices giving with a mind intent on subduing evil persons, they do not give rise to obstacles upon seeing an evil person come to beg;
rather, they subdue their mind and enter the equal Dharma-realm, practicing universal giving. As a sutra says:

"One who gives rise to the profound mind through the dharma of renunciation" refers to a bodhisattva practicing giving who perceives the single reality-Truth (*ekasatyadharma*) and departs from the two extremes of the house of birth-and-death.

Because all who receive the teachings on skillful means know that the dharma of renunciation ultimately returns to the single Great Vehicle dharma of renunciation, they give rise to the profound mind (*adhyāśaya*).
As the Sūtra says: "By practicing according to what is taught, one gives rise to great learning.

When a Bodhisattva practices giving while contemplating the single ultimate truth (*ekasatyatā*), their mind becomes pliant and compliant, enabling them to practice according to the teaching and give rise to great learning, desiring to hear it universally.
This is the teaching of the four vehicles as three provisional means and one ultimate reality.

When the sutra says, "By means of the dharma of non-contention, one arises in a secluded place," it means that when a bodhisattva practices giving and knows the four things that cannot be spoken of, they are without contention;

through skillful means, they arise in various secluded places to gather in sentient beings who are amidst the clamor of the world. When the sutra says, "One proceeds toward the Buddha-wisdom by arising in meditative seclusion," [it refers to this].

When a bodhisattva practices giving and perceives the single truth of reality (*ekasatyatā*), thereby turning toward the wisdom of a Buddha and engaging in meditative seclusion (*pratisaṃlayanam āsīnaḥ*), this is explained in detail according to the chapter on Śāriputra.
As the Sūtra says, "releasing the bonds of sentient beings and arising on the stage of cultivation":

when a bodhisattva practices giving and contemplates the single truth of reality, they are able to use skillful means (*upāya*) to release the internal and external realms within the realm of sentient beings.

Regarding external constraints, the various distinctions made concerning the stages of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*) according to different doctrinal systems—such as the differences in the realization, abandonment, and suppression of afflictions within the true ranks of the noble ones (*ārya*)—are as analyzed previously in the *Xuan-yi* (Profound Meaning).
As the Sūtra states: "By means of possessing the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) and purifying the Buddha-lands, one initiates the karma of merit.
This refers to a Bodhisattva’s practice of giving (*dāna*), which initiates the karma for the thirty-two marks, as explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
It has already been explained in the preceding "Chapter on the Buddha-land" that the karma for purifying the buddha-field arises from giving;
this is what the Sūtra means when it says, "knowing the mental inclinations of all sentient beings and preaching the Dharma accordingly gives rise to the karma of wisdom.

When a bodhisattva practices giving and perceives the single ultimate truth (*ekābhisamaya*), they immediately know the mental inclinations of all sentient beings and are able to preach the Dharma in accordance with their capacities, thereby giving rise to [the karma of wisdom].

This is the activity of the two wisdoms—expedient and ultimate—according to circumstances. As the Sūtra says: "Knowing all dharmas without grasping or abandoning, one enters the gate of the single characteristic and gives rise to the activity of wisdom.

When a Bodhisattva practices giving, they know that all dharmas converge in *dāna* (generosity) and perceive the single true reality (*ekasatyatattva*), thereby being without grasping or abandoning and entering the single characteristic.
Regarding the statement that "one gives rise to the activity of wisdom," this refers to the forgetting of what preceded.
These are the two wisdoms of the provisional and the real. As the Sūtra says: "To sever all afflictions, all hindrances, and all unwholesome dharmas;
to give rise to all wholesome karmas and to attain all wisdom and all wholesome dharmas;
and to bring forth all factors that assist the path to Buddhahood"—when a Bodhisattva practices giving and perceives the single Truth of Reality (*ekābhisamaya*), true cultivation is manifested.

If one is thus able [to practice], yet desires to advance further in both self-cultivation and the transformation of others, one must give rise to conditions and cultivate the dharmas that assist the Buddha-way.
Such, son of good family, is the assembly for the gift of Dharma; if a bodhisattva abides in this assembly for the gift of Dharma, [he shall attain great merit].
He becomes a great donor and a field of merit for all the world.
This is the fifth assembly that perfects the giving of the Dharma; it is also dwelling within generosity while possessing all Buddha-dharmas.
Just as the scent of medicinal herbs applied to a poisoned arrow, wherever it reaches, it immediately [neutralizes] all... [afflictions].
The extinction of afflictions and the fulfillment of all roots of goodness constitute the assembly for the gift of Dharma;
such a person is a great donor. As the Sūtra says, they also serve as a field of merit for all sentient beings:
if a Bodhisattva has internally accomplished all Buddha-dharmas, then anyone who makes offerings to them will be able to cultivate and grow all those roots of goodness; this is what is truly so.
It is also a field of merit.
When the World-Honored One and Vimalakīrti preached this Dharma,
two hundred people from among the assembly of Brahmins all resolved to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This is the section on the benefits gained by the assembly during the six periods of light. It consists of two parts: first, the Brahmin’s generation of the bodhicitta;
second, the explanation of how the mind of Sudatta attained purity. Regarding the Brahmin’s generation of the bodhicitta:

upon hearing the teaching that the perfection of *dāna-pāramitā* encompasses all Buddha-dharmas, his mind was opened and his understanding clarified at this assembly of Dharma-giving, reaching the unsurpassed state.
The aspiration for the Way immediately arose within me.

At that time, my heart attained purity, and I marveled at this unprecedented occurrence; I prostrated myself to pay homage at the feet of Vimalakīrti and offered him a necklace worth hundreds of thousands.
This is the second section, "Subhūti Attains Purity of Mind," which consists of four parts:
(1) Subhūti attains purity of mind and pays homage and makes offerings; (2) Viśuddhamati modestly declines the honor; (3) Subhūti respectfully requests again and accepts the necklace;
(4) Viśuddhamati accepts the necklace and dedicates the merit so that Subhūti may attain purity of mind. Regarding "Subhūti attains purity of mind": Subhūti heard [the teaching].
To preach the Dharma is to see all Buddha-dharmas within giving, which, being thoroughly illuminated and untainted, constitutes the purification of the mind.
Because he had never before heard this teaching—which was previously only received through provisional instructions—he attained what he had never experienced before.
Moved by the great benefit of Vimalakīrti, he felt profound gratitude and paid his respects; he offered his necklace as an offering to repay his debt of gratitude.
He was unwilling to accept it.
This second clarification shows that Vimalakīrti declined to receive it because his original intent was to benefit others through the Dharma and he had no attachment to material things;
furthermore, had he accepted it suddenly, it might have led to public censure, and it also serves to demonstrate that the Bodhisattva inwardly maintains the non-acceptance of all dharmas.
I said, "Householder, I pray that you will certainly accept whatever you wish to give.
