This is because [the donor] has not yet expressed the intent of a formal invitation, a request for repeated acceptance, a respectful offering out of gratitude, or a gift to be accepted as a necessary requirement;
therefore, one accepts it repeatedly so that it may be redirected as a dedication, thereby fulfilling the sincere devotion of the donor."
Then Vimalakīrti accepted the necklace, divided it into two portions, gave one portion as a gift to the lowliest beggar in this assembly,
and offered the other portion to that Tathāgata Duṣprasaha.
This is the fourth: Mañjuśrī accepts the pure name [of the necklace] and dedicates it as a gift, thereby causing the assembly to attain a profound sense of reverence;

it also signifies that a Bodhisattva, for the sake of transforming sentient beings, accepts all sensations through non-acceptance, and having accepted them, dedicates them to the two fields of compassion and respect.
The text contains four points: first, the dedication to the two fields of compassion and respect; second, the members of the assembly seeing the necklace upon him.
The Buddha’s three supreme purities are titled "A Brief Discourse on the Assembly for the Gift of Dharma.

When the beggars from the four cities resolve their minds on Bodhi, they offer their gifts once to both the field of compassion and the field of reverence; this manifestation that the field of merit is non-dual is precisely the assembly for the gift of Dharma.
The entire assembly beheld the Tathāgata Duṣpradharṣa of the land of Prabhāsa,
and they also saw the pearl necklace above that Buddha transform into a four-pillared jeweled terrace, magnificently adorned on all four sides and not obstructing one another.
This manifestation— wherein the assembly sees the Tathāgata Duṣprasaha receive the pure Mañjuśrī-garbha necklace and transform it into a four-pillared jeweled terrace—
is intended to signify that because of this offering, Mañjuśrī will, in the future,
attain the fruit of the four supreme virtues of unobstructed Great Parinirvāṇa.
When Vimalakīrti had manifested these supernatural transformations, he spoke these words: "If a donor gives with an impartial mind even to the lowliest beggar,
regarding them as identical to the field of merit of the Tathāgata— without making distinctions, out of great compassion,
and seeking no reward for the fruit of their action— this is called the fulfillment of the gift of Dharma."

This is the assembly for the Dharma-giving of Vimalakīrti, who, possessing the purity of the three knowledges (*traividyā*), bestowed a jeweled necklace as an offering. Regarding the purity of the name:
even when giving to a beggar, one regards them as having the characteristics of the Tathāgata’s field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), without making any discrimination.

This is precisely the contemplation of the field of giving as the equal *dharmadhātu*, free from dualistic marks, thereby accomplishing unconditional great compassion (*nirālambanā mahākaruṇā*) and attaining perfection in the One Vehicle.
To not seek the retribution for practicing based on conditions regarding all Buddha-dharmas is itself the fulfillment of the assembly for the gift of Dharma (*dharma-dāna*);
since such is the explicit text, how can the various Dharma masters rely solely on the act of preaching to explain the gift of Dharma?
A most lowly beggar within the city, seeing this supernatural power and hearing what was said, all gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This is the beggar within the city of Caturmukha who, upon witnessing the supernatural power, gave rise to the bodhicitta. Furthermore—
Upon hearing the discourse on the assembly for the gift of Dharma, his mind was opened and he attained awakening, immediately resolving upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment.
Therefore, I am not fit to go to him to inquire after his illness.
This is the fourth [reason], concluding that the Elder’s son Śrīgupta is unable [to visit]. He himself reflected thus upon his past life in his father’s house.
"If one organizes a gathering without being proficient in the gift of Dharma, it results in mere reputation and censure;
how could such a person, whose mind is not yet purified, be worthy of transmitting the Tathāgata’s intent to go inquire after his illness?
Thus, each of these bodhisattvas spoke to the Buddha regarding their own past causes and recounted what Vimalakīrti had said.
They all said, "We are not fit to go there to inquire after his illness.

This is the second major section of this chapter; as for the variations in the extant scriptures, they are not uniform—some may have been brought from the original texts, while others may not have been fully translated.
Thus, when the various Bodhisattvas were commanded, they all declined, citing their own unfitness for the task.
If one clarifies this based on the praise of their virtues, there are thirty-two thousand bodhisattvas;
if one follows the text regarding Mañjuśrī’s entry into the chamber, it speaks only of a number of eight thousand bodhisattvas, so a definitive judgment cannot yet be made.
As for the four bodhisattvas who recounted the words of their past rebukes, the scribe used several sheets of paper to describe these various bodhisattvas.
Each person has presented their own exposition, and these texts amount to several thousand scrolls.

Since this entire great assembly has heard them together and the Tathāgata has certified them as all constituting the meaning of the five kinds of benefits, how could they be categorized as belonging exclusively to the Introductory Section?
Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra, Scroll 18;
Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra, Scroll 19 (The Fifth Chapter: Visiting the Sick, Part One).
This chapter follows the "Bodhisattva" chapter because the Buddha previously commanded his disciples and bodhisattvas to go inquire after [Vimalakīrti’s] illness.
Each [of the disciples] respectfully declined, deeming themselves unable to fulfill this current command; it was Mañjuśrī who respectfully accepted the command to inquire after his illness.

Therefore, it is titled "The Chapter on Mañjuśrī’s Inquiry into the Illness. The preceding section clarifies how Vimalakīrti manifests illness to give rise to the teaching; broadly categorizing the text, it consists of two main parts.
The first two chapters and a half constitute the teaching given by Vimalakīrti outside his room; this present chapter concerns what takes place inside his room.

When expounding the Dharma outside the chamber, he frequently uses the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint of therapeutic treatment) to rebuke and subdue others, thereby leading them into the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*).
When entering the chamber, he frequently employs the *puruṣakāra-siddhānta* (the standpoint of individual guidance) to attract and sustain them, as this leads them into the ultimate meaning.
Thus, the *Śrīmālādevī Sūtra* states: "By means of subduing and sustaining, the True Dharma is enabled to abide for a long time. That which enables the Dharma to abide for a long time is...
This entry into the primary meaning results in the attainment of untainted, true dharmas that shall never again be lost.

Having concluded the section on subduing outside the house, this chapter and the following five chapters now clarify the process of gathering [disciples] within the house; thus they follow in sequence.
Now, I shall briefly employ five meanings to explain the textual and doctrinal sense of this chapter and the subsequent five.
First, clarifying the purpose of this chapter’s introduction; second, clarifying that Mañjuśrī is capable of inquiring after the illness;
third, explaining the two types of illness—the provisional and the real; fourth, how the six chapters emerge from the illness;
fifth, entering the text for a detailed commentary.

First, to clarify the intent of this chapter: the Great Being Vimalakīrti, dwelling in inconceivable skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), assists the Great Sage in manifesting the teaching of the causes and conditions for attaining a Buddha-land through inconceivable true nature and liberation.
Previously, he used the four teachings to subdue ordinary beings, those of the two vehicles, and all partial-practicing bodhisattvas; now, he praises [the Buddha].

The fruit of the three liberations of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) receives and guides [practitioners], causing them to cultivate the causes of the three contemplations (sanguan), enter the inconceivable liberation, and attain the practice of being born in pure Buddha-lands according to their karma through beholding pure lands.
For this reason, this chapter and the following five chapters have come forth. Briefly summarized, there are five points regarding this: first, to respond to the times.
1. To respond to the hearts of the assembly who look up with thirsting longing; 2. To be subsumed and introduced by the three contemplations; 3.
To support and perfect the teaching on purifying the Buddha-land; 4. To enter the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* as its progeny; 5.

To return to the place where the Buddha established his meditative concentration. Regarding the first—responding to the hearts of the assembly who look up with thirsting longing—though there are kings, officials, commoners, disciples, and bodhisattvas...

Śāriputra stated that while the great assembly had long been filled with sincere longing and thirst for the noble wisdom and supreme virtues of the Mahāsattva, they had not yet been able to see or hear him;

however, if those who come to inquire after his illness were to follow him and receive his personal instruction, they would all be able to behold and hear of the Mahāsattva’s inconceivable divine wisdom and his deeds in benefiting sentient beings through the pretext of illness. Therefore, Mañjuśrī accepted the command and went at the appointed time to the assembly.

The mind [of the Buddha] causes them to see that their illness is entrusted to an empty room, which represents the hearing of the discourse on the inconceivable duality of the provisional and the real illnesses.

Second, regarding the inclusion and introduction through the three contemplations: outside the room, he rebukes those bodhisattvas who follow partial teachings, those of the three vehicles who have not yet entered the true position, and all ordinary beings;
although their hearts are broken with longing and admiration, they do not yet contemplate the inconceivable.
When discussing the right path, one finds that few know how to enter its proper track; it is as when Mañjuśrī entered the chamber to inquire after the Bodhisattva’s illness.
In the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, both briefly and extensively, it clarifies the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) for the subduing of the mind.

This "subduing" (*vinaya*) is precisely the meaning of "gathering," "receiving," and "introducing. Third, regarding the support and completion of the teaching on the Pure Land: if, following Mañjuśrī’s inquiry...
One is able to swiftly cultivate the three contemplations to exhaust all obstacles of conditions, whether they be few or many;
thus one attains vision of pure lands and is born in each of those pure realms. All such vows and practices constitute the conduct for purifying a Buddha-land.

Fourth, as for those who enter the lineage of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* sūtras: even if those of the two vehicles have already entered the stage of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*), at that time, although they hear [these teachings]...
The Buddha’s preaching of the Mahāyāna sūtras was like milk that had not yet turned into curd;

now, as Mañjuśrī enters the chamber and further hears the exposition of the six chapters, he immediately attains the transformation of curd into fresh butter (*navanīta*). Thus, when Kāśyapa said, "Now all the śrāvakas should exclaim and cry out," this refers precisely to this matter.
If one reaches the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* [Sūtra], it becomes clarified butter (*ghṛta*); if one reaches the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, it becomes ghee (*sarpirmaṇḍa*).
Nirvāṇa is itself the attainment of *amṛta* (the finest essence).

Those of dull faculties who receive the Tripiṭaka teachings, as well as Bodhisattvas who progress through the five-flavor teachings, share the same general intent as the Two Vehicles. As for those of sharp faculties whose stage is not fixed, this is as explained previously;
it has already been fully clarified in the "Bodhisattva Chapter. Fifth, regarding returning to the Buddha’s place to receive the definitive seal: if one does not rely on the text...
When Śāriputra inquired after his illness and entered the room, he engaged in a dialogue with Vimalakīrti that culminated in the sixth chapter on ultimate purity.

How could Vimalakīrti have otherwise physically lifted the great assembly and returned them to the Āmra Garden before the Tathāgata? There, the Tathāgata confirmed the preceding and subsequent teachings;
subsequently, Śāriputra addressed the Tathāgata at length to clarify the Pure Land, wherein the world of Sukhāvatī was brought into this land.

Causing the entire great assembly to see and hear [this teaching], to make vows for rebirth, and to cultivate the practices of Akṣobhya Tathāgata—this is the essential summary of everything expounded both outside and inside the Vimalakīrti chamber;
it entirely supports and completes the Great Sage’s teaching on the cause and effect of the inconceivable liberation, the Dharma-body, and the purification of Buddha-lands. First...

Second, explaining why Mañjuśrī alone is capable of inquiring after the illness: regarding the Emperor’s command that the five hundred disciples and the great bodhisattvas each recount their own rebukes and decline the task of inquiring after the illness, while Mañjuśrī alone is able to fulfill the Buddha’s sacred intent, there are briefly five reasons:
first, his high station; second, his manifestation of traces; third, the revelation of perfection; fourth... [text ends].
This is what satisfies the sentiments of the multitude; it is a single stage that adapts to capacities, yet its loftiness makes it fit for one to inquire after the illness [of the Buddha].
Although Mañjuśrī and the various Bodhisattvas dwell together in the rank of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), within this single stage there is nonetheless a distinction of high and low.
Therefore, the *Ratnavyūha Sūtra* clarifies that those dwelling in the rank of Equal Enlightenment enter the Gate of the Double Profundity and receive their retribution for immeasurable kalpas.

Mañjuśrī has long cultivated the practices of ordinary beings; his wisdom and virtue have long since reached the highest excellence, and as he is now equal to Vimalakīrti, he is fit to be the one who inquires after his illness.
This is the primary meaning. Second, regarding his being fit to inquire after the illness by way of manifesting a trace:
while most bodhisattvas occupy the stage of true attainment and dwell in the position of a successor, it is Mañjuśrī alone—[who manifests such traces].
Furthermore, his original ground is that of the Tathāgata Nāga-king, who now manifests traces by dwelling in the stage of the "Successor" (Upapadya);

since his meaning of original and manifested ground is identical to that of Vimalakīrti, he is qualified to inquire after the illness. Moreover, this is merely an explanation from one perspective. Third, to reveal the perfect [teaching]:

how could the original and manifested grounds of the various bodhisattvas be definitively measured? However, when these bodhisattvas assist the Teacher of the Dharma, they frequently manifest the propagation of the methods [of salvation].
Because he was instructed in the gate [of the teaching], he was entirely refuted by Vimalakīrti.

Mañjuśrī assisted the Teacher in extensively demonstrating the Mahāyāna (the broad and perfect teaching), and since his task of assisting the Buddha to propagate the Dharma was identical to that of Vimalakīrti, he was qualified to go inquire after the illness. Question:
If that is so, how could he have been refuted by Aṅgulimāla? Answer: This is discussed from the perspective of the majority; it was by Aṅgulimāla that he was refuted.
This is merely a minor point of interpretation. Although Mañjuśrī was not previously rebuked by Vimalakīrti, there is no contradiction in principle for him to do so now under the sacred command.

As for the fact that the feelings of sentient beings are satisfied: since all the bodhisattvas assist the Great Master according to the capacities of beings, how could he fail to propagate the Perfect Teaching at all?
It is simply that although Maitreya has succeeded the Teacher of Śākyamuni, [he does not yet appear in this world].
Regarding the affairs and protocols of the bodhisattvas who serve as attendants on the right side, these are mostly characterized by a formal and distant demeanor;
whereas those who occupy the position of the "Successor" (kṣetra) co-residing with Mañjuśrī serve as the Master’s attendants on the left side.

Just as a state minister on the left side of a kingdom possesses the sovereign authority to adjudicate matters more effectively than one on the right, this is what accords with the inclinations of sentient beings. Fifth, [the teaching] adapts to capacities.

While all other bodhisattvas possess a capacity for interaction with Vimalakīrti that is like a block of wood and a hammer working together to form an object, Mañjuśrī and Vimalakīrti possess a capacity for interaction like two hammers striking one another to form an object; thus, Mañjuśrī is fit to be the one who inquires after his illness.

Therefore, when he enters the room and engages in dialogue with Vimalakīrti, his words are never faltering or obstructed, delighting the hearts of the multitude, and he often acts as Vimalakīrti’s interlocutor.
To praise him in this way is surely not the same as the speech of other bodhisattvas, which is always met with rebuke and refutation;
for these reasons, Mañjuśrī is fit to inquire after his illness. Third, regarding the explanation of the two types of illness—the provisional and the real:

although the meanings of "illness" are numerous, when their essential intent is traced, they do not exceed these two kinds: the provisional and the real. The provisional refers to the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas and the bodhi...

The Bodhisattva manifests illness where there is no illness; therefore, this is called the provisional (upāya). Because the ninefold path of sentient beings truly possesses the afflictions of cause and effect, this is called the real (tattva).
If one follows the perspective of the capacity for transformation, then logically the provisional should come first and the real second, as this sutra text asks:
"Is this illness endurable? and further states: "How does a sick bodhisattva practice self-discipline?"

As for his mind, it follows the order of the transformation [of beings], wherein reality precedes and skillful means follow; thus, the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra states: "Because sentient beings are ill, I am ill.
Now, regarding this illness of reality as presented in the sequence of the transformation, we shall briefly analyze it according to four meanings:
first, distinguishing the two aspects of cause and effect; second, the characteristics of the two types of illness; third, the explanation; and fourth... [the remainder of the text].
Clarifying the fourfold classification of the distinct and common [teachings] by way of the lands, first, distinguishing the signs of swiftness in cause and fruit:
Now, illness (*vyādhi*) is a phenomenon of obstruction; because it obstructs both form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*), it is called illness, and it is also called disease and affliction (*ābādha*).
What is termed "illness due to causes" refers to the fourfold afflictions within the causal stage that obstruct the mind and spirit.

To give rise to various afflictions and calamities is precisely the sickness of the mind; as for the term "cause," it is because afflictions (*kleśa*) are the cause that they are called the "sickness of the cause.

As for the "sickness of the fruit," if one brings forth a body composed of the four great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—these abide together within a single vessel, yet their natures are each distinct, mutually opposing, and alternately giving rise to increase or decrease, thereby causing obstruction and impairment to the physical form.

The various afflictions and ailments are themselves the diseases of the body; yet they are called "diseases of the fruit" because they serve as the retribution for the "diseases of the cause," which are the afflictions.
Regarding the second explanation: within the fourfold division of afflictions in the causal stage, one first distinguishes the three poisons in opposition to the three great diseases.
As for the "equal-part" (sāmya) afflictions, this is because the grasping at a self exists equally across the three locations [the body, speech, and mind].
Names and so forth are the great diseases of this birth-ground. Why is this so? First, regarding the disease of desire in contrast to the water element, the Sūtra says:
"The river of craving swirls back and forth, drowning sentient beings; blinded by ignorance, they cannot escape.
Furthermore, craving can moisten karma, just as water moistens growth. Second, regarding the affliction of hatred in contrast to the fire element: as soon as a mind of hatred arises, [it burns].
Because it burns away the roots of goodness, anger is likened to fire; because delusion is a defilement, it is likened to the disease of wind.
Since delusion gives rise to the four inversions (*catur-viparyāsa*), the Sūtra states that the violent winds of the four inversions can topple mountains and level peaks.
Thus, one knows that the inversions of delusion correspond to the disease of wind. Because the disease of the fourth stage possesses three kinds of discrimination, it is like water.

Because fire and wind disorders gather together within a single body, and because the balanced humors (sannipāta) correspond to earth-related ailments, the fourfold afflictions constitute the four causes of disease.
When ordinary, base worldlings possess these fourfold afflictions, there arise eighty-four thousand causal diseases of affliction;
following conditions, they are activated and bring torment and harm to the minds and spirits of sentient beings.

Therefore, it is said that the cause is swift and the result is swift. That which is the "swift result" refers to the various afflictions of the constituent parts (*skandhas*) which bring about the retribution-body (*vipākakāya*).

When even one of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) is disturbed, one hundred and one diseases arise; when all four great elements are disturbed, four hundred and four diseases arise, resulting in manifold afflictions and illnesses.
Furthermore, it is by means of the afflictions of the four parts that the retribution-body is brought into being.
The existence of birth, old age, sickness, and death is likewise a great affliction for sentient beings;
therefore, the latter part of this sutra states that the presence of birth and death constitutes a great affliction. This, too, arises from the fourfold afflictions (*kleśa*).
Why is this so? As the *Śrī-sūtra* (or *Śrī-garbha-sūtra*) states: "Greed leads to old age, hatred leads to sickness, and delusion leads to death. Now...
Inferring from these meanings, the "equal portions" (samabhāga) lead to birth;
once born, there is a body composed of the four great elements, and with a body, there is the suffering of the four diseases—this is precisely the meaning of the result of illness.

However, as the sūtras and śāstras vary according to circumstances, sometimes fire is used as a metaphor for greed, sometimes water for hatred, and even wind is not fixed; now, [we shall discuss] the first.

If one follows the extensive discourse to extract its specific meaning, it is relevant as previously discussed regarding the supernormal power of the divine ear; what, then, could not be illustrated by this?

As for the distinction between the three types of supernormal knowledge (*vidyā*) and the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), there are two aspects—cause and effect—each having both general and specific dimensions.

Regarding the specific dimensions of the causal aspect, the four grave offenses constitute the general category, while the ten unwholesome paths, the four pārājika offenses, the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya-karma*), and the slandering of the Vaipulya sutras constitute the specific instances. Regarding the specific dimensions of the resultant aspect, the fourfold division constitutes the general category, while the aforementioned [offenses] constitute the specific instances.

The icchantika is mentioned for the sake of distinction. Regarding the illnesses of the fruits, there are both general and specific types. The four great elements and the four sufferings constitute the general category;

the increase of the four great elements, severe and sudden ailments, or the occasional intensification of the four sufferings, up to the heavy sufferings of the three miserable realms—all these are the specific illnesses within the fruits.
This is truly because within the causes there exist both general and specific illnesses. Therefore...
Regarding the results, there are both general and specific defects; since in the causes there are only general defects, at the time of the result there are likewise only general defects.
If at the time of the cause the general defect is strong and the specific defect is weak, then at the time of the result the general defect is also strong and the specific defect is weak.
If at the time of the cause the specific defect is strong and the general defect is weak, then at the time of the result the specific defect is also strong and the general defect is weak.
The fourth point, concerning the gravity or lightness of afflictions according to the lands, is the differentiation of gravity and lightness based on the four lands:
first, regarding the Land of Common Dwelling; second, the Land of Shared Reward; third, regarding the Land of Fruitional Reward;
and fourth, regarding the Land of Eternal Quiescent Light. First, regarding the differentiation of gravity and lightness within the Land of Common Dwelling: [it is] the same as...
The dwelling-place is the conditioned arising of the four aggregates; the afflictions are the causal illness, and the segmented birth-and-death within the three realms is the resultant illness.
This has two types: first, the defiled, and second, the pure. In the defiled, the illness is heavy; in the pure, the illness is light.
It is for this reason that the defiled constitutes an illness: in the shared defiled land, all five destinies are present. If one is among the devas...

Regarding the fruits of the Path, the illnesses of the three realms of humans, animals, and ghosts consist only of common afflictions and lack distinct causal illnesses; thus, their causal illnesses are not fixed.
If one explains the causes and fruits of these three paths according to their respective meanings, they possess both common and distinct aspects, varying in degree.
As for the fruits of the illnesses of the hell realm, there are only distinct heavy sufferings and no common afflictions; likewise, their causal illnesses are also not fixed. If it is the same...
Dwelling in the Pure Land, there is exclusively only general illness and no specific illness.

The reason for this is that although the fourfold afflictions (*kleśa*) exist in the Pure Land, the ten evil deeds, the five heinous crimes, and other such grave offenses are absent; likewise, the four evil realms and the four heavy sufferings do not exist.
Therefore, illnesses resulting from cause and effect are merely general and both are light. Second, explaining the illnesses in the Land of Residual Defilement (*sāvaśeṣabhūmi*).
This refers to the illness of those outside the [true] realm; it is the suffering of the fruit of *parināmi-ja* (transformative) birth-and-death experienced by the sages of the Three Vehicles.
Having seen only the partial truth and exhausted the delusions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), they remain attached to the one true reality (*eka-tattva-satya*) and to the *śūnyatā-nirvāṇa*.

Thus, they give rise to the fourfold afflictions of unconditioned conditions and collections, which induce the fruit of suffering of transformative birth-and-death; this is also termed "expedient birth-and-death. This pertains to the Separate Teaching and the Perfect Teaching.
The teaching for Bodhisattvas involves the exhaustion of afflictions within the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) while not yet having seen the Middle Way;

thus, they do not sever ignorance or the specific delusions (*pṛthagmoha*), and all are born in the Land of Expedient Means (*upāyabhūmi*). The causal and resultant afflictions of this stage are identical to those of the Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas.

These causal and resultant afflictions constitute what are termed the "disease of the cause" and the "disease of the result. This is explained according to the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavahāra*); it does not refer to the "common" (*sāmānya*) or "distinct" (*bheda*) aspects as explained in the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇavyavahāra*).
This explains the general and specific aspects of "sickness. A question is asked: "In other lands, how can there still be the causes of sickness categorized into four parts?
The answer is: "The unconditioned (*asamskrta*) is divided into four parts based on its conditions. Why is this so? Grasping at partial truth (*ekadeśa-satya*) is precisely craving (*rāga*);

abandoning conventional existence (*saṃvṛti-sat*) is precisely hatred (*dveṣa*); and being deluded regarding the single ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is precisely ignorance (*moha*). These three parts are taken as equal."

This refers to the equal distribution [of these factors]; these four parts are precisely the causes of the distinct afflictions of *dṛṣṭi* (views) and *saṃjñā* (perception), as well as the disease of rapidity. Question:

Since the remaining lands already possess the causal diseases of these four parts, do they also possess the resultant diseases of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the four types of suffering?

Answer: They also possess the four great elements of transformation (*pariṇāma*) and the four types of suffering in their general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). Question: Regarding the upper realms...
Question: "If even the various devas are free from old age and sickness, how could there be the suffering of old age and sickness in this Pure Land?

Answer: "There is no distinct old age and sickness; rather, there is a common old age and sickness. As the preceding text of this sutra states, 'to be born and to age' refers precisely to this common old age and sickness.
If the transformation of the four great elements does not conflict [with the Dharma-body], then there is no further transformation."
Although there are common afflictions, those beyond the realms have lightened the burdens and complications of the fourfold afflictions and the transformation of existence;

how could these compare to the heavy, conditioned, and causally accumulated afflictions of the threefold segmented realm? Thirdly, regarding the fruit-retribution lands to clarify the swiftness of cause and effect:

"swiftness" refers to the Bodhisattvas of the Distinct Teaching who, upon entering the first stage (*bhūmi*), perceive the one true reality and give rise to true awakening. As for the Bodhisattvas of the Perfect Teaching...
When the Bodhisattva first abides in the stage of the Initial Resolve (prathamacittotpāda), he perceives the one True Truth and gives rise to true illumination (*bhūtapratyavekṣā*).

Although he simultaneously abandons the afflictions that take the unconditioned as their object (*asaṃskṛtālambana-kleśa*), because the collection of conditions pertaining to the self-substance of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) has not yet been exhausted, there remain four categories of afflictions based on ignorance (*avidyā*).

These constitute the "disease of the cause," which brings about the fruit of the suffering of *pariṇāmika-vaiparītya-janman* (transformative birth that lacks substantial reality). This is the "disease of the fruit. Furthermore—

The cycle of birth and death caused by names and conditions is called "the affliction of the lack of substantiality in its own essence. Because these afflictions are slight, it is said that the illness is not truly established in its own essence.
However, the term "transformation" (pariṇāma) applies generally to the preceding stage of birth and death during the preparatory practices (*pūrvayoga*), which is also called "transformation.

If the characteristics of transformation are coarse, then the afflictions are also coarse; yet, compared to the affliction of the lack of substantiality in its own essence, those preceding [afflictions] are slight.

In other lands, illness is a heavy burden; in the land of retribution, illness is light. This extends even to the existence of subsequent birth and death versus the absence of subsequent birth and death;
the afflictions and burdens of cause and effect become increasingly subtle and slight.

Yet, though they are subtle and slight, they are likewise the illnesses of cause and effect within the truly retributive land of non-obstruction. Thus, from the very beginning, for those who are icchantikas—

From the fruit of Avīci hell up to the source-grade ignorance and the adamantine perfect enlightenment, although there are distinctions in the stages of gravity and lightness, one cannot say that none of them are truly illnesses. Question:

In the Land of True Reward and Non-obstruction, how can there still be the fourfold causal illnesses? Answer: This is because the dharma-realm of the self-substance is opened through the convergence of conditions.
There are thus four divisions. The reason for this is as follows: grasping at one's own self is the single reality-truth (*ekasatyatā*), which is precisely craving (*rāga*);
abandoning the two extremes of birth and death is hatred (*dveṣa*); and because ignorance (*avidyā*) regarding the single reality-truth has not yet been exhausted, there is still delusion (*moha*).
Taking these three factors equally is the "equal-part" (*samabhāga*) type. These constitute the three fundamental [afflictions].
Regarding the request to Avalokiteśvara because of the poisons, it was said: "Purify the roots of the three poisons, and there will be no doubt regarding the attainment of the Buddha-way. Question:
"In the Land of True Reward and Non-obstruction, if there are causes for the four divisions [of the aggregates], would there not still be the four great elements and the four sufferings?
Answer: "Since there is already the self-substance of birth and death that is not truly established, how could there not be the lack of self-substance and the lack of true establishment?"

These are the four great sufferings. Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "All dharmas tend toward earth; yet this 'tending' does not transcend earth, for even earth itself cannot be apprehended.
How then could there be such a thing as 'tending'? This applies likewise to water, fire, and wind.

If the self-nature of these four great elements is not established as real, and the four types of suffering are exhausted, this is precisely what the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* clarifies as the subtle and wondrous.
Form is serene and eternally abiding, not subject to the transformations of birth, old age, sickness, and death.
If various masters claim that in the Dharma-cloud Bodhisattva’s awakening there is no birth, old age, sickness, or death, how could the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* contain such a statement?
Therefore, the subsequent passage of this sūtra says: "From ignorance and craving, my illness arises. If it were [merely] like a diamond...
Fourth, regarding the Land of Tranquil Light (*śāntaprabhāsa-kṣetra*), there are two interpretations.
If the Land of Tranquil Light is exclusively the dwelling place of Vairocana at the ultimate stage of wondrous enlightenment,
then it is the dharma-realm of the self-substance itself, wherein the afflictions of cause and effect still persist.

Ultimately, there is forever an end to this discussion of the gravity of illness. If one considers the Constant Quiescent Light Land (*sada-prabhāsvara-kṣetra*) as being accessible to the dwellings of Bodhisattvas, then there exists the illness of subtle cause and effect.
This refers either to the absence of future birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) or to the presence of future birth-and-death;
if one relies on the *Ratnaketu-Parivarta* (Renwang jing) to clarify the stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmamegha-bhūmi*), [it is the latter].

"Three births have no subsequent birth-and-death" means that what constitutes the final birth is precisely the absence of subsequent birth-and-death. "Subsequent birth-and-death" refers to the birth of abiding;
from the initial birth prior to the Dharma-Cloud stage up to the Joyful Stage (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), all belong to the birth-and-death of causes and conditions.

This is the expedient teaching for the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavasthāna*). If one infers according to the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya*), the absence of subsequent birth-and-death refers to the Stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samantaprabhā-bhūmi*).
Regarding the subsequent cycle of birth and death, whether it proceeds from the Dharma-cloud stage down to the thirty minds of the Joyful Stage, all are instances of causal-condition birth and death.
The principles of their relative gravity may be understood through successive analogies. Although this interpretation has been provided, it should not yet be taken as definitive;
rather, one should rely on the previous explanation: in the eternally quiescent land of light, there is ultimate purity—how could there be even the subtlest distinction between cause and effect?

"Is it not like waiting for a physician to diagnose and determine the severity of an illness? He asked: "What is the intention behind using the principles of Vasubandhu to explain the teachings of Nāgārjuna?
He replied: "How could Nāgārjuna and Vasubandhu not have entered together into the Dharma-gate of non-duality?
Now, this text is intended to provide a comprehensive understanding of Buddhism; as we apply its interpretations according to specific contexts, how can one arbitrarily accept or reject them?"

This is a definitive interpretation. If one were to analyze the names and meanings of the fetters, afflictions, birth-and-death, and all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) outside the realms, one should carefully model them after the work composed by Vasubandhu.
As for the gate of contemplation that dispels [delusions], settles the mind, and enters the Way—what fault could there be in following Nāgārjuna?

However, while this sutra text clearly elucidates the meaning of "speed," I have not yet seen such explicit statements in other sutras; thus, if one does not adopt the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages) system to encompass it, [the meaning remains incomplete].
Regarding those who look upon the Mahāyāna with mutual suspicion, some may claim that it is a manifold of forced explanations regarding what is not the true principle.
Second, to clarify the provisional and expedient: when a Bodhisattva dwells in Great Nirvāṇa, there are five kinds of practice.

That is to say, if one attains the three truths and the samādhi of the three truths, and is endowed with the twenty-five samādhis, one immediately accomplishes the noble practice (*ārya-caryā*). From this noble practice, [the remaining practices] arise.
The practice of heaven and the Brahma-practice arise from the Brahma-practice; the practice of an infant and the practice of illness arise from the roots of goodness of great kindness;
the practice of illness arises from the roots of goodness of great compassion. Why is this so?

Because for the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, whose pure Dharma-body has eternally severed all evils and universally gathered all virtues, what further skillful means could there be? What small [remedy] would there be?
In the practice of goodness, what illness of cause and effect could there be within or without the realms?
It is solely because of the roots of goodness of great compassion that one desires to uproot the afflictions and burdens of cause and effect for sentient beings both within and without the realms;

thus, manifesting as the Dharma-realm, one manifests illness without being ill, making one’s own illness identical to the illnesses of sentient beings—this is the "practice of illness. Furthermore, it demonstrates expedient means through minor virtues.
When the conditions that gather from within and without the realms for sentient beings are eliminated, this is the practice of an infant.

If the causes and effects of sentient beings within and without the realms are swiftly healed, then all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas would relinquish their manifestations and return to the ultimate truth;
however, because sentient beings are inexhaustible and their illnesses arise and cease, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas accordingly heal the ailments of the sentient beings they deliver.
The Bodhisattva likewise follows the sentient beings of the ten directions wherever illness arises, whether it be severe or slight;
the Bodhisattva manifests an illness corresponding to their severity or mildness. Therefore, this sutra says that a Bodhisattva arises from great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*);
because sentient beings are ill, the Bodhisattva is also ill. If sentient beings attain freedom from illness, then the Bodhisattva is likewise without illness.
Furthermore, this is also a matter of illness. Now, the Great Being Vimalakīrti dwells in a room of ten feet square within Vaiśālī;

he has vacated the interior of the room, leaving only a single couch upon which he lies prostrate with sickness. This is the manifestation of being without illness while appearing to be ill, intended to signify something profound.
That which it signifies is that all buddha-lands possess the skillful manifestation of illness; however, actual physical illness is indeed grave.
Briefly summarizing the four lands to distinguish them, this section clarifies that the manifestation of expedient illness is likewise based on the four lands.

Specifically, there are four: first, the manifestation of expedient illness in the *sahā-loka* (co-resident) land; second, the manifestation of expedient illness in the land with remainder (*sa-upadhiśeṣa*);

third, the manifestation of expedient illness in the land of retribution (*vipākabhūmi*); and fourth, the manifestation of expedient illness in the land of eternal quiescent light (*nityapraśāntaprakāśa*). First, the manifestation of expedient illness in the *sahā-loka* land.

As for "the sick," those who dwell together in the same land consist of both the defiled and the pure. Since the defiled land possesses the reality of the causes and effects of sentient beings within the ten dharma realms, it is called "sickness.
Because there is this sickness, Vimalakīrti likewise manifests the provisional sickness of the causes and effects within the ten dharma realms.
If the causes and effects of the sentient beings of the ten dharma realms who have a connection with him within those realms are healed of their sickness, then he is pure.

It is said that wherever one manifests illness in the Land of Common Dwelling (*sābhāsā-lokadhātu*), all such ailments are healed. A question is asked: "The causes and effects of illness within the six realms of existence can be understood;
however, regarding the four types of practitioners, what are the causes and effects within the realm? The answer is:
"This refers to those whose karmic afflictions and burdens within the realm have not yet been exhausted. If one is in the Pure Land of Common Dwelling, there are only humans and devas."
The practitioners of the six types of dharma-realms possess the reality of illness regarding the causes and effects of the dharma-realm;
because they have this illness, Vimalakīrti likewise possesses the expedient illness of the sixfold causes and effects.

If these practitioners of the four types of human and celestial realms are cured of their illness within the mundane realm, then Vimalakīrti attains the expedient illness of the Pure Land of Non-Shared Co-residence. Second, the explanation.

There are others who possess provisional illnesses: Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and the three types of Bodhisattvas all have the illness of the unconditioned causal collection—the actual cause of the fruit of the death-and-rebirth of transformation.

Because they possess this illness, Vimalakīrti likewise possesses the provisional illness of cause and effect. If this illness were to be cured, then Vimalakīrti’s [provisional] illness [would likewise cease].

The illness is likewise healed. In the realm of the unobstructed fruition of the Threefold Wisdom (*trividyā*), those who manifest as having an illness are merely Bodhisattvas of the thirty minds of the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya-yāna*) and Bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samāpatti-bodhi*). They have received the Dharma-nature body (*dharmatā-kāya*), each possessing its own intrinsic nature.

Because the real causes and conditions for the collection of [the illness] do not constitute a truly established intrinsic nature, there is no subsequent birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) resulting from such causal conditions.
In birth-and-death there is no subsequent birth-and-death; the fruit of reality is swift.
Because these bodhisattvas possess this illness of the cause and effect of reality, Vimalakīrti likewise possesses this provisional illness of cause and effect.

If the illnesses of the cause and effect of reality of these bodhisattvas are healed, then Vimalakīrti will attain freedom from illness. This is the Constant, Quiescent, and Radiant Light (Cang-jig-guang) of the Fourth Clarification (Sì-míng).
Regarding the meaning of the lands having illness or being free from illness, as previously analyzed and categorized, it may be understood accordingly.

Thus, the Great Compassion of Vimalakīrti manifests illness through expedient means (*upāya*) within the four lands; by manifesting illness while remaining free from it, he bears the burden of sentient beings across the ten dharma-realms, and is therefore called "expedient illness.
Question: Since Vimalakīrti is of the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), his ignorance (*avidyā*) is fundamentally non-existent; how can he truly have illness?

Question: Since the actual fruit of future birth and death has not yet been exhausted and the illness still persists, how can one clarify the provisional illness by reference to the land of unobstructed true retribution?
Answer: The meaning of the unfathomable distinctions between the fundamental and the manifest has already been fully elucidated in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning).
Why, then, do you pose this question again? However, the meaning of provisional illness is established according to the stages [of spiritual development].

The stages and grades differ; if one refers to the ultimate stage of wondrous enlightenment (*miao-jue*), there is no "speed of the dharma-realm" (*fa-jie ji*) because it manifests the speed of the dharma-realm.
The provisional speed is fully explained in the commentary on the provisional and real speeds in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*.

If one’s rank is that of Equal Enlightenment (*samyag-avabodha*), there still remains the causal speed of the final grade of ignorance (*avidyā*), and thus the resultant speed of future birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) does not yet exist.

The present experience of the cycle of birth and death in future existences, up to and including the illness of the causes and effects of the segmented birth and death within the triple world—all these are provisional.
Such categories of transmission regarding the birth and death of future existences are truly provisional causes and conditions;
this being the case, the illnesses at the same level are real, while the illnesses at lower levels are all provisional illnesses, and so on.
Any other sickness manifested in the Sahā world as cause and effect is entirely provisional. If there are Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas,

or Bodhisattvas of the three stages in other lands who equally possess the real cause of sickness arising from unconditioned conditions and the real fruit of sickness within the cycle of birth and death through skillful means,
they enter the segmented triple world of the Sahā Pure Land by means of their supernatural powers and vows.
The swift progression of cause and effect within the realm of humans and devas for the four types of practitioners is like a supernatural power;

their entry into the segmented three realms and cohabitation in the defiled land, sharing the same path as the six classes of beings, constitutes the swift progression of cause and effect for these four types of practitioners—all of which are provisional illnesses.
If, in the Land of Co-habitation, the four types of practitioners have not yet exhausted the delusions of the internal realm...

When the afflictions within the realm of cessation are exhausted, yet the *saṃbhogakāya* still remains in the *sahā-lokadhātu*, if one manifests illness despite being free from disease for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, this is all "expedient illness" (*upāya-vyādhi*).

Even when the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) of sages or the various devas—attained as the fruition of their karma—allow them to perform various deeds without being subject to illness, these too are called "expedient illnesses. If we consider this in terms of contemplating the mind:

For a practitioner of meditation who is skillful in the meaning of clarity, whether for their own sake or for the sake of transforming others, manifesting the illness of cause and effect when there is no such illness is also the meaning of provisional illness;
even all sentient beings possess this meaning. Thus, all phenomena tend toward illness; they do not exceed illness. Such is the ultimate.

Since it is unattainable, how could there be any coming or going? One who clearly and swiftly understands this meaning penetrates vertically to the profound source of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and extends horizontally to be as vast as the dharma-realm of empty space. Within this, the principles are subtle and profound;
were it not for the perfect clarity of the wondrous awakening of the all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñājñāna*), who could ultimately attain unhindered penetration? Now, [this] purity...
Because his illness was manifested to symbolize this, it was something that neither Śrāvakas nor Bodhisattvas could endure; none dared to transmit the Tathāgata’s intent.

Mañjuśrī, knowing for himself that he well understood the meaning of illness, was thus able to respectfully receive the Buddha’s sacred command and enter Vimalakīrti’s room to inquire about his ailment.
Through the exchange regarding the two types of illness—the provisional and the real—there was no impediment. Fourth, it clarifies how six chapters emerge based on the illness.
Regarding the scriptural text: Vimalakīrti feigned illness with the intent of promoting the teaching.

Because Mañjuśrī inquired after his illness and Vimalakīrti responded regarding his provisional illness, the first half of this chapter’s scriptural text was produced. Because Mañjuśrī inquired after his real illness and Vimalakīrti responded regarding his real illness, the second half of this chapter’s scriptural text was produced.
Thus, the scriptural text of this single chapter proceeds from the single theme of "illness."

Because the "character" (the teaching) possesses both the provisional and the real, it exists. Furthermore, because of the provisional illness, the *Acintyavimokṣa-parivarta* was extensively expounded;
because of the real illness, the *Sattvaparīkṣā-parivarta*, the *Buddhamārga-parivarta*, the *Advayadharmamukha-parivarta*, and the *Gandhavyūha-parivarta* were extensively expounded.
For this reason, the six chapters within the inner chamber all emerge from and enter into the single character "illness."
The explanatory postscript should be understood as being like a tally and its seal. Question: A certain master says that this chapter represents the five sources and eight beginnings;
what does this mean? Answer: This [explanation] appears similar yet is loose, and in some respects it does not sufficiently correspond to the core meaning.

The reason for this is that the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* originally established its teaching by means of the pretext of illness; however, it develops the six [teachings] within the chamber based solely on the single character "illness" (疾).
Why do these chapters rely on the empty room and so forth as their fivefold basis? Now, it is clarified that within this single division there are fourteen chapters;
the text of only the first chapter, "The Buddha-land," was spoken by the Great Sage, the Dharma King himself.
The remaining thirteen chapters all concern Vimalakīrti, none of which fail to arise from his feigned illness. If one carefully examines the single character "illness" (疾), it is as follows:
These three "arising from" (*yīyou*) result from six sources, two beginnings, and two causes. Regarding what is called the "three arising from":

because Vimalakīrti manifested illness, kings, officials, and commoners came to inquire after him; likewise, the Tathāgata commanded his disciples and the great bodhisattvas to inquire after his illness.
Thus, it is through this illness that the three grades of external [interactions] come to be. As for the "six sources," they consist in the manifestation of illness.
Mañjuśrī, having received this command, entered the room to inquire about the two illnesses of provisional and ultimate reality; Vimalakīrti answered briefly and then explained at length.
This constitutes the six chapters within the room, which arise from the room; "illness" is precisely the source and root from which these six chapters emerge.
As for the two beginnings, they refer to the two chapters on the Bodhisattva’s practice after leaving the room and the vision of Akṣobhya; these two chapters likewise [arise from the same source].

It was because of Vimalakīrti’s feigned illness that [the teaching] first began to unfold in this manner. This is because when it was heard that he had an affinity with the *Ṣaṭparivarta* (Six Chapters), his illness was cured;
since Vimalakīrti was thereafter free from illness, he personally bore the great assembly on his palms back to the Āmra grove.

This gave rise to the Tathāgata’s re-establishment of the fundamental doctrine to clarify the meaning of the causes and effects of the Buddha-land in two chapters. Since these two chapters begin from the point where the illness was cured, they are called the "two beginnings."
Regarding the two causes, the two chapters on "Dharma-offering" and "Entrustment" also arise because of the pretext of illness.
The reason for this is that since these two chapters constitute the circulation of the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*, they exist by virtue of the pretext of illness;

and as the circulation of the formal teaching (*samyag-deśanā*), they are precisely the circulation of the formal teaching based on the pretext of illness. Thus, the circulation of these two chapters exists because of the illness.
Therefore, it is said that there are two causes. Now, in clarifying the six chapters within the "Interior" section, they are broadly divided into three parts:
this first chapter briefly explains the two types of illness—the provisional and the real; the next chapter, "Inconceivable," extensively explains the illness of the provisional;
and the final four chapters extensively explain the illness of the real.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī: "Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness.
This is the fifth section, the formal explanation of entering the text. Regarding this chapter, there are two parts:

first, the Buddha commands Mañjuśrī to inquire after his illness; second, Mañjuśrī respectfully accepts the command and inquires after his illness. First: the Buddha commands Mañjuśrī to inquire after his illness.
As mentioned above, the World-Honored One has already summoned five hundred disciples and various bodhisattvas, each of whom, upon being rebuked, declined on the grounds of incapacity.
However, entering the chamber to inquire after his illness is a matter of grave benefit;
therefore, he summoned Mañjuśrī, for none other than he possesses the aforementioned five qualities and is capable of going there. Thus was he summoned.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, that superior person is difficult to respond to.
This was the second time Mañjuśrī respectfully accepted the command to inquire after his illness.
After the Tathāgata had already commanded five hundred disciples and various great bodhisattvas, they were all unable to do so, as each had previously been rebuked [by Vimalakīrti].
Since Mañjuśrī is free from such faults, there is no ground for further reproach. Furthermore, the purpose of inquiring after his illness is of great significance;
as previously stated, it briefly yields five benefits. This is no small matter, so how could one contravene the lofty intent of the Great Sage and abandon these great benefits?
Therefore, in deference to his command, he went to inquire after his illness. Regarding this, there are briefly five points of meaning: first, inquiring out of respect for the command.
1. The Illness; 2. The Two Assemblies Go Together; 3. The Exchange between Guest and Host; 4. The Formal Inquiry Regarding the Illness;

5. The Assembly Gains Benefit at That Time. Regarding the text of the inquiry into the illness, there are two intentions: first, self-humility; second, formally accepting the command to inquire after the illness.
Within the section on self-humility, there are further two parts: first, the expression of self-humility; second, the presentation of the grounds for such humility.

First, to begin with self-humility is the constant practice of a practitioner; yet, as for saying that he is difficult to respond to in debate, this is because this superior person’s wisdom is profound and his virtue is weighty, making it no easy matter to engage him in exchange.
He has deeply penetrated the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*), is skilled in expounding the essential points of the Dharma, possesses unimpeded eloquence, and his wisdom is without obstruction.

This concerns the textual passage on the two types of "exiting" [the state of] humility and difficulty; it consists of four points: first, the two types of wisdom are profound and vast, and thus are difficult to revere;
second, the qualities of cause and effect are perfected, and thus are difficult to revere; third, the merit of transforming others is great, and thus is difficult to revere;
fourth, the two types of wisdom are ultimately consummated, and thus are difficult to be humble before. First, regarding the profundity and vastness of the two types of wisdom:
Regarding "venerating and honoring," there are two aspects: first, the real, and second, the provisional. One who profoundly penetrates the true aspect possesses real wisdom;

because this wisdom is profound and vast, they are worthy of veneration and honor. If the Tripiṭaka Teaching explains the bodhisattva's origin but does not discuss their entry into the true aspect, how could one judge its depth or shallowness?
If the Shared Teaching explains the bodhisattva, it concerns entry into the partial true aspect.
This is not yet sufficient to sigh over the fact that the true wisdom of the Mahāsattva is so venerable and difficult to attain.

If, according to the Separate Teaching (biejiao), one clarifies that a Bodhisattva ascending to the first stage of Joy perceives the true reality of the Middle Way, and continues until reaching Equal Enlightenment (samyaksaṃbodhi) by merely destroying eleven grades of ignorance, then this constitutes a failure to achieve profound penetration of true reality.
Furthermore, since there would be no person [to realize it] under such a teaching, how could it be worthy of veneration?

This is difficult to understand; it refers to what is elucidated in the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao): from the initial stage of the Ten Abidings (shizhu) one penetrates the Middle Way and the True Reality (zhongdao shixiang), continuing through to the Stage of Equal Enlightenment (dengjue).
Having shattered the forty-one grades of ignorance and being on the verge of exhausting the source and bottom of the True Reality, one’s wisdom is adjacent to Sublime Enlightenment (miaojue);
therefore, it is said that one "profoundly penetrates the True Reality. "Skillfully expounding the essentials of the Dharma" means precisely knowing non-arising (wusheng).
The "unborn" cannot be described; yet, by employing the four *siddhāntas* to reach those with perfect capacities, the Dharma of the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) is taught through the four gates.

If one were to compare the many teachings spoken through provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) to the benefit gained by the listeners, the latter would be insufficient to mention; thus, [provisional teaching] is not the essential point.

Now, when the wisdom of reality (*tattva-jñāna*) teaches the single dharma of the true reality, the benefit gained by the listeners is profound and vast. Therefore, [the teaching of reality] is the essential point.

Regarding the statement that the Dharma-essence (dharmāvadāna) is as clarified in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*: how could the extensive bestowal of gold, silver, and precious objects be the same as untying the hair-knot to give the jewel?
This should be analyzed according to four propositions: (1) little spoken with little contained;
(2) much spoken with little contained—this is not the Dharma-essence; (3) little spoken with much contained; (4) much spoken with much contained—this is the Dharma-essence. Thus says the Sūtra.
To say that "eloquence is unimpeded" means that because one clearly possesses profound and vast skillful means and wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), one is worthy of reverence and difficult to surpass.
This refers to the fact that the arising of arising, non-arising of arising, and arising of non-arising cannot be expressed in words;

yet, by employing the four *siddhāntas* and the four types of eloquence (*pratibhāna*) to respond to conditions, one teaches the three vehicles (*triyāna*) without obstruction. That "wisdom is unimpeded" refers precisely to these three teachings.

Because they are fully endowed with the perfection of skillful means— the knowledge of the principles to be expounded, the diagnosis of illnesses, the identification of medicines, and the administration of medicine according to each illness—
and possess unimpeded wisdom, it is said that their wisdom is unobstructed.
They thoroughly know all the ritual methods of the bodhisattvas and there is nothing among the secret treasuries of the Buddhas that they cannot enter.
This refers to the second [point]: because the virtues of cause and effect are perfected, they are worthy of veneration and difficult to fathom.
The Sūtra speaks of "all the ritual methods (*vidhi*) of Bodhisattvas," which refers to the two types of ritual methods: the provisional and the real.
The provisional ritual methods are the rules for the practice of Bodhisattvas as elucidated in the three teachings; the real ritual methods are those of the Perfect Teaching (*paripūrṇa-śāsana*).
This clarifies the ritual procedures for the practice of Bodhisattvas. Being neither provisional nor ultimate, they are able to penetrate both the provisional and the ultimate;
these are the Bodhisattva methods for self-cultivation and teaching others. Not only does one fully know them, but one is also able to accomplish them all entirely.
Because the virtues of the cause are thus fulfilled, they are worthy of reverence and difficult to master. As the Sūtra says: "The secret treasury of all Buddhas has no..."
Regarding those who are not permitted to enter, the secret treasury of all Buddhas also has two kinds: first, the provisional, and second, the real.

The provisional refers to the secret treasury of all Buddhas as elucidated by the three teachings; the real refers to the secret treasury of all Buddhas as elucidated by the Perfect Teaching (*yāna*).

If one regards the real in light of the provisional, it is a teaching spoken according to the intentions of others; how could it be the true secret treasury? The real is that which accords with [the ultimate truth].
I have long intended to explain this essential point, yet I did not strive to speak of it hastily;

this is precisely the meaning of the "Secret Treasury. Not a single dharma-gate fails to contain [all others], for the fact that all dharma-gates are contained therein is the very meaning of "Treasury.
Thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states, "Various treasuries are all overflowing," which is its meaning. Since the fruit of virtue is about to be fulfilled, it is so called.
There is no one who cannot enter [this state]; since Vimalakīrti has already perfected such merits within the fruition, he is truly worthy of profound reverence and awe.
He subdues all māras and sports with supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).
This is because he has perfected the skill of converting others through the Threefold Knowledge (*traividyā*), and thus he is worthy of veneration and difficult to surpass.

As for the scriptural statement "subduing all Māras," the meaning of subduing Māra is fully explained as previously set forth in various places; however, Māra is the lord of the sentient beings to be converted.
If the lord does not submit, how could the sentient beings to be converted ever turn their hearts toward him? Since the Great Being is able to subdue [him], [the beings] attain faith.
Having subdued the various Māras in the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there are no sentient beings who do not take refuge in and enter the Way.

As the Sūtra says regarding "sporting with supernatural powers" (*abhijñā-vikrīḍita*): once the Lord of Māras has been subdued, there are none among the sentient beings with whom one has a karmic connection throughout the ten directions who do not take refuge.
Therefore, through mastery over supernatural powers, one manifests transformations to bring sentient beings to maturity and purify Buddha-lands.
Because the bodhisattvas of the lower stages cannot compare to his vast and great [practice], he is venerable and difficult to emulate.

Since both his wisdom and skillful means have already reached the further shore, and because this constitutes the culmination of the four knots and two knowledges, he is venerable and difficult to emulate; his wisdom is precisely the realization of the fruit.

Skillful means are precisely the two provisional and ultimate wisdoms that guide all practices; because both practice and understanding have attained their ultimate consummation, it is said that "all have already attained deliverance.
Nevertheless, you should now follow the Buddha’s holy command and go there to inquire after his illness.
This constitutes the second formal inquiry into his illness in accordance with the Buddha’s command. Mañjuśrī has already prepared the etiquette of humble submission;
although Vimalakīrti’s wisdom and virtue are profoundly lofty, whatever a disciple of the Buddha undertakes is never without the empowerment of the Buddha’s spiritual power.

Now, since he has been sent by the Buddha, he relies on the Buddha’s spiritual power for its hidden assistance to transmit this message and inquire after the illness, hoping that there shall be no error.
Because he was free from the faults of leakage, contraction, and stagnation, it was said: "I shall now follow the Buddha’s holy intent and go to inquire after his illness. Question:
If one is capable of going by virtue of receiving the Buddha’s hidden empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), then all the bodhisattvas mentioned above who were empowered should also have been capable of going.
Answer: Empowerment is bestowed upon those who are worthy of it. Mañjuśrī possesses five conditions; therefore, he is worthy of empowerment. Furthermore, it is like... [text fragment].
In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, when the fourfold assembly of Maitreya has doubts, they are resolved solely by relying on Mañjuśrī;
how could this be compared to other bodhisattvas? Thereupon, within the assembly, the various bodhisattvas, great disciples, Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings all had this thought: "Now..."
As the two great beings, Mañjuśrī and Vimalakīrti, conversed together, they were certain to discourse upon the wondrous Dharma;
immediately, eight thousand bodhisattvas, five hundred śrāvakas, and hundreds of thousands of devas and humans all desired to follow them.
This is the second section on the great assembly proceeding together; the text consists of two parts: first, the assembly’s desire to follow along;
second, Mañjuśrī proceeding with the assembly. As for why the assembly desired to follow Mañjuśrī:
Vimalakīrti’s spiritual wisdom was difficult to fathom, and among the śrāvakas and bodhisattvas of the past, none had not been stymied or hindered by him; none dared [to approach].

"Your Honor, Mañjuśrī’s wisdom and virtue are now lofty and far-reaching; having received the holy mandate of the Buddha, we shall surely discuss the Great Dharma upon meeting, reaching its depths in the most profound mysteries. Therefore, all wish to follow you."
Thereupon, Mañjuśrī, together with the assembly of bodhisattvas, great disciples, and devas and humans,
entered the great city of Vaiśālī, respectfully surrounded by them.
This was the second instance where Mañjuśrī went to the chamber with the great assembly to hear the Dharma.
It was because Mañjuśrī always accompanied those who were destined to receive benefit as they entered the city together.

At that time, the elder Vimalakīrti thought to himself, "Now Mañjuśrī is coming with a great assembly," and immediately used his supernormal powers to empty the interior of his room, removing all furnishings as well as his attendants.
This is the third section, clarifying the exchange between host and guest; the text consists of four parts:
first, Vimalakīrti manifests a sign by means of his empty room; second, Mañjuśrī perceives the sign and knows that something is being indicated;
third, Vimalakīrti praises Mañjuśrī’s arrival; and fourth, Mañjuśrī confirms his words. Regarding "Vimalakīrti manifests a sign by means of his empty room":
The Pure Name (Vimalakīrti) knew in his heart that Mañjuśrī had received the command and come specifically to manifest and expound [the teaching].

Since he intended to rely on illness to give rise to the teaching, it was necessary for him to appear in an empty room to provide a sign that would open the beginning of their dialogue. Regarding this passage, there are two points:
first, the emptying of the room through supernatural power; second, lying ill in the empty room to signify his desire to conform to the realization of a Buddha-land.
This teaching manifests illness to reveal the inconceivable liberation of the three virtues. First, regarding the manifestation of the empty room:
Vimalakīrti thought to himself and, by means of his supernatural power, emptied the interior of the room, removing all furnishings as well as the attendants.
By this supernatural power, he manifested the use of the power of wisdom to empty the room; this signifies that the Buddha-lands are likewise empty.

The manifestation of emptiness represents the True, Constant, and Quiescent Light Land (*prabhāsvara-kṣetra*). The removal of all furnishings signifies the removal of the *paribhoga-niśraya* (the environment of enjoyment) and the various attendants;

the removal of the primary physical form (*ātmabhāva*) signifies the elimination of Māras and non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). This is fully explained in the passage of the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* where Vimalakīrti provides his response.
The empty room symbolizes the Buddha-land, which carries two meanings: first, to fulfill what preceded it; second, to... [text fragment ends].

Regarding the first point concerning birth after [attaining] realization: as explained above by the Tathāgata, it is precisely because sentient beings have committed offenses that they do not perceive the pure Buddha-land, cannot be born in a pure realm, and are unable to accomplish the practices for a pure Buddha-land;
therefore, the Tathāgata extensively taught the "Buddha-land Chapter" specifically to destroy the defilements and karmic conditions of all sentient beings.
He binds all impure karmic actions to become the causes for the realization of a pure Buddha-land.
Vimalakīrti previously came forth to support the Buddha’s teaching by employing skillful means in reverse to humble the śrāvakas and rebuke the bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, he manifested illness as an occasion to establish the Dharma and preach it for the sake of ordinary beings, desiring once again to issue the rebukes of the past.
All these matters serve to support and complete the discourse on the purification of the Buddha-lands.
Now that Mañjuśrī has come to inquire after his illness, he manifests this appearance of the room’s emptiness to signify that all Buddha-lands are empty;
thus, his desire to discuss the Buddha-lands extensively with Mañjuśrī is precisely intended to fulfill the meaning of what preceded it. Second, it serves to introduce the subsequent meaning.
Furthermore, when the room appeared empty, it signified that all Buddha-lands are entirely empty.

Mañjuśrī, perceiving this sign and knowing what it portended, immediately went forth to discuss the meaning of the Buddha-lands with Śāriputra; thus, this chapter clarifies the nature of the Buddha-lands.
Moreover, because of the empty room, when Śāriputra thought of a seat for the assembly and food for the mealtime, the assembly was able to see the Lamp-King Buddha.
From afar, Tuṣita beheld the Pure Land of Universal Fragrance; therein, chapter after chapter, he expounded upon the causes and effects of the Buddha-lands.
Having concluded this meaning, he took the great assembly in his palms and proceeded to the place of the Tathāgata.

There, he initiated the Tathāgata to once again expound extensively upon the chapters on Bodhisattvas, clarifying the causes and effects of the lands. In the "Chapter on Seeing the Buddha Akṣobhya," a boundless great assembly was seen.

All those Buddha-lands are within this land; it is because of this that they give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment and are born in those lands. Each person resolves to cultivate the practices for the Pure Land of Akṣobhya Buddha, and it is precisely through the manifestation of signs in this empty room that their birth there is established—this is the meaning of "immediate birth" (*upapadya*).

Now, I shall explain the signs manifested in the empty room by categorizing and interpreting them according to the four lands. First: [The first category: The sign of the empty room represents the Land of Common Residence (*sādhāraṇāvāsa-bhūmi*). This signifies that all sentient beings, regardless of whether they are ordinary persons or noble ones, share this same realm of emptiness as their dwelling place. It indicates that the nature of emptiness is the common ground upon which all phenomena arise and abide. By contemplating this, one realizes that the true nature of the mind is originally pure and non-dual, and thus one attains the realization of the equality of self and others. This is the meaning of the empty room as the Land of Common Residence. [The second category: The sign of the empty room represents the Land of Expedient Means (*upāya-bhūmi*). This signifies that within the state of emptiness, all skillful means are spontaneously manifest. Although the room is empty, it can accommodate all things; likewise, within the wisdom of emptiness, all the various gates of practice and teaching are fully present. It shows that the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the six perfections and other virtues does not depart from the essence of emptiness, yet through these expedients, they lead sentient beings to liberation. This is the meaning of the empty room as the Land of Expedient Means. [The third category: The sign of the empty room represents the Land of Realization (*abhisamaya-bhūmi*).

This signifies that within the state of emptiness, one directly realizes the true nature of reality. The room is devoid of all conceptual constructs and sensory objects; likewise, when the practitioner dwells in the wisdom of emptiness, they sever all delusions and attachments, realizing the suchness of all dharmas. This is the meaning of the empty room as the Land of Realization. [The fourth category: The sign of the empty room represents the Land of Dharma-nature (*dharmatā-bhūmi*). This signifies that the ultimate nature of all phenomena is itself the empty room. It is neither created nor destroyed, neither increasing nor decreasing. All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas dwell within this very nature, which is eternally quiescent and unconditioned. To enter this room is to enter the realm of the Tathāgata’s inconceivable liberation. This is the meaning of the empty room as the Land of Dharma-nature. Thus, the manifestation of signs in this empty room serves as a profound metaphor for the fourfold classification of the Buddha-lands. By understanding these meanings, one may truly give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment and attain birth in the Pure Land of Akṣobhya.
The shared lands may be defiled or pure; if one relies upon a defiled land, the environmental retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*) is a mixture of impurities.

Within this, there are the primary retributions (*vipāka-phala*) of celestial Māras, non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), and sentient beings bound by craving and views. The Pure Name manifests within these defiled lands, knowing that the defiled land is itself empty.
One seeks to use the power of wisdom to demolish defiled karma; if defiled karma were not empty, it could not be destroyed.

Now, because defiled karma is empty, the dependent retribution can be demolished; this is the removal of all that exists and the destruction of all evil Māras, externalists, and those possessed of craving and views.
The primary retribution of sentient beings is thus the removal of all attendants.

Next, this symbolizes the Pure Land of Shared Residence, where although there is no defiled dependent retribution, there are likewise no evil Māras, externalists, or primary retributions [of afflicted beings].
Yet, within these realms of fragmented, pure dependent retribution and fragmented sentient beings governed by craving and views, the Pure Name manifests birth therein;
