knowing that this Land of Shared Dwelling is itself empty, one uses the power of wisdom to sever the karma of fragmented dependent retribution, and thus it is said:
"removing all that exists" means to destroy the conditioned accumulation of craving and views belonging to these sentient beings.

The "correct retribution" (*samyag-vipāka*) refers to both [the environment] and the exclusion of attendants. Regarding the two manifestations in the Land of Expedient Means with Remainder (*upāya-avaśeṣa-bhūmi*):
although this land lacks the impure or pure "dependent retribution" (*niśraya-vipāka*) of segmented existence, it possesses the "correct retribution" of conditioned bonds of craving and views;

yet it does possess the "dependent retribution" of transformation (*pariṇāma*) and the "correct retribution" of unconditioned causal accumulation. These sentient beings are precisely those driven by craving.
Because he perceives the heavenly Māras and non-Buddhists, Vimalakīrti rebukes Subhūti, saying that he is "equal to afflictions" and has "entered into various views.
When Vimalakīrti manifests birth in that land, he knows that there are still residual karmic conditions;

thus, by the power of wisdom, he eliminates the karma of the transformed environment (*pariṇāmika-karma*) and the afflictions of craving and views (*tṛṣṇā-dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), thereby eliminating the primary retribution (*pratyaya-phala*).
Having eliminated all possessions as well as attendants, the text next clarifies the land of true retribution free from obstacles (*niṣparigraha-nirāvaraṇa-bhoga-kṣetra*).

Although this land lacks the provisional, transformational *upādāya-pratyaya* (dependent support) and the conditioned accumulation of non-active causes, it does possess its own substantial body consisting of the primary retribution (*mukhya-phala*) of craving and views; yet, this substantial body is not truly established.

It consists of a pure, wondrous, and unobstructed *upādāya-pratyaya* (dependent support), while the primary retribution of craving and views constitutes its own substantial body and conditioned accumulation.
Sentient beings whose names are pure should be born in that land; they know that the Land of True Reward is the Unobstructed Nation.

By the power of wisdom, they eliminate the karma of the unobstructed *pariṇāmanīya* (dependent) retribution—the collection of conditions consisting of craving and views—which constitutes their own true (*svabhāva*) *pratyaya-saṃnipāta* (conjunction of causes).
Therefore, it is said that they "eliminate all possessions as well as all attendants. The Land of Constant Quiescent Light is the ultimate.

Ultimate emptiness, being pure and devoid of anything whatsoever, is precisely the dwelling place of Vairocana’s stage of wondrous enlightenment, for there is nothing therein to be eliminated or severed.
Thus, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* clarifies that one who has nothing to sever is called the Unsurpassed One (*anuttara*).
Now, Vimalakīrti employs his supernormal powers to empty the interior of his room, removing all possessions as well as his attendants.
To manifest the ultimate fruit of retribution and enter the land of eternal quiescence, he displays supernatural power such that the room becomes empty, removing all possessions and attendants;
this is precisely the meaning of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra*’s explanation of the "pure dhyāna of abandoning the two obstacles" as being pure through its freedom from all views.
If it were to manifest expedient means while remaining in the present land, [the situation would be different].
The "convenient objects" are to be understood as previously explained. Furthermore, when a country, material things, and attendants exist, these are skillful means (*upāya*);
that they are now all removed is to manifest the reality (*tattva*). The brief explanation of the manifestation of signs in the empty chamber is thus concluded.
Only a single bed was set out, upon which he lay down in illness.
This is the second illumination, intended to manifest the characteristics of the three virtues of liberation (*vimukti*). The bed symbolizes the liberation of true nature (*svabhāva-vimukti*);
the illness symbolizes the liberation of skillful means (*upāya-vimukti*); and lying down symbolizes the liberation of actual wisdom (*prajñā-vimukti*). This also has two meanings: first, for...

The accomplishment of the former two serves to give rise to the latter; thus, the accomplishment of the former is precisely what supports the teaching on the Dharma-body of inconceivable liberation and the three virtues as expounded by the Buddha.
The reason for this is that the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* establishes the Tathāgata’s inconceivable liberation;
therefore, after first reproaching the various disciples and bodhisattvas, it subsequently resorts to the pretext of illness to teach for the sake of ordinary beings.
Furthermore, in order to reiterate the teaching from the past that rebuking [the Arhats] brings about the inconceivable liberation, Mañjuśrī manifested illness despite being free from disease.
Now, as Mañjuśrī received the command to enter the chamber and inquire after his illness, it was necessary to manifest this sign of illness to initiate the dialogue.
Through this, one can discuss the two types of illness—the provisional and the real—as taught by the Tathāgata.
The explanations regarding the "inconceivable liberation" and Vimalakīrti’s past instances of rebuking and supporting [the Buddha's teaching] are all now clearly and distinctly revealed.
As for the second part concerning his birth, this refers to the six chapters on his birth in the chamber and the two chapters on his departure from the chamber.
The reason for this is that his manifestation of illness serves as a symbolic expression, leading to Mañjuśrī’s inquiry into the two types of illness—the provisional and the real.
Furthermore, because this chapter is subsequently explained in detail by Vimalakīrti, it gives rise to the five subsequent chapters.

[The sections on] presiding over the great assembly and returning to the Āmra Garden serve to establish the teaching of the inconceivable liberation; thus, they give rise to the two chapters on the Bodhisattva seeing the Buddha Akṣobhya.
Therefore, they are called "subsequent" (*shenghou*). When one reaches the later textual commentary, their meaning will become manifest of itself. This is why.

The phrase "only placing a single bed to represent the mark of inconceivable true nature liberation" means that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* clarifies that the emptiness of all phenomena (*dharmas*) constitutes the seat;
this chapter on the Emptiness of All Phenomena is the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), and true reality is precisely true nature liberation.
"Illness" represents great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*); since great compassion gives rise to skillful means (*upāya*), liberation should likewise correspond to having illness.

Furthermore, "lying down" (*śayana*) signifies the manifestation of true wisdom-liberation; true wisdom is precisely the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body). "Lying down" is the mark of the body being at rest.
If true wisdom-liberation accords with the true nature (*dharmatā*), then all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) come to rest and the mind abides unmoving.
This is the perfection of the wisdom that cuts off [afflictions]. Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* asks: "Who attains peaceful sleep? It refers to this.
This means that those who possess compassion constantly cultivate heedfulness and regard all beings as their only child.
By means of the unconditioned great compassion (*nirālamba-mahākaruṇā*) of the Buddhas, they extract all suffering; it is not through heedless conduct that one is said to attain peaceful sleep.
Just as a magnet attracts iron without effort or thought, this very lack of conditioned intention is what constitutes peaceful sleep. It is like a person who is naturally free from illness.
Just as one naturally falls into a sick sleep, so too is the true wisdom of the Dharma-body.

If sentient beings are without illness, then the true wisdom of the Dharma-body has no "sickness" that arises from shared conditions. If there are sentient beings with the capacity who are ill, then the great compassion of the true wisdom Dharma-body gives rise to a "responsive sickness.
It is for this reason that Vimalakīrti dwells together with those in the defiled land, manifesting this [sickness] for the sake of those with whom he has a karmic connection.
Those who are ill, having a karmic affinity for the Pure Land, likewise manifest this illness;

even those in the lands of remaining traces (*sopadhiśeṣa*) and the lands of retribution (*vipākabhūmi*) are all like this. Question: Illness is a phenomenon produced by the aggregation of conditions, characterized by affliction, suffering, and obstruction.
How can it manifest the virtue of liberation? Answer: This meaning differs from what is explained in the Tripiṭaka and the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-śāsana*).
They regard the absence of afflictions within birth and death as liberation;

yet now, through inconceivable skillful means, they undergo afflictions and birth and death while remaining themselves unbound, thereby liberating others from their bonds. Therefore, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Wherever Buddhas and Bodhisattvas tame sentient beings, that place is called liberation. Question:
Question: This sutra clarifies that the four dhyānas serve as a bed and seat; how can it be that the bed symbolizes true nature and liberation? Answer:
The teachings of the sutras employ metaphors according to circumstances and are not fixed. How can one dogmatically cling to them?

To understand the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, one must realize that awakening to the "imageless" (the ineffable) is like obtaining a pearl—this constitutes liberation. One must investigate thoroughly so as not to lose the treasure. It is just as this sutra clarifies.
The house of ultimate emptiness and quiescence is now manifest as an empty chamber; it represents all buddha-fields as empty, such that they cannot be described as a "house.
When Mañjuśrī entered the house, he saw that the chamber was empty and devoid of anything at all, with only a single bed upon which [the woman] lay alone.
This is the second clear indication that when Mañjuśrī entered the room and saw its signs, he understood what was being manifested.

Seeing that the room was empty and devoid of all things, he immediately knew this manifested the emptiness of all Buddha-lands; it must be intended to reveal the teaching that accords with the realization of the Buddha-land.
Seeing Vimalakīrti alone upon a single couch due to illness, he immediately knew this manifested the liberation of the three virtues (*triguṇa*).
This must surely be intended to manifest the teaching of inconceivable liberation, which accords with the Buddha’s own discourse.
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The wise are able to know wisdom, just as a snake knows its own feet. Question:
How is it known that when Mañjuśrī saw the signs, he immediately understood the intention expressed by Vimalakīrti? Answer: It is because Vimalakīrti greeted him, saying, "Welcome! (svāgata).
To see the mark of non-seeing while not seeing marks—that is, to see the marks of the four inexpressible [realms]:
the dependent reward of the land and the primary reward of the Dharma-body—is to see these manifested marks that represent the land and the body.
If it were otherwise, how could Mañjuśrī, being below, inquire after the illness and ask about the emptiness of the room? It is because of this exchange that he proceeded in such a manner.
Furthermore, since Mañjuśrī already knew that [Vimalakīrti] was about to preach the Lotus Sūtra and manifested signs to indicate this,

how could he not know that Vimalakīrti’s manifestation of signs had something to signify? If he did not know this, how could he have respectfully followed the Tathāgata’s intent and been worthy of being the one to inquire after his illness?
Then Vimalakīrti said, "Welcome, Mañjuśrī!
This is the Pure Name of the Threefold Knowledge. As for why he praised him in this way: it was because he knew that Mañjuśrī possessed the five aforementioned qualities;
thus, his coming now to inquire after my illness would surely enable him to manifest the inconceivable liberation of the Buddha.
The teaching on the causes and effects of the nation supports and completes what was spoken by the Dharma King to extensively benefit those with the karmic affinity;
thus, he praises them, saying, "Welcome. This passage consists of two parts: first, the actual praise of "welcome," and second, the explanation of that praise.
Regarding the first, the actual praise of "welcome": this is a praise of "welcome" in contrast to what is not welcome. As for what is called "not welcome," if...

The various ordinary beings, the five hundred great disciples, and the bodhisattvas who came to inquire after his illness were unable to give rise to the teaching on the causes and effects of the Pure Land—the inconceivable dharma-gate of liberation—thereby failing to extensively benefit all classes of beings;
therefore, their arrival was not "well-come. Now, Mañjuśrī possesses the five qualities previously explained.
Yigong has come at the sacred command to inquire after my illness and to give rise to the causes and conditions for the inconceivable liberation and the Buddha-land;
therefore, his coming will surely be able to support and complete the Great Teaching of the Dharma King, bringing great benefit—this may truly be called a "Welcome.
Thus, while ordinary beings, the great disciples, and the various bodhisattvas are all not "well-come," this present case is distinguished as being so.
The meaning of "Welcome" (*svāgata*) is briefly of seven kinds. First, if kings, officials, or commoners come to inquire after one's illness, this is not a true "Welcome.
Why is this so? Because all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are bound by the conditions of views and afflictions (*kleśa*);

even if they receive the teaching of the Dharma to eliminate their fetters and delusions, how could they possibly bring forth and manifest the Great Dharma? Therefore, it is not a true "Welcome. Second...
If the great disciples were to come at will to inquire after the Illustrious One’s illness upon receiving his command, this would not be a "welcome arrival.
Why is this so? Because those of the Two Vehicles perceive only partial truth; they have severed their fetters but lack the heart of great compassion.

Not seeking wondrous enlightenment, they are unable to guide and lead sentient beings out of the burning house. Although they come from causes and reach the *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana with remainder), [they remain thus].
If one enters a state of extinction through the ashes [of the body], severing what is not true *nirvāṇa*, how could this be called "Welcome"?
Third, if a Bodhisattva of the Tripiṭaka Teaching were to suddenly come to inquire after the illness of the Tathāgata at his command, this would not be "Welcome. Why is this so?
Although such a Bodhisattva possesses compassion and aspires to seek the fruit of Buddhahood, they have suppressed their afflictions (*kleśas*) but have not yet severed them from the mind.
If one who is not yet pure merely seeks the Buddha-fruit at the Bodhi tree and enters nirvana, what they seek is not the reality;
it is essential to transform the mind and transform one's contemplation—how then could this be called a "welcome"? Fourth, regarding bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching (Sādhāraṇa-yāna):
if they were to come to inquire after the illness [of the Buddha] merely by following the Great Sage’s command, this would not be a "welcome. Why is this so? Because these bodhisattvas perceive...

Those who realize partial truth and sever the fetters, though they possess compassion for transforming sentient beings, ultimately seek the fruits of Buddhahood—both with remainder and without remainder—which are impermanent;
since that which they seek is not the ultimate reality, they too must transform their minds and transform their contemplations. How could they be said to have come "well"?
Fifth, if a Bodhisattva of the Separate Teaching should suddenly pay respects to the holy intent and come to inquire after his illness, this is not a "welcoming arrival. This is why:
However, although this Bodhisattva seeks the fruit of Buddhahood which is eternally abiding, they are unable to perfectly contemplate the Middle Way Dharma-realm;

because they sever the afflictions of the internal and external realms through a gradual and sequential process, they must still undergo the transformation of mind and the transformation of contemplation upon entering the ten stages—how, then, can they be said to have "come well"?
As for a Bodhisattva at the initial stage of the Sixth Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), if they were to suddenly...
"To come and inquire after your illness by imperial decree is not a 'Welcome' (svāgata). Why is this so?

Although this Bodhisattva is able to perceive the Middle Way and the Dharma-realm, he does not sever his afflictions; his great compassion without object universally covers all beings, yet he does not abide in the first stage (*bhūmi*).
His mind is quiescent at every moment, naturally flowing into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (omniscience); it is merely through wisdom..."
My virtue is still shallow and not yet equal to that of Vimalakīrti; how could I be called one who has "come well"?

Seventh, as for a Bodhisattva of the final mind in the Perfect Teaching, whether in terms of their fundamental nature or their manifested traces, although their virtue is equal to that of Vimalakīrti, they lack the karmic conditions to inquire after the illness of others.
If such a person were to suddenly accept the command and come, it would provide no benefit to sentient beings due to a lack of conditions, nor could they manifest the Dharma; how could this be right?

He is named "Welcome" (Svāgata). This is because when the Tathāgata commanded five hundred śrāvakas and various great bodhisattvas to come inquire after his illness, none dared to respectfully accept the command;
this was due to the presence of such matters that were not "welcome. When he commanded Mañjuśrī, there were no such unwelcome matters;
this is precisely because the fundamental and manifested traces of the Great Being of the Perfect Teaching are identical with Vimalakīrti.

Having measured himself to know that there was an occasion for the assembly to inquire after his illness and to engage in a profound dialogue, he led the great multitude—like an elephant king leading its herd out of the enclosure—and entered together with them into the chamber of Vimalakīrti in Vaiśālī.
There, he delivered the imperial decree to inquire after his illness; this served as an excellent opportunity for the assembly to enter into the inconceivable and behold the Pure Name.

Because he has come to inquire after the illness for the purpose of accomplishing the practice of purifying a buddha-field by being born in a pure land, Vimalakīrti—who possesses profound insight—exclaims, "Welcome, welcome! as a true and virtuous greeting.
"It comes without the characteristic of coming; it is seen without the characteristic of being seen.

This is the second interpretation praising [the Buddha]. There is a master who explains: "In the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) there is no characteristic of coming, whereas in the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) there is coming;
therefore, it is said that 'it comes without the characteristic of coming. If this were so, then Vimalakīrti should also praise the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas).
Furthermore, the Master says that because the Dharma-body has no coming while the Response-body (nirmāṇakāya) does have a coming, it is said that "the aspect of non-coming comes.
If this were so, then Vimalakīrti should praise all bodhisattvas. Moreover, the Master says:
if "coming" is a coming, then that coming is the coming of self-nature; if one says "coming" is a non-coming, then that coming is a conventional coming—a conventional coming.
That which is "not coming" is precisely the characteristic of not-coming while yet coming. Now, to say "coming" refers to a coming that is a coming of self-nature;
such a coming is a non-coming, and a coming of self-nature would mean a coming of other-nature. How could Vimalakīrti have praised him [for such a coming]?
Now, regarding why Vimalakīrti praised Mañjuśrī by saying, "Welcome," if it were a coming characterized by the mark of coming, then—
It is not that Mañjuśrī has come well now, because he has come with the characteristic of non-coming; therefore, he is praised as having "come well.
As for those who say one has come with the characteristic of coming, they have not come well. All ordinary worldlings who come to inquire after your illness do so with craving and views;
this is coming with the grasping of signs, not coming with the characteristic of non-coming. This is not the case for the disciples of the Śrāvakas.
To shatter the conventional and enter the true, thus coming here, is to take a winding path to grasp the characteristics of the partial truth; it is not a case of "coming while not coming.
If it is a Bodhisattva of the Tripiṭaka Teaching who comes having suppressed the fetters, yet whose delusive characteristics are not yet severed, this is also not a case of "coming while not coming.

If it is a Bodhisattva of the Shared Teaching who, from the perspective of the essence of the provisional, perceives the true and enters the stage of vision (darśana-bhūmi), [this is likewise not a case of "coming while not coming"].
Up to and including the stages of Arhat and Pratyekabuddha, they enter the rank of Bodhisattva and come here;
this is coming by taking the characteristics of the two truths, not coming by way of the characteristic of non-coming.

If it is a Bodhisattva of the Separate Teaching who, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment, passes through distinct contemplations of the three truths and enters the First Ground to come here, this is coming by relying on the characteristics of the three truths, and not...

To come by way of the characteristic of not coming: if one understands through the Perfect Teaching that the four [realms] are ineffable, one does not perceive any marks whatsoever, yet is able to contemplate the Middle Way and simultaneously illumine the two truths.

Thus, one naturally flows into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge) to transform sentient beings throughout the dharma-realm, desiring that they likewise enter the land of eternal quiescent light. This is "coming by way of the characteristic of not coming."

This indeed accords with the meaning of the chapter on "Accordance with the Tathāgata’s Command" regarding the exposition of the Pure Land, and it is also consistent with the intention of Vimalakīrti.
However, as for the Bodhisattvas of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), they lack the karmic conditions to inquire after the illness during this assembly;

how could they dare to respectfully follow the Tathāgata’s command to come and inquire after his illness? Because of this deficiency, they do not venture to act as those who inquire after the illness.
That which is not praised by names—now Mañjuśrī, from his first generation of the mind, has known that the four [realms] are ineffable and devoid of provisional or ultimate [distinctions].
Because he understands the signs of coming in both self-cultivation and the transformation of others, it is said that "he comes with the sign of not coming.

Thus, he is able to let the path and contemplation flow as a dual stream, and through both the provisional and the ultimate, in self-cultivation and the transformation of others, his every thought is quiescent and extinguished.

However, they have entered the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge) and come forth to align themselves with the virtues of Vimalakīrti’s fundamental and manifested traces; thus it is said that they "come.

Furthermore, one should know that this entire assembly is itself the fourfold "unspeakable," yet because there is now a specific cause and condition, they appear as the "speakable" through a provisional manifestation.
Therefore, leading them along, he enters the room; therein they shall hear of inconceivable liberation.
Since all teachings on purifying the Buddha-lands result in great benefit, Vimalakīrti explains and praises this by saying, "He comes with the characteristic of not coming.
When the Sūtra says, "He sees with the characteristic of not seeing," this is likewise an explanation praising the meaning of a "welcome arrival.
For Mañjuśrī, having entered the room with the characteristic of not coming, and having arrived, he sees with the characteristic of not seeing.

While lying ill in an empty room, he immediately realized that [Vimalakīrti] intended to propagate the teachings of the Pure Land and the wondrous path of liberation through the inconceivable three virtues;
thus, by manifesting these signs, he attained the intended meaning and was found worthy of Vimalakīrti’s aspirations—this is why he offered praise.
As for what was said regarding "seeing while not seeing forms," this refers to seeing in contrast to the perception of forms; it is not [the case that one sees] otherwise.
Because they have come well, it is said that seeing without seeing marks is what constitutes "coming well.

This is because if ordinary worldlings possess only the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*) and the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), and see the coarse and subtle marks of the causes and conditions of worldly truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*), this is precisely "seeing by means of marks.
If the disciples of the Śrāvakas possess only three eyes—the fleshly eye, the divine eye, and the wisdom eye (*prajñācakṣus*)—and see only the causes...

The wisdom-eye perceives the coarse and subtle characteristics of the *satya* (truth) based on conditions; seeing the characteristics of the *satya* of causes and conditions is precisely to see the characteristics of the two truths.
If a Bodhisattva of the Tripiṭaka Teaching has not yet realized the truth or severed the fetters, they do not see the characteristics of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*);
rather, they possess only the fleshly eye and the divine eye to see the coarse and subtle characteristics of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), which is to say, they see only characteristics.

As for "seeing," if a Bodhisattva of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) also merely attains the three eyes, seeing the two truths as having the characteristics of illusions and transformations, this is likewise "seeing through the characteristics.
If a Bodhisattva of the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao) attains the four eyes, the three eyes see as previously described;
additionally, they attain the Dharma-eye, seeing the countless principles of the Four Truths and the Buddha-dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, both within and beyond the realms.

This refers to the "seeing of characteristics" (xiang-jian). Although a Bodhisattva in the ten abodes (shizhu) of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) possesses the fleshly eye (rouyan), it is called the Buddha-eye (foyian) as a semblance of the perfect vision of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
However, because the delusions regarding the characteristics of the Dharma-realm have not yet been eliminated, it is still termed "seeing of characteristics.

Once they enter the first abode, the Abode of Initial Resolve (chufaxin zhu), and truly give rise to the outflow-free wisdom (anāsrava-jñāna), the five eyes open perfectly; thus, although they possess the five eyes, [it is no longer merely a semblance].

To know that the four are ineffable and not to perceive the existence of the three categories of sentient beings is precisely to not perceive characteristics while attaining a perfect vision of the Dharma-realm;
this is to see by means of non-seeing. This applies even up to the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*miao-jue*).

Now, regarding the text’s provisional and ultimate [teachings], the five eyes are identical in purity to those of Vimalakīrti. Vimalakīrti does not manifest characteristics, yet he manifests them; this has its expression in the text.

It is particularly because, by not seeing [external] marks, one sees the manifestation of marks by Vimalakīrti, which expresses the inconceivable threefold virtue and liberation regarding the causes and effects of the Buddha-land;
since this intent is in profound harmony with that of Vimalakīrti, he is praised. Question:
What is the distinction between "coming" (*āgata*) and "seeing"? Answer: "Coming" refers to the threefold wisdom within a single mind, while "seeing" refers to the five [eyes].
The *Lotus Sūtra* states: "To cause sentient beings to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision," and it further says: "The Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision is vast and immeasurable.

This is precisely its meaning. Furthermore, from the stage of the Initial Resolve (*cittotpāda-vihāra*) onward, the Bodhisattva of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) knows the four inexpressibles and attains the threefold wisdoms within one mind and the five eyes;
looking back at the cause from the perspective of the fruit, every thought is quiescent and extinguished.
Because one naturally flows into the great ocean of wondrous enlightenment, it is said that "one comes with the aspect of not coming.
As the five eyes become increasingly clear until the fruit is perfected and one perceives the Dharma-realm, it is said that "one sees with the aspect of not seeing."
Mañjuśrī said: "It is so, householder. If one has come, there is no further coming;
if one has gone, there is no further going. Why is this? That which comes comes from nowhere, and that which goes goes nowhere.
What can be seen cannot be seen again."
This is the confirmation and formal articulation by Mañjuśrī of the Four Gates.

Thus, whereas previously the householder had praised [the Buddha] from afar with "Welcome," now Mañjuśrī confirms it from afar. Such a person of wisdom can know wisdom, just as one who knows a snake understands the snake's feet.
This consists of two parts: first, Mañjuśrī’s realization and confirmation through formal articulation; second, the explanation.
This is a restatement for confirmation. Regarding the "restatement for confirmation" by Mañjuśrī: "Householder, this is the true seal;
having come, one does not come again. These three phrases constitute the Great Being’s words of restatement for confirmation.
As for "having come, one does not come again," this restates the previous "Welcome" in contrast to what is not a "Welcome."
The reason for this is that because the practitioners of the previous five types have come with [defiled] characteristics, their coming is not a "Welcome Coming" (*svāgata*).

Having already come, there remains the sense of coming again; just as ordinary people and non-Buddhists practice dhyāna up to the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception and then fall back into the three miserable realms, such cyclic existence constitutes coming again after having already come. If those of the two vehicles come by practicing the Path...
Having emerged from the triple world and traveled three hundred *yojanas*, one dwells in the illusory city of *nirvāṇa*.
If that illusory city is extinguished, one must return once more to the place of the treasure; this is what is meant by "having come, coming again.

When Bodhisattvas of the Tripiṭaka Teaching resolve their minds, desiring to seek the fruit of Buddhahood, they practice the six *pāramitās* and thus "come"—yet this is not a "good coming," for it does not reach the stage of *samyak-saṃbodhi*. If one hears...

In the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*), one must immediately resolve upon *bodhicitta* and transform the mind’s contemplation; coming from the contemplation of non-arising (*anutpāda-darśana*) constitutes "having already come, yet coming again.

If a Bodhisattva of the Shared Teaching comes seeking the Subtle Enlightenment (*sūkṣma-bodhi*) and hears the Distinct Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*), transforming the mind’s contemplation to follow the Distinct Contemplation, this constitutes "having already come, yet coming again. If a Bodhisattva of the Distinct Teaching practices...
To seek the wondrous enlightenment through the three contemplations of distinct characteristics is like the winding course of a river;
if one hears the Perfect Teaching, one must immediately change one’s mind and change one’s contemplation. To come from the Perfect Teaching is to "come again after having already come.
All such cases are instances of coming again after having already come. Now, the Bodhisattva of the Perfect Teaching, within the correct contemplation of the Middle Way Dharma-realm, gives rise to...

The carriage has no deviation and never alters its course midway; changing one's mind and transforming one's perspective is like the great river of golden sand flowing directly into the Western Sea—having already come, there is no further coming.

Furthermore, although a Bodhisattva at the initial or middle stage of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) comes by way of the direct path, there is no matter of altering the mind or transforming the perspective; it is simply that they have come but have not yet arrived.
If there is still the sense of "coming" regarding the fruit, Mañjuśrī and Vimalakīrti have both reached the ultimate stage;

since they have already come, there is no further sense of coming, and thus it is said, "If one has already come, one does not come again. This passage explains and confirms the praise of "coming with the characteristic of non-coming.
When Mañjuśrī says, "Having departed, one does not depart again," this is a further confirmation of the meaning of "coming."
Furthermore, regarding the five types of people, although they have departed, they do so by means of the characteristic of departure; thus, their departure is not a "skillful departure.

Consequently, even after having departed, they would still need to depart further. However, according to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), when one arouses the mind and correctly contemplates the Middle Way, this single departure is such that there is no longer any principle of changing the mind, changing the contemplation, or departing again. Therefore, it is said that "if one has already departed, one does not depart further. This—

These two phrases have the same essential meaning; they are merely different names used for distinct aspects of the same reality. If one considers the fruit in relation to the cause, it is because [the Buddha] has come from the cause;

therefore, it is said that "the Great Vehicle of Prajñāpāramitā is that from which the Buddha has come. Conversely, if one considers the cause in relation to the fruit, it carries the sense of "going";
thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "This vehicle comes from within the triple world and proceeds out to reach omniscience (*sarvajñatā*)."
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The various sages come in this manner, and the Buddha also comes in this manner;

the various sages depart in this manner, and the Buddha also departs in this manner. This is as described in the passage concerning Vimalakīrti’s empty room: when Mañjuśrī enters, it is called "coming";

when he receives the Buddha's command and departs to inquire after his illness, it is called "going. It was for the sake of Vimalakīrti that Mañjuśrī explained these matters regarding coming and going.
Furthermore, this is further elucidated through the meaning of "departure. Mañjuśrī said: "If one has already seen [it], one does not see it again.
This describes seeing by means of the characteristic of non-seeing. That which is seen while being invisible is the seeing of the empty room;

the manifestation of illness represents the environment and inhabitants (*āśraya-adhiṣṭhāna*) of the stage of fruition. Beyond what is represented here, there is no further Pure Land or Dharmakāya to be seen.

Regarding the meaning of "attaining Buddhahood in the Land": if one leads sentient beings to enter and perceive the Dharma-body of the Pure Land, there is nothing further beyond this that can be seen;
therefore, it is said that "if one has already seen it, one sees nothing more.
Furthermore, just as the human eye perceives coarse forms but cannot see subtle forms—this being a perception of form that is not ultimate—if one further cultivates the celestial [eye]...
The physical eye sees coarse forms; although the divine eye sees subtle forms, it cannot see the Truth.

If those of the Two Vehicles or Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching cultivate and attain the Wisdom Eye, they then see the Truth; yet although the Wisdom Eye sees the Truth, it cannot perceive the methods for discerning medicines and illnesses.
When Bodhisattvas of the Distinct Teaching cultivate the Dharma Eye, they further perceive the various differentiated dharmas.

Although the Dharma-eye perceives phenomena, it cannot see them perfectly; it does not see the three truths, nor all phenomena, nor that all phenomena enter into a single phenomenon, and that a single phenomenon contains all phenomena.

A Bodhisattva of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), if they attain the Buddha-eye, can then see the Dharma-realm perfectly, even to its ultimate source and bottom, equal to empty space. Beyond what is seen by the Buddha-eye, there is nothing further.
Because there is nothing that can be seen, it is said that "having seen, one sees no more. The Sūtra asks: "Why is this so?
That which comes comes from nowhere; that which goes goes nowhere. What can be seen cannot be seen again.
This is the clear explanation by Mañjuśrī, which elucidates and establishes the intended meaning. As for what was said—"that which comes comes from nowhere"—this is...
The commentary states: "If one has already come, there is no further coming.

This fourfold ineffability is the equal Dharma-realm, which even all Buddhas cannot traverse. Since this has no characteristic of coming, to speak of "coming" in reference to this is precisely the meaning of "having nowhere from which to come";
it establishes that non-coming is itself coming. As the Sūtra says: "That which goes has no destination"—this fourfold [ineffability]...
To say that it is the equal and true *dharmadhātu* is because it is a place where even all Buddhas cannot arrive; thus, it is said that the one who goes has nowhere to go.
This reiterates and establishes the characteristic of not coming while yet coming, and that this coming reaches nowhere. Mañjuśrī said:
"That which can be seen is further not to be seen; within the fourfold ineffable, equal, and true *dharmadhātu*, there is nothing [to be seen]."

Regarding that which can be seen and is called "seeing," it is the Buddha-eye that sees; when there is ultimately nothing further to be seen, this is precisely the explanation of the aforementioned seeing of the mark of non-seeing.
*Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra Commentary*, Scroll Nineteen.
Commentary on the Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra, Scroll Twenty (Part Two of the "Inquiry into the Illness" Chapter).
Let us set aside this matter for now.
From here on follows the fourth section, which correctly elucidates the inquiry into the illness; the preceding discourse constitutes the initial stage of the interaction between host and guest.
The formalities of their meeting were not yet the true intent of Mañjuśrī.

Since the spiritual understanding of the two was equal and their eloquence inexhaustible, if they had allowed their unimpeded discourse to continue unchecked, it would have hindered the proclamation of the Buddha’s purpose; therefore, he said, "Let us set this matter aside for now.

Now, to clarify the text concerning the actual inquiry after his illness, there are two parts: first, the proclamation of the Buddha’s purpose regarding the inquiry after the illness; second, Mañjuśrī himself [proceeding with the inquiry].

Explaining one’s own feelings while inquiring after the illness: First, one must proclaim the Buddha’s intent. Those who inquire after the illness do so fundamentally by carrying the Buddha’s command;

because the Master’s intent is revered, it must be proclaimed first. Next, one must inquire into the profound cause of the pretext for the illness, in order to investigate and bring forth how the Mahāsattva propagates the Dharma to benefit all beings;
thus, one explains one’s own feelings while inquiring after the illness. If one were to merely proclaim the Buddha’s intent, [the various śrāvakas...]
Upon hearing this, it was understood that the Bodhisattvas should not each decline on the grounds of incapacity;

rather, the principle of inquiring after the illness of a superior person is profound and vast, and the process of such an exchange is difficult, being beyond the capacity of others. This is the underlying meaning, and for this reason, Mañjuśrī followed by must state his own feelings.
"Householder, can this illness of yours be endured?
This is the first section, which proclaims the Buddha’s intent in inquiring after his illness; it consists of two parts:

first, the actual proclamation of the intent, and second, a general summary of the Buddha’s meaning. Regarding the first, the text proclaiming the intent has three phrases, which constitute three points. The first says:
"Is this illness bearable? [The Buddha replied: "Impurity is called the Dharma-body; fundamentally, it is itself without illness. What could there be that is bearable or unbearable?
Since I manifest this illness for the sake of sentient beings, I shall discuss 'bearability' and 'unbearability' in reference to those very beings.

However, because the Buddha is the World-Honored One who dwells in the world to benefit all things, his traces conform to the mundane world; thus, there is the inquiry regarding fatigue, as in the case of Vimalakīrti."
Among the nuns, the Buddha comforted the bhikṣus, asking whether they were not fatigued by the journey and whether alms-food was easy to obtain;

furthermore, as clarified in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the Buddhas themselves comfort one another, inquiring after their lack of illness and lack of affliction—the commentaries on the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* all contain profound significance regarding this.
Now, when the Buddha asks Vimalakīrti, "Is your illness bearable? it refers to Vimalakīrti.
For the sake of sentient beings, their illnesses are diverse; some illnesses can be endured, while others cannot.
For example, when a person is ill yet still able to walk back and forth, this is an illness that can be endured.

However, when there is the suffering of illness so acute that it presses upon one such that one cannot even rise or sit, this is an illness that cannot be endured. Now, let us distinguish these according to the four lands (*catur-bhūmi*). First, regarding...

Regarding the four types of lands: first, the land of common residence; second, the land of partial fulfillment; third, the land of retributive fruition; and fourth, the land of eternal quiescent light.
To clarify what is endurable and what is not endurable within the land of common residence, there are two kinds of such lands.

First is the defiled land. Within this defiled land, there are the six paths of existence. If one commits the ten evil deeds, the four grave offenses, the five heinous crimes, or slanders the Vaipulya (Mahāyāna) sutras, [it is not endurable].
To act as an icchantika is the causal illness of the three evil paths; the resulting suffering of the three miserable realms is the resultant illness.
This causal illness is heavy and its characteristics are unbearable. If the ten wholesome deeds are the causal illness for asuras, humans, and devas;

the eight sufferings and five decays are the resultant illnesses. These sufferings are slight and light, and their characteristics are bearable. Now, Vimalakīrti’s provisional illness is identical to these.
The causes of the illness of the segmented body and its results are likewise subject to being either endurable or unbearable.
Furthermore, while those dwelling together in this defiled land share the same result-illness, there are nine different types of cause-illnesses.

For example, humans may have the cause-illnesses of the six destinies, or they may possess the root-natures of the three vehicles; if they have the cause-illnesses of the six destinies, they lack the three vehicles.
That the root-natures (*indriya*) cannot be delivered is the mark of "intolerance" (*akṣānti*); if there were root-natures of the three vehicles that could be delivered, it would be "tolerable.
Vimalakīrti’s skillful illness is likewise such that there is both the tolerable and the intolerable.

Furthermore, if ordinary beings possess the wholesome natures of the three vehicles and cultivate the practices of the two vehicles, their faculties may be sharp or dull, and their hindrances may be light or heavy.
When those of sharp faculties conceal their light afflictions, they can endure them; when those of dull faculties conceal their heavy afflictions, they cannot endure them.
Vimalakīrti’s skillful concealment of his illness is likewise a case of what can and cannot be endured. Furthermore, regarding the progress of those in the Three Vehicles who sever their fetters:

for those who have severed them, the illness is light and can be endured; for those who have not yet severed them, the illness is heavy and cannot be endured. Vimalakīrti’s skillful [concealment] is the same.
Illness is likewise like that, being either endurable or unbearable. Next, regarding the presence of both endurable and unbearable aspects of illness while dwelling together in the Pure Land:
excluding the four evil destinies, which are unbearable, one may clarify the endurable and unbearable according to the types of persons;
the three vehicles are as explained previously. Furthermore, one may clarify the endurable and unbearable by way of the remaining lands (sāvaśeṣa-bhūmi).
In those lands, there is no suffering of the fragmented body; generally speaking, all illnesses therein are tolerable.

However, when compared in terms of coarseness and subtlety, for those of the Two Vehicles and Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching who are born in those lands, their dull faculties find it intolerable;

whereas for Bodhisattvas of the Distinct and Perfect Teachings who are born there, their sharp faculties find it tolerable. This is because the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* employs skillful means to appear identical [to them].

Third, regarding the distinction of the *vipākabhūmi* (land of retribution): the bodhisattvas in the land of retribution are all the Dharma-body of the Middle Way, and thus there is no differentiation between the three vehicles.

Although their individual afflictions of ignorance have not yet been exhausted, the maladies of birth-and-death—consisting of causes and effects that lack a self-substance and are not ultimately real—are all slight and entirely tolerable. This is also the provisional manifestation of Vimalakīrti.
One may regard it as tolerable if one compares it with the characteristics of other stages;
it is not that it cannot be tolerated, but rather that it is not like the previous cases where there are horizontal manifestations of tolerable characteristics in other lands.

Fourth, since the Land of Constant Quiescent Light is the ultimate stage where all evils are forever exhausted and all virtues are fully realized, being free from illness and affliction, there is no actual disease.

Whether an illness can be endured or cannot be endured can be distinguished in this way; thus it is clear. One must not definitively judge that because the words of the sutras and treatises speak of existence, one must immediately follow them in interpreting existence, or because they speak of non-existence, one must accordingly explain non-existence;
for now, based on the ultimate stage, there is no distinction between provisional and real, nor between swift and slow.
"Treating with harm" refers to this:
following the second of the two illuminations, the Buddha proclaimed the second phrase of the inquiry regarding "treating with harm.

This means that when there is illness in the world, one must necessarily employ medical treatment; likewise, since Vimalakīrti acts for the sake of sentient beings who have disease, he must necessarily employ the Dharma.
To treat the illnesses of sentient beings with medicine is precisely to treat the illness of Vimalakīrti. However, there are three distinct types of illness among sentient beings:
first, the illness of grasping at signs (*nimitta*) and views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-cetanā*); second, the illness of ignorance as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
and third, the illness of fundamental nescience (*avidyā*). These three types of illness are the very root of all causes and effects of illness, both within and beyond the realms.

If one employs the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*) to cure these three kinds of ailments so that they are extinguished, then all ailments of cause and effect—both within and beyond the realms (*dhātu*)—are extinguished.
This meaning is fully contained within the "Three Contemplations" section of the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning), where it has already been clarified;

furthermore, the subsequent explanation of this chapter will naturally become evident. Now, distinguishing according to the four lands (*catasraḥ bhūmayaḥ*): first, entering emptiness from the conventional (*saṃvṛti*).
The contemplation of correct cultivation (*samyak-pratipatti*) primarily treats the illnesses of views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) in the Land of Common Dwelling (*sahā-loka-dhātu*);

it enters from emptiness (*śūnyatā*) into the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti*), thereby swiftly treating the illnesses of the sands of afflictions in the Land of Residual Defilements (*śeṣa-kleśa-bhūmi*) and the sands of ignorance (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*) in the Land of Common Dwelling as secondary treatments.

Third, the contemplation of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*) correctly treats the illness of ignorance (*avidyā*) in the Land of Residual Defilements and the illness of ignorance in the Land of Fruitional Retribution (*vipāka-bhūmi*), providing sharp benefit.

The faculties of the Bodhisattvas incidentally treat the *dṛṣṭi-āsrava* (afflictions of views) and *kleśa-āsrava* (afflictions of existence) within the *sahā-loka-dhātu* (the land of shared residence), as well as the sands-of-the-Ganges number of types of ignorance (*ajñāna*).

They also incidentally treat the sands-of-the-Ganges number of types of ignorance within the *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa-dhātu* (the land with remainder). In the *sadā-praśānta-prabhāsvara-dhātu* (the land of constant quiescent light), there are no ailments to be treated;

therefore, this section now clarifies the treatment [of ailments] in the *sahā-loka-dhātu*. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* provides a fourfold analysis: first, those with dull faculties and heavy obstructions—namely, those of dull faculties who are ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Now, there are those whose afflictions, transgressions, and defilements are so deep and heavy that they seem incurable; yet if their faculties are dull and their obstacles light— like Cūḍapanthaka,
who in a single summer could only recite the *Kumāra* verse, yet was able to give rise to true outflow-free wisdom, sever his fetters, and become a powerful Arhat—
or those whose faculties are sharp and their obstacles heavy— like Aṅgulimāla, who in a single day [attained realization].
He killed nine hundred and ninety-nine people, yet because his faculties were sharp, even though there was a grave obstruction, he could not hinder him from seeing the Buddha;

he immediately attained awakening. Furthermore, four types of faculties are sharp such that obstructions are light; for example, Śāriputra heard a single verse on the Three Truths spoken by Aśvajit and immediately attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
Vimalakīrti is similar to these cases: those with such illnesses are difficult to diminish [in their spiritual progress] and easy to diminish [their afflictions].
As for the fourfold analysis regarding those such as Pāṇḍaka, Aṅgulimāla, and Śāriputra—all these are remedies for those who have been impaired.

If one considers those in the *sāvaśeṣa-bhūmi* (the stage with remainder), their ignorance is never truly impaired; yet, when the three vehicles are compared to one another, they are likewise distinguished into three types of impairment.
The provisional illness of Vimalakīrti is also the same as that. If one enters the dharma of the equality of karmic fruition, [there is no longer any distinction].
In this realm, these are those of sharp faculties; they have only a single ignorance as an obstruction.

Discussing this according to the stages (*avasthā*), there is no distinction in lightness or gravity, yet it is horizontally obstructed and treated as a single "existence" (*bhava*) with impairment. If one considers the initial mind or past karma, one may distinguish two phrases, though there is no difference from those of dull faculties.
The provisional illness of Vimalakīrti is also like that. As for the ultimate *dharmadhātu* of the Constant Quiescent Light Land...
Because the ground is tranquil and free from such conceptual discrimination, the Buddha asked whether the treatment had caused any harm, or whether it had led to an increase.
This was the third time the Buddha uttered his third question: "Has it not increased? It is for this reason that he posed this inquiry.
For example, there are four types of illnesses common among people in the world:
first, those that from the onset of the illness increase despite taking medicine and do not diminish, such that there is ultimately no possibility of recovery; this is called "increasing increase.

Second, those where although the illness is severe and the condition is critical, it is cured as soon as treatment begins; this is called "increasing decrease. Third, those where upon taking medicine, there is initially a temporary decrease...

Thereafter, further increasing it is called "increasing the decrease. From the initial reduction of the medicine during its administration until it returns to normal dosage, this is called "decreasing the decrease.
Regarding the Pure Name, it is said that one should be born in the Land of Common Residence to preach the twelve divisions of the sūtras and treat the illnesses of sentient beings;
herein there are also four kinds of increase and decrease. First, as for "increasing the increase," this refers to those of inferior capacity.
First, if one preaches the Dharma to ordinary beings and they further give rise to slander, they incur the sin of an icchantika, as in the cases of Sunakṣatra, Devadatta, and others.
Second, regarding increase and decrease [of merit], it is as in the cases of Śrīgupta, Aṅgulimāla, and others.

Third, regarding decrease and increase [of realization], it is as explained in the *Śāstra*: a certain bhikṣu cultivated and attained the four dhyānas and claimed they were the four fruits; at the time of his death...

Seeing those born in [such] places who slander the absence of *nirvāṇa*, they fall into hell; furthermore, those described in the *Abhidharma* and the *Tattvasiddhi* as persons subject to regression (*parihāṇadharman*) all possess these characteristics.
Regarding the "four types of impairment," this refers to Śāriputra and other noble ones who have attained the Way;
even though they dwell together with Vimalakīrti, their skillful display of illness is likewise intended for the four different types of sentient beings to be transformed.
Second, regarding the lands with residual defilements (*sopadhiśeṣa-bhūmi*), there are three kinds of non-increase.

This is because those who have attained the stage [of non-retrogression] do not fall back or return to birth within the triple world; yet, for those of the three vehicles born in those lands, since there are those who regress from their practice or regress from their mindfulness, there are likewise three kinds [of increase].
When the provisional illness of Vimalakīrti was in that land, he was identical to them. If it were the fruit...

In the Reward Land (*vipākakṣetra*), all are those whose minds do not regress; their every thought is quiescent and extinguished, flowing spontaneously into [the ultimate]. This is entirely a matter of "diminishing the diminishing.
Alternatively, according to the meaning of entering and emerging from contemplation, there are three phrases: when the provisional illness of Vimalakīrti was in that land, he was identical to them;

if it were the Ultimate Ground of the Constant Quiescent Light Land (*nityaprabhāsvara-kṣetra*), it would be utterly serene. Thus, Vimalakīrti’s provisional manifestation was identical [to the inhabitants of that land].

If the illnesses of the first three lands—which are taught as a Dharma for governing sentient beings—actually diminish and do not increase, then the provisional illness of Vimalakīrti must likewise diminish and not increase; therefore, he was asked in greeting, "Has it not increased?"
"The World-Honored One sends his most earnest and boundless greetings.
This is the second passage where Mañjuśrī proclaims the Buddha’s intent to offer consolation. Regarding "the World-Honored One sends his most earnest and boundless greetings":

the sentient beings within the ten directions and the dharma-realm across the three lands are truly infinite; since their illnesses are likewise infinite, Vimalakīrti’s compassion [is likewise boundless].
Since mindfulness is also immeasurable, the expedient illness is likewise immeasurable; thus, the World-Honored One’s inquiries are also immeasurable.
The reason these three phrases were previously cited was to indicate the opening of the inquiry, though there may well have been further phrases.
Those who translated the scriptures abbreviated them—for example, [the assemblies of] five hundred and eight thousand were all mentioned, yet they were omitted and not transmitted.
This was merely a general proclamation of the immeasurable [teachings] sufficient to express the Buddha’s intent; he did not elaborate further.
"Householder, what is the cause from which this illness arises? How long has it been present? And how shall it be extinguished?"
This is the second section, in which Mañjuśrī describes his own feelings in order to inquire about the illness [of Vimalakīrti] and receive the imperial decree;

the difficulty of the intent lies herein. Regarding the text itself, there are two parts: first, the formal inquiry concerning the provisional illness within the fruit [of Buddhahood]; second, the inquiry concerning the real illness within the cause [of practice].
Within these two inquiries, there are two responses; the first is Mañjuśrī’s inquiry regarding the provisional illness, and the second is Vimalakīrti’s response based upon that.
Following the chapter "Inconceivable" (*Acintya*), there is the sequence where Mañjuśrī asks about the illness of the Real and Vimalakīrti answers;
from this point, the subsequent four chapters proceed to the explanation of the fifth chapter, which can be clearly seen as it stands.

Regarding the provisional illness within the fruit [of Buddhahood] as addressed in the questions, there are three points: first, from the passage "Householder, what is the cause from which this illness arises? it is as follows:

The first question concerns the cause for manifesting illness: "Since the Dharma-body of a Great Being on the stage of fruition is pure and forever free from affliction and suffering, by what cause has this illness now appeared?
The second question concerns the emptiness of the chamber and the absence of attendants: "Why is this room empty and devoid of servants?
This is a question regarding the Dharma-body's 'dependent retribution' (the environment and retinue); where, then, are the land and the followers now located?"
Yet one sees only ultimate emptiness. Third, "What are the characteristics of this illness? This asks regarding the characteristics of the Illusory Body (nirmāṇakāya) being the same as the illness:
is it the same as the characteristics of the Dharma Body (dharmakāya), or is it the same as the characteristics of an ordinary person?
Thus, he asks about its appearance. Now, regarding the first question, there are two parts: first, Mañjuśrī’s question; second, [the Buddha’s response].
In Vimalakīrti’s response to Mañjuśrī’s question regarding the causes for the manifestation of illness on the ground of fruition—the Dharma-body—there are three parts:

first, the question concerning what causes the illness to arise; second, the question concerning how long the illness has been present; and third, the question concerning the method for extinguishing the illness.
Regarding the first question, "What causes this illness to arise? [the answer is: if one is on the ground of fruition as the Dharma-body, all evils have already been exhausted.
When all virtues are universally assembled, what illness or affliction could there possibly be? That you should now suddenly say you are ill—by what cause does this illness arise?

Next, I ask how long it has been since you were born: since the Dharma-body has been free from illness from its very inception, how much time has passed since this provisional illness first appeared? Finally, I ask how it shall be extinguished.

"If this [illness] arose for the sake of sentient beings, and since the sentient beings of the lands in the ten directions are inexhaustible and cannot be extinguished, by what method can this illness be extinguished?
Such are the three successive questions posed by Mañjuśrī; the general meaning lies herein.
Vimalakīrti said: "From ignorance and craving my illness arises; because all sentient beings are ill, I am ill.
If all sentient beings were free from illness, then my illness would cease."

This is the second response by Vimalakīrti. Regarding this response, it is divided into two parts: first, a direct answer to Mañjuśrī’s second question concerning how long the illness has been present;
and second, an answer to his third question concerning how it shall be extinguished. Next, he answers the first question: "What is the cause from which this illness arises?
As for why the questions and answers appear in different sequences, each of these [sections] has its own specific purpose.
The intention behind Mañjuśrī’s question was to cause sentient beings to know how the trace arises from the source;

the intention behind Vimalakīrti’s answer was to cause sentient beings to seek the trace in order to enter the source, while also manifesting the principle that the characteristics of arising and ceasing are established.

Regarding the preceding answer-text, there are three parts: first, the direct restatement of the two questions; second, the explanation; and third, the manifestation through analogy. As for the first, the direct restatement:

The text for answering the two questions consists of two parts: first, answering the second question regarding the rapid arising [of illness], and second, answering the third question regarding the rapid cessation [of illness].
This is the first part; it first answers the second question concerning the duration of the arising of purity.

Regarding the statement, "From ignorance and craving there is existence, and thus my illness arises," this is the direct answer to the second question concerning how long it has been since the illness arose. From ignorance...
"Affection gives rise to my illness" means that the disease arises from the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) of sentient beings.
If the arising of the twelve links of dependent origination in sentient beings is recent, the manifestation of Vimalakīrti’s provisional illness is also recent;

if the arising of the twelve links of dependent origination in sentient beings has been long, the manifestation of Vimalakīrti’s provisional illness has also been long. This is known by way of this analogy.
Regarding the answer concerning the twelve links of dependent origination, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states that there are two fundamental origins of birth and death:
ignorance (*avidyā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Between these two lies birth, old age, sickness, and death. Ignorance belongs to the past, while craving belongs to the present;
because the characteristics of these two periods differ, they are established as two distinct names. Past ignorance moistens the formative forces (*saṃskāra*).

It is because one can cause the five fruits, such as consciousness, to exist in the present; when birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is moistened by craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*), existence (*bhava*) arises, and thus there is future birth-and-death.
Consequently, as one transmigrates through the three realms and twenty-five states of existence, undergoing successive births and deaths, there is both causal illness and resultant illness.
Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states that sentient beings give rise to delusion and craving.
The Great Compassion of the Dharma-body gives rise to expedient illness within sentient beings;

it arises from ignorance and craving, and its coming is neither near nor far—this is precisely the intended meaning of the response regarding the duration of the visit to inquire after the illness. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī manifests this illness for the sake of a single sentient being;
why would it be limited only to sentient beings in the Land of Common Residence (Sahā-lokadhātu) as a conditioned cause?
The moment delusion and craving arise rapidly as a collection, this is precisely the provisional illness manifested by the Pure Name (Vimalakīrti) arising in the Land of有余 (Sāvaśeṣa).
When delusion and craving arise through the unconditioned causal collection, this is likewise the provisional illness manifested by the Pure Name. Why is this so?

Because when delusion and craving are exhausted in the Sahā world (the Land of Co-residence), delusion and craving immediately arise in the Land of有余. This is because these sentient beings are deluded regarding the Middle Way.

Because one is stained by *nirvāṇa*, delusion and craving arise; between these two lies birth and death, the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), where the cause is swift and the effect is swift.
However, this is merely the *pariṇāmika* (transformational) twelve links of dependent origination, which differs from the *bheda-bhava* (segmented) type.

If it were the segmented type, there would be ascending and descending, coming and going—from the heavens back down to the three miserable realms (*tridurgati*). This [latter] is the transformational [type].
The twelve links of dependent origination are not like this; rather, it is simply a matter of their causes.

When craving for birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is extinguished, one immediately attains a higher stage and undergoes birth-and-death in that higher realm, never again falling back to be born in a lower stage. This is because one has already severed the fetters and delusions of the three realms entirely;
thus, one does not return to be born within the coarse, segmented (*bheda*) three realms, nor does one fall back into the subtle, transformative (*pariṇāma*) realm.
Receiving coarse transformation and change is similar to the case of an Anāgāmin who, while in a body within the desire realm, attains the first dhyāna;
if he is born into the first dhyāna and dies, he is immediately born into the second dhyāna, never again receiving birth in the desire realm, nor ever regressing to be born in the first dhyāna.
If this is so even for a noble one within the realms, how much more so for a noble one outside the realms who would regress to be born in the *pratisaṃdhi* (segmented) existence?

One subsequently undergoes coarse transformation and change (*pariṇāma-vipariṇāma*). If sentient beings subject to transformation and change possess this delusion and craving, it is termed "Great Compassion" (*mahākaruṇā*) as being pure;
yet if they immediately give rise to delusion and craving, this answers the question regarding the duration of that rapid arising.

If the sentient beings in the land of retribution (*vipākabhūmi*) have not yet exhausted the ignorance (*avidyā*) that conditions their own bodies and the collection of external objects, this constitutes defilement through delusion; that which relies upon and is manifested by these [bodies and objects] constitutes craving.
Seeing that within these two [extremes] there is the non-substantiality of self-nature, yet the causes and effects of birth-and-death—the twelve links of dependent origination—arise with rapidity;
therefore, the *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra* states: "The power of the ground of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*) is the greatest;
it can only be severed by the Buddha's Bodhi-wisdom. If delusion and craving are extinguished in other lands, that is the land of retribution (*vipākabhūmi*). Regarding this delusion:

When affliction arises from craving, the Dharma-body of Vimalakīrti manifests great compassion and appears as if born together with them; this is the answer regarding the duration of the arising of that affliction.
If one dwells in the eternal Samantaprabhā-land at the ultimate stage where there is no delusion or craving, then there is no actual illness;
therefore, there is no duration for the arising of either provisional illness. Question: If it is explained that [affliction] arises based on the delusion and craving of sentient beings, then...
Regarding the question of how long or short the arising of Vimalakīrti’s illness was, [the answer is that] because ignorance and craving have no beginning, it is neither long nor short;
how then could one receive such an answer to Mañjuśrī’s question? The reply states: "The ignorance and craving of sentient beings have no beginning and are neither long nor short;
Vimalakīrti’s unconditioned great compassion is likewise so. Yet, as for discussing its duration or brevity, this principle can also be established in terms of conventional phenomena."
The reason for this is that the Great Compassion of the stage of fruition exhausts the source through quiescent illumination;

it follows without obstruction the delusory illnesses arising in sentient beings, and from this, Great Compassion of Identical Substance is born. This is precisely what is meant by "long" or "near. As this sutra says:
"From the root of non-abiding, all dharmas are established. Beginningless ignorance gives rise to a realm of countless ignorances beyond the four [realms].
Abiding within the realm, the four inversions are purified; the name "exhausting dependent origination" is likewise so.
If one relies on principle, the land of retribution is attained quickly while birth in the land of remainder is gradual.

If one relies on phenomena, birth in the land of cohabitation is attained quickly while the lands of remainder and retribution are approached gradually. This is like severing the delusion of the land of cohabitation.
Attachment is precisely what remains; from delusion and attachment, [the illness] arises. This is the second response by Mañjuśrī.
Regarding the third question on the cessation of illness: "Cessation" refers to purity. If the illnesses of sentient beings cease, then my illness ceases.

Since the illnesses of sentient beings arise due to the three kinds of delusion and attachment, if one employs the four teachings and the three contemplations to sever the delusion and attachment of sentient beings in the three lands, this is the true cessation of illness.
When [the illness] ceases, it is called "purity," for the provisional illnesses of the three lands also cease; therefore, it is said, "Then my illness ceases. The reason for this is as follows:

if, in the Land of Common Residence (*sahā-loka-dhātu*), [illness] arises from the causes and effects of ignorance and craving, the Pure Name (Vimalakīrti) undergoes an illness identical to theirs and preaches the Four Teachings to them, causing them to cultivate the Three Contemplations.
When the sentient beings' illnesses of the causes and effects of ignorance and craving cease, the illness of the Pure Name likewise ceases.

When the illness of those beings is extinguished along with their [delusions], if there are sentient beings in other lands whose delusions and cravings constitute the cause of illness and the fruit of illness,
then Vimalakīrti manifests a provisional illness for them and preaches the Separate Teaching and the Perfect Teaching,

causing them to cultivate the entry from emptiness into the provisional and the correct contemplation of the Middle Way. When the disease of those sentient beings' delusions and cravings is extinguished, it is Vimalakīrti who has [extinguished it].

Vimalakīrti’s illness subsides in accordance with the cessation of those [afflictions]. If the sentient beings in the land of retribution possess the illness of cause and the illness of effect due to ignorance and craving, then Vimalakīrti likewise possesses a provisional illness;
however, he speaks only to teach the Perfect Teaching (Ekayāna) so that they may cultivate the correct contemplation of the Middle Way.
If those sentient beings eliminate the forty-one grades of ignorance and craving one by one, Vimalakīrti likewise eliminates them one by one in forty-one grades.

This refers to the cessation [of illness] within the *dharmadhātu*. In the eternal *sambhogakāya* (Constant Quiescent Light), the ultimate stage of all Buddhas of the ten directions is a single body and a single wisdom;

since their knowledge and severance (*jñāna-prahāṇa*) are perfectly consummate, there is no cessation. This concludes the brief explanation answering the third question regarding the meaning of Vimalakīrti’s sudden illness.
If various Dharma masters do not permit explaining the provisional illness by way of the two lands outside the *dharmadhātu*, then those two lands outside the *dharmadhātu* should...
There is no such thing as non-ignorance (*avidyā*). If there were a real ignorance existing outside the realms, how could Vimalakīrti’s skillful illness have its arising and ceasing?
Question: The illnesses of delusion and craving among the sentient beings of the three lands throughout the ten directions are inexhaustible;
when, then, will Vimalakīrti’s skillful illness ever come to an end? Answer: Speaking in general terms, as long as sentient beings are not exhausted, Vimalakīrti’s skillful illness does not cease.
The illness is likewise inexhaustible; for now, let us speak according to those with whom there is a karmic affinity within a single period.
When the sentient beings with whom there is affinity among those transformed in the three lands pass away, the provisional illness of Vimalakīrti also ceases.
Why is this? Because Bodhisattvas enter into birth and death for the sake of sentient beings; where there is birth and death, there is illness.
If sentient beings can become free from illness, then the Bodhisattva will no longer have illness.
This constitutes two interpretations of the preceding two answers, which thus contain two meanings.

The first statement—that for the sake of sentient beings entering birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), there is birth-and-death, and that there are three kinds of "illness" arising therein—explains the answer regarding the existence of provisional illness and the duration of its arising.
The second statement—that if sentient beings attain freedom from illness, then the Bodhisattva will no longer have illness—is...
This explains the reason why Śākyamuni later answered that his provisional illness had been extinguished.
It is like an elder who has only one son: when the son falls ill, the parents also fall ill;
when the son recovers, the parents also recover.
These three analogies reveal that the text itself consists of two parts: first, the introduction of the analogies; second, the application of the analogies.
The introduction of the analogies contains two points: first, the introduction of the analogy for having illness; second, the introduction of the analogy for the recovery from illness.

Regarding the introduction of the analogy for having illness, the parents are used as the analogy because a Bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion from the two types of wisdom; if they abide in the stage of the "only child," then...
Because all sentient beings equally possess the principle of Buddha-nature, they are the parents of all beings; thus it is said that there is "but one child.

If the sentient beings of the three lands suffer from the maladies of delusion and craving, the Dharma-body, the two wisdoms, and Great Compassion must accordingly manifest birth within those three lands.
Therefore, there is the provisional illness and the twofold clarity; once the illness is opened and cured, liberation is attained.

In this way, the Bodhisattva loves all sentient beings as if they were his own children; when sentient beings are ill, the Bodhisattva is ill, and when the illness of sentient beings is cured, the Bodhisattva is also cured.

This is the passage on the combined analogies, which consists of two parts: first, the combined analogy of the feigned illness, and second, the combined analogy of the recovery from that feigned illness.
This can be understood through analogy.
Furthermore, as for the statement "What causes this illness to arise?
The illness of a bodhisattva arises from great compassion," this is the second response to Mañjuśrī’s first question; it is answered later, though its meaning is the same as before.

The commentary seeks to trace the traces back to the source. Having already distinguished the arising and ceasing of the provisional illness, it now answers the cause and conditions for the arising of this provisional illness:
it is due to the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

This mind of great compassion is precisely non-referential compassion, the compassionate mercy of inconceivable liberation. By the power of the roots of goodness of this compassionate mercy, it is able to...
Manifesting illness in his physical body to benefit sentient beings in the three lands—this is being without a deliberate mind toward objects.
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states that from his five fingers, he manifested five lion-like Tathāgatas; although the Buddha did not actually form the thought [to do so], the elephant perceived lions.

One should know that all such things are the power of the roots of goodness of loving-kindness and compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā-kuśalamūla*). Now, when Vimalakīrti’s great compassion perfumes his mind, such manifestations immediately arise.

The illnesses in the three lands are likewise so: if one possesses only compassion based on sentient beings or phenomena, one cannot be universal, nor can one manifest illness in response within the three lands.

Now, because Vimalakīrti possesses great compassion without conditions (*anālambana-mahākaruṇā*), he is able to manifest his body with illness in the three lands and preach the four teachings and the three contemplations.
