It is like a person born blind whose faculty of the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*) is impaired; though confronted with various forms, they cannot give rise to consciousness to perceive them.
It is so seen.
Upon hearing this, what wise person would not resolve their mind toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
This is the second exhortation for the wise to resolve their minds, excluding those of the two vehicles who have already entered the stage of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
"Any practitioners of the five vehicles who possess wisdom may resolve their minds to study this inconceivable dharma-gate of liberation. Why have we,
all śrāvakas, eternally severed our roots regarding this Mahāyāna, becoming like withered seeds?"
Upon hearing this inconceivable Dharma-door of liberation, all should weep aloud until their voices shake the trichiliocosm.
This is the third point clarifying that Kāśyapa reproaches himself for the fact that the śrāvakas have no share in this; it is the voice of all beings.
"Hearing that the roots have been severed forever" means that the seeds can no longer produce sprouts.
"Hearing this, all should wail until their voices shake the trichiliocosm" clarifies that there is no longer any function within the three realms;
because there will forever be no inconceivable benefit for beings throughout the great thousandfold world-system, Mahākāśyapa laments and reproaches himself.
The intention here is to lead those of the Lesser Vehicle who have entered the stage of correctness to become "fresh butter" (navanīta) entering the Mahāyāna; to mature them into "ghee" (ghṛta);
and finally, through the Lotus Sūtra, to bring them to the state of "clarified butter" (sarpis).

All Bodhisattvas should rejoice greatly and receive this Dharma upon the crown of their heads. If there are Bodhisattvas who possess faith and understanding, it is impossible [that they would not do so].
Regarding this inconceivable dharma-gate of liberation, all Māras can do nothing against it.
This is the fourth section, clarifying Mahākāśyapa’s celebration of the benefits gained by the bodhisattvas; it consists of two parts:

first, celebrating and exhorting them to receive [the teaching] upon their heads as the text describes; second, clarifying that having attained this true Dharma, the Great Beings abide within this dharma-gate.
Because he knows the illusions of Māra, it is said that for a bodhisattva who has attained faith and understanding of the Dharma-gate, no Māras whatsoever can do anything to him.
When Mahākāśyapa spoke these words, thirty-two thousand devaputras all resolved upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The thought of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

This is the benefit gained by the assembly upon hearing the Dharma during the fifth period. That the devas and humans gained this benefit was precisely due to hearing Vimalakīrti’s discourse on the inconceivable great function;
it was also because Kāśyapa himself praised and exhorted them, whereby they all gave rise to [the resolve for enlightenment].
It is the bodhicitta.

At that time, Vimalakīrti said to Mahākāśyapa: "O worthy one, those who act as Māras in the immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya worlds of the ten directions are for the most part bodhisattvas dwelling in the inconceivable liberation who employ skillful means."
Therefore, he teaches and transforms sentient beings while manifesting as a Māra king.
This is the sixth instance where Vimalakīrti validates Mahākāśyapa. Kāśyapa previously stated, "This Dharma-gate cannot be destroyed by Māras.
Now, the Great Being (Mahāsattva) validates this meaning in two ways: first, [he shows] that Māras cannot...
Those who have destroyed the two [obstructions], dwell in the inconceivable, and are able to accomplish the goal of the practitioner such that no demon can destroy them—
those who act as demon-kings are mostly those dwelling in this dharma-gate who strike at beginner practitioners of skillful means and beginners cultivating the Perfect Path.
If it were the true path, it would be indestructible, like gold.
Just as a vase made of adamantine jewels cannot be broken, and just as a wild boar rubbing against a golden pillar only causes its luster and color to increase further,
so too when Māras come while one cultivates the Path, they only cause one's merit, virtue, wisdom, and insight to increase all the more.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, suppose there are immeasurable bodhisattvas in the ten directions, and someone comes to them begging for their hands,
feet, ears, nose, head, eyes, marrow, brain, blood, flesh, skin, bones, villages, cities, wives, children, male and female servants,
elephants, horses, carriages, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, musaragalva, agate, coral, amber, pearls, conch shells, clothing, or food and drink— such as these.
Most of those who beg are bodhisattvas dwelling in the inconceivable liberation who, through the power of skillful means, go to test them in order to make their resolve firm.
Why is this? Because bodhisattvas dwelling in the inconceivable liberation possess the power of majestic virtue;
they employ coercive methods to demonstrate such difficult tasks to sentient beings, for ordinary, inferior people do not possess such capacity.
No power can thus oppress such a bodhisattva; it is like a dragon-elephant treading with its feet, which a donkey cannot endure.
This is called the gate of wisdom and skillful means of a bodhisattva who dwells in inconceivable liberation.
This is the second clarification regarding how bodhisattvas dwelling in the inconceivable can bring practitioners to fulfillment.

For those who receive the teachings of the provisional methods as well as the initial learners of the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya*) who practice the six perfections such as *dāna*, these bodhisattvas dwelling in the inconceivable frequently come to test them, causing their resolve to become firm; this is explained in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
When Kāśyapa was practicing on the causal stage, he was constantly obstructed by Devadatta; a minor bodhisattva could not do so.
The analogy is presented to clarify this point, and the comparison may be understood according to the text.
Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra, Scroll Twenty-two;
Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra, Scroll Twenty-three (Part One of the Chapter on Contemplating Sentient Beings).
The Seventh Chapter: Contemplating Sentient Beings, as Spoken by Vimalakīrti.
Below this, there are four chapters of sūtra text that follow the "Chapter on the Inconceivable. These shall be briefly explained using three points:
first, clarifying the intent behind this chapter and those that follow; second, briefly explaining the title of this chapter; and third, providing a word-by-word commentary on the text.
First, regarding the clarification of the intent behind this chapter: if one considers the aforementioned "Inconceivable" [chapter] alone...
The meaning of this chapter’s attainment of the supreme fruit is proximate; thus, the discourse constitutes the "Chapter on Inquiring after the Illness.
Within the room, all possessions are removed to signify that the Buddha-lands of the ten directions are entirely empty, leaving only a single bed upon which he lies ill.

This precisely symbolizes the inconceivable application of the Great Compassion of the Dharma-body. To establish this meaning, the "Inconceivable" chapter extensively elucidates abiding in the inconceivable.
Liberation possesses various unfathomable functions; this establishes the aforementioned clarity that expedient skill (*upāya*) manifests as illness or non-illness.

This is the inconceivable causal condition for benefiting sentient beings through the manifestation of illness. Speaking from a distant perspective, it establishes the "Buddha-land Chapter" (*Buddhakṣetra-parivarta*), clarifying that because Śāriputra and other sentient beings possess karmic offenses, they do not perceive the Pure Land; whereas Śaṅkhaśikha, being free from offense, does perceive it.
Seeing this inconceivable and boundless great function of adornment, only those who are to be delivered can perceive it;
therefore, the preceding chapter on "Inconceivability" establishes the meaning of the function of the supreme fruit.

Now, from the chapter "Observing Sentient Beings" onwards, there are four chapters that serve as the proximate discourse, primarily intended to establish the meaning of the "Inquiry into the Illness" chapter through three types of instruction and consolation.
Because the "Contemplation of the Threefold Subduing of Illness" is explained in detail herein, it serves to explain and establish what precedes it.
Furthermore, speaking from a broader perspective, it also concurrently establishes the four chapters outside [the main body].

The four chapters on the stages of existence (*bhavāgra*) correspond to the three teachings and consolations in the preceding "Inquiry into the Illness" chapter; the three contemplations for subduing those with actual illness refer to the contemplation of sentient beings.
This chapter constitutes the "Chapter on Inquiring after the Illness," which is the subduing through the contemplation of entering emptiness from the conventional.
The previous passage stated: "My illness arises from the delusions of past lives... even 'self' and 'nirvāṇa'—these two are both empty. One who attains this Dharma has no remaining illness;
there is only the "illness of emptiness," and even that illness of emptiness is empty. The preceding text directly addressed the entry [into emptiness].
The previous section did not yet distinguish how the four immeasurable minds arise based on emptiness; this chapter provides that full distinction, and thus it differs slightly.

Furthermore, while the preceding section merely clarified entering into emptiness, in this chapter Mañjuśrī asks about the ultimate source, and Vimalakīrti’s response reaches the source of non-abiding before concluding.
Moreover, because the dialogue between the heavenly maiden and Śāriputra is presented here with such clarity, this chapter is more extensive than the preceding one.

Furthermore, the second chapter, "The Buddha Path," explains and establishes the "Inquiry into the Illness" chapter. Regarding the contemplation of entering the provisional from emptiness (*śūnyatā-praveśa-prajñapti-vipaśyanā*) for the purpose of subduing [afflictions]:

it was previously stated that one should accept all sensations by means of non-acceptance; yet, as long as one has not yet perfected the Buddha-dharmas, one should not extinguish sensation to attain realization.

This is precisely the contemplation of entering the provisional from emptiness. Now, the "Buddha Path" chapter states that one practices within what are not paths in order to achieve thorough penetration.
The Buddha-way is precisely resolved in the "Inquiry into the Illness" chapter, which clarifies the entry into the conventional;

the third section, the "Entry into the Dharma-gate of Non-duality" and the "Incense Accumulation" chapter, both explain and establish what was clarified in the preceding "Inquiry into the Illness" chapter regarding the Middle Way and correct contemplation.
As stated in the "Inquiry into the Illness" chapter: "My illness is neither real nor existent; so too is the illness of sentient beings."
Furthermore, it is neither real nor existent; moreover, it is said that it is neither a path of defilement nor a path of purity.

The "Chapter on Entering the Dharma-Gate of Non-Duality" clarifies that all bodhisattvas enter the dharma-gate of non-duality, thereby fulfilling the "Chapter on Inquiring after Illness," which clarifies that [all things] are neither real nor existent.
The "Chapter on Fragrant Accumulation" shows the simultaneous engagement in both defilement and purity, thereby fulfilling the "Chapter on Inquiring after Illness," which clarifies the Path.
This is the contemplation of the meaning of the two streams (*dvayadhārā*). If discussed from a broader perspective, it simultaneously achieves the four chapters above the "Outer" section:

the "Contemplation of Sentient Beings" chapter achieves the aforementioned teaching for kings and elders regarding the impermanence of the body, its nature as a dream or illusion, and so forth, thereby inducing them to seek the *dharmakāya*.

The text of the "Expedient Means" chapter merely clarifies that, according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*), conditioned phenomena arise through dependent origination; it serves as a general teaching on the provisional nature of the essence, leading one to enter emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

Previously, the defiled and the true, nirvana and emptiness, as well as the sickness and the emptiness of that sickness, were not yet fully distinguished; now, because these are all thoroughly distinguished, this is considered "extensive and superior.
Next, regarding the "Chapter on the Buddha-way" which completes the "Chapter on the Disciples" by clarifying the meaning of the Separate Teaching:
it rebukes the disciples for seeking the true truth and nirvana without possessing the skillful means for entering into the conventional. Now, it clarifies practicing within what is not the Way.

He penetrates the Buddha-way and extensively explains the entry into conventional designations; he shatters ignorance as vast as the sands of the Ganges and excels in knowledge and vision, attaining non-obstruction.

Next, the "Chapter on Entering the Dharma-gate of Non-duality" and the "Chapter on Fragrant Accumulation" complete the preceding "Chapter on Bodhisattvas" to clarify the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).
As for the Bodhisattvas of the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*), although they practice through distinct stages while still in the causal state, even though...

One who can enter the conventional but cannot simultaneously traverse both the ultimate and the conventional now enters the "Chapter on Entering the Dharma-gate of Non-duality," wherein both arising and ceasing are extinguished;
and when emerging in the "Chapter on Fragrant Accumulation," one traverses equally through existence and non-existence, purity and impurity.

This reveals the dharma-gates of the perfect teaching, excluding only the dharma-realm of self-substance and its conditional aggregation. Now, that which accords with obtaining the Buddha-land is the attainment of the Buddha-land itself.
This refers to the meaning of "causes. The reason for this is that if the bonds of conditions are severed, one immediately attains rebirth;
furthermore, when one becomes a Buddha, the sentient beings whom one transforms will be able to come and be born in that land. These four chapters constitute three sections:

Chapter One, "Contemplating Sentient Beings," correctly clarifies the contemplation from the provisional to the empty; Chapter Two, "The Buddha Path," correctly clarifies the entry from the empty into the provisional.
The two chapters "Observing the Three Entrances into the Dharma-gate of Non-duality" and "The Fragrant Accumulation" clarify the dual flow of the Middle Way and correct contemplation.
This present chapter clarifies the initial common characteristic: the contemplation of entering emptiness from the conventional.
To briefly explain the title of this chapter, "Observing Sentient Beings," it refers to what was elucidated in the preceding "Inquiry into Ailment" chapter.

Entering emptiness from the conventional involves contemplating only one's own body; now, in the "Chapter on Sentient Beings," it clarifies that entering emptiness from the conventional is precisely the contemplation of others.
Self and other are one and non-dual. As previously cited from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:
"Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction. Here, self and other are mentioned interchangeably, each representing one side of the same reality.

Furthermore, while the former [chapter] clarifies that one must first understand oneself and then discipline oneself, this chapter clarifies that one understands others and embraces sentient beings with compassion;

thus, it is called the "Chapter on Contemplating Sentient Beings. "Contemplation" (guan) takes "penetrative understanding" (guanda) as its meaning, and it also takes "puncturing through" (guanchuan) as its meaning.

What is meant by "penetrative understanding" is to penetrate the source of sentient beings as being fundamentally pure, which is like the contemplation of entering emptiness from the conventional (from the false into the empty).

Although there is a distinction between ordinary beings and sages regarding what is illuminated and realized, they all ultimately converge in emptiness and stillness, being as one and non-dual as suchness.
As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "As is the mind, so are the Buddhas; as are the Buddhas, so are sentient beings.

Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without differentiation. The preceding passage states: "Maitreya, the suchness of sentient beings and the suchness of [the Buddha] are one suchness, without duality. Thus it is.

This is precisely the thorough realization that sentient beings are ultimately pure: the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) in the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and the equality of emptiness in the supreme truth of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad-paramārtha-satya*).

For one who penetrates the profound meaning of these three principles, although there are three types of afflictive hindrances within the three truths of sentient beings—namely, the distinctions between grasping at signs, ignorance, and fundamental nescience (*avidyā*)—[they are ultimately non-dual].
Because the Bodhisattva illuminates and penetrates the principles of the three truths without obstruction, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states:
"Using a sharp pickaxe to strike it, the boulders, sand, and gravel are passed through directly and without hindrance, penetrating all the way to the diamond [layer].

This is the meaning of "observing and penetrating," and it also carries the meaning of "observing and piercing. When the Bodhisattva enters the contemplation of emptiness from the conventional, [this occurs].

It pierces through the boulders of delusive views and afflictions within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), and penetrates the sands of stagnant ignorance that obscure the single reality-truth (*eka-astitva-satya*).
To penetrate without obstruction is precisely to reach the ultimate limit of the mind-nature’s primordial source—the diamond-like [wisdom].
Thus, the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "For example, suppose there is a person who, parched with thirst and needing water, digs at a high spring and still sees..."
Seeing dry earth, one knows that water is still far off; yet by continuing the work without ceasing, one eventually sees moist soil and gradually reaches mud.
This resolute mind knows that water must be near. Seeing dry earth represents contemplating the provisional while perceiving the ultimate truth;
seeing moist soil represents contemplating the ultimate without dwelling upon it and contemplating the provisional without obstruction; and gradually reaching the mud represents this...
Because the clarity of the Middle Way merges with ignorance like water merging with mud, it is said to reach the mud.
When one obtains clear water, this is precisely the manifestation of the principle of the Middle Way; being free from the mud of ignorance, settled and pure, is true liberation.
Therefore, entering this chapter to contemplate sentient beings involves three kinds of intentions, which correspond to this.
The contemplation of the three truths is precisely the meaning of "contemplative penetration. Furthermore, the text states:

"To exhaust the source and investigate until reaching the foundation of non-abiding" means to penetrate through the five stages of dwelling (*pañca-vāsabhūmi*) to the adamantine limit of the mind's fundamental boundary.

That which is called "sentient beings" refers to the dharmas of the five aggregates, the six sense bases, and the eighteen elements; by grasping these real dharmas, one forms a body, and thus they are called sentient beings. If...
According to the Abhidharma, the sentient beings established by its principles ultimately lack any truly existent dharma that constitutes them.

If one follows the Vātsīputrīya school, which posits a "self" within the fifth, inexpressible category (*avaktavyaka-nikāya*), or according to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, it is not only the sentient beings established therein that are provisional, but even the dharmas that constitute them are likewise provisional;
thus, they take the three types of provisional designations (*prajñapti*) as their basis.

In the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), there are provisionally existent sentient beings; yet when one enters the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) through the emptiness of the three provisional designations, there are no sentient beings.
Not only is there no sentient being who is established, but there are also no real dharmas that establish them. This analysis of the provisional clarifies that the establishing factors are empty.
Furthermore, according to the Mahāyāna practitioners, all real dharmas of sentient beings are like dreams and illusions—neither arising nor ceasing.
The *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* ultimately refutes the loss of the Mahāyāna meaning.

This sutra clarifies that the sentient beings who are formed by the essence and the real dharmas that form them are all like illusions, water-moons, mirror-images, lightning, and so forth; this is the entry into emptiness via the provisional nature of the essence.
Question: If they are empty just as an illusion is, how does this differ from what is taught by those of the Vaipulya path?

The answer is: That which clarifies [the truth] as being like an illusion and so forth is precisely emptiness (*śūnyatā*). To grasp at the marks of emptiness is to destroy the wisdom-eye through conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*);

if one cannot even attain emptiness to enter the Truth, how could one attain true emptiness to enter the Middle Way? This sutra clarifies the contemplation of the three truths (*trīṇi satyāni*) to exhaust their source and fully realize their nature.
By inferring this meaning, there are three kinds of sentient beings: first, those of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); second, ... [text continues].

Among the three truths of sentient beings, those of the Middle Way: if one views them according to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), they grasp the five aggregates of fragmentation (*pariccheda-pañca-skandha*) to form nominally designated sentient beings, all of whom are like illusions and dreams;
if one views them according to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), they likewise grasp the five aggregates of transformation (*pariṇāma-pañca-skandha*) to form sentient beings;
if one views them according to the Middle Way, it is by means of the five aggregates of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā-pañca-skandha*) that they constitute sentient beings.
Because it arises, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* clarifies that the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is not separate from the six dharmas. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Sentient beings are unsurpassed; the Buddha is the unsurpassed Dharma; and this Dharma is unsurpassed, which is Nirvana.

Now, since the Middle Way is the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), why should the five aggregates not be called "contemplating sentient beings"? It exhausts the source of sentient beings and reaches the ultimate limit of the three [realms].
Question: This sutra clarifies that contemplating sentient beings is the meaning of a bodhisattva observing sentient beings;

it states that they enter true reality (*tattva*) like the "fifth great element" and so forth, and does not speak of the existence of the five aggregates subject to transformation (*pariṇāma*). How, then, can this interpretation be applied here?
Answer: When contemplating true reality, one does not perceive conventional sentient beings, just as one does not perceive a fifth great element and so forth.
Based on reality, it is not that there are no sentient beings composed of the five aggregates that undergo transformation through the conditions of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva’s contemplation of emptiness differs from that of the Two Vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas). The Two Vehicles contemplate the emptiness of sentient beings but do not contemplate the emptiness of *nirvāṇa*;

since they do not even contemplate the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) of *nirvāṇa*, how could they contemplate the emptiness of the Middle Way? Now, this clarifies the entry from the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) into [the ultimate].
Since emptiness means that all three truths are empty, the text of the "Inquiry into the Illness" chapter states: "Both 'I' and 'nirvāṇa'—these two are both empty.
Here, "I" refers to the conventional truth of birth-and-death, which is the emptiness of sentient beings; "nirvāṇa" refers to the dharma of the ultimate truth, which is the emptiness of phenomena.
It further states: "The illness of emptiness is also empty. One should know that these words clarify that within the grasping of delusion, even this illness is empty. This is the Middle Way.
When the Middle Way is explained by means of emptiness at certain times, it is because emptiness [negates] the two extremes of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
If one were to conceive of a "Middle Way" as being existent, that would constitute a disease regarding the Middle Way; since this disease is also empty, it is said that even the Middle Way is empty.
When one enters the contemplation of emptiness for the time being, all three truths are empty; yet, although they are all empty, they are not [non-existent].
Those who sever [delusions] by perceiving the true Middle Way realize that the myriad practices are but the One Mind; how could this be a mere void annihilation?
Therefore, this chapter explains the ultimate realization of the Middle Way, using analogies such as the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

One should know that when a Bodhisattva enters from the conventional into the void, although they likewise enter the void, their omniscience (*sarvajñā*)—according to its designation—perceives the three [realms].
Since the Truth (satya) possesses the three wisdoms (*trijñāna*), the Commentary states: "The three wisdoms are actually attained simultaneously;

however, for the sake of explaining them to people so they may easily understand, they are distinguished as a sequence. If one can thus enter emptiness (*śūnyatā*) while simultaneously possessing the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*), then although one uses the name of the first contemplation when entering emptiness, one actually possesses all three contemplations, which inherently include loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), and sympathetic joy (*muditā*).

This is what is clarified in this chapter on "Renunciation. If one enters emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and possesses the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*) to perceive the three truths (*trīṇi satyāni*), this is precisely the meaning of "contemplative penetration" (*guan-da*) and "contemplative piercing" (*guan-chuan*); therefore, it is called the "Chapter on Contemplating Sentient Beings. Question:

If you say that the Middle Way is emptiness, then previously, the conventional was sublated by the ultimate, and subsequently, the ultimate was sublated by the Middle Way; thus, emptiness could be taught. Now...
By what means is the Middle Way refuted? It is answered: because that which is non-arising cannot be described as arising, its nature is inherently empty.

Furthermore, it is refuted because it prevents the false conceptualization and grasping at proliferation regarding the un-realized Middle Way; thus, it is called the "refutation of emptiness" within the Middle Way.
Moreover, it is now taught as emptiness in order to refute attachment to phenomena (*dharmatṛṣṇā*); there is no other distinct principle of truth that refutes the Middle Way.
If there were some other principle of truth (satya) distinct from the Path that could refute the Right Path, then that principle of truth would itself require another principle of truth to refute it;
thus, there would be an infinite regress of principles of truth.
At that time, Mañjuśrī asked Vimalakīrti: "How does a bodhisattva contemplate sentient beings?
This is the third entry into the textual commentary. As before, the four chapters are divided into three sections;

this chapter specifically clarifies contemplating sentient beings by entering emptiness from the conventional, resolving the previous "Inquiry into the Illness" chapter’s entry from the conventional into emptiness.
The "Subtle Commentary" (*Kongōshaku*) thus treats this single passage as four sections: first, the primary exposition on contemplating sentient beings as they enter emptiness from the conventional;
second, the exposition on giving rise to immeasurable minds to benefit others; third, the investigation into the ultimate source of sentient beings;
and fourth, the section on the celestial maidens scattering flowers. Regarding the first, the primary exposition on contemplating sentient beings, the text is as follows:
There are two parts: first, Mañjuśrī’s question; second, Vimalakīrti’s answer. As for why Mañjuśrī asks:

in the preceding "Inquiry into the Illness" chapter, it was clarified that a bodhisattva who is truly ill enters emptiness from the conventional; this precisely expounded the meaning of self-discipline, yet it did not clarify how this contemplation benefits others.
Now, Mañjuśrī asks: if a bodhisattva employs the aforementioned contemplation of entering emptiness from the conventional...
Regarding the question of how a bodhisattva who benefits sentient beings contemplates their birth, Vimalakīrti replied:
"It is just as a magician views the illusory person he has conjured; a bodhisattva contemplates sentient beings in this same way."

This is the answer-text concerning the names of the two purities, which consists of three parts: first, observing sentient beings from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) through ten analogies such as being like an illusion;
second, observing sentient beings from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) through five analogies such as being like a fifth great element;

and third, observing sentient beings from the perspective of the Middle Way, the primary ultimate truth (*madhyamā-prathamārtha-satya*), through analogies such as being like the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Regarding the former observation...
By means of analogies such as illusions, the arising [of phenomena] is analyzed to refute the notion that conventional reality possesses an inherent nature; this clarifies that their nature is empty.

One merely eliminates the false conceptualization of a fixed nature, yet it does not preclude the continued existence of conventionally designated sentient beings. If one discusses their conventional body, it is ultimately real as a phantom-like existence;

this is precisely what is called "emptiness of nature" within the context of the three types of conventional designations that accord with principle. It is not that there is nothing remaining that accords with principle.
Regarding the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases of sentient beings within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) as being like an illusion and the three types of provisional existence:

through these ten metaphors, the observation of sentient beings in the conventional truth is revealed with two intentions. The first five similes illustrate provisional existence according to principle (*yathā-yukti*), while the latter five similes illustrate provisional existence according to sentiment (*yathā-lobha*).

To establish this [latter] "according to principle," the text itself has two parts: first, an analysis based on the metaphor of an illusion; second, an analysis based on the [remaining] nine [metaphors].
For example, it is like a person who, from the outset, relies on a magician to observe the illusory figures created by that magician;

such a person, through their own recognition of the magician’s art, knows that the phenomena produced by illusion are not real, whereas the people before them do not know they are illusions and claim them to be real persons.
It is just so with the Bodhisattva observing the aggregates, sense bases, elements, and sentient beings of conventional truth. It is as with the Bodhisattva.
When there is the illusory principle of ignorance, there are both self-sentient beings and other-sentient beings.
If, as in the previous "Inquiry into Ailments" chapter, one contemplates that self-sentient beings exist only through delusion, then external sentient beings are likewise all like illusions.

However, because those deluded by externals do not understand this and instead regard them as truly existent, there are also "three provisional [categories of] sentient beings" according to their subjective perceptions. Now...
This clarifies that although Bodhisattvas observe sentient beings as having an illusory and empty nature, this does not preclude the existence of those who still possess inversions;

because there are, according to principle, sentient beings of the three provisional designations within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), it is said that the Bodhisattva observes sentient beings in this manner.
It is like the wise person seeing the moon in water, like seeing the reflection of one's own face in a mirror, like a mirage in the heat, like an echo, like clouds in the sky,
like foam gathered on water, like bubbles on the surface of water, like the solidity of a plantain tree, and like a flash of lightning that lingers for but a moment.

Of these nine analogies, four belong to the category of "conforming to principle" (*yathā-artha-prajñapti*) and five belong to the category of "conforming to sentiment" (*yathā-āśaya-prajñapti*). To take the analogy of the moon in water:
the moon in the water exists because of the celestial moon; while one knows that the moon in the water cannot be grasped, this does not preclude the existence of the [celestial] moon.

In the same way, when a Bodhisattva knows for themselves whether the bright moon exists, it is precisely within the water of the *dharmatā* that there is the moon of sentient beings, just as in a mirror.
When a Bodhisattva beholds the appearance of a face, they know that there is the face of ignorance within the mirror of the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

To see conventional beings in this mirror of the true nature of phenomena is like seeing a mirage in the heat; ignorance is like the heat, and from this nature of phenomena arises the mirage of conventional beings.
It is like an echo responding to a call: if there is the call of ignorance, then immediately—
The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is like an empty valley that produces the echoes of sentient beings.

If one follows the eight analogies in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, which maintain that based on the *ālayavijñāna* each has its own specific referent, this reflects the intent of the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyākaraṇa*).

Now, using the analogy of sentient beings in general—as in "clouds in the sky"—is the intent of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇavyākaraṇa*) and the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulyavyākaraṇa*). These five analogies below are those of the Tripitaka Teaching (*piṭakatrayavyākaraṇa*).
These three conventional truths according to worldly sentiment serve as analogies to assist in establishing the three conventional truths according to principle,
just as the "Expedient Means" chapter clarifies that while there is no person within the five aggregates, the cloud of sentient beings arises through the power of ignorance and the view of a self.
Just as with the mass of foam upon water— these four analogies are all from the "Expedient Means" chapter.
This has already been explained.
Just as with the fifth great element, the sixth aggregate, the seventh sense-faculty, the thirteenth base, and the nineteenth realm,
so too does the Bodhisattva contemplate sentient beings in this manner.
From this point on, these five analogies clarify the second point: observing that sentient beings are empty of true reality (*tattva*). Why is this so?

The preceding analogies observed that sentient beings have no fixed nature, yet they do not preclude the existence of sentient beings as provisional names and illusory echoes perceived through inversion.
Now, these five analogies clarify that sentient beings are like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit—ultimately non-existent.
It is unobtainable not only because there are no sentient beings, but also because there are no real dharmas; thus, the path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity ceases.
Just as the fifth great element or the nineteenth realm are ultimately non-existent, this principle is established.
Therefore, one should know that these five phrases constitute the contemplation of sentient beings to enter the ultimate truth, wherein sentient beings are ultimately not seen.
It is like form in the formless realm; like a sprout from scorched grain; like the view of a self in the body of a stream-enterer;
like entering a womb for a non-returner; like the three poisons in an arhat; like greed, anger, and violation of precepts in a bodhisattva who has attained patient acceptance;

like the habitual tendencies of afflictions in a Buddha; like seeing forms by one who is blind; like inhalation and exhalation in one who has entered the meditative absorption of cessation; like the tracks of a bird in the sky; and like a stone.
A daughter is like a conjured person; the arising of fetters is like the birth of a Tathāgata; the production of afflictions is like what is seen in a dream after one has awakened;
receiving a body is like the state of one who has entered parinirvāṇa; and [the body] is like a fire without a cause. Thus does the Bodhisattva contemplate sentient beings.
The sixteen similes below are precisely the three insights for observing the Middle Way of sentient beings.

The reason for this is that the Dharma of the Middle Way is neither existent nor empty; it is not like the similes of "existence" such as illusions, nor is it like the similes of "non-existence" such as the five great elements (*mahābhūta*).
As the Sūtra says, "Form is like form in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)," which refers to the provisional teachings of the skillful means (*upāya*).

The definitive teachings clarify that the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is entirely without form; yet, because the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* clarifies that there is indeed form in the formless realm, it states:
"Regarding the form in the formless realm, how could there be coming, going, staying, or dwelling?
Such meanings are not within the sphere of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, but are known only by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
The same applies to seeing liberation. That which is both form and non-form—the "non-form" refers to the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas;
the "form" refers to the Buddhas and Tathāgatas. This form is not like the material obstructions of the mundane world;

it is wondrous form (*prabhāsvara-rūpa*), serene and eternally abiding, never subject to the transformations of birth, old age, sickness, or death. If one discusses "form that is formless," according to the Hīnayāna:

As for the teaching, according to the Mahāyāna teachings, it possesses form and possesses persons. Some say that the *Śāriputrābhidharma* clarifies that there is form within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

This is analogous to the Middle Way, which differs from the conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) in its designation of existence as "emptiness," yet differs from the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) in its lack of non-existence; therefore, it possesses wondrous form. Thus we know that from this point onward...
The following analogies all explain the Middle Way by way of the wise person’s vision of both emptiness and non-emptiness;
thus the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "All phenomena are non-existent, yet they exist in this manner. Not knowing this is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
The ground of abiding ignorance possesses the greatest power, and it is only through the Buddha’s bodhi-wisdom that it can be severed. Now, [this ignorance] is absent.
One should know that the form of the form realm is the Buddha’s domain;

from this point onward, it is all an exposition on observing sentient beings and entering the meaning of the emptiness of the Middle Way. Furthermore, since the preceding text concluded the discussion on the nineteen realms, it then concludes by stating:
"The Bodhisattva observes sentient beings in this manner. Now, a new chapter begins to clarify the form of the formless realm; how could these be the same?
The fifth great element and the nineteenth realm are ultimately non-existent; this fully explains and establishes the preceding passage from the "Inquiry into the Illness" chapter:

"Entering from the conventional into emptiness, both 'self' and 'nirvāṇa' are empty. When one attains this Dharma, there is no remaining illness, only the illness of emptiness, and even the illness of emptiness is empty.
This corresponds with the text here which observes that the three truths are mutually established for sentient beings.
Regarding the intent of the "Chapter on Observing Sentient Beings," the present section explains the various phrases concerning scorched seeds sprouting buds.

In the preceding passage, Kāśyapa reflects that he is like a rotten seed; if he were permanently ruined, he would not be eligible for the prediction of attaining Buddhahood according to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
However, if he is to attain Buddhahood, his seed is not scorched. The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "If a person uses skillful means such as ghee and oil..."
Since watering [a parched seed] causes the sprout of a scorched seed to grow, we know that even a scorched seed possesses the principle of producing a sprout;

how could it be the same as the fifth great element or the nineteen realms? Regarding the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) in a *srotāpanna*: this person has severed the afflictions of the truths (*satyadarśana-kleśa*) and entered the first fruit;

because the view of a self is permanently eliminated, they are said to be "without" the view of a self. However, this refers to its absence within the three realms of segmented existence (*prādeśika*).

If one considers the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) in relation to the specific afflictions of the distinct teachings that have not yet been eliminated—whereby the vision of the truths (*darśana-mārga*) still remains—then it carries the sense of "possessing a body-view.

How could this be like the fifth great element or the nineteenth realm? An Anāgāmin enters the womb having exhausted the nine grades of afflictions of the desire realm and thus does not return to the lower stages of the desire realm to receive a womb-birth;
yet, if they have not severed the specific afflictions [of the higher realms] and then resolve their minds [on awakening], [the situation is different].

Because one enters the "sacred embryo" (āryagarbha) only by practicing the Mahāyāna, it is said that one dwells securely in conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). At the moment of first emerging from this embryo, it is called "non-arising arising.
How could this be like the fifth great element or the nineteenth realm?

For example, although an Arhat has severed the three poisons of the desire realm and exhausted the eighteen grades of afflictions of the form and formless realms—thus being free from the three poisons within those realms—they still possess the [afflictions] of the [higher] realms.
The three poisons external to the [five] aggregates are not ultimately non-existent, just as the fifth great element or the nineteenth realm are not.
When a Bodhisattva attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), it is only then that greed, anger, and the violation of precepts within the realms are ultimately non-existent.
How could one claim that greed, anger, and the violation of precepts arising from views and attachments external to the realms are also ultimately non-existent? Therefore...
There is a sutra which states that only the Buddha alone dwells in pure precepts, while all others are said to have defiled precepts.
One should know that even Bodhisattvas who have attained *kṣānti* (patience) possess the sense of violating prohibitions; how could they be like the nineteen elements (*dhātu*) and so forth?

Regarding the Buddha’s afflictions and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), the Buddha has severed the primary afflictions and their habits, eternally eliminating them so that his wisdom of all modes (*sarvajñatā*) is perfected. If it were as [the case for] sentient beings...

Vasanas (habitual tendencies) can be transcended, yet they may also manifest; for example, when [the Buddha] rebuked Devadatta while praising Śāriputra, although [the underlying defilements] were already severed, there was still a sense of similarity [to them].
This is not like the nineteen elements and so forth, which absolutely cannot possibly exist.
Question: If that is so, then why do the actual outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) also arise? Why speak only of the vasanas? Answer: Because the actual outbursts have already...

For Arhats, those who have attained patience (kṣānti), and Bodhisattvas, although these [afflictions] are exhausted, their residual habits (vāsanā) have not yet been severed; unless it is a deliberate manifestation, one cannot say they exist.
It is like a blind person seeing colors: though they do not see them manifest before their eyes, they nevertheless conceive mental images of forms and appearances within their inner mind.
This is like desiring to see something—the occurrence of mental movement and conceptualization still exists—but it is not like the nineteenth realm.
Furthermore, there is the principle that [something] may eventually be perceived. Regarding the fifth great element and the nineteen realms, they ultimately do not exist from beginning to end.

This is like the case of one who has entered the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) and the inhalation and exhalation of breath: once one has entered the absorption of cessation, there should no longer be any breath, because it is sustained by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi-bala*).
Although the breath cannot enter or exit, it is not obstructed; the phenomena of breathing still remain perfectly intact.
Regarding the body, it is like a fish held in ice; though it does not move while the ice remains, it moves as soon as the ice melts.

Furthermore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* clarifies that although consciousness ceases in the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), it can arise again because it depends upon the *ālayavijñāna*. Thus, those who emerge from this state do so by relying on it; this principle should be understood accordingly.
However, the nineteenth *dhātu* cannot be so, for it would be like the tracks of a bird in the sky. This is if one considers it in terms of physical substance.
The eye does not see it, and thus one says there are no tracks. The *Aṅgulimālīya Sūtra* states that those with the divine eye can see the tracks of birds in the sky;
how could this be the same as the nineteen elements and so forth, which are ultimately invisible like the son of a barren woman?

As for the nature of a barren woman, she never gives birth to a child; how then could there be a retribution for such a thing? If the karmic obstruction is transformed, it is no longer [an obstruction].

Just as the fruit of a barren woman might, through transformation, give birth to a child, so too—just as Śāriputra became a woman and that woman became Śāriputra—all female bodies lack a fixed nature;
this case should be understood by analogy. How could it be the same as the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) and so forth, which are ultimately incapable of transformation?
For instance, when a manifested person (*nirmāṇapuruṣa*) possesses afflictions, that manifested person is actually without afflictions; yet at times, they are seen [to have them].

In walking, standing, sitting, and reclining, one manifests the signs of the three poisons; how can this be the same as the nineteen realms (*dhātu*), which ultimately possess no characteristics whatsoever?
It is like what is seen in a dream: once awakened, although the dream is no longer present, the dream cannot be said to be non-existent.

It does not hinder the existence of a recollective consciousness that remembers the events of the dream, nor is there any principle that precludes dreaming again. How could this be the same as the nineteen realms?

These are ultimately and utterly beyond recollection or cognition, just as one who has entered parinirvāṇa. Regarding those who receive a body, it is said in general that an Arhat who enters parinirvāṇa has no permanent location;
yet, since they take birth in the land of transformation (*pariṇāmiki-bhūmi*), how could this be the same as the nineteenth realm, which is ultimately without birth?
It is like a fire without a cause; if one were to analyze such a fire through the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), it would be refuted.
Causes and conditions arise neither from themselves nor from another; this too is causeless fire. Furthermore, it is like the light of a *vaiḍūrya* gem emitting rays:
when blue light is seen, it appears as blue, yet these various lights are emitted without cause. This emission of light is simply the illumination of fire.
(Verse 19) Regarding the elements (*dhātu*) and so forth, this principle never exists. These fifteen phrases collectively constitute the discernment of sentient beings.

Entering the Middle Way of the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*), although it is empty, it is not the same as the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), being like a "fifth great element" or a "nineteenth realm.
Although it exists, it is unlike the provisional existence of conventional truth; it is neither empty nor existent, yet it can make emptiness and existence appear perfectly distinct.
It is like form that is not of the formless realm—non-existent yet existent. Thus one should know that this is the inconceivable realm of all Buddhas.

The Bodhisattva contemplates sentient beings as they enter from the provisional into the empty, thoroughly seeing the Three Truths; this constitutes the preceding "Inquiry into the Illness" chapter. Question:
In the "Inquiry into the Illness" chapter, one contemplates up to the Middle Way and thereby shatters the illness of emptiness;

yet in this text, one contemplates the Middle Way without shattering it. How can these two be the same? Answer: In the former case, because there was attachment to grasping, it was necessary to shatter [emptiness]. Now, it clarifies abiding.
In principle, that which is not itself a disease need not be cured.
Mañjuśrī said: "If a bodhisattva practices contemplation in this way, how does he practice loving-kindness?
This is the second [section], clarifying how a bodhisattva enters from the conventional into emptiness and gives rise to the four immeasurable minds toward sentient beings.
The reason one must give rise to the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*) is that these four immeasurable minds are the foundation for benefiting sentient beings;
if one lacks this mind, one falls into the stage of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*). According to this text, there are four rounds of question and answer:

first, Mañjuśrī asks about the immeasurable mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*); second, he asks about the immeasurable mind of compassion (*karuṇā*); third, he asks about the immeasurable mind of sympathetic joy (*muditā*).

Regarding the four questions on the mind and the first question on the immeasurable mind of equanimity (*upekṣā-apramāṇa-citta*): the text concerning the entry into emptiness and the clarification of the immeasurable mind of compassion (*maitrī-apramāṇa-citta*) consists of two parts:
first, Mañjuśrī’s question; second, Vimalakīrti’s answer. As for why Mañjuśrī asks:

when a bodhisattva observes sentient beings entering the emptiness of the three truths from the conventional, if they enter the emptiness of the mundane, there would be no such thing as illusory conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta*).
If sentient beings who are a collection of conditions enter true emptiness, then there are no unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) sentient beings who are a collection of conditions.

If they enter the right path, then emptiness itself has no self-nature; within the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), where sentient beings are a collection of conditions, for what reason would a mind of compassion arise, and furthermore, what sentient beings would there be to be transformed?
Yet, the path of the Bodhisattva is fundamentally for the purpose of transforming others.
If things are primary [and now] all are empty, what is there for compassion to encompass? If one contemplates emptiness and loses compassion, how does this differ from the two vehicles?
It is for this reason that this question was asked. Vimalakīrti said:
"After a bodhisattva has made such an observation, he reflects to himself: 'I shall preach such a teaching as this for the sake of sentient beings.'"
The Dharma is precisely true compassion.
This is the meaning of the two Pure Names' responses:

they speak these three truths of emptiness solely for the sake of sentient beings, so that sentient beings may awaken to this principle of the emptiness of the three truths, enter the secret treasury of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), and attain permanence, bliss, self, and purity.

"Purity" refers to the thirty-two kinds of true compassion (*maitrī*). Regarding this response, there are four parts: first, explaining that this Dharma is precisely the meaning of compassion as the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*);
second, clarifying compassion in terms of the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*); third, clarifying compassion in terms of the virtue of the noble ones (*ārya-guṇa*);
and fourth, clarifying compassion in terms of all practices (*sarva-caryā*). First, regarding the clarification of compassion in terms of the virtue of wisdom: if one wishes to know—
Wisdom consists in speaking now for the sake of sentient beings; to speak thus of true compassion means that the Bodhisattva, practicing the path, now realizes Great Nirvana.
Knowing that the non-arising of arising is ineffable, he employs the four bodies to respond to conditions and preach this Dharma.
This is precisely the virtue of wisdom, which causes sentient beings to see their Buddha-nature and attain the bliss of Great Nirvana. This is...
Compassion (*maitrī*) is able to bestow happiness. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Compassion is the Tathāgata; compassion is liberation (*vimukti*).

Liberation is seeing the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*), which is seeing the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), and abiding in Great Nirvāṇa. This constitutes the hundredfold liberation. This refers to what was explained above:
the contemplation of emptiness that penetrates all the way to the Middle Way. The Middle Way is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), the unconditioned great...
Compassion is like a magnet that attracts iron; this is true compassion. Apart from this compassion, where else could one seek true compassion?
Because those of the Two Vehicles do not perceive the True Path, they enter into emptiness and lack a compassionate heart. If we speak of these in distinct categories:

what has been explained above regarding the contemplation of conventional truth is "compassion for sentient beings" (*sattvālambana-maitrī*), while that of ultimate truth is "compassion for phenomena" (*dharmālambana-maitrī*).
One should know that seeing the Middle Way within compassion is precisely "unconditioned compassion" (anālambana-maitrī). Thus, contemplating the three truths is itself the three virtues (triguṇa).
If a bodhisattva who contemplates sentient beings enters into emptiness and possesses such compassion, this takes emptiness as its primary function;
although it is designated by the name "all-knowledge" (sarvajñā), in reality it possesses all three contemplations and may also be discussed in terms of the three types of compassion.
If a sick Bodhisattva contemplates their own body and is able to cultivate this contemplation, they personally discipline their own mind;
if they can cultivate this compassion and preach it for the sake of sentient beings, this is the meaning of transforming others by bestowing happiness.

Therefore, it is said that preaching such a Dharma for sentient beings is true compassion. This is why the *Lotus Sūtra* clarifies that even if one has not yet attained [the state of] non-... [the text continues].
By means of the outflows (āsrava), one enters the Tathāgata’s chamber, dons the Tathāgata’s robe, and sits upon the Tathāgata’s seat.
Now, a sick bodhisattva who has not yet attained the dharma-nature body is one who dons the Tathāgata’s robe and practices the Tathāgata’s unconditioned compassion (anālambana-maitrī).
Furthermore, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* clarifies that a bodhisattva who initially relies [on this practice] possesses afflictions (kleśa) and is thus able to know the Tathāgata.
The secret treasury is that which people may also believe and accept when it is spoken;
since this is already so even at the stage of semblance, how much more so when one truly enters into compassion and preaches the Dharma for sentient beings—
is this not indeed true great compassion?
He practices the compassion of quiescence because there is nothing produced; he practices the compassion that is not feverish because there are no afflictions;

he practices the compassion of equality because it is equal throughout the three periods of time; he practices the compassion free from contention because there is nothing that arises; he practices the compassion of non-duality because the internal and external do not meet;

he practices the compassion that is indestructible because it is ultimately exhausted; he practices the compassion that is firm because the mind is not subject to ruin; he practices the compassion that is pure.
Because the nature of all dharmas is pure, one practices boundless compassion, which is like space.
The following nine phrases clarify compassion from the perspective of true severance (*tathatā-prahāṇa*). The Sūtra says: "Compassion that is quiescent and without arising.
This means that when one contemplates sentient beings and enters emptiness up to the Middle Way, one sees that all dharmas have been so from the very beginning.
The coming [of all things] is always characterized by inherent quiescence;

because they are originally devoid of the dualistic marks of birth-and-death and agitation, the Dharma of Middle-Way Quiescence is itself compassion and the principle of neither-arising-nor-non-arising.
If one perceives this principle, the birth-and-death of the two extremes are both severed; therefore, it is said that "nothing is produced. Question: If there is production from the two extremes...
Question: Since "death and severance" is called "that which is non-arising," how can there still be forty-one grades of birth remaining in the first dwelling?
Answer: The severance of even one grade of *pariṇāma-utpāda* (transformative birth) is itself "non-arising.

Although there are forty-one grades of that which is produced, because none of them possess a determinate nature (*niyata-svabhāva*), they are all "non-arising. Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:
Although one has not yet escaped the realm of death, it is as if one has already attained liberation. As the Sūtra says:

"One who practices the compassion of non-affliction (anupatāpa-maitrī) perceives the True Path and immediately enters the cool pool of Great Nirvāṇa, free from the heat of the afflictions of the two extremes.
One who practices the compassion of equality (samatā-maitrī) regards saṃsāra and nirvāṇa as equal; when contemplating sentient beings, they enter into emptiness and perceive the Truth.
The equality of the three periods of time is the true Dharma-body, the "stone of compassion.

A sutra states that those who practice the compassion of non-contention are free from contention because they see that saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are not distinct; because there is contention, various afflictions arise, leading to old age and death.

However, if one contemplates sentient beings and enters the vision of emptiness, perceiving the correct path, then the contention of the two extremes does not arise—this is the true stone of compassion. Thus says the sutra.

Regarding "the compassion of non-duality between speech and action": when one observes sentient beings entering emptiness and seeing the right path, this is precisely the single path of pure compassion, termed "non-dual compassion," because it does not conjoin with the afflictions or the cycle of birth and death within or without the realms;

thus it is said that there is no conjunction between the internal and external. The Sūtra states that "the compassion of unimpaired speech" refers to when one observes sentient beings entering emptiness and seeing...

The True Path is the Single Ultimate Truth; this single ultimate is unconditioned true compassion (*anālambana-satya-maitrī*), which cannot be destroyed by the afflictions of the two extremes or the fruits of birth and death.
As the Sūtra says: "One who practices firm compassion observes sentient beings, enters emptiness, and reaches the True Path;
then their mind becomes like a vajra, realizing true compassion, and their mind is not disturbed by the eight worldly concerns of the internal or external realms."

It is that which is destroyed by the wind. The Sūtra says: "Practicing the purity of loving-kindness" means that if one contemplates sentient beings, enters emptiness, perceives the right path, and attains true reality (*satya*), one knows that all phenomena (*dharma*) are pure and free from defilement or attachment. The Sūtra says:

"Practicing boundless loving-kindness" means that if one contemplates sentient beings, enters emptiness, and perceives the single ultimate truth (*ekābhisamaya*), this is itself the boundless reality.

Compassion enters the nature of phenomena through goodness and does not stagnate in any extreme; great compassion universally covers all because it perceives emptiness and the Buddha-nature, and is therefore said to be like space.

One practices the compassion of an Arhat to destroy the thieves of the fetters, practices the compassion of a Bodhisattva to bring peace to sentient beings, and practices the compassion of a Tathāgata...

Because they have attained the mark of suchness, they practice the compassion of a Buddha; because they awaken sentient beings, they practice spontaneous compassion; because it is obtained without cause, they practice the compassion of bodhi;
and because it is of one equal flavor, [they practice it].
The following six phrases constitute the third illumination, which defines true compassion by means of the noble virtues. As the Sūtra says:
"That which is called the compassion of an Arhat—'Arhat' being translated here as 'slayer of thieves'—the Arhat perceives emptiness and slays only the afflictions within the realm.
The Bodhisattva, however, contemplates sentient beings entering into emptiness; he perceives not only mere emptiness, but also the emptiness of the unobtainable (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*)."
This is the true path and the single ultimate truth. Within the realm, one slays the thieves of affliction; without the realm, one slays the great thieves of affliction.
Because the Bodhisattva prioritizes benefiting sentient beings, he not only slays his own thieves but also slays the internal and external thieves of affliction of all sentient beings;
therefore, it is said that he "destroys the thieves of the fetters. As the Sūtra says, those who practice the Bodhisattva’s compassion attain [this].
The knowledge of the modes of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) is that which can benefit sentient beings; thus it is called the Bodhisattva.

If one contemplates sentient beings and enters into emptiness, seeing the single ultimate truth (*ekasatyam*), the principle of this single ultimate truth can benefit the Bodhisattva and can also benefit all sentient beings;
this is true compassion (*maitrī*), which brings benefit, peace, and happiness to sentient beings. The Arhat Ciming of the preceding era attained the Right Path through its cultivation.

Regarding the various illnesses, it is now said that the Bodhisattva’s attainment of clarity allows them to realize the Middle Way, thereby nurturing the roots of goodness in sentient beings and bringing peace to those who have not yet found peace.

As the Sūtra says: "The compassion of the Tathāgata is as follows: if one contemplates sentient beings and enters emptiness to see the Right Path—the Right Path being precisely True Suchness (tathatā) and the Single Ultimate Truth—this is called the compassion of riding upon the path of reality."
The Tathāgata’s compassion consists in attaining the mark of suchness, which is free from the distinct marks of the two extremes.

One who practices the compassion of a Buddha, if they contemplate sentient beings and enter emptiness to see the right path—this is precisely the wisdom of the primary meaning of the Middle Way, called the Buddha-Jewel.
This is what it means to practice the compassion of a Buddha; to awaken oneself and awaken others is called awakening sentient beings. Thus says the Sūtra.

Regarding "natural compassion" (*anābhoga-maitrī*) in speech and action: if one observes sentient beings, enters into emptiness, perceives the right path, and the mind becomes tranquil and extinguished, naturally flowing into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), this is natural compassion encompassing all.
As for "attaining it without cause": the right path does not arise from causes and conditions; therefore, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* speaks of the "ultimate truth" (*paramārtha-satya*).
It is not produced from causes and conditions. A sutra states that those who practice the compassion of awakening (*bodhicitta*) observe sentient beings entering into emptiness and the Middle Way;

this Middle Way is itself unsurpassed awakening (*anuttara-bodhi*). To attain the single flavor (*ekarasa*) is as clarified in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* regarding the single characteristic and single flavor.
These four types all pertain to the Buddha-dharma, as the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* clarifies their existence.
The four dharmas are: the Buddha-dharma, the Tathāgata-dharma, the dharma of self-natured persons, and the dharma of those with all-knowledge.
One practices incomparable loving-kindness because it severs all craving; one practices great compassionate loving-kindness because it guides others by means of the Mahāyāna;

one practices tireless loving-kindness because it contemplates emptiness and non-self; one practices the loving-kindness of Dharma-giving because it is free from regret or stinginess; and one practices the loving-kindness of upholding the precepts because it transforms those who violate them.

One practices the compassion of forbearance because of restraint; one practices the compassion of diligence because of protecting both self and others; one practices the compassion of meditative concentration because of bearing the burden of sentient beings;
one practices the compassion of wisdom because of not relishing [meditative states]; one practices the compassion of skillful means because of knowing the proper time for all things;

one practices the compassion of non-concealment because of manifesting everything; one practices the compassion of the profound mind because of the purity of the straightforward mind; and it is unmixed with anything else.

Because it is practiced, it is the compassion that is non-deceptive; because it is not false or artificial, it is the compassion that brings peace and happiness, causing others to attain the bliss of Buddhahood.
Such is the compassion of a bodhisattva.
The fourteen phrases that follow clarify this compassion through four aspects of its practice. The Sūtra says: "Its practice is incomparable."

Regarding "loving-kindness" (*maitrī*): when one observes sentient beings and enters emptiness to perceive the single ultimate truth (*ekābhisamaya*), all attachment and aversion are severed. As the Sūtra says:

"The great compassion of loving-kindness (*mahākaruṇāmaitrī*) is such that if one observes sentient beings and enters emptiness to perceive the single ultimate truth, one is then able to extract them from the suffering of birth and death at both extremes;
therefore it is called the great compassion of loving-kindness. Loving-kindness can lead sentient beings from the two extremes into the single ultimate truth.
One attains the bliss of the Mahāyāna. A sutra states that for one whose compassion is never weary of action:

if they observe sentient beings and enter into true emptiness (*bhūta-śūnyatā*), seeing the single ultimate truth (*eka-bhūtārtha-satya*), they know that the two extremes of birth and death are ultimately unobtainable; thus, there is no mind of difficulty.

If the mind is fundamentally without weariness, it is because through observation, the birth and death of the two extremes are found to be unobtainable, which is precisely what constitutes the ultimate.

Regarding the *Śūnyatā-nairātmya-sūtra*, which speaks of the "compassion of the gift of Dharma," some masters claim that from this point onward it corresponds to the practice of compassion on the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

This interpretation is not adopted here. If one instead employs right contemplation (*samyag-darśana*) to observe sentient beings and enter into emptiness (*śūnyatā*), thereby seeing the true path, one then possesses all wholesome dharmas;
being neither stingy nor parsimonious is called the "compassion of the gift of Dharma," for one constantly practices relinquishment.
Because of this practice, one transforms others externally, leaving no sentient beings behind or neglected. The Sūtra says:
"The loving-kindness of upholding the precepts consists in observing sentient beings, entering emptiness, and seeing the single ultimate truth;

this is neither upholding nor violating, and is called the loving-kindness of upholding the precepts, which can transform those who fall into the two extremes of breaking the prohibitions. The Sūtra says: "The loving-kindness of patience consists in observing sentient beings and entering..."
The insight into emptiness and the realization of the single ultimate truth constitute patience; not being angry and not failing to endure are called the "patience of compassion.
Not afflicting sentient beings who dwell in the two extremes is precisely protecting both others and oneself.

A sutra states that the "compassion of vigor" means that if one contemplates sentient beings and enters emptiness to see the right path, then neither advancing nor flagging is called the "vigor of compassion," for it is able to bear the burden of sentient beings.

The Sūtra says that practicing the meditative concentration of loving-kindness (*dhyāna-samādhi-maitrī*) means not receiving the flavors of the two extremes—the ultimate and the conventional—within meditative concentration.

The Sūtra says that practicing wisdom (*prajñā*) means that if one contemplates sentient beings and enters emptiness to see the right path, being neither wise nor foolish is called the "wisdom of loving-kindness";
furthermore, it is able to adapt to capacities and respond to conditions, never failing to know the proper time. The Sūtra says that practicing skillful means (*upāya*)...
Regarding "compassion through kindness": if one contemplates sentient beings and enters emptiness to perceive the single True Dharma-realm, one is skilled in knowledge and vision;

attaining non-obstruction is called "expedient compassion. Therefore, one is able to manifest various dignified conducts from within the samādhi of cessation without arising from it, performing the inconceivable transformations of the ten dharma-realms and the three wheels.
As the sutra says, "conduct without hidden compassion" refers to contemplating sentient beings.
One who enters emptiness and perceives the single ultimate truth is precisely the Dharmakāya; this is true, unhidden compassion and the eightfold right mind of non-action.
Because it is not defiled by the afflictions of the internal or external realms, it attains purity. As the Sūtra says:
"Regarding the profound mind of compassion, if one contemplates sentient beings and enters emptiness to perceive the single ultimate truth, this is to enter deeply."
The compassion arising from dependent origination is the practice of skillful means that is not mixed with the two extremes.

As the Sūtra says, "compassion that is non-deceptive in action" means that if one contemplates sentient beings and enters emptiness to see the single ultimate truth, this is compassion free from the deception of dualistic afflictions;
it does not engage in the false dharmas of the two extremes. As the Sūtra says, "compassion that brings peace and happiness" means if one contemplates sentient beings and enters...
When one perceives the single ultimate truth through the view of emptiness, one abides in the peace and bliss of all phenomena;
such compassion is precisely that which enables sentient beings to attain the nirvana of a Buddha. As the sutra says, "The compassion of a bodhisattva is like this.

When a bodhisattva contemplates sentient beings, enters into the realization of emptiness, and attains the Middle Way, they achieve such compassion. How, then, could one ask how to practice compassion?
Mañjuśrī asked again, "What is compassion? He replied, "Whatever meritorious virtues a bodhisattva performs, he shares them all with all sentient beings.
This is the second instance where Mañjuśrī successively asks about the practice of compassion; regarding this passage, there are two parts.
Mañjuśrī asks about the two names of purity, and Vimalakīrti answers with one. 1. Mañjuśrī’s Question:

Having already heard the practice of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), he next asks about contemplating sentient beings, entering into emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and seeing the Middle Way as the practice of compassion (*karuṇā*). 2. Vimalakīrti’s Answer:

If loving-kindness is the bestowing of happiness and compassion is the removal of suffering, then by means of this very "unconditioned" (*anālambana*) loving-kindness, one causes sentient beings to share in it and attain the Middle Way.

The supreme and eternal bliss of the Path is called "loving-kindness" (*maitrī*); to uproot the attachments to the two extremes and to be free from the suffering of the two kinds of birth-and-death within the afflictions of those two extremes is called "compassion" (*karuṇā*).
Question: What is meant by "joy" (muditā)? Answer: To feel joy when there is benefit to others, without regret;

this is the third point. When Mañjuśrī asks how one enters the Middle Way through observing sentient beings within emptiness and gives rise to immeasurable joy, there are two parts to this passage: first, Mañjuśrī’s question, and second, Vimalakīrti’s answer.
The intention behind Mañjuśrī’s question may be understood as before. Regarding Vimalakīrti’s response:

he rejoices that these sentient beings have been able to leave behind the suffering of birth and death within the two extremes and have attained the joy of conditions upon perceiving the Middle Way; this is what is termed "rejoicing" (*prāmodya*).

If one were to rejoice in a joy that leaves something remaining or in a joy that leaves nothing remaining, there would subsequently be regret; however, since one rejoices in ultimate bliss, there is no such regret.
There is no regret.
What is meant by "renunciation"? The answer is: performing meritorious deeds without any expectation of reward.
This is the fourth point. Mañjuśrī asked: How does one enter the vision of emptiness by contemplating all phenomena and realize the single True Reality? How is this accomplished?
Regarding the "immeasurable mind of equanimity," this passage consists of two parts: first, Mañjuśrī’s question; second, Vimalakīrti’s answer.
Mañjuśrī’s question may be understood by analogy with the preceding section. As for Vimalakīrti’s answer:

if one contemplates sentient beings and enters into emptiness, one perceives the nature of the single true reality (*ekābhisamaya-satya*), which—like space—is eternally present whether a Buddha appears or not; its essential characteristics are ever-abiding, and all things possess them.
Regarding the nature of equanimity (*upekṣā*): although it is said to bestow happiness and extract suffering, in reality there is no happiness to be bestowed and no suffering to be extracted.
What, then, is there to rejoice in? Because one relinquishes these three mental states without any expectation, it is called equanimity.
Mañjuśrī asked again, "In the face of the fear of birth and death, upon what should a bodhisattva rely?
Vimalakīrti replied, "Within the fear of birth and death, a bodhisattva should rely on the power of the Tathāgata’s merits."
This is the third section, in which Mañjuśrī thoroughly investigates the source of sentient beings.

Within this section, there are twelve rounds of question and answer, which comprise two main intentions: first, the initial six rounds establish the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa-citta*) based on the four great vows;

second, the subsequent six rounds of question and answer exhaustively investigate the source of sentient beings, thereby correctly establishing the preceding contemplation of sentient beings as entering emptiness and reaching the Middle Way.
Regarding the Way, now, based on the first six rounds of question and answer, the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) are established through the four great vows (*mahāpraṇidhāna*).
If one merely gives rise to the immeasurable mind without the great vows, it is like painting without glue; the colors will inevitably flake off.

Now, regarding these six rounds of question and answer, they constitute four parts: the first two rounds establish loving-kindness (*maitrī*); the next round establishes sympathetic joy (*muditā*); the next...

The second section establishes the relinquishment through two parts. In the first part, the preceding question and answer correctly clarify that when practicing loving-kindness (*maitrī*), if fear arises, one must rely on the power of the Tathāgata’s merits.
In the subsequent question and answer, the merits of the Tathāgata are specifically set forth.
The text of the first question and answer consists of two parts: first, Mañjuśrī’s question; second, Vimalakīrti’s answer. The purport of Mañjuśrī’s question is as follows:
