At that time, as the Buddha was preaching the Dharma in the Āmra Grove, the ground suddenly became vast and magnificent, and the entire assembly turned the color of gold.
Regarding the text of these two chapters, they are divided into two parts: first, from the beginning of this chapter until Ānanda’s exclamation of the unprecedented.
There is the chapter titled "Pure Name" (Jingming), which describes the great assembly entering the garden together as if carried by the palms [of the Buddha], titled "Returning to the Buddha.
Section Two begins from the Buddha’s discourse to Ānanda, starting with "It is so, it is so," and concludes with the "Akṣobhya Chapter.

This is titled "Restoring the Original Thesis to Explain the Causes and Conditions of the Buddha-land. At that time, two chapters are first opened; of these two, the first chapter clarifies the Buddha-land.
This practice further clarifies the fundamental tenets; next, in the "Chapter on Seeing the Buddha Akṣobhya," the manifest fruit is clearly revealed:
first, the entire assembly is carried by a single palm to the Āmra Garden; second, Ānanda, upon smelling the fragrance, immediately raises a question;

regarding this first instance of being carried by a single palm, there are six parts: (1) the manifestation of signs, (2) Ānanda seeing the signs and addressing the Buddha, (3) the Buddha’s explanation for him.
1. Vimalakīrti announces his intention to depart; 2. Mañjuśrī asks about it; 3. He employs supernatural power to carry them to the garden;

4. Those who share the same golden color symbolize that those transformed by Vimalakīrti have already eliminated the bonds of conditions and all enter the land of innate purity and eternal quiescence, which is uniformly of golden light.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, by what causes and conditions has this auspicious omen appeared?
This place has suddenly become vast and magnificent, and the entire assembly has turned the color of gold.

The Buddha told Ānanda, "This is because Vimalakīrti and Mañjuśrī, together with the great multitude, have respectfully surrounded them and intend to come; therefore, they have first manifested this auspicious sign."
"Vimalakīrti, you should go with Mañjuśrī to see the Buddha and all the bodhisattvas to pay them homage and make offerings.
Mañjuśrī said, "Excellent! Let us go; now is precisely the right time."
Vimalakīrti then, by means of his supernatural powers, took the entire great assembly along with the lion-thrones and placed them upon his right palm;

he proceeded to the place where the Buddha was, and having arrived, he set them down on the ground, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him seven times to the right, and stood to one side with palms joined in single-minded devotion.

Within the assembly of the six types of beings, there were three [sections]: first, the Bodhisattvas paid their respects to the Buddha; second, the Buddha comforted them and they offered their respects;
third, the Great Beings (Mahāsattvas) paid their respects.
All those Bodhisattvas immediately vacated their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him seven times, and stood to one side.
Second, all the bodhisattvas proffered their respects;
the great disciples, Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, and others likewise rose from their seats, bowed their heads at the Buddha’s feet,
and stood to one side.
Then Śakra and Brahmā prostrated themselves in reverence.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, having comforted the bodhisattvas according to the Dharma, offered two kinds of consolation, which are threefold:
first, consolation; second, consolation; [and third, consolation]. (Note: The repetition of "consolation" likely reflects a textual redundancy in the source.)
He commanded each of them to return to their seats.
After he had twice commanded them to return to their seats,
they all received his instruction and the assembly was settled in their places.
Third, receiving the command, they returned to their seats.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra: "Do you see the deeds performed by the sovereign spiritual powers of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas?
In the second section, Ānanda’s inquiry, there are two parts: first, the Buddha’s questioning of Śāriputra; second, Ānanda’s doubt regarding the fragrance.
He then asked Śāriputra four questions: first, "Do you see the great being's supernatural power? second, [Śāriputra] answered "No"; third, he asked again, "How is it?
and fourth, [Śāriputra] answered, "It is an inconceivable dharma that cannot be fathomed or measured by a mind that relies on conceptual thought.
The reason the Buddha asked these questions was solely to authenticate what had occurred within the room. Furthermore—
For those within the assembly who harbor doubts that have not yet been resolved, upon hearing the Buddha’s seal, they will no longer have doubt;
because they give rise to the seal of faith, it becomes a sūtra.
"Yes, indeed. I have perceived your intention, World-Honored One. I observe that this is inconceivable and beyond the reach of the mind."
"What is intended here cannot be measured by ordinary calculation.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, the fragrance now perceived has never been experienced since antiquity; what kind of fragrance is this?"

From Ānanda’s questions, there are two parts: first, a question regarding the fragrance; second, a question regarding its disappearance. Within the question concerning the fragrance, there are five sections:
first, Ānanda’s question.
The Buddha told Ānanda, "That is the fragrance from the pores of those bodhisattvas."
The two Buddhas replied.
Thereupon, Śāriputra said to Ānanda, "Fragrance also issues from our pores.
Then the Son of the Śākya (Śāriputra) said, "My body, too, is fragrant."
Ānanda asked where this had come from.
The four Ānandas questioned the conditions for obtaining the fragrance, saying:
"It was from the house of the elder Vimalakīrti, who took the remains of the Buddha’s meal from the Land of Universal Fragrance and ate it."
All the pores of his body were fragrant in this manner.
Śāriputra replied that he had obtained the meal from the land of Vimalakīrti.
Ānanda then asked Vimalakīrti, "How long will this fragrance remain?"
Regarding the inquiry into the digestion [of the food], it is divided into three parts: first, Ānanda’s question; second, Vimalakīrti’s answer; third, Ānanda’s praise.
Within Vimalakīrti’s response, there are two sections: first, the general answer; second, the specific answer. The general answer states: "This fragrance follows the rice."
"If the rice is digested, the fragrance will likewise be digested.
He asked, "How long will it take for this rice to be digested? He replied, "The potency of this rice will last for seven days before it is finally digested."
He asked again how long it would take for it to be digested, to which he replied separately in two parts: first, the matter; second, the principle.
Regarding the matter, he replied that it would be digested in seven days. For example, ordinary food sustains the body and relieves hunger, yet it ceases [its effect] after one day;

this food, however, is digested only after seven days. Furthermore, it is like taking a certain medicine: the medicine sustains the body for seven days until it is digested, and its potency continues to permeate.
The body reaches such a state that the illness is cured; this is the explanation of the matter.
Furthermore, Ānanda, if a śrāvaka who has not yet entered the stage of certainty eats this food, he will enter the stage of certainty and only then be digested.
If one who has already entered the stage of certainty eats this food, he will attain liberation of mind and only then be digested. If...
For those who have not yet resolved upon the Mahāyāna to eat this food, it will only be digested once they have generated that resolve;

for those who have already generated the resolve to eat this food, it will be digested only after they attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); and for those who have already attained the patience of non-arising to eat this food, it will be digested only when they reach the stage of being "born only once more" (*ekajātipratibaddha*).
It is, for example, like a medicine called "Supreme Flavor" (*agrarasa*); whoever consumes it, their body...
Just as this rice is digested only after all poisons have been neutralized, so too is this [food] digested only after all the poisons of affliction (*kleśa*) have been eliminated.
If one’s understanding is not thus, then regarding the turning of the wheel of Dharma spoken of in terms of sound, there are the teachings of the Half and the Full in this land.

If the Two Vehicles are called "half-syllables" (*ardha-akṣara*) and the Mahāyāna is called "full-syllables" (*pūrṇa-akṣara*), then within the half-syllables, the Wheel of Dharma is turned in three ways:
first, showing; second, encouraging; and third, realizing. "Showing" means showing the Four Noble Truths so that by seeing them, one awakens to the truth.

"Encouraging" means encouraging the severance of the delusions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). "Realizing" refers to the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*); therefore, these are called the three turnings. Now, the incense comes to manifest this principle.

It also elucidates the half-syllables (*ardhākṣara*) and the three turnings of the Wheel of Dharma; herein its functional meaning is complete. The first seven days constitute the preparatory stage (*prayoga*);
the five stages of mental abiding (*pañca-vastuka-citta-sthiti*) and the general and specific applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) pertain to the four dharmas of *ūṣmagata* and *mūrdhan*.

What is now said—that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who consume this fragrant food enter the seven stages of preparation (*saptavidha-prayoga*)—means that those who consume the food within these seven stages of preparation subsequently enter the state of correctness (*samyaktva*).

As for the nutriment of status (*sthāna-āhāra*), it is not eliminated upon entering [the path]; it must be seen through the realization of the truths (*satyadarśana*) and the manifestation of the true nature before it can be eliminated. This is called "turning toward demonstration" (*darśanavartana*).

As for those who consume the nutriment of the correct position (*samyagavasthā*), they do not enter the stage of reflection (*cintāmayī bhūmi*); it is not eliminated until they enter the stage of reflection, at which point it is eliminated. This is called "turning toward exhortation" (*preraṇāvartana*).
As for those who consume the nutriment of reflection, they do not attain the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*); it is not eliminated until they attain liberation of mind (*cetovimukti*).

Upon attaining the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), one eliminates this designation; the realization of the four stages clearly demonstrates the meaning of the three turnings and four aspects of the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra-pravartana*), consisting of demonstration, exhortation, and realization.
Furthermore, regarding the meaning of the three turnings of the full-syllable (*paripūrṇākṣara*) Mahāyāna as expressed by this fragrance:

first, it critiques the half-syllables (*ardhākṣara*); those who have not yet entered the stage of correctness (*samyaktva-niyāma*) consume [the food], but upon entering that stage, they are able to digest it, just as with the human body.

"You, sirs, have already severed the bonds of the three realms and realized the liberation of mind; you have attained the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).

What fruit would there be in further advancing this meal? If it does not advance toward a fruit, the meal will not be digested; if it advances toward a fruit, that is precisely the meaning of the Mahāyāna.
You should know that although an Arhat has realized the four fruits and severed the fetters of the three realms, if they have not yet set forth upon the Mahāyāna..."
The mind is still outside the principle of the Mahāyāna and has not yet entered the stage of skillful means; therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says:

"Dwelling and lodging outside the gate, staying in a grass hut—if one can give rise to the Mahāyāna mind, it is called 'the food being digested,' which refers to abiding in the stage of skillful means.
Thus it is said that after seven days the food is digested; from this stage of skillful means, those who eat enter the stage of the true position (*samyaktva-niyāma*).

This is then extinguished; it is just as Śāriputra, within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, entered the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and received a prediction, being named as having "entered the stage of certainty" (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
In terms of the Mahāyāna, this constitutes the three faculties: the faculty of "not yet knowing but desiring to know," the faculty of "knowing," and the faculty of "having known.

If one enters the arousal of the bodhicitta, this is the faculty of "desiring to know"; from the moment of arousing the mind until reaching the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), one proceeds through these stages.

Then, that which was called the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*) is eliminated within the state of non-arising; when one eats the meal until reaching the stage of "one who is to be filled" (*paripūraka*), that which was called the faculty of "having known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*) is eliminated.
This is because the fragrant teaching explains the three untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*);

thus it is said that he turns the wheel of the *pūrṇākṣara* (the perfect syllable), catering to those with the karmic affinity for the Mahāyāna. For example, just as a superior medicine removes [poisons], what is meant by "the poisons of the manifest body are extinguished"?

It merely extinguishes the poison of the segmented birth within the triple world; it further penetrates to extinguish the distinct poisons of the transformational birth of the Shared and Distinct Teachings, as well as the poison of the various portions of ignorance within the realm of true retribution.
This should be explained by using the metaphor of the "poisonous drum" to establish this meaning: whether near or far, all who hear it die, as fully explained previously (etc.).
Ānanda said to the Buddha, “It is unprecedented, World-Honored One! Such fragrant food is able to perform the work of a Buddha.
For the third time, Ānanda marveled at this unprecedented event: “In the past, I only heard the sounds that explained the three turnings of the wheel of Dharma—the Half and the Full Teachings;
now, within this fragrance, the exhortation, the demonstration, and the realization are all fully present. Therefore, I praise it as unprecedented.”
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is, Ānanda! There are some buddha-fields where the work of a buddha is performed by the light of the Buddha;
some where it is performed by bodhisattvas; some where it is performed by persons emanated by the Buddha;
some where it is performed by the Bodhi tree; and some where it is performed by the Buddha’s robes and bedding."
There are those who perform the Buddha-work through food and drink; there are those who perform the Buddha-work through gardens, groves, and palatial towers;
there are those who perform the Buddha-work through the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics; there are those who perform the Buddha-work through the Buddha-body;
and there are those who perform the Buddha-work through empty space. Sentient beings may enter into the practice of discipline by means of these conditions. There are also those who...
There are those who perform the work of a Buddha through metaphors such as dreams, illusions, echoes, reflections in a mirror, the moon in water, and a mirage;
there are those who perform the work of a Buddha through sounds, speech, and written words;

and there are those who perform the work of a Buddha in pure buddha-fields that are silent, wordless, without speaking, without teaching, without cognition, without action, and without conditioned activity.
The second reason is that Ānanda’s inquiry clarifies the restoration of the primary thesis; this section is divided into two parts.

First, from here until the end of this chapter, it clarifies that the Buddha-lands differ and the faculties of beings vary—this is the purpose for the introduction of this chapter and constitutes two of the five layers of meaning.
If the work of transformation is complete, then [the Buddha] will simply hold the great assembly in his palm.

Entering the Āmra grove is its primary meaning. Next, regarding the state in which doubts within the chamber have not yet been resolved, or where further confirmation is required, this refers to the Buddha’s address to Śāriputra:
"Do you see the deeds performed by the Great Being through his sovereign spiritual power?
The internal intent here is precisely to provide definitive confirmation. Furthermore, whatever was spoken within the chamber that involved doubt is all severed [by this]. If it is great...
Although the praise by the noble one (*śrāvaka*) discusses other dharmas separately, they all serve to manifest the Pure Land.
Once the Pure Land has been manifested, the fundamental principle returns once more to that which was taught by the Buddha; this is precisely the meaning of the text here.

Furthermore, while the awakening of sentient beings' faculties depends upon the Buddha's intention, the present text first establishes the fundamental principle: the elder first asked about the fruit, and subsequently asked about the cause. The Buddha—
The first response addresses its fruit; the second response addresses both its cause and fruit. Within the discussion of the cause, there are two parts:
first, clarifying the cause; second, providing an explanation. Within this explanation, the re-establishment of the thesis (*pūrvapakṣa*) also possesses two meanings:

first, the re-establishment of the thesis stating that the fruit is itself the Buddha-land and that the Buddha-activities are not uniform; second, the re-establishment of the thesis clarifying that the cause is itself the various... [text truncated].

The Bodhisattva’s request concerning the Bodhisattva practice is divided into two parts within the section on the fruit: first, the explicit clarification of the fruit; second, the explanation of its meaning.

Within the section on the cause, there are likewise two parts: first, the explicit clarification of the Bodhisattva practice; second, the explanation of the significance of the relationship between the preceding and succeeding sections.

Because they are equal in their essential nature, it should be understood that this is a restatement of the fundamental doctrine to clarify the meaning. Regarding the first point, the clarification of the meaning within the section on the fruit: first, according to what has been taught.
1. Transforming sentient beings while taking up a Buddha-field; 2. Taming sentient beings while taking up a field; 3.
Entering the Buddha-wisdom by means of whatever dharma while taking up a field; 4. Arousing the faculties by means of whatever dharma while taking up a field.

This present section on the fruit also fully possesses these four meanings, establishing the doctrine of the Buddha-land according to our own school; it is identical in substance, though the sequence differs from what preceded.
That they differ later on is simply because words do not emerge repeatedly and speech is not redundant;

thus, they are explained alternately so as to prevent practitioners from fixating on the sequence of before and after. This is like the Dharma Flower Sūtra’s threefold exposition of the Dharma, where the names differ but the meaning is the same;
or like the thirty-six questions and answers in the Nirvāṇa Sūtra, where the meanings correspond while the terminology differs.
The underlying meaning is that although the names differ, there is no cause for suspicion; herein, even though the sequence is not chronological, the names and meanings correspond perfectly.
Although the first explanation above corresponds to the fourth [below] and the fourth explanation above corresponds to the first [below], their names differ yet their meaning is one and the same.
The full enumeration is present in the text; herein, the explanation of the arising of the bodhisattva-faculties consists of thirteen phrases, clarifying [this point].
The faculties that arise in the various Buddha-lands differ; yet they all function by means of the six objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) to give rise to the six faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*).

If one follows the *Abhidharma*, matter (*rūpa*) is defined as having physical obstruction and cannot be extended to other objects; thus, the eye sees only form and cannot simultaneously employ other functions.
However, the meaning clarified in the Mahāyāna differs from this: within the relationship between the faculties and their objects, they are capable of mutual interchangeability.
All phenomena are universally penetrating, just as when the eye confronts the colors of paper and ink;

these colors can express all phenomena—whether empty, provisional, or the Middle Way—and among all mundane and supramundane phenomena, there is not one that does not possess this quality, being nothing more than a single stroke of ink.
Because its virtue of containment is universally penetrating and unobstructed, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "All..."
The dharma-tendency toward form is the tendency that does not exceed it, and so on until the dharma-tendency toward all dharmas is the tendency that does not exceed them.

Just as there is equality regarding food, there is also equality regarding dharmas; one should know that because the faculties and objects encompass all dharmas, these faculties and objects give rise to the faculties of this Bodhisattva.
Now, when taking a single object (*viṣaya*) as the subject of discourse, this is designated according to its preeminence.

Just as the nose faculty is most acute for entering the Path and thus employs the object of fragrance to arouse it, and the body faculty is acute and thus employs the touch of light to stimulate it, so too here the ear faculty is acute and employs the object of sound to arouse it.

It is not necessarily the case that there are only objects of sound and no other five objects; just as in this world the Buddha’s work is performed through sound, he likewise emits light and so forth.

Incense clouds, incense canopies, robes, and so forth constitute Buddha-activities; these are considered primary from the perspective of their excellence, while others are judged as secondary Buddha-activities.
This same principle applies even if one were to raise a single speck of dust in other lands.
Regarding light as a Buddha-activity: when light is emitted and touches the body, it fully explains all dharmas, such that through the mere touch, one attains liberation.
Not only do other lands take light as the Buddha-work; this land also transforms people through radiance.
As in all Mahāyāna sūtras, they emit light to startle and move all beings; however, this is not the primary intent for entering the Path in this land.

Here, the Buddha-work primarily functions through the correct principle. One should know that within the radiance, all dharmas are fully present, just as stated in the *Saṃghabhedavastu* (or *Sahagata-sūtra*).
The analysis is as follows: In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (Dapin), it is said that when sentient beings encounter the emitted light, they immediately give rise to the bodhicitta;
likewise, in the *Avataṃsaka*, the "Light of Non-Attachment" is named because it extinguishes and eliminates all obscurations of greed and desire.

In all such cases, light is taken as the primary means, and it is fully endowed with all dharmas. However, within the Hīnayāna, it is sometimes said that the light must reach and touch [the object], whereas in the Mahāyāna, this is not considered necessary.

In deliberation and analysis, it is understood that employing transformed beings (*nirmāṇapuruṣa*) to perform the Buddha-work is as follows: for instance, the Buddha Susaṃbhava left behind a transformed Buddha to deliver sentient beings;

or there are Buddhas who, in order to perform beneficial deeds for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, employ transformed beings, transformed bodhisattvas, and so forth, to arouse the faculties of the masses.
Furthermore, it is said that when the Prajñāpāramitā transforms bodhisattvas, the Prajñā itself is the transformation.
In this realm, transformation is the Buddha-work. Regarding the Bodhisattva as the Buddha-work:

there are some Buddha-lands where Bodhisattvas alone are employed as retinues to benefit others and lead the multitudes, while the Buddha serves merely as the presiding lord. This same principle applies here as well;
for example, when it is said that the four great Bodhisattvas of the *Avataṃsaka* manifest the merits of the various stages (*bhūmi*), the Buddha merely acts as [the presiding lord].

Lord, you should know that bodhisattvas also perform the work of a Buddha. Since the speech of these bodhisattvas is universal, it cannot be definitively categorized as belonging solely to the transformation-body;
therefore, it pertains to the sense faculties and their objects. The Bodhi tree performs the work of a Buddha:
when the Buddha attained the Way beneath it, he adorned this tree so that it emitted light and preached the Dharma to mature sentient beings, providing them with shade.
To perform Buddha-work through the coolness [of the grove] is to activate the faculty of the body (*kāyendriya*) by specifically practicing the contemplation of the tree;

likewise, to walk back and forth (*caṅkrama*) is to activate the faculty of the eye (*cakṣurindriya*). Just as here [in this world], one attains the Way while sitting under the Bodhi tree, so too in the sutras there may be instances where the Bodhi tree is employed to perform Buddha-work;
this is precisely what is meant by [the passage] "the gardens, groves, terraces, and pavilions" (and so forth). This is also...
When one observes the two meanings of the "obscured aggregate" (āvṛta-skandha), the marks and signs (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana) cannot be definitively categorized as belonging to either.

These marks and signs arise from the dust of form (rūpa-rasa) to activate the eye-faculty; yet, while they are seen, the marks and signs themselves possess that which is signified, enabling sentient beings to attain awakening and understanding.

This is like when the Prajñāpāramitā is being taught here: sometimes the exalted, extraordinary body (vairocana-kāya) appears, majestic and towering, and sometimes the ordinary body (sādhāraṇa-kāya) appears, appearing to be severed.
One should know that doubt also performs the Buddha-work through its marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*). As for space, it merely manifests the characteristic of emptiness;
this characteristic of emptiness can express all dharmas. As stated in the "Gate of Non-duality": "The four kinds of emptiness and the elements of space constitute duality.
If one realizes that the four kinds of emptiness are not different from the elements of space, one enters the gate of non-duality. If one perceives this space as...
When emptiness is empty, there is no seeing; where there is seeing, it is not emptiness. It is utterly open and without obstruction.

By awakening to the fact that all phenomena function solely as the work of the Buddha, it is like when Ānanda wished to see the Buddha’s abdomen: the Buddha told him to look at his own head, and he saw that the interior of the abdomen was empty and possessed nothing.
Just as when the Gaganagañja Bodhisattva came to this realm, all phenomena were seen to be empty. This is so.
At times, they also employ emptiness as a Buddha-work, using the ten metaphors such as dreams and illusions to perform Buddha-works, constantly preaching this Dharma.
This Dharma has many points of exposition; some may awaken to the emptiness of dreams and illusions, while others may even awaken to the fact that dreams and illusions are neither empty nor existent.
This is consistent with the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), which applies the ten metaphors to both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna; however, the Hīnayāna takes only the emptiness of dreams and illusions.

If a Bodhisattva were to encounter a master of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* who regards the ten similes as signs of deception, this would mean they have attained the emptiness (*śūnyatā*) of the Hīnayāna and have forever lost the existence (*bhāva*) of the Mahāyāna.

If one says that since these are signs of deception, Prajñāpāramitā takes them as its "Mother," then if the Mother is deceptive, the Son must also be unreal. Therefore, one should know that the meaning of "dreams and illusions" applies universally.
If one were to fixate rigidly [on this], one would lose the meaning of the Mahāyāna.

If it is said that there are buddha-fields and that buddha-activities are performed through dreams and illusions, such buddha-fields are deceptive appearances and unreal sounds; they arise as the faculty of hearing within this very realm.
As for "tranquility" (*śānti*), it demonstrates the wheel of mind (*citta-cakra*): although there is no verbal expression, it does not preclude the presence of the bliss of tranquility.
If it were not a matter of joy, how could one speak of performing the Buddha-work? If the Buddha did not reveal the mind, the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) would remain unknown;
yet if he were to reveal the mind, even insects would be able to know it. One should understand that this is the meaning of revealing the mind:
here too, employing "no speech" and "no revelation" constitutes the Buddha-work. As in the case of Vimalakīrti’s silence, Mañjuśrī recounted the Buddha’s words, or as the Buddha sometimes [acted].
Śāriputra remained silent, and [the Buddha] remained silent as well. To explain extensively would be immeasurable; briefly indicated, there are thirteen kinds of lands.
This concludes the re-establishment of the thesis clarifying the Buddha-lands, which was the fourth section on the meaning of "arousing the roots of bodhisattvas."
Thus, Ānanda, in all the majestic deportment, movements, and actions of the Buddhas, there is nothing that is not the work of a Buddha.

Although Ānanda has these four māras and eighty-four thousand gateways of affliction through which sentient beings become exhausted, the Buddhas perform the work of a Buddha by means of these very things; this is called entering the dharma-gate of all Buddhas.

The second section, from "In this way, Ānanda, the majestic deportment and activities of all Buddhas" to "this is the Buddha-work," corresponds to the third [section] above which clarifies the meaning of entering the Buddha-wisdom;
this constitutes two parts: first, clarifying the gate of goodness, and second, clarifying the gate of evil.
From "the deportment of advancing and halting" onwards, the gate of goodness is clarified, which is the meaning of the Pure Land, and it clarifies the four Māras.

The departure from defilement is the illumination; the gate of evil is the land of impurity. The meaning of the preceding text is that, according to the capacities of sentient beings, one enters the Buddha-wisdom by means of whichever land [is appropriate].
"Buddha-wisdom" is what the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* calls the "Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Herein it is clarified that there are gates for entering the Buddha-dharma.
The Buddhas manifest lands of differing purity and impurity in order to enable sentient beings to attain entry into Buddha-wisdom. If...

Sentient beings who should perceive the majestic deportment and dignified composure of the sublime Dharma, and who are worthy of entering through the manifestation of the supreme and extraordinary marks of radiance, shall have these manifested to them.
For those who should enter by way of the unwholesome, [the Buddha] manifests as the four evil afflictions to enable their entry.
As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "A woman demonstrates the dharma-gate of lust; if an ordinary person were to fall for this, they would be ruined."

As soon as Sudhana touched [the image], he immediately awakened to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Dharma-gates; this demonstrates how one enters the Buddha’s wisdom through the demon of desire (*kāma-māra*).
Just as Sudhana fulfilled the King’s practice of the "Illusory Dharma-gate" (*māyā-dharmaparyāya*), he slew immeasurable people out of rage and thereby attained awakening;
this is entering through the demon of hatred (*dveṣa-māra*). It is like seeing a Brahmin who threw himself from a cliff...
When the fire is released from the body and departs, the Buddha-dharma manifests before one; this is precisely the use of the delusion-demon to enter the Buddha-wisdom.
From these three poisons arise the four equal parts, giving birth to the eighty-four thousand afflictions and latent tendencies.
Once sentient beings have entered the Buddha-wisdom, because the two gates of good and evil enter wisdom differently, the Buddhas manifest the two lands of defilement and purity.
Although there is a distinction between defilement and purity, the gateway for entry is of one kind; this concludes the third section: the meaning of entering the Buddha’s wisdom.
When a bodhisattva enters this gateway, if they see all pure and beautiful buddha-fields, they do not feel joy, nor do they become greedy or conceited;
if they see all impure buddha-fields, they do not feel sorrow, nor are they hindered or discouraged. Rather, in regard to...
All Buddhas give rise to a pure mind of joy and reverence such as has never been before.
Third, if one enters this gate, seeing purity does not bring joy and seeing defilement does not bring sorrow; this explains the second [point] above:
that while sentient beings are tamed and a Buddha-land is attained, all Buddhas act to subdue those who are entirely stubborn and fierce.
When people manifest both defilement and purity, how can one perceive this purity and impurity as to give rise to thoughts of superiority and inferiority, or sorrow and joy?
If the mind experiences sorrow or joy, it is not said to be "tamed"; being without sorrow and without joy is the mark of taming.
It is like a skilled physician who, in order to cure a disease, prescribes two medicines—one sweet and one bitter; though the medicines differ, the curing of the disease is no different. If...
Seeing this skilled physician administer two kinds of medicine for the sake of curing a disease, one does not give rise to feelings of aversion or attachment toward the physician;
the Buddha is likewise, acting solely to discipline sentient beings, without perceiving purity or defilement—this is what is meant by "doubt."
The merits of all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are equal; yet, for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings, they manifest different Buddha-lands.

The fourth section, beginning from "The equality of all Buddhas," explains the first point—that all Buddhas take up Buddha-lands for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings—clarifying herein that the merits of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions are equal and constitute a single body.
The power of wisdom and fearlessness are likewise equal. Since they are equal, why is it that one Buddha-land is pure while another Buddha-land is defiled?
If purity and defilement differ, how can they be called equal?

It is only for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings that compassion and pity arise within this equality, manifesting as both equal and unequal; it is through the transformation of sentient beings that the differences between purity and defilement come to exist.

The ear [of the listener] immediately confirms and establishes that the aforementioned was for the purpose of teaching and transforming sentient beings. Regarding the fourfold meaning of the lands: first, there is no deviation;

second, one realizes and returns to the fundamental source; third, the proclamation and exposition; and fourth, the summary of the beginning and end. These establish the preceding and succeeding stages, clarifying the meaning of purifying the Buddha-lands.
"Ānanda, you see that while the lands of the various Buddha-fields differ in their characteristics, space itself does not differ.

Second, departing from the various Buddha-fields [to explain this] serves to clarify the meaning of the four types of defilement and purity, thereby revealing the land of the tranquil light of inherent purity that accords with conditions; this is divided into four parts, the first of which concerns space."

1. A brief explanation of the connection between the vows and the liberation; 2. A brief clarification of body and wisdom; 3. An extensive clarification of body and wisdom; 4. An analysis based on the three titles.
Now, regarding the connection and explanation through the analogy of space, this is contrasted with the aforementioned Buddha-land to clarify the meaning of the fruit.

It is like a person who wishes to construct a palace in space: it can never be completed. Yet, by relying upon the earth, it is successfully established. Even though it relies upon the earth, if there were no...

Space itself does not constitute this [attainment]. This means that if one proceeds directly to the principle of the true emptiness of the *dharmatā*, there are no myriad practices, merits, or *pāramitās* to adorn the *dharmakāya*.
However, if one relies on conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), there is the accomplishment of sentient beings and the purification of Buddha-lands;
yet, even though these involve myriad practices and merits, they ultimately pertain to the *dharmatā*.
If there were nothing accomplished through emptiness, and if phenomena lacked the nature of emptiness, then whatever actions were performed could not be fulfilled.

Now, this commentary on the verse clarifies that the lands manifested according to conditions—whether the ground consists of sand and gravel or the seven treasures—are for the purpose of transforming sentient beings, desiring to subdue them and lead them into the Buddha-wisdom, thereby giving rise to the roots of a bodhisattva. Thus it is said: "Whether the ground be of sand and gravel or of the seven treasures."

From the lands of skillful means (*upāya*) and the remaining self-nature (*śeṣa-svabhāva*), through the lands of true recompense (*vipāka*) and the various [pure lands], there are numerous distinctions and differences according to sentient beings;

yet in the land of the perfectly pure nature (*prakṛti-viśuddha-kṣetra*), which is the dwelling place of ultimate wisdom, there are no matters of defilement or purity, high or low, superior or inferior.
Therefore, it cites empty space as an analogy for its lack of plurality, even though it is empty.
Emptiness is without plurality, yet it pervades all plural lands; those plural lands cannot be separated from emptiness that is without plurality.
Ultimately, there is no emptiness without plurality that exists apart from plurality.
Now, although the four kinds of lands according to conditions differ in being defiled or pure, they are all defined in relation to the land of eternal, quiescent light.
There is also the Land of Constant Quiescence and Light that manifests for others in accordance with conditions, which likewise pervades all lands of skillful means;

for apart from the lands of skillful means, there is no separate land of constant quiescence and light. Thus the Sūtra says: "The dwelling place of that Buddha is named Constant Quiescence and Light, pervading all places and existing nowhere not present.
It is what ultimate wisdom contemplates; it contemplates all dharmas, for there is nothing that is not the Dharma-nature."
To know the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is called "eternal quiescence. A sutra states: "The absence of ignorance is called ultimate emptiness;
ultimate emptiness is precisely the nature of ignorance. Because this nature is luminous, it is called "quiescent light" (*śānta-prabhā*).
Being eternally abiding and unchanging, it is termed "constant" (*nitya*). Therefore, like space, it is without differentiation; this explains the establishment of the defiled and pure lands.
Thus, while the physical bodies (*rūpakāya*) of the various Buddhas may differ in size, their unimpeded wisdom (*anāvaraṇajñāna*) does not differ.

Second, the text briefly cites the bodies and wisdom of the Buddhas to explain and establish the two kinds of lands: for instance, Śākyamuni’s body is sixteen feet tall, while Maitreya’s is a thousand or even ten thousand *chi* (cubits).
This refers to the differences in the *nirmāṇakāya* (response-body) as it manifests to transform sentient beings according to their varying capacities.
If there is such a difference in duration, then what further distinction is there between the wisdom and abandonment attained by Śākyamuni Buddha of the Tripiṭaka—
who has acquired the fivefold Dharma-body and unimpeded wisdom— and the unimpeded wisdom attained by Maitreya, in whom both active and latent afflictions have been eliminated?
Furthermore, what difference is there between the single body, single wisdom, power, and fearlessness of all Buddhas of the ten directions?

The extraordinary, quiescent dharma-nature has no distinction here; it is merely that the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) manifests images of varying lengths according to circumstances, and because these differ in quality—superior or inferior—there appear differences such as being sixteen feet tall or a thousand feet tall, or being defiled or pure.
Therefore, it is said that by means of body and wisdom, the lands of defilement and purity are explained and established.
Ānanda, the physical bodies, majestic marks, lineage, precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, the knowledge and vision of liberation,
the powers, the fearlessnesses, the unique qualities, great kindness, great compassion, deportment, conduct, as well as their lifespans,
preaching of the Dharma, teaching and transforming, the maturing of sentient beings, the purification of Buddha-lands, and the possession of all Buddha-dharmas of all Buddhas are entirely equal.
Third, the extensive explanation of the body and wisdom: if one explains the meaning by way of the concise and the extensive, the former belongs to the concise and the latter to the extensive;
if one explains the meaning by way of the conceivable and the inconceivable, the concise belongs to the conceivable.

The two truths and the three baskets clarify the Buddha’s unimpeded wisdom from the perspective of the extensive explanation of body and wisdom as belonging to the inconceivable two truths; it is not only...

The inconceivable ultimate truth differs from the conceivable [truth] within the Three Baskets; the inconceivable conventional also differs from the various conventionalities within the Three Baskets.
The distinctions between the characteristics of bodies are likewise so. Why is this?
If one takes the bodies of parents from whom one is to be born within the Three Baskets and distinguishes their various [aspects], and then takes the five aspects of the ultimate truth—
When distinguishing the Dharma-body, there is no plurality; ultimate wisdom dwells within the realm of the eternally quiescent Dharma-nature, where no plurality exists.
However, when clarifying the gate of the Form-body, the long, majestic, and preeminent bodies within the Lotus Treasury World manifest major and minor marks;
these supreme manifestations appear as pluralities, yet they are taken up by that which dwells in ultimate wisdom. Constantly.
One should know that the realm of the quiescent *dharmakāya* is without plurality, for the ultimate (*paramārtha*) and the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) are eternally distinct.
As for the "form and so forth" of the Buddhas of the ten directions: first, the bodies of the *nirmāṇakāya*, their lands, and their activities of transformation are all equal;
the sublime form of the *dharmakāya* likewise abides equally in this state. Regarding "wisdom and so forth," these refer to the three baskets (*tripiṭaka*) of the *nirmāṇakāya*.

The Buddha’s ten powers, fearlessnesses, and great compassion are equal, and this extends even to the Dharma-body; the ten powers and fearlessnesses of the supreme Nirmāṇakāya (Emanation Body) are likewise no different.
Regarding the equality of lineage: the Nirmāṇakāya is born into noble lineages such as the Kṣatriya or Brāhmaṇa, and these matters are identical.

As for the lineage of the Dharmakāya, it consists of the lineage of the stage of habituation (*śaikṣa*), the lineage of the noble ones (*ārya*), and so forth, up to the Dharma-nature of wondrous enlightenment.

Furthermore, they are all equally identical in their transformation of sentient beings through the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*). This supreme response-body for transforming sentient beings is also a transformation within the realm of true retribution (*vipākaphala*).
Since these various aspects are equal, the pure and impure environments (*bhājanaloka*) upon which they rely are likewise equal.
How could it be that only the Buddhas possess pure lands? Śākyamuni also possesses a pure land named "Invincible" (*Anabhibhūta*), which exists therein.
In the West, why is it that Śākyamuni alone transforms beings in the Sahā world and enters nirvāṇa?

It is because all Buddhas likewise manifest and turn the wheel of Dharma within this realm; thus we know that all Buddhas possess various lands according to conditions, as well as the wisdom of eternal quiescence and non-obstruction.
Therefore, it is said that by extensively explaining the body and wisdom, the nature of defilement and purity is established.
The land and this body-and-wisdom are mutually interdependent and can explain one another.

If, for the sake of sentient beings, one takes up a land, there arises a distinction between purity and defilement; thus, the excellence or inferiority of the *niśraya-vipāka* (the environment) is unequal.
Since the *niśraya-vipāka* is unequal, the *pratisthā-vipāka* (the physical bodies and wisdom experienced by sentient beings) is likewise unequal. This is—
Because the wisdom of the body explains the meaning of the land, this constitutes an explanation of the land by means of the wisdom of the body;
based on this, it reveals both the pure and the impure (and so forth).
For this reason, he is named Samyaksaṃbuddha, named Tathāgata, and named Buddha.
Fourth, regarding the explanation of the two country names based on these three titles, there are two parts: first, the formal explanation of the three titles;
second, the detailed analysis of their meanings, which is difficult to receive. First, as for the formal explanation: *Samyaksaṃbuddha* means "Perfectly and Universally Enlightened. If it is...

The Tripiṭaka clarifies *samyak-saṃbuddha*. "Right" (*samyak*) is so named in contrast to the sixty-two heterodox views; it refers to observing the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) while not observing the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Although it is called "omniscience" (*saṃbuddha*), from the perspective of the Mahāyāna, it is ultimately termed "partial" and is not the ultimate rightness.

"Knowing" (*jña*) means that one thoroughly understands both the ultimate and the conventional, being clearly enlightened regarding them all. As the *Śāstra* (Treatise) clearly explains, this knowledge pertains to the numerical dharmas (*saṃkhyeya-dharma*).

Whether non-enumerated phenomena (*asaṃkhyeya-dharma*) are permanent or impermanent, one knows and fully understands them; that non-enumerated phenomenon is itself the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and its wisdom is without differentiation.
To fully understand enumerated phenomena (*saṃkhyeya-dharma*) is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*);

it involves deeply discerning the faculties and conditions, employing skillful means according to those conditions, and thus having various distinctions. It is based on this that they are called "fully understanding. One who is self-awakened awakens to the ultimate.
To awaken others means to awaken to the conventional; because one awakens to the conventional, it is the various and diverse skillful means that accord with conditions.
To awaken to the ultimate truth is the intrinsically pure, unimpeded wisdom, which is without diversity.

Regarding the inconceivable Middle Way: the universal illumination of the three truths is called "omniscience" (*sarvajñā*); because one knows the three truths, it is called "knowledge. However, within the Middle Way itself, it is neither a numerical category nor...

That which is neither numerical nor eternal, and neither non-eternal—profoundly awakening to this principle is called unimpeded wisdom (*anāvaraṇa-prajñā*). It simultaneously illuminates the two truths:

within the conventional truth, it distinguishes differences, recognizes ailments, and identifies remedies; according to conditions, it employs skillful means, as impurity and purity differ, and thus there are various methods for taming sentient beings.

Regarding the self-awakening and awakening of others within both the ultimate and conventional truths, the examples are as previously stated (*etc.*). Therefore, it is called "Right and Universal" (*samyak-saṃbuddha*).
"Knowledge" refers to the Tathāgata, who understands according to the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) and explains according to the characteristics of phenomena.

If, within the Three Baskets (*tripiṭaka*), one clarifies understanding according to the characteristics of phenomena, this is precisely to be in accord with the principle of True Suchness (*tathatā*);

it is also called knowing conventional principles, and thus such knowledge is termed "understanding according to the characteristics of phenomena. Therefore, this is unimpeded wisdom (*pratisaṃvid-jñāna*), which is without differentiation and should be so regarded.
What dharmas are taught? What dharmas are disciplined? What dharmas enter the Buddha-wisdom? What dharmas give rise to the differences in the awakening of faculties and responses?
Thus, although various explanations are given, they are all real and not false;

therefore, it is said that he teaches according to the characteristics of phenomena, and is thus called the Tathāgata. This explains the meaning of defilement and purity within the inconceivable. As in... [the inconceivable].
This Buddha is named "Awakened" (Buddha) and also named "Knower," as explained previously.
Ānanda, if I were to explain the meaning of these three phrases in detail, you would not be able to receive it all even with a lifespan of an eon.

Regarding the second section, the explanation of the meaning of the three phrases, there are five parts. First, it clarifies that the meaning of the three phrases is so vast that Ānanda was unable to retain it;
even if all sentient beings filling the trichiliocosm were like Ānanda, foremost in erudition.
Ānanda, even if these people were to possess the lifespan of an eon and attain the *dhāraṇī* of mindfulness, they would still be unable to receive such an immeasurable,
inconceivable wisdom and eloquence as that of the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all the Buddhas.
Second, it is explained that even if there were many Ānandas, they would still be unable to uphold [this teaching].
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "From this day forward, I dare not claim for myself the title of 'one of great learning'."
The three knowledges (vidyās) caused Ānanda to feel remorse and reproach himself.
The Buddha told Ānanda, "Do not give rise to thoughts of retreat. Why is this?
I have said that among the śrāvakas, you are the most learned; I did not say this regarding bodhisattvas."
The Buddha of the Fourth Illumination consoled him, saying:
"Cease, Ānanda! One who possesses wisdom should not attempt to limit the measure of bodhisattvas.
While all the depths of the oceans may still be measured, the bodhisattva’s meditative concentration, wisdom, dhāraṇīs, eloquence, and all their merits cannot."
"Furthermore, Ānanda, set aside for a moment the conduct of bodhisattvas;

the supernatural power manifested by Vimalakīrti in a single instant is something that all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas could not accomplish even by exerting their full transformative powers throughout hundreds of thousands of kalpas."
The five explanations regarding the meaning of "unable to sustain" are as stated in the text.
At that time, the bodhisattvas who had come from the World of Universal Fragrance joined their palms and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, when we first saw this land, we conceived thoughts of inferiority; we now repent and reproach ourselves, and shall abandon such a mind."
Second, it clarifies that the Bodhisattva’s request for the practice of a Bodhisattva is precisely a reaffirmation of the preceding point regarding the causes of a Buddha-land;

this consists of three parts: first, the request for the Dharma; second, the Buddha’s exposition; and third, the praise and return to one's original state. Within the request, there are three further sections, the first of which is the confession and repentance.
Why is this? Because the skillful means of the Buddhas are inconceivable; for the sake of delivering sentient beings, they manifest different Buddha-lands according to what is appropriate for them.
Second, the comprehension and understanding.
"So be it, World-Honored One; we pray that you grant us a small portion of the Dharma so that we may return to that land and there mindfully remember the Tathāgata.

They requested the Dharma three times. As for this request for the Dharma: it clarifies that the Land of Accumulated Fragrance uses the two dharmas of fragrance and flavor to come here and deliver sentient beings.
Now, they wish to take the dharmas of this land back to that land to perform Buddha-work; this is why they requested the Dharma. That...
Although the Bodhisattvas are recipients of the Mahāyāna who have attained awakening to the Middle Way, they have not yet reached a profound depth in the simultaneous illumination of the two truths;
nor have they fully understood the cessation and suppression of the conventional within the Lesser Vehicle.

For this reason, the Tathāgata explains for them the meaning of simultaneous illumination, so that they may be unimpeded in their transformation and guidance of others—just as a kingdom is fully provided with both civil and military officials.
According to their respective states of stillness or agitation, there is the arising or ceasing of activity: in an age without thieves, the vessels [of the world] are dull and people are weak;
in times of invasion, the weapons are sharp and the generals are brave. Now it is clear that the Buddha-dharma of the ten directions possesses the meaning of the three truths;
however, because the Sahā world has many difficulties, the provisional transformation is emphasized to clarify that the various bodhisattvas are fully matured in the dual illumination.
Because the roots of goodness in the soil are profound and thick, those with true wisdom attain penetration swiftly along the Middle Way, whereas those on the provisional path harbor doubts;
since a Bodhisattva who wishes to travel through the ten directions must practice the three truths universally, they must make this request.
The Buddha told the bodhisattvas: "You should study the dharma-gate of liberation known as 'the Exhaustible and the Inexhaustible.

The Buddha’s initial answer regarding the meaning of causes has two aspects: first, horizontal clarification; second, vertical clarification. Within this, there are also two parts: a general explanation and a specific explanation.
Although the terminology differs from the preceding text, the meaning is the same. Now, based on the Buddha’s response, it shall be divided into three sections."
First, a general statement exhorting study; second, the detailed explanation; third, the conclusion. What is meant by "exhaustion"?
It refers to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). What is meant by "non-exhaustion"? It refers to unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
As for a bodhisattva, they do not exhaust the conditioned, nor do they abide in the unconditioned.
The commentary further divides this into two parts: first, a brief explanation; second, a detailed and specific explanation.
What is meant by "not exhausting the conditioned"?
Within the detailed explanation, there are three sections: first, clarifying not exhausting the conditioned; second, clarifying not abiding in the unconditioned; and third...

The double explanation of these two types, concerning the inexhaustibility within conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), consists of three parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation; and third, the conclusion. That is to say:
not being separated from great loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and not abandoning great compassion (*karuṇā*); deeply generating the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*) without ever forgetting it;

never becoming weary in teaching and transforming sentient beings; constantly and consistently practicing the four methods of attraction (*saṃgraha-vastu*); and protecting and upholding the true Dharma.
Cherishing their lives while planting all roots of goodness without weariness, their resolve is always to abide securely in skillful means and dedication;
they seek the Dharma without slackening and preach it without stinginess. Diligently making offerings to all Buddhas, they enter the cycle of birth and death without fear;

regarding all honors and insults, their minds are free from sorrow or joy. They do not disparage those who have not yet studied, but honor those who study as if they were Buddhas, and cause those fallen into afflictions to...
One should arouse right mindfulness regarding the joy of seclusion without regarding it as precious; one should not be attached to one’s own pleasure but rejoice in the pleasure of others.
One should regard all meditative absoritions (*dhyāna*) as if they were hells, and the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) as if it were a pleasure garden.

One should regard those who come seeking [help] as virtuous teachers, and the relinquishing of all possessions as being endowed with omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). One should regard those who violate the precepts as persons to be rescued and protected.
One should regard the various *pāramitās* as one's parents; the dharmas of the path-factors (*mārgāṅga*) as one's kinsmen; the cultivation of roots of goodness as being without limit;
the adornment of all pure lands as the means to accomplish one’s own Buddha-field; the practice of boundless giving as the fulfillment of the primary and secondary marks;
the elimination of all evil as the purification of body, speech, and mind; and the passage through countless kalpas of birth and death as being undertaken with resolve.

Having heard of the Buddha’s immeasurable virtues, he applied himself with tireless resolve; using the sword of wisdom, he shattered the thieves of affliction and emerged from the aggregates and realms.
Bearing the burden of sentient beings, he brought them forever to liberation. With great vigor, he subdued the armies of Māra, constantly seeking the wisdom of the true mark of non-conceptuality.
He practiced few desires and contentment, yet did not abandon worldly dharmas, nor did he violate his dignified deportment.

Yet they are able to manifest supernatural powers and wisdom in accordance with worldly conventions to guide sentient beings, enabling them to attain mindfulness and dhāraṇī so that what they have heard is never forgotten;
they skillfully discern the faculties of others, sever the doubts of sentient beings, and expound the Dharma without impediment through the eloquence of joyful speech.

They purify the ten paths of wholesome action to receive the blessings of humans and devas, cultivate the four immeasurables to open the path to the Brahma-world, and exhort others to preach the Dharma while rejoicing in and praising their goodness.

They attain the Buddha’s voice; their body, speech, and mind become virtuous; they master the Buddha’s majestic deportment; they cultivate wholesome dharmas deeply; their practice becomes increasingly superior;
through the teaching of the Mahāyāna, they establish the community of Bodhisattvas; their minds are free from negligence, and they do not lose any of their manifold virtues.
In this commentary, forty sentences are generally traversed to clarify that one does not exhaust the conditioned;

now, to speak of "exhausting the inexhaustible" means not exhausting the conventional while extensively practicing the ten thousand practices, neither abiding in the unconditioned nor being identical to the annihilation of ashes, but rather illuminating both the true and the conventional simultaneously, traveling through both contemplation and the path together, and integrating the pure and the defiled with mastery over the provisional and the real. The conventional truth is birth and death.

Because conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are dharmas subject to exhaustion, they are called the "Truth of Exhaustion" (*kṣaya-satya*). Nirvāṇa is an unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and empty dharma, and is thus called "inexhaustible.
Therefore, the gate of "exhaustion and inexhaustibility" is the means by which sentient beings should attain liberation.
By means of this very dharma, they give rise to the roots of a bodhisattva and enter the wisdom of the Buddha. This also serves to explain and establish what was clarified within the chamber.
This illness is neither real nor existent; if one enters this gate, one can then travel simultaneously through both the pure and the defiled, attaining mastery over the contemplation of the Path.

Thus, one will not be rebuked by the One of Pure Name (Vimalakīrti). [A private question: If the Bodhisattvas from the Fragrant Land have only just requested this Dharma, how can they already travel through this Sahā world?
[A private answer: It is because they use skillful means (*upāya*) to lead toward the ultimate reality (*bhūtārtha*) that such a thing occurs.
Question: It is said that because one follows expedient means with reality, one is able to roam the Sahā world (and so forth).

In the text, the comparison of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) to a prison and birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) to a garden is borrowed from the analogy of a son in distress while his father remains at home: although he possesses the five desires, he constantly experiences suffering as if undergoing torment;
only when he is rescued from the distress does his mind find joy (and so forth).
Practicing such dharmas is called a bodhisattva’s non-exhaustion of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
What is meant by a bodhisattva not dwelling in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)?
Regarding the second point, "not dwelling in the unconditioned," there are also three parts: first, the general indication; second, the detailed explanation; and third, the conclusion.

This means that while practicing and studying emptiness (*śūnyatā*), one does not take emptiness as a basis for realization; while practicing and studying signlessness (*animitta*) and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), one does not take signlessness and wishlessness as bases for realization;

while practicing and studying non-arising (*anutpāda*), one does not take non-arising as a basis for realization. One contemplates impermanence (*anitya*) without becoming weary of the roots of goodness;
one contemplates the suffering of the world (*loka-duḥkha*) without loathing birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*); and one contemplates selflessness (*anātman*) without growing weary of instructing others.
Contemplating quiescence, yet not remaining in eternal quiescence; contemplating detachment, yet cultivating goodness in body and mind;
contemplating the absence of a place of return, yet returning to and taking refuge in wholesome dharmas; contemplating non-arising, yet bearing all beings upon oneself through the dharma of arising;
contemplating the outflow-free, yet not severing the various outflows; contemplating the absence of activity, yet teaching and transforming sentient beings through the dharma of activity.
He contemplates emptiness and non-existence yet does not abandon great compassion; he contemplates the stage of the True Dharma yet does not follow the Lesser Vehicle;

he contemplates all phenomena as illusory, unstable, without self, without master, and without marks, yet because his original vows are not yet fulfilled, he does not let his merit, meditative concentration, and wisdom become empty.
In the commentary, sixteen phrases are sequentially explained in detail to clarify non-abiding in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), as per the text.
Cultivating such dharmas is called a bodhisattva’s non-abiding in the unconditioned.

This third section provides a layered explanation of "not exhausting" and "not abiding," thereby establishing the horizontal and vertical dimensions within the Buddha-land mentioned above.

Regarding the two aspects of "horizontal" and "vertical": as for the horizontal, within each of the seventeen phrases, the transverse characteristics are clarified by means of the four teachings (Tripitaka, Shared, Distinct, and Perfect) and the four gates.
As for the vertical, from the direct mind up to the fruit of Buddhahood, there are thirteen phrases of varying depth;

The forty phrases extensively distinguish the inexhaustibility of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); next, the sixteen phrases extensively distinguish non-abiding in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

These clarify, through horizontal and vertical perspectives, the profound and vast nature of the *dharmalakṣaṇa*. Following this, there are four pairs that provide layered explanations of the three types of provisional and ultimate wisdom.

This explains the fulfillment of vows for the vertical deepening within one’s own stage and the horizontal benefit of others, thereby establishing the meaning of the preceding horizontal and [vertical] dimensions.

Within the vertical exposition, it is not exhausted by what precedes nor does it abide in what follows; within the layered explanation, it does not abide in what precedes nor is it exhausted by what follows.
This mutual clarification between the subsequent and the preceding reveals the meaning of being neither before nor after, and the simultaneous fusion of before and after.

What is now called "non-abiding in the unconditioned" (apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa) means that there is no obstruction regarding the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), and thus one spontaneously accomplishes the practice of the Way.

To exhaust all that is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is to possess universal knowledge of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), whereby one’s transformation of others is unimpeded; thus, the provisional and the real are simultaneously illumined, and self and other are both mastered.
If the three truths are perfectly clear and one penetrates them deeply from within, this constitutes unimpeded wisdom (*anāvaraṇa-prajñā*) that is non-dual.
Because there is no obstruction in transforming others, one is able to traverse both the defiled and the pure, employing various skillful means (*upāya*).
Regarding this layered explanation, there are four pairs: first, merit and wisdom form one pair; second, compassion and the vow form one pair;
third, knowing the disease and administering the medicine form one pair; fourth, knowing the illness and diagnosing the illness form one pair.

Based on these, one should clarify that within the two wisdoms of the provisional and the real, there are both the provisional and real aspects of self-cultivation and the provisional and real aspects of cultivation for others.

Regarding the provisional and the real for the sake of transforming others: taking the principle of cultivating the Middle Way oneself as the real, and the simultaneous illumination of the two truths as the provisional—this is clarifying the provisional and the real regarding one's own practice.

If taking the observation of the principle of the two truths for oneself as the real, and speaking of the two truths for others as the provisional—this is called clarifying the provisional and the real regarding both one's own practice and the transformation of others. If... [the text continues].

Regarding the transformation of others through the clarification of the provisional and the real: this refers to the lack of fixedness regarding conditions, wherein one may speak of the provisional as the real, or the real as the provisional;
or one may distinguish the provisional and the real within the provisional, or distinguish the provisional and the real within the real.

Adapting to the depth or shallowness of the faculties of beings and following what is expedient for the circumstances of things, these matters cannot be fixed again. Based on this, one judges between the conceivable and the inconceivable.

Regarding the two kinds of the Two Truths: if these pertain solely to one's own practice (*svayam-pratipatti*), the provisional and the real are definitively categorized as the inconceivable and the conceivable, respectively.
However, if they pertain to both one's own practice and the transformation of others (*parārtha*), then among them, some belong to the inconceivable and some belong to the conceivable.
Why is this so? It is because, as clarified in the Shared Teaching (*pāryāya-yāna*), the Two Truths encompass the Middle Way within the Truth of Reality (*satyadharma*).
It is said that those of the three vehicles equally sever afflictions and enter *nirvāṇa* by means of the path of non-discourse.

If this refers to "containing the truth while entering the conventional," it is as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: "I and Maitreya have discussed worldly truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), yet five hundred bhikṣus claim we were speaking of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
This is precisely that meaning. Although the specific name of the Middle Way is not explicitly used, its substance is present.

Because the meaning of the Middle Way belongs to both [categories], it is called "penetration" (*tong*). "Penetration" means to penetrate the emptiness of the True Truth (*satyadharma*) as seen by the Two Vehicles;
if one penetrates through the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*) or the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), then one sees both emptiness and non-emptiness.
To be able to penetrate and see emptiness is the conceivable vision of emptiness; to see both emptiness and non-emptiness is the inconceivable vision of emptiness-wisdom.
Wisdom like that of a firefly perceives neither emptiness nor non-emptiness; wisdom like that of the sun and moon has both broad illumination and great efficacy in treating delusions.
Since the wisdom of those of the Two Vehicles is small, that which they sever is also small.

If a Bodhisattva practices for themselves, they perceive both emptiness and non-emptiness; yet in transforming others and benefiting beings, they perceive only emptiness and do not perceive non-emptiness. Thus it is known.
The provisional and ultimate [teachings] for both self-cultivation and transforming others belong to both the conceivable and the inconceivable.
If these are the provisional and ultimate [teachings] for transforming others, they are exclusively conceivable. Why? Because the two truths of the conceivable lack the essence of the Middle Way.
When the Truth of Reality (the ultimate) is clarified, it is eternally quiescent like space; when the Truth of Phenomena (the provisional) is clarified, it is like gold within stone.
