Within this conceptually conceived True Suchness, there are the meanings of gradual and sudden, just as stone and gold must be gradually smelted and refined until the ore is entirely exhausted.
The manifestation of the inconceivable gold is likewise of three kinds:

first, like all the myriad phenomena arrayed before one’s eyes—in their thousands and tens of thousands of forms—when one traces them back to their origin, they are all equally composed of the four great elements; this is called the "lower" kind.

Second, although these four great elements pervasively constitute all things, they are all impermanent phenomena subject to arising and ceasing; this is called the "middle" kind. Third, although arising and ceasing... [text continues]

Furthermore, that which undergoes transition and cessation is likewise without birth and without extinction, entering into the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Is this not both gradual and sudden?
It is not so with the inconceivable. Rather, there is the fundamental substance of the Middle Way; by means of this substance, the two truths are clarified, and this is termed "inconceivable.
It is like a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*) which can rain down all kinds of the seven treasures, yet within the jewel itself, there is ultimately nothing at all.
There is nothing to be sought, for it cannot be apprehended; it is simply called ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), yet it can rain down jewels.
This inconceivable principle is likewise so: neither true nor conventional, yet ultimately pure, it is able to fully and perfectly embody both the true and the conventional.
Since all aspects of the true and the conventional are beyond calculation or measurement, it is termed "inconceivable" (*acintya*). If one considers it from this perspective:
The jewel is used as a metaphor for those of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*): when the jewel rains down treasures, there is no appearance of gold or silver;
how does this differ from an ordinary jewel? It is precisely by means of the conventional that it is broken down, seeking the ultimate emptiness of the treasure.

How does this emptiness differ from the emptiness of cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) in the Truth of Ultimate Reality (*paramārtha-satya*)? By means of this, the conceivable aspect is clarified; this is the conceivable [teaching] of the Tripiṭaka.
Regarding the two truths: if one understands their efficacy and makes a vow to seek the treasure, various articles for sustaining life can immediately emerge from within space.
This emptiness is not the same as the "true emptiness" of those of the Two Vehicles. The treasures produced differ from the worldly ornaments and playthings;
this is not like the mundane reality of ordinary people. It is because the Bodhisattva possesses profound insight.
The two inconceivable truths (*advaya-satya*) likewise open up and consolidate the ultimate and the conventional, fully presenting two types as previously described;
now, by means of the threefold provisional and real, we shall explain the meaning of the inexhaustible and the simultaneous roaming in both the provisional and the real.

Furthermore, having examined the four teachings to clarify the inexhaustible and the non-abiding, we shall now clarify this according to the Tripiṭaka Teaching (*śrāvaka-piṭaka*). If one contemplates the ultimate truth to sever the fetters...
If one takes emptiness as the realization, one would be the same as the two vehicles, abiding in the extinction of ashes and dwelling in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
how then could one achieve the Buddha-dharmas over three *asaṃkhyeya*-kalpas? Therefore, one must not dwell in the unconditioned while exhausting the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

This is because compassion, the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), and so forth are fundamentally based on practice within the conditioned; they are for the purpose of teaching and transforming sentient beings within the mundane world. If one enters the ultimate truth, these cease to exist.
If this matter were now to exhaust the causes of all existence (*bhava*), then with the exhaustion of the cause, the fruit would perish;

how then could one dwell within the three realms and extensively practice the Buddha-dharma? Now, by not exhausting the outflows (*āsrava*) of conditioned existence while practicing the Buddha-dharma, one is able to accomplish the Way and turn the wheel of Dharma, transforming others through the Three Piṭakas, fully endowed with both the provisional and the real.
This is the "not exhausting" of the Shared Teaching (*pāryāyika-śāsana*).

If one who does not abide were to exhaust all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), they would be the same as the followers of the two vehicles; if one were to abide in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it would contradict the path of a bodhisattva.
Therefore, through skillful means (*upāya*), one emerges from emptiness into the provisional to benefit sentient beings.

Because these skillful means are as subtle and marvelous as planting trees in the sky, one does not exhaust conditioned phenomena, and because one does not grasp at the realization of emptiness, one does not abide in the unconditioned. This is the distinction.

Regarding the teaching that one neither exhausts nor dwells [in the conditioned]: if one were to enter the Middle Way by employing only the two contemplations as the path of skillful means, this would constitute dwelling in the unconditioned and exhausting the conditioned.
Now, although one has entered the principle of the Middle Way, the Buddha-dharma, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, has not yet all manifested before one;
since one must know and study them all, how can one guarantee this Middle Way? One must therefore illuminate it.

Because the conventional is thus, one reflects back from within it upon the two truths; this is called "not abiding in the unconditioned. If one were to remove the conventionality of the two truths, there would be no further conventionality to be observed.
Now, because one illuminates these two truths and universally practices the Buddha-way, it is said that one does not exhaust the conditioned.

Because one does not preserve [a fixed] middle way, it is said that one does not abide in the unconditioned. Within the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), this is still explained in terms of the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao).

Regarding the clarification of the meaning: if one contemplates only the Middle [Truth], this is exhausting the Two Truths; if one does not illuminate the Two Truths, this is abiding in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Now, when the Three Truths are contemplated together, one can simultaneously and clearly comprehend them: by not abiding in the True [Truth], one does not exhaust the Conventional;
by neither abiding nor exhausting, one simultaneously illuminates both the provisional and the real (*upāya* and *paramārtha*) (and so forth). If it is thus...
Because there is much evil in this world, he trains his army and lectures on military arts;

yet, he employs the two truths for the sake of transforming others, while regarding his own practice, he has not yet fully realized those two truths. Therefore, the fragrant rice is brought here so that those of the three vehicles, both near and far—such as the class of Śāriputra—may eat this rice.
For those who eat it, it will only be digested once they have resolved their minds [for enlightenment]; within the *Lotus Sūtra*, the Buddha-knowledge is revealed.
Seeing that the three types of provisional and ultimate [teachings] are fully perfected therein, and that while that land is free from evil and merely regulates ritual and music,
it has not yet realized the provisional and ultimate [teachings] regarding the transformation of others through one's own practice; for this reason,

he earnestly requested these skillful means to return to the Land of Fragrant Accumulation to perform Buddha-work, so that those who practice the ultimate [truth] there might realize the three types [of teachings].
Both the provisional and the ultimate are entirely perfect, pervasive, sovereign, and unimpeded. Question:

If the bodhisattvas in that land attain the Samādhi of the Treasury of Merit while beneath the fragrant trees, such that all Buddha-dharmas are contained therein, why do you say they have not yet mastered the provisional and ultimate means for transforming others?
Answer: There are two meanings. First, although they possess these [means], they do not employ them. Second, [they do not employ them] because they do not practice them.
This transformation [of the Buddha] is not clearly understood by those of the Two Vehicles on their minor paths, for two reasons:

first, although that land is pure, it possesses both the provisional and the real; as for the real, they have only received the teaching of the single reality and have not yet received the teachings of skillful means, and therefore they request the Dharma.
Furthermore, they must pass through the four pairs of categories—merit, vows, knowledge of medicines, and knowledge of illnesses.
The four teachings each manifest their characteristics clearly and are fully accomplished (and so forth). Now, let us briefly apply this according to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

The adornment of merit and virtue consists of the dharmas of the five perfections; these must universally encompass both the conditioned (*sābhisaṃskāra*) and the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*) two kinds of Four Noble Truths.
Within that land, one cultivates the various perfections to perfection, possessing sands-of-the-Ganges numbers of Buddha-dharmas. If, within the realm of segmented birth and death (*pariccheda*),...

Because one who has perfected the cultivation of merit can sit at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) within the Three Piṭakas to perform the Buddha’s teaching and transform sentient beings, it is said that they do not exhaust the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
If one cultivates the perfection of merit through skillful means in the stage of "having a remainder," they will sit at the site of enlightenment in that very land.
Furthermore, when the perfection of merit is attained in the Reward Land (*vipākabhūmi*) of the Distinct Teaching or the Perfect Teaching, one sits at the site of enlightenment and becomes a Buddha.
Now, for the sake of universally fulfilling these adornments of merit, one does not exhaust the two types of conditioned phenomena—the manifest (*vijñapti*) and the unmanifest (*avijñapti*).

For the sake of wisdom, one does not exhaust the conditioned; that is, the objective realm is able to give rise to wisdom. If one were to reject the realms of segmented existence (*paricchinna-bhava*) and the remaining transformational existence (*pariṇāmi-bhava*), what would there be to observe?
Since one would no longer know the characteristics of the realms of segmented existence, which are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, [how could wisdom arise]?

If one’s appearance is thus, yet wisdom is not yet full, and because wisdom is not yet full, one cannot attain the ability to sit at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) in various lands according to conditions;
therefore, one does not exhaust the conditioned in order to increase wisdom. This is how one utilizes the two adornments of merit and wisdom to perfect the bodhisattva practice.
Second, regarding the pair of "not exhausting the conditioned": this is because one desires great compassion.
Compassion uproots suffering and bestows happiness; this is great loving-kindness (*maitrī*).

It not only uproots the suffering of the two truths of the conceivable (*cintya*) and the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), and bestows the happiness of the conceivable truth of reality (*tattva*), but also uproots the suffering of the inconceivable (*acintya*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) four truths, and bestows the ultimate happiness of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*) therein.
If the suffering of the segmented [birth-and-death] (*paricchinna*) is exhausted, one can then sever it at the Bodhi tree.

When the three baskets are completed and the Buddha reaches the exhaustion of even the suffering of transformation (*pariṇāma-duḥkha*), he constitutes the Buddha of the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-śāsana*).
Because he benefits all beings through this great compassion, it is said that he does not exhaust the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

To fulfill his original vows means that in the past he gave rise to the four great vows (*catur-mahāpraṇidhāna*) and extensively took as objects both the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*) and conditioned (*abhisaṃskṛta*) two kinds of Four Noble Truths.
Since this vow has not yet been fulfilled, how could one exhaust all conditioned phenomena? The third collection of the Dharma-medicine is likewise:

regarding the *buddhadharmas* as numerous as motes of dust, one must universally know them according to their depth or shallowness, the capacities of sentient beings—whether great or small—their various inclinations and desires, and the remedies for their virtues and evils, whether in form or fragrance.
One should not [cease] until the *buddhadharmas* are fully realized.

By extinguishing sensation, one realizes [nirvana]; therefore, one does not abide in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Within the unconditioned, there is neither illness nor medicine, neither a teacher nor a recipient.

Now, wishing to act as the Great King of Physicians who delivers beings from old age, sickness, and death, and bestowing upon sentient beings the medicine that cures afflictions (*kleśa*), how could one exhaustively terminate the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*)?
Because it is not exhausted, he establishes the Three Piṭakas; thus the Buddha knows the two vehicles.
The medicinal teachings of the Four Truths and Dependent Origination cure the diseases of the *paricchinna-bhava* (segmented existence);

even the distinct teaching (*bhedavyavahāra*) of Vairocana Buddha bestows the medicinal teaching of the Middle Way. If one exhausts all that is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), these [teachings] no longer exist. Fourth, sentient beings are conditioned;
if they now abide in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), they do not enter the great ocean of the conditioned. How, then, could they possess cognition?

Since they do not recognize the various manifestations of the diseases of greed, anger, and delusion, they preach the Dharma according to their own mechanical notions rather than the patient's specific needs;

thus, they act as enemies to sentient beings by prescribing medicine falsely. They are not enlightened physicians. Because they understand the nature of illness, they do not abide in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
because they seek to extinguish illness, they do not exhaust the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). What is called "extinction" is not an extinction into non-existence.
The places where the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas tame sentient beings are called "liberation.

Within these, they themselves are without bondage and are able to untie the bonds of others; yet they neither bind nor liberate, causing sentient beings to attain the state of being neither bound nor liberated—this is termed "extinction" (*nirvāṇa*).
Because it serves to tame them, and because one attains liberation without exhausting the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it is called the "extinction of illness."
This is called the Dharma-gate of the Exhaustible and the Inexhaustible Liberation; you should all study it.

he paid homage, took his leave, and returned to his own land. Regarding the passage above concerning his initial request for the Dharma, where he expressed shame and repented his errors:

he repented because he had not yet clearly understood the provisional and ultimate teachings for transforming others; through this repentance and the removal of hindrances, he requested the supreme Dharma and immediately attained it.
To open up and understand the three types [of teachings] such that the provisional and the real are fully perfected is what constitutes gaining benefit by coming here from another land.

As for those who gain benefit by repenting their transgressions within this land—such as Śāriputra and others who, after eating the fragrant rice, felt shame and reproached themselves in the *Lotus Sūtra* to repent their own faults—this is merely repenting one's transgressions; it is not yet seen as the practice of the provisional and the real.

Once the covering has been stripped away through self-reproach, one opens the Buddha’s knowledge and vision within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, enters the Buddha’s wisdom, receives the prediction of enlightenment, and achieves the path;

This is precisely how one receives benefit from others in this land. By traveling between both lands simultaneously, the non-duality of defilement and purity is realized, achieving the perfection of the two [realms].
The ultimate meaning of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) lies herein (and so forth).

It is like a person shooting at a target [as described in the Dharma-discourse]...

If one contemplates this mark correctly, as fully explained in the *Entrance into Nonduality*, one abandons the two extremes and truly manifests the Middle Way. Herein, the intent is further clarified, which is why the Tathāgata asked.
Based on the preceding analysis of unimpeded wisdom, there are no distinctions among the bodies, knowledge, or meritorious qualities of the various Buddhas.
Because the Buddha wishes to demonstrate that the Dharma-body of the Great Being is not different from that of all Buddhas, he asks:
"How does one contemplate the Dharma-body? If one analyzes the Dharma-body, the Dharma-body must have a specific referent; that which is referred to is precisely the Buddha.

Therefore, this question arises in the [present] treatise: "If the Buddha as the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) can possess the names of boundaries, domains, and lands, what lands could there be for the *dharmakāya* (dharma body), which is profound and quiescent? The present explanation is not so.

The *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas is neither defiled nor pure, yet it is able to follow conditions (*pratyaya*) to traverse both the defiled and the pure simultaneously. Now, the *dharmakāya* is neither an object...
Since wisdom also illuminates both object and subject simultaneously, for what reason could it not discern the realm of the land? Thus, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states:
"The realm of inconceivable wisdom is inconceivable; the illumination of inconceivable wisdom is inconceivable.
Is this not precisely where the numinous wisdom of the Dharmakāya dwells? Furthermore, the *Vairocanābhisaṃbodhi-sūtra* (Puxian guan jing) speaks of Vairocana...
This most wondrous Dharmakāya is said to possess a land called Constant Quiescence and Radiance (*nitya-praśānta-raśmi*), which pervades all places;
is this not indeed the true realm?
As I contemplate the Tathāgata, he does not come from the past, he does not go to the future, and he does not abide in the present; he does not perceive form, nor...

One contemplates form as not contemplating the nature of form; one does not contemplate sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor does one contemplate consciousness as such, nor contemplate the nature of consciousness.

It does not arise from the four great elements and is identical to empty space. The six sense bases do not accumulate; the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind have already transcended them and do not abide within the three realms.
The three fetters have been severed, and one accords with the three gates of liberation. Wisdom and ignorance are equal.
It is a single characteristic, not a different characteristic; it is neither its own characteristic nor another’s characteristic; it is not without characteristic, yet not a grasped characteristic.

It is not this shore, not the other shore, and not the middle stream, yet it transforms sentient beings. It contemplates quiescence, yet does not undergo eternal extinction; it is neither here nor there, neither by this nor by that.
It cannot be known by wisdom, nor can it be cognized by consciousness; it is without darkness.

It is without ignorance, without name, without characteristics, without strength, and without weakness; it is neither pure nor defiled; it does not abide in any direction, yet is not separate from any direction;
it is neither conditioned nor unconditioned; it is without demonstration and without explanation;

it is without giving and without stinginess, without precepts and without transgression, without patience and without anger, without vigor and without indolence, without concentration and without distraction, without wisdom and without folly, without sincerity and without deception, and it does not come.
Neither going nor coming, neither entering; all paths of speech are severed. It is not a field of merit, nor is it not a field of merit;
it is not one to whom offerings should be made, nor is it one to whom offerings should not be made. It is neither grasping nor abandoning; it is neither with signs nor without signs.

It is identical to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and equal to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); it is ineffable and immeasurable, transcending all calculation and measurement. It is neither great nor small, and it is not seen.
It is neither heard, nor perceived, nor known; it is free from all fetters and bonds. Its various wisdoms are equal to those of ordinary beings.

Regarding all phenomena, it is without discrimination, entirely without loss, without turbidity, without affliction, without action, without arising, without birth, without cessation, without fear, without sorrow, without joy, without weariness, without attachment, without having existed in the past, without existing in the future, and without existing in the present; it cannot be [grasped].
All verbal expressions are conceptualizations and manifestations.
To answer specifically regarding the second point—contemplating the three periods of time—the past does not come;
yet, as if there were future dharmas, they enter the present where their arising and arrival can be apprehended. As for whether they have limits or are limitless, fundamentally they do not.
Since one perceives that there is future birth, how much more so for a person who has come into the present?

Therefore, that which does not come from the prior limit (pūrvānta) nor go to the subsequent limit (aparānta)—if there were a phenomenon that ceased and entered the past, one could say it "came" or speak of it as "having gone" or "not having gone.
However, since no phenomenon is seen entering the past, therefore [there is no coming] at the subsequent limit.

That which does not go and does not abide in the present: if there were a dharma existing in the present, one could say it exists, one could say it abides, and one could speak of its being permanent or impermanent.
Since no such dharma can be found existing in the present, how can one say that it abides?
Thus, when sought throughout the three times, it cannot be obtained. Having understood the Vajra [Sūtra], one realizes that what was previously considered impermanent is, in fact, eternal bliss.
Regarding "permanence, bliss, self, and purity after the Vajra": the permanence, bliss, self, and purity [attained] prior to this Vajra are not as they are now.
Why is this? Because the Dharma of Buddha-nature has existed inherently from the beginning; it is not something that has only arisen recently.
Regarding "there is no permanence, bliss, self, or purity after the Vajra": why is this? As the Sūtra says, Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages [still have further...]

If one were to practice all ordinary matters in reverse for immeasurable kalpas, and if the Dharmakāya were to arise in response to the six realms and undergo birth and death like an ordinary person, then it would likewise possess impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity.
Therefore, while it is identical to others in some respects, it is not identical in others, each according to its own reason.

According to the interpretation of others, "response" (應) refers only to transformation (化), and transformation is response; however, my current understanding is not so: response is capable of being transformation, and transformation is response.
It cannot perform transformations like those of ordinary people, non-Buddhists, transcendental immortals, or various devas and spirits;

yet it can perform transformations like those of the "transformation-body" (nirmāṇakāya). Furthermore, that which is transformed by the transformation-body is also temporarily and provisionally existent, unable to complete its beginning and end.

Now, we shall distinguish this "response-body" (nirmāṇakāya): when its response is identical [to the original] and its beginning and end coincide throughout the entirety of a single period of existence, it is termed [the true transformation-body].
The Tathāgata, by means of non-conceptual and spontaneous wisdom, responds to conditions as they arise;

he employs this without obstruction and without the exertion of deliberate thought. It is like a bright mirror in which images appear as soon as they are present—the reflection and the object are identical, without any difference.
This is unlike the emanations of celestial beings, which can only be accomplished through intentional mental effort and planning.
There is transformation like a painting: when one moves the hand and applies the mind to sketch a human form, it is not necessarily entirely devoid of mental activity;
whether it is skillful or unskillful can be understood through these two analogies. For one who does not contemplate form, the mind is like a magician conjuring various forms;
if one knows the magician is a deceiver, one will not grasp the conjured forms. Now, form arises from the mind.
Even a magician who conjures illusions cannot find this mind; where, then, can such form be seen? Therefore, one does not contemplate form, nor does one contemplate the "suchness" (tathatā) of form.
If one were to see form as distinct from suchness, that would mean dissolving form into suchness.
Since one does not currently perceive a distinction between form and suchness, one does not contemplate the nature of suchness. Some say that suchness is simply nature, and nature is simply...
This *tathatā* may have this meaning: now, the Sage does not permit the repetition of a single dharma with two proclamations;

what is indicated here is that this very nature is taken as the Buddha-nature. One does not contemplate form as empty—this is the conventional—and one does not contemplate such emptiness as real—this is the ultimate.
One does not contemplate the Buddha-nature within emptiness as the Middle Way. Because they conceive of the Middle Way as having a Buddha-nature, they give rise to a compliance with the Path.
The arising of craving constitutes a "fall from the summit"; therefore, the preceding text states: "Both 'self' and 'nirvāṇa' are empty;
there is only the sickness of emptiness, and even the sickness of emptiness is empty. Now, not contemplating the nature [of things] is because one lacks the craving that accords with the Path.

As for "not contemplating the nature as arising from the four great elements": although one contemplates this body, one does not give rise to delusion regarding the four great elements, unlike ordinary people.
One does not give rise to conceptual understanding regarding the four great elements, for, like those of the Two Vehicles, there is neither delusion nor understanding;

thus it is said that they do not arise and are identical to empty space—this is called the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). As for the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), they are able to accumulate the six objects and construct birth and death;
yet, unlike the six sense bases of ordinary beings which merely accumulate, these have already transcended the spheres of the ordinary person's six faculties.

"Not abiding in the three realms" means that one has emerged from both the ultimate and the conventional truths. "Having already departed from the three defilements" means being free from the impurities of the three realms.
"Accordant with the three liberations" means taking the single true reality as an object, thereby acceding to the three liberations.

"The three insights (*vidyā*) are equal to ignorance" means that the source of ignorance is precisely the true reality, the *dharmatā*. This *dharmatā* is peerless; there is nothing that can equal it.
Wisdom equal to this is called the "Unequaled Threefold Knowledge" (*tisro vidyāḥ*). That is to say: the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) can thoroughly illuminate the future;

the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*) reaches the present; and the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*) exhaustively contemplates the past, reaching back to the beginning of ignorance.
Even those in the tenth stage do not see its beginning; only a Buddha can know both the beginning and the end. Since it is said that one contemplates the true mark of the body, one contemplates...
The Buddha is likewise; the Buddha has reached the beginning of ignorance, and now he knows that beginning.

One who is equal [to him] in the exhaustion of the outflows of ignorance can know the outflows of the five stages (*pañca-vihāra*). Because the delusions of ignorance are exhausted, it is said they are "equal. The single characteristic (*eka-lakṣaṇa*) is the characteristic of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*);

different characteristics (*nānā-lakṣaṇa*) are the distinctions of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Now, the true reality (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa*) is neither ultimate nor conventional; therefore, it is not [either].

That which is neither identical nor different is not self-existent; when one travels to another country, it is called "other-characteristic" (*paralakṣaṇa*), whereas arriving at one's own father’s house is called "self-characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*).
This [teaching] should employ the true cultivation and the cultivation of conditions to extensively refute and sever the notions of self-arising and other-arising.

By transcending these notions of self and other, one enters into the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). It is not a state of non-appearance (*animitta*), nor is it the grasping of appearances (*nimittagraha*).
Neither birth-and-death nor beyond birth-and-death, neither ordinary person nor nirvana, neither the two vehicles nor this shore,
neither conventional truth nor the other shore, neither ultimate truth nor the middle current, and free from all afflictions and delusions—

reaching the "this shore" that is detached from both "this" and "that," and reaching the "other shore" that is neither "this" nor "that" to thereby transform sentient beings: this is the general [principle].
The manifestation of the application of the Dharma-body is neither here nor there; this is precisely the state of neither birth-and-death nor nirvana.
Being neither by means of this nor by means of that, it is the wisdom that contemplates the two truths.

When both object and wisdom are simultaneously manifest, that which cannot be known by wisdom is so because all phenomena are dispersed; that which cannot be cognized by consciousness is so because all phenomena are gathered.

That which is called "consciousness" is precisely birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). That which is neither darkness nor light is precisely the resolution of delusion and the attainment of awakening.

The resolution of delusion and the attainment of awakening are precisely birth-and-death and *nirvāṇa*. Because names are the characteristics of the world, they are themselves the transcendence of the world;

therefore, ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is named the "true aspect" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). That which is neither strong nor weak refers to birth-and-death, which is a method of coarse ore and is thus named "strength"; wisdom is [the opposite].

This is because it is supported by principle and easy to awaken to; it is called "weak" not because it is weak, but because it is neither strong nor weak. Therefore, this true aspect (*dharmatā*) does not reside within spatial directions.
Since the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) does not exist within the boundaries of birth and death, how could there be any delimited realm? Thus, it is said that it "neither dwells nor departs.
This means that the Constant Quiescent Light Land (*nitya-śānti-prabhāsa-kṣetra*) is also spatially pervasive throughout all places; therefore, it is said not to depart, yet it is not [limited].
The conditioned is not the unconditioned, like the Gate of the Inexhaustible; there is neither demonstration nor exposition, like Vimalakīrti’s silence.
There is no giving that is not the other shore of *dānapāramitā*, and no stinginess that is not this shore of the ordinary person’s secret hoarding;
the same applies to the six perfections. Nirvāṇa, being thoroughly examined, is the truth; saṃsāra, being false and illusory, is the deception.

This vehicle does not come, for it comes by means of the path of suchness to achieve perfect enlightenment; it does not go, for this vehicle emerges from the triple world and reaches omniscience (*sarvajñā*).
It is free from coming and going, yet it is not that there is no emerging; it is not the vehicle of the two [vehicles], yet it is not that they do not enter;
it is not the realm of ordinary beings, for the path of speech is severed—like the silence of Vimalakīrti. It is not a field of merit, as when he rebuked Subhūti, yet it is not without merit.
The Tathāgata’s consolation of Subhūti is not like [the way one might treat] an Arhat; his censure of Subhūti is not like [the way one might treat] one who is not an Arhat.

The Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One, knows that he is worthy of offerings (arhat). He is identical with the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) and equal to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), in profound accord with the ultimate truth.
He is immeasurable, which is to say he possesses the dharma of inconceivable liberation, and even his immovability is likewise so.

It is also the same as all sentient beings; all sentient beings are likewise suchness (*tathatā*). For those who are without discrimination, they enter the single true reality (*ekasatyalakṣaṇa*) and do not perceive high or low.
There is no loss, nor are there three kinds of falling into the three lands (*tridhātu*). There is neither joy nor weariness;
all these are explained in terms of the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three lands. Since there is already nothing and there will be nothing, this should be explained in terms of *nirvāṇa*.
The verse on the three periods of time explains this meaning.
The World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, contemplates his own body as being thus.
Next, he concludes.
"To view it in this way is called right view; to view it otherwise is called wrong view.
Next, the distinction between the wrong and the right follows the text.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Vimalakīrti: "From where did you pass away to come and be born here?"
Regarding the second [question] asked by Śāriputra: Śāriputra is the one who initiates the teaching.

Having already understood that the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) of the Great Being is identical in its true nature (*tathatā*) to that of all Buddhas, he further asks in order to manifest the capacity for the unimpeded great function of the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), which transforms sentient beings according to conditions.
This question is still narrow, as it arises from the perspective of the Tripiṭaka. If it were according to the Tripiṭaka...
If the Buddha has passed into extinction, then there is no birth; yet if a Bodhisattva of the Tripiṭaka still possesses delusions and defilements, then there is birth.
If this is so, one may ask: from where did he pass away to come and be born here?

This involves two points: first, refuting Śāriputra; second, [discussing] the land where the Buddha resided. Regarding the first, the refutation of Śāriputra, there are two parts: first, explaining Śāriputra’s question.
Vimalakīrti said, "Does the Dharma you have realized have passing away and birth? Śāriputra replied, "It has neither passing away nor birth.
Vimalakīrti said, "If all dharmas possess no characteristic of passing away or birth, why do you ask, 'From where did you pass away to come and be born here'?"
The second part, the response, is divided into five sections: first, a counter-interrogation; second, an illustration by analogy; third, a question; fourth, an answer;
and fifth, a citation of the Buddha’s words as an explanation. Regarding the counter-interrogation: "In your state of liberation, there is still no passing away or birth;
how then can there be passing away or birth within my Dharma-body? Since you do not possess such [passing away and birth], how can you pose this question?"
What do you think? For example, suppose a magician conjures up men and women through illusion.
Or suppose that magician himself dies and is reborn. Would these be real? Since they are not real, one cannot say that there is death and rebirth.
"Would you rather undergo death and birth? Śāriputra replied, "There is no death or birth.
[The interlocutor asked,] "Have you not heard the Buddha teach that all phenomena have the characteristic of being like an illusion? He answered, "It is so.
If all phenomena have the characteristic of being like an illusion, why do you ask, 'From where did you die to come and be born here'? Śāriputra died.
That which arises is a phenomenon of falsehood and deception, characterized by decay and ruin; that which is born is a phenomenon of falsehood and deception, characterized by continuity.
Although a bodhisattva passes away, they do not exhaust their roots of goodness; although they are born, they do not increase their various evils.

In the fifth section, the commentary on the interpretation states: Although a Bodhisattva passes away, they do not exhaust their roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), unlike those of the Two Vehicles who "extinguish the body and exhaust wisdom," which is called the exhaustion of the roots of goodness.
The Bodhisattva does not extinguish wisdom; because wisdom is not extinguished, the merit produced by that wisdom is also not extinguished.
By means of these roots of goodness, they are able to benefit sentient beings. Although they may not perceive evil as such, it is not [the same as]... [the case of the Two Vehicles].
The accumulation of ordinary beings is not exhausted, and their roots of goodness differ from those of the Two Vehicles in that they do not perish; because these roots of goodness do not perish,
they are able to respond to lands of defilement and purity, yet they do not increase the good or evil of either the land of defilement or the land of purity.
At that time, the Buddha told Śāriputra: "There is a land named Abhirati and a Buddha named Akṣobhya;
it was from that land that this Vimalakīrti passed away to be born here.

The Buddha further explained that among the pure lands, there are three types: those where a single Buddha resides, those where he teaches according to conditions, and those that are pure lands by their very nature.
Śāriputra said, "It is unprecedented, World-Honored One! How can these people abandon a pure land to come to delight in this place of much anger and harm?
Thus did the two Śāris praise him.
Vimalakīrti said to Śāriputra, "What do you think? When the sun rises, does it coincide with darkness?
This question regarding whether the sun coincides with darkness constitutes the first of the five points concerning the emergence of the three great beings from their concealment.
He replied, "No; when the sunlight appears, there is no longer any darkness.
A second time, Vimalakīrti asked, "For what reason does the sun travel over Jambudvīpa?"
The third question asked: "With what intention does the sun rise?
He replied: "It intends to illuminate and thereby dispel the darkness.
This was the fourth answer.
Vimalakīrti said, "In this way, although a bodhisattva is born in an impure buddha-field for the sake of transforming sentient beings, they do not associate with ignorance;
rather, they merely extinguish the darkness of the afflictions of sentient beings."

Fifth, the explanation of the "releasing of the boundary" clarifies that this person is identical to all Buddhas in possessing the two bodies of the Dharma and the Response (nirmāṇakāya) [and so forth].
At that time, the great assembly, thirsting with longing, desired to behold the world of Abhirati, the Tathāgata Akṣobhya,
and his host of Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas.

The second [section], from "The Great Assembly yearned with thirsting longing to see the Land of Wonderful Joy" up to "departing for that land," concerns the manifestation of the Pure Land as the dwelling place where this Great Being dwells.
This may be divided into three points: first, to verify the purity of the Great Being’s land;
second, to cause the assembly of that time to initiate practices directed toward a pure land; and third, to cause them to resolve to be reborn there. For these reasons, this section exists.

This passage is divided into seven sections: (1) the great assembly’s longing desire to see [the Buddhas]; (2) the two Buddhas’ command for them to appear; (3) their compliance with the command and arrival; (4) the Buddhas’ exhortation for the assembly to practice; (5) the great assembly’s arousal of the bodhicitta; (6) their return to their original abodes after having benefited others; and (7) Śāriputra’s praise. Regarding the first point, "the great assembly’s longing desire to see": [The Buddha] said: "Śāriputra, you should know that in this Sahā world there is a Buddha named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who is currently teaching the Dharma. He has appeared in the world for the sake of sentient beings who are difficult to save, and he manifests various skillful means to bring them to maturity. At that time, the great assembly, hearing these words, was filled with joy and wonder. They all rose from their seats, joined their palms, and gazed toward the World-Honored One. Their hearts were filled with longing and they yearned to see those two Buddhas. They thought to themselves:

"How wonderful it would be if we could behold the physical forms of those two Buddhas! Then, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the great assembly, addressed Śāriputra: "Śāriputra, do you wish to see the two Buddhas? Śāriputra replied to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, I do indeed wish to see those two Buddhas. The Buddha said: "Śāriputra, if you and the great assembly truly wish to see those two Buddhas, you must arouse a mind of supreme faith and respect, and cultivate the roots of goodness that lead to the vision of the Buddhas. At that moment, the World-Honored One extended his right hand and stroked the crown of Śāriputra’s head. Simultaneously, by the power of the Buddha’s spiritual authority, the two Buddhas—the Tathāgatas Amitābha and Akṣobhya—manifested their bodies in the Sahā world. Then, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly: "All of you should now generate a mind of pure faith and reverence. You must practice the path diligently and not be negligent. Upon hearing this, the great assembly aroused the aspiration for supreme, perfect enlightenment. Having brought benefit to all, the two Buddhas returned to their own lands. Finally, Śāriputra praised the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how inconceivable is the power of the Buddha! How rare is the appearance of such a Tathāgata! Now, regarding the phrase "the great assembly’s longing desire to see":

it refers to the initial state of the multitude before the manifestation of the Buddhas. As the text states: "At that time, the great assembly, hearing these words, was filled with joy and wonder... Their hearts were filled with longing and they yearned to see those two Buddhas. This describes the state of the assembly prior to the actual appearance of the Buddhas. It is the stage where, having heard the description of the Buddha’s skillful means, they felt a deep sense of yearning and desired to behold the physical forms of the two Buddhas. Thus, it is called "longing desire to see. It is not yet the actual sight of the Buddhas, but rather the intense aspiration and mental visualization that precedes it. This is why it is described as "longing" and "desiring to see. It serves as the necessary condition for the subsequent manifestation of the Buddhas through the Buddha’s power. Therefore, it is designated as the first section: the great assembly’s longing desire to see.
Having heard that the Land of Wondrous Joy mentioned above is the dwelling place of this Great Being, they all looked up to it with single-minded longing.
The Buddha, knowing the thoughts of the entire assembly, first manifested himself as two Buddhas; this initial act clarifies how the Buddha’s tranquil illumination perceives and knows their thoughts.

He addressed Vimalakīrti, saying, "Good son, for the sake of this great assembly, please manifest the Land of Wonderful Joy, the Tathāgata Akṣobhya, and the multitude of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas; everyone here desires to see them."
Second, he manifested the command of the true order.

Thereupon, Vimalakīrti thought to himself: "Without rising from my seat, I shall bring forth the Iron Ring Mountains, rivers, mountains, valleys, streams, great oceans, springs, Mount Sumeru, and all the various mountains, as well as the sun, moon, and stars, along with the devas and nāgas of the Land of Wonderful Joy."
The palaces of the spirits, ghosts, and Brahmā-devas, along with the assemblies of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas; the cities, villages, men and women, great and small;

and even the Tathāgata Akṣobhya and his Bodhi tree with its various exquisite lotuses—all those capable of performing buddha-work throughout the ten directions—possess three precious stairways that extend from Jambudvīpa up to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven by means of these precious steps.
The devas descended and all paid homage to the Tathāgata Acala as they listened to and received the Dharma.
The people of Jambudvīpa also ascended its steps to rise up to the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, where they beheld those devas. In the world-system Abhirati, such immeasurable merit was accomplished;
from the Akaniṣṭha heaven above down to the water’s edge below, he took it up in his right hand as if it were a mere blade of grass.
The potter’s wheel entered this world like one holding a flower garland to show it to all the assemblies.
Thirdly, by command, he became the foremost of the six in his resolve to move the world-system of Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa in the Land of Bliss.
Having formed this thought, he entered into samādhi and manifested his supernormal powers, using his right hand to sever and take up the world-system of Abhirati and place it within this land.
Second, the actual manifestation of his supernormal powers.
Then the Bodhisattva Prāptābhijña, along with the assembly of śrāvakas and the other devas and humans, cried out in unison:
"Indeed, World-Honored One! Who has taken us away? We pray that you will grant us protection!"
Third, those who had attained supernatural powers were startled and marveled;
the Buddha Akṣobhya declared that this was not his own doing, but was produced by the spiritual power of Vimalakīrti.
Fourth, the Buddha praised this as the work of the Pure Name (Vimalakīrti).
Those others who have not yet attained supernormal powers (abhijñā) are neither aware of nor know where they themselves are going.
Those five who have not attained the powers are unaware;
although the world of Abhirati enters this land, it neither increases nor decreases, and this world is not made cramped by it.
It was exactly as it was originally, without any difference;
the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) were not diminished in this land.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha addressed the great assembly: "You all should now observe the world of Abhirati."
The Tathāgata Akṣobhya’s land is adorned and magnificent; the bodhisattvas’ conduct is pure and the disciples are immaculate.
Fourth, the Buddha exhorts the assembly at that time to cultivate the practice of the Tathāgata Akṣobhya, which consists of three parts:
first, exhorting them to contemplate the magnificence and purity of that land.
They all replied, "Indeed, we have seen it.
At both times, the assembly responded, "We have seen it.
The Buddha said, "If a bodhisattva wishes to attain such a pure buddha-field, they should train as the Tathāgata Akṣobhya did."
The Way of Practice.
Third, correctly exhorting the practice of unshakable conduct, as clarified by the Buddha in his response to the son of the householder in the *Buddhakṣetrasamālaṃkāra-sūtra*.
Furthermore, it is like entering a room to offer consolation and subdue [the mind], practicing on what is not the Way to penetrate the Buddha-way, as in the *Akṣayamati-paripṛcchā-sūtra*.
The gate of exhaustion is precisely the practice of the Pure Land.
