The deva replied, "You should go and ask the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja; he will explain the offering of the Dharma to you in detail.
Thereupon, Prince Candracchattra went to the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja, prostrated at the Buddha's feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
He addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, among all forms of offering, the offering of the Dharma is supreme. What is meant by the 'offering of the Dharma'?
The Buddha replied, "Good son, the offering of the Dharma refers to the profound sutras spoken by all Buddhas, which are difficult for the entire world to understand."
Faith is difficult to attain; it is subtle, difficult to see, pure, and untainted—it cannot be obtained merely through conceptual discrimination or deliberation.
Regarding the sixth Buddha, the exposition of the text is divided into two parts: first, the clarification of the supreme and wondrous Dharma; second, from "If... onwards.
Those who hear and believe in such sutras as these manifest a mind of supreme worship; now, within this superior Dharma, there are four points:

first, from "following the words of the Buddha" onward, it clarifies the most wondrous Dharma; second, regarding "the Dharma-treasury of the Bodhisattvas," it clarifies the discussion of causes based on the Dharma;
third, from "being able to cause sentient beings to sit at the site of enlightenment" onward, this discusses [the result] based on the Dharma.
Regarding the four fruits: from the departure of the Buddhas and noble sages, these are the seals praised by the Buddhas concerning their causes and effects.
Now, to explain the first point regarding the profound sutras taught: the principle of the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) is neither deep nor shallow;

yet, for the sake of two types of conditions—those for whom it is deep and those for whom it is shallow—it is explained as being both deep and shallow within that which is neither deep nor shallow. That which is "shallow" is as follows:
Among the profound sūtras that encompass both the general and specific teachings of the Tripiṭaka, these are precisely the Perfect and Ultimate doctrine; therefore, they are called "profound sūtras.
The characteristics of these profound sūtras are as described above by the Great Being regarding the meaning of contemplating the true reality of the body, which is the pure and profound sūtra.
As for their being difficult to believe: within a single minute mote of dust, there are three thousand great chiliocosms.
Regarding this sutra, there are none who believe it; the principle of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) resides solely within the mind, so there is no need to seek it afar.
Because people do not recognize what is near, they do not believe the teaching; thus it is said to be difficult to believe and difficult to accept.
If there is something accepted, there will be something practiced; if there is nothing accepted, what would there be to practice? By believing and accepting the true mark, one is able to cultivate.
If one does not believe and accept these practices, one cannot cultivate the subtle and wondrous; this is another name for the inconceivable liberation.
It is also the subtle and wondrous self and dharma of the three virtues, which are wondrous and difficult to conceive, pure and untainted.
Being unstained by the three types of views and afflictions, it is like space, devoid of both purity and defilement, and beyond discursive thought.
That which can be attained through discernment cannot be realized by the movement of thought or the application of conceptualization; rather,

it is through non-thought and non-discrimination that one naturally flows into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), a state that cannot be fathomed even by those who possess the general or specific expedient means of the Tripiṭaka.
Sealed with the dhāraṇī-mudrās contained within the Dharma-treasury of the Bodhisattvas, it leads to the stage of non-retrogression and the accomplishment of the six pāramitās;
it skillfully distinguishes meanings, accords with the Dharma of Bodhi, and stands at the head of all sūtras.

It enters into great compassion, leaves behind all demonic activities and various false views, accords with the Dharma of dependent origination, and is empty of self, person, sentient beings, and life-span. It is emptiness.
The marks are without activity and without arising.
Second, regarding the explanation of what is subsumed within the Dharma-treasury of the Bodhisattva:

it clarifies that the preliminary practice of the Bodhisattva’s Dharma-treasury—consisting of hearing, retention, and the three virtues—is a secret treasury that is neither vertical nor horizontal and has no accumulation; this is precisely what is called a "treasury" (kośa).
The dhāraṇī-seal that encompasses all phenomena and causes them to enter therein is as follows: "dhāraṇī" means that which can obstruct and sustain;
it sustains the good so it is not lost and obstructs the evil so it does not arise. That which neither arises nor is lost is called a "seal" (*mudrā*).
"Reaching non-retrogression" means precisely obstructing and sustaining all virtues such that there is no falling back; this is also non-arising (*anutpāda*).

The stage of non-retrogression through the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*), wherein one accomplishes the six perfections (and so forth), involves skillfully discerning that which accords with bodhi;
this is precisely the ability to skillfully discern the characteristics of all phenomena while remaining unmoved within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Being "at the head of all sutras" means being at the head of the various sutras of the Tripiṭaka, the Shared Teaching, and the Distinct Teaching. Thus, one enters into great compassion.

This is the arising of objectless *maitrī* (compassion). As with the thirty kinds of *maitrī* mentioned above, being free from all *māras* means one is free from the eight *māras*, the ten *māras*, and so forth;
it also means being free from the three kinds of craving (*tṛṣṇā*). The celestial *māra* belongs to birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and is the flow of craving;
because the Bodhisattva is free from this, they are said to be "free from *māras*. Furthermore, those who possess wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) also fall into these three categories.
All views whatsoever prior to this are termed false views; within the true mark (lakṣaṇa), one is entirely free from these various views.
For those who accord with dependent origination, the nature of dependent origination is itself the true mark.

To accord with this true mark and deeply contemplate all phenomena as possessing both the emptiness of arising and the emptiness of dharmas—dependent origination is the emptiness of dharmas, and conditions are the true mark.
They cultivate the three samādhis of emptiness together,
enabling sentient beings to sit at the site of enlightenment and turn the wheel of Dharma; they are praised by devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and others,
and enable sentient beings to enter the treasury of the Buddha-dharma, encompassing the wisdom of all worthies and sages.
He expounds the path practiced by all bodhisattvas based on the meaning of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, clearly proclaiming the teachings of impermanence,
suffering, emptiness, non-self, and cessation; he is able to rescue all beings who violate the precepts, as well as māras, non-Buddhists, and those who are greedily attached,
and he can cause them to feel awe.

Third, regarding the manifestation of sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) by way of the fruit: if one can thus contemplate the true reality (*dharmatā*) in its perfection and enter into the *prajñā* of *nirvāṇa*, this is called "abiding.

At the moment of abiding in the stage of the initial resolve for enlightenment, one is immediately able to achieve the eightfold marks of enlightenment and manifest as a Buddha according to conditions;
therefore, it is said that "at the very moment of the initial resolve, one sits at the site of enlightenment and turns the wheel of Dharma. This is the Perfect Sudden Teaching.
Because it gradually unfolds the three teachings, it is said that the turning of the Dharma wheel is praised by devas and nāgas.

Having sat at the site of enlightenment for the benefit of all Buddhas, humans, and devas, those who enter the treasury of the Buddha-dharma are established within the secret treasury of the sons [of the Buddha].
The Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) encompasses forty-two stages of worthies and sages, while the Partial Teachings (Pianjiao) encompass twenty-seven stages of worthies and sages.
All are the treasury of the Buddha-dharma. All those of universal wisdom cause even those who have received partial teachings to enter the Buddha-wisdom.
As the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "Such persons as these, I now likewise cause to enter the Buddha-wisdom.
Regarding the exposition of the path practiced by the various bodhisattvas: although bodhisattvas take the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as their path, they may still receive other teachings.
Ultimately, it leads back to the reliance on the true aspect (*dharmatā*). Regarding the meaning of relying on the true aspect: whether cause or fruit, nothing can be separated from the true aspect.
It is by reference to this true aspect that the teachings of the partial and the perfect are established. Therefore, the *Lotus Sūtra* says:

"If there are those of profound wisdom, for them one preaches this Dharma"—this is precisely preaching the true aspect. It further says: "If one does not understand this Dharma, [one is far] from the Tathāgata."

To instruct, benefit, and gladden others regarding other profound dharmas is to preach the partial and gradual teachings—proclaiming non-self, suffering, emptiness, and cessation—which, among the skillful means intended to save those who have violated the precepts, all deviate from the perfect and ultimate; thus they are termed "violation of the precepts.
However, once one enters the Perfect [Teaching], there is no longer the fault of such skillful means, even if one had previously been a violator of the precepts within the Lesser Vehicle.

For those who revere [the precepts] heavily, there is no need for repentance; however, if one possesses the Mahāyāna’s correct contemplation of non-arising (*anutpāda-samyag-darśana*), it can wash away [all defilements].

Therefore, it is said that it "rescues all who have violated the prohibitions. As for those who fear demons and externalists, because it severs the two types of mind—craving and views—they are free from the five fears.

It is praised by all Buddhas and worthy sages; it turns one’s back on the suffering of birth and death and reveals the bliss of nirvana; it is that which has been taught by all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
Fourth, because it is praised by all Buddhas, it accords with the true nature (*dharmatā*); thus, at the very first thought, one is able to become a Buddha. Therefore, it is [the supreme vehicle].
That which is praised by all the sages refers to turning one's back on the three kinds of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).

That which demonstrates *nirvāṇa* is precisely the demonstration of the hundredfold liberation. That which is spoken by the Buddhas of the ten directions means that the path of all Buddhas is identical and they all together proclaim this true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
If one hears such sutras as these, believes, understands, upholds, reads, and recites them, and by the power of skillful means explains, analyzes,

and clearly reveals them for the sake of all sentient beings— protecting the Dharma for this reason— this is called the "Dharma-offering. Furthermore, regarding all dharmas, practicing according to what is taught,
conforming to the twelve links of dependent origination, departing from all false views, and attaining the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharmakṣānti).
It is determined that there is no self and no sentient beings; yet, regarding causes, conditions, fruits, and retributions, there is neither contradiction nor contention.

One is free from all notions of "mine," relying on the meaning rather than the words, relying on wisdom rather than consciousness, relying on sūtras of definitive meaning rather than sūtras of interpretable meaning, and relying on the Dharma rather than the person.
One accords with the characteristics of phenomena, having nothing to enter and nothing to which to return.

Because ignorance is ultimately extinguished, volitional formations are also ultimately extinguished; and so on, until because birth is ultimately extinguished, old age and death are also ultimately extinguished.

To contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination in this way as having no characteristic of exhaustion, and not to give rise to further views—this is called the supreme offering of the Dharma.
The second [section], "If one hears such sūtras as these," clarifies the mind of worship, which is here divided into two parts:
first, it clarifies the practice of faith (*śraddhā-caryā*); second, it clarifies the practice of the Dharma (*dharma-caryā*).

If, upon hearing the teaching of the reality-mark (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa*), one generates understanding within that hearing and attains unimpeded penetration, this is called the mind of worship through the practice of faith. If one hears what is not heard... [as before].

To practice the contemplation of the Dharma, to realize that causes and conditions are empty, to sever all deluded views, and to perceive the principle of the true mark (*dharmatā*) so as to attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*)—this is called the mind of the offering of Dharma-practice. Furthermore, this is explained by means of the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*):

not understanding the Dharma-practice is called "relying on the person. The teachings of all Buddhas are fundamentally intended to suit the capacities and inclinations of beings; they cannot be fixed.
Because it is characterized by grasping, consciousness that relies on words is not to be relied upon; because it is a phenomenon possessed of afflictions, consciousness is not to be relied upon.

The Sūtras are teachings of expedient means and are not ultimate reality, and thus they are not to be relied upon. Only the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) is to be relied upon. As for persons, because they are bodies born of birth-and-death, they are not to be relied upon.
One who has reached the bottom of the source of ignorance knows that all things are originally unborn; therefore, they are ultimately without cessation.
To contemplate that causes and conditions are inexhaustible is itself delusion, for they are as inexhaustible as space.
The Buddha told Prince Candracchattra: "Having heard this Dharma from Bhaisajyaraja Buddha, you have attained the patience of compliance (anulomikī kṣānti)."
Seventh, regarding attaining the patience of docility (*kṣānti*) through hearing the Dharma, this consists of two parts: first, the benefit of initially attaining the patience of conformity;

second, repaying the kindness by offering the gift of the precious robe. If one explains the patience of docility according to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), "docile" means to be subdued and compliant;

this refers to the stage of the ten faiths (*śraddhā*) within the Perfect Teaching—the position of the iron wheel—during which the six sense faculties are purified. If [this patience] were to arise...
Truly illuminating and entering into principle is precisely the attainment of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
Having understood this, he took off his precious robes and ornaments to offer them to the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, I shall practice the offering of the Dharma and protect the true Dharma. I pray that you will empower me with your majestic spiritual power and compassion to establish it."
I have attained the subduing of demonic adversaries while practicing the bodhisattva path.
Stripping my garments to offer them constitutes two types of offering: first, the material offering; second, the offering of the Dharma through the practice of making vows.
I pray that you will bestow your majestic spiritual power upon me, enabling me to subdue all enemies and proclaim the Great Dharma.
The Buddha, knowing the thoughts in his deep mind, prophesied to him, saying: "In the final age, you shall guard the city of the Dharma.

Regarding this eighth prophecy of Buddhahood, it merely records that he will be a person of later generations who propagates the Dharma and protects it, having a karmic affinity with the people and things that can cause the Great Dharma to flourish and manifest;
no text is seen that records him as becoming a Buddha. To speak of this from a broader perspective:
This meaning should indeed exist, though it has not yet appeared in the text.
At that time, Prince Candracchattra, having seen the purity of the Dharma and heard the Buddha’s prophecy, left the household life out of faith.
He cultivated wholesome dharmas with diligence and, before long, attained the five supernormal powers, reached the bodhisattva path, and acquired dharanis.
After the parinirvāṇa of the Buddha, Dhanvantari, by means of the power of his attained supernormal knowledges, dhāraṇīs, and eloquence,
shall propagate for ten intermediate kalpas the wheel of Dharma turned by the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja.

The ninth section clarifies the practice of the Dharma-offering through leaving the household life and cultivating the path; this is divided into two parts. First, it clarifies the protection of the Dharma by those who have left the household life.
For instance, the bhikṣu Candracchattra, through his diligent application of vigor in guarding the Dharma, transformed himself into one hundred trillion [bodies] within this very lifetime.
He established fourteen nayutas of people in non-retrogression regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
caused immeasurable sentient beings to deeply resolve upon the mind of a *śrāvaka* or *pratyekabuddha*, and enabled countless beings to be reborn in the heavens.

Second, it clarifies the number of people transformed: millions, billions, and tens of millions of beings who resolve to attain Bodhicitta do so by means of what is taught in the Perfect Teaching (the *yuanjiao*).
Those who give rise to the minds of the Two Vehicles do so by means of expedient means used for induction and guidance.
Because these two methods—the Perfect and the Partial—are employed to lead and benefit sentient beings, this constitutes the offering of the Dharma.
"O Devendra, was King Ratnacchattra of that time anyone else? He is none other than the present Buddha named Ratnārcis Tathāgata.
The thousand sons of that king are precisely the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa, beginning with Krakucchanda and ending with the Tathāgata named Loushi (Locanābha).
As for the bhikṣu Candracchattra, he is my own self."
The third section concludes by correlating the ancient and the present as written in the text.
Thus, O Śakra, you should know that this essential Dharma-offering is the highest, the most supreme, the foremost, and peerless among all offerings.
Therefore, O Śakra, you should honor the Buddha with the offering of the Dharma.
The Fourth: A Statement Confirming the Previous Vow to Propagate and Uphold the Sūtra and Proclaim It, as Well as Protecting Those Who Practice the Sūtra, Causing All to Be Harmonious and Peaceful;
The Chapter on Entrustment.
In the second section of the circulation text (*parīndanā*) of this chapter, it was previously explained that Śakra, Lord of Devas, made a vow to propagate the sutra;

here, the entrustment by the Tathāgata’s own golden mouth is clarified. "Entrustment" (*parīndanā*) has the sense of handing over; it refers to the entrusting of the reality-dharma of non-characteristic (*animitta*) to those who shall propagate and protect it.
"To carry" (*bhāra*) has the sense of bearing a burden amidst repeated toil; now, this Great Dharma is specifically intended for—
Because it has already been entrusted so that external obstacles may be eliminated and internal practice may be proclaimed and made to flow forth, it is called "entrustment" (*parindanā*).
Thereupon, the Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying:
"Maitreya, I now entrust to you this *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* which I have accumulated over immeasurable billions of *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas."
Regarding this text, there are three parts: first, the Buddha’s entrustment to Maitreya; second, the entrustment to Ānanda;
and third, the great assembly’s joyful reception of the sutra. Now, within the first section—the entrustment to Maitreya—there are two parts:
first, the Buddha’s entrustment; second, Maitreya’s acceptance of the mandate. Within the Buddha’s entrustment, there are three parts: the first is the actual entrustment.

This second commentary on the entrustment of this sutra consists of three parts; the third part distinguishes between gain and loss. Now, regarding the first section—the entrustment—it is divided into two:
(1) the entrustment of the honored sutra, and (2) the command to protect it through supernatural powers. As for that which was gathered over immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas and entrusted to you:
if one follows the explanation by Kātyāyanīputra within the Tripiṭaka, it clarifies the cultivation of three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
To study the Buddha-dharma for a hundred kalpas so that the marks of a Buddha appear before one is the shallow and proximate teaching of the Tripitaka’s Hinayana;
the time spent in cultivation, study, and practice is relatively brief. However, according to the *Śāstra* (the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*), this interpretation is refuted:
the Buddha-dharma is immeasurable; how could what is learned in three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* be all-encompassing? It must pass through immeasurable billions of *kalpas*.
Only by practicing the vast number of Buddha-dharmas and all profound dharma-gates can one bring the deep and wondrous Mahāyāna to fulfillment;

therefore, the time spent in study is also vast. Since it is said here that [this teaching] was accumulated over immeasurable kalpas, we know this is a sublime Mahāyāna scripture entrusted to Maitreya.
After the parinirvāṇa of the Buddha, during the final age, you all must use your supernormal powers to widely proclaim and disseminate sūtras such as these throughout Jambudvīpa,
so that they shall not be cut off.
Second, one should employ supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) to propagate [the teaching] extensively so that it remains uninterrupted; this is the command to provide protection.

To entrust this Great Dharma specifically to Maitreya clearly demonstrates that he is the immediate successor to the Honored One’s position, whose wisdom and severance of afflictions are perfect and complete, who has a karmic affinity with sentient beings, and who is fully endowed with supernormal powers, capable of widely propagating and protecting [the teaching] so that it does not cease. If...
Sentient beings of the final age have been far removed from the Sages for a long time; not only are their spiritual faculties dark and turbid, but obstacles also arise in great numbers.

Just as places where the *Prabhūtaratna* [Stūpa] resides are inevitably rife with enemies and bandits, so too when the Way is lofty, demonic forces flourish, giving rise to hindrances and difficulties.
If one does not receive the secret support of the Sages' power, external hardships will invade and oppress; yet if one is graced by the addition of the divine light, it shall likewise cause the mind—
Having untied [the knots] and integrated both internal causes and external conditions, the Dharma-treasure is thus rendered uninterrupted.

For this reason, I command that your supernatural powers be bestowed upon those sentient beings capable of hearing [the Dharma]. In this regard, one should cite the case of Upagupta, who was harassed by Māra;
consequently, countless people were prevented from attaining enlightenment, and those who were to have been transformed were instead led astray by Māra.

Regarding those who were deluded, he used his supernatural powers to bind the Māras; all who heard the sutra obtained benefits beyond measure, and it was likely with this intention that he used his supernatural powers to propagate the sutra (and so forth).
Why is this? Because in future ages there will be sons of good family, daughters of good family, as well as devas, nāgas, yakṣas,
gandharvas, rākṣasas, and others, who will resolve their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and take delight in the Great Dharma.
Regarding the second explanation: as for the phrase "Why is this so? it is divided into two parts.
First, it clarifies that even in the final age there are those with the capacity to attain the Way; second, it clarifies that if one does not hear this sutra, one will lose the benefit of goodness.
As for the first point, clarifying that there are those in the final age who can attain the Way: although ordinary beings differ in their conditions for awakening, some may perceive the Dharma King.
Benefit may be gained in the presence [of the Buddha], or through awakening born of longing after his passing; thus the Sūtra says:

"Those who are to be delivered by means of parinirvāṇa, for them he manifests parinirvāṇa. It is like when, in order to cure a mad son, one says he is dead while actually remaining alive, leaving behind fragrant medicinal powders and scents;
when the son feels remorse and grief, he takes the medicine and is healed. If he did not see the Buddha...
Through self-reproach and diligent effort, he felt shame at not having encountered the Buddha’s era; by this means he entered the Path and attained liberation from afflictions.
Thus, about one hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, one hundred thousand went forth as monastics and ninety thousand attained the Path.

One should know that the capacities of those who followed after the Buddha were likewise immeasurable. This refers to Kukkuta, who sought to go forth while the Buddha was still alive, searching for him [to do so].
The Buddha said that since his wisdom was equal to that of Śāriputra, he could not immediately return to the teachings of the non-Buddhists;

the Buddha then gave a prediction concerning him, saying that this man’s opportunity to attain the Way would come after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa. Having become a disciple of Ānanda, he will deliver immeasurable people and lead countless beings to the Way, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
People of that time will revere and praise him as the "Buddha of Formlessness" (Animitta-buddha); he is none other than Śākyamuni in a future age.

Among the gods, humans, dragons, and spirits of this world, there are those who possess the conditions for generating the aspiration for enlightenment and who delight in the Great Dharma; they must surely attain liberation.
Therefore, one must propagate such a sublime teaching so that they may hear it.

If they were not permitted to hear such sūtras as these, they would lose this excellent benefit. However, when people of this kind hear such sūtras, they will surely feel great faith and joy, giving rise to a sense of rare wonder;
they should receive them upon the crown of their heads and preach them extensively for the sake of all sentient beings, according to the benefits each should obtain.
Second, regarding the statement that "if one does not hear this sutra, it will be a great loss":
if one hears only the provisional teachings of the Tripiṭaka, one loses the benefit of the "poisonous drum" of the Mahāyāna. As the *Bhadracaryā-praṇidhāna* (Puxian guan) states:

"When the Dharma is nearing extinction, during the five hundred-year period, if one single-mindedly cultivates this Lotus Samādhi, one will immediately attain the purity of the six sense faculties. Thus we know [this].
Even in the final age, there may still be those with the capacity to enter the Mahāyāna; yet, if they do not hear this sutra, they will forever lose the benefit of the Dharma.
Therefore, it must be proclaimed and disseminated.
Maitreya, you should know that bodhisattvas have two characteristics.
Third, regarding the two characteristics arising from the bodhisattva, this serves to distinguish between gain and loss; herein there are two parts: first, distinguishing gain and loss;
second, extensively citing what is not [the case] to explain. Within the section on distinguishing gain and loss, there are three parts: first, indicating the characteristics.
What are these two? First, delighting in miscellaneous phrases and literary embellishments; second, not fearing profound meanings and being able to enter them as they truly are.
This is the brief explanation of the two.
If one delights in miscellaneous phrases, literary embellishments, and worldly matters, you should know that such a person is a newly initiated bodhisattva. If, however,
one has no fear regarding such profound sūtras that are untainted and unattached, is able to enter into them, and having heard them,
purifies the mind, upholds, recites, and practices them as taught, you should know that such a person is one who has long cultivated the path of practice.

Third, the explanation by way of persons: regarding persons, if one follows the Tripitaka Teaching, one mostly clarifies all dharmas within the context of distinct causal conditions and individual phenomena.
Those who study according to this are persons of newly awakened intent.

As for the distinct and perfect teachings of the Mahayana sutras—which speak of being without dependence or reliance and transcending all mind and consciousness—these are what are called "profound sutras."
This very greed is the path; hatred and delusion are likewise so. Within these three dharmas, all dharmas are fully contained.
If one seeks bodhi apart from these three dharmas, it is like seeking heaven and earth apart from each other.
By penetrating the nature of these three poisons, one realizes that they are ungraspable, just like empty space.
That sutra states: "One who deeply penetrates this Dharma does not violate the precepts;
one who deeply penetrates this Dharma also does not cling to non-obstruction.

Many practitioners claim that the three poisons are the Way, yet they cling to this non-obstruction and thereby destroy right precepts and right view. What, then, is meant by "penetrating the three poisons"?
Those who thoroughly penetrate this nature find neither destruction nor attachment; this is what is called the meaning of the sutras—the Dharma of the true mark (*dharmatā*).

It is neither cause nor fruit, yet it is spoken of as cause and fruit. Therefore, it is said that [the nature of] causes is not the fruit, just as the Buddha-nature is the fruit and not the cause, as in the case of Great Nirvana.
Now, the nature of the three poisons is likewise neither cause nor fruit, yet it is spoken of as a cause.
If one explains the effect as the cause, it means that the three poisons are the complete fulfillment of all Buddha-dharmas;
if one explains the cause as the effect, it means that all sentient beings possess the mark of eternal quiescence, which cannot be extinguished further.
If one can hear this and discern the two paths of cause and effect within desire—remaining without attachment or disparagement, and giving rise to no fear—one should know that this is [the path].

A bodhisattva who has practiced for a long time is one who delights only in the profound Dharma of the true nature (*dharmatā*) and no longer takes pleasure in flowery rhetoric, elegant compositions, or ornate language;
they instead explain the Dharma of the steadfast trunk. By inferring from this, one knows them to be a bodhisattva who has practiced for a long time.
If they delight in verbal expressions and their speech is adorned with elegance, consisting of literary phrases and sections, then they should be considered [a beginner].

While it may initially please the listener, in the end it becomes like milk with water added, obscuring the true nature (*dharmatā*); it is not the practice of those who have long cultivated the path.
By this one may discern that such a person is a bodhisattva newly resolved upon enlightenment.

Just as when one speaks of the number of people present, they ask about their features, saying they have eyes and eyebrows; yet though they hear the Mahāyāna teaching of non-reliance, they regard it as mere empty verbiage.
Regarding those who do not give rise to faith or joy, one should cite the case of Sudatta requesting the Buddha to preach the Dharma for his aged mother.

Although the Buddha manifested his form in all ten directions to her, she would not believe or accept it. Subsequently, Ānanda transformed himself into a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) to skillfully guide her;
once her heart was filled with joy and she submitted in faith, she returned to the Buddha and heard the Dharma.

Why is it that you practice the Way in this manner? This is because in the past, your preceptor as a śrāmaṇera frequently spoke of the profound words regarding the true nature (*dharmatā*), which you heard but could not understand, nor did you give rise to faith or admiration for them.

Your *ācārya*, however, frequently taught the causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) of all phenomena (*dharma*) and their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), instructing you through various events and circumstances. Consequently, your mind developed an attachment to these teachings and took delight in them. For this reason, upon hearing my [teachings] now...
The words did not enter his mental faculties; Ānanda had to turn his mind toward the Way.

Although Ānanda was made to give rise to faith, it was ultimately through me that he was able to attain the Way. Thus we know that the method of literary adornment is merely a condition for pleasing the ear, not the ultimate principle.
It is a skillful means for introduction, serving as a gradual stage for advancing toward awakening. Therefore...
Whether it be the profound reality of the ear or the essential method for attaining the Way, this is what is meant by the analogy of the "poisonous drum.

By means of this, the two types of persons—those who have newly resolved their minds and those who have long practiced—are distinguished; one need only observe their ornate rhetoric or direct speech to know their strengths and weaknesses.
Maitreya, there are further two dharmas such that a beginner cannot attain certainty regarding the profound Dharma.
What are these two? First, upon hearing a profound sūtra never heard before, they are struck with alarm and fear, giving rise to doubt;
unable to accord with it, they slander and do not believe it, saying: "I have never heard this before; from where has it come? Second, if there is one who protects...
If those who uphold and explain such profound sutras as these refuse to draw near, make offerings to, or show respect toward them,
or even occasionally speak of their faults and evils— know that by these two factors, such individuals are newly initiated bodhisattvas who bring about their own ruin and injury,
being unable to discipline their minds within the profound Dharma.

The second [section] further contains two dharmas. From the point where it says "regarding the sūtras not yet heard," this clearly and extensively enumerates what is not [to be done], rather than treating these as the two [dharmas] themselves.
Previously, two dharmas were explained to interpret how those newly trained in the teachings should not slander or stay far away [from them];

subsequently, two dharmas are explained to interpret how those who have long studied should not treat [others] with contempt or grasp at signs. Regarding the section on "slandering and staying far away" mentioned previously: herein...

When the Bodhisattva Nandendriya spoke only of the Dharma of the true mark (*dharmatā*), clarifying that within all things there exists the nature of bliss, those who had received the teachings of the Tripiṭaka, whose majestic deportment was flawless, and who maintained the precepts and dhūta practices, were suddenly startled upon hearing what Nandendriya said.
Because it contradicted what they had studied, their minds were greatly shocked; they reviled, slandered, and refused to believe it.
Upon receiving the ritual for immediate expulsion, this person, Rāhula, was expelled; the rite of expulsion was thus accomplished, and he immediately entered hell.
This refers to those who have newly resolved their minds [to attain awakening] but, having received provisional teachings, slander the *Prajñāpāramitā* and do not believe in the profound sūtras.
Such individuals must understand both the deep and the shallow. Alternatively, there may be those who at times do not slander this Dharma, yet [slander] those who uphold the Dharma.
Furthermore, there are times when one speaks of the faults of those who lack a respectful and intimate mind;
this too is a sign of failure, as such individuals have not long practiced the taming of the mind.
Maitreya, there are two further dharmas by which a bodhisattva, despite having faith and understanding in the profound Dharma, still brings about self-injury and is unable to [progress].
What are the two [obstacles] to attaining the patience of the non-arising of dharmas? First, to treat newly initiated bodhisattvas with contempt and fail to instruct them;
second, although understanding the profound Dharma, to grasp at signs and engage in conceptual discrimination—these are the two dharmas.

The second section, the "Great Chapter on Elevating and Contemptuously Grasping at Characteristics," clarifies that if a bodhisattva conceives thoughts of contempt toward a fellow practitioner who has newly resolved their mind for enlightenment—
thinking, "This person knows nothing"— and gives rise to this single thought of pride,

they will instead diminish the merit of countless kalpas and must undergo further retribution. Only after the retribution for such offenses is fully exhausted can they again resolve their mind for enlightenment.
Furthermore, regarding today’s conduct and virtue, to speak thus with a mind of contempt is a grave transgression;
it not only obstructs the attainment of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), but leads further to the reaping of karmic retribution. Therefore, this is specifically excluded.

Moreover, there are bodhisattvas who, although they understand the profound Dharma, still grasp at signs and engage in conceptual discrimination regarding the stages, gradual progressions, and hierarchical levels.

To ascend and descend, to restrict and cut off, to clarify meanings, to grasp signs, and to engage in conceptual discrimination to produce fixed notions—this is again a method of mental agitation and not the ultimate path.
Why is this so? Because the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is pure and serene;
it does not even possess a single mark, let alone two, three, four, or five. It is beyond words and beyond demonstration. To speak of it is to miss it; it is that which should be pointed out.
Those who deviate from the fundamental tenets—how can a mind that discriminates and deliberates ever be in accord with the Dharma of quiescent extinction?

Whether it be the doctrines of the three periods, four periods, five periods, the half-full and full [cycles], or the four schools and six schools—all such meanings are merely the works of dharma masters who have extracted the intent of the sutras to establish terminology and analyze doctrinal categories. To claim they are consistent with the truth is entirely incorrect.
Regarding the ultimate art of ineffability, the true intention of our school is not like this. We seek a harmonious fusion with the Dharma-realm and a profound resonance with the ultimate truth;
we do not wish for the mind to be at variance or in conflict with sentient beings.

Although we establish these four teachings, it is solely for the purpose of providing a comprehensive explanation of the texts of the various sutras; it is not intended to exhaustively investigate the ultimate source, nor do we ultimately maintain fixed attachments to them.
The meanings of the four teachings—sometimes three, two, one, or none of the teachings—appear and disappear without constancy;
their number is not fixed, and they transform with sovereign ease according to how individuals interpret and explain them.

One must not allow this mind to harbor even the slightest attachment or self-clinging to one's own views while deeming the interpretations of others to be incorrect. If one acts in such a manner, it is merely a matter of contentious debate and is not [the true teaching].
Regarding the method of entering the Way, as Master Nanyue said in verse: "When a dog sees its own reflection, it immediately fights;
though it fights, it refuses to desist, until it eventually dies of thirst... (and so forth). Now, this is a concise summary and does not intend to encompass every detail of the Way.
However, the mental paths of practitioners differ; although they are manifold, they do not exceed two categories: first, the Sage’s teaching through speech; second, the Sage’s silence.
However, one must recognize the suitability and skillful means of one's own mind.

If at times it becomes stagnant or obstructed within the path of silence, such that the mind cannot be opened, one should for a short while listen to the Dharma; or approach a virtuous friend who can open the person's mind;
or seek out the principles within the scriptures to awaken and develop this mind; or occasionally listen to the Dharma with focused attention.
If one is restless and unable to maintain stillness, searching through sutras and investigating their meanings will result in a chaotic proliferation of affairs.

If one realizes that this brings no profound benefit to the mind and spirit, one should immediately close the eyes, bind the body, and naturally quiet the mind. Entering the path of silence, one practices both speech and silence to subdue the mind.
One investigates the coarse to achieve harmony and adaptability, skillfully mastering what to accept and what to reject, and thus discerning the true from the false. It is thus.
At one time, one should cultivate tranquility; at another time, one should cultivate wisdom. It is like heaven and earth:
whether it is sunny or rainy, they regulate the yin and yang so that all things may grow.
If it rains constantly without sunshine, the seeds will rot; if it is constantly sunny without rain, the sprouts will wither. In either case, they cannot bring forth growth.
All things must be brought into harmony before they can be perfected; likewise, if a practitioner remains in one-sided silence, they will fall into a state of dullness and obstruction.

Conversely, if they employ only conceptual discrimination, various views will arise in competition, such that the provisional and the ultimate do not accord and the Guide does not give rise to skillful activity.
Only when one suddenly enters the Way—like seeing a flash of lightning in the night—is one able to enter the Noble Dharma.
This is how those who study the Way skillfully discern right from wrong and distinguish the heterodox from the orthodox. Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Just as timely rain falls repeatedly and the five grains grow repeatedly, so too does the rain of Dharma fall repeatedly and wholesome dharmas grow repeatedly.
If one does not employ the Sage’s speech or the Sage’s silence to repeatedly train and discipline them, the grain of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) will not grow. If...

Because one who is biased toward and attached to intellectual views will never enter into the principle, it is said: "Though one may read a hundred thousand sutras, if false views flourish, the poison of the 'self' remains most virulent;
though one claims to carry the eternal child, a barren woman will never give birth.
If, amidst the teachings of the Sages, one can hear them and immediately awaken, penetrating all dharmas with mastery and clarity, this is the practice of faith.
Hearing [the Dharma] yet not attaining awakening, one contemplates the four foundations of mindfulness with profound penetration and deep illumination until reaching their very depths;
this is called the "practice of the Dharma" (dharmānusārin) within the noble silence. Within this, there are likewise those who practice through faith (śraddhānusārin).

When practicing such meditative contemplation, if one contemplates a single object, it then universally penetrates all objects; the mind-ground becomes clear and bright, free from even the slightest doubt or obstruction, like space.

This "middle wind" is called the practice of the Dharma (*dharmacaryā*). If, when applying oneself to contemplation, one cannot attain awakening and continues to exert effort yet remains muddled and confused without understanding, it is as follows:
if one hears [the truth] from a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) or hears it within the sūtras, there is a sudden clarity like a sky free of clouds, with inner and outer completely penetrating;

this is the practice of faith (*śraddhācaryā*). Furthermore, receiving transformation and manifesting it as speech, acting exactly according to what was heard—this is the practice of transformation (*parivartacaryā*).
To practice noble silence as it is practiced, and to hear the noble teaching of the Dharma as it is heard;
furthermore, after being transformed by that teaching, to speak as it is spoken, and to hear the noble teaching of the Dharma as it is heard; and to practice as it is heard—this is noble silence.
Having heard this teaching, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, it is unprecedented!
As the Buddha has taught, I shall distance myself from such evils."

Regarding the second section, where Maitreya addresses the Buddha, this clearly elucidates the reception of the command and the mandate; herein it is divided into three parts: first, Maitreya receives the mandate;
second, the various bodhisattvas receive the mandate; third, the four kings receive the mandate. Regarding the first of these, there are two sections:
first, the reception of the mandate, and second, the subsequent confirmation. Within the first of these, there are again two parts: first, the clarification of receiving the admonitory mandate.
One upholds the Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, which the Tathāgata has accumulated over countless asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
From the point of upholding the Tathāgata’s [Dharma] throughout those countless kalpas, there follows the reception of his exhortation; herein, two pairs are established.
Of the two aforementioned types, the first is to respectfully transmit the purport of the sutras. If, in future ages,
there are sons or daughters of good family who seek the Mahāyāna, you should cause them to obtain such sutras as these in their own hands,
granting them the power of mindfulness so that they may receive, uphold, read, recite, and extensively explain them to others, O World-Honored One, in the final dharma-ending age.
If there are those in the world who are able to receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain it to others, you should know that this is established through the supernatural power of Maitreya.

Second, regarding the protection and upholding of the meaning through the power of reverence, the text itself states therein that he provides them with the power of mindfulness (*smṛti-bala*) and thereby establishes it.
If such a person, relying on the practice of peaceful conduct (*sukha-vihāra*), preaches the Dharma, they will secretly accord with emptiness and augment their power of mindfulness.
It is like a person who, while contemplating the Dharma, reaches only one or two points, yet by the time they actually preach it, they suddenly perceive three or four sections of its meaning.
This may be because their mind has entered the gateway of the principles (*artha-mukha*) and can clearly discern them, or it may be because they are in secret accord with emptiness.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent, Maitreya! It is as you have said; the Buddha rejoices in your words.
This was the second time the Buddha confirmed and completed his statement.

Then all these bodhisattvas joined their palms and addressed the Buddha: "We, too, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, shall widely proclaim and disseminate this anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in the lands of the ten directions;
furthermore, we shall guide and instruct those who preach the Dharma so that they may obtain this sutra."
The second assembly of bodhisattvas received the command and made their vow.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, wherever there may be cities, towns, villages, mountain forests, or wildernesses where this sutra scroll is read, recited, explained, or expounded, we shall lead our respective officials and retinues to listen to the Dharma."
Therefore, they went to that place and protected the person for a hundred yojanas around their face, ensuring that no one seeking an opportunity could find an opening against them.
The third and fourth kings received the command and made their vows according to the text.
At that time, the Buddha told Ānanda, "Receive and uphold this sutra, and propagate it widely.
Ānanda said, "I have received and upheld it, World-Honored One. However, by what name should this sutra be called?
The Buddha said, "Ānanda, this sutra is named 'The Teaching of Vimalakīrti,' and it is also named 'The Dharma-Gate of Inconceivable Liberation. You should receive and uphold it thus."

Regarding the second point, as for the command to Ānanda to proclaim the sūtra: although Ānanda’s traces remained within the Lesser Vehicle and he subsequently attained the body of an Arhat, at the time of entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, his rebirth (*jāti*) would have been forever exhausted. How, then, could he have been able to receive and proclaim this Great Sūtra?

The intention here is merely that he be entrusted with the transmission so that there might be no error in the compilation of the Dharma-treasury; thus, he was commanded to proclaim the sūtra. If one considers this from the perspective of the fundamental [teaching]:
Since speech can sustain all the Buddha-dharmas of the ten directions, how could it be allowed to be extinguished like ashes and fail to proclaim this sutra?
According to the text, there are three parts: first, receiving the command; second, inquiring about the name of the sutra; third, the Buddha’s answer regarding the two types of names.
"The essential" refers to the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa); the true mark universally encompasses all dharmas, and to obtain the essential is to obtain all dharmas.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the elder Vimalakīrti, Mañjuśrī, Śāriputra, Ānanda,
and the entire assembly— including devas, humans, asuras, and others— having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced, paid their respects, and departed.
The third assembly, having heard this sutra, was filled with great joy.
*Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra-vyākhyā*, Fascicle 28 (End).
This entire commentary on the sutra consists of thirty-four fascicles; the first thirty-one fascicles are the work of Xuánwén.

The Great Master Zhi of the Tiantai school produced this commentary for the Ruler of Yang, consisting of three fascicles from the "Chapter on the Buddha-way" to the end of the "Chapter on the Dharma-gate of Non-duality.

This was compiled by joining together the private notes previously taken by the Venerable Ding, who was a candidate for Buddhahood (Bodhisattva of the Final Birth), and thus transmitted to later generations;
it is therefore designated as a "Record" (*ji*). It was completed in the first year of the Ruyi era of the Great Zhou dynasty, the cyclical year *Renchen*.
In the eighth month, the monk Yiwei of Tiangong Temple transcribed this vow and pledged to uphold it, seeking the Buddha’s wisdom as his recompense for the Three Jewels;
he then traveled south to Fahua Temple. From that time on, his writings came to an end.
At the age of sixty, he spent his days and nights in various places, never wearying until death.
In the twelfth month of the twenty-second year of the Kaiyuan era of the Great Tang,
the monk Daoyi of Fahuasī in Kuaiji Prefecture went to Qingtaisi in Puyang and, relying on the manuscript from Tiantongsi, completed the transcription.
In the thirteenth year of the Tiānbǎo era, it was transcribed at Fuyan.
